t.maisons de la weissenhof siedlung@48.8,9:
In 1927, on a hillside overlooking Stuttgart, a group of the most radical architects in Europe built an entire housing estate in a few months as an exhibition of what modern living could look like. The Weissenhof Estate, organised by the Deutscher Werkbund under the direction of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, brought together Le Corbusier, Walter Gropius, Hans Scharoun, J.J.P. Oud and others, and their flat-roofed, white-walled houses became a manifesto for the International Style.

The estate was controversial from the start. Conservative critics mocked it, and the Nazis later used doctored postcards showing it as an Arab village to attack modernism; some houses were destroyed in the war. About half of the original buildings survive, and the two houses by Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret were added to the UNESCO list in 2016 as part of a transnational site of Le Corbusier's architectural works. One of them now houses a museum where you can see restored interiors and learn the history of the estate.

The estate is a quiet residential area today, with people living in most houses, so be respectful. It sits on the Killesberg, a hill on the north side of the city, close to the Killesberg park and its observation tower. Stuttgart itself sits in a basin surrounded by vineyards and forest, and its streets climb steeply in every direction; the city has hundreds of public staircases.

For motorcyclists, Stuttgart is the home of both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, and their museums are excellent. Riding in the city is slow and congested, with many traffic lights, but the surrounding hills offer good roads. The Swabian Jura, the Schwäbische Alb, about an hour south, has some of the best biking roads in Germany, with winding climbs up the escarpment. Closer to town, the vineyards along the Neckar valley and the Rems valley make for pleasant rides.

Stuttgart has every service. Note that the city has a low-emission zone that applies to cars but not to motorcycles. Local food includes Maultaschen, large stuffed pasta, and Spätzle, and the local wines, especially Trollinger, are drunk in wine taverns all over the city.
On the western shore of Lake Como, above the village of Ossuccio and facing the little Isola Comacina, a cobbled path climbs the hillside through olive groves and woods, past fourteen small chapels, to a sanctuary at the top. This is the Sacro Monte of Ossuccio, one of nine sacred mountains in Piedmont and Lombardy listed together by UNESCO. Built in the seventeenth century, the chapels illustrate the Mysteries of the Rosary with life-size terracotta and plaster figures arranged in dramatic scenes, each one a small piece of theatre.

The Sacri Monti were created in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, during the Counter-Reformation, as a way of bringing the sacred story to people who could not make the pilgrimage to the Holy Land. They were meant to be walked, with each chapel a station for prayer and contemplation. Ossuccio's is one of the most beautiful because of its setting: the path offers changing views of the lake, the island and the mountains across the water. The walk up takes about half an hour.

Isola Comacina, the only island on Lake Como, has the ruins of early medieval churches and a famous restaurant that serves the same menu it has for decades. The nearby villages of Lenno and Sala Comacina are lovely, and Villa del Balbianello, on a promontory near Lenno, is one of the most famous villas on the lake, used as a film location.

The road along the western shore of Lake Como is narrow, busy and full of character. It hugs the water, passes through villages and tunnels, with bends and views. In summer, traffic is heavy, and coaches and cars can make it slow going. The roads that climb from the lake into the mountains, toward the Val d'Intelvi or over to Lake Lugano, are quieter and offer great riding. On the eastern shore lies Mandello del Lario, the home of Moto Guzzi, where the factory has a museum.

Mandello del Lario, about thirteen kilometres away by water, is the nearest larger town, but Lenno has fuel and food. Lake fish, such as missoltini, dried shad, are a local speciality. Spring and autumn are best for riding.
t.monte san giorgio@45.9,8.9:
Monte San Giorgio is a wooded, pyramid-shaped mountain on the shores of Lake Lugano, straddling the border between Switzerland and Italy. To the eye, it is a pleasant green hill with villages on its slopes. To palaeontologists, it is one of the most important fossil sites in the world. About two hundred and forty million years ago, during the Middle Triassic, this area was a tropical lagoon, and its sediments preserved an extraordinary range of marine reptiles, fish, invertebrates and plants. The mountain was added to the UNESCO list in 2003 on the Swiss side, and in 2010 on the Italian side.

The fossils include ichthyosaurs, marine reptiles that looked like dolphins, and the bizarre Tanystropheus, a reptile with a neck longer than its body. Excavations have been going on since the nineteenth century, and the finds are displayed in museums at Meride on the Swiss side and at Besano on the Italian side. The museum in Meride, designed by the architect Mario Botta, is excellent.

Porto Ceresio, on the Italian side, is a small lake town with a waterfront promenade and views of the mountain across the water. The villages on the slopes, like Besano and Saltrio, are quiet and pleasant; Saltrio is known for its stone quarries.

The riding around Monte San Giorgio is very pleasant. The roads along Lake Lugano are scenic, with bends and views, but can be busy. The roads that climb over the hills between Porto Ceresio, Viggiù and the Valganna are twisty and quieter. On the Swiss side, the road from Mendrisio up through Meride and around the mountain is narrow and scenic. Crossing the border is usually easy, but remember that Switzerland requires a motorway vignette and that Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, with heavy fines.

Porto Ceresio has fuel and restaurants, and Mendrisio, about six kilometres away, is the nearest Swiss town. Local food includes lake fish, risotto and polenta, and the wines of the Mendrisiotto, especially Merlot. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.city of luxembourg its old quarters and:
Luxembourg City is built on a rocky plateau above the deep, green valleys of the Alzette and Pétrusse rivers, and for centuries it was one of the most powerful fortresses in Europe, nicknamed the Gibraltar of the North. Spanish, French, Austrian and Prussian armies all held it, and each added to its walls, bastions and tunnels. In 1867, after an international treaty, most of the fortifications were dismantled, but enough remains to make the old quarters and fortifications a UNESCO World Heritage site, inscribed in 1994.

The most remarkable remains are the casemates, a network of tunnels carved into the rock. The Bock casemates, on the promontory where the city's first castle stood in the tenth century, can be visited, and the views from them over the valley and the suburb of Grund are superb. The Chemin de la Corniche, a promenade along the old ramparts, has been called the most beautiful balcony in Europe. The old town, with the grand ducal palace, the cathedral and the narrow streets, is compact and easy to walk.

Luxembourg is a small country with a big role. It is a founding member of the European Union and home to many of its institutions, as well as a major financial centre. The Kirchberg plateau, across the valley, is home to the European Court of Justice and a cluster of modern office towers. Luxembourgish, French and German are all official languages, and most people speak all three, as well as English.

Riding in Luxembourg City is slow, with heavy traffic and lots of one-way streets, so park and walk. But the country is a joy for riders. The Ardennes in the north, around Clervaux and Vianden, have twisting roads through forest and over hills, with castles at every turn. The Moselle valley, in the east, is lined with vineyards, and the road along the river is scenic. Luxembourg is also famous for its cheap fuel, and there are long lines of cars at the stations near the borders.

Local food includes judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork with broad beans. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.old city of berne@46.9,7.5:
Bern does not shout. The Swiss capital sits on a sandstone spur in a tight loop of the green Aare, with six kilometres of arcaded streets that let you walk the whole old town in the rain without getting wet. It was founded in 1191 by Duke Berthold V of Zähringen, and legend says he named it after the first animal he killed hunting nearby, a bear. The bears have been the town's mascots ever since, and a few still live in the BärenPark down by the river at the end of the Nydeggbrücke.

The old town is a UNESCO site, and it earns it with a rare consistency: sandstone facades, colourful fountains topped with figures, red-tiled roofs and the great late-Gothic Minster, whose tower is the tallest church tower in Switzerland and worth the climb for the view to the Bernese Alps on a clear day. The Zytglogge clock tower puts on its little mechanical show a few minutes before each hour, and on Kramgasse you can visit the apartment where Albert Einstein lived while working out special relativity. In summer, locals jump into the Aare upstream and drift back through town with the current, which says a lot about the water quality and the Bernese temperament.

Riding into Bern is straightforward but not glamorous. The centre has narrow streets, trams, buses, pedestrian zones and strict parking rules, so find a designated motorcycle parking area on the edge of the old town and walk. Switzerland requires a vignette for motorways, and speed enforcement is notoriously strict and expensive, so keep to the limits even when the road feels empty. The good news is that leaving the city takes minutes: the Emmental's rolling hills, the Gantrisch nature park with the Gurnigel pass, and the lakes of Thun and Brienz with the Alps behind them are all within an hour.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere, though Swiss prices will catch your breath. A local tip is to buy picnic supplies at a supermarket and eat by the river or in the Rose Garden above the bear park, which has the best view over the rooftops and the Aare loop. If the weather is fine, an early evening stroll under the arcades, when the shops close and the light warms the sandstone, is the best way to feel the city.
t.fort site and civil settlement of welhei:
Welzheim sits up in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, a rolling upland of spruce, beech, deep stream valleys and old sawmills east of Stuttgart, and the Romans chose it for the same reason the forest still feels remote today: it was the edge. The Upper German-Raetian Limes ran dead straight through these woods, and Welzheim had not one fort but two, an east and a west fort, with a civilian settlement of traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families packed around them. The east fort has a reconstructed gate and a small archaeological park that gives you a good sense of scale, and the whole frontier line is part of a UNESCO site.

What strikes many visitors is the straightness of that line. For tens of kilometres north of here, the Romans laid out the frontier with almost no deviation, ignoring hills and valleys, a feat of surveying that still puzzles historians. You can follow its course on small roads and forest tracks, with reconstructed watchtowers popping up along the way.

The riding is the reason to linger. The roads around Welzheim, Kaisersbach and Althütte twist through forest and clearings, dropping into narrow valleys and climbing back out over short, sharp ridges, with villages, lakes and the occasional water mill along the way; the Schwäbische Waldstraße and the Mühlenstraße are both signposted themes worth following. Surfaces are generally good, but shade keeps some corners damp long after rain, and in autumn the leaves make them slick. Weekend traffic includes plenty of other riders and cyclists, and local authorities do enforce speed limits, so a calm rhythm pays.

Welzheim is a town of about eleven thousand with fuel, bakeries, a Swabian inn or two serving Maultaschen and Spätzle, and a pleasant centre. The Ebnisee, a forest lake a few kilometres away, is popular for a swim in summer and a coffee on its terrace any time of year. For a lunch with a view, push on toward the edge of the Rems valley, where the forest opens and vineyards fall away toward Schorndorf, the birthplace of Gottlieb Daimler, which seems fitting for a day spent on two wheels.
t.fort site and civil settlement of jagsth:
Jagsthausen is a village of around fifteen hundred people in the Jagst valley of northern Württemberg, and it punches far above its weight in history. The Romans built a fort here on the Upper German-Raetian Limes, with a civilian settlement and a bath house, part of the UNESCO-listed frontier. But the village is better known for a later resident: Götz von Berlichingen, the knight with the iron hand, who was born in the castle here around 1480. He lost his right hand in battle and had a mechanical one made, led peasants in the war of 1525, and became the hero of a play by Goethe that contains a famously rude line that Germans still quote.

The castle, known as the Götzenburg, still belongs to the Berlichingen family and houses a hotel and restaurant, and every summer it hosts open-air theatre festivals, with Goethe's play as a regular feature. The Roman remains, including the foundations of the bath house, are displayed near the castle, and a small museum tells the story of both Romans and knights.

The Jagst valley is one of the most beautiful in southern Germany for riders, and one of the least crowded. The river winds lazily through meadows, past old mills and villages, between steep wooded slopes, and the road follows it with gentle curves, occasionally climbing onto the plateau for wide views. The nearby Kocher valley, running parallel to the south, offers similar pleasures, and the roads connecting the two valleys over the hills are short and twisty. Surfaces are good, traffic light, and the landscape changes with the seasons, from spring blossom to autumn colours.

Jagsthausen has an inn or two, but for fuel and more services, Forchtenberg, Möckmühl or Öhringen are better bets. The region is known for its wine, especially in the Kocher and Tauber valleys, and for hearty Swabian and Franconian food, including Maultaschen, Schäufele and Spätzle. Schöntal Abbey, a baroque monastery a few kilometres upstream, is a beautiful stop, and the castle-studded valley of the Neckar is less than an hour away.
t.civil settlement of niedernberg northern:
Niedernberg is a quiet village on the left bank of the Main, a few kilometres downstream from Aschaffenburg, where the river was the Roman frontier. The Upper German-Raetian Limes, after running across the Odenwald, used the Main as its boundary between Großkrotzenburg and Miltenberg, and a fort with a civil settlement stood at Niedernberg, guarding the river line. The northern part of the civil settlement is listed separately as part of the UNESCO site. There is little to see above ground, as the remains lie under fields and houses, but the location by the river makes the Roman logic clear.

Today Niedernberg is best known for its lakes. Gravel extraction has left a series of large ponds along the Main valley, and the Niedernberger See has become a popular leisure area, with beaches, a camping site, swimming and water sports, and in summer it is crowded with families from the Rhine-Main area. The river itself, wide and slow, is busy with barges and pleasure boats, and the riverside path is popular with cyclists.

The riding in the immediate area is flat and suburban, but the hills are close. To the east, the Spessart, a large forested upland, offers some of the best riding in the region, with winding roads through beech and oak forests, quiet villages and the castle of Mespelbrunn, a beautiful moated castle in a forest valley. To the south, the Odenwald has more twisty roads, climbing through forests and valleys with views over the Main and the Rhine plain. Traffic around Aschaffenburg can be heavy, but the forests are quiet, especially on weekdays.

Sulzbach am Main, just over a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Aschaffenburg, a short ride upstream, has everything, including the Renaissance castle of Johannisburg, built of red sandstone on the riverbank, and the Pompejanum, a replica of a Roman villa built for King Ludwig I of Bavaria. Local food includes Franconian dishes like Schäufele, roast pork shoulder, and the wines of the Main valley, which are bottled in the distinctive flat, round Bocksbeutel. Miltenberg, further upstream, is one of the prettiest towns on the Main.
t.ivrea@45.5,7.9:
Ivrea is the town Olivetti built, or at least rebuilt. In the twentieth century the Olivetti company, famous for typewriters, calculators and some of the first personal computers, turned this small Piedmontese town into a showcase of what industry could be: factories with glass walls and natural light, worker housing, libraries, nurseries and social services designed by the best architects of the day. Adriano Olivetti believed a company should serve its community, and the result was listed by UNESCO in 2018 as an industrial city of the twentieth century. Walk along Corso Jervis and you can see the buildings still standing, some reused, some waiting.

The older town is lovely too. It climbs a hill above the river Dora Baltea, crowned by a red-brick castle with four towers and a cathedral, and the river rushes through below, green and fast with snowmelt from the Valle d'Aosta. Every winter Ivrea hosts its notorious Carnival and the Battle of the Oranges, when teams on foot pelt teams on carts with oranges for three days. The streets turn orange and sticky, and the smell lingers for weeks.

The landscape around Ivrea is a geologist's favourite. Glaciers coming down from the Aosta valley pushed huge walls of debris ahead of them, and the Serra d'Ivrea, a long, straight, wooded ridge running east of town, is one of the largest moraines in Europe. Small lakes lie scattered in the hollows left behind, Sirio and its neighbours, good for a swim in summer.

On the bike, Ivrea is a gateway. The road north-west follows the Dora Baltea into the Valle d'Aosta, past castles and terraced vineyards, towards the high passes. Lanes climbing onto the Serra and into the hills of the Canavese have plenty of bends and few cars, and the sacred mountains of Piedmont, including Belmonte above Valperga, are within easy reach. Watch for cobbles in the old town and narrow streets that turn into pedestrian zones without much warning.

As a town of over twenty thousand people, Ivrea has fuel, shops, mechanics and good food. Try the local white wine, Erbaluce di Caluso, with a plate of agnolotti, or the toasted hazelnut sweets of Piedmont with a coffee in one of the arcaded streets.
t.konstanz hinterhausen@47.7,9.2:
There is nothing to see at Konstanz-Hinterhausen, and that is precisely the point. Below the surface of Lake Constance, along the shore near the city, lie the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings: wooden posts, floors, pottery and food remains preserved in the mud for thousands of years. They are part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, a World Heritage site that spans six countries and over a hundred locations. Archaeologists dive to study them, but the rest of us have to make do with the view of the lake and a bit of imagination.

For an idea of what those villages looked like, cross the lake to Unteruhldingen, where an open-air museum has reconstructed whole settlements of thatched huts on stilts over the water. It is a popular stop and makes the abstract real.

Konstanz itself is one of the most pleasant cities on the lake, with an old town that survived the Second World War largely intact, reportedly because it sat right against the Swiss border and kept its lights on, confusing bombers. Between 1414 and 1418 it hosted the Council of Constance, which ended a schism in the Catholic Church and condemned the Czech reformer Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake here in 1415. At the harbour entrance stands Imperia, a towering, rotating statue of a courtesan holding two small figures representing a pope and an emperor, a cheeky comment on the council that still amuses visitors.

The riding around the city is varied. The Bodanrück peninsula to the north has quiet lanes through orchards and woods, and the flower island of Mainau draws crowds. Over the border in Switzerland, the Seerücken ridge along the southern shore offers lovely views over the lake, and a car ferry links Konstanz with Meersburg on the northern shore, saving a long ride around. Traffic in and around the city is heavy, particularly on weekends with shoppers crossing from Switzerland, and the border crossings can be congested.

Konstanz has over eighty thousand people and every service you might need. Fuel tends to be cheaper on the German side than in Kreuzlingen, and remember that Swiss motorways require a vignette. Grab a coffee by the harbour and watch the ferries come and go.
t.watchtower wp 7 37@49.6,9.4:
The Romans liked straight lines, and nowhere more than here. On the edge of Walldürn, in the hilly country between the Odenwald and the Tauber valley, runs the course of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, the frontier wall that marked the edge of the Roman Empire across what is now southern Germany. Watchtower WP 7/37 is one of hundreds of small posts that lined it, each within sight of the next, so that signals could be passed along the frontier. The Limes here famously runs almost dead straight for many kilometres, regardless of hills and valleys, a statement of Roman confidence and surveying skill.

At the site itself, expect modest remains, perhaps a low mound or the outline of foundations, along with an information board. The interest lies in the wider picture: a watchtower, a palisade and ditch, and soldiers posted on this ridge two thousand years ago, keeping an eye on the Germanic lands beyond. Walldürn also has the remains of a Roman bath house, which belonged to a small fort and is worth a short detour.

The town is better known as a place of pilgrimage. According to tradition, in the fourteenth century a priest knocked over a chalice during mass, and the spilled wine formed an image of Christ on the cloth. The relic drew pilgrims for centuries, and the large baroque basilica still welcomes thousands each summer, especially during the main pilgrimage weeks.

The riding in this part of Germany is very good. To the west lies the Odenwald, a favourite of riders from Frankfurt and Heidelberg, with wooded hills, winding roads and small half-timbered villages. To the north, the Main valley around Miltenberg and Amorbach is beautiful, with red sandstone towns and river bends. The landscape around Walldürn itself, the Bauland, is more open and rolling, with farmland and quiet roads ideal for relaxed touring. Be aware that some Odenwald routes have weekend restrictions or speed limits for motorbikes because of noise and accidents, and police checks are frequent in summer.

Walldürn, with around twelve thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of bakeries and inns. Try a local Schäufele, roast pork shoulder, or a slice of cake with coffee, and take a short walk along the line of the old frontier.
t.building remains south of the watchtower:
Mainhardt sits high in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, between Heilbronn and Schwäbisch Hall, on a wooded plateau that the Romans chose for one of the forts guarding their frontier. The Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes runs through here on its long, ruler-straight stretch heading south towards Welzheim, and along it stood watchtowers every few hundred metres, with small buildings nearby for the soldiers who manned them. The remains south of one of these towers are modest, low foundations in a clearing or under the forest floor, but they are part of the World Heritage frontier that runs for more than five hundred kilometres across Germany. The village has a small Roman museum that explains the fort and its garrison.

The forest is the reason to come. Dense spruce and beech woods cover rolling hills cut by deep valleys, with clear streams, mills and scattered farms. It is cool and green in summer, often misty in autumn, and snowy in winter. The area is popular with hikers, and the Limes path follows the line of the old frontier through the trees.

Schwäbisch Hall, about a quarter of an hour east, is one of the most beautiful towns in southern Germany, with half-timbered houses climbing the slopes above the river Kocher and a grand flight of steps in front of St Michael's church. It grew rich on salt, and the Heller, a small silver coin minted there, gave its name to small change across the German-speaking world. The surrounding Hohenlohe region is famous for its food, including a heritage breed of pig with a black head and tail.

The riding around Mainhardt is excellent. The main road between Heilbronn and Schwäbisch Hall climbs over the plateau with long bends, and the minor roads through the forest offer endless curves, climbs and descents with little traffic. Watch for forestry vehicles, wildlife at dawn and dusk, and patches of mud or wet leaves on shaded corners. Speed limits and police checks are common on popular routes, especially on weekends.

Mainhardt has over five thousand residents, so fuel, a bakery and inns are close at hand. Try a plate of Maultaschen, the Swabian pasta parcels, or a slice of Black Forest cake, and stretch out on a bench at the edge of the forest before heading on.
t.lavaux@46.5,6.7:
From the shore of Lake Geneva the vineyards of Lavaux climb almost vertically, terrace upon terrace, held up by stone walls, to villages perched on the slopes above. Monks from Cistercian abbeys began shaping these hillsides in the Middle Ages, and generations of winegrowers have rebuilt the walls ever since, carrying soil back up when rain washes it down. The result is one of the most striking wine landscapes in the world, stretching about thirty kilometres between Lausanne and Montreux, and listed by UNESCO in 2007. Locals like to say that the vines here enjoy three suns: the one in the sky, its reflection off the lake and the warmth stored in the stone walls.

The grape of Lavaux is Chasselas, a delicate white that expresses the soil and slope in subtle ways, and the small appellations, Dézaley, Epesses, Saint-Saphorin, Calamin, each have devoted followers. Village cellars open their doors for tastings, especially at weekends, and a glass on a terrace overlooking the water with the Savoy Alps opposite is a fine thing.

Cully, a lakeside village with a small harbour, hosts a well-known jazz festival in spring, and Chexbres, up on the slope, has a terrace with views across the lake.

The riding is short but spectacular. The Route de la Corniche runs along the middle of the slopes between Lutry and Chexbres, narrow and winding, with stone walls on both sides and views that make concentration difficult. It is busy with cyclists, walkers, small tractors and the occasional tourist train, so ride gently and expect to stop often. The lakeside road below is faster but less interesting. Above Lavaux, roads climb into the hills of the Jorat and towards Fribourg through farmland and woods, with little traffic.

Switzerland has strict speed limits and very high fines, with cameras everywhere, so keep to the limits. A vignette is required for motorways. The weather is mild, with warm summers and mild winters, though fog can lie on the lake in autumn and winter.

Lutry, about five kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Lausanne and Vevey offer more. Try filets de perche, perch fillets from the lake, with chips and a glass of Chasselas, or a plate of local cheese and dried meat in a village pinte.
t.old jewish cemetery worms@49.6,8.4:
The Heiliger Sand in Worms is the oldest surviving Jewish cemetery in Europe, with gravestones going back to the eleventh century. Weathered sandstone slabs lean at angles among the grass and trees, carved with Hebrew inscriptions, some barely legible after nearly a thousand years. Pebbles and small notes lie on many of them, left by visitors as a sign of remembrance, especially on the grave of Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, a great scholar of the thirteenth century who died in captivity. Together with the synagogue and ritual bath of Worms and the Jewish sites of Speyer and Mainz, the cemetery forms the ShUM Sites, listed by UNESCO in 2021, recognising the Rhineland communities that shaped Ashkenazi Jewish culture in the Middle Ages.

The communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz were centres of learning, attracting scholars from across Europe. The famous commentator Rashi studied in Worms, and a small chapel near the synagogue is named after him. Their history was also marked by persecution, including massacres during the Crusades and the destruction of the Nazi era, and the cemetery survived almost miraculously.

Worms has other stories too. In 1521 Martin Luther stood before the emperor at the Diet of Worms and refused to recant his writings, and a large monument to the Reformation stands in the town. The city is linked to the Nibelungenlied, the medieval epic of Siegfried and the treasure of the Nibelungs, with a museum devoted to it. The Romanesque cathedral of St Peter dominates the skyline, and the vineyards around the Liebfrauenkirche gave their name to Liebfraumilch, once a famous export wine.

The riding around Worms is flat along the Rhine, with busy roads and traffic, but interesting routes lie on both sides. To the west, the Pfälzerwald, a vast forest, and the German Wine Route offer twisty roads through vineyards and wooded hills, while to the east, across the river, the Odenwald provides more curves and climbs.

Worms has fuel, shops and restaurants. When visiting the cemetery, men should cover their heads, and it is closed on the Sabbath and Jewish holidays. Afterwards, sit with a glass of Rheinhessen wine and a plate of Saumagen, a stuffed pork belly dish from the Palatinate.
t.egelsee@47.6,8.9:
There is almost nothing to see at the Egelsee, and that is part of its charm. It is a small, reed-fringed bog lake in the rolling Thurgau countryside between Gachnang and Frauenfeld, and under its peat and mud lie the remains of a Neolithic lakeside settlement, timber piles and floor layers preserved for thousands of years because air never reached them. It is one of the many sites that make up the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps on the UNESCO list, and unlike the reconstructed villages you find elsewhere, this one has been left in the ground on purpose. Archaeologists consider the soggy earth the best museum there is.

So you come here less for a monument than for the setting. Thurgau is the gentle, agricultural corner of Switzerland that the rest of the country teases as Mostindien, cider India, for its endless orchards and its pear and apple juice. In spring the trees between the farms are white with blossom; in autumn the roadside stalls sell freshly pressed sweet must. The lake itself is ringed with reeds and willows, quiet enough that you will hear frogs and the odd heron lifting off before you see it.

The roads around it suit a relaxed day. Small lanes thread between Niederwil, Gachnang and Hüttwilen, rising and falling over moraine hills left by the Rhine glacier, with views north toward the Seerücken ridge and, on clear days, south to the Alps. Surfaces are good, villages are tidy and speed limits are enforced with Swiss seriousness, so this is not a place for heroics. Tractors and cyclists share the lanes, and the Thur plain to the south can be windy.

Frauenfeld, the cantonal capital, is less than three kilometres away and has everything you need: fuel stations on the edge of town, supermarkets, cafés and a compact old centre around a castle whose stone keep dates back to the Middle Ages. It is a good place for lunch before heading on toward the Untersee or back toward Winterthur. If you want a swim on a hot day, Hüttwilen's little lakes nearby are popular with locals, but the Egelsee itself is a protected wetland, and it is better to leave it to the frogs and the buried village.
t.foret de la bettlachstock@47.2,7.4:
Above the watchmaking towns of Grenchen and Bettlach, the first chain of the Jura rises like a wall out of the Aare plain, and on its steep southern flank grows the beech forest of the Bettlachstock. In 2021 it became one of the Swiss components of the UNESCO Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a serial site that stretches across the continent to show how beech spread after the last Ice Age. What makes this patch special is that it has been left largely to itself for decades, on slopes so steep and rocky that nobody bothered to log them hard, and so the trees grow old, fall, rot and feed the next generation.

You feel the geology as soon as you leave the valley. The Jura here is folded limestone, pale and fractured, and the roads climbing toward the Grenchenberg and the high pastures are narrow, steep and full of tight bends, with gradients that keep you in first and second gear. Surfaces are generally sound, but expect gravel at the edges, cows on the upper stretches and walkers on weekends. Looking back, the view opens over the Aare plain to the whole Alpine chain from the Säntis to the Bernese giants, best in the clear air of autumn mornings when fog fills the lowlands below you.

The forest itself smells of damp leaves and wild garlic in spring, and in high summer it stays cool even when the plain bakes. Woodpeckers, including the big black species, work the dead trunks, and the understory is full of ferns and orchids on the lime soil. Please treat it as a reserve: park where parking is marked and walk in, rather than trying to find a track.

Grenchen, just below, is a town of about sixteen thousand with fuel, food and a long industrial history built on watch movements, and it also has a small airfield whose gliders often hang over the ridge on thermal days. Solothurn, the baroque little capital with its eleven churches and fountains, is a short ride east and makes a fine lunch stop. The upper farms on the ridge sometimes serve simple food in summer, but do not count on it; bring water and tank up before you start climbing.
t.schreckensee@47.9,9.6:
The Schreckensee, the lake of terror, is a disappointingly peaceful place for such a dramatic name. It is a small kettle lake in the moraine country of Upper Swabia, between Ravensburg and Aulendorf, left behind when a block of glacial ice melted at the end of the last Ice Age. Its shores, now partly bog and reed bed, hide the remains of prehistoric settlements, and it is one of the German sites in the UNESCO listing of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. As at most of these sites, nothing is visible on the surface; the timbers and household waste lie preserved underwater and in the peat, waiting for future archaeologists.

The countryside around it is gently rolling, with meadows, forests and the boggy wetlands the Swabians call Ried. Upper Swabia is also famous for its baroque churches and monasteries, and the Upper Swabian Baroque Route links many of them. A few kilometres south, the basilica of Weingarten is one of the largest baroque churches north of the Alps, and every year on the day after Ascension it hosts the Blutritt, a procession of thousands of horsemen honouring a relic of the Holy Blood. Ravensburg, with its medieval towers and gates, is a fine old trading town, and the home of a well-known board game and puzzle maker.

The riding is pleasant rather than thrilling. Country roads wind between farms and villages, over low hills and through forests, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. Expect tractors in summer and autumn, and watch for deer at dawn and dusk. On clear days, especially when the warm föhn wind blows from the south, the Alps appear on the horizon across Lake Constance, looking close enough to touch.

Fronreute and Wolpertswende are small villages with limited services, so head to Aulendorf, nine kilometres away, or Ravensburg and Weingarten for fuel and a broader choice of food. Look for Swabian dishes such as Maultaschen, big pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, or Kässpätzle, egg noodles with melted cheese and fried onions. A cold local beer on a terrace is a reward at the end of the day.
t.unteruhldingen stollenwiesen@47.7,9.2:
Unteruhldingen is where most people first meet the prehistoric lake dwellers of the Alps, thanks to the Pfahlbaumuseum, an open-air museum of reconstructed houses on stilts standing in the shallow water of Lake Constance. It started in the 1920s and has been adding houses ever since, and walking along the wooden walkways between thatched huts gives you a vivid idea of village life thousands of years ago. The real archaeological sites, like Stollenwiesen just offshore, lie underwater, a series of settlements preserved in lake mud and listed by UNESCO in 2011 as part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps.

The northern shore of the lake, the Überlinger See arm, is one of the most beautiful stretches of the Bodensee. Vineyards and orchards climb the slopes above the water, and the views across to Switzerland and the Alps are spectacular on clear days. Just up the hill from Unteruhldingen stands the pilgrimage church of Birnau, a rococo masterpiece in pink and white, famous for a little cherub licking honey from his finger. A few kilometres east, Meersburg is a lovely town of steep lanes, half-timbered houses and an old castle where the poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff spent her last years. Car ferries run from Meersburg across to Konstanz.

The riding is scenic but often slow. The lakeside road is beautiful, but in summer it is busy with tourists, caravans, cyclists and buses, and the towns along the shore have low speed limits. For more fun, head inland into the hills of the Linzgau and toward the Hegau volcanoes, where the roads are quieter and the bends tighter. Spring, when the fruit trees are in blossom, and autumn, when the vineyards turn gold, are the best seasons.

Uhldingen-Mühlhofen, two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and a choice of restaurants and cafés. Meersburg and Überlingen offer more. Try Felchen, a whitefish from the lake, often served fried or smoked, with a glass of local Müller-Thurgau wine or a Spätburgunder from the Meersburg slopes, if you are done riding. Parking can be tight near the museum, but bikes have an easier time.
t.storen wildsberg@47.4,8.7:
The Greifensee lies just east of Zurich, a shallow, quiet lake of about six kilometres in length, framed by reeds, meadows and the gentle hills of the Zurich Oberland. Its shores are largely protected, and there is no road running right along the water, which keeps it remarkably calm for a lake so close to Switzerland's biggest city. At Storen-Wildsberg near the village of Greifensee, the remains of a prehistoric settlement lie under the water and in the shoreline sediments, one of the Swiss sites in the UNESCO listing of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. As with all of them, it is the ground itself that is protected; there is nothing to see except the reeds and the water.

The village of Greifensee has a small castle, and a dark episode in its past. In 1444, during the Old Zurich War, the Confederates besieged the castle, and after its surrender they executed most of the garrison in a meadow nearby, an event still remembered as the Murder of Greifensee. Later, in the eighteenth century, the castle was home to Salomon Landolt, a colourful bailiff, painter and military reformer whose life inspired a novella by Gottfried Keller.

The lake is a magnet for walkers, cyclists, inline skaters and families on weekends, so riding here is more about enjoying the scenery than covering distance. The roads around the lake are narrow, with frequent villages and low speed limits, and cyclists are everywhere. For more interesting riding, head east into the Zurich Oberland, where the roads climb into the hills toward the Bachtel and the Hörnli, with views over the Alps and plenty of curves. As always in Switzerland, speed limits are strictly enforced, with fixed and mobile cameras.

Greifensee itself, a commuter village of five thousand, has a few shops and restaurants, and Uster, the nearest larger town, has more choice, including fuel. On a hot day, there are bathing areas around the lake, popular with locals. Try a plate of Zürcher Geschnetzeltes, sliced veal in a creamy mushroom sauce with rösti, or simply sit with an ice cream by the water and watch the sailing boats drift past.
t.stations de morges@46.5,6.5:
On a calm morning the lake off Morges is as flat as polished pewter, with the Savoy Alps on the far shore and Mont Blanc floating above them, and it is hard to believe that anyone ever had to fight for this view. Yet people have been living right here for millennia. Just off the shore, in the shallow water near the town, lie the remains of prehistoric villages built on piles, the Stations de Morges, one of the Swiss components of the UNESCO Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. Divers and archaeologists have mapped wooden posts and objects from the Bronze Age, but from the shore you will see only water, swans and the occasional paddleboarder.

Morges itself is a cheerful little town on Lake Geneva, between Lausanne and Geneva. Its squat lakeside castle, built by the Savoyards in the thirteenth century, now houses military museums, and the lakeside park next to it hosts a famous tulip festival every spring, when hundreds of thousands of blooms turn the lawns into a riot of colour. The Polish pianist and statesman Ignacy Paderewski lived in Morges for decades, and Audrey Hepburn spent her last years in nearby Tolochenaz, where she is buried in the village cemetery.

The riding along the lake is beautiful but often frustrating. The main road through the towns of La Côte is busy, with roundabouts, traffic lights and strict speed limits. Better to climb into the vineyards above the lake, where narrow lanes wind between the vines and villages, with stunning views over the water. Further up, the roads cross the Jura foothills to the Col du Marchairuz and the Vallée de Joux, with long, flowing curves through pine forests and pastures. In summer, the lake breeze offers some relief from the heat; in winter, fog can sit on the water for days.

Morges, with fourteen thousand inhabitants, has everything: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants along the lakefront. Try filets de perche, fried perch fillets from the lake, with chips and tartare sauce, or malakoffs, deep-fried cheese fritters from nearby Vinzel. Chasselas from the slopes of La Côte is the classic accompaniment, though only when the riding is done.
t.castello di aglie@45.4,7.8:
Agliè is a small town in the Canavese, the hilly district north of Turin that spreads between the Po plain and the mouths of the Alpine valleys, and its castle is far grander than the town around it. Begun as a medieval fortress by the San Martino counts, it was transformed in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries into a baroque residence and later bought by the House of Savoy, who turned it into a summer palace with richly decorated rooms, a chapel, a theatre and a large park with fountains and a lake. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, a ring of palaces around Turin, and Italian television viewers may recognise it from a popular costume drama filmed there.

The Canavese has plenty of character. The poet Guido Gozzano spent time in a villa at Agliè and wrote about its gardens with gentle irony. Nearby Castellamonte has a long tradition of ceramics, especially the big terracotta stoves that once heated Piedmontese homes. Ivrea, a little to the north, is known for the Olivetti company town, also on the UNESCO list, and for its carnival, when teams pelt each other with oranges in a mock battle.

The riding is excellent, with variety on every side. The hills around Agliè are crossed by quiet country roads, winding through vineyards, woods and villages, with the morainic ridge of the Serra d'Ivrea on the horizon. To the northwest, the Valle Orco leads up into the Gran Paradiso National Park, with a spectacular climb toward the Colle del Nivolet, a high road among lakes and glaciers that is open only in summer and sometimes restricted to traffic on certain days. Traffic is light, but watch for tractors and gravel on the smaller roads.

Agliè is a small town with cafés and a few restaurants, and Castellamonte, five kilometres away, has fuel and supermarkets. Try the local wine, Erbaluce di Caluso, a crisp white, or a red Canavese. For food, look for agnolotti, tajarin and, in the cold months, bagna càuda, a hot dip of garlic, anchovies and olive oil, eaten with vegetables.
t.watchtowers wp 8 31 to 8 41@49.4,9.4:
Somewhere between Walldürn and the hills north of Stuttgart, the Roman surveyors drew a line on the map and simply refused to bend it. For about eighty kilometres, the Upper Germanic Limes runs almost perfectly straight across hill and valley, one of the most remarkable feats of ancient surveying in Europe. The watchtowers WP 8/31 to 8/41 near Osterburken and Adelsheim lie on that straight stretch, and like the rest of the frontier they are part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Most are now low mounds in fields and woods, but here and there you will find a reconstructed tower or a stretch of wall to give you an idea of what it looked like.

Osterburken is the place to understand it all. The town has a Roman museum built around the remains of a military bath house, and the double fort here was one of the main garrisons on this part of the frontier. Among the finds is a large and beautifully carved relief of the god Mithras slaying the bull, a sign of how popular this mystery religion was among Roman soldiers. The fort walls are partly visible on a hill above the town.

The area is called the Bauland, a quiet, rural part of northern Baden-Württemberg, with gently rolling hills, wheat fields and small villages. It is also known for Grünkern, spelt harvested while still green and then smoked and dried, used in soups and patties. The riding is relaxed, with country roads winding through fields and forests, little traffic and good surfaces. The Jagst and Kocher valleys to the east offer more scenic routes, with castles, vineyards and tight bends along the rivers.

Adelsheim and Osterburken, both a few kilometres away, are small towns with fuel, shops and inns. The local food is hearty: Grünkern soup, Schäufele, roast pork shoulder, and Kässpätzle. The wines from the nearby Tauber valley and the Württemberg slopes are worth trying, if you have finished riding for the day. On a clear evening, the light over the fields makes this quiet frontier land surprisingly beautiful.
t.villages on kashiragashima island@33.0,1:
Kashiragashima is a scrap of rock off the northeast coast of Nakadōri, in the Gotō Islands west of Nagasaki, and for a long time nobody wanted to live there. In the nineteenth century the island was used as a place to isolate smallpox patients, and that very isolation drew a small group of Hidden Christians, Japanese Catholics who had kept their faith in secret through more than two centuries of persecution. They settled in a cove, farmed the steep slopes and fished. After the ban on Christianity was lifted, they built a church out of the local sandstone, quarried and carried by hand, under the direction of the master builder Tetsukawa Yosuke, who designed many churches across the region. Completed in 1919, it is a sturdy, beautiful building, and the village is part of the UNESCO listing of Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region, inscribed in 2018.

The church is small and still cared for by the community, so visits usually need to be arranged in advance through the local information centre, and you may be asked to take a shuttle rather than ride to the door. Inside, the stone walls and a ceiling painted with flowers create a calm, gentle atmosphere.

Getting to the Gotō Islands takes some planning: ferries run from Nagasaki and Sasebo, carrying vehicles, and the crossing takes a few hours, less on the fast boats that do not carry bikes. On the islands, the roads are narrow and winding, following the coast around inlets and over headlands, with views of the sea, cliffs and small fishing harbours. Traffic is light, but watch for fallen rocks, gravel and the occasional slow truck. Typhoons can disrupt ferries and roads in late summer and autumn.

Services on the main island of Nakadōri are limited but adequate, with fuel stations and shops in the town of Shinkamigotō, but do not expect to find them on the smaller islands. Plan ahead and keep your tank full. Gotō udon, thin noodles made with camellia oil, are a local speciality, often eaten as jigoku-daki, dipped straight from the boiling pot, and the seafood, especially fresh fish and squid, is superb.
t.sacro monte della ss trinita@46.0,8.6:
High above the western shore of Lake Maggiore, in a forest of chestnut and beech above the village of Ghiffa, a small sanctuary dedicated to the Holy Trinity looks out over the water to the hills of Lombardy. The Sacro Monte of Ghiffa began in the seventeenth century as a series of chapels along a path, each meant to illustrate a scene from sacred history for pilgrims, but it was never completed as planned. It is the smallest of the nine Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy listed by UNESCO in 2003, and its charm lies in its intimacy and its setting: a few chapels, a porticoed walkway and a church in the woods, with the lake shining below.

The area around Ghiffa is part of the Verbano, the stretch of Lake Maggiore between Verbania and Cannobio. The lake is famous for its gardens: the Borromean Islands, with their palaces and terraced gardens, are just south, and the Villa Taranto gardens in Verbania hold thousands of species of plants from all over the world. The mild climate allows camellias, azaleas, rhododendrons and even citrus to flourish.

The riding here is varied and fun. The lake road, the SS34, runs along the shore from Verbania to Cannobio and the Swiss border, with views of the water and the mountains, but it is busy in summer and the villages slow you down. Better are the roads that climb into the hills behind the lake, such as the road up to Premeno and Pian di Sole, with hairpins, forests and great views, or the road from Cannobio into the Valle Cannobina, narrow and twisty, following a river through deep gorges. Watch out for gravel, leaves and other bikers on weekends.

Ghiffa is a small village with a few cafés, and Verbania, four kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels. The lake towns are full of places to eat, from simple trattorias to elegant restaurants. Try lake fish, such as perch or whitefish, risotto with perch fillets or polenta with local cheese. In autumn, look for chestnuts roasted by the roadside, a perfect snack on a cool day.
t.sacro monte della beata vergine@45.6,8.0:
Oropa is a sanctuary on a scale that surprises everyone who comes up the valley from Biella for the first time. At almost twelve hundred metres, in a bowl of mountains, a vast complex of churches, courtyards, porticoes and pilgrim lodgings rises in terraces, built over several centuries around an ancient chapel that holds a Black Madonna, a wooden statue of the Virgin that legend attributes to St Luke. Above the main buildings, a Sacro Monte of chapels with life-size statues illustrates the life of Mary along a wooded path. It is one of the nine Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy listed by UNESCO in 2003, and one of the most important Marian shrines in the Alps.

Biella, at the foot of the valley, is a town built on wool. For centuries, its mills processed fine wool into cloth, and today some of the most famous names in Italian textiles still have their factories here. A short ride east, the Panoramica Zegna, a scenic road created by the textile industrialist Ermenegildo Zegna in the 1930s, winds through forests and over ridges, with spectacular views of the plain and the Alps, and the Oasi Zegna park has trails and rhododendron gardens.

The climb to Oropa is famous among cyclists: it has been a summit finish in the Giro d'Italia, and Marco Pantani's attack here in 1999 is the stuff of legend. On a motorcycle, it is a pleasure, with a smooth surface, regular gradients and plenty of curves, though busy with pilgrims and tourists on weekends. From Oropa, a road continues over the mountain to the Cervo valley and the sanctuary of San Giovanni d'Andorno, narrow and steep, closed in winter.

Biella, ten kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the sanctuary has restaurants, a bar and pilgrim lodgings where you can stay overnight. Try polenta concia, polenta layered with melted local cheese and butter, or a plate of cured meats and cheese from the mountain pastures. The water from the sanctuary's fountains is cold and clear, perfect for filling a bottle before heading back down.
t.ruine altenmuster@49.7,8.6:
Lorsch Abbey, founded in the eighth century, became one of the most powerful monasteries of the Carolingian empire, with vast estates, a famous library and the patronage of Charlemagne himself. Its first home, however, was not on the site of the later abbey, but a short distance away, on an island in the Weschnitz river, a place known as Altenmünster, the old minster. The ruins of that first foundation, a few low walls in a meadow, are a quiet counterpoint to the abbey's most famous building, the Torhalle, a gatehouse with a façade of red and white stone panels, one of the few surviving examples of Carolingian architecture. The abbey and Altenmünster together have been on the UNESCO list since 1991.

The abbey's library produced the Lorsch Pharmacopoeia, one of the oldest surviving medical texts in the German-speaking world, and the Lorsch Codex, a register of the abbey's lands and privileges, which is an invaluable source for the history of the region. Today, the abbey grounds include a herb garden, a museum and an experimental Carolingian farm, where you can see how people lived and worked in the early Middle Ages.

Lorsch lies in the flat Rhine plain, between the river and the Odenwald hills. Just east, the Bergstraße, the mountain road, runs along the foot of the hills, through towns like Bensheim and Heppenheim, with half-timbered houses, castles and vineyards. It is one of the first places in Germany where spring arrives, with almond and cherry trees in blossom. The Nibelungenstraße climbs from Bensheim into the Odenwald, with long curves and views, and the roads through the forests and valleys of the Odenwald are a favourite with riders from Frankfurt and Mannheim.

Lorsch, a town of thirteen thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Bensheim, four kilometres away, has more choice. The Hessian Ried around Lorsch is famous for its asparagus, harvested in spring and served with ham, potatoes and hollandaise sauce. Try a glass of wine from the Bergstraße, one of the smallest wine regions in Germany, or a local apple wine, if you are done for the day.
t.watchtowers wp 7 1 to 7 36 including for:
At Miltenberg, the Roman frontier did something unusual: it stopped being a wall and became a river. North of the town, the Main served as the frontier for some fifty kilometres, guarded by forts and watchtowers along its western bank, and here, where the river bends, the land frontier began again, heading south through the Odenwald. The watchtowers WP 7/1 to 7/36 belong to this stretch, and while most are only traces in fields and forests, they are part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The Romans built forts at Miltenberg, too, and some of their finds are displayed in the town museum.

Miltenberg is one of the prettiest towns on the Main. Its old town stretches along the river at the foot of a steep, wooded hill, with a long main street lined with half-timbered houses, many of them with carved and painted beams. At the heart of it lies the Schnatterloch, a small, sloping square surrounded by timber-framed houses, with a fountain and a castle on the hill above. The local red sandstone was quarried here for centuries and used in buildings across the region, including in Roman times.

The riding in the area is a delight. The roads along the Main follow the curves of the river, with views of vineyards, forests and villages, and the roads that climb into the hills of the Spessart to the north and the Odenwald to the south are winding and fun, with tight bends, steep climbs and very little traffic on weekdays. In summer, the riverside roads are busy with cyclists, and the towns slow you down. Spring, with blossoms, and autumn, with golden forests, are the best seasons.

Miltenberg, with nearly ten thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants and inns. Bürgstadt and Großheubach, nearby, are wine villages with taverns serving local wines, especially the red wines grown on the sandstone slopes. Try a Frankish Bratwurst with sauerkraut, a Schäufele, or a fish from the Main. And if you have time, a short walk up to the castle gives you a fine view of the town and the river.
t.chenevieres de guevaux i@46.9,7.1:
Lake Murten is small, shallow and warm, framed on its north side by the vine-covered whale back of Mont Vully. Under its shallows near the Vully shore lie the remains of prehistoric pile-dwelling villages, and Chenevières de Guévaux is one of them, part of the UNESCO site of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. Between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, people built houses on timber posts along lake shores like this one. Waterlogged conditions preserved posts, tools, textiles and food remains for thousands of years, and the finds transformed what we know about early farming communities in Europe.

There is nothing to see from the shore except the lake itself, so the stop is about context and setting. The Vully is wine country, with small villages of stone houses where producers sell Chasselas and Pinot Noir from their cellars, and the road along the lake between Môtier and Praz is narrow and gentle, a place to cruise slowly with the windows of the old houses almost within reach. The climb up Mont Vully gives a wide view over the Three Lakes region, with the Jura on one side and, on clear days, the Bernese Alps on the other.

Across the lake, Murten is one of the most complete walled towns in Switzerland. You can walk the ramparts and look down over tiled roofs to the water. In 1476 the Swiss Confederates crushed the army of Charles the Bold of Burgundy near here, a victory that still features in Swiss history lessons. The town has fuel nearby, cafés under arcades and plenty of places to eat lake fish. Try a gâteau du Vully, a sweet bread with a sugary cream topping, from a local bakery.

Swiss rules apply: strict speed limits, unforgiving fines, and a vignette is needed if you use the motorway. Summer weekends bring cyclists and boaters, so the lanes can be busy. Late September, during the grape harvest, is perhaps the best time, when the air smells of crushed fruit and the lake turns silver in the evening light.
t.robenhausen@47.3,8.8:
In 1858 a local man named Jakob Messikommer began digging in the peat bog at Robenhausen, on the southern end of the Pfäffikersee in the Zurich Oberland, and he spent decades uncovering a remarkably rich Neolithic pile-dwelling settlement. His finds, from stone axes to woven textiles and charred bread, travelled to museums around the world and helped make Swiss lake dwellings famous. Today Robenhausen is one of the components of the UNESCO Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, though what remains lies underground in a protected wetland.

The Robenhauser Ried is a nature reserve of reed beds, wet meadows and peat, and it is a refuge for birds, frogs and dragonflies. Footpaths and boardwalks lead through it, and in early summer the meadows are bright with orchids and irises. The Pfäffikersee itself is a small, clean lake popular for swimming, with a quiet shoreline that feels remote even though Zurich is only half an hour away.

On a bike, the Zurich Oberland is a pleasant surprise. Lanes climb from Wetzikon and Pfäffikon onto rolling hills toward the Bachtel and the Hörnli, with farm roads that twist through woods and open onto views of the Alps on clear days. Traffic around Wetzikon can be heavy, and Swiss speed limits are enforced rigorously, but once you leave the main roads the riding becomes quiet and rhythmic, the kind of hill country where you are always going up, down or around something.

Wetzikon, a town of over twelve thousand people right next door, has fuel, supermarkets and cafés, so there is no need to plan ahead. The Oberland was an early industrial region, and old spinning mills along the streams are reminders of a time when water power drove the local textile trade. Take a swim in summer if the weather is kind, walk a stretch of the reserve, and imagine this lake shore five thousand years ago, with smoke rising from houses on stilts and canoes drawn up on the mud.
t.sacro monte calvario@46.1,8.3:
Domodossola's holy mountain rises immediately above the town, on the wooded Mattarella hill, and the walk or ride up gives you the whole Ossola valley at your feet. The Sacro Monte Calvario was begun in the seventeenth century as a devotional path of chapels depicting the Passion of Christ, each holding painted and sculpted scenes, leading up to a sanctuary church at the top. It is one of the nine Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy inscribed together on the UNESCO list, and it has a particular link with Antonio Rosmini, the philosopher-priest who founded his religious institute here in the nineteenth century.

The hill was also a fortress long before it was holy ground. Remains of a medieval castle stand near the summit, which makes sense once you see the position: the hill controls the junction where the Simplon road comes down from Switzerland and the side valleys of Vigezzo, Antigorio and Bognanco open out. Domodossola has always been a crossroads, and its Saturday market, held for centuries, still draws people from both sides of the border.

For riders, the town is a superb base. The Simplon pass, at 2005 metres, is one of the great Alpine crossings, with a gorge section through Gondo on the Italian approach and broad, fast bends higher up toward the Swiss side; a Swiss vignette is only needed if you go on to the motorway. The Valle Vigezzo road east toward Locarno is twistier and more intimate, through larch woods and villages of stone-roofed houses, and the Valle Antigorio leads north to the waterfall of the Toce in Val Formazza.

Domodossola has fuel, mechanics and plenty of places to eat, and the old centre around Piazza Mercato, with its arcades and balconies, is lovely for an evening walk. Ossola cooking leans to mountain food: cured meats, cheeses from the high pastures, and rye bread. The chapel path is steep but short, and in early morning or late afternoon the light across the valley is wonderful, with the snow peaks above the Simplon catching the last sun.
t.odenahlen@48.1,9.6:
The Federsee basin in Upper Swabia is one of those landscapes that hides its importance. It looks like a flat expanse of reeds, wet meadows and woodland around a shrinking lake, but beneath the peat lie dozens of prehistoric settlements, preserved because the bog kept the oxygen out. Ödenahlen is one of these sites, a Neolithic village on the edge of the moor, and the Federsee settlements are part of the UNESCO Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. Wooden floors, house walls, wheels and everyday objects have been excavated here, and some of the oldest wooden wheels in Europe come from this region.

To understand it, go to the Federseemuseum in Bad Buchau, which tells the story of the moor settlements and has reconstructed houses outside. A boardwalk stretches across the reeds to the open water, and in spring and early summer the moor is full of birdsong; it is one of the important wetland bird sites in southern Germany, and you may hear bitterns booming or watch marsh harriers quartering the reeds.

Riding in Upper Swabia is gentle and open. The roads between Biberach, Bad Buchau and Bad Schussenried run through rolling farmland and small woods, with onion-domed church towers marking each village. This is Baroque country, and the Oberschwäbische Barockstraße links some extraordinary churches. Steinhausen, just a short ride away, has a pilgrimage church by Dominikus Zimmermann often called the most beautiful village church in the world, and it is hard to argue once you stand under its pastel ceiling.

Fuel and supplies are easy in Bad Buchau or Biberach an der Riß, a pleasant town of around thirty thousand with a well-preserved old centre. Expect speed cameras and tractors. Summer evenings are the best time to be here, with the sky reflected in the bog pools and the smell of hay drifting off the meadows, and a beer from one of the many small Swabian breweries waiting in town.
t.sacro monte di belmonte@45.4,7.6:
On a granite hill rising above the Canavese plain north of Turin, the Sacro Monte di Belmonte looks out over the foothills toward the Alps. The sanctuary, run by Franciscan friars, has a church and a circuit of chapels representing the stations of the Passion, built in the early eighteenth century on a site that had long been a place of pilgrimage. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy, and the walk around the chapels, under chestnut and oak trees, is calm and shady even in summer.

The hill has an older story too. Archaeologists have found evidence of prehistoric and early medieval settlement on Belmonte, and the strategic view over the Orco and Soana valleys explains why people have long sought refuge here. From the top, on a clear day, you can see across the plain toward Turin and up toward the peaks of the Gran Paradiso.

Riding up from Valperga or Cuorgnè, the road climbs through woods in a series of tight hairpins, narrow but well surfaced, and it makes a short, satisfying detour. The real riding lies further up the Orco valley, past Locana and Noasca to Ceresole Reale and the Colle del Nivolet, at 2612 metres one of the highest roads in the Alps, ending in a dead end amid lakes and high pastures within the Gran Paradiso national park. The upper road is open only in summer and is sometimes subject to traffic restrictions on certain days, so check before you go.

Cuorgnè, three kilometres away, is the local centre, with fuel, shops and a pleasant arcaded main street. The Canavese is known for its wines, especially Erbaluce di Caluso, and for its cheeses and cured meats. Come in spring or autumn, when the chestnut woods are fresh or golden, and avoid summer weekends, when Turin escapes to the mountains and the valley roads fill with traffic.
t.les greves@46.9,6.9:
Reeds, mostly. That is the first thing you notice when you roll down to Les Grèves on the southern shore of Lake Neuchâtel: a soft wall of reed and willow between the fields and the water, with the Jura sitting long and blue on the far side of the lake. This stretch between Portalban, Gletterens and Chevroux belongs to the Grande Cariçaie, the biggest lakeshore marsh in Switzerland, and it only exists because people once moved an entire lake level.

In the late nineteenth century the First Jura Water Correction tamed the Aare and dropped Lakes Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten by a couple of metres. The old shallows fell dry, the marsh crept out onto them, and the archaeologists followed. Under the mud lay the posts of prehistoric lake villages, and the southern shore turned out to be thick with them; several belong to the UNESCO group of Alpine pile dwellings. At Gletterens there is a reconstructed village of thatched huts if you want to see what the Neolithic looked like in daylight rather than in a museum drawer.

The riding around here is gentle and agricultural rather than dramatic. Little roads cut through tobacco and vegetable fields of the Broye plain, tractors appear from nowhere, and the lake road links a string of harbour villages where the speed limit drops constantly. Ride it for the light, which is wonderful in the early evening when the low sun turns the reeds copper and the Jura goes violet. In summer the mosquitoes come out at the same moment, so keep the visor down when you stop by the water. Wind can come across the lake surprisingly hard, and the Joran, the cold evening wind off the Jura, is well known to sailors here.

Nature is the real show. The Cariçaie is a stopover and nesting ground for an absurd number of birds, from great crested grebes to marsh harriers, and the paths and observation hides are made for walking boots, not bikes, so park at a harbour and wander for twenty minutes. Fuel is not in the hamlets: head to Estavayer-le-Lac with its fine medieval old town, or to Domdidier and Avenches, where the Roman amphitheatre of Aventicum makes a fine excuse for a second stop. Across the water on the Mont Vully slopes they grow a light white wine that tastes very good with lake perch, which every harbour café along this shore will happily put in front of you.
t.isolino virginia camilla isola di san bi:
Lago di Varese is the quiet one. The big lakes, Maggiore and Lugano, grab the postcards and the coach tours, while this shallow, reedy sheet of water just west of Varese gets on with being pretty in a modest way. Off its western shore, a few hundred metres out from Biandronno, floats a tiny wooded island called Isolino Virginia, and that speck of land is one of the most important prehistoric sites in the Alpine world.

People were living here on timber platforms in the Neolithic, some seven thousand years ago, and kept coming back for millennia into the Bronze Age. That long sequence is why the island sits on the UNESCO list of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. The island once belonged to the Ponti family, who named it after a daughter, and today a small museum tells the story. In season a little boat crosses from the Biandronno shore, so check the timetable before you plan your day around it, because outside summer weekends it may not run.

The road around the lake is a pleasant loop of perhaps thirty kilometres, mostly flat and rarely fast, threading through Gavirate, Biandronno, Bodio and Calcinate with the water appearing between villas and reed beds. It is a road for an unhurried morning. The real riding begins when you point the front wheel uphill: the Campo dei Fiori massif rises right behind Gavirate and Varese, and the climbs to the Sacro Monte di Varese and beyond twist through chestnut forest with proper hairpins and views back over five or six lakes on a clear day. Weekends bring cyclists in great numbers, so ride the climbs with patience.

Gavirate is your practical base. It is a lively little town with fuel, cafés and a lakeside promenade, and it claims the invention of the brutti ma buoni, the lumpy hazelnut and meringue biscuits whose name means ugly but good. Buy a bag; they survive a tank bag surprisingly well. The lake itself has had a long battle with pollution and swimming is not what it was decades ago, but the cycle path that rings it is lovely for a short walk after parking. Late afternoon is the hour to be here, when the Monte Rosa glows pink far to the west and the water goes perfectly still around the island.
t.spitz@46.9,7.1:
On the southern shore of the Murtensee, just west of the medieval town of Murten, a little point of land juts into the water at Greng, and here, beneath the shallows, archaeologists found the posts of prehistoric lake villages. Greng-Spitz is one of the Swiss sites in the UNESCO group of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, and while there is nothing to see but reeds, water and the occasional marker, it is pleasant to know that people lived on this shore some five thousand years ago.

Murten, two kilometres away, is the real star. Its old town is one of the best preserved in Switzerland, with arcaded streets, a castle and a complete ring of medieval walls that you can walk along, looking down on red roofs and across the lake. In 1476 the Swiss Confederates defeated the army of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, outside the town in one of the decisive battles of Swiss history. The town sits on the language border, French to the west and German to the east, and both Murten and Morat are used.

The riding around the lake is gentle and lovely. Roads follow the shore through vineyards and villages, and the Mont Vully, a hill of 653 metres between the Murtensee and Lake Neuchâtel, has small roads climbing through vineyards with views over the Three Lakes region and the Alps on clear days. The Seeland, to the east, is a flat land of vegetable fields, reclaimed from marshes by the Jura water corrections in the nineteenth century. Traffic can be busy on summer weekends, especially in Murten, and speed limits in villages are strictly enforced.

Murten has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Lake fish, especially perch fillets, are the local specialty, and the Vully wines, mostly whites made from Chasselas, are light and fresh. A special local treat is the Nidelkuchen, a sweet cream cake from the region. Swimming in the lake is popular in summer, and boats link Murten with Neuchâtel and Biel through canals. In the evening, the walls of Murten glow in the setting sun, and the lake turns gold.
t.les roseaux@46.5,6.5:
Morges sits on the north shore of Lake Geneva between Lausanne and Geneva, with its castle by the harbour and the Alps of Savoy rising across the water. Just east of the town, at a place called Les Roseaux, the reeds, archaeologists found one of the oldest pile dwelling sites on the lake, dating back to the early Bronze Age, and it is part of the UNESCO group of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. Its remains lie underwater and are not visible, but the name and the shore keep the memory.

Morges itself is a pleasant small town with a long history. Its castle was built by the Savoy family in the thirteenth century and now houses military museums. The town is famous for its tulip festival in spring, when the lakeside park of the Parc de l'Indépendance blooms with thousands of tulips. The actress Audrey Hepburn lived in nearby Tolochenaz and is buried there. Wine is everywhere, as the slopes of La Côte, between Lausanne and Geneva, are covered with vineyards producing mostly Chasselas.

The riding around Morges is mostly about the lake and the vineyards. The lake road between Lausanne and Geneva is often busy, but the roads climbing up through the vineyards of La Côte offer lovely views over the lake and the Alps, with Mont Blanc visible on clear days. Further north, the Jura mountains have winding roads and passes such as the Col du Marchairuz, which is popular with riders. Swiss speed limits are low and strictly enforced, with heavy fines, so ride with care. The Lavaux vineyards, east of Lausanne, are spectacular and worth a detour.

Morges has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the lakeside promenade is pleasant for a walk. Lake fish, especially perch, is the local specialty, and the wines of La Côte are best enjoyed after the riding is over. The town has a weekly market, and cafés along the main street. In the evening, the sun sets over the lake, and the Alps on the French side glow pink. It is a peaceful place to end a day of riding.
t.mercurago@45.7,8.6:
Just south of Arona, at the southern tip of Lago Maggiore, a small regional park protects a landscape of woods, meadows and peat bogs called the Lagoni di Mercurago. The lagoni are small ponds and wetlands formed after the retreat of the glaciers, and in the nineteenth century, while peat was being dug, the remains of a Bronze Age pile dwelling settlement were found here, including a wooden wheel. Mercurago is part of the UNESCO site of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

The park is a quiet place for a walk, with paths through oak and chestnut woods and around the ponds. It is also known for its horses: the area has long been a centre of thoroughbred breeding, and you may see horses grazing in the meadows. Arona, three kilometres north, is a lakeside town with a long promenade and a historic centre. Above the town stands the San Carlone, a huge copper statue of Saint Charles Borromeo, the archbishop of Milan who was born in Arona in 1538; visitors can climb inside it and look out through the eyes.

The riding around Arona is varied. The lake road north along the western shore of Lago Maggiore, towards Stresa and Verbania, is scenic but often busy, with views of the Borromean Islands. The hills behind, towards Lake Orta and the Mottarone, have winding roads through forests with fine views over the lakes and the Alps. The Mottarone, between the two lakes, is reached by a road with many hairpins. South of Arona, the plain of Novara is flat and agricultural, with rice fields. Traffic around the lake on summer weekends can be heavy.

Arona has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Dormelletto and Comignago, nearby, are small villages with basic services. The local cuisine combines Piedmontese and Lombard traditions: risotto, lake fish and gorgonzola, which comes from the Novara area. A coffee on the lakeside promenade in Arona, looking across to the castle of Angera on the Lombard shore, is a pleasant way to take a break. In autumn, the woods of Mercurago turn gold, and the park is particularly beautiful.
t.watchtowers wp 9 101 to 9 131 including:
There is a stretch of the Roman frontier in southern Germany that runs almost perfectly straight for about eighty kilometres, from Walldürn in the Odenwald to near Welzheim in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, ignoring hills and valleys alike, as if the surveyors had simply drawn a line on a map. The watchtowers numbered WP 9/101 to 9/131 stand near the southern end of that line, in the forests around Kaisersbach and Welzheim, where the Limes finally turns.

How the Romans managed such precision is still debated, but the result was a frontier that stretched across rough terrain, through forests and over ridges, with towers at regular intervals. At Welzheim there were two forts, and the eastern fort has a reconstructed gate in an archaeological park. Along the trails in the forest, you can find the remains of tower foundations and the bank and ditch of the frontier, and information boards explain what you are looking at.

The Swabian-Franconian Forest is wonderful riding country. The hills are covered with dense forests of spruce and beech, cut by deep valleys, and the roads wind through them with constant bends, climbs and descents. The Ebnisee, a small lake in the forest near Kaisersbach, is a popular destination for riders and families on weekends. The roads are generally well surfaced, but shaded sections can stay damp, and forest roads can have leaves and gravel. Weekends are busy with riders and cyclists, and police controls are frequent.
