Kaisersbach and Althütte are small villages with basic services, and Welzheim, six kilometres away, is a town of eleven thousand with fuel and shops. The forest is dotted with inns serving Swabian food: Maultaschen, large stuffed pasta squares, Spätzle, egg noodles, and roast meat with gravy. In the forests, the air is cool and smells of resin, even in summer, and the silence is broken only by birds and the occasional motorcycle. Walking a short stretch of the Limes path in the forest is a good way to understand the scale of the Roman frontier.
t.port conty@46.9,6.8:
Under the shallow water off Port-Conty lie the remains of villages that were built on stilts more than five thousand years ago, and you will see none of them from the shore. The site, near Saint-Aubin-Sauges on the north-western side of Lake Neuchâtel, is one of the many locations in the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. Archaeologists have found posts, tools, pottery and remains of food preserved in the lake mud, painting a picture of Neolithic and Bronze Age communities who farmed, fished and built their houses along the water's edge.

What you do see is a lovely stretch of lake, with reed beds, small harbours and the long blue line of the water stretching toward the Alps on clear days. Saint-Aubin and Gorgier are small wine villages on the slopes of the Béroche, with vineyards running down to the lake and old stone houses lining the streets.

The road along the north shore between Neuchâtel and Yverdon is pleasant but busy, with steady traffic, frequent villages, speed limits that change often and Swiss enforcement that is not known for its mercy. The real fun begins when you turn uphill into the Jura. Roads climb steeply through vineyards and forest toward Provence and Mauborget, with tight bends, great views back over the lake and the cliffs of the Creux du Van not far away, a vast natural amphitheatre of limestone that rewards a walk if you have the time. Remember the vignette if you join the motorway.

For practical stops, Saint-Aubin-Sauges has the basics, and Bevaix and Estavayer-le-Lac across the water are bigger. Neuchâtel, further east, is a full-sized town with every service. The local wines are worth tasting, especially the light whites made from Chasselas and the Oeil-de-Perdrix rosé, though of course not before riding.

The lake changes colour constantly, from silver in the morning to deep blue at noon and pink at sunset, and the smell of reed, water and vines is lovely on a summer evening. Stand by the shore at Port-Conty and think about the people who stood here thousands of years ago, watching the same light on the water from their houses on stilts.
t.saline royale d arc et senans@47.0,5.8:
Claude-Nicolas Ledoux wanted to build an ideal city, and he started with a salt factory. The Saline Royale at Arc-et-Senans was built between 1775 and 1779 on the orders of Louis XV's administration, to boil brine into salt, and Ledoux designed it as a perfect half circle of buildings around the director's house, with the workers, the boiling halls and the management all arranged in a geometric order meant to express reason, hierarchy and efficiency. It never grew into the full circular city he imagined, but what was built is astonishing, and it was listed by UNESCO in 1982, later joined by the great saltworks at Salins-les-Bains.

The brine came from Salins, around twenty kilometres away, through a pipeline of hollowed wooden trunks, because it was cheaper to move salty water to the forest than to haul firewood to the springs. The nearby Forêt de Chaux, one of the largest oak forests in France, provided the fuel for the boiling pans. Today the site hosts exhibitions, gardens and a museum of Ledoux's architecture, and it is worth an hour or two even for riders who usually skip museums.

The riding around here is classic Franche-Comté. The valley of the Loue to the east is superb, with gorges, limestone cliffs and the town of Ornans, where the painter Gustave Courbet was born. Further up, the roads climb into the Jura plateau through forest and pasture, with smooth tarmac, flowing corners and little traffic outside the summer holidays. Salins-les-Bains, wedged in a narrow valley, is a natural pairing for the saltworks theme.

Arc-et-Senans is a small village with basic services, and Quingey and Mouchard nearby are similar. For a sure range of fuel stations and shops, Dole is about twenty-three kilometres away. Food here means Comté cheese, the region's pride, as well as smoked Morteau sausage and the yellow wine of the Jura, vin jaune, which tastes like nothing else.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the light is clear and the meadows green or golden. Walk into the great courtyard, stand in front of the director's house with its heavy columns, and try to imagine the clatter, steam and salt of a royal factory built like a temple.
t.vorder au@47.2,8.7:
The Au peninsula pokes out into Lake Zurich like a green thumb, and at its tip, Vorder Au, the shallow water hides traces of villages built on piles thousands of years ago. It is one of the Swiss sites in the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, though as with most of them, the archaeology lies under the lake bed and is protected rather than displayed. What you see is a wooded little hill with a castle-like house, vineyards running down to the water, reed beds and a small harbour.

The peninsula belongs to Wädenswil, a lively town on the left bank of the lake known for its research institutes in agriculture, horticulture and wine, and for the views across to the Pfannenstiel hills on the other side. A ferry crosses the lake between Horgen and Meilen just to the north, which is a handy way to switch shores without sitting in traffic around the city.

The lake road along the left bank is a typical Swiss lakeshore run: busy, often slow, lined with villages, traffic lights and speed cameras. It is pleasant for the views but not for spirited riding. Head uphill instead, onto the Zimmerberg and toward the Hirzel or the Höhronen, and the roads open out into rolling farmland with forest patches, good tarmac and lovely views over the lake and to the Alps on clear days. Weekend afternoons bring plenty of cyclists and motorbikes, so a quiet morning is better.

Practical needs are easy. Wädenswil, about three kilometres away, has fuel, shops and plenty of cafés, and Au has a railway station and small services of its own. The area is known for its fruit and wine, and a glass of local white or a slice of cake from a lakeside café is a fine reward after a ride.

The peninsula is lovely to walk on a summer evening, when the light turns gold, swans drift along the shore and the Alps glow at the end of the lake. Spring brings fruit blossom, autumn the colour of the vines. Park, walk to the point and look out over the water, imagining those Neolithic villages perched on their stilts where the sailing boats now drift by.
t.the castrum with the torba tower and the:
The Lombards get a bad press in most history books, which tend to treat them as the barbarians who arrived in Italy in 568 and broke what was left of Roman order. Castelseprio tells a subtler story. On a wooded spur above the Olona valley, north-west of Milan, stand the ruins of a late Roman and Lombard castrum, a fortified town that controlled the road between the plain and the Alpine lakes, and just outside its walls is the little church of Santa Maria foris portas, whose frescoes are among the most mysterious and beautiful paintings of early medieval Europe. Down by the river, the stout stone Torba tower, later part of a Benedictine nunnery, completes the group. Together they form one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of the Lombards in Italy.

The frescoes are the reason art historians argue in loud voices. Nobody agrees exactly when they were painted or by whom, and their soft, almost classical style feels centuries ahead of its supposed time. The Torba monastery is looked after by the Italian heritage trust FAI and opens to visitors, with a lovely courtyard, the tower and faded paintings of nuns on its upper floor.

The riding is a pleasant surprise for an area so close to Milan. The Olona valley is green and wooded, and the roads that climb through the hills toward Varese and the lakes are twisty, narrow and full of character, if sometimes busy with commuter traffic and lined with villages. Head north and you reach Lago di Varese and the Campo dei Fiori, whose climb toward the Sacro Monte gives fine curves and views. Weekday mornings are quieter; weekends bring cyclists and Sunday drivers.

Carnago, a couple of kilometres away, has petrol and shops, and Castiglione Olona nearby is a small Renaissance gem with its own collegiate church and frescoes by Masolino, an easy addition to a culture-heavy day. For food, look for a trattoria serving risotto or polenta with local cheeses and cured meats.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the woods are fresh or golden and the light is gentle. Summer can be hot and humid in the valley. Walk among the ruins in the late afternoon, then step into the little church and stand in front of those faded faces painted by an unknown hand more than a thousand years ago.
t.fort site and civil settlement of trennf:
For a stretch of about fifty kilometres the Romans let the River Main do the work of a wall. Between Miltenberg and Grosskrotzenburg, the frontier of the Upper Germanic Limes followed the river instead of running as a palisade across country, and a chain of forts sat along its west bank. Trennfurt, a village now part of Klingenberg am Main, was one of them: a fort with its civilian settlement, the vicus, where traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived. It is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and as with many Limes sites, most of what survives lies under fields and gardens rather than standing proud.

What stands proud instead is the town. Klingenberg climbs steeply from the river, with half-timbered houses, narrow lanes and terraced vineyards on red sandstone slopes, crowned by the ruins of the Clingenburg castle. The local red wines, especially Spätburgunder, have a fine reputation, and the steep terraces were hard work to build and still are to tend.

Riding here means a mix of river valley and forest hills. The roads along the Main are easy and scenic, following the curves of the river past small towns like Wörth and Erlenbach, with good surfaces but plenty of traffic and towns with low limits. Cross the river or head west and you climb into the Odenwald, or east into the Spessart, both forested ranges with plenty of twisting roads that are popular with motorcyclists on summer weekends. Be wary of noise-related restrictions on some local routes and the attention police pay to popular biker roads.

Klingenberg has a few thousand residents and the basics, and Erlenbach just downstream is a bigger town with more choice for fuel and shopping. Wineries offer tastings and sometimes seasonal taverns, and bakeries and cafés line the small main streets.

Come in early autumn when the vineyards turn colour and the new wine appears in the taverns, or in spring when the hills are fresh. The red sandstone glows in the low sun, and the river slides past with barges heading toward Frankfurt. Stand by the water and imagine Roman soldiers watching the far bank for trouble, with the river as their moat and the forest beyond as the unknown.
t.villages on kuroshima island@33.1,129.5:
For more than two centuries after Christianity was banned in Japan in the early seventeenth century, small communities of believers kept their faith in secret, disguising prayers as Buddhist chants and images of the Virgin Mary as Buddhist figures. Kuroshima, a small island off the coast of Sasebo in Nagasaki Prefecture, was one of the places where these hidden Christians lived and farmed, and when the ban was lifted in the 1870s they emerged openly. Their villages are part of the UNESCO listing of Hidden Christian sites in the Nagasaki region, listed in 2018.

The centre of the island is the Kuroshima church, a beautiful red brick building completed in 1902 under the direction of a French missionary priest, Father Marmand, with the islanders themselves contributing labour and materials. Inside, the arches, the wooden ceiling and the stained glass create a calm, luminous space, and the floor of the sanctuary is laid with tiles of local Arita porcelain. The church is still used by the community, so visitors should be quiet and respectful.

Getting there means taking a ferry from Ainoura port in Sasebo; check timetables and whether you can take the bike, as services are limited. The island is small, with a quiet road winding past farms, stone walls, forest and coastal views, and it is easy to explore at a gentle pace. On the mainland, the coast around Sasebo is beautiful, with the Kujukushima islands, a scatter of more than two hundred small wooded islands, visible from viewpoints above the city.

Fuel, food and lodging are available in Sasebo, a city of about a quarter of a million people, famous for its large naval base and for the Sasebo burger, a local take on the American hamburger introduced by the base. On Kuroshima itself, services are limited, so bring water and something to eat.

Riding in this part of Kyushu means driving on the left, narrow coastal roads with plenty of curves, and generally courteous traffic. Typhoons can bring heavy rain and wind in late summer and autumn, and ferries may be cancelled. Come in spring or autumn, take the early boat, and spend a few quiet hours on an island where faith survived in secret for generations.
t.les graviers@47.0,6.9:
Auvernier is a wine village with its feet in the water. Its old stone houses, cellars and narrow lanes climb from the shore of Lake Neuchâtel into vineyards, and the lake bed just off its little harbour holds the remains of prehistoric villages. Les Graviers is one of the sites in the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, where archaeologists have found the traces of Neolithic and Bronze Age settlements, with wooden piles, tools, pottery and food remains preserved in the lake mud. Many of the finds from the region are displayed at the Laténium, a superb archaeology museum by the lake at Hauterive, on the other side of Neuchâtel.

The village is one of the main wine centres of the canton, with family estates producing Chasselas, Pinot Noir and the local rosé, Oeil-de-Perdrix, the partridge's eye. In autumn the wine festival in Neuchâtel brings parades and celebrations, and the cellars of Auvernier open their doors for tastings.

The riding here starts gently along the lake, then climbs steeply into the Jura. The road north from Neuchâtel over the Vue des Alpes pass toward La Chaux-de-Fonds is a classic, with sweeping bends, good surfaces and, as the name promises, views across the lake to the Alps on clear days. La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle, the watchmaking towns, are part of a UNESCO listing for their urban planning built around the watch industry. To the west, the Val-de-Travers is the birthplace of absinthe, the green fairy, which was banned in Switzerland for nearly a century and is now made legally again in the valley's distilleries.

Auvernier has a few cafés and restaurants, and Peseux and Neuchâtel, close by, have fuel, shops and every service. Swiss roads are well maintained, but speed limits are strictly enforced, cameras are common and fines steep. The motorway vignette is needed if you use the motorways.

Come in late spring, when the vineyards turn green, or in autumn for the harvest. Summer evenings by the lake are lovely, with swimmers and sailors making the most of the light. Sit in a café by the harbour with a glass of local wine, after the riding is done, and look out over water that has drawn people to its shores for thousands of years.
t.immeuble clarte@46.2,6.2:
In 1932, while most of Geneva was building in stone, Le Corbusier put up an apartment block made almost entirely of steel and glass. The Immeuble Clarté, in the Eaux-Vives district on the east side of the city, was revolutionary for its time: a prefabricated steel frame, huge windows that flood the apartments with light, duplex flats with double-height living rooms and a structure that allowed flexible layouts. The name means clarity, and the building lives up to it. Since 2016 it has been part of the UNESCO listing of the architectural work of Le Corbusier, alongside the Villa Savoye, the Unité d'Habitation and other buildings on several continents.

The building is still lived in, so admire it from the street. Look at the rhythm of the windows, the balconies and the stairwells with their glass block floors, designed to bring light down through the building. It was restored in recent years, and its clean, modern look still surprises in a neighbourhood of nineteenth-century houses.

Riding in Geneva is city riding: busy traffic, trams, many traffic lights, cyclists and strict speed limits enforced by cameras. Parking for motorcycles is generally available in designated areas. Once you leave the city, the riding gets much better. The Salève, just across the French border, has a winding road to the top with views over the city and the lake, and the Jura and the Alps are within easy reach, with the roads around the Col de la Faucille and the Chablais offering superb curves.

Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere, though prices in Geneva are high, and fuel is often cheaper just across the border in France. The lakefront, with the Jet d'eau shooting water high into the air, is a short walk from the Clarté building, and the old town, with its cathedral and narrow lanes, is close by.

Local food includes perch fillets from the lake, cheese fondue, longeole, a Geneva pork sausage flavoured with fennel, and chocolate in every form. Spring and early autumn bring mild days and clear light. Summer can be hot, winter grey and cold, with the bise, a cold north-east wind, sweeping across the lake. Nearly a century on, it still looks like the future that Geneva politely declined to build around it.
t.sacro monte di san francesco d orta san:
Lake Orta is the quiet sister of Lake Maggiore, smaller, calmer and more mysterious, and on a wooded hill above its prettiest town stands a holy mountain dedicated to Saint Francis of Assisi. The Sacro Monte di Orta is a path through a park of beech and chestnut trees, linking twenty chapels built from the end of the sixteenth century onward, each containing life-size terracotta statues and frescoes depicting scenes from the life of the saint. It is one of the nine holy mountains of Piedmont and Lombardy listed together by UNESCO in 2003, created during the Counter-Reformation as places of pilgrimage and devotion.

The chapels are a blend of architecture, sculpture and painting, with hundreds of figures arranged in dramatic scenes, and walking from one to the next, with glimpses of the lake through the trees, is a peaceful, gently theatrical experience. Below, Orta San Giulio is a jewel of a town, with a cobbled square by the water, old palaces with frescoed façades and the island of San Giulio just offshore, crowned by a Romanesque basilica and a Benedictine convent.

The riding around Lake Orta is beautiful and varied. The lakeside roads are narrow and twisting, with villages, views and limited traffic outside summer weekends. Climbing above the lake, the road to the Mottarone, between Lake Orta and Lake Maggiore, is a superb ride with tight curves and views over both lakes and the Alps, though part of the summit road is a private toll road. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for cyclists and tourists in the villages.

Orta San Giulio is a small, mostly pedestrian town, and vehicles must park above it. For fuel and full services, head for Omegna, about nine kilometres away at the northern end of the lake, an industrial town known for its kitchenware manufacturers and as the birthplace of the children's writer Gianni Rodari. Local food includes risotto, polenta with cheeses and game, lake fish and the cured meats of the Ossola valleys.

Come in spring, when the gardens bloom and the beech woods turn green, or in autumn, when the chestnuts ripen and the colours glow. Summer weekends can be busy. Walk up to the Sacro Monte in the early morning, before the crowds, and look down through the trees at the island floating on the still water.
t.weier i iii@47.7,8.7:
Just outside Thayngen, almost on the German border, a small wetland hides the remains of Neolithic villages that stood here more than five thousand years ago. The sites known as Weier I to III were built on the edge of a former lake or moor, now mostly filled in, and excavations revealed well-preserved timber houses, tools, pottery and food remains that give a detailed picture of early farming communities. They form part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, though as with most such sites, there is little to see above ground today beyond the landscape itself.

Thayngen has an even older claim to fame. In the Kesslerloch cave nearby, excavations in the nineteenth century uncovered Ice Age artefacts from the Magdalenian period, including a famous carving on reindeer antler of a grazing reindeer, one of the finest pieces of Palaeolithic art found in Switzerland. The cave is right next to the railway line and the road, an unlikely setting for such treasures.

The canton of Schaffhausen is a pocket of Switzerland north of the Rhine, almost surrounded by Germany, and the border wanders through fields and forests in seemingly random ways. Büsingen, nearby, is a German village entirely surrounded by Swiss territory. The riding is pleasant and varied, with rolling farmland, forests and vineyards, and the volcanic hills of the Hegau rising across the border to the north, crowned by castle ruins such as Hohentwiel. Roads are generally excellent, traffic moderate, but speed limits are strictly enforced on both sides of the border.

Thayngen has a few thousand inhabitants and basic services, and Gottmadingen, just across the border, about five kilometres away, has more choice. Schaffhausen, the cantonal capital, has a beautiful old town with painted houses and the round fortress of the Munot, and the Rhine Falls, the largest waterfall in central Europe, are just a short ride away.

Local food includes the wines of the Klettgau, fish from the Rhine and hearty Swiss and Swabian dishes. Come in spring or early autumn, when the weather is mild and the light clear. Ride through the gentle hills, cross the border a few times without noticing, and stop at the Rhine Falls to feel the spray before heading on.
t.baden baden@48.8,8.2:
Baden-Baden is so nice they named it twice, as the old joke goes, though the doubling actually comes from distinguishing it from other places called Baden. Romans soaked in its hot springs, and the remains of their baths lie under the old town, but the town's golden age came in the nineteenth century, when European royalty, aristocrats, writers and gamblers flocked here to take the waters, stroll the avenues and lose fortunes at the casino. Dostoevsky, Turgenev and Brahms all spent time here. Baden-Baden is one of the eleven Great Spa Towns of Europe, listed together by UNESCO in 2021.

The town is elegant and green, with the Lichtentaler Allee, a long park along the river Oos lined with old trees, villas and museums, and the Kurhaus with its grand casino, often called one of the most beautiful in the world. The Friedrichsbad, a nineteenth-century bathhouse, offers a Roman-Irish bathing ritual, and the modern Caracalla spa has pools fed by thermal water. The old town climbs the hillside behind, with narrow lanes and the collegiate church.

For riders, Baden-Baden is the northern starting point of the Black Forest High Road, the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse, which runs south along the ridge of the northern Black Forest toward Freudenstadt, passing the Mummelsee, a small dark lake below the Hornisgrinde, the highest peak in the northern Black Forest. The road has long sweeping bends, good surfaces and great views over the Rhine plain to the Vosges, and it is very popular with motorcyclists, so expect police checks, speed limits and noise controls, especially on weekends.

Baden-Baden has fuel, food and every service, though prices reflect the town's upmarket image. Cafés serve Black Forest cake, cherry gateau with cream and kirsch, and the vineyards of the Ortenau and the Baden wine region on the slopes nearby produce excellent Pinot Noir and Riesling.

May and October are the gentle months, with fresh or golden forests and fewer visitors in town. Summer brings festivals and horse racing at nearby Iffezheim, winter can bring snow to the high road. Ride the high road in the early morning, when the mist lies in the valleys below, then come back down for a soak and a slice of cake in the afternoon.
t.watchtowers wp 9 14 to 9 32 including th:
For about eighty kilometres through northern Württemberg, the Roman frontier runs in a nearly perfectly straight line, ignoring hills, valleys and rivers as if someone had drawn it with a ruler on a map. Surveyors still argue about how the Romans managed it. The stretch with watchtowers 9/14 to 9/32, near Öhringen in the Hohenlohe region, lies along this remarkable line, and Öhringen itself grew from Roman forts, two of them, which guarded the frontier here. The line is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and the Limes trail follows it through fields and forests.

Öhringen is a handsome small town with a collegiate church and a palace of the princes of Hohenlohe, whose family dominated the region for centuries. The Hohenlohe is a land of castles and palaces, with Neuenstein, Langenburg and Waldenburg all within easy reach, perched on hills or above river valleys.

The riding in the Hohenlohe is superb. The Kocher and Jagst valleys, cutting deep into the plateau, have twisting roads along the rivers, past mills, villages and castles, while the plateau above offers open, gently rolling roads through farmland and forests. Surfaces are generally excellent, traffic moderate, and the region is popular with motorcyclists on weekends. The Waldenburg hills, east of Öhringen, give fine views over the plain toward Heilbronn.

Öhringen, about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Pfedelbach, nearby, is a small wine town. The Hohenlohe is known for its food: the Schwäbisch-Hällisches pig, a local breed raised in the region, Maultaschen, Swabian filled pasta, and Spätzle with cheese or gravy. The vineyards on the southern slopes produce good red and white wines.

Come in late spring, when the fields are bright with rapeseed, or in autumn, when the vineyards turn and the forests glow. Find a stretch of the Limes on the plateau, look along the line as it runs straight to the horizon, and marvel at the stubborn precision of Roman surveyors.
t.fort site and civil settlement of schire:
On the southern edge of Schwäbisch Gmünd, near the Schirenhof farm, the outline of a Roman fort and the foundations of its bath house lie in the grass, with walls and hypocaust heating systems laid out for visitors to see. The fort guarded the point where the Upper Germanic Limes met the Raetian Limes, the two great frontier lines of Roman Germany, and a civilian settlement grew up around it. The site is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and it is one of the more rewarding Limes stops in Baden-Württemberg, with visible remains and a lovely setting above the town.

Schwäbisch Gmünd is one of the oldest Staufer towns, with a cathedral-like church, the Heilig-Kreuz-Münster, among the earliest late Gothic hall churches in southern Germany, and a long tradition of gold and silversmithing that continues in workshops and a design school. The old town has half-timbered houses, fountains and a lively market square.

To the north rise the three Kaiserberge, the emperor mountains: Hohenstaufen, Hohenrechberg and Stuifen, conical hills on the edge of the Swabian Jura. The Hohenstaufen was the seat of the Staufer dynasty, which produced emperors such as Frederick Barbarossa, and the ruins on top give wide views over the countryside. The roads around these hills are a rider's delight, winding up and down through forests and farmland, with tight bends, good surfaces and plenty of other motorcyclists on sunny weekends.

The Rems valley, running west from Gmünd toward Stuttgart, has easier roads through vineyards and orchards, and the Swabian Jura, to the south, offers steep climbs, limestone cliffs and the high plateau of the Alb. Speed checks and noise controls are common on popular biker roads.

Schwäbisch Gmünd, about two kilometres away, has fuel, food and every service. Swabian food is hearty and delicious: Maultaschen, Spätzle, Linsen mit Spätzle, lentils with noodles and sausages, and Zwiebelrostbraten, roast beef with crispy onions. The Kaiserberge are greenest in May and at their most golden in October. Climb the Hohenstaufen for the view, then come back down and walk among the foundations of the Roman bath house, where soldiers once relaxed after a day on the frontier.
t.fort site and civil settlement of milten:
Miltenberg is one of those German towns that seem almost too pretty to be real, with half-timbered houses leaning over the cobbled streets, a market square sloping down toward the river, a castle on the hill above and the Main flowing slowly past. The Romans were here first. Two forts guarded this point on the frontier, one near the old town and another to the east, where the Limes left the river and ran overland through the Odenwald, and the sites, with their civilian settlements, are part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. A museum in the town displays finds from the forts.

The Mildenburg, the castle above the town, now houses a museum of modern art and icons, and the views over the Main valley and the red sandstone roofs of Miltenberg are superb. The market square, known locally as the Schnatterloch, is one of the most photographed in Germany, surrounded by timber-framed houses and a fountain. Across the river, Kleinheubach has a baroque palace in a large park, and Großheubach climbs up to the Engelberg, a Franciscan monastery reached by a long flight of steps.

The riding around Miltenberg is varied and excellent. The Main valley roads follow the river through vineyards and small towns, with gentle curves and moderate traffic. South and west, the roads climb into the Odenwald, a forested upland with twisting roads, small villages and the baroque abbey of Amorbach, famous for its organ, one of the largest baroque organs in the world. East, the Spessart offers more forest roads. Weekends bring many motorcyclists, and police checks are common.

Großheubach, about two kilometres away, and Miltenberg have fuel, shops and restaurants. Local food includes Franconian dishes such as roast pork with dumplings, Schäufele, and the red wines of the Churfranken region, especially Spätburgunder from the slopes along the Main. Cafés and wine taverns line the old town streets.

Come in spring, when the orchards bloom, or in autumn, when the vineyards turn and the wine festivals begin. Summer weekends can be crowded. Walk up to the castle in the late afternoon for the view down over the red roofs to the river, then come back to the square for a glass of Franconian red once the bike is parked for the night.
t.watchtowers wp 8 11 to 8 28 including fo:
The Romans did not much care for the shape of the land when they drew this frontier. Around Osterburken the Upper Germanic Limes stops following valleys and ridges and simply runs in long, stubborn straight lines across the Bauland, the rolling limestone country between the Odenwald and the Jagst. The watchtower sites numbered in this stretch were once timber, then stone, posts spaced so that each could see its neighbours, strung along a palisade and ditch that marked where the province ended and the unconquered north began.

Osterburken itself is the reason to stop. It held a cohort fort with an annexe bolted on later, and the town grew a Roman museum around the excavated remains. The prize there is the collection of altars set up by beneficiarii, the soldiers posted to police roads and collect tolls, who thanked Jupiter in stone at the end of their tours. There is also a great Mithras relief found in the area, a carved bull-slaying scene that says a lot about what frontier soldiers believed in when the winters came. You do not need to be a history buff to enjoy it; it is the kind of museum you finish in an hour with your helmet under your arm.

The riding around here is gentle and honest. Roads run between wheat, rapeseed and dark blocks of beech forest, rising and falling over low ridges with long sightlines and very little traffic outside the commuter hours. The Kirnau stream cuts a small, green valley through the town, and the lanes toward Adelsheim and Seckach have that easy rhythm where you sit in third gear and let the bike breathe. In early summer the fields smell of hay and the light at evening goes golden across the plateau. In autumn, morning fog lies in the hollows and the tarmac stays damp under the trees well into the day, so be gentle on the first corners.

Osterburken is a proper small town with fuel, bakeries and a station, so it is a sensible place to refill both bike and rider before heading off along the frontier line. Adelsheim, a few kilometres away, has a pleasant old centre if you want a second coffee. The Limes itself is mostly invisible now, a low bank in the woods or a reconstructed tower here and there, so treat the ride as a game of spotting traces rather than expecting walls. That is half the fun: once you know the line was ruler-straight, you start to see it in field boundaries and forest tracks everywhere.
Nozaki is a long, steep island in the Goto archipelago, off the western coast of Kyushu, and almost nobody lives there now. In the nineteenth century, Christians who had kept their faith secretly for over two hundred years of persecution under the Tokugawa shogunate settled on the island, farming its steep slopes alongside the community that served a Shinto shrine. When the ban on Christianity was lifted in 1873, they built a church, and the brick church of Nokubi, completed in 1908, still stands on a hill above the sea. The island and its abandoned villages are a piece of the World Heritage property for Hidden Christian sites in the Nagasaki region.

The island was gradually abandoned in the twentieth century, as people moved to the cities, and the last inhabitants left in the early 2000s. Now it is home to wild deer, in large numbers, and to the ruins of houses, terraces and stone walls slowly being reclaimed by the forest. A small visitor facility in a former school offers basic accommodation for those who want to stay overnight, and walking trails lead to the church and around the island.

Riding here, honestly, is not an option. Nozaki has no roads for private vehicles, and it is reached by small ferry from Ojika island, which in turn is connected by ferry to Sasebo and Fukuoka on Kyushu. You can take your bike to Ojika on the larger ferry and explore its quiet roads, which wind around volcanic hills and along the coast with very little traffic, and then leave it at the port for the day trip to Nozaki. Check the ferry schedules carefully, as they are infrequent and weather-dependent.

Ojika has a few shops and inns, and fuel should be found there, but it is wise to fill up before boarding on Kyushu. Food on the islands is simple and fresh, with fish, seaweed and sweet potatoes. On Nozaki, bring water, food and everything else you need, as there are no shops. Walk up to the church, sit on the steps and look across the sea toward the other islands, and think of the families who lived here, holding on to their faith in secret, generation after generation.
t.wangen hinterhorn@47.7,8.9:
When the water of the Untersee, the western arm of Lake Constance, was unusually low in the winter of 1853 to 1854, people around the Swiss and German shores noticed wooden posts sticking out of the mud. They were the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, villages built on the lakeshore thousands of years ago, and the find sparked a wave of research and a craze for lake-dwelling romance across Europe. Wangen, on the German shore of the Untersee, was one of the first sites studied, and Wangen-Hinterhorn belongs to the World Heritage inscription for prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, though there is nothing to see above the water.

Wangen is a village on the Höri peninsula, a gentle land of orchards, vegetable gardens and reeds between the Untersee and the Zeller See. In the early twentieth century, artists and writers found refuge here: Hermann Hesse lived in Gaienhofen, and the painter Otto Dix spent his later years in Hemmenhofen, where his house is now a museum. Across the water lies the Swiss shore, with Steckborn and its castle, and to the east, the island of Reichenau, with its medieval monastery churches, is also on the UNESCO list.

The riding is calm and lovely. The roads around the Höri and along the Untersee are narrow and gentle, with views of the lake and the hills, and traffic is light except in summer. Stein am Rhein, a short ride west, is a medieval town with painted facades, and the road along the Rhine toward Schaffhausen and its falls is beautiful. The surface is good, and the main hazards are cyclists, tractors and the occasional tourist stopping suddenly for a view. Weather is mild, with fog on the lake in autumn.

For fuel, Radolfzell, about nine kilometres away, and Steckborn on the Swiss side are good options, though Swiss prices are higher. Food around the lake includes fish, especially whitefish called Felchen, local vegetables from the Höri and wines from the shore. A café terrace by the water is a good place to rest. Look out over the lake and imagine the villages of wooden huts on stilts that once stood in the shallows; the water has kept them for five thousand years.
t.egolzwil 3@47.2,8.0:
Archaeologists named a whole Neolithic culture after Egolzwil, a small village in the canton of Lucerne, because the settlements found in the Wauwiler Moos, a former lake turned into peat bog, revealed a way of life older than anything else known in the region at the time. Egolzwil 3, one of these sites, was a village of farmers who lived on the shore of a small lake over six thousand years ago, and it counts as one component of UNESCO's inscription of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. The lake was drained in the nineteenth century to create farmland, and the remains were preserved in the wet peat.

Today the Wauwiler Moos is a flat expanse of fields and meadows, with drainage ditches, a few patches of reeds and wetland, and the small villages of Egolzwil, Wauwil and Schötz around its edge. Bird life is rich, especially in spring and autumn. The rolling hills of the Lucerne countryside rise around the plain, with farms, orchards and forests. Sursee, a pretty small town with a fine town hall, lies to the east, and Lake Sempach, a little further on, was the scene of the battle in 1386 in which the Swiss confederates defeated the Habsburgs.

The riding here is relaxed. The roads across the plain are flat and straight, but the hills around offer curves, and to the west, the Napf region has some of the twistiest small roads in Switzerland, climbing through steep valleys and over ridges with views of the Alps on clear days. The surface is excellent, as everywhere in Switzerland, and traffic is light on minor roads. Speed limits are strictly enforced, with heavy fines, so stay alert. Weather can be foggy in autumn and winter.

Sursee, about seven kilometres away, has a filling station and somewhere to eat, and Nebikon, closer by, also has services. Swiss food here means rösti, sausages, cheese and, in the Lucerne region, the Luzerner Chügelipastete, a puff pastry filled with veal and mushrooms. A stop at a farmhouse café for cake and coffee is a pleasant break. There is nothing to see of the Neolithic village itself, but standing on the edge of the old lake, you can imagine the smoke rising from the huts and the dugout canoes on the water.
t.sumpf@47.2,8.5:
Zug-Sumpf was a Bronze Age village on the northern shore of Lake Zug, near the mouth of the river Lorze between Cham and Steinhausen, and the waterlogged ground preserved wooden floors, posts and objects for over three thousand years. Excavations in the twentieth century recovered pottery, bronze tools and even remains of food, and the site sits on the World Heritage list as part of the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. Some of the finds are displayed in the museum of prehistory in Zug. Today the site lies under modern buildings and meadows, and only the name, which means swamp, recalls its watery origin.

The town of Zug, a few kilometres away, is a curious mix of tradition and money. It has a medieval old town with a clock tower, narrow streets and lakeside promenades, where the sunsets over the lake are famous. It is also one of the lowest-tax cantons in Switzerland, which has made it home to many international companies and a lot of wealth. The local speciality is the Zuger Kirschtorte, a cherry brandy cake, and the region is known for its cherry orchards, which blossom in spring.

The riding is pleasant. The roads along Lake Zug are scenic, with views of the water and the mountains, especially the Rigi to the south. The road climbing from Zug to the Zugerberg offers views over the lake, and further east, the Ägerisee and the passes toward Sattel and Einsiedeln have curves and fine scenery. Traffic around Zug can be heavy, especially in rush hour, and speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras everywhere. The surface is excellent. Weather is variable, with fog on the lake in autumn and winter.

Cham and Steinhausen have fuel, shops and cafés, and Zug has everything. Food here includes lake fish, such as Zuger Röteli, a local char, and the famous cherry cake, along with all the Swiss classics. A coffee by the lake in Zug at sunset is a fine way to end a ride. As for the Bronze Age village, it lives on in the museum cases, a reminder that people have enjoyed this lakeshore for a very long time, even before the tax advantages.
t.baie de chatillon@45.8,5.9:
At the northern tip of the Lac du Bourget, the largest natural lake entirely in France, the shore curves into a shallow bay below the village of Châtillon and its castle. In the shallows, divers and archaeologists have found the remains of prehistoric lake villages, and the Baie de Châtillon is one of the French sites included in the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. The castle, perched on a rocky hill above the bay, was the seat of local lords in the Middle Ages and has a commanding view over the lake.

The lake is long and deep, framed by mountains: the Mont du Chat and the Dent du Chat to the west, the Bauges massif to the east. On the western shore stands the Abbaye d'Hautecombe, the burial place of the princes of the House of Savoy, its neo-Gothic church reflected in the water. Aix-les-Bains, at the southern end, is an old spa town with grand hotels from the Belle Époque, and the lake inspired the poet Lamartine, whose poem Le Lac, a meditation on love and time, was written here. The Canal de Savières links the lake to the Rhône at Chanaz, a pretty village with boats.

The riding is superb. The road along the eastern shore is pleasant, and the roads climbing into the mountains around the lake are excellent. The Col du Chat crosses the ridge west of the lake with curves and views, and further north, the Grand Colombier, one of the toughest climbs in the Tour de France, rises to over fifteen hundred metres, with steep hairpins and views of Mont Blanc on clear days. The surface is generally good, but there are cyclists in large numbers on the climbs. Summer is warm, and the high roads close in winter.

Châtillon and Chindrieux are small villages; for fuel and supplies, head to Albens, Rumilly or Aix-les-Bains. Savoyard food is mountain fare: tartiflette, fondue, diots, local sausages, cooked in white wine, and lake fish such as lavaret. The wines of Savoie, including the crisp whites from Chignin and Jongieux, are refreshing. Stop by the bay, look across the lake toward the mountains, and think of the prehistoric villagers who chose this spot: they had good taste in views.
t.vingelz hafen@47.1,7.2:
Biel and Bienne are the same city, one name in German and one in French, and street signs, conversations and even jokes switch between the two languages without anyone noticing. At its western edge, the lakeside district of Vingelz, with its small harbour, has given archaeologists remains of prehistoric pile dwellings in the shallow water of Lake Biel, and the site is one piece of the World Heritage property for pile dwellings around the Alps. The lake, long and narrow, lies at the foot of the Jura mountains, and its shores have been inhabited for thousands of years.

Biel is the capital of Swiss watchmaking, home to Omega, Swatch and the movement factories that supply some of the most famous names in the business, and a museum tells the story. The old town, on a hill above the modern centre, has fountains, arcades and medieval houses. A funicular climbs to Magglingen, or Macolin, on the slopes of the Jura, with views over the lake and the Alps, and the Taubenloch gorge offers a walk through a narrow canyon. In the lake, St Peter's Island, connected to the shore by a narrow strip of land, was where Jean-Jacques Rousseau spent a happy few weeks in 1765.

The riding is excellent. The road along the northern shore of the lake runs between vineyards and the water, through the wine villages of Twann and Ligerz, with tunnels and views, though it can be busy. Above, the roads climb into the Jura, with curves, forests and pastures, toward the Chasseral, the highest summit in the region, reached by a road with views over the Alps on clear days. The surface is excellent, and traffic is light on minor roads. Speed limits are strict, and the police are vigilant. Weather is variable, with fog in autumn and winter, and snow on the high roads.

Nidau and Biel have fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. Food here mixes Swiss German and French traditions, with lake fish, especially perch and whitefish, wines from the northern shore, mostly Chasselas, and treats like the Treberwurst, a sausage cooked in grape pomace, a winter speciality of the wine villages. A meal by the lake in Ligerz or Twann is lovely. Park at Vingelz, look out over the water, and imagine the prehistoric villages in the shallows, their smoke rising against the green slopes of the Jura.
t.watchtowers wp 9 70 to 9 99a including t:
Mainhardt sits on a ridge in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, and the Roman frontier ran right through it, on its way south in one of the longest straight lines ever drawn across European landscape. Here, the Upper Germanic Limes runs for some eighty kilometres from Walldürn to near Welzheim almost perfectly straight, ignoring hills and valleys, as if surveyors had laid a ruler on the map. The watchtowers numbered in this section stood along that line in the forest, and Mainhardt had a fort, whose site is marked in the village, with a small museum.

The Swabian-Franconian Forest is a nature park of wooded hills, deep valleys and small villages, between Stuttgart, Heilbronn and Schwäbisch Hall. Its forests of beech, spruce and fir are cut by streams, and there are lakes, mills and lookout towers. The Löwenstein hills rise to the west. Schwäbisch Hall, a short ride north-east, is a beautiful medieval town on the Kocher, with half-timbered houses and a grand church above a monumental flight of steps, and it was once famous for its salt and for the Heller, a coin that gave its name to small change.

The riding is excellent. The B14, the main road between Stuttgart and Schwäbisch Hall, passes through Mainhardt, but the minor roads through the forest are the real joy, winding through valleys and over ridges, with curves, forests and views. Road quality is fair to good, but there are tractors, cyclists and wildlife. Some roads in the region have weekend restrictions or speed limits for motorcycles, due to noise complaints, so watch the signs. Weather can be cool and damp, with fog in autumn and snow in winter.

Mainhardt has a filling station and somewhere to eat. Swabian food is hearty: Maultaschen, large pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, Spätzle, soft egg noodles, and roast meat with gravy. The forest inns serve local trout and game. Look for the reconstructed watchtower and the information boards along the Limes trail, and notice how the line runs straight through the forest; once you know it, you see the Roman obsession with order in every clearing.
t.watchtowers wp 9 33 to 9 35@49.2,9.5:
Öhringen had not one but two Roman forts, known today as the Bürgkastell and the Rendelkastell, both on the Upper Germanic Limes, which ran past the town on its way south. The watchtowers numbered here were part of that frontier, and the town grew partly on the remains of the Roman settlement that clustered around the forts. Little is visible above ground, but finds are displayed in the local museum, and the line of the Limes can be followed on foot or by bike through the surrounding countryside.

Öhringen is the main town of the Hohenlohe region, a rolling plateau of fields, orchards and woods, with river valleys cut into it, such as the Kocher and the Jagst. The princes of Hohenlohe ruled here for centuries, and their palace in Öhringen, a large Renaissance building, now houses the town hall. Neuenstein, a few kilometres east, has a fairy-tale moated castle, and the collegiate church of Öhringen contains the tombs of the Hohenlohe family. The region is known for its pigs, the Schwäbisch-Hällisches Landschwein, a traditional breed, and for good food in general.

The riding is pleasant. The plateau roads are open and gently rolling, with long views, and the valleys of the Kocher and Jagst offer more curves, with castles, villages and vineyards. Grip is usually reliable, and traffic is light outside the towns. Watch for tractors and cyclists, and for mud on the roads at harvest time. The region can be foggy in autumn and winter, and summer brings thunderstorms. Some valley roads have speed limits for motorcycles at weekends.

Öhringen has fuel, beds and plenty of places to eat. Hohenlohe food is substantial: roast pork, sausages, dumplings, and local wines from the slopes along the valleys. The town has a pleasant old centre with cafés. Combine a visit to the Limes sites with a ride through the Hohenlohe valleys; the landscape is gentle and unhurried, and the contrast between the Roman frontier and the castles of the princes gives the day a sense of history layered upon history.
t.fort site and civil settlement of murrha:
A Roman cohort fort once stood where Murrhardt's streets now run, on the Upper Germanic Limes as it cut south through the forest toward Welzheim, and a civilian settlement of traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families grew up around it. Some remains have been found under the town, and the local museum tells the story. The Romans left, but the site remained attractive, and in the early Middle Ages a monastery was founded here, associated with Saint Walterich, a hermit whose small chapel, the Walterichskapelle, is a jewel of late Romanesque architecture.

Murrhardt is a town of about fourteen thousand in the valley of the Murr, in the heart of the Swabian-Franconian Forest nature park. The forest surrounds it on all sides, with deep, narrow valleys, streams, mills and lakes such as the Ebnisee, a popular spot for swimming and walking in summer. The town has a pleasant old centre with half-timbered houses and the monastery church. Kaisersbach and Sulzbach an der Murr are small neighbours, and the city of Backnang is a short ride downstream.

The riding is good and relaxed. The Murr valley road is gentle and scenic, and the roads climbing out of the valley into the forest have curves, gradients and views over the wooded hills. Toward Welzheim and the Ebnisee, the roads are particularly enjoyable, but some have weekend restrictions or speed limits for motorcycles due to noise complaints, so watch the signs. The surface is generally good, but there are tractors, cyclists and wildlife, especially at dawn and dusk. Weather in the forest is cool and damp, with fog in autumn and snow in winter.

Murrhardt has fuel, shops, restaurants and a railway station. Swabian food includes Maultaschen, Spätzle and Zwiebelrostbraten, roast beef with crispy onions, and the forest inns serve trout and game. Local cider, Most, is a traditional drink, though better saved for later. Visit the Walterichskapelle, a small building of great beauty, and then ride into the forest. Between the Roman fort, the medieval monastery and the deep green woods, Murrhardt is a place where history and nature have been comfortable neighbours for a long time.
t.fortlet lehnenwiesen@49.4,9.5:
Götz von Berlichingen, the knight with the iron hand, was born in Jagsthausen around 1480, and he is remembered for a rude phrase he supposedly shouted at an enemy, made famous by Goethe in his play about the knight. Jagsthausen's castle, where Götz grew up, hosts an open-air theatre festival every summer, and the iron hand, a prosthesis he wore after losing his right hand in battle, is displayed there. A few kilometres away, in the fields near Widdern, the fortlet of Lehnenwiesen was a small Roman post on the Upper Germanic Limes, part of the chain of forts and watchtowers that ran through this landscape.

The area lies in the valley of the Jagst, a river that meanders through a deep, green valley between the plateaus of Hohenlohe and the Bauland. The valley is lined with villages, castles and mills, and its slopes are covered with woods, meadows and, in places, vineyards. Jagsthausen also had a Roman fort, and its remains have been excavated, with a bath house. Widdern is a small town with a medieval centre, and Möckmühl, downstream, has a castle above the river.

The riding in the Jagst valley is a pleasure. The valley road follows the river with gentle curves, past villages and castles, and the roads climbing out onto the plateaus offer more curves and views. Surfaces are mostly sound, and traffic is light. Watch for cyclists, as the Jagst valley cycle route is popular, and for tractors. Some roads have weekend restrictions for motorcycles. Weather is mild, with fog in the valley in autumn and occasional snow in winter.

The villages around the fortlet are small; for fuel, head to Adelsheim, Möckmühl or Jagsthausen. The cooking here is Swabian and Franconian, with roast meats, dumplings and local wine. Jagsthausen's castle has a hotel and restaurant. The fortlet itself is a modest site in a field, with information boards, but the view over the valley is pleasant. Combine it with a visit to Jagsthausen to see Götz's iron hand; the knight lived a long and turbulent life, and his story is a fine counterpoint to the quiet Roman post in the fields.
t.church and dominican convent of santa ma:
Most people who come to Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan are here for one painting, and they are right to be. On the wall of the old refectory of the Dominican convent, Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper in the 1490s for Duke Ludovico Sforza, and despite his experimental technique, which began to fail almost at once, despite centuries of damage and despite a bomb that destroyed much of the building in 1943, the painting survives. The wall was protected with sandbags, and the long restoration completed in 1999 revealed colours and faces that had been hidden for centuries.

Visits are tightly controlled, in small groups for a short time, and tickets often sell out weeks in advance, so book ahead. If you cannot get in, the church itself is worth a visit. Its tribune, the domed east end, is attributed to Donato Bramante, one of the great architects of the Renaissance, and its graceful proportions contrast with the Gothic brick nave. The cloisters are peaceful. The whole complex, church, convent and painting, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The neighbourhood around Corso Magenta is elegant and quiet, with old palazzi and courtyards. A short walk away is the Sforza Castle, the Duomo and the shopping streets of the centre, and to the south lie the Navigli, the old canals, now lined with bars and restaurants.

Riding in Milan is not a relaxing experience. Traffic is heavy, the streets are often narrow and cobbled, and tram tracks can catch a front wheel, especially in the wet; cross them at an angle and with care. Scooters weave everywhere. The centre is covered by Area C, a congestion zone with restrictions and charges for some vehicles, and the rules for motorcycles have changed over the years, so check before you ride in. Parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, with dedicated bays in many streets.

For fuel, there are stations throughout the city, and food is everywhere: try a risotto alla milanese, golden with saffron, or a cotoletta. To escape the city, the lakes are an hour to the north, Como and Maggiore, with some superb riding along their shores and up into the mountains.
t.burgaschisee ost@47.2,7.7:
Burgäschisee is a small, quiet lake on the border between the cantons of Bern and Solothurn, surrounded by reeds, woods and farmland. It would be easy to ride past without noticing, but it holds a secret: along its shores, archaeologists have found the remains of Neolithic villages built on piles, dating back more than five thousand years. The eastern shore site, Burgäschisee Ost, is one of the components of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps World Heritage site, listed by UNESCO in 2011. There is nothing much to see on the surface, as the remains lie underwater or in the soft ground, but the peaceful setting makes it easy to imagine the wooden houses, canoes and fishing nets of those early farmers.

The lake is a nature reserve, home to birds, frogs and dragonflies, and in summer there is a small swimming area where locals come to cool off. A path runs around the shore, a pleasant walk of about an hour, through reeds and woods.

The area around is the Oberaargau, a gentle region of rolling hills, farms and villages, with the Jura mountains rising to the north and, on clear days, the Bernese Alps visible to the south. To the east lies the Emmental, famous for its cheese with holes, its wooden farmhouses with huge roofs and its winding roads through green hills. Herzogenbuchsee, the nearest town, is a small, friendly place with shops and cafés.

The riding here is relaxed and pleasant, on quiet roads with gentle bends, through farmland and forest. The roads into the Emmental are more interesting, with more curves, climbs and views. Swiss roads are generally in excellent condition, but speed limits are strict and enforced with cameras and heavy fines, so keep an eye on your speed. A vignette is required for motorways.

Herzogenbuchsee has fuel, shops and restaurants; the villages around have small shops and inns. Try a plate of rösti, crispy potatoes, or a slice of Emmental cheese with bread. The weather is variable, with rain likely at any time of year; summers are warm, winters cold, with occasional snow. Spring and autumn are lovely, with blossom in the orchards or golden leaves in the forests. Bring a swimsuit in summer and take a dip in the lake.
t.riedmatt@47.2,8.5:
Zug has a reputation as one of the wealthiest places in Switzerland, a small canton of low taxes, glass office blocks and companies registered by the hundred. But beneath the surface, quite literally, lies a much older story. Along the shores of Lake Zug, archaeologists have found the remains of Neolithic and Bronze Age villages built on piles in the shallow water and marshy ground, and Riedmatt, near the border between Steinhausen, Cham and Zug, is one of the sites included in the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps World Heritage listing. As with most such sites, there is nothing visible on the surface; the remains are preserved in the waterlogged ground.

The old town of Zug, on the lakeshore, is charming, with narrow lanes, painted houses and the Zytturm, a clock tower with a colourful tiled roof. The lakefront promenade is famous for its sunsets, when the sky turns orange over the water and the mountains. The town is also known for its Kirschtorte, a cake soaked in cherry brandy, and for the cherry orchards on the surrounding hills.

Above the town rises the Zugerberg, reached by a funicular or a winding road, with views over the lake to the Rigi and Pilatus. To the east lies the Ägerisee, a smaller lake in a quiet valley, and beyond it the road climbs towards the Raten pass and the Sattel, with good bends and views of the mountains.

The riding around Zug is mixed. The roads near the towns are busy, with traffic, roundabouts and speed cameras. Away from the towns, the roads into the hills are quieter and more interesting, with curves, climbs and views. To the north, the Albis pass, near Zurich, is a popular road with riders. Swiss speed limits are strict and fines are heavy, so stay alert.

Cham, Zug and Steinhausen all have fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a slice of Kirschtorte with coffee, or a plate of lake fish, such as perch or whitefish. The weather can change quickly, with rain likely at any time of year, and foehn winds can bring sudden warmth and clear skies. Spring, with the cherry blossom, and autumn are the best seasons. Take a walk along the lakeshore at sunset.
t.lobsigensee@47.0,7.3:
Lobsigensee is a tiny lake, barely more than a pond, hidden among fields and woods on a low hill above Aarberg in the Bernese Seeland. It is a nature reserve, ringed with reeds and alder trees, and it is home to frogs, newts, dragonflies and birds. It also hides one of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps World Heritage sites: the remains of Neolithic settlements along its shore. There is nothing visible on the surface, but the quiet, green setting gives a sense of what the landscape might have looked like thousands of years ago.

The Seeland, the land of lakes, lies between the lakes of Biel, Neuchâtel and Murten, and for centuries it was a marshy, flood-prone area. In the nineteenth century, the Jura Water Correction, a huge engineering project, redirected the Aare river into Lake Biel and lowered the level of the lakes, draining the marshes and creating fertile farmland. Today the Seeland is known as the vegetable garden of Switzerland, with fields of carrots, lettuce, onions and potatoes stretching to the horizon. The lowering of the lakes also exposed many of the pile dwelling sites, which is why so many have been found in this region.

Aarberg, just below the lake, is a charming small town built on a rocky island in the old course of the Aare. Its long, cobbled market square is lined with old houses and inns, and a covered wooden bridge crosses the river. The town is also home to one of Switzerland's two sugar factories, processing sugar beet from the surrounding fields, and in autumn the smell of cooking beet hangs in the air.

The riding in the Seeland is flat and easy, with straight roads across the fields and gentle bends through villages. It is pleasant rather than exciting. To the north, the Jura mountains offer much better riding, with winding roads, passes and views over the lakes and the Alps. The roads to Chasseral, the highest point in the Bernese Jura, are particularly good.

Aarberg has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try local vegetables, fresh from the fields, or fish from the lakes. Lowland fog is the local speciality in autumn and winter, often lingering until noon while the hills above sit in sunshine. Spring and summer are the best seasons for riding.
t.l abbaye 2@46.9,6.8:
The north shore of Lake Neuchâtel is a long, gentle slope of vineyards running down to the water, with villages of honey-coloured stone and the Jura rising behind. At Bevaix, on the shore below the village, archaeologists have found traces of prehistoric pile dwellings at a site known as L'Abbaye, named after a medieval priory that once stood nearby. It is one of the Swiss components of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps World Heritage site. Nothing is visible on the surface; the remains lie underwater or in the lake sediments. But the lakeshore is beautiful, and there is a pleasant path along the water.

The region around Neuchâtel has a special place in European archaeology. At La Tène, at the northern tip of the lake, nineteenth-century excavations uncovered a huge collection of Iron Age weapons and objects, and the name La Tène was given to an entire Celtic culture. The Laténium, a museum at Hauterive near Neuchâtel, displays many of these finds, along with objects from the pile dwellings, and it is one of the best archaeological museums in Switzerland.

The vineyards around Bevaix, Cortaillod and Boudry produce some of the best wines of western Switzerland: Chasselas, Pinot Noir and the local rosé, Œil-de-Perdrix, the partridge's eye. Boudry also has a museum of the vine and wine in its castle. A tasting in a village cellar is a fine way to end a ride.

The riding here is varied and excellent. The lakeshore road is busy, but the roads that climb into the Jura are a pleasure: from Boudry, a road follows the gorges of the Areuse towards Val-de-Travers, the home of absinthe, and the climb towards Creux du Van, a vast natural rock amphitheatre, offers views over the lake and the Alps. The Jura passes, such as La Tourne and the Vue des Alpes, have good surfaces and many bends. Speed limits are strict, as everywhere in Switzerland.

Bevaix, Cortaillod and Boudry have fuel, shops and restaurants; Neuchâtel, a short ride away, has everything. Try fish from the lake, such as perch, or a Neuchâtel fondue. Autumn here brings the grape harvest and golden vines, and the wine festival in Neuchâtel in late September is a lively celebration. Wet spells roll in from the west, so watch the sky above the Jura.
t.littoral de chens sur leman@46.3,6.3:
On the French shore of Lake Geneva, just across the border from Switzerland, the village of Chens-sur-Léman sits among fields and woods above the water. Along its shoreline, at places such as Tougues and Les Grèves, the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings lie in the shallow water, and they are part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps World Heritage site. On calm days, when the water is clear and low, it is sometimes possible to see the stumps of ancient wooden piles sticking out of the lakebed, a quiet reminder of the people who lived here thousands of years ago.

This stretch of the lake, in the Chablais region of Haute-Savoie, is quieter than the Swiss shore opposite, with small villages, beaches and harbours. A short ride east, Yvoire is a medieval walled village on a point jutting into the lake, with stone houses covered in flowers, a castle and a famous garden. It is one of the most visited villages in France, and in summer it can be crowded, but early in the morning it is lovely. To the west, the Swiss village of Hermance marks the border, with its own old centre and harbour.

The lake itself is a constant presence, changing colour with the weather and the time of day, from deep blue to grey to silver. On clear days, the Jura mountains stand out on the far shore, and to the south the Alps rise above the hills. Sailing boats, paddle steamers and swimmers share the water in summer.

The riding along the lakeshore is pleasant but often busy, with traffic heading between Geneva and Thonon-les-Bains. The minor roads inland are quieter, through farmland and woods, with gentle bends. For more challenging riding, the mountains are close: the Chablais Alps, with passes and winding roads towards Morzine and Avoriaz, or the Salève, a long ridge south of Geneva with a road along its crest and views over the city and the lake.

Douvaine, a few kilometres inland, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try fish from the lake, such as perch or féra, a local whitefish, often served with fries. Summer is warm and sunny, with occasional storms; winter is cold, with fog over the lake. Spring and autumn are lovely, with fewer crowds.
t.the architectural work of le corbusier@4:
On the shore of Lake Geneva at Corseaux, just west of Vevey, stands a low white house, long and narrow, with a single strip window running along its lakeside facade. It looks modest, almost plain, but it is one of the key buildings of modern architecture. Le Corbusier, born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Swiss Jura, designed it in the early 1920s for his parents, and the Villa Le Lac, also called the Petite Maison, was an early demonstration of his ideas: a ribbon window framing the view, a roof garden, an open plan. Since 2016 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, which includes seventeen sites in seven countries.

The house is small, and it opens to visitors on certain days. Inside, the long window frames the lake and the Alps like a panoramic painting, and the garden, with a small opening in the wall, is a delight. It is a strange feeling to stand in a house that changed the way people think about living space.

Vevey, next door, is an elegant lakeside town with a long promenade, a market square and a statue of Charlie Chaplin, who spent the last decades of his life in Corsier-sur-Vevey, just above the town. His house is now a museum, Chaplin's World. Vevey is also the home of Nestlé, and the Alimentarium, a museum about food, has a giant fork standing in the lake in front of it.

Above Vevey, the hills are covered with the terraced vineyards of Lavaux, listed by UNESCO in 2007. The stone terraces climb steeply from the lake, and the narrow roads that wind through them, especially the Route de la Corniche, offer some of the most stunning views in Switzerland. The riding is slow and scenic, with tight bends, narrow lanes and walls close to the road. Watch for walkers, cyclists, tractors and delivery vans, and be prepared to stop often for the views.

Vevey has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a glass of Chasselas from Lavaux, or a plate of filets de perche from the lake. The climate is mild, with warm summers and relatively gentle winters. Spring and autumn are perfect, with the harvest in late September and October.
t.fort site and civil settlement of nieder:
For one stretch of the Roman frontier in Germany, the soldiers did not need to build a wall at all. Between Großkrotzenburg and Miltenberg, the Main river itself served as the border, the so-called wet Limes, guarded by a chain of forts along its western bank. Niedernberg, a village on the river just below Aschaffenburg, was one of them, with a fort and a civilian settlement beside it. Little survives above ground today; the remains lie beneath fields and houses. But the Main still flows past, broad and slow, and it is easy to picture patrol boats and soldiers watching the far bank. The site is part of the Upper German-Raetian Limes World Heritage listing.

The river valley here is a gentle landscape of meadows, gravel pits turned into lakes, villages and vineyards on the slopes. Niedernberg has a popular bathing lake, and in summer people come to swim, sail and lie on the beaches. A cycle path runs along the river, busy at weekends.

Aschaffenburg, a few kilometres downstream, was for centuries the second residence of the Archbishops of Mainz, and their great red sandstone palace, Schloss Johannisburg, stands above the river. Nearby, King Ludwig I of Bavaria built the Pompejanum, a replica of a Roman villa from Pompeii, with painted walls and a garden, an unexpected sight in a German town.

The riding in the valley itself is flat and often busy, but the hills on both sides are excellent. To the east, the Spessart is a vast forest of oak and beech, with winding roads, small villages and very little traffic, a favourite with riders. To the south, the Odenwald offers similar pleasures, with roads that twist through wooded valleys and over ridges, past castles and half-timbered towns such as Miltenberg and Amorbach. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for deer, forestry vehicles and cyclists, and note that some popular roads in the region have speed limits for motorcycles.

Niedernberg and Sulzbach have fuel, shops and inns; Aschaffenburg has everything. The vineyards along the Main produce Franconian wine, often sold in the distinctive round, flat Bocksbeutel bottle. Try a Schoppen, a glass of local wine, in a village tavern. The weather is mild, with warm summers and cool winters; spring and autumn are lovely.
t.pointe de montbec i@46.9,7.0:
The south shore of Lake Neuchâtel is a long, soft margin of reeds, shallow water and woodland, and it hides one of the richest archaeological records in Europe. Pointe de Montbec, near the villages along the Fribourg and Vaud shore opposite Neuchâtel, is one of the places where prehistoric lake dwellers built their villages on the water's edge thousands of years ago. Their houses stood on piles driven into the soft lake shore, and when lake levels rose, the remains were sealed under water and mud, preserving wood, textiles, seeds and tools in astonishing detail. The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps were inscribed by UNESCO in 2011 as a single serial site spanning six countries, and this shore contributes a good number of them.

What brought many of these sites to light was a feat of nineteenth-century engineering. The first Jura Waters Correction, carried out from the 1860s onward, lowered the levels of the lakes of Neuchâtel, Biel and Morat by around two and a half metres to stop the flooding of the Seeland plain, and suddenly the remains of ancient villages appeared along the shores. Collectors and archaeologists rushed in, and the so-called lake-dweller fever spread across Switzerland, shaping a national myth of early ancestors living on the water.

Today the shore is protected as the Grande Cariçaie, the largest lakeshore marshland in Switzerland, a haven for herons, grebes, reed warblers and countless insects. The roads that follow the shore, a little inland from the reeds, run through farmland and villages with gentle curves and good surfaces, and the slight rise of the land gives views across the lake to the Jura mountains. Traffic is light outside the summer weekends, but watch for tractors, cyclists and the odd wandering family. Evenings are glorious, with the sun setting over the Jura.

The villages along the shore, such as Portalban and Gletterens, have cafés and small restaurants, often serving perch fillets from the lake, and Gletterens has a reconstructed prehistoric village that brings the pile-dwelling story to life. Fuel is available in larger towns like Estavayer-le-Lac or Avenches, the latter also home to the remains of the Roman capital of Helvetia. Make your break by the shore, walk to the edge of the reeds, and look out over the water. It is calm, green and quietly fascinating.
t.bahnhof@47.1,7.2:
The label says only "Bahnhof", which is a nicely Swiss joke, because the real attraction here is not a station at all but the south shore of Lake Biel between Täuffelen, Gerolfingen and Lüscherz. This is the Seeland, a low, fertile plain between the lakes, and the villages along the shore are surrounded by vegetable fields, orchards and vineyards on the gentle slopes. Like the shores of Lake Neuchâtel to the south, this lake edge was home to prehistoric pile-dwelling villages, and several sites around Lake Biel form part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. The finds, from pottery to wooden tools, tell of farming communities that lived here thousands of years ago.

Across the water, the steep slopes of the Jura rise above the north shore, covered in vineyards, with the wine villages of Twann and Ligerz clinging to the hillside. In the middle of the lake lies the St. Petersinsel, a long, wooded island joined to the land by a narrow causeway, where the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau spent a few happy weeks in 1765 and later wrote about it lovingly. The Hagneck canal, which brings the Aare into the lake just north of Lüscherz, was part of the great Jura Waters Correction of the nineteenth century, which tamed the floods of the Seeland.

The riding on the south shore is gentle and relaxed. The road from Biel through Nidau, Täuffelen and Lüscherz toward Erlach is mostly flat with gentle curves, passing through villages and fields with occasional views of the lake. It is popular with cyclists, so be patient. For more challenging riding, cross to the north shore and climb into the Jura, where the roads over the Chasseral and through the valleys of the Bernese Jura offer superb curves and views. Weather in the Seeland is often mild, though fog can settle over the lake in autumn and winter.

Täuffelen and the neighbouring villages have small shops and cafés, and Nidau and Biel, a short ride away, have fuel and every service. Local food includes lake fish, especially perch and whitefish, and wines from the north shore vineyards. Take a break by the lake at Lüscherz or Gerolfingen, watch the boats on the water, and enjoy the view across to the vineyards and the Jura. It is one of the quietest corners of the Swiss lowlands.
t.hornstaad hornle@47.7,9.0:
On the Höri peninsula, the long finger of land that pokes into the Untersee arm of Lake Constance, the shallow water off the point of Hornstaad hides the remains of a village burned some six thousand years ago. Hornstaad-Hörnle is one of the most important Neolithic sites in the region: the settlement was destroyed by fire, and the charred remains, sealed in lake mud, preserved an extraordinary record of daily life, including food, textiles, tools and house timbers, which dendrochronology has dated with great precision. It is part of the World Heritage inscription of the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, and finds from the site are displayed in museums around the lake.

The Höri has a special place in German cultural history. In the early twentieth century, it became a refuge for artists and writers seeking a simple life away from the cities. Hermann Hesse lived in Gaienhofen with his first wife from 1904 to 1912, and his house and garden can be visited. During the Nazi era, painters such as Otto Dix, labelled "degenerate", retreated here, and Dix lived and painted in Hemmenhofen for the rest of his life. The peninsula's gentle landscape of orchards, reeds and lake views has a quiet, timeless appeal.

The roads on the Höri are narrow and winding, following the shore through small villages and orchards, with frequent views of the lake and the Swiss shore across the water. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with cyclists and tourists everywhere, but on a weekday or out of season the riding is a pleasure. The island of Reichenau, with its UNESCO-listed churches, is a short ride away, reached by a causeway, and the roads across the Bodanrück toward Konstanz offer more curves and hills. Crossing into Switzerland at Stein am Rhein or Steckborn opens up more scenic routes.
