Gaienhofen and the other Höri villages have cafés, small restaurants and guesthouses, and Radolfzell, at the base of the peninsula, has fuel and every service. Local food includes fish from the lake, especially whitefish known here as Felchen, and the Höri bulb onion, a local speciality. Find a quiet spot by the shore, look out at the reeds and the water, and imagine the village that stood there six thousand years ago, its houses on piles and its people fishing the lake.
t.fort site and civil settlement of walldu:
Walldürn sits on the high, rolling plateau where the Odenwald meets the Bauland, a gentle landscape of fields, woods and small towns in the northeast of Baden-Württemberg. The Romans came here in the second century AD, when the Upper German Limes was pushed forward to a new line running almost straight through the countryside, and they built a small fort at Walldürn with a civil settlement beside it, where soldiers' families, traders and craftsmen lived. The remains of a bath house have been excavated and conserved, and the line of the frontier, with its watchtowers and palisade, runs nearby. The Upper German-Raetian Limes, more than five hundred kilometres long, became a UNESCO site in 2005.

Walldürn is best known in Germany for its pilgrimage. Since the Middle Ages, pilgrims have come to the town to venerate the Holy Blood, a relic associated with a legendary miracle in the fourteenth century when a priest spilled consecrated wine on a corporal cloth and an image of Christ appeared. The great baroque basilica in the town centre, built in the eighteenth century, is the focus of the pilgrimage, which still draws large crowds every year, especially in the weeks after Pentecost.

The riding around Walldürn is varied and pleasant. The Odenwald, to the west, is a classic motorcycle area, with winding roads through deep forests, valleys and small villages, and plenty of curves and gradients. The roads toward Amorbach and Miltenberg on the Main river are particularly good, descending through the forest into the river valley. To the east, the Bauland is flatter and more agricultural, with long, straight roads and gentle undulations. Traffic is light on weekdays, but the Odenwald attracts many bikers on weekends, and police controls are common.

Walldürn is a town of about twelve thousand people with fuel, cafés, bakeries and restaurants, so you are well supplied. Try local dishes such as Grünkern, an unripe spelt grain traditionally grown in the Bauland and used in soups and patties, or a slice of cake with coffee in the town centre. Visit the basilica, take a look at the Roman remains, and imagine the frontier running through these fields, with soldiers watching from their towers over the forests beyond.
t.fort site and civil settlement of osterb:
Osterburken is a small town in the Bauland of northern Baden-Württemberg, and the Romans left it one of the most interesting fort sites on the Upper German Limes. The fort here was built in the second century AD, when the frontier was moved forward, and it had an unusual annex fort added later, with walls that ran down the slope toward the stream, making it one of the few double fort complexes on the Limes. Large sections of the walls have been excavated and conserved, and the Roman museum next to the site displays finds from the fort and the civil settlement. The Upper German-Raetian Limes became a UNESCO site in 2005.

The museum's highlight is a sanctuary of beneficiarii, soldiers who served as officials controlling traffic and trade at important points along the frontier. In the 1980s, archaeologists excavating a waterlogged site in the town found dozens of altar stones dedicated by these soldiers, many still standing in their original positions, along with wooden remains of the sanctuary. The altars, with their inscriptions, give a vivid sense of the people who manned the frontier and their religious practices. Osterburken also produced a famous relief of the god Mithras, now in a museum in Karlsruhe.

The riding in the Bauland is relaxed and pleasant. The roads wind through gentle hills, fields and forests, with small villages and good surfaces. The Odenwald, to the north and west, offers more challenging riding, with winding roads through dense forests and deep valleys, while the Jagst and Kocher valleys, to the south, are beautiful river valleys with castles, vineyards and winding roads. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays, but watch out for agricultural vehicles in the fields.

Osterburken is a modest town of some six thousand people with fuel, cafés, a bakery and a few restaurants, and Adelsheim, nearby, has more. Local food includes Grünkern dishes, made from unripe spelt, and Swabian classics such as Maultaschen. Visit the museum, walk around the conserved walls, and look at the altar stones. They are among the most moving testimonies of Roman life on the frontier, and the town makes a pleasant stop for an hour or two.
t.la manufacture a saint die@48.3,7.0:
Le Corbusier designed only one factory in his long career, and it stands in Saint-Dié-des-Vosges, a town in the Meurthe valley on the western side of the Vosges mountains. The Manufacture Claude et Duval, a hosiery factory built between 1946 and 1951, is a concrete block raised on pilotis, with a roof terrace and brightly coloured interiors, and it embodies many of the architect's principles. It was part of his plans for the reconstruction of Saint-Dié after the town was largely destroyed by the retreating German army in November 1944, though most of his grand urban plan was never built. In 2016, the factory was included in the UNESCO listing of the architectural work of Le Corbusier, alongside buildings in seven countries.

Saint-Dié has another claim to fame: it is known as the "godmother of America". In 1507, a group of scholars here published a cosmography with a world map that used the name "America" for the first time, in honour of the Italian navigator Amerigo Vespucci. The town celebrates the connection, and the international geography festival held here each autumn draws visitors from around the world. The cathedral, rebuilt after the war, and the cloister next to it, are worth a look.

The riding around Saint-Dié is excellent. The town is a gateway to the Vosges, with roads climbing east toward Alsace over passes such as the Col de Saales and the Col du Bonhomme, with forests, curves and views. The Route des Crêtes, the famous ridge road along the crest of the Vosges, is within reach, offering spectacular riding with wide views over Alsace and the Rhine plain. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and some high roads are closed in winter. The forests are dense and dark, and the weather can turn quickly, with rain and fog common.

Saint-Dié is a town of around twenty-five thousand people with fuel, cafés, restaurants and supermarkets. Local food includes Vosges dishes such as tourte lorraine, a meat pie, and Munster cheese, together with bilberry tarts in season. The factory is still in use and can be visited only at certain times, so check ahead. Even from the outside, its clean lines and pilotis are striking. Then head up into the mountains for a ride through the forests.
t.dorfstation@47.0,7.1:
The south shore of Lake Biel is a gentle place of reeds, vineyards on the far bank and farmland stretching back towards the Seeland plain, and at Lüscherz, one of the small lakeside villages, the remains of a prehistoric pile-dwelling settlement lie in the shallows. Dorfstation, as the site is known, is part of the transnational World Heritage Site of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, inscribed in 2011. Neolithic and Bronze Age farmers built their houses on wooden piles along the shore, and the waterlogged ground preserved timbers, tools, textiles and food remains for thousands of years.

Nothing is visible from the shore: the remains are underwater or buried in mud. But knowing they are there changes how you look at the lake. People have been living, fishing and farming here for six thousand years.

Across the water, St Peter's Island, actually a peninsula since the lake level was lowered in the nineteenth century, is where Jean-Jacques Rousseau spent a few happy weeks in 1765, later writing that they were among the best of his life. On the north shore, the wine villages of Twann, Ligerz and La Neuveville cling to the slopes beneath the Jura, and their white wines are worth tasting.

The riding around Lake Biel is varied. The south shore roads are flat and pastoral, through villages and fields of vegetables, as the Seeland is Switzerland's market garden. The north shore road is busier and squeezed between the lake, the railway and the vineyards. For real curves, climb into the Jura: the road from La Neuveville or Nods up to the Chasseral, the highest point of the Bernese Jura, offers a fine climb with views over three lakes and, on clear days, the whole chain of the Alps. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, and the fines can be eye-watering.

Erlach, four kilometres away, is a charming small town with a castle, a covered arcade street and a lakeside promenade. For fuel and more services, head to Ins or to Nidau and Biel at the north-eastern end of the lake. Remember that Swiss motorways require a vignette, and that many roads in the Jura can be foggy in autumn.
t.sacro monte del rosario di varese@45.9,8:
Above Varese, on the flank of the Campo dei Fiori, a cobbled path climbs two kilometres or so through woods and past fourteen chapels to a medieval sanctuary and the tiny village of Santa Maria del Monte. Each chapel contains a life-size scene of the mysteries of the Rosary, with painted terracotta figures and frescoed backgrounds, and the whole ensemble, built in the seventeenth century under the architect Giuseppe Bernascone, is one of the nine Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2003.

The Sacri Monti were built in the age of the Counter-Reformation as a kind of pilgrimage substitute, bringing the Holy Land and the mysteries of the faith to the Alps in a form ordinary people could walk through and understand. At Varese the effect is theatrical and moving: the path opens up as you climb, the chapels become grander, and the views over the lakes and the Po plain widen with every bend. At the top, the village is a cluster of old houses, a church and a few cafés, with views reaching on a clear day to the Monte Rosa.

Varese has a special place in motorcycle history. MV Agusta builds its bikes on the shores of the Lake of Varese, and the area has a long tradition of motorcycle and aircraft manufacturing. The roads above the city are a favourite with local riders: the climb to the Sacro Monte and further up to the Campo dei Fiori, with its old Art Nouveau hotel and astronomical observatory, is a twisting, steep road through chestnut and beech woods. Weekends are busy, with cyclists and walkers on the narrow sections.

The surrounding area is full of lakes: Maggiore to the west, Lugano to the north and the small Lake of Varese below the city. Roads around them offer endless combinations of curves, views and villages, though traffic and Swiss border crossings add complexity.

Induno Olona, four kilometres away, and Varese itself have fuel and all services. The region's food is Lombard: risotto, polenta, cured meats and cheeses, and the local amaretti and sweets. A coffee at the top of the Sacro Monte, after the climb, with the lakes shimmering below, earns its place in the day.
t.bodman schachen lochle@47.8,9.0:
Lake Constance takes its German name, Bodensee, from this village. Bodman, at the western tip of the Überlinger See arm of the lake, was the site of a royal palace in the early Middle Ages, and the name of the place spread to the water. Below the village, in the shallows at Schachen and Löchle, lie the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, part of the transnational World Heritage Site of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, inscribed in 2011.

The pile dwellings of Lake Constance are among the best known in Europe. At Unteruhldingen, on the north shore a short ride east, a museum has reconstructed several villages on stilts in the lake, giving a vivid picture of what life looked like. At Bodman the remains are underwater and invisible, but the shoreline, with reed beds, old trees and the steep wooded slopes of the Bodanrück, is lovely in its own right.

The landscape around Bodman is varied. To the west lies the Hegau, a volcanic landscape of extinct cones topped by castle ruins, including the Hohentwiel near Singen, one of the largest fortress ruins in Germany. To the north, the hills of the Linzgau roll away towards the Danube, with orchards, forests and small villages. The lake itself is always close, with ferries, sailing boats and swans.

Riding in this area is a pleasure, especially on the smaller roads. The B31 along the north shore is busy and slow in summer, but the back roads through the hills offer curves, views and little traffic. The road from Bodman up to the Bodanrück and the routes into the Hegau are particularly nice. Watch for cyclists, tractors and speed cameras, which are common in Baden-Württemberg.

Stockach, five kilometres away, is the place to refuel. It is also known for its carnival court, the Narrengericht, a tradition said to go back to the fourteenth century in which a prominent figure is put on mock trial each year. The local food includes fish from the lake, such as Felchen, a whitefish, and wines from the slopes around the lake. On a hot afternoon, a swim from the shore near Bodman with the Alps floating above the far end of the lake beats any café stop.
t.segelboothafen@46.9,7.1:
Murten is the rare Swiss town where you can walk the medieval walls almost all the way round, looking down on brown tiled roofs on one side and the lake on the other. Its sailing harbour, the Segelboothafen, lies just below the old town on the shore of Lake Murten, and in the shallows here are the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, one of the Swiss components of the transnational World Heritage Site of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. Nothing shows above the water, but the lakeshore has been a place to live for thousands of years.

Murten's most famous date is 1476. Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, besieged the town, and the Swiss Confederates came to its relief and crushed his army in a battle that ended Burgundian ambitions in the region. Legend has it that a runner carried the news to Fribourg, collapsing as he arrived with a linden twig in his hand; a modern race between the two towns commemorates it every autumn. The town is bilingual, Murten in German and Morat in French, and its arcaded main street is full of shops, cafés and restaurants.

Across the lake rises Mont Vully, a long, low hill covered with vineyards on its southern slope, which produces some of Switzerland's most pleasant white wines. On its summit are the remains of a Celtic oppidum, and the views over the three lakes of the region, Murten, Neuchâtel and Biel, are wide. The local speciality is the gâteau du Vully, a flat, sweet bread topped with cream and sugar, which goes very well with a glass of Chasselas.

The riding is relaxed. The roads around the lake and through the Vully are gentle, with vineyards and villages, and the Seeland to the north is flat farmland. For more excitement, the Jura is within an hour, with the climbs to the Chasseral or the Vue des Alpes. Swiss rules apply: low speed limits, strict enforcement and a vignette for motorways. The lake is popular with cyclists and walkers, so watch out on the narrow roads near the water.

Murten has fuel and all services. Park outside the walls, walk through the old town, climb the ramparts and end at the harbour, where a swim or a boat ride on the lake on a hot day washes off the road dust nicely.
t.welzheim ost civil settlement northern p:
In the Swabian Forest east of Stuttgart, the Roman frontier ran as straight as a ruler for some eighty kilometres, ignoring hills and valleys in a way that still puzzles historians. Welzheim lies on this straight stretch of the Upper German-Raetian Limes, and the town had two Roman forts, the west and east forts, with a civil settlement around them. The northern part of the settlement near the east fort is one of the components of the Limes World Heritage Site, and the Ostkastell has been turned into an archaeological park with a reconstructed gate.

The Swabian Forest is a region of wooded hills, deep valleys and small villages, a green island between the busy urban areas of Stuttgart and Schwäbisch Hall. The forests are mostly spruce and beech, and the valleys are cut by streams and rivers that once powered mills. The landscape is gentle but varied, with plenty of viewpoints, lakes and old farms.

The riding is excellent, with countless curves and little traffic outside weekends. Roads wind through the forests and valleys, and the climbs and descents are steep in places. The roads to Murrhardt, Gschwend and Kaisersbach are all worth exploring, and the Ebnisee, a small lake in the forest, is a popular stop. Watch for cyclists, hikers and speed cameras, especially on weekends, when the area is popular with day trippers from Stuttgart.

Welzheim is a small town with a pleasant centre and a long history. Nearby Alfdorf and Kaisersbach are quiet villages, and Schorndorf, the birthplace of Gottlieb Daimler, is a short ride south in the Rems valley. The Swabian Forest is also known for its mills, and a mill trail links several restored mills in the valleys.

Welzheim, right beside the site, can handle fuel and lunch. Swabian cooking is generous and unfussy: Maultaschen, large pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, Spätzle, egg noodles often served with cheese, and Rostbraten, roast beef with onions. Several forest inns around the Ebnisee serve exactly that under the trees.
On the southern edge of Turin, at the end of a long straight avenue lined with trees, a bronze stag stands on the dome of a palace that looks like a star dropped on the plain. The Palazzina di Caccia di Stupinigi was built from 1729 by the architect Filippo Juvarra for King Vittorio Amedeo II of Savoy as a hunting lodge, though the word lodge hardly does justice to its grand halls, frescoed ceilings and sprawling wings. It is part of the World Heritage Site of the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, inscribed in 1997.

Juvarra designed the building around a central oval hall, from which wings radiate in the shape of a St Andrew's cross, giving views down the avenues of the hunting park. The interior is full of hunting scenes, paintings and furniture, and the central hall, with its galleries and frescoes, is enormous, a ballroom dressed up as a hunting hall. The park, once a hunting reserve, is now a natural park with woods, fields and farms.

Turin is a city of the Savoy dynasty, of baroque palaces and arcaded streets, but also of industry, the home of Fiat and a long history of car and motorcycle manufacturing. The Museo Nazionale dell'Automobile is one of the best car museums in the world. The city's cafés serve bicerin, a layered drink of coffee, chocolate and cream, and the region's food and wine are among the best in Italy.

For riders, Stupinigi is a gateway to the south. The Langhe and Roero hills, with their vineyards, castles and villages, are an hour away, and the roads through them are winding and scenic. Pollenzo, with its royal estate and the University of Gastronomic Sciences founded by the Slow Food movement, and Govone, with another Savoy castle, are on the way. The Alps rise to the west, with passes into France.

Beinasco, four kilometres away, will fill your tank, and Turin covers every other need, from tyres to a proper espresso. A ride from Stupinigi into the Langhe, with a lunch of tajarin, thin egg pasta, or vitello tonnato and a glass of Barolo or Barbaresco, is one of the great pleasures of Piedmont.
t.takashima coal mine takashima coal mine@:
Out in the sea off Nagasaki, a low island called Takashima was the place where modern Japan dug its first Western-style coal shaft. In 1868, in the very year of the Meiji Restoration, the Scottish merchant Thomas Glover went into partnership with the Saga domain to sink a shaft here using steam-powered machinery from Britain. The mine later passed to Mitsubishi and became one of the pillars of the company's rise, fuelling steamships, factories and the rapid industrialisation of the country. Takashima is now part of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, listed by UNESCO in 2015.

There is not much left of the early workings, but the site of the original shaft and a small coal museum tell the story, along with the island's own memories of mining life. The mine closed in the 1980s, and like the other coal islands off this coast, the population fell sharply afterwards. From Takashima you can see Hashima, better known as Gunkanjima or Battleship Island, an abandoned undersea coal mine whose concrete apartment blocks still crowd the rock like the superstructure of a ship. The history of these mines includes the forced labour of Korean and Chinese workers during the war years, a part of the story that remains sensitive and worth reading about before you go.

Takashima is reached by passenger ferry from Nagasaki port, so most riders will leave the bike in the city for the half day. The mainland ride compensates. Route 499 runs south from Nagasaki along the Nomozaki peninsula, a coastal road of headlands, fishing villages and long sea views, with good vantage points facing Gunkanjima offshore. The road is narrow in places and can be busy at weekends, but early on a clear morning, with the sun behind you and the islands sharp on the horizon, it is one of the loveliest coast rides on Kyushu.

Nagasaki itself is a city of steep hills and a deep harbour, with a history unlike any other in Japan: centuries of contact with Portuguese, Dutch and Chinese traders, a hidden Christian community, and the atomic bombing of 1945, remembered at the Peace Park and museum. Fuel and food are no trouble. Eat champon, a hearty noodle soup with seafood and vegetables born in the city's Chinese quarter, and take a slice of castella sponge cake for the road.
t.olzreute enzisholz@48.0,9.7:
Some five thousand years ago, someone in Upper Swabia built a wheel out of a single maple plank, mounted it on an axle and used it to move loads across the soft ground near what is now Bad Schussenried. The wheel turned up during excavations at the moor settlement of Olzreute-Enzisholz and is among the oldest wheels ever found in Central Europe, dated to around 2900 BC. The settlement, a group of pile dwellings on the edge of a former lake, is one of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps listed by UNESCO in 2011, a transnational site across six countries.

There is little to see on the ground: the remains lie preserved in the waterlogged peat, which is precisely why the wood survived. To understand the site, visit the Federseemuseum in Bad Buchau, a short ride to the north-west, which has reconstructed houses on stilts, finds from the moors of the region and a walkway out across the Federsee marshes, a lovely place with reeds, birds and wide skies.

Upper Swabia is gently rolling country between the Danube and Lake Constance, shaped by the glaciers of the last ice age, with moors, small lakes, forests and farmland. It is also baroque country: the Upper Swabian Baroque Route links the great monasteries and churches of the region. In Bad Schussenried, the former monastery has a library hall of great beauty, with a painted ceiling and carved figures, and nearby Steinhausen has a pilgrimage church often called the most beautiful village church in the world.

For riders, the area offers relaxed, scenic riding on small roads through villages, fields and woods, with gentle curves and good surfaces. Traffic is light outside the towns. It is a good place to unwind, and to link up with more demanding routes in the Allgäu, to the south-east, or the Swabian Jura, to the north. Lake Constance, with Bregenz and the Alps on its far shore, is about an hour away.

Bad Schussenried, a town of over eight thousand people two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The town has a brewery with a beer museum, and Upper Swabian food is hearty: try Maultaschen, large ravioli filled with meat and spinach, or Käsespätzle, egg noodles with cheese and fried onions. Late spring and early autumn are the loveliest seasons, when the meadows are green and the light is soft.
t.chur@46.9,9.5:
At 593 metres, in a wide bend of the Rhine valley, Chur makes a strong claim to be the oldest town in Switzerland, with traces of settlement going back thousands of years and a Roman presence from the first century BC. It has been the seat of a bishop since late antiquity, and the bishop's court, with its cathedral, sits on a terrace above the old town. Down below, the narrow streets and squares of the Altstadt, with painted houses, fountains and arcades, are a pleasant place to wander after a morning in the saddle.

For riders, Chur is the hub of Graubünden, the largest and most mountainous canton in Switzerland, and the starting point for some of the best roads in the Alps. South of the town, the road climbs over the Lenzerheide to the Albula and Julier passes and the Engadine; west, it runs past Flims and the Rhine gorge to the Oberalp pass; east, the dead-end road to Arosa climbs a famous sequence of hundreds of bends up a narrow valley. North, the Rhine valley runs down past the vineyards of the Bündner Herrschaft toward Liechtenstein and Lake Constance. Chur is on the Grand Tour of Switzerland, and you will see plenty of other riders.

The town has all the services you could want: fuel stations on the main roads, motorcycle dealers and workshops, shops and restaurants. Fill up here before heading into the mountains, where stations are fewer and prices higher. The motorway, the A13, requires a Swiss vignette, but the main roads through the valleys do not. Speed limits are strictly enforced in Switzerland, with radar cameras and heavy fines, so ride within the limits.

The Rhaetian Railway, Graubünden's narrow-gauge mountain railway, has its headquarters in Chur, and its trains climb into the mountains from here, including the line to Arosa and the routes over the Albula and Bernina to St. Moritz and Tirano. Watching a red train winding up a valley is part of the scenery of Graubünden.

Graubünden's cuisine is hearty and distinctive. Try capuns, chard leaves wrapped around a dough of flour, egg and dried meat, cooked in milk and cheese, or pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta with potatoes, cabbage and cheese. For dessert, the Bündner Nusstorte, a pastry filled with caramelised walnuts, keeps well and makes a good snack on the road. The Bündner Herrschaft produces excellent Pinot Noir, best enjoyed in the evening, once the bike is parked for the night.
t.rhaetian railway in the albula bernina l:
The Rhaetian Railway's Albula and Bernina lines were built in the early twentieth century to connect the Engadine with the rest of Switzerland and with Italy, and they are masterpieces of mountain railway engineering, with spiral tunnels, viaducts and gradients that seem impossible for a train. They were listed by UNESCO in 2008 together with the landscapes they cross, and St. If you ride in this area, you will see the red trains everywhere, and you will often be riding beside them.

The Albula line climbs from Thusis to St. Moritz through a series of spiral tunnels and viaducts, including the famous Landwasser viaduct near Filisur, where the train emerges from a tunnel in a cliff and crosses a deep gorge on tall stone arches. The Albula pass road, at 2,312 metres, runs parallel to the railway for part of the way, a narrow, winding road with spectacular views, closed in winter. The Bernina line runs from St. Moritz over the Bernina pass, at 2,253 metres the highest point of the railway, and down to Tirano in Italy, without rack assistance, with the circular viaduct at Brusio, where the train loops around a stone spiral, a highlight.

The Bernina pass road, at 2,328 metres, is one of the great alpine rides, with views of the Morteratsch glacier and the Piz Bernina, the highest peak in the eastern Alps, from the Montebello bend. The road descends into the Valposchiavo, through tight bends and past lakes, to Tirano. It is generally open all year, though conditions can be difficult in winter.

St. Moritz is the glamorous heart of the Engadine, a resort famous for its winter sports, luxury hotels and shops, set above a lake surrounded by mountains. The Upper Engadine is a high, broad valley with a chain of lakes, larch forests and villages with sgraffito-decorated houses, and the light here is famously clear and bright. Romansh, Switzerland's fourth national language, is still spoken in the valley.

St. Moritz has fuel, shops and restaurants, though prices are high. Fuel stations are also found in other villages of the Engadine, and Davos, about thirty-four kilometres away, is another larger town. Try an Engadiner Nusstorte with a coffee, and ride the Bernina early in the morning, when the light on the glacier is at its best and the road is quiet.
t.la bessime@46.9,6.9:
Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely within Switzerland, a long, narrow body of water at the foot of the Jura mountains, and its shallow shores have been home to people for thousands of years. La Bessime is one of the prehistoric pile-dwelling sites of the lake, part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, listed by UNESCO in 2011. Like most such sites, it lies underwater or buried in the lake bed, with the remains of wooden posts, tools, pottery and food preserved in the mud, invisible to the visitor but invaluable to archaeologists.

To understand the pile dwellings, visit the Laténium in Hauterive, near Neuchâtel, one of the largest archaeological museums in Switzerland, with reconstructed houses and finds from the lake. Near the museum, at La Tène, a famous Iron Age site gave its name to the entire La Tène culture of the Celts, which spread across much of Europe.

The south shore of the lake, around Estavayer-le-Lac, is quite different from the north. Here, the Grande Cariçaie, the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland, stretches for kilometres, with reeds, marshes and forests, home to many birds. Estavayer-le-Lac is a charming medieval town, with a castle, narrow streets and arcades, and a quirky museum with a collection of stuffed frogs posed in nineteenth-century scenes.

For riders, the roads around the lake offer pleasant, relaxed riding. The road along the south shore passes through villages, fields and woods, with views of the lake and the Jura beyond. The north shore road, through Neuchâtel, is busier, with vineyards on the slopes above the lake. From the north shore, roads climb into the Jura, with winding routes through forests and pastures to the high plateaus around La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle, famous for watchmaking. Swiss police take speeding seriously, and fixed cameras are common at village entrances.

Estavayer-le-Lac, a town of over five thousand people about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants; Cortaillod and Bevaix, on the opposite shore, are smaller. Try perch fillets from the lake, filets de perche, served with fries and tartare sauce, a classic dish of the region, with a glass of white wine from the vineyards of Neuchâtel. On a calm evening, the lake reflects the sunset over the Jura, and the view across the water is wonderfully peaceful.
t.fortifications of vauban@47.2,6.0:
Victor Hugo was born in Besançon in 1802, and so were the Lumière brothers, the pioneers of cinema, a generation later. The capital of Franche-Comté sits in a tight loop of the river Doubs, with the old town on the peninsula inside the loop and the citadel on a rock at the neck, closing the only side not protected by water. The citadel was built by Vauban, Louis XIV's great military engineer, after the French conquest of the region in the late seventeenth century, and it is one of the twelve groups of Fortifications of Vauban listed by UNESCO in 2008.

The citadel is a massive complex of walls, bastions and buildings perched above the river, with views over the old town and the Doubs valley. It houses several museums, including a museum of the Resistance and Deportation, and a zoo. Down in the old town, the streets are lined with elegant buildings of grey-blue and ochre stone, and the town is known for watchmaking, with an astronomical clock in the cathedral and a museum of time.

For riders, Besançon is a good base for exploring the Jura and the valleys of Franche-Comté. The Doubs valley, upstream toward Ornans and beyond, and the Loue valley, with its spectacular source gushing from a cliff, offer winding roads through limestone gorges, forests and pastures. Ornans, the birthplace of the painter Gustave Courbet, is a charming town on the Loue, with houses built over the river. Further south and east, the roads climb onto the high plateaus of the Jura, with long, sweeping bends through forests and pastures where Montbéliarde cows graze.

The city itself has heavy traffic and a complex road system, and the old town is partly restricted, so park and walk. The roads up to the citadel are steep and narrow.

Besançon, a city of over a hundred thousand people about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind. Franche-Comté is famous for its cheeses, especially Comté, aged for months in cellars and with a rich, nutty flavour, and Mont d'Or, a soft cheese in a spruce box, eaten warm in winter. The Morteau sausage, smoked over resinous wood, is another speciality. Try them all with a glass of vin jaune, the extraordinary yellow wine of the Jura, aged under a layer of yeast for more than six years, and raise a toast to Hugo and the Lumières.
t.lac de chalain@46.7,5.8:
Lac de Chalain is the largest natural lake in the French Jura, a long, green-blue lake set in a valley among forested limestone cliffs, and its shores were home to farming villages built on piles thousands of years ago. The remains of these villages, preserved in the lake bed, are part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, listed by UNESCO in 2011. In the 1900s, when the lake level was lowered for a hydroelectric project, a dugout canoe and the remains of houses were found, and excavations since then have revealed a remarkable picture of life in the Neolithic.

Today, the lake is a popular spot for swimming, boating and camping in summer, with a beach and a large campsite on the shore. The surrounding area is the Region of the Lakes, the Pays des Lacs, a plateau dotted with small lakes, forests and waterfalls. The Cascades du Hérisson, a series of waterfalls on the Hérisson river, are among the most beautiful in France, and a trail leads up the valley past them. Nearby, the Belvédère des Quatre Lacs offers a view of four lakes from a cliff top.

For riders, the Jura is a delightful region, with quiet, well-surfaced roads winding through forests, valleys and pastures, gentle bends and moderate gradients, and little traffic outside the summer holidays. The roads around the lakes, between Clairvaux-les-Lacs, Doucier, Ménétrux-en-Joux and Champagnole, are particularly scenic, with views of lakes and cliffs. Further east, the roads climb toward the high plateaus and the Swiss border, through the Forêt de la Joux, one of the finest fir forests in France.

The climate here is cool and wet, with cold winters and snow on the high plateaus, and the roads can be slippery in rain. Summer is the best time to visit, though the area is busy in July and August.

Champagnole, about thirteen kilometres away, is a small industrial town on the Ain with fuel, supermarkets and a few restaurants; Clairvaux-les-Lacs is smaller but has a station and cafés in season. Pack a picnic, because the best lunches here are eaten on a rock above the water: a loaf from the bakery, a wedge of Morbier with its thin line of ash through the middle, and a bottle of cold water from the spring. If you want a proper meal, look for poulet aux morilles, chicken in a cream sauce with morel mushrooms gathered from these forests, and save the swim for after, once lunch has settled.
t.swiss tectonic arena sardona@46.9,9.3:
Twice a year, in spring and autumn, the sun shines through a hole in a mountain ridge and lights up the church tower of Elm, a village in the Sernf valley of canton Glarus. The hole is the Martinsloch, a natural window in the Tschingelhörner, and it sits right on one of the most famous geological features in the world: a sharp line along the cliffs, clearly visible from the valley, where older rock lies on top of much younger rock. This is the Glarus thrust, and it helped geologists understand how mountains are built by the stacking of enormous slabs of the earth's crust. The Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona was listed by UNESCO in 2008.

The arena covers a high, rugged area between the Linth, Rhine and Seez valleys, with peaks rising to over three thousand metres around the Piz Sardona, and glaciers, high pastures and deep valleys. Hiking trails lead to viewpoints where the thrust line can be seen up close, and information points explain the geology. On the Graubünden side, Flims and Laax are known for their skiing, and the Segnes plateau above Flims offers a superb view of the Tschingelhörner and the Martinsloch.

Nearby, the Rhine gorge, the Ruinaulta, was carved through the debris of the Flims landslide, the largest known landslide in the Alps, which fell some ten thousand years ago and buried the valley under billions of cubic metres of rock. The road from Flims toward Ilanz runs above the gorge, with viewpoints looking down onto the white cliffs and the river below.

For riders, the area offers a mix of great roads. The Oberalp road runs west from Chur past Flims and Laax and up the Surselva valley to the Oberalp pass and Andermatt, a long, fast route with lovely views. On the Glarus side, the road up the Sernf valley to Elm is a narrow dead end, but scenic, and the Klausen pass, connecting Glarus with Uri, is one of the classic alpine passes, with a twisting climb and spectacular views. The Klausen is closed in winter.

Domat/Ems, about eighteen kilometres away, and Chur have fuel and services; Flims and Laax have stations as well, and the villages of the Glarus valleys have more limited facilities. Try a Glarner Pastete, a pastry filled with almonds and plums, or Glarner Schabziger, a pungent herb cheese made in the canton for centuries, and look up at the mountains as you eat, imagining the slow collision that built them.
t.baie de gresine@45.7,5.9:
Lac du Bourget is the largest natural lake in France, a long, deep lake in Savoie between the Jura and the Alps, and the poet Alphonse de Lamartine made it famous with his poem Le Lac, written after a love affair that began on its shores. The Baie de Grésine, near Brison-Saint-Innocent on the eastern shore, is one of the prehistoric pile-dwelling sites of the lake, part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps listed by UNESCO in 2011. As with other such sites, the remains lie underwater, but the bay and its surroundings are a beautiful place to stop.

The eastern shore is dominated by the spa town of Aix-les-Bains, popular since Roman times for its hot springs and a fashionable resort in the nineteenth century, with grand hotels, a casino and a lakeside promenade. Across the lake, on the western shore, the Abbaye de Hautecombe, a Cistercian abbey on the water, holds the tombs of many members of the House of Savoy, the dynasty that once ruled this region and later became the royal family of Italy.

For riders, the area offers superb roads. Above the western shore, the Dent du Chat road and the Col du Chat climb steeply over the mountain ridge, with tight bends and views over the lake. The road along the western shore is narrow and winding, with tunnels and cliffs. To the east, the road from Aix-les-Bains up to Mont Revard climbs through forests to a plateau with a spectacular view over the lake and, on a clear day, Mont Blanc. Further afield, the Bauges massif offers quiet, twisty roads through limestone mountains and pastures, and the Chartreuse massif, to the south, has famous passes and gorges.

Traffic around Aix-les-Bains and Chambéry can be heavy, especially in summer, and the roads around the lake are busy on weekends. The weather is generally mild, but storms can build up quickly over the mountains in summer.

Aix-les-Bains, a town of over twenty-five thousand people about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants of every kind; Brison-Saint-Innocent and Grésy-sur-Aix have more limited facilities. Try lavaret, a white fish from the lake, served with butter and lemon, or a plate of diots, Savoyard sausages cooked in white wine, with crozets, small square pasta made from buckwheat. And sit by the lake at dusk, as Lamartine did, and watch the light fade over the water.
t.les marais de saint jorioz@45.8,6.2:
Lake Annecy is often called the cleanest lake in Europe, and on a summer day its water is such a startling shade of turquoise that it looks retouched. The lake fills a long valley among the limestone mountains of Haute-Savoie, with the town of Annecy at its northern end, and its western shore, around Saint-Jorioz, is a flat area of reeds and meadows, the Marais de Saint-Jorioz, where prehistoric people built villages on piles. The remains are part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, listed by UNESCO in 2011, and lie hidden under the water and the marshes.

The lake is surrounded by mountains. On the eastern shore, the Dents de Lanfon and the Tournette rise steeply above Talloires and Menthon-Saint-Bernard, home of a fairy-tale château; on the western shore, the Semnoz forms a long ridge above the lake. The Roc de Chère, a forested headland on the eastern shore, is a nature reserve with walking trails and views over the water.

For riders, the area is a playground. The roads around the lake are scenic but often busy, especially in summer and on weekends, when traffic can be heavy and slow. The climbs are the real attraction: the Col de la Forclaz de Montmin, above the southern end of the lake, is famous for its view and its paragliders, who launch from a meadow above the road; the Semnoz road climbs through forests to a summit with views over the lake and toward Mont Blanc. Further east, the Aravis range offers classic passes like the Col des Aravis and the Col de la Colombière.

Annecy itself has a charming old town, with canals, flower-filled balconies and the Palais de l'Isle, a former prison on an island in the Thiou canal, but traffic and parking in the town can be difficult. Saint-Jorioz, a town of over five thousand people about two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants; the other villages around the lake have more limited facilities.

Haute-Savoie is the home of reblochon, a soft, creamy cheese, and of tartiflette, a dish of potatoes, onions, bacon and reblochon baked in the oven, which is hearty enough to fuel a whole afternoon of riding. In summer, the lake is perfect for swimming, and a dip in the clear water after a hot morning on the road is a great pleasure.
t.bodio centrale o delle monete@45.8,8.8:
Gavirate, on the northern shore of the Lago di Varese in Lombardy, has a sweet claim to fame: it is the home of the brutti ma buoni, ugly but good, crunchy biscuits made with hazelnuts and egg whites, which were reportedly invented here in the nineteenth century and are still sold in local pastry shops. The lake itself is a small, shallow lake surrounded by low hills, and its shores were home to some of the earliest pile-dwelling villages in Italy. The site of Bodio Centrale, also known as delle Monete, on the southern shore near Bodio Lomnago, is part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, listed by UNESCO in 2011.

The most famous pile-dwelling site of the lake is the Isolino Virginia, a small island near Biandronno, where a museum displays finds from the prehistoric villages. The lake is a peaceful place, with reeds, birds and a cycle path around the shore, and the views toward the Alps on a clear day are lovely.

The city of Varese, a short ride to the east, sits at the foot of the Campo dei Fiori, a mountain covered in forest, with a road that climbs to a summit with views over the lakes and the plain. On its slopes, the Sacro Monte di Varese, a pilgrimage route lined with chapels leading up to a sanctuary and village, is part of the UNESCO-listed Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy. The road up is steep and twisting, and the views from the top are splendid.

For riders, the area around Varese offers a mix of good roads. The hills between the Lago di Varese, Lago Maggiore and Lago di Lugano are crossed by small, winding roads through forests and villages, and the roads along Lago Maggiore, toward Luino and the Swiss border, are scenic though often busy. To the north, the Valganna and the Valcuvia lead toward Switzerland and the Ticino, with Bellinzona and its three castles further on. Traffic around Varese and on the main roads can be heavy, especially on weekdays.

Gavirate, a town of over nine thousand people about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of risotto with perch fillets from the lake, risotto con filetti di pesce persico, a classic dish of the Lombard lakes, and of course a bag of brutti ma buoni for the road, a perfect snack to munch at a viewpoint with the lake shining below.
t.worms synagogue compound@49.6,8.4:
In the Middle Ages, three Rhineland cities, Speyer, Worms and Mainz, were the centres of Jewish learning in northern Europe, and they gave their initials, in Hebrew, to a community known as ShUM. The Jewish communities of these cities developed traditions, laws and customs that influenced Ashkenazi Jewry for centuries, and their monuments were listed together by UNESCO in 2021. In Worms, the synagogue compound includes the synagogue, rebuilt after its destruction by the Nazis in 1938, the women's synagogue, the mikveh, a ritual bath dating from the twelfth century, and the Rashi house, now a Jewish museum, named after the great medieval scholar who studied here.

Just outside the old city walls, the cemetery known as the Heiliger Sand is one of the oldest surviving Jewish cemeteries in Europe, with gravestones dating back to the eleventh century, tilted at odd angles among the trees and grass. It is a moving, peaceful place, and visitors often leave small stones on the graves of the famous rabbis buried there.

Worms is also famous for other chapters of history. Its great Romanesque cathedral, built in red sandstone, is one of the finest in Germany. In 1521, Martin Luther appeared before the Imperial Diet here and refused to recant his writings, a key moment in the Reformation, and a large monument in the town commemorates him. The city is also the setting of much of the Nibelungenlied, the medieval epic poem, and the Nibelungen Museum explores the legend.

For riders, Worms lies on the left bank of the Rhine, in a flat, fertile plain, and the roads around it are fast and busy. To the west, however, the Palatinate offers excellent riding: the German Wine Route, the Deutsche Weinstraße, winds through vineyards and wine villages at the foot of the Palatinate Forest, and the forest itself, one of the largest continuous forests in Germany, has many twisty roads through hills and valleys. To the east, across the Rhine, the Odenwald offers more winding roads through forests and villages.

Worms, a city of over eighty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The region is one of Germany's great wine areas, and Worms is the home of Liebfraumilch, a sweet white wine whose name comes from the vineyards around the Liebfrauenkirche in the town. Try a plate of Saumagen, stuffed pig's stomach, a speciality of the Palatinate, with a glass of dry Riesling, and take a walk through the quiet paths of the Heiliger Sand.
t.la place forte de neuf brisach@48.0,7.5:
After the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, France had to give the fortress of Breisach, on the right bank of the Rhine, back to the Habsburgs, and Louis XIV needed a new stronghold to guard the river. His engineer Vauban designed it from scratch on an empty plain on the left bank: Neuf-Brisach, a perfect octagon of walls, bastions and moats, with a grid of streets inside and a large central square with a church and a parade ground. Built between 1698 and the early eighteenth century, it was Vauban's last great work and is often considered his masterpiece. It is one of the twelve groups of Fortifications of Vauban, listed by UNESCO in 2008.

Seen from the air, the town looks like a star-shaped diagram, and even from the ground, walking along the walls and through the gates, the geometric order is striking. The Porte de Belfort, one of the gates, houses a small museum about Vauban and the fortifications. The town itself is quiet, with a few shops and cafés around the square.

Across the Rhine, Breisach am Rhein sits on a hill above the river, with its cathedral, St Stephen's, on the summit, and it is the gateway to the Kaiserstuhl, a small volcanic range covered in vineyards, with winding roads through terraced hills, and to the Black Forest beyond. On the French side, the Alsace Wine Route winds through vineyards and villages at the foot of the Vosges, with half-timbered houses, storks' nests on the rooftops, and wine cellars at every turn. Colmar, about twenty kilometres away, is one of the most charming towns in Alsace, with canals and colourful houses.

For riders, the area offers a mix of flat riding on the Rhine plain and more interesting roads in the Kaiserstuhl, the Vosges and the Black Forest. The Route des Crêtes, along the ridges of the Vosges, is a classic ride, with views over the Rhine plain and the Black Forest. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads, especially around Colmar.

Volgelsheim, about two kilometres away, has fuel and basic services; Breisach, about five kilometres away, is larger. Try a tarte flambée, a thin, crispy flatbread topped with cream, onions and bacon, or a choucroute garnie, sauerkraut with sausages and pork, with a glass of Alsace Riesling or Gewürztraminer. And walk the ramparts of Neuf-Brisach at sunset, when the light catches the stone and the shadows reveal the geometry of Vauban's design.
t.littoral de tresserve@45.7,5.9:
The Lac du Bourget is the largest natural lake entirely in France, a long blue trough in the Savoie Prealps, and the shore at Tresserve, just south of Aix-les-Bains, is one of the quiet places to see it. Beneath the water here lie the remains of prehistoric lake dwellings, villages of timber houses built on piles along the shore thousands of years ago. The site is part of the UNESCO-listed Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, a series of more than a hundred settlements in six countries. There is nothing to see above the surface, but knowing it is there changes the way you look at the reeds and shallows.

The lake has a literary fame too. Alphonse de Lamartine met his great love, Julie Charles, in Aix-les-Bains in 1816, and after her death he wrote Le Lac, one of the most famous poems in the French language, about the lake that saw their happiness. Across the water, on the steep western shore, the Abbey of Hautecombe sits by the water at the foot of the Mont du Chat, burial place of the princes of the House of Savoy.

Aix-les-Bains is an old spa town, with Belle Époque hotels, a casino and thermal baths, and it makes an excellent base. The riding around the lake is superb. The road along the western shore, below the Dent du Chat, is narrow and winding, with the cliffs on one side and the water on the other. Above it, the climb to the Mont du Chat is steep and tight, with long drops on the outside of the hairpins and no room for daydreaming. On the eastern side, the road up to Mont Revard climbs in long bends to a plateau with views over the lake and, on clear days, Mont Blanc.

The lake is a place to swim in summer, with beaches and lidos around the shore; the water is clear and warms up well by July. Mornings are often hazy; afternoons can bring thunderstorms that roll in over the mountains.

Aix-les-Bains has fuel, garages and every kind of food, from lakeside cafés to restaurants serving lake fish such as lavaret, a whitefish found in the Alpine lakes. Tresserve, the residential village above the shore, is quiet and green. Park by the water, take off your helmet, and listen to the lake.
t.venetian works of defence between the 16:
Bergamo is two cities: the busy modern town on the plain, and the Città Alta on the hill above, enclosed by massive walls built by the Republic of Venice between 1561 and 1588. Bergamo was then the westernmost outpost of Venice's mainland territory, facing the Spanish-ruled Duchy of Milan, and the walls, more than five kilometres long, were designed to withstand artillery, with bastions, platforms and gates. They were never seriously tested in battle, which is why they are so well preserved. In 2017 UNESCO listed them, together with other Venetian fortifications in Italy, Croatia and Montenegro, as the Venetian Works of Defence.

The upper town is a joy to explore on foot, a compact maze of medieval and Renaissance streets, with the Piazza Vecchia at its heart, the Colleoni Chapel with its multicoloured marble facade, and the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore. The walls themselves are now a tree-lined promenade, with views over the plain on clear days as far as the Apennines. You reach the upper town by funicular from the lower town, or on foot along steep, cobbled lanes; vehicle access is restricted, so leave the bike below.

Bergamo has its own food traditions: casoncelli, stuffed pasta with butter and sage, polenta in every form, and a sweet called polenta e osei, a yellow cake shaped like a dome with chocolate birds on top. The local cheeses, from the valleys above, include Taleggio and Branzi.

The riding from Bergamo is outstanding. North of the city, the valleys of the Brembo and the Serio cut deep into the Bergamo Alps. The Val Brembana leads to San Pellegrino Terme, the spa town famous for its mineral water, with a Belle Époque casino and grand hotels, and then climbs towards the passes of the Orobie. The Val Seriana leads to Clusone and the Presolana pass, a classic climb with views of the limestone peaks. Lake Iseo, to the east, has roads along its shores with tunnels and bends, and the island of Monte Isola in the middle. The roads can be busy on weekends with Milanese heading for the mountains.

Bergamo has fuel and every service, and the airport at Orio al Serio is close if you are flying in to rent a bike. The best seasons are spring and autumn; summer in the plain is hot and humid.
t.kasuga village and sacred places in hira:
Hirado is an island off the northwest coast of Kyushu, connected to the mainland by a bright red suspension bridge, and for a brief moment in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries it was one of Japan's windows on the world. Portuguese traders arrived in 1550, followed by Jesuit missionaries, and later the Dutch and English East India Companies set up trading posts here. When Christianity was banned in the early seventeenth century and foreign trade was moved to Nagasaki, the Christians of Hirado went underground. Kasuga, a farming village on the western side of the island, is one of the places where these Hidden Christians, the Kakure Kirishitan, maintained their faith in secret for more than two centuries, outwardly following Buddhism and Shinto while worshipping Christian images disguised as Buddhist statues and reciting prayers in a garbled mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese. The village and the sacred mountain of Yasumandake above it are part of the UNESCO listing of the Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region.

The village is beautiful in a quiet way: terraced rice fields stepping down a valley towards the sea, farmhouses with stone walls, and forested hills behind. The terraces have been farmed in the same way for centuries, and in early summer, when they are flooded, they reflect the sky. A small visitor centre explains the history.

The riding on Hirado is pleasant and unhurried. The roads circle the island along the coast and through the hills, with tight bends, steep climbs and views over the sea and the scattered islands. Traffic is light, the surface excellent, as everywhere in Japan, and the speed limits are low and enforced. Japan drives on the left. Watch for farm vehicles and elderly drivers in tiny kei trucks.

Hirado town, on the eastern side, has a reconstructed Dutch trading house, a castle overlooking the harbour, and a striking view of a Buddhist temple and a Catholic church together on the same hillside. It has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants serving fresh seafood. Try the local flying fish, ago, dried and used in soups, or grilled squid.

The best seasons are spring and autumn. The rainy season in June brings heavy rain, and typhoons can strike in late summer and early autumn, so check the forecast.
t.nagasaki shipyard mitsubishi former patt:
Nagasaki's harbour is a long, narrow inlet surrounded by steep hills, and on its western shore the Mitsubishi shipyard has been building ships since the late nineteenth century. The yard was one of the engines of Japan's rapid industrialisation in the Meiji era, when the country transformed itself from a feudal society into an industrial power in a few decades. Several of its historic structures are part of the UNESCO listing of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, inscribed in 2015. The Former Pattern Shop, a red-brick building from 1898 where wooden patterns were made for casting metal parts, now houses a museum of the yard's history. The Giant Cantilever Crane, installed in 1909 and made in Scotland, is still in working order, and it dominates the waterfront. The yard built many famous ships, including the battleship Musashi, one of the largest warships ever constructed.

The Scottish connection runs deep. Thomas Glover, a merchant from Aberdeen, arrived in Nagasaki in 1859 and played a key role in the industrialisation of Japan, helping to import machinery, establish the shipyard and develop coal mining. His house, the oldest Western-style wooden building in Japan, stands in the Glover Garden on the hill opposite, with views over the harbour.

Nagasaki is a city of layered history: the Portuguese traders and Jesuits of the sixteenth century, the Dutch trading post on the artificial island of Dejima during the centuries of Japanese isolation, the Chinese community with its temples and lantern festival, and the atomic bomb of 9 August 1945, commemorated in the Peace Park and the Atomic Bomb Museum. Offshore, the abandoned coal mining island of Hashima, Gunkanjima, the battleship island, can be visited by boat.

Riding in Nagasaki is challenging. The streets are narrow, steep and crowded, with trams running through the centre, and parking is difficult. Outside the city, the coastal roads of the Nagasaki peninsula, south towards Nomozaki and west towards Sotome, are lovely, with sea views, tight bends and little traffic.

The city has fuel, garages and every service. Try champon, a hearty noodle soup with seafood and vegetables, and castella, a sponge cake introduced by the Portuguese. The night view from Mount Inasa is one of the finest in Japan.
t.shitsu village in sotome@32.8,129.7:
Sotome is a stretch of rugged coast north of Nagasaki, where steep hills drop into the East China Sea, and the village of Shitsu clings to its slopes. During the centuries when Christianity was banned in Japan, the farmers and fishermen of this remote area kept their faith in secret, passing down prayers and rituals from generation to generation, hiding their devotion behind Buddhist and Shinto practices. When the ban was lifted in 1873, many of them returned to the Catholic Church. The Shitsu church, built in 1882 under the direction of the French missionary Marc Marie de Rotz, stands on a hill above the sea, a simple white building with a low profile designed to resist the strong winds. De Rotz was more than a priest: he taught the villagers to make bread, pasta and textiles, built a clinic and a workshop, and his legacy is still honoured locally. The village and church are part of the UNESCO listing of the Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region.

The area has a literary connection. Shūsaku Endō, one of Japan's greatest twentieth-century novelists, set his novel Silence, about the persecution of Christians and the anguish of a Portuguese priest, in a fictional village inspired by Sotome. A literary museum dedicated to Endō stands on the coast nearby, overlooking the sea, and a stone monument bears a line from the book about the blueness of the sea.

The coastline is magnificent. Route 202 runs along it, high above the water, with tight bends, short tunnels and constant views over the sea and the islands. The sunsets here are famous, and the road is known as the sunset road for good reason; on a clear evening, the sun sinks into the East China Sea in a blaze of orange. Traffic is light outside Nagasaki, the surface excellent, and the speed limits low.

The nearest towns with full services are Togitsu and Nagasaki, about twenty kilometres away. There are a few roadside stations along the coast where you can buy local produce and snacks, and small restaurants serving seafood. Try the local pasta, inspired by de Rotz, sold in the village shop.

The weather on this coast can be wild, with strong winds and typhoons in late summer and autumn. Spring and autumn days, clear and mild, are perfect for the ride.
t.monastic island of reichenau@47.7,9.1:
Reichenau is a flat, green island in the Untersee, the western arm of Lake Constance, connected to the mainland by a long causeway lined with poplars. A wandering bishop named Pirmin founded the monastery here in 724, and over the next centuries it became one of the great centres of learning and art in Europe, famous for its scriptorium and its illuminated manuscripts. The island's three Romanesque churches survive, and UNESCO listed the whole as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

The most striking of them is St George at Oberzell, where tenth-century wall paintings of the miracles of Christ cover the nave, remarkably clear after a thousand years. The minster at Mittelzell is larger and holds the monastery's treasures, and the little church of St Peter and Paul at Niederzell sits near the shore. The monk Walahfrid Strabo wrote a poem here about his herb garden, the Hortulus, and the island's gardening tradition has never stopped: the greenhouses and vegetable fields you see today produce lettuces, tomatoes and cucumbers sold across southern Germany. Fish from the lake, especially the whitefish called Felchen, appear on every menu.

The riding on the island is gentle. Roads are flat and narrow, with cyclists everywhere, so keep to modest speeds and enjoy the views across the water to the Swiss shore and the hills of the Hegau. Approach it from the mainland along the causeway at a steady pace, especially on summer weekends when traffic and visitors are heavy. The ride around the lake, from Konstanz to Bregenz and beyond, is the real draw, with lakeside bends, orchards, vineyards and views of the Alps on a clear day. Autumn is lovely, with mist on the water and apples ripening in the orchards.

The island has a few petrol options, but Allensbach, a couple of kilometres away, and Konstanz are better bets, with larger stations and supermarkets. Cafés and inns on the island serve Kuchen and coffee, and the lakeside terraces are good places to sit with a glass of local wine. Park on the mainland side if the island is busy, and walk or cycle the short distances between the churches.
t.watchtowers wp 9 100@49.0,9.6:
The Limes in the Swabian-Franconian Forest has a quality that surprises people who expect Roman walls to follow hills: it runs in a dead-straight line, for kilometres at a stretch, regardless of what stands in the way. Near Murrhardt the line dives through woodland and valleys, and the signposted watchtower sites mark points where a timber and later stone tower stood on the frontier, with a ditch and a palisade or bank beside it. The numbering, with its slash, comes from the nineteenth-century surveyors who first mapped the frontier, and archaeologists still use it.

Murrhardt itself is an attractive town in a green valley, founded around a Benedictine monastery whose origins go back to the Carolingian period, and there is a small museum of the Roman and early medieval history of the area, in a former abbey building. The Walterichskirche, a Romanesque chapel, has a strange, quiet charm. The surroundings are forested hills and narrow valleys cut by the river Murr, and the wooded country is dark and cool even in summer.

Roads in the area are a pleasure for riders. The minor roads through the Swabian-Franconian Forest climb and drop through beech and spruce, with a long series of medium-speed curves, occasional hairpins and good views from clearings, and the surface is usually decent, though damp and slippery under trees. Traffic is modest, but expect cyclists and walkers, especially on summer weekends. The best months are May to October, and in autumn the colours are superb, though leaves on the road need respect. Rain is frequent, so pack waterproofs.

Murrhardt, only two kilometres away, has fuel, shops, bakeries and cafés, and the neighbouring Kaisersbach and Oberrot have smaller services. The region is known for hearty Swabian dishes, including Maultaschen, a kind of large ravioli served in broth or fried with egg, and spaetzle with lentils. If you want to follow the Limes on foot, a marked trail leads along the frontier, and a short walk will give you a better sense of its straightness than any map.
t.watchtowers wp 8 29 to 8 30@49.4,9.4:
Osterburken is the place on the German Limes where you really can see the Romans in the town. The fort here sat on the frontier in the Bauland, a hilly farming district between the Odenwald and the Neckar, and the museum in the town houses the remains of the fort baths and a rare relief of the god Mithras, an eastern cult favoured by soldiers, whose followers met in small, dark temples to share a sacred meal. The watchtowers 8/29 and 8/30 stand out in the fields a short distance away, part of the line that ran straight over the hills.

The geography explains why Rome put a fort here. The Kirnau valley offers a natural passage through the hills, and the Romans wanted to control who came through. Later, in the third century, Germanic raiding grew, and the garrisons were pulled back. The fort at Osterburken was one of the more strongly built on the Upper Germanic Limes, and its name, which means something like east fort, may preserve the memory of its role.

The surrounding landscape is quiet and rolling, with orchards, meadows and small woods, and the Neckar valley and its castles lie a short ride to the west. Roads through the Bauland are among the better ones in northern Baden: they curve over low ridges, drop into villages with half-timbered houses, and have good surfaces with moderate traffic. Spring blossom, golden autumn and the long evening light of June are the best times. Be careful with farm traffic, and with mud on the road after harvest or heavy rain.

Osterburken itself has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and a couple of restaurants, and Adelsheim, a little further, has more of the same. A plate of roast pork with dumplings or a wedge of Black Forest cake is the local solution to tiredness. If you want to see the Romans, visit the museum first, because it makes the lonely tower sites much easier to read, then ride out to the fields and stand where the watchmen stood.
t.boseong suncheon yeosu goheung getbol@34:
Korea's southern coast is a place where land and sea cannot decide who owns what. The tides here rise and fall by several metres, leaving wide mud flats, called getbol, that glitter in low light and fill with life. The Getbol, Korean Tidal Flats, were added to the UNESCO list in 2021 because they are a feeding ground for migratory birds travelling along the East Asian flyway, including rare ones such as the black-faced spoonbill. Boseong, Suncheon, Yeosu and Goheung are the four stretches here, strung along a coast of bays, islands and reed beds.

Suncheon Bay is the highlight. Wooden walkways run through a huge bed of reeds, and a hill viewpoint above gives the shape of the channels, curling like a river map in gold and green in autumn. In winter, hooded cranes arrive in numbers, and in spring and summer fiddler crabs and mudskippers crawl over the mud, with fishermen out for cockles. Nearby Boseong is known for green tea, and the terraced hillsides of tea bushes are one of the most photographed views in Korea.

Yeosu, a port city of about three hundred thousand, hosted the 2012 World Expo and sits on a dramatic harbour with islands and bridges, including the long cable-stayed bridge to Dolsan. It has fuel, hotels and a lively waterfront. The local food is the point of a visit, with raw fish, marinated crab, mustard-leaf kimchi and grilled eel, all served with a table full of side dishes. Suncheon, another big town of over two hundred thousand, is close, so supplies are never an issue.

The riding is a pleasure on a bike, with smooth, quiet coast roads that curve around bays, climb headlands for views and pass fishing villages, oyster racks and salt pans. Traffic is light outside holidays, but tolls on bridges and expressways are common. Spring is lovely, with fresh green and blooming camellias, and October and November turn the reed beds gold. The best time for the mud flats is low tide, so check the tide tables, and summers are hot and humid, with typhoons in late summer.
t.prehistoric pile dwellings around the al:
Five thousand years ago, people were building houses on stilts at the edge of lakes across the Alps, and then the lakes rose, buried the houses and kept them almost perfectly in the mud. The remains of these pile dwellings, found in the nineteenth century when a drought lowered the water, include posts, tools, textiles, food and even bread, and they gave archaeologists an extraordinary view of Stone Age and Bronze Age life. A hundred and eleven of the sites, in six countries, were listed by UNESCO in 2011, and the Swiss share is the largest.

Meisterschwanden lies on the Hallwilersee, a long narrow lake in the canton of Aargau, and the shallows of its shore hold some of the remains. I must be honest here, since there is little to see above water. Most sites are covered by the lake or buried in the mud, protected on purpose, and what you find on land are information boards, a view of the shore and perhaps a museum with finds. Robenhausen, in the ride title, is a classic site on the Pfäffikersee in canton Zurich, known since the 1850s, and has a small display of reconstructions.

The Seetal, the valley around the Hallwilersee, is lovely riding country, with gentle hills, orchards, villages with half-timbered farmhouses and the lake glinting below. The roads are in excellent condition, speed limits are firmly enforced and there are cameras, so keep within the limit. Schloss Hallwyl, a moated castle at the north end of the lake in Seengen, is one of the finest water castles in Switzerland, and well worth a stop.

Reinach, with nearly eight thousand people, and Meisterschwanden, with about twenty-five hundred, have fuel and cafes. Remember that motorways in Switzerland need a vignette, a sticker that costs about forty francs a year, so buy one at the border or a petrol station. The best seasons are spring, with blossom, and autumn, with the apple harvest and cooler air. Swim in the lake in summer, and eat a cheese fondue or a plate of fried lake fish with a glass of local white wine.
t.bellerive i@46.3,6.2:
Lake Geneva has a gentle northern shore and a steep one, and Bellerive lies on the quiet side. Collonge-Bellerive is a village on the Geneva side of the lake, a few kilometres from the city, with lawns running down to the water, old villas and a small harbour where sailing boats bob. Some five thousand years ago, people built houses on piles in the shallows here, and what remains of that settlement lies below the surface, protected as part of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, listed by UNESCO in 2011. There is nothing to see from the shore except the lake and the Alps, so the visit is about the setting.

The setting is good. On a clear day the Mont Blanc massif shows in the far south-east, white and enormous, and in the evening the light on the lake turns copper. Bellevue and Corsier, the neighbouring villages, are small, wealthy places with cafes and walks, and Geneva itself, with its famous fountain and old town, is only fifteen minutes away.

The ride list pairs this with Lavaux, the terraced vineyard slope between Lausanne and Vevey, which UNESCO listed in 2007. Monks began the terraces in the twelfth century, and today about eight hundred hectares of stone-walled vineyards climb from the lake to the hills, producing Chasselas, a delicate white wine. The road through the villages, such as Cully, Epesses and Chexbres, is narrow, winding and lined with walls, and it is best taken slowly, on a quiet weekday, with stops for a glass of wine in a cellar.

Between the two, the lakeside road runs west to east along the water, with plenty of traffic around Lausanne and Geneva, so leave early and avoid rush hours. Fuel is easy everywhere, though Swiss prices are high, and you need a vignette for the motorway. Spring and autumn are lovely, with autumn the best, when the vines turn gold and the grape harvest fills the villages with festivals. Summer is warm and crowded, with swimmers on every landing stage, and winter brings the cold bise wind from the north-east.
t.en praz des gueux@46.8,7.0:
Fribourg is the town where French and German meet. It was founded in 1157 by the dukes of Zähringen on a rock in a loop of the Sarine river, and the old city still sits above the water, with a Gothic cathedral, covered wooden bridges and steep cobbled lanes. The border between the languages runs through the city, so locals switch between French and a Swiss German dialect, and the divide has a name, the Röstigraben, after the potato dish that lies on one side. Beyond the city, the canton is green and rolling, with farms, forests and pastures that produce the famous cheese of Gruyères.

En Praz des Gueux lies in this farmland, south-west of Fribourg, near the villages of Avry-sur-Matran and Grolley, which are small, quiet places with a couple of thousand people each. The land is gently hilly, with orchards, barns with low roofs and views to the Fribourg Alps on a clear day.

For riders, Fribourg canton is a pleasure. Roads are well maintained, quiet and varied, running through villages with fountains and flower boxes, and on to the pre-Alps, with the Gruyères region and its medieval castle to the south and Lake Neuchâtel to the north. Estavayer-le-Lac, on the lake, has a walled old town and a good promenade, and Murten, with its complete town wall, was the site of a famous battle in 1476, in which the Swiss defeated Charles the Bold of Burgundy.

Fuel and food are easy in Fribourg, a city of about forty thousand, and in the larger villages. Remember the vignette for the motorway, and speed cameras on many roads. Spring and autumn are best, with clear air and autumn colour, and the cheese is a year-round pleasure. Eat a fondue moitié-moitié, with half Gruyère and half Vacherin, or try meringues with thick cream, and finish with a coffee on the cathedral square.
t.sacro monte della beata vergine del socc:
The Madonna of Succour sits above Ossuccio, on the western shore of Lake Como, about halfway between Como and Menaggio. A cobbled path climbs through the village with fourteen small chapels along it, each holding painted terracotta figures that act out a scene from the life of Mary, and at the top there is a sanctuary with a terrace and a view across the water. It is one of the Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy, a group of hillside devotional complexes that UNESCO listed together in 2003. These were built in the Counter-Reformation as walkable theology: you could not read, so you walked and looked. The Ossuccio chapels date from the seventeenth century, and the little island you see below the slope is the Isola Comacina, the only island on the lake, with its own long and rather stormy history.

The riding here is the lake road itself, the old Strada Regina that follows the shore in a series of tight bends, short tunnels and villages where the carriageway shrinks to the width of a delivery van. It is glorious on a weekday morning in spring or in October and a slow parade on a sunny Sunday, when cars, cyclists and German tour buses all share the same ribbon. Do not plan to make time. The corners are lovely precisely because you cannot take them quickly, and the surface is generally good, with the odd patch of polished stone in the village centres that gets greasy after rain.

Parking at the foot of the path is easy enough for a bike, and the climb on foot takes about as long as a coffee, with steps and shade from chestnut and oak. Wear shoes you can walk in, as the cobbles are old and uneven. At the top the lake lies spread out below, with the mountains of the Grigna pale on the far side and the light changing by the hour. Villages in the immediate neighbourhood, Ossuccio, Sala Comacina and Lenno, are small, so do not count on a pump in every one of them. Top up in Como or Menaggio before you commit to the shore, because the nearest big town in the data, Mandello del Lario, is across the water and a long way round.

Lenno has lakeside cafes and the pull of Villa del Balbianello along the headland, which is worth knowing about if the rest of the family wants something other than motorcycles. Order a risotto with lake perch if you see it, and finish with a coffee on a terrace. This is a short, quiet detour that rewards patience more than speed.
Lorsch looks like a regular small town of the Hessian Bergstrasse, and then you see the Torhalle, a little gatehouse of red and white stone with an arcade at the bottom and a pitched roof above, which is one of the very few surviving buildings of the Carolingian age in Germany. The abbey was founded in 764, rose to enormous wealth and influence under Charlemagne's family, and its library produced and preserved a startling number of manuscripts. The Lorsch Pharmacopoeia, written around 795, is one of the earliest known medical texts from German lands, and the monks' collection of books is scattered through libraries in Rome, Heidelberg and the Vatican today. UNESCO listed the abbey and nearby Altenmünster in 1991.

Altenmünster is the older monastery site, a short distance away, and little remains there beyond a modest ruin and an outline in the ground, but the sense of continuity is strong. The monks chose this flat land at the edge of the Rhine plain, near the foot of the Odenwald, and the abbey became a powerful landowner whose records show the landscape being shaped, tilled and drained around it.
