In the sixteenth century the abbey was dissolved and lost its role, and the buildings were damaged over time, including in a fire in the Thirty Years' War.

The ride in is easy, mostly flat farm roads and town streets from Heppenheim, Einhausen or from the A5 motorway, which runs to the west. Lorsch is a town of about thirteen thousand, so fuel, bakeries, cafes and a pharmacy within walking distance are all there. The better riding lies east, where the Odenwald rises and the road to Fürth and Lindenfels winds through beech forest with tidy bends and fewer trucks. Cycle traffic is heavy on weekends, and the Bergstrasse is famous for almonds, early blossom in March, and good wine on the slopes above.

The abbey grounds are open and green, with a museum and a long wall of old sandstone. Give it an hour. A museum entry fee is small, and it is a quiet half day that suits an afternoon between more demanding roads. If it rains, you are close to the gatehouse door in any case, and the red and white pattern of the stone looks best then, when it is wet and the light is flat.
t.hamberg ditch@49.0,8.9:
Maulbronn is a small town in the folded country where the Kraichgau meets the Stromberg hills, and its Cistercian monastery is the best-preserved medieval monastery north of the Alps. The Hamberg ditch belongs to a very different part of the story, the hydrology that kept the monks fed and powered. The Cistercians were famous engineers, and at Maulbronn they dug ditches, built dams and shaped ponds so that the water supply could drive mills, fill fish ponds and flush drains. Parts of this system still survive in the surrounding woods, and UNESCO included the monastery and its water works in the 1993 listing.

The monastery itself is a short ride away, and it should not be skipped. Founded in the twelfth century, it has a cloister, a vaulted refectory, a fountain house and fortified walls that make it look like a small town. Legend says Johann Faust, the alchemist of the old stories, studied here, and the town has made the most of it. Later, the poet Hermann Hesse spent a miserable half year at the monastery school, an experience he used in his novel Beneath the Wheel.

For riding, this is a gentle, winding landscape, with roads that follow wooded ridges and drop into little valleys of vines and orchards. Traffic is mostly local, with the busy A8 motorway to the south and Pforzheim to the east, so the lanes in between feel quiet. Surfaces are generally smooth, though farm tractors leave mud in autumn. The Stromberg is wine country, and Württemberg red is the thing to try if you have time, with Trollinger and Lemberger as the usual names.

Maulbronn itself has almost seven thousand people, so you can find fuel and a bakery without trouble, and Mühlacker is larger and a short ride away. A late-afternoon walk around the monastery wall, with the light on the pale stone, is the best use of the hour. Spring blossom and autumn colour are the seasons to choose.
t.watchtowers wp 8 44 to 9 2@49.3,9.5:
The Jagst is a small, winding river in northern Württemberg, and between Jagsthausen and Möckmühl it runs through a valley of orchards, wooded slopes and half-timbered villages. The Roman frontier ran along this side of the river, and watchtowers 8/44 to 9/2 sit on the high ground above. They belong to the Upper German-Raetian Limes, inscribed by UNESCO in 2005, which here ran in a remarkably straight line for many kilometres, a feat of surveying that still impresses. The Romans needed to hold a rim of high ground and chose a line that ignored the little hills, which is why the old frontier looks like a ruler line across the map.

Jagsthausen has a more famous resident than any Roman. The castle on the edge of the village was the birthplace of Götz von Berlichingen, the imperial knight with an iron hand, whose name entered German literature through Goethe's play, and the castle hosts open-air performances in summer. The Roman fort at Jagsthausen once had substantial baths, and part of the layout can still be seen. Möckmühl has a handsome old town centre with an imposing gate, and with eight thousand people, a better supply of fuel and supermarkets.

The riding is lovely in a quiet way. The roads follow the river and cut across hills, with gentle gradients, good surfaces and little traffic outside the commuter hours around Möckmühl. In spring the fruit trees flower in pale drifts along the lower slopes, and in autumn the vineyard and orchard colours are rich. There are no long straights, but nothing is tight enough to demand your full concentration, and the whole district invites a gentle loop with a lunch stop. The Hohenlohe plain to the east has broader fields and wider views.

Regional food here is robust, with Schwäbisch Hall pork, noodles and spätzle, and fresh bread in village bakeries. If you stay for the evening, a glass of local Württemberg wine or cider makes sense. The watchtower stop itself is a small clearing with a sign. Take a minute, look down the line towards the next post, and picture the soldiers who lived in tidy stone-footed towers above a river valley not much different from this one.
t.wollmatingen langenrain@47.7,9.1:
Konstanz is the German city that sits on Switzerland's lap, so close to the border that the two towns, Konstanz and Kreuzlingen, run into each other with a fence in between. The old town lies on the narrows between the Obersee and the Untersee, the two halves of Lake Constance, where the Rhine leaves the lake, and it has one of the best preserved medieval centres in southern Germany. Its survival has a simple explanation: it was not bombed in the Second World War, partly because of its closeness to neutral Switzerland. In the early fifteenth century, it hosted the Council of Constance, which ended a split in the Catholic Church and condemned the reformer Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake in 1415.

The pile-dwelling remains at Wollmatingen-Langenrain are the older story, and they belong to the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. They date from the Neolithic and Bronze Age and lie preserved under the shallows near the nature reserve of the Wollmatinger Ried, a huge reedbed on the lake shore that is one of the most important bird habitats in central Europe. Nothing is visible from the land, but the reedbeds, with their thousands of waterfowl, are a spectacle in autumn and winter.

The roads around the Untersee are among the nicest in the region. Cross the border into Switzerland, and the road follows the shore through Tagerwilen and Ermatingen, with orchards, vineyards, villas and views of the lake and the green island of Reichenau, which holds a UNESCO-listed monastery with Carolingian wall paintings. The corners are gentle and the scenery is pastoral, with the Alps visible on a clear day to the south. Weekend traffic is heavy in summer, with cyclists and families, so go early. In autumn, the fruit stands sell apples and pears, and the vineyards turn red and gold.

Konstanz has plenty of fuel and restaurants, and Tagerwilen is a few minutes away. Check the border formalities before you cross, as you will need your passport, and remember that the Swiss motorway vignette applies to motorbikes. Try the lake fish, Felchen, fried in butter, and a glass of local wine.
t.la chaux de fonds@47.1,6.8:
La Chaux-de-Fonds sits at nearly a thousand metres in the Swiss Jura, on a high, windswept plateau where the winters are long and cold, and it should not really exist. There is no river, no great harbour and no easy farmland, but the people who settled here in the seventeenth century turned to making clocks in their farmhouses during the winter, and the town became the world's capital of watchmaking. After a great fire in 1794, it was rebuilt on a grid pattern, with wide, straight streets that allowed light to reach the workshops and homes, and with the long, high windows that watchmakers needed. That orderly plan is why it is listed by UNESCO, together with its neighbour Le Locle.

Karl Marx called it a single huge factory town in Das Kapital, and the observation holds. The town's culture runs on precision, and its museum of horology is one of the best in the world, with timepieces from sundials to atomic clocks. Le Corbusier was born here in 1887, and several early houses he designed in the town, in a regional style quite unlike his later work, still stand. The Jura landscape beyond is open and green, with spruce forest, pastures and old farms with huge overhanging roofs, and horses that graze in the meadows.

For riders, the Jura is a gentle pleasure. The roads climb and descend through the hills in long, easy curves, with views of the Alps on clear days, and the nearby gorges of the Doubs river, which forms the border with France, are dramatic. The Saut du Doubs waterfall is a short ride away. The high plateau is cold, and winter can bring snow as early as October and as late as April, with the valley of La Brevine nearby known as the Siberia of Switzerland. In summer, the weather is fresh and often windy.

Fuel and food are easy in the city, which has about thirty-seven thousand people. Look for cheese such as Tete de Moine and Gruyere, and for the saucisson neuchatelois, a smoked sausage, as well as the absinthe made in the nearby Val-de-Travers. A Swiss motorway vignette is required for motorbikes on the autoroutes.
t.agelmoos@47.3,8.2:
Lake Hallwil is a long, narrow lake in the Aargau, lying north to south between low hills, and it is the quiet cousin of the bigger Swiss lakes. At its northern end stands a moated castle, Schloss Hallwyl, a grey medieval fortress surrounded by water that looks as if it belongs on a stage, and which holds a museum of its centuries of family life. The lake's shore is a mix of reed beds, meadows and villages, and the water is clean enough for swimming in summer. Rowing boats and small sailboats drift across it on warm afternoons.

Agelmoos, on the eastern shore near Meisterschwanden and Reinach, belongs to the very old story of the lake. Over the last five thousand years, Neolithic and Bronze Age people built villages on posts at the water's edge here, and the wetland and marsh soils that later covered them preserved wood, textiles, seeds and tools in extraordinary condition. The names in the label, Halbinsel and Sumpf, meaning peninsula and swamp, hint at the landscape of that time. This is part of the UNESCO listing for the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, but there is nothing to see in the open air, and the real finds are kept in museums, such as the one in the castle at Lenzburg and in the national museum in Zurich.

The riding is what you would want from the Swiss midland: gentle, green and well kept. The roads in the Seetal, the lake valley, wind over low ridges among apple orchards, fields and small villages, with views of the Alps on clear days and a pleasant sense of calm. Corners are open, gradients are mild and the surface is smooth, though weekend traffic can be heavy and cyclists are everywhere. On the ridge of the Lindenberg to the east, a road runs along the top with views across the lake and the plains.

Reinach, three kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes. Look for the local specialities, such as Bernese platter in the winter, and the smoked sausages from the region. A Swiss motorway vignette is required if you use the autobahn, and speed limits are strictly enforced, so keep to them. The best seasons are May to October, with the lake at its warmest in July and August.
t.motier i@46.9,7.1:
Murten, or Morat as the French speakers call it, is a small walled town on the shore of a lake of the same name, on the language frontier of Switzerland. Its ramparts are among the best preserved in the country, and its main street is lined with arcades and painted fountains. In 1476, it was the site of a decisive battle, when the Swiss Confederates defeated the army of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and ended his attempt to conquer the region. A stone memorial to the battle, and the legend that a runner carried the news of victory to Fribourg, gave Switzerland a long-lasting patriotic story.

Across the water rises Mont Vully, a low, gently rounded ridge covered in vineyards, and Motier, on the lake, lies at its foot. The first part of the label refers to prehistoric pile dwellings in the shallows, part of the UNESCO listing for such sites around the Alps, though the posts are underwater and the real treasure is in the museums. The second part, Kehrsiten, is far away on Lake Lucerne, which shows how a route can jump across the whole country. The Vully wines, a white Chasselas and a fruity Pinot noir, are made on the slopes, and a local speciality is the gateau du Vully, a sweet tart topped with cream and sugar.

The riding here is mellow. The Three Lakes region, with Neuchatel, Biel and Murten, has flat roads along the shores, vegetable fields in the Seeland, and gentle bends through vineyards on the slopes. The surface is generally excellent, and traffic is moderate, though it grows heavy in summer. The road over the Vully hill offers fine views of the lake and, on a clear day, a line of Alpine peaks across the water. Autumn, with the grape harvest and golden light, is particularly lovely.

Murten has fuel nearby, as well as bakeries and restaurants, and the old town is easy to explore on foot. It is worth walking along the town wall for the view over the roofs and the lake. If the weather is hot, a swim in the lake is a pleasure, and boats run on the water in season. A Swiss vignette is required for motorway use. The best times are May and September, when the weather is mild and the lakeside is calm.
t.port@46.3,6.2:
Lake Geneva, which the locals call the Leman, is the largest lake in western Europe, and its southern shore, curving between Geneva and the French border, is where the river Rhone leaves the water. The little places of Corsier-Port and Anieres lie on the left bank, among villas, vineyards and gardens that slope down to the water, and they are among the most elegant addresses in the canton. The French shore across the lake rises into the mountains of Chablais, and on a clear day the whole range of the Mont Blanc can be seen to the south-east, a white line above the water.

The prehistoric pile dwellings that give this stretch its place on the UNESCO list lie in the shallow water near the shore, and they date back to the Bronze Age, about three thousand years ago. As elsewhere, they are only seen underwater or in museum displays. On land, the interest is in the villages, with their old stone houses, little harbours and lakeside promenades. The Mouettes Genevoises, small yellow ferries, cross the harbour in the city, and the lake steamers of the Compagnie Generale de Navigation are a pleasure on a sunny day.

The ride along the shore road is easy and pleasant. It runs from the city past Cologny and Corsier to Hermance, close to the French border, with views of the lake through gaps in the hedges. It is a quiet road, but with a speed limit, many cyclists and plenty of cameras, so slow riding is the rule. Beyond the villages, the road climbs into the hills of the Genevan countryside, where vineyards and fields run toward the Jura, and the quiet lanes are a pleasure. The wind known as the bise, a cold north-east wind, can blow strongly in winter, while the vent, a warm south-west wind, brings rain.

Versoix and Geneva have fuel at several stations, and there are cafes in the villages. Switzerland is expensive, so a coffee on a terrace is a small luxury, but the lake and the light make it worthwhile. A Swiss motorway vignette applies for the autoroutes, and crossing into France for fuel is a common way of saving money.
t.zona di commando@45.1,7.7:
Turin is the city that made the Savoy dynasty into the kings of Italy, and the area known as the Zona di Comando, the Command Zone, is the heart of that story. In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the dukes of Savoy, who had moved their capital to Turin in 1563, laid out a grand ensemble of palaces, courtyards and arcades around the old castle, turning a provincial town into a stage for royal power. Piazza Castello is the centre, with the Palazzo Madama, a medieval castle with a baroque facade, and the Palazzo Reale, the royal palace, with its gardens and the Royal Armoury. It is part of the UNESCO group of the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, listed in 1997.

The city beyond is less stiff than its reputation. Turin has long, straight arcaded streets, grand cafes that serve the bicerin, a drink of coffee, chocolate and cream, and a large Egyptian museum, the biggest outside Cairo. The Mole Antonelliana, a tall tower with a pointed dome, houses the cinema museum and has a glass lift to a viewing platform. Fiat, the carmaker, shaped the modern city, and the old Lingotto factory, with its rooftop test track, has been turned into a shopping and cultural centre. In the evening, the aperitivo hour fills the bars with free snacks.

Riding here is straightforward if you accept the rules of Italian city traffic. Scooters and cars share the lanes, trams run on tracks, and many central streets are restricted zones, called ZTL, where entry without a permit can lead to a fine, so be careful with navigation. The best rides start outside the city: the hill of Superga, with its baroque basilica, gives a view over the Po and the Alps, and the road to Ivrea, with its Olivetti factories of the early twentieth century, runs through the Canavese, a countryside of lakes, vineyards and castles. The Langhe hills to the south, famous for Barolo wine, are a great destination.

Turin has fuel at many stations on the ring road and the main avenues, and good restaurants everywhere. Try agnolotti, the little stuffed pasta, and the Piedmont hazelnut chocolates. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter fog can settle in the plain.
t.oura cathedral@32.7,129.9:
Nagasaki is a city of steep hills around a deep harbour, and on one of those slopes above the old foreign settlement stands a small white Gothic church that is, in its quiet way, one of the most important in Japan. Oura Cathedral was built in the early 1860s by French missionaries, who had been allowed to serve the foreign community in the treaty port after Japan's long seclusion, and it was dedicated to the twenty-six Christians who were executed on a hill in Nagasaki in 1597. The church faces the site of that martyrdom, and it is the oldest surviving Gothic-style church in the country.

Its fame comes from what happened a few weeks after it opened. In March 1865, a group of local people came to the church and told the French priest, Bernard Petitjean, that their hearts were the same as his. They were Kakure Kirishitan, hidden Christians whose families had practised the faith in secret for more than two centuries after it was banned, passing down prayers by word of mouth and disguising their images as Buddhist figures. The meeting was seen as a miracle in Europe, and the so-called finding of the hidden Christians led to a new wave of persecution before the ban was lifted in 1873. The cathedral stands as a monument to that long, quiet fidelity and is part of the Hidden Christian Sites World Heritage listing.

Nagasaki is a hard city to ride in and an easy one to love. Roads are narrow and steep, the old Dutch and Chinese quarters are tangled with one-way streets, and trams share the main roads, so tracks and wet rails call for care. A short walk takes you to Glover Garden, laid out around the former houses of foreign merchants, and the view from the hillside across the harbour is the reward. The Nagasaki ropeway to Mount Inasa gives a famous night view, and the peace park and atomic bomb museum are essential for understanding the city's modern history.

With over four hundred thousand people, Nagasaki has fuel, food and everything else. Try champon, a noodle soup with seafood and vegetables invented here by Chinese immigrants, and castella, a sponge cake brought by Portuguese traders in the sixteenth century. Spring and autumn offer the best weather, and the rainy season in early summer can be heavy.
t.hidden christian sites in the nagasaki r:
Far west of the Japanese mainland, the Goto Islands trail out into the East China Sea in a scatter of volcanic hills, cliffs and quiet harbours, and on them stand some of the most moving small churches in Asia. The Hidden Christian Sites of the Nagasaki Region belong to the same World Heritage listing as Oura Cathedral, but this corner of it feels very different. Here the faith was kept alive in remote farming and fishing villages, to which Christian families moved in the late eighteenth century, partly because the authorities of the Goto domain wanted settlers to open up poor land.

When the ban on Christianity finally ended in 1873, the villagers began building churches, often with their own hands and their own money. Many were put up in wood or brick by local carpenters in the decades that followed, which is why they have the look of village halls that happen to have stained glass. The result is a series of modest, beautiful buildings, set above small harbours or at the end of narrow lanes, and the sight of a white church above a green hillside and a blue sea is one of the lasting pictures of the islands.

Fukue Island is the largest of the group, and the town of Fukue, with about twenty-seven thousand people, is the place for petrol, food and lodging. The island is reached by ferry or plane from Nagasaki or Fukuoka, and a bike would need a ferry crossing planned in advance. The roads on the island are narrow, winding and quiet, passing through camellia woods, rice terraces and small fishing hamlets, with sudden views of cliffs and surf. Camellia oil has long been a local product, and the flowers bloom in winter and early spring. The weather can be rough, with strong winds and sudden rain off the sea, so always carry waterproofs.

Many of the churches are still active parishes, and visitors are asked to be quiet, respectful and sometimes to follow dress or photo guidelines, so check beforehand. Spring and autumn offer the most settled conditions. In summer the heat is strong and typhoons can shut ferries for days. The beaches here are among the clearest in Japan, and the Takahama sands on Fukue make a good afternoon after a morning on the church trail.
Under the northeastern slopes of Jeju there is a hollow world made by fire. Geomunoreum is a small volcanic cone, one of the hundreds that dot the island's flanks, and in the long prehistory of the island it spilled lava that ran downhill in rivers. The surface of each flow cooled and hardened while the molten rock inside kept moving, and when it finally drained away it left long empty tunnels. The Geomunoreum lava tube system, a family of caves including Manjanggul, Gimnyeonggul and others, is among the finest in the world, and it is the core of the Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes World Heritage site, inscribed in 2007.

Manjanggul is the one you can visit, and the visit is memorable. The tunnel is more than seven kilometres long in total, though only a kilometre or so is open to the public, and walking in feels like entering a giant's drain pipe, thirty metres wide in places and as high as a house. The air is cool all year round, about the temperature of a cellar, so bring a jacket even in August, and wear shoes with grip, as the floor is rough and wet. At the end a tall column of lava, about seven metres high, stands where molten rock once poured down from a hole in the roof. The ripple marks on the walls show the levels of the flow, and tiny bats still use the darker sections.

The roads of north-east Jeju are a pleasure, though they are not mountain roads in the alpine sense. Farm lanes, walled with black basalt, wind through fields of tangerines, canola, and sweet potatoes, and nearby the Bijarim forest holds a grove of ancient nutmeg trees, some well over five hundred years old. Hallasan, the great shield volcano at the island's centre, reaches 1,947 metres, the highest in South Korea. Cross-island roads climb its flanks through deciduous forest and pass through cloud, and these mist-wrapped sections can have a sudden damp chill and low visibility.

Jeju City, about twenty kilometres away, has everything, from fuel and restaurants to bike hire. Wind is a serious factor on the island, especially in spring and autumn, and in summer typhoons can ground ferries and flights. Eat black pork, grilled abalone and local tangerines, and check opening days before you go, because caves can close after heavy rain or for maintenance.
t.allensbach strandbad@47.7,9.1:
Lake Constance does not do dramatic. It does soft: a huge sheet of water, a far shore that comes and goes with the haze, and little towns with tidy promenades that seem to have been tidied again while you were not looking. Allensbach's Strandbad is one of those spots, a lido on the Gnadensee, the western arm of the lake, with a swimming area, grass banks and a view across to the Reichenau island and the Swiss shore beyond.

That island is the reason the ride exists. Reichenau holds a monastery founded in the eighth century that became one of the great centres of learning and manuscript painting in medieval Europe, and its churches carry a UNESCO listing. A few minutes away by road, a causeway leads out to it. On the way, Allensbach itself, with about 7,000 people, is a quiet lakeside town with a long history of fishing and market gardening, and the mild lake climate is why Reichenau is also covered in vegetable plots and greenhouses.

For riders the pleasure is gentle. The lake roads here are flat, with the odd rise through orchards, and the best times are early morning and early evening, when traffic thins and the water is calm. On a warm Saturday the roads fill with cyclists, day-trippers and caravans, and the little car parks near the water fill by mid-morning. If you want a quiet swim, go early or late, and bring something to lock your kit into, since a bike jacket and boots on a beach towel are an odd sight.

Practical bits are straightforward. Allensbach has shops and cafés, and the Radolfzell side to the west and Konstanz to the east have the bigger fuel stops and supermarkets. Swimming here is a straightforward pleasure from late spring through early autumn, and the water on the Untersee side warms quicker than the deep main lake. Allow time for fish: Felchen, the whitefish of Lake Constance, are served pan-fried across the shore, and the local vegetables from Reichenau are worth asking for. The border with Switzerland is only a few kilometres off, so carry a passport or ID card if the day's plans wander.
t.feldbach@47.2,8.8:
Feldbach is a small village on the northern shore of Lake Zurich, and a very Swiss kind of calm hangs over it. It belongs to the municipality of Hombrechtikon and lies on the sunny stretch locals call the Gold Coast, where steep vineyards and orchards slope down to the water and the houses cost more than most people care to say aloud. The village has a lakeside park with big old trees, a small harbour and a place to swim in summer, and across the water the opposite shore climbs toward the Albis hills.

Rapperswil, just two and a half kilometres away, is the town to know. It is a medieval walled town on a spit of land that reaches into the lake, with a castle on a hill, a rose garden that is famous in June and a long wooden footbridge across to Hurden that follows a line pilgrims have used for centuries. The town used to be called the town of roses and has a long tradition as a stopover on the pilgrim road to Einsiedeln. The castle holds a Polish museum that dates back to the nineteenth century, when Polish exiles gathered here. Rapperswil is also where you will find fuel, supermarkets and a train station, with a population of about 35,000.

For riders, the roads around this end of the lake are a mixed bag. The lakeside road through Feldbach and Wolfhausen is slow and busy, especially on summer weekends, when walkers and cyclists dominate. Better riding lies up behind the shore, over the Pfannenstiel ridge or towards the Zürcher Oberland, where lanes run through farmland and woods with views of the Alps on clear days. Morning is the time for quiet roads, and in winter the lake can be shrouded in fog while the hills above are bright.

Take your time at the water. The lake is clean enough to swim in, and the little harbour at Feldbach is a pleasant place for a coffee and a look at the boats. If you are heading to Zurich, the Enge Alpenquai on the other side of the lake is the next stop, about 40 minutes by road with traffic. Keep an eye on the speed cameras along the main roads, and remember that Swiss fines are not small. A vignette is required for the motorways, but the lake roads do not need one.
t.chateau de montebello@46.2,9.0:
Bellinzona has three castles and a wall, and together they once decided who got through the Alps. The town sits at the head of the Ticino valley where several routes meet, including the roads to the San Bernardino and Gotthard passes, and whoever held it controlled the north-south traffic between Milan and the Swiss lands. Montebello is the middle one of the three, perched on a small hill on the east side of town, and the smallest of the trio. It was built in stages from the thirteenth century onward and expanded by the Visconti and Sforza dukes of Milan before the Swiss cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden took over around 1500.

The three castles and the walls that link them are a UNESCO site, and the view from Montebello is one of the best. The castle has a drawbridge, a keep and ramparts, and the inside holds a small museum and a courtyard with a neat lawn. From the walls you see the roofs of Bellinzona, the broad Magadino plain and the mountains on both sides. Opening hours and entry fees vary by season, so check before you plan a visit, but the grounds are rewarding in any case.

Getting here puts you in a pleasant corner of Switzerland. Ticino has a mild climate, and the town carries a southern feel, with palm trees, café terraces and Italian spoken on the streets. The ride south from the Gotthard or San Bernardino passes takes you down a long valley with chestnut woods and small villages, with plenty of hairpins and a clear change of mood as the vegetation becomes more Mediterranean. Traffic can be heavy on the A2 motorway, especially at weekends and during holiday periods, when queues form near the Gotthard tunnel, so a mountain road is often more fun than the highway.

Bellinzona has about 17,000 people and all the services a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and parking. Use the town as a base for the afternoon, with a risotto or a plate of polenta with braised meat as the local choice, and wine from the Merlot grapes grown on the slopes. The market on Saturday morning in the old town is lively and worth a look. Wind and rain are rare in the valley, and spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and fewer visitors than in midsummer.
t.village@46.9,6.9:
The label is simply Village, which tells you the scouts did not have a better name, so this entry is really about the shore of Lake Neuchâtel between Estavayer-le-Lac and Cortaillod. Here the lake is wide and calm, a long sliver of water set between the Jura mountains to the northwest and the rolling Fribourg country to the southeast. The southern shore is special. A broad belt of reeds, marsh and woodland runs along it, known as the Grande Cariçaie, which is the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland and a refuge for many birds, dragonflies and amphibians.

People have lived on this water for a very long time. The shores of Lake Neuchâtel and nearby lakes preserve the remains of prehistoric pile-dwelling settlements, built on wooden stilts by farming communities thousands of years ago. A group of such sites across the Alps was added to the UNESCO list, and the lake's waters, with low oxygen in the mud, kept the wood and objects in remarkable condition. Nothing dramatic remains for visitors to see in most places, but museums in the area show finds and reconstructions.

Estavayer-le-Lac, with about 5,000 people and a medieval old town, is the nearest proper town, with a castle, narrow lanes, a harbour and the restaurants where perch fillets are served with fries and a glass of local white. It is a good place for fuel, food and a stretch. The ride along this shore is smooth and relaxed: flat, with pleasant bends through farmland, villages with fountains and small vineyards on the sunny slopes. Traffic can pick up around the main towns and during summer weekends.

If you want a bigger ride, the Jura roads above the north shore climb to viewpoints with a sweep of the lake and, on a clear day, a line of Alps. Cortaillod and Bevaix on the Neuchâtel side belong to wine country, where the reds and whites carry the name of the village. Weather here can switch from sun to haze, and in autumn and winter a sea of fog often fills the lake basin while the heights above stay bright. Spring and September are the nicest times, and a short swim in the lake is possible in high summer, though the water stays cool.
t.speyer jewry court@49.3,8.4:
Speyer is known for its cathedral, a huge Romanesque church where several medieval emperors are buried, but a few hundred metres away lies a quieter site that matters just as much. The Judenhof, the Jewry Court, was the centre of the medieval Jewish community, and it contains the ruins of a synagogue from the early twelfth century and a mikveh, a ritual bath, that is generally regarded as the oldest in Europe. The mikveh is reached by steep steps down into a cool, vaulted chamber where groundwater still collects. It is a remarkable place, and the stone is beautifully worked.

Speyer, together with Worms and Mainz, formed a trio of Jewish communities in the Rhineland known by the acronym SchUM, from the first letters of their medieval Hebrew names. They were centres of learning and law that shaped Ashkenazi Jewish life for centuries, and the sites were added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2021. The story also includes persecution, as the communities suffered massacres in the time of the Crusades and again in the fourteenth century, and the history of the court is part of that.

The riding around Speyer is flat and easy. The city lies on the western bank of the Rhine, in the Palatinate, and the roads run through the plain with its asparagus fields, tobacco and orchards. To the west, the Pfälzer Wald and the Wine Route offer more varied riding, with vineyards and half-timbered villages. Within the city, expect cobbles near the cathedral, a busy centre and bridges across the Rhine, with traffic building at rush hour. Spring and early autumn are the pleasant seasons, and the city has a well-known market and festival culture.

Speyer has about 50,000 people and all the services you need, with fuel, supermarkets and many restaurants and cafés, and parking for bikes is easy outside the pedestrian centre. The Technik Museum on the edge of town is surprisingly big, with aircraft and a Soviet space shuttle on display. Try a Saumagen, the stuffed pig's stomach that is the Palatinate's most famous dish, if you are brave, or a slice of Zwiebelkuchen, onion tart, with a glass of young wine in the autumn. Walk down to the Rhine and look across the flat river towards the Black Forest on a clear day.
t.hochenacker pond@49.0,8.8:
Hermann Hesse ran away from Maulbronn after seven months. He was fourteen, a pupil at the Protestant seminary housed in the old monastery, and one day in 1892 he walked out and was found a day later in a field, cold and hungry. He later turned the experience into his novel Beneath the Wheel, and the monastery has not forgotten. The seminary buildings are still a school, and the cloister is among the best-preserved medieval monasteries in Germany, listed by UNESCO since 1993. Johannes Kepler and the poet Friedrich Hölderlin also studied here, which tells you the standard.

The pond at Hochenacker is one of a ring of artificial lakes around the monastery. The Cistercian monks who founded Maulbronn in the twelfth century were practical people, and they built a system of ponds, dams and ditches to supply the monastery with water, to power mills and to breed fish. Many of the ponds survive, and they are now wooded lakes where herons stand in the shallows and walkers follow the banks. It is easy to forget that the water is man-made, and the landscape has a settled, old feeling.

Maulbronn is in the Stromberg-Heuchelberg country, a low, rolling region of vineyards, orchards and mixed woods between the Black Forest and the Kraichgau. The roads here are narrow and winding, with farm traffic and cyclists, and the riding is relaxed rather than demanding. Spring brings blossom, and autumn colours the vineyards red and gold. After rain, the lower roads can be slick with mud and leaves, especially near fields.

Maulbronn, with about 7,000 people, has fuel and basic shops, while Mühlacker, a larger town, is closer to the motorway. A café near the monastery gate is the obvious place for coffee, and the area is known for Württemberg wines, such as Trollinger and Riesling, and for Maultaschen, the local filled pasta, which monks are said to have invented to hide meat from God during Lent. Whether or not that is true, it is a good story and a good lunch. Allow time for a stroll round the pond and a look at the monastery's cloister and fountain house.
t.aalkisten pond@49.0,8.8:
The name sounds like a joke, Eel Boxes, but it is a literal description. The Aalkistensee is another of the ponds that the Cistercian monks of Maulbronn built to hold fish, and a kiste was a wooden box or a pen in which eels were kept alive. The monks needed fish for the many days of the year when meat was forbidden, and a monastery that held land and water could supply its own table and sell the surplus. The Maulbronn system, with its dams, channels and sluices, was a clever piece of hydraulic engineering for the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and it works on the principle of gravity and careful levels.

You can still follow the logic on foot. Water from the surrounding hills is gathered in the upper ponds, passed down a chain of lakes, and finally reaches the monastery and its mills. The dams have survived because they were built to last, with clay cores, and the ponds provide a habitat for many birds, frogs and dragonflies. In spring the banks are bright with marsh marigolds, and in autumn the beech woods reflect in the water.

The country around is a mix of wooded ridges and vineyards, and the riding is gentle. The roads wind through small villages like Ölbronn-Dürrn and Knittlingen, the latter claiming to be the birthplace of the real Doctor Faustus, the sixteenth-century alchemist who inspired the legend. Traffic is light on the minor roads, though the area is popular with cyclists and walkers on fine weekends. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn.

Maulbronn is a short ride away, and has bakeries and cafés and a small supermarket. For fuel and a wider choice of shops, Mühlacker, with about 26,000 people, is the nearest larger town, and Knittlingen has basic services. If you have time, look in at the monastery itself, where the cloister, the refectory and the beautiful fountain house show how a medieval community looked after its body and soul. A local fish dish, a plate of trout from a nearby stream, is a fitting meal after a walk by the water.
t.chapelle notre dame du haut de ronchamp@:
Notre-Dame-du-Haut sits on a hill above Ronchamp, at the foot of the Vosges, and it is one of the strangest and most beautiful buildings of the twentieth century. Le Corbusier designed it in the early 1950s and it was consecrated in 1955. The white walls curve and lean, the roof sweeps up like a hull or a hat, and the thick walls are pierced by small deep windows filled with coloured glass. Inside, light falls in coloured pools on the floor, and the whole room feels carved rather than built. There has been a pilgrim chapel on this hill for centuries, and the earlier church was destroyed in the war, which is what led to the commission.

Ronchamp itself is a small former coal-mining town of just over three thousand people, and the mining past is visible in the museum and in the slag heaps. Lure, about ten kilometres off, is the closest real town, with fuel, shops and a reasonable range of cafes. In Ronchamp you will find small restaurants and a bakery or two. The hill is a short, steep climb from the village, with a car park near the top, and motorbikes can get close.

The country here is the southern edge of the Vosges, a landscape of rounded, forested hills, meadows and small lakes, and from the chapel terrace you can look south toward the Jura and, on a very clear day, even the Alps. The roads of the Haute-Saône around Ronchamp are quiet and winding, with tight turns through the woods, and they link easily to the Ballon d'Alsace to the north. Mornings are best; weekends and August fill the hill with coach parties.

The chapel charges an entry fee and has set opening hours that change with the season, so check before you go. Dress for weather, because a wind can whip across the exposed summit even in summer. A newer neighbour, a monastery for the Poor Clares designed by Renzo Piano, lies just below the hill, and is worth a look from outside.
t.castello del valentino@45.1,7.7:
The Castello del Valentino stands on the left bank of the Po in the middle of Turin, in a park where students lie about on the grass and rowing crews slide past on the river. It looks like a French château, with pitched grey roofs, corner towers and a courtyard open to the water, and that is no accident. It was built for the dukes of Savoy and transformed in the seventeenth century by Christine of France, widow of Duke Victor Amadeus I, who wanted something of home in her adopted capital. Later it became a school of engineering and then a faculty of architecture, which gives the courtyard a pleasant, slightly scruffy academic life.

The palace is part of a ring of Savoy residences around Turin that together form a World Heritage listing, and you can happily spend a day moving between them. The nearby Parco del Valentino has a reconstructed medieval village with a castle built for an exhibition in 1884, and a botanical garden. On warm evenings the riverbank fills with people drinking aperitivo and listening to music.

For riders, Turin is a city to arrive in carefully. The centre has a restricted traffic zone, the ZTL, where cameras fine vehicles that enter without permission, and motorbikes are not always exempt. Park outside it and walk or use the tram. The wide avenues around the Valentino are handsome, and the tree-lined roads along the river are a pleasure early on a Sunday. In the hills across the Po, a road climbs toward the Basilica of Superga with views over the whole city and the Alpine arc, a good riding reward after the grid of the town.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of this size. Turin invented the chocolate-and-hazelnut spread and the bicerin, a layered coffee, chocolate and cream drink served in small glasses in the old cafes. Pick spring or autumn: summer is hot and heavy, and winter fog can hide the mountains. The Alps, when they appear, are a remarkable backdrop.
t.egami village on naru island@32.9,128.9:
Egami is a small Catholic church on Naru Island in the Goto archipelago, off western Kyushu, and its story is one of the most remarkable in the history of Japanese Christianity. After missionaries arrived in the sixteenth century, the shogunate banned the faith and for about two and a half centuries persecuted believers. Some communities went underground, hiding their rosaries and their prayers in the guise of Buddhist or Shinto customs, and became known as the Hidden Christians. In the Goto islands, families who had fled from Nagasaki in the late eighteenth century cleared poor land and kept their faith quietly, and when the ban was lifted in the 1870s they came into the open.

The present Egami church, a small wooden building with a painted interior, was built in 1918 by the carpenter Tetsukawa Yosuke, who gave it the look of a Gothic nave with Japanese craftsmanship. It stands among camellias and ferns near the water. The church is part of the Hidden Christian sites in the Nagasaki region, recognised by UNESCO in 2018.

You cannot simply ride to Naru. Fukue, the main island of the Gotos, is reached by ferry or plane from Nagasaki or Fukuoka, and from Fukue you take a smaller boat across to Naru. Once there the roads are narrow, hilly and winding, with tight bends through forest and sudden views of the sea. Surfaces are generally fine but rough in places, and rain and sea mist make them slippery. Distances are small, but the ferry timetables rule everything, so plan around them. Fuel stations are limited and located mostly in Fukue, about eighteen kilometres away, so fill up there.

The islands are famous for camellia oil, udon noodles called Goto udon, and fresh fish. Visitors are asked to respect the church as a place of worship, to dress modestly and keep quiet, and to check opening times and any requirements for visiting. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with clear light and calm seas, while winter storms and summer typhoons can disrupt travel.
t.zurich@47.4,8.5:
Zurich is the polite, prosperous kind of city that keeps its history discreet. It lies at the northern end of Lake Zurich, where the Limmat river runs out of the lake and through the old town, and it began as a Roman customs post called Turicum on the hill now known as the Lindenhof. By the sixteenth century it was a centre of the Reformation under Huldrych Zwingli, who preached at the Grossmunster, the twin-towered church that still dominates the skyline. Across the river, the Fraumunster holds stained glass windows by Marc Chagall, and the light inside on a bright morning is worth a short detour.

As a rider you will probably come here by the motorway network, and the traffic can be heavy at rush hour, with trams, buses and bicycles all claiming their share of the road. Parking for motorbikes is generally reasonable if you look for the marked bays, and the old town is mostly pedestrian, so you will have to walk. Remember that Switzerland requires a vignette for motorways, and it applies to motorcycles too. Fuel is easy to find anywhere in the city, but it is not cheap, so filling up a little outside town can save money.

The Grand Tour of Switzerland starts here for many riders, and you can see why. The lake and the Uetliberg, a ridge that rises above the city and offers a long view over the water and the Alps on a clear day, make a good first view. From the city centre, roads lead south along the lakeshore towards Rapperswil and the Sihl valley, or east towards the hills of the Zurich Oberland, where narrow roads wind through apple orchards and farms.

Zurich is also a city for eating and wandering. Bahnhofstrasse is one of the most expensive shopping streets in the world, and the cafes along the Limmat are good for people-watching. Try a local classic such as Zurcher Geschnetzeltes, thin veal in a cream sauce, usually served with rosti. The lake is cold but clean enough for swimming in summer, and the bathing spots are full of locals after work.
t.st gallen@47.4,9.4:
St Gallen grew up around a hermit's cell. In the early seventh century an Irish monk called Gallus settled in a forest valley here, and a monastery grew up that became one of the great centres of learning in medieval Europe. Today the abbey district is a UNESCO site, with a baroque cathedral, an abbey library, and a plan of the cloister, a famous ninth-century drawing that shows what an ideal monastery should look like.

The library is the highlight. It is one of the oldest and finest in the world, with a hall of carved wood, painted ceilings and gleaming parquet floors, and it holds about a hundred and seventy thousand volumes, many of them medieval manuscripts. Visitors put on felt slippers to protect the floor, which gives the place a hushed quality. The town later became a centre of textile production, famous for embroidery and lace, and the grand merchants' houses of the old town, with their oriel windows, show how rich it became.

The town sits at about six hundred and seventy metres above sea level, in a hilly region between Lake Constance and the Appenzell hills, and the roads leaving it are the draw for riders. To the south, the Appenzell loop runs through green rolling country of farms, wooden houses and cow bells, with the Santis mountain towering above. Teufen is a village on the way, and the pass road up to Schwagalp climbs to the foot of the Santis. Traffic is moderate, and the surface is excellent, but the corners tighten quickly and the weather can change from sun to rain in minutes.

St Gallen has about seventy thousand people and every kind of service, with fuel, workshops and plenty of cafes. Try the St Galler Bratwurst, a veal sausage that is traditionally eaten without mustard, with a piece of bread called a Bürli. In the Appenzell hills, cheese is the local pride, with a spicy hard cheese washed in a secret herbal brine. Autumn is lovely, when the cows come down from the Alps in decorated processions. Spring brings fresh grass and blossom.
t.hurden seefeld@47.2,8.8:
Lake Zurich has a narrow waist, and at the waist stands a long causeway called the Seedamm. It links Rapperswil on the north shore with the Pfaffikon side on the south, and the peninsula of Hurden sits at its northern end. The upper lake, the Obersee, lies to the east, a quieter, shallower basin with reed beds, while the main lake stretches away to the west. Behind it all, the Glarus Alps and the Churfirsten rise to the horizon on a clear day.

Hurden Seefeld is one of the prehistoric pile dwelling sites that UNESCO listed in 2011 across six countries around the Alps. About five thousand years ago, and again in the Bronze Age, people built villages on timber piles in the shallows here, and the wet lakebed preserved wood, pottery and tools in remarkable condition. The Seefeld site lies in the shallows, and there is little to see from the shore, but divers and archaeologists have recovered remains. The rich finds show that this was a busy crossing even in prehistoric times.

The crossing is still busy. A wooden footbridge, the Holzsteg, re-opened in 2001 on the line of a medieval pilgrim route, carries walkers and cyclists across the water from Rapperswil to Hurden. It is part of the Way of St James, which leads to Einsiedeln and on to Spain. Riding across the Seedamm is a short, easy affair, with a straight, flat road, but traffic can be heavy, especially on summer weekends, and the lake wind can be strong.

Rapperswil, called the town of roses, has a castle on a hill and a lovely old town of arcades and cobbled lanes, and it has all the fuel, food and cafes you need, with Pfaffikon a smaller alternative. Perch fillets are the local dish in lake restaurants, and a glass of Zurich wine goes well with them. The hills above, towards Einsiedeln and the Sihlsee, offer curving roads and good views. Go early on a summer morning, when the water is still and the light is clear.
t.litzelstetten krahenhorn 32@47.7,9.2:
The Bodanrueck is a wooded peninsula that sticks out into the western end of Lake Constance, between the Uberlinger See and the Zeller See, and Litzelstetten is a small village on its southern side, close to the city of Konstanz. The Krahenhorn is a little promontory on the shore, and the whole area is an easy, gentle mix of orchards, forest, reeds and quiet beaches. Mainau Island, the flower island, lies just off the coast, with its palm trees and rhododendrons.

The site is another of the prehistoric pile dwelling settlements around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011. The shallow water at the edge of Lake Constance was a good place to live five thousand years ago, with fish, reeds and fertile soil, and villages of timber houses stood on stilts at the shore. On the German side of the lake the story is told at the open-air pile dwelling museum at Unteruhldingen, where reconstructed houses give a lively picture of Stone Age and Bronze Age life. At Litzelstetten itself, the remains lie beneath the water.

For a rider, the area is a pleasure. The roads around the peninsula wind through woods and farmland, with the lake appearing between the trees. They are narrow and not fast, and cyclists use them in numbers in summer, so patience is needed. Further west, the road to Uberlingen follows the shore, through small towns and vineyards, and the old town of Uberlingen has a lakeside promenade, a Gothic minster and a good choice of cafes. The city has fuel and shops, and Uhldingen-Muhlhofen, a bigger village, is another possibility.

Take the ferry from Meersburg to Konstanz if you want a change of pace. The crossing takes about fifteen minutes, and the view of the Alps across the lake is lovely on a clear day. Weather can be changeable, with sudden fog and cool winds off the water, but autumn often brings warm sun and soft light. Eat fresh whitefish, called Felchen, from the lake, and drink the local Muller-Thurgau. A swim in the clear lake is a fine way to end the ride.
t.saline de salins les bains@46.9,5.9:
Salt built Salins-les-Bains, and the name gives it away. A salt spring, rich in brine, rises in this narrow valley in the Jura, and people have been boiling it for salt since Roman times or earlier. In the Middle Ages the saltworks were among the largest in the region, and the spring made the town and its lords rich. The Grande Saline, the great saltworks, is now a museum, and together with the Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans, the neoclassical complex designed by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux, it has been listed by UNESCO.

The two sites were linked. Brine was piped from Salins to Arc-et-Senans, about twenty kilometres away, where forest wood was abundant for fuel, and the pipeline was an early feat of engineering. At Salins, you can walk through underground galleries, where the salt water was drawn from deep wells, and see old pumps and great wooden machines. The town sits in a deep valley, with steep slopes of forest, and two forts, Belin and Saint-Andre, built by the military engineer Vauban, stand guard on the hills above.

The riding in the area is wonderful. The Jura is a land of limestone plateaux, deep valleys and green hills, and the roads around Salins wind up and down with good surface and moderate traffic. The Cret de Chalam, a high ridge in the southern Jura, is a longer ride away, but the road up to the villages above Salins gives long views over the valley. Autumn is lovely, with golden beech forests, and in winter snow can close the higher roads.

The town has about three and a half thousand people, with fuel, bakeries, cafes and a thermal spa that uses the same salty water. Jura food is rich and satisfying: Comte cheese, smoked sausages from Morteau, Morbier cheese, and the strange yellow wine called vin jaune, which is aged for years under a film of yeast. Take time to look at the old town hall and the church, and consider a visit to the spa. A long dip in warm brine is a good remedy for a day in the saddle.
t.hautecombe@45.7,5.8:
Hautecombe Abbey stands on the western shore of Lac du Bourget, in Savoy, and it is almost impossible to reach without seeing the lake first. The Lac du Bourget is the largest natural lake entirely in France, a deep blue sheet under limestone cliffs, and the abbey sits on a small rocky spur above the water, with a boat landing and a church whose tower is visible across the bay. The poet Lamartine, who fell in love here in 1816, wrote a famous poem called Le Lac, about a lost love at this water.

The abbey was founded by Cistercian monks in the twelfth century, and in the following centuries it became the burial place of the counts and dukes of Savoy. The House of Savoy later became the royal family of Italy, and it is a strange fact that the last king of Italy, Umberto II, who died in exile in 1983, was buried here. The church is full of tombs and sculpture, and the style is a mixture of Gothic and nineteenth-century revival. The abbey was damaged in the Revolution and restored in the nineteenth century, and today it is home to a Catholic community that welcomes visitors.

The road there runs along the lake's western shore, a quiet and narrow route with views across the water to Aix-les-Bains, and traffic can build in summer. The surface is generally good, with gentle bends rather than anything dramatic. Further north, the Rhone flows through the marshes of Chautagne, and the village of Chanaz has a canal that links the lake to the river. Mont du Chat, the ridge on the west side, offers a steep, winding road for those who want more of a challenge.

Brison-Saint-Innocent and Chatillon are the nearest villages with a few thousand people, and Aix-les-Bains, on the eastern shore, is a spa town with everything you need, including fuel. Try fish from the lake, such as perch and omble chevalier, served with local white wine. Quiet early mornings give the best light on the water, and the abbey itself is calm outside peak hours. Dress modestly, and be prepared to speak softly inside the church.
t.la citadelle@47.2,6.0:
Besancon sits in a tight loop of the Doubs river, almost an island, and above the loop a great rock rises more than a hundred metres. On top of it stands the Citadel, the fortress that the military engineer Vauban built for Louis XIV after the king captured the region from Spain in 1674. It is one of the twelve fortified sites that UNESCO listed together in 2008 as the Fortifications of Vauban, and it is a fine example of his work, with thick walls, bastions and long ramparts that follow the line of the rock.

Vauban designed the fortress to dominate the town and the river, and its walls and bastions look inwards as well as outwards, as a warning to the local people. From the ramparts you look out over the roofs of the old town, the cathedral tower and the green loop of the river, with the hills of the Jura beyond. Inside, the Citadel holds three museums, a zoo and a garden, which makes it a popular family outing, and you could spend several hours walking the walls.

The city is a pleasant, lively place, with about a hundred and thirty thousand people and a big student population. It is the birthplace of Victor Hugo, who was born here in 1802, and of the Lumiere brothers, who invented the cinema. It was also the heart of French watchmaking, and the tradition survives in a museum of time. The old town is full of Renaissance houses and shaded squares, and the river is a good place for a walk.

Riding here is easy. The roads climb out of the Doubs valley into forested hills, and a short ride in any direction brings you to the Jura, with its plateaux and deep valleys. The streets in the centre are narrow and sometimes steep, so park the bike near the river and walk up. Fuel is plentiful on the edges of town, with Beure and other villages nearby. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good light. Taste a plate of Comte cheese and a glass of Arbois wine, and look at the view from the ramparts.
t.exhibition grounds 1901@49.9,8.7:
In 1899 the Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse did something unusual for a ruler: he invited a group of young artists to Darmstadt and gave them a hill to build on. The Mathildenhohe, a low rise on the edge of the old town, became an artists' colony where architects, painters and designers could live, work and experiment. The first great exhibition, in 1901, was called A Document of German Art, and the houses and studios built for it were part of the show. UNESCO listed the colony as a World Heritage site in 2021.

The leading figure was the Austrian architect Joseph Maria Olbrich, who designed the Ernst Ludwig House with its great arched entrance, the exhibition halls and the Wedding Tower, a tall brick tower with a five-fingered top, built in 1908 to mark the Grand Duke's marriage. Peter Behrens, who later became a pioneer of industrial design, built his own house on the hill. Elsewhere, the gold-domed Russian Chapel, built for the Tsar's family, adds a strange touch of Orthodox colour. The style is Jugendstil, the German form of Art Nouveau, with flowing lines, stylised plants and patterned tiles.

Darmstadt is a university town with about a hundred and forty thousand people, and the Mathildenhohe is a short walk from the centre. For riders, the city is a good starting point for the Odenwald, the hilly forested area to the south and east, with roads that curve through valleys and over ridges, and for the Bergstrasse, the old road along the western edge of the hills, famous for blossom in spring. Weiterstadt, to the north, is a smaller town, and there are fuel stations all around the city.

Traffic in Darmstadt is moderate, and parking for motorbikes on the edge of the old town is easy. Enjoy a coffee in the park, with the plane trees and lily pond, before you set off. Spring brings blossom and autumn brings colour, and the brick of the Wedding Tower glows in low sun. Take your time to walk around the buildings, which reward careful looking.
t.building remains north of gotzingen@49.5:
The Odenwald is old, rounded country, a forested upland between the Rhine and the Main, and the Limes crosses its eastern edge in a line so straight that it looks drawn with a ruler. Near Gotzingen, a village in the Buchen district of Baden-Wurttemberg, the frontier ran past a small Roman building that archaeologists found in the fields. The remains are the foundations of a small military station or a farm building, in a place where the soldiers lived close to the line. It is a modest site, but it shows that the frontier was more than a wall.

The Odenwald Limes was the earliest part of the Upper German frontier, built in the 150s AD when the Romans pushed the border forward from the Main to the Neckar. The soldiers manned watchtowers set within sight of one another and lived in small forts. Local people called the line the Devil's Wall for centuries. UNESCO listed the Limes in 2005, and this section is marked with posts and paths.

Buchen, the nearest big town, has about nineteen thousand people and has fuel, shops and cafes, and Seckach is a smaller place beside it. The countryside is the Bauland, a patchwork of fields, orchards and small woods in a gentle landscape, and the roads run over low hills with long views and quiet villages. The surface is generally good, and the bends are mild, with very little traffic. Spring brings blossom, and autumn brings mist and colour.

For a longer ride, the hills of the Odenwald to the west offer more curves, with good roads through beech and oak forest and past old castles on the Neckar. Take care at dusk, when deer cross the road. The Limes walking trail follows the line for many kilometres, and a short stroll along it is a good way to stretch before a long ride. The Bauland is a quiet place that few visitors notice, and its people are friendly and unhurried. Local inns serve solid food, with roast pork, dumplings and a glass of beer or cider.
t.residenz@49.8,9.9:
The Residenz in Wurzburg is a palace that people go to see for a staircase. Balthasar Neumann, one of the great architects of the baroque, designed it for the prince-bishops of Wurzburg, who ruled this part of Franconia, and it was built between 1720 and 1744. The grand staircase is a single, unsupported vault, and above it, covering the whole ceiling, is a fresco by the Venetian painter Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, painted in 1752 and 1753. It shows the four continents, with Apollo and the gods above, and at roughly 600 square metres it is one of the largest ceiling paintings in the world.

The palace was badly damaged on 16 March 1945, when British bombers destroyed most of the city in a single night. The roof burned, but the great vault and its fresco survived, thanks to emergency repairs by the local people, and the building was restored over the following decades. UNESCO listed it in 1981, and it is now a magnificent museum with rooms of mirrors, gilding and stucco. The Hofgarten behind it is a pleasant place for a walk.

Wurzburg sits on the river Main, in the middle of a wine region, and the city is full of wine. The local wine, Franken, is dry and crisp, and it is sold in a squat, flat bottle called a Bocksbeutel. You can taste it in wine bars and at the old Bürgerspital cellars. The old bridge across the Main is lined with statues of saints, and the fortress of Marienberg stands above on the opposite bank. The city has about a hundred and thirty thousand people, and Hochberg is a smaller town on the western side.

Wurzburg is the start of the Romantic Road, a famous tourist route that runs south through medieval towns to the Alps. The riding around the city is gentle, with roads through vineyards and woods, and the Main valley is pretty. Fuel and food are easy. In the city, park near the edge, as the centre has many one-way streets. Autumn, when the grapes are harvested, is a wonderful time to visit.
t.les climats du vignoble de bourgogne dij:
Dijon sits at the top of the Côte d'Or, where the Burgundian plain meets the long limestone escarpment that carries some of the most expensive vineyards in the world. The UNESCO listing called the Climats of Burgundy covers those vineyards and the towns that grew around them, and the label's last word, cut short, means Dijon itself, the old ducal capital where the Valois dukes ruled a territory that rivalled the French crown. The Palace of the Dukes and Estates, now a museum and town hall, still dominates the central square, and the pedestrian streets around it are full of half-timbered houses and fine stone doorways.

A climat, in Burgundian speech, is a named plot of vineyard, with its own soil, slope and microclimate recognised over centuries, mostly through the work of Cistercian monks at Cîteaux and Cluniac monks elsewhere. The point of the listing is that the label on the bottle is a piece of geography, and that two vines a few metres apart can give wines of different price. For a rider that means the Route des Grands Crus, the D974, which heads south from Dijon through Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée and Nuits-Saint-Georges to Beaune and onward, with the names of famous wines flashing past on road signs.

The riding is gentle rather than dramatic, a procession of low stone villages, vineyard walls and small churches. Turn off onto the little lanes through the vines, where you can ride slowly and see the individual plots, usually marked by stone walls and the occasional cross. Late September and October bring harvest traffic and tractors, but also golden leaves and the smell of crushed grapes. In July the hills shimmer, and on winter mornings frost can sit on the slope.

Dijon is a city of about a hundred and fifty thousand, so fuel, parking and food are easy. Mustard has been made here since the Middle Ages, and the gingerbread called pain d'épices is a local specialty, along with the blackcurrant liqueur crème de cassis that, mixed with white wine, became the kir named after a wartime mayor, Canon Félix Kir. Look for the little owl carved on the wall of Notre-Dame church, which people stroke for luck. Take care in the city, where tram tracks and cobbles can catch a wheel.
t.residences of the royal house of savoy@4:
Turin was the capital of a duchy, then a kingdom, and finally, from 1861 until 1865, of the new Italy, and the Savoy family left a ring of palaces and hunting lodges around it that UNESCO lists together. The Royal Palace in the centre, the Palazzo Madama, the vast Reggia di Venaria on the northern edge, the Stupinigi hunting lodge to the south-west and the Superga basilica on its hill are the best known.

Turin has a rational, rather austere beauty, a grid of arcaded streets laid out under Roman and then baroque plans, with the Alps filling the western sky when the air is clear. On a motorcycle the centre is easy and fast, but beware the limited traffic zones, which are enforced with cameras and which cost visitors a fine months later; check with your hotel or the municipal map. Trams and cobbles can be slick when wet. Park in the paid bays or garages near Piazza Castello, and walk from there.

For riding, the hill road to Superga is the treat. It winds up through trees from the east bank of the Po, with views that open suddenly over the city, and the basilica at the top was built after the Savoys won the siege of Turin in 1706. The football story is also here: in 1949 the plane carrying the great Torino team crashed into the hill, and a memorial stands beside the church. Beyond, the Langhe and Monferrato wine hills lie an hour to the south-east, full of good riding in autumn.

The city has nearly nine hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and repairs are plentiful. Coffee is serious in Turin, and the bicerin, a drink of espresso, chocolate and cream served in a small glass, is the local ritual. Gianduiotti chocolates, aperitivo with vermouth, and agnolotti are the obvious tastes. The Egyptian Museum is one of the best in the world outside Cairo. The Savoy palaces are best visited in spring or autumn, when the gardens are in colour and the crowds are thinner.
t.nagasaki shipyard kosuge slip dock@32.7,:
Nagasaki has always lived off its harbour, and the harbour is a long, deep, hill-framed bay that looks, from the hillside streets, like a Scottish loch with a Japanese accent. The Kosuge Slip Dock sits on the eastern shore, a stone-lined cradle where ships were once hauled out of the water for repair. It dates from the very start of the Meiji era, the late 1860s, and was built with the help of Scottish engineers and a Scottish merchant, Thomas Glover. Mitsubishi took over the yard in the 1880s and the company is still building ships on the same shoreline today, which is why most of the neighbourhood is working industry rather than a museum.

This is a quiet corner of a loud industrial story. The stonework is fitted with great care and has the neat, almost fussy look of Victorian dock engineering, surrounded by brick sheds and cranes. Around the bay you can also spot the giant cantilever crane, a monster from the early twentieth century, and the old pattern-shop buildings that now carry a World Heritage label as part of the Meiji industrial sites group. It is the sort of place a naval architect would weep over and an ordinary rider would walk past in ten minutes.

Riding in Nagasaki is a lesson in gradients. The city climbs the hills in tight terraces and the roads can be astonishingly steep, with hairpins and one-way lanes hardly wider than a bike and a bicycle. Trams still rattle along the main streets. Fuel and food are no problem, as this is a city of four hundred thousand, and you should treat it as a place for slow, low-gear pottering. Head up Mount Inasa after dark if the weather allows; the harbour lights from there are the best view in Kyushu.

Do not skip the food: champon, a noodle soup piled with seafood and vegetables, and sara udon with its crispy fried noodles both grew out of the Chinese community here, and castella sponge cake came with Portuguese traders. The city was the only Japanese port open to Europeans during the long isolation, through the Dutch trading post on the island of Dejima, which is why it feels different from anywhere else in the country.

Spring and autumn are gentle. Summers are muggy, and typhoons in September can shut the roads for a day.
t.glover house and office@32.7,129.9:
Thomas Blake Glover arrived in Nagasaki in 1859 as a young Scot in his early twenties, and within a decade he had become one of the most influential foreigners in Japan. His house stands on Minamiyamate hill above the harbour, built in the early 1860s, and it is the oldest surviving Western-style building in the country. It has wide verandas, a stone-flagged garden and a view of the bay that must have been a sales tool in itself. Glover traded tea and ships and, more controversially, guns and warships, supplying the domains that overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate. He also helped smuggle young Choshu samurai out of Japan to study in London, and later worked with Mitsubishi on shipbuilding. Some historians say he brought the Industrial Revolution to Japan through the back door.

The house is now part of Glover Garden, a hillside park with other old foreign residences, and it forms part of the Meiji industrial sites on the World Heritage list. The grounds are laid out as a gentle uphill stroll, with ponds, flower beds and views over Mitsubishi's shipyards across the water. A short walk away is Oura Church, the oldest surviving Gothic-style wooden church in Japan, which is also where the so-called hidden Christians revealed themselves to a French priest in 1865 after more than two centuries of secret worship.

Nagasaki is not a place for fast riding. The streets near the garden are steep and tight, cars park half on the pavement and the trams grind along the main road, so come by bike if you can manage hills and leave it at the bottom if you cannot. The city is large enough for any fuel, food or repair, and you will find parking more of a challenge than petrol.

The legend of Madame Butterfly is associated with the garden, because the opera is set in Nagasaki and tourist guides like to connect it to Glover's Japanese wife. Treat that as folklore, not fact. What is factual is the harbour view, still among the finest in Japan.

Visit in spring for the azaleas, in autumn for the clear air, or at dusk when the harbour lights come on.
t.barbara baths@49.8,6.6:
Trier is the city that Germans call the oldest in the country, and the Barbara Baths are among the reasons it can say so with a straight face. Built in the second century AD, when Augusta Treverorum was one of the leading cities of the Roman north, they were once among the largest bathing complexes anywhere outside Rome, a vast rectangle of hot rooms, cold plunges, exercise yards and furnace tunnels. Later centuries treated the building as a quarry, and medieval Trier built houses and a monastery over parts of it, which is why what survives is a maze of walls, arches and basement passages rather than a roofed hall. Walk down into the underground service tunnels and you can see the sooty vaults where slaves tended the fires.

The ruin is right in the south of the old town, within a short walk of the Roman bridge and the amphitheatre, and it forms part of the Roman monuments of Trier that were listed by UNESCO in 1986 along with the Porta Nigra, the Basilica of Constantine and the cathedral. Spend a morning with all of them and you understand why Constantine liked the place.

For a rider, Trier is a joy because of what surrounds it. The Moselle winds west and northeast through steep vineyards, and the road along the river, with its long smooth bends, castles on the ridges and wine villages every few kilometres, is one of the best slow rides in Germany. In the other direction the Hunsruck and the Eifel give you forest roads, climbs and more demanding twisties. Fuel is plentiful in a city of a hundred thousand, and Luxembourg is only a short ride away, where petrol is often cheaper.

Riesling is the wine here, grown on slate slopes so steep that harvest is done by hand. Stop for a glass in a village on the river and plan to sleep over. The city also claims Karl Marx as a native son, with his birthplace now a museum.

April brings blossom on the slopes, September and October the harvest and the golden colours. Summer weekends are busy. Winters are grey but cheap and quiet, and the Christmas market under the Roman gate is excellent.
t.furka pass@46.6,8.4:
Furka is one of the Alps' great stage roads: 2,429 metres of switchbacks linking Uri and Valais, with the Rhône Glacier at the western foot. From Andermatt the road climbs through the high Urseren valley, past Realp, up a series of hairpins to a pass where the air is thin and cold, and the views unfold across rock, snow and sky. The mountains here are bare and grand, and the sense of altitude is real.

The glacier is the star. The Rhône starts here as a meltwater stream under the ice, and until recent decades the glacier tongue reached down almost to the road at Gletsch. It has retreated sharply and now sits high on the slope, with an ice grotto cut into it each summer. The old Hotel Belvédère, a grand building from the days of the stagecoach, stands at a bend and became famous when it appeared in the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger, in which Bond's Aston Martin raced the Furka's bends.

Riding it is a pleasure and a test. Bends are tight and well engineered, the tarmac is generally good, and the traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with buses, cars and motorbikes sharing hairpins. Go early or late for the best light and emptier road. Weather matters: cold mornings, sudden fog or snow even in summer, and rain on the Valais side. The pass is closed in winter and typically reopens in late spring, though dates vary with snowfall, so check before planning.

Andermatt, about fifteen kilometres east, and Airolo, a similar distance to the south through the Gotthard side, are the closest fuel stops, so fill up beforehand. Mountain restaurants at the summit serve coffee, soup and apple pie, and the cold means you will want them. Wear a warm layer under your jacket and keep a visor-cleaning cloth handy.
t.altdorf@46.9,8.6:
Altdorf is the capital of the canton of Uri, a small town at the head of Lake Lucerne's southern arm where the Reuss river leaves the mountains and the Gotthard route begins. It is a practical, low-key place, flat and sheltered, with a pretty centre and a roar of traffic nearby from the motorway, and it is the sort of town where riders refill the tank, buy a coffee and look up at the wall of peaks above.

The centre of attention is Wilhelm Tell. The legend says that Tell, a crossbowman from Uri, was forced by the tyrannical Austrian bailiff Gessler to shoot an apple from his son's head, and that he later killed Gessler and helped spark the Swiss rebellion. In the main square stands a statue of Tell and his son, put up in the 1890s, and the story is told with pride. Historians doubt that Tell ever existed, but locals tend to treat that as irrelevant.

The roads from here are some of the best in Switzerland. South, the Gotthard route climbs through the Reuss valley, with its old stone bridges and the Devil's Bridge legend. East, the Klausen pass links to Glarus, and the Susten pass heads west toward Meiringen, with its sweeping bends and glacier views, closed in winter. Altdorf is also the gateway to the Axenstrasse, a lake-side road cut through rock, with tunnels, balconies and glimpses of the water far below. These are famous riding routes, and they get busy on sunny weekends.

Fuel is straightforward here, with several stations, and the town has plenty of cafes and bakeries. Altdorf lies at only 458 metres, so it warms up early, though the mountain passes above are still snowed up in spring. Give yourself time for breakfast before the big climbs. Note that the Gotthard road tunnel can have long queues, so plan around the holiday traffic.
t.lausanne@46.5,6.6:
Lausanne tips down a steep hillside to Lake Geneva, and you feel it in your legs, your brakes and your bike's low gears.
