The city sprawls over three hills and a lake front, with the old town at the top and the harbour district of Ouchy at the bottom, joined by one of the world's smallest metro systems. The Gothic cathedral looks out over the roofs and the water toward the French Alps across the lake.

Lausanne has been the home of the International Olympic Committee since 1915, and the Olympic Museum, near the lakeside, shows the story of the Games in a handsome setting. The city is also a centre of learning, with a major university and a technical institute, which gives it a youthful side. Food and wine are the regular pleasures, with cheese fondue, filets of perch from the lake and the pale white wine of the region on every menu.

The ride that starts here is the Lavaux, a hillside of terraced vineyards that tumbles down to the lake east of the city. Monks from the Cistercian order began building the terraces in the twelfth century, and they are now a World Heritage Site. The road threads between stone walls, through villages such as Cully, Epesses and Chexbres, with narrow lanes and tight bends. The grape is mainly chasselas, and the hillside faces south, so it soaks up the sun and reflects the light from the lake, which helps ripen the grapes. The best time is autumn, during the harvest, when the leaves turn gold and the air smells of fermenting juice, though spring and summer are lovely too.

The city has all you need: fuel stations around the edges, plenty of parking for bikes, and lakeside cafes. Traffic can be heavy at rush hour, and some of the old-town streets are steep cobbles, so be careful when wet. Plan a break at one of the wine cellars in the Lavaux, but keep the helmet on until the end of the day.
t.tasch for zermatt@46.1,7.8:
Täsch is a place most people pass through on the way to somewhere more famous, and it has made peace with that. Zermatt, a few kilometres up the valley, is closed to private cars, so the road ends here, at a large terminal beside the railway, where visitors leave their vehicles and ride the shuttle train for around twelve minutes to the village under the Matterhorn. For a motorcyclist the arrangement is simple. Park at the terminal, change out of the leathers, and take the train in.

The drive up the Mattertal is rewarding in itself. From the Rhône valley at Visp the road follows the Vispa river upstream, narrow and steep sided, through tunnels and past avalanche galleries, with the rail line wrapping around you. At Randa the cliffs show scars of the rockfall in 1991, when millions of cubic metres of mountain collapsed across the valley floor, and a long suspension footbridge, said to be among the longest in the world, crosses the gorge nearby. Surfaces are good, but the road is narrow, and tour buses and delivery vans share it, so take your time and leave early.

The mountain is the star. The Matterhorn rises to 4,478 metres, a pyramid of dark rock that looks almost too perfect to be real, and it was first climbed in 1865 by Edward Whymper and his party, four of whom died on the way down when a rope broke. The tragedy shocked Victorian Britain, and made the peak more famous. It still holds the imagination, especially at dawn when the first light turns the summit pink.

Before you head up the valley, fill the tank down the valley in or near Visp, because fuel supplies in the narrow upper valley are limited and expensive. Täsch has plenty of parking and some restaurants and shops, though most people spend their nights in Zermatt. The roads here are fully usable in summer and mostly clear in winter, but heavy snow can close the valley, so check reports. Autumn gives clear air, golden larch woods and fewer visitors.
t.innertkirchen@46.7,8.2:
Innertkirchen sits at 625 metres where the Haslital opens out, and in practice it is a junction. Two famous passes start here, the Grimsel climbing southeast toward the Rhône glacier and the Susten rising east toward the Reuss valley, and the roads divide at the edge of the village. The Aare river runs through, fresh from the glaciers, and just downstream the Aare Gorge cuts a narrow slot of polished limestone that can be walked on timber galleries. The valley is also the heart of the Oberhasli hydropower scheme, with turbines and tunnels bored deep inside the mountains, which explains the large grey buildings you pass.

Four kilometres down the valley is Meiringen, the bigger place and the one with more services. The town says it invented the meringue, a claim that is hard to prove but cheerfully repeated in every bakery window. It also has a more literary link. Arthur Conan Doyle sent Sherlock Holmes and Professor Moriarty over the nearby Reichenbach Falls in 1893, and there is a small Holmes museum in town and a funicular to the falls. For fuel, groceries and a proper meal, Meiringen is the answer, and a stop here before the passes is sound planning.

The riding from Innertkirchen is as good as Swiss riding gets. Susten has long, perfectly graded curves up to a summit near 2,224 metres, with views of glaciers, while Grimsel goes up to around 2,164 metres past big reservoirs and rock walls before reaching the Furka and Nufenen roads beyond. Surfaces are good, but traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, and weather turns quickly, with cold rain or fog at the top while the valley basks. The passes close in winter, typically from around late October or November until late spring or early June, with dates depending on snow, so check before you plan a trip.

Morning is the best time to leave, when the air is cold and the tarmac empty. Pack a warm layer, because even in July the summits can be close to freezing, and keep a hand on the fuel gauge, since there are no stations on the passes themselves.
t.st moritz@46.5,9.8:
St. Moritz is not subtle, and the world's most famous winter resort does not intend to be. It sits at about 1,800 metres in the Upper Engadine, on a sunlit shelf above a lake, with ranges of white peaks on every side and a record of sunny days that the tourist board advertises with some pride. Its mineral springs were known in the Bronze Age, and in the Middle Ages pilgrims came to drink the water. Winter tourism, legend says, started in 1864 when the hotelier Johannes Badrutt bet English summer guests that they would enjoy the Alps in the snow. The town has hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1928 and 1948, and the Cresta Run, an ice toboggan track, still runs every winter.

Today the centre is hotels, designer shops and some very expensive cars, which makes a dusty motorcycle feel agreeably subversive. It is still worth a stop. Walk the lakeshore, look back at the town from the lower end, and notice how the light makes everything seem sharp and bright. The valley beyond is gentler than many Swiss valleys, with a chain of lakes along the floor from Maloja to Celerina.

For riders, St. Moritz is a star hub for passes. The Julier Pass heads northeast to the Albula valley, and the Bernina road climbs south to a pass of around 2,300 metres before dropping to Italy at Tirano, with the Rhaetian Railway beside it for much of the way. West, the Maloja road descends to Chiavenna through a dramatic series of hairpins. All are well surfaced and have good views, but weather in the high Alps changes fast. Summer is the easy season, and snow can close passes at any time from October through spring.

Fuel is available in the town and nearby villages, though prices are among the highest in the country. Cafés in the centre serve the local Engadiner nusstorte, a rich pastry filled with caramel and walnuts, which is a good reason to stop. Leave time for a short walk beside the lake in the evening.
t.lindau@47.6,9.7:
Lindau is an island that behaves like a postcard. The old town sits on a small piece of land in the eastern corner of Lake Constance, linked to the mainland by a causeway and a railway bridge, with a harbour entrance guarded by two monuments, a stone lighthouse and a tall statue of the Bavarian lion. Boats cross to Bregenz in Austria and to the Swiss shore, and behind the harbour wall are cobbled streets, painted houses and cafés that spill onto the quay. The Bodensee, as the Germans call it, is the third largest lake in Central Europe and the surrounding land is orchard country, apple trees and vineyards, with the Alps rising over the south shore on a clear day.

The town has a quietly distinguished record. Lindau was a free imperial city in the Middle Ages, and an old tower that once served as a lighthouse still stands at the harbour. Since 1951 it has hosted a meeting each summer where Nobel laureates talk with young scientists. For the motorcyclist it is also the starting point of the German Alpine Road, which heads east along the foot of the mountains toward Berchtesgaden near the Austrian border, a long journey through the Allgäu and Upper Bavaria.

The ride up toward Schwägalp is a typical Alpine foothills loop, with smooth bends through meadows and forest, church towers appearing between hills, and the snowy peaks of the Säntis in view. Surfaces are generally excellent, but the area is popular, and weekends bring caravans, cyclists and other riders, so go early. Austrian and Swiss borders are close, and each country has its own rules for vignettes and speed limits, so plan your route accordingly. Fog can sit on the lake until midmorning in autumn and spring.

Fuel is easy in Lindau's mainland districts and in nearby towns, while the island itself is for walking. Coffee and cake beside the harbour is the usual reward, and freshly caught lake whitefish, called Felchen, is the local fish. Evening is a good time to sit at the water's edge and watch the sun go down behind the mountains across the lake.
t.sion@46.2,7.4:
Sion is the capital of the Valais, the Swiss canton that runs along the upper Rhône between two walls of high mountains, and it is dominated by two hills. On one, the ruins of the Tourbillon castle crown the rock, and on the other, the fortified church of Valère holds what is said to be the oldest playable pipe organ in the world, dating from around the fifteenth century. You climb to it by a steep stone lane, and in summer the organ is used for a festival. The two hills rise straight out of the town and give Sion a theatrical appearance, like a backdrop for something medieval.

Around the town the valley floor is flat and wide, but the hillsides are covered in terraced vineyards that climb surprisingly high up the slope. The Valais is the driest part of Switzerland, because the mountains wring the rain out of the clouds before they arrive, and the vines get abundant sun. Fendant, made from chasselas grapes, is the local white, and the region also produces Petite Arvine, Cornalin and Humagne Rouge, all wines you rarely see abroad. Sion's old town has narrow streets, small wine bars and stalls selling raclette, the melted cheese scraped onto potatoes that the Valais proudly claims as its own.

The Valais Wine Road is a pleasure for riders. It threads between the main valley highway and the vineyards on the northern slope, along narrow lanes through villages, stone terraces and orchards, with the Alps rising on the far side. The roads are small and well kept, but they carry farm vehicles and walkers, so ride slowly, especially in autumn at harvest time, when tractors and pickers fill the lanes. The warm sunny weather makes spring and early autumn ideal, while summer can be hot, and winter is generally dry but cold.

Sion has fuel, shops, workshops and a good selection of restaurants, and it is also a transport hub, with the Simplon road toward Italy and the Rhône valley highway nearby. Many riders use it as a base for the passes of the Valais, including the Grand St Bernard to the southwest. Set aside an hour for Valère, and allow another for tasting a glass or two in the evening, once the bike is parked.
t.chamonix@45.9,6.9:
Mont Blanc does not so much loom over Chamonix as lean on it. The valley is a deep, narrow trench of the Arve river with the highest peak in the Alps, just under 4,810 metres, standing right at the top of it, and the glaciers come down so close that you can see the cracks in the ice from the main street. Modern mountaineering has a birthday here. In 1786 two local men, Jacques Balmat and Michel Paccard, reached the summit for the first time, and the town has been selling the idea of going up high ever since. In 1924 it also hosted the first Winter Olympics.

You do not need to be a climber to feel the scale. The cable car from the valley to the Aiguille du Midi rises to about 3,840 metres in a single, rather pale-faced journey, and the rack railway to the Montenvers drops you at the edge of the Mer de Glace, the longest glacier in France, which has visibly shrunk over the last few decades. Down in the centre, the statue of Balmat pointing at the summit stands in the middle of the square, and the cafés are full of people in boots and sunburn.

The roads are a mixed blessing. North, the Col des Montets climbs gently through Argentière and Vallorcine to the Swiss border, and onward over the Col de la Forclaz to the Rhône valley, a pleasant and well-surfaced ride. South, the road runs down the valley through Les Houches toward Sallanches. In summer, traffic is heavy, and lorries bound for the Mont Blanc tunnel, which opened in 1965 and runs 11.6 kilometres to Italy, fill the valley road. After the 1999 fire in the tunnel, safety rules were tightened. Go early, since the light is gentle and the air is cold.

Chamonix has plenty of fuel, bike-friendly cafés and rental shops. Expect high prices, especially in July and August, and avoid parking on streets marked for residents or pedestrians. Afternoon thunderstorms in the mountains can arrive quickly, so keep an eye on the clouds. On a clear evening, sit by the river as the last light climbs the Aiguilles and turns the granite pink.
t.bregenz@47.5,9.8:
Bregenz is where Austria touches Lake Constance, the Bodensee, and the town makes the most of a small piece of shoreline. The lake is huge, shared with Germany and Switzerland, and on a clear day the far shore melts into haze. Behind the town the Pfänder rises to just over a thousand metres, with a cable car that carries you from the harbour to a ridge in a few minutes, and from the top you see the whole lake, the Rhine delta, the Alps and, with luck, a good part of three countries at once.

The best-known thing here is the festival. Each summer an opera is staged on a floating platform in the lake, with a set so large it seems to belong to a different scale of theatre, and the audience sits on a steep grandstand on the shore. The tradition goes back to the 1940s, and the sets keep getting more ambitious. The town also has the Kunsthaus, a glass box designed by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, which glows at night like a lantern. Higher up lies the Oberstadt, the old town, with the Martinsturm, a tower with a big onion dome from the seventeenth century. The Romans called the place Brigantium, and the lake was a highway for them long before it was a holiday destination.

For a rider the town is a gateway. East of it, the Bregenzerwald rolls out in green valleys of wooden farmhouses, cheese dairies and good, flowing roads that climb toward Alpine passes. West, you can follow the lake to Switzerland or north to Germany along the shore. Traffic in town can be heavy on summer weekends, and the lakeside road clogs when the weather is warm. Föhn, the warm southerly wind, sometimes blows through here, bringing sharp clear views and a mildly restless mood.

Bregenz has about thirty thousand people and every service: fuel stations on the ring road, bakeries, lakeside cafés where a coffee costs more than it should and is still worth it. Parking for bikes is easier near the harbour than in the old town. Autumn is calm and often clear, when the lake mist burns off by noon and the leaves turn on the hills. Spring brings fruit blossom around the lake and a general feeling of release after winter.
t.neuchatel@47.0,6.9:
Neuchâtel looks across its lake from a long, gentle shoreline, with the Jura mountains rising behind and, on a clear day, the Bernese Alps floating above the far side like a distant promise. The town takes its yellowish tint from the local limestone, a warm honey colour in evening light, and its centre is a tidy lattice of old lanes between the castle and the lakefront. The castle and the Collegiate church sit together on a small hill above the old town, and it was from here that the counts, and later the Prussian kings, ruled. Neuchâtel was under the Prussian crown from 1707 until a republican revolution in 1848, a curious detail that explains its odd, independent character.

This is a town of watchmakers, scholars and wine. The hills along the lake are lined with vineyards, and the local white, made from Chasselas, is crisp and slightly spritzy, while the pale pink Œil de Perdrix is a regional curiosity. In the nearby Val-de-Travers, the absinthe once banned across Europe was distilled in secret and is now legal again, with a gentle smugness. Rousseau lived in the area for a while, and Le Corbusier was born a short way up the hill in La Chaux-de-Fonds.

As a riding base, Neuchâtel works nicely as either end of a day. To the north, roads climb up from the lake through the vineyards to the Jura plateau, with long, open curves, pastures and spruce, and the rolling uplands of the Val-de-Ruz and the Chaumont ridge are quiet and pleasant. Along the shore, the lake road toward Yverdon or Biel is flat and quick but busy. The Swiss vignette is needed for motorways, and you should assume speed cameras are common and tolerance is low.

Fuel, food and parking are all easy in a town of over thirty thousand, though central parking is metered. Lake fish, particularly perch fillets, are the dish to order, and the lakeside promenade makes a good place for a slow coffee before the climb into the Jura. In winter, be alert for ice on the high roads and fog on the lake.
t.thusis@46.7,9.4:
Thusis is a gateway town, and it knows its job well. It sits where the Hinterrhein, the young Rhine, comes out of the gorge of the Viamala and into the wide, orchard-lined valley of the Domleschg, and from here roads and railway lines fan out into the Graubünden mountains: south over the Splügen and San Bernardino passes, east through the Schin gorge toward the Albula and Davos. At about seven hundred metres in altitude, it is a fairly low base for such high terrain, and that makes it a useful place to be at the start of a mountain day.

The Viamala itself, the bad road, is just south of the town. For centuries it was one of the great hazards of alpine travel, a gorge so narrow and deep that the old mule track clung to the cliff over the river. The Romans and medieval merchants used it to reach the southern passes, and the toll traffic made nearby villages rich. The modern road runs through tunnels and over high bridges, but you can still stop and walk down into the gorge itself, where the river has carved a ribbon of polished rock far below. The Domleschg valley to the north is full of castles, more per square kilometre than almost anywhere in Switzerland.

The ride south from Thusis is among the best in the country. The old road through the Viamala and Rofla gorges and up to the Splügen is a feat of nineteenth-century engineering, while the motorway tunnel carries the heavy traffic toward San Bernardino. If you take the pass road over the San Bernardino, the road climbs in long, easy curves and ends with a generous run of hairpins on the southern side toward Mesocco and Ticino. Be ready for cool air at the top even in summer, and snow can close some of these roads from late autumn to spring, so check ahead.

Thusis is a small, practical town with a fuel station, supermarkets, bakeries and several cafes beside the Rhaetian Railway station, which is a good place to watch the red trains setting off for the Albula. The nearest bigger town is Domat/Ems, about fifteen kilometres to the north, and Chur is just beyond. If you plan a long mountain day, fill up and eat something here first.
t.sargans@47.0,9.4:
Sargans is a small town doing something unexpectedly big. It sits on a low saddle in the Rhine valley where the river, instead of flowing on west toward Lake Constance as it now does, once could just as easily have turned toward the Walensee and Zurich. The ridge between the two directions is barely a rise in the ground, which is why geographers like to point at Sargans and say the whole river's fate depended on a patch of gravel. Today the Rhine runs north, and the town's modest castle on its rocky knoll watches over the valley and the Liechtenstein hills across the water.

For a rider it is a junction more than a destination. The motorway from Zurich arrives along the Walensee, the main railway crosses here, and roads lead north to Liechtenstein and Feldkirch, south to Chur, and east across the border into Austria toward Bludenz and the Montafon valley. That is exactly what makes it a useful meeting point and fuel stop at the start of a trip to the Silvretta. At around five thousand people, it has what you need: a station, fuel, bakeries, supermarkets and cheap, practical meals, with Bad Ragaz and its thermal baths just a few kilometres south.

The surroundings are dramatic, as the Alps rise steeply on both sides of a wide, flat valley. To the west the jagged Churfirsten wall above the Walensee, and to the south the Falknis range above Balzers. In spring the Föhn, a warm, dry wind from the south, can blow strongly down the valley, so gusts may push you around on the open stretches of road, and it is common to see clear sky and stable weather on the Föhn side while rain waits to the north.

Be aware that the vignette is needed in Switzerland, and the nearby crossings into Liechtenstein and Austria are quick but have their own road charges for motorways. Prices at the pumps in Liechtenstein tend to be lower than in Switzerland, which is an open secret among locals. Heidiland, as the area is marketed, is a pastoral name for a valley that is very good for riding, with quiet side roads climbing into the Alpine meadows above the Rhine.
t.montreux@46.4,6.9:
Montreux is the Swiss Riviera in its most polished form, a ribbon of hotels, gardens and promenades stacked up the steep north shore of Lake Geneva, with the French Alps standing on the far side of the water like a stage set. The slopes behind are so sheltered that palms and magnolias survive outdoors, and the lakeside walk is lined with flowerbeds from early spring. It was a retreat for Victorian invalids and then for writers: Byron wrote about the nearby Château de Chillon, and Nabokov spent his last years in a suite at the Montreux Palace hotel, where his statue stands in the gardens today.

Music is the other local industry. The Montreux Jazz Festival began in 1967 and still takes over the lakefront each July, and the town has a deeper rock footnote, too. In December 1971 a fire destroyed the casino during a Frank Zappa concert, and Deep Purple, who had come to record nearby, turned the scene into Smoke on the Water. Queen later bought a studio here and Freddie Mercury lived part of the year in Montreux, so the bronze statue of him on the promenade is rarely without a visitor.

For riding, the lake itself is not the highlight. The lakeside road is busy, slow and lined with traffic lights. The reward is up the hill: roads climb steeply from town into the vineyard terraces of Lavaux to the west, a UNESCO landscape of walled terraces dropping to the lake, and up behind Montreux toward Caux and the Rochers-de-Naye, where a cog railway climbs to the summit. From the Col de Jaman, further up, you can look back down to the lake. For longer distances, the Col des Mosses and the Col du Pillon lead east and south into the Vaud and Valais Alps.

Montreux has a population of about twenty-three thousand, and that brings fuel, parking garages, and everything from bakeries to fine dining. Prices are decidedly Swiss. A lakeside coffee is expensive and worth it. Spring and early autumn are best, as summer weekends are crowded and festival weeks are chaos. A Swiss motorway vignette is needed on the A9 that runs above the town, and speed limits are strictly enforced.
t.geneva@46.2,6.1:
Geneva sits at the south-western tip of Lake Geneva, which locals call Lac Léman, and on a clear day the white shoulder of Mont Blanc rises over the far shore, more than sixty kilometres away. The Rhône leaves the lake here, fast and blue-green, and the city spreads along both banks. The most famous thing is the Jet d'Eau, a fountain that throws a plume of water about a hundred and forty metres into the air from the lake, visible from far across the water.

The old town climbs a hill on the south bank, with the Cathedral of Saint-Pierre at the top, where John Calvin preached in the sixteenth century and made Geneva the centre of Protestant thought, so that the city came to be called the Protestant Rome. Calvin's city later became home to the Red Cross, founded here by Henri Dunant in 1863, and then to the League of Nations and the United Nations, so that today it hosts dozens of international organisations. A short distance to the west, under the countryside near the French border, lies the ring of CERN, where physicists smash particles together in the largest machine ever built. The whole place has an air of quiet prosperity, with watchmakers, banks, chocolatiers and lakeside parks full of swans.

Riding from Geneva is easy and rewarding. Swiss motorways require a vignette, and you will need one for any section, so buy it at the border or online. The road along the northern shore leads to Lausanne and the terraced vineyards of Lavaux, which are a landscape of their own, steep slopes of vines above the lake, while the French side, toward Annecy and the Alps, rises into bigger mountains. Traffic in the city can be heavy, and the border crossings fill at rush hour, with tens of thousands of commuters from France every morning.

Fuel is plentiful, though Swiss prices are higher than in neighbouring France, so many riders cross the border to refuel. Cheese fondue and a plate of lake perch are the local specialities, best taken with a glass of local white. The best months are May to September, but a clear October day, when the first snow dusts the Jura and the lake shines like steel, can be the finest of the year. Beware of the bise, a cold north-easterly wind that comes down the lake in winter and spring.
t.upper pond hilsenbeuertal@49.0,8.8:
Hermann Hesse arrived in Maulbronn in 1891 as a fourteen-year-old seminary student, and left after seven months, having run away across the fields and been found in the cold. The boy became a writer, and the old Cistercian monastery turned up in his novels as the place where a young person's spirit is crushed or set free. The Hilsenbeuertal is one of the quiet valleys on the edge of town, and the upper pond there is a good place to think about all this, because it is still and shaded and has no interest in your opinion.

Maulbronn Monastery, founded in the middle of the twelfth century, is the best-preserved medieval monastic complex north of the Alps, and UNESCO listed it in 1993. The Cistercians settled here in a wet valley and made it work, building a network of dams, ponds and channels that fed the mill, the fish tanks and the kitchen, and kept the monastery supplied through winter and Lent. The ponds in the surrounding woods, including this one, are survivors of that system. Fish was a staple on the many fasting days, and carp and tench were raised in these waters for centuries. Some of the old stonework of the dams is still visible if you look.

The ride around Maulbronn takes you through the Stromberg and Kraichgau, a countryside of low wooded hills, orchards and vineyards in north-western Württemberg. Roads here are quiet, well surfaced and gently curving, with long views from the ridges and villages of half-timbered houses. Narrow lanes through the woods are shaded and damp, with moss on the edges, and in autumn leaves cover the tarmac in a slippery skin. Deer are common at dusk. The nearest place of any size is Maulbronn itself, which is small but has fuel, bakeries, a couple of inns and a good choice of Swabian dishes, such as Maultaschen, a kind of large stuffed pasta, and Spätzle.

The pond is within walking distance of town. Leave the bike and follow the path, and you may see herons, ducks and, in early summer, dragonflies skimming the surface. Visit in the early morning or at evening, when the light comes low through the trees. Spring is bright with new leaves, and October brings mist and colour. In winter the ponds sometimes freeze, and the path can be icy.
t.trier@49.8,6.6:
Trier claims to be the oldest city in Germany, and it can make a respectable case. The Romans founded it as Augusta Treverorum around the end of the first century before Christ, and by the fourth century it was one of the capitals of the empire, a city of emperors, with palaces, baths and a circus. Constantine the Great lived here for years before he moved east, and the city's buildings from this period are so impressive that UNESCO lists a group of them together with the cathedral and the Church of Our Lady.

The Porta Nigra, the Black Gate, is the icon. It is a huge fortified city gate of massive sandstone blocks, built in the second century and darkened by time into a deep grey. In the Middle Ages a monk named Simeon lived in it as a hermit, and a church was built into the structure, which saved the gate from being dismantled for building material. The Basilica of Constantine, with a vast brick hall, is still used as a church, and the Imperial Baths, which are the ruins of an enormous complex, show how the Romans liked to bathe on a grand scale. An amphitheatre on the hillside once held twenty thousand spectators. In the narrow cobbled streets of the centre, the Hauptmarkt is the pleasant heart of the city, with a market cross and old houses.

Trier is also the birthplace of Karl Marx, born here in 1818 in a house that is now a museum. The city lies on the Moselle, in a valley of steep vineyards producing some of the best Riesling in the world, and the Moselle road is a classic ride, a series of long bends following the river through villages and terraces of vines, with castles on the heights. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. In summer, the road fills with campervans and cyclists, so start early.

Luxembourg lies only about ten kilometres to the south-west, and many riders cross the border to take fuel, which is cheaper there. Trier itself, with about a hundred thousand people, has everything, from supermarkets to wine cellars. The wine is white and crisp, and the local food is hearty, with sausages, potatoes and cheese. The best way to see the monuments is on foot, because parking in the centre is limited and expensive. A short ride to Völklingen, across the border in Saarland, takes you to the ironworks, another UNESCO site and a monument of a different age.
t.kloster lorsch@49.7,8.6:
Lorsch is a quiet town of about thirteen thousand in the Rhine plain, between Worms and Darmstadt, and in the ninth century it was one of the most important places in the Frankish empire. A Benedictine abbey was founded here in 764, and under the patronage of Charlemagne's family it grew rich and learned, with a library that was among the best in Europe. The abbey's scriptorium produced the Lorsch Codex, a record of its lands and gifts, and the Lorsch Pharmacopoeia, a medical manuscript of the eighth century that is among the oldest of its kind, now on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

What survives of the abbey is the gatehouse, a small building known as the Torhalle or Königshalle, finished in about 880. It is one of the rare Carolingian buildings that still stand in Germany, and it is a delight: a two-storey hall with a facade covered in a pattern of red and white sandstone tiles set like a chessboard, and a row of half-columns topped by decorative capitals. Nobody knows quite what its original purpose was, whether as a ceremonial entrance, a chapel or a place to receive the king. The rest of the abbey was destroyed in the seventeenth century, and the empty site now holds a park, a museum and the foundations of the church.

The surrounding landscape is flat, fertile and warm, the sort of land where asparagus and tobacco were grown, and the wine hills of the Bergstrasse rise just to the east, with the Odenwald forest beyond. Roads on the plain are straight and quiet, while the Bergstrasse and the Odenwald offer the winding roads that riders prefer, with views over the plain and blossom in April. Local drivers are easygoing, but weekends bring plenty of motorcyclists into the Odenwald. Traffic can be heavy on the main roads near Darmstadt.

Lorsch has fuel stations, bakeries and a decent choice of restaurants, with local dishes including asparagus in season and white wine from the Bergstrasse. The ride goes on to Darmstadt, where the Mathildenhöhe, an artists' colony from the early twentieth century, preserves Jugendstil buildings, and the exhibition of 1904 is a landmark. Spring is a fine time, and late summer brings warm evenings and fresh wine.
t.elfinger pond@49.0,8.8:
Elfinger Pond belongs to the same Cistercian water system as the others around Maulbronn, but its label travels with a surprising companion: a Roman watchtower, number twelve of thirty-nine on a ride devoted to the frontier of the empire. The Roman limes ran well to the east of here, so there is no Roman connection on the ground, only the odd fact that this hill country has been a place of lines and boundaries, in one form or another, for two thousand years. The ponds belong to a gentler kind of border, the one between wilderness and a well-run estate.

For the monks, the pond was a working thing. A dam of earth and stone held back the water of a small stream, and sluices controlled the level. Fish were raised in the ponds for the monastery's table, particularly carp, which were fed, harvested in autumn and kept alive in tanks until needed. The Cistercian rule demanded abstinence from meat on many days, so fish was a necessity rather than a luxury. The water also drove mills and, in times of fire, supplied a reserve. Today the pond is a quiet corner of the forest, with reeds along the edge and the occasional angler.

The ride in this part of the Stromberg and Kraichgau is a pleasure for those who like quiet. Roads wind between woods and fields, past orchards and vineyards, with a succession of small villages where the church tower and the village pump mark the centre. Surfaces are generally good, with a few rough patches near forest tracks. Weekends bring cyclists and walkers, but the weekdays are almost empty. Watch out for tractors at harvest time and for wet leaves in autumn.

Maulbronn is two kilometres away and has fuel, bakeries and a couple of inns, with Swabian cooking such as lentils with Spätzle and sausages, a hearty meal for a cool day. The larger towns of Bretten and Mühlacker lie a short ride off. Spring brings blossom and birdsong, summer is warm and green, and early autumn is the best of all, when the vines turn red and the mist lies in the valleys. Take a layer, because the woods are cooler than you expect.
t.abt gerhard pond@49.0,8.8:
Abbot Gerhard is one of those figures who appear in a local pond name and then disappear back into the archive, and there is no need to invent a biography for him. What matters is the office. A Cistercian abbot was the head of a self-governing community of monks, elected by them, responsible for their souls and their accounts, and Maulbronn's abbots were notable managers, who took on the work of draining marshes, laying out ponds and building mills. A pond named for one of them is a small monument to the idea that holiness and good drainage could go together.

The Cistercians arrived in the Stromberg region in the twelfth century, bringing a way of working that had been developed in Burgundy and spread across Europe. They preferred remote valleys, because they wanted solitude, and they made them productive with hard work. Monks and lay brothers cleared forest, planted vineyards, kept bees and bred fish, and the monastery's wine was famous. The huge cellar, the Kelter, still stands, and the abbey was a model of rational estate management that influenced the surrounding countryside for centuries. After the Reformation, the monastery became a Protestant school, and that tradition continues in the seminary buildings, where the likes of Johannes Kepler and Hermann Hesse once studied.

The pond itself is a modest sheet of water in the woods a kilometre from town, reached by a path through beech and oak. It is a good place to see how the monks used the land, with the dam, the sluice and the channel still readable in the shape of the ground. A rest here, on a bench in the shade, is pleasant. In early morning, you may see a heron fishing in the shallows, and in spring, frogs make a surprising amount of noise.

For riders, the roads around Maulbronn are quiet and generally smooth, curving through woods, vineyards and fields. Fuel is available in Maulbronn, along with bakeries, cafés and inns serving Swabian food. If the weather is bad, the monastery itself is a fine place to spend an hour or two. A visit in May or in October is ideal, and in winter the forest paths are muddy or icy.
t.middle pond hilsenbeuertal@49.0,8.8:
The middle pond in the Hilsenbeuertal is where the valley shows its character most clearly. It sits between the upper and lower waters in a chain, each held by its own dam, and the Cistercian monks arranged them so that the stream passed from one to the next, feeding fish at each stage and powering a mill at the bottom. It is cool engineering for the twelfth century, and it has lasted. Part of what UNESCO lists at Maulbronn is this whole hydraulic landscape, the dams, ditches and ponds spread through the forest around the monastery.

What you notice at the water's edge is life. Reeds crowd the margins, water lilies float on the surface in summer, and dragonflies hover and dart in the sun. Kingfishers sometimes flash along the bank, grey herons stand like statues in the shallows, and frogs and newts spawn in the spring. In the evening, bats come out to hunt insects over the water. Old beech and oak trees lean over the pond, and the quiet is broken by wind and birdsong. In autumn the leaves fall and float on the water, and the surface turns to gold.

The roads that lead there run across a pleasant countryside, the northern Stromberg, with wooded ridges, orchards, small vineyards and villages. They are mostly narrow and well surfaced, with gentle bends and little traffic, though farm vehicles sometimes slow you down. Forest tracks near the ponds may be gravel or mud, and a road bike is better left on the tarmac. In summer, thunderstorms build quickly in the afternoon and can bring hail, so keep an eye on the sky.

Maulbronn, only about four hundred metres away, has fuel, bakeries, restaurants and small hotels, and the monastery itself is open to visitors during the day. The old refectory and the cloister are among the finest in Germany, and a guided tour explains the layout of the complex. Late April and May, when the beeches burst into leaf, and October, when the air is crisp and the colours rich, are the best months. Bring a waterproof, because the forest holds the damp.
t.pond at elfingerhof@49.0,8.8:
Elfingerhof is a farm, and the pond that bears its name is a reminder that a monastery of this kind was also a very large agricultural business. Maulbronn owned villages, fields, forests, vineyards and farms across the region, run by lay brothers and later by tenants, and the estates produced grain, wine, wood and fish in quantities that kept the whole enterprise rich. The monastery's grange farms were outlying centres, where animals were kept and crops stored, and Elfingerhof is a descendant of that world.

The land around is the western edge of the Stromberg, with its loess soils, which give good wheat and sugar beet, and rows of fruit trees along the roads. Cherry blossom in April is a local event, and in autumn the apple and plum harvest fills the farm shops. The pond lies in a hollow among fields, with a tree-lined shore and a view across open farmland that is rare in the forested hills. In the evening the sun sinks behind the ridge and the sky turns pink, and the wind drops. You may see a buzzard circling above the fields, and in winter flocks of geese pass overhead.

The ride here is mellow. Country roads connect the farms and villages, quiet and smooth, with long straights over the fields and a few bends where they enter a wood or cross a stream. Farm traffic is common, especially at harvest, and mud on the road after rain can be slippery. A few of the lanes are unsurfaced or have rough patches, and signs of local access restrictions are worth respecting. Speed limits are enforced in villages, and cameras operate at some junctions.

Maulbronn, about two kilometres away, has fuel stations, bakeries and a few inns. A farm shop on the way may sell eggs, honey and local fruit juice, and in season fresh asparagus from spring, strawberries in June and pumpkins in autumn. Spring is lovely when the fields turn green and the blossom opens, and early autumn brings a golden light. On a still evening, the quiet is so deep that you can hear the church bell from the town.
t.pond at aschberg@49.0,8.8:
Aschberg is a low hill on the edge of Maulbronn's forest, and the pond at its foot is the quietest of the monastery's waters. There are no signs to speak of, no ticket booth and no explanation, only a patch of water with a dam, a margin of reeds and trees leaning in from every side. That absence is itself a kind of history. The monks who built it worked without fanfare, and the land has gone back to ordinary use, so what you find is a working landscape that has become a nature reserve without anybody planning it.

Maulbronn Monastery was founded in 1147 and is a UNESCO site, but its fame rests on the quality of its preservation. Almost every building of the medieval monastery survives, from the church and cloister to the refectory, the fountain house, the mill and the encircling wall, so you can read the full life of a Cistercian community in one place. The ponds, ditches and dams that fed all this make up part of the listing, and though the pond at Aschberg is not one of the stars, it belongs to the same story. The Faust legend is also tied to the place. The real Johann Georg Faust, an alchemist and charlatan of the sixteenth century, is said to have visited the monastery, and a tower in town carries his name.

The woods around the pond are a mixture of beech, oak and hornbeam, with a good carpet of wild garlic in spring that you can smell before you see it. Roe deer step out at dawn, and woodpeckers drum on the trunks. Paths are gravel or earth, suitable for a walk of a few minutes from the nearest lane, and roads in the area are narrow, quiet and well surfaced, with gentle curves. Tractors and cyclists are the main hazards, and fallen leaves and mud on the forest roads need respect.

Maulbronn is about two and a half kilometres away and has fuel, bakeries and a couple of inns, while Mühlacker and Bretten offer larger supermarkets. Spring, when the wild garlic blooms, and autumn, when the leaves turn, are the best times. Come in the early morning or the evening, when the light slants between the trunks and the surface of the pond is smooth enough to hold a perfect reflection.
t.bern@46.9,7.4:
Bern is the odd capital, one that never calls itself a capital: the Swiss federal government sits here but the official term is federal city. It is also one of the best places in the country to park a bike and walk, because the old town fills a tight loop of the Aare river, with the water running green and fast on three sides far below the bridges. UNESCO put the medieval centre on its list in 1983, and the sandstone arcades along the main streets, about six kilometres of them in total, mean you can shop in the rain without an umbrella.

The founding story is the usual mix of legend and politics. The Zähringen dukes established the town around 1191 on the peninsula, and by tradition they named it after the first animal they killed on the hunt, a bear, which is why bears are everywhere, from the coat of arms to the pit by the river where live ones are kept in a park. The clock tower, the Zytglogge, puts on a little show of mechanical figures a few minutes before each hour, which draws a small crowd. Einstein lived on the Kramgasse while working at the patent office and developing his early papers, and his flat is open as a museum.

For a rider, the place is a city stop on the Grand Tour of Switzerland, with all the fuel, food and sleep that implies, and not much of a route in itself. Traffic is dense on weekdays, with trams, buses and restricted zones in the centre, and parking for motorbikes is well provided at the edges. The pleasant approach is from the Aare valley or from the Emmental hills, with their big farmhouses and cheese dairies, and the way out towards Thun and Interlaken is a gentle run to the foot of the Alps.

A good tip is to cross the river by the Nydeggbrücke and ride up to the rose garden on the hillside for the classic view of the old town, then stop for a coffee in one of the cafés. In summer, Bernese locals drift down the Aare in the water on their backs, and on warm days you will see swimmers in the river. Be careful with tram rails when they are wet.
t.mesocco@46.4,9.2:
Mesocco is a valley village of about thirteen hundred people on the southern side of the San Bernardino, in the Misox, the Italian-speaking arm of Graubünden that opens toward Bellinzona and Lake Maggiore. At nearly eight hundred metres it is the last place of any size before the road climbs to the pass, and it is the right place for a breakfast or a late lunch, with a handful of simple restaurants and cafés serving polenta, cheese, local salami and chestnut dishes, and a small stretch of fuel and shops.

The beautiful thing about the village is its castle. Above the road, on a rock, stand the ruins of the Castello di Mesocco, once a stronghold of the Sax family who controlled the pass in the Middle Ages, and the Romanesque church of Santa Maria del Castello nearby, with frescoes inside, lies on a ledge beneath it. The place was important because the San Bernardino pass was an old trade route over the Alps, used since Roman times, and the lords took tolls from every mule train. The pass road itself took its modern form in the nineteenth century, and since 1967 a long road tunnel has carried most of the heavy traffic underneath, which leaves the old road for those with time to enjoy it.

The ride is the real attraction. From Mesocco the road climbs in a succession of hairpins and gallery stretches through chestnut and beech forest and then spruce, reaching the summit at 2,066 metres beside a small lake, and then descending towards Hinterrhein and the Rhine valley. The corners are well graded, the surface usually good, and the traffic is thinner than on the Gotthard. The pass is closed by snow in winter, so riders should only plan to cross in the warmer months, usually from late spring.

Weather often differs on the two sides: the south may be warm and sunny while cloud sits over the summit, so carry a warm layer. The old road is best early, before the heat, and the smell of woodsmoke and wet stone in the village is a pleasant thing to ride into.
t.realp@46.6,8.5:
Realp is the last village on the Urseren valley road before the Furka, a hamlet at about fifteen hundred metres that most people ride through without stopping. That would be a mistake, because the railway station here is the starting point of the Furka cogwheel steam railway, a heritage line run by volunteers, which was rebuilt from abandoned track after the original was closed in 1981. Steam locomotives climb to Oberwald by way of the old mountain route in summer, and even if you do not ride the train, the sight and smell of the engines in the station yard make a decent coffee stop.

The valley itself is wide, flat and treeless, with the Reuss river wandering through meadows between Andermatt and Realp, and long winters that bring serious snow. Andermatt, a couple of villages down the valley with about thirteen hundred inhabitants and the nearest place with fuel, has long been a garrison and holiday town, and has seen big new hotel developments. Airolo, on the south side of the Gotthard, is the next town with services in the other direction. If your tank is low, fill it before you commit to the high roads, because the passes have no stations.

Ahead, the Furka Pass road climbs in a series of hairpins to 2,429 metres, with the Rhone glacier waiting on the far side, and the whole run to Gletsch and onwards to Grimsel or the Nufenen is among the great motorcycle roads of the Alps. This pairing with the Nufenen, the highest fully paved pass in Switzerland at 2,478 metres, has made the area a favourite. Surfaces are generally good, but the road can be rough at the edges and has tight corners with drops on the outside.

Snow closes the passes from about late October until May or June, depending on the year, and the opening dates are announced locally, so check them before you go. In summer, mornings are cold at this height and can be frosty even in August, and afternoon storms build quickly. Early starts give you empty roads, which is what makes a dawn run here so memorable.
t.davos food and weather@46.8,9.8:
Davos sits at about 1,560 metres in a long, high valley in eastern Graubünden, and it claims to be the highest city in Europe, which depends on how you count. It has about eleven thousand people and has been a health resort since the nineteenth century, when the dry mountain air was prescribed for tuberculosis, and a sanatorium culture grew up here. Thomas Mann, who visited his wife during her treatment in 1912, based his novel The Magic Mountain on the experience, and the expressionist painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner moved to the valley and spent his last years working in the hills.

Today the town is better known for skiing, mountain biking and the annual World Economic Forum in January, when it fills with security staff and black cars. In summer it is a lively but not very beautiful place, with long Promenade shopping streets and a mixture of hotels and apartment blocks, but it is practical: there is fuel, plenty of food, bike shops and supermarkets. Klosters, down the valley to the north-east, is smaller and prettier.

The reason riders stop is the weather check. From Davos you can go west on the Flüela pass towards the Engadin or south over the Albula and Julier routes, and conditions on the high roads can change fast, so it is worth reading the sky and looking up the road reports before you set off. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and snow can fall on the passes even in August, so it is wise to start in the morning.

For lunch, Graubünden has its own dishes: Bündnerfleisch, the air-dried beef; pizokel, small dumplings with cheese; Capuns, chard parcels; and nusstorte, the walnut cake from the Engadin. The valley is dry and sunny for much of the year, and the air has a clean, resinous smell. The town fills with traffic on summer weekends and when the Forum meets, so you can save time by avoiding the main street.
t.rhine falls@47.7,8.6:
The Rhine Falls, at Neuhausen near Schaffhausen, are the biggest plain waterfall in Europe, not in height, which is about twenty-three metres, but in volume, with a stream some hundred and fifty metres wide pouring over the rock in the early summer when the snow melts in the Alps. The water thunders and the spray hangs in the air, and a central rock, a stump of limestone, stands in the middle of the torrent. A walkway and a set of platforms take you almost to the foam, and the whole thing smells of wet stone and minerals.

The falls were created at the end of the last ice age, about fourteen to seventeen thousand years ago, when the Rhine was pushed into a new bed by the glaciers and found a hard band of limestone across its path. Goethe visited in the eighteenth century and wrote of the effect on him, and painters including Turner came to paint it. On the north bank sits Schloss Laufen, a castle with a restaurant and a viewing platform, and boats run from both banks to the central rock, which you can climb in season.

The surroundings are mixed: factories and rail lines nestle close, and the town of Neuhausen, with ten thousand inhabitants, is largely industrial. It is not a place for corners, and this is where the Grand Tour starts to bite on a ride from Zurich to Davos, a day of about two hundred and fifty kilometres heading east and south. The riding near the falls is on flat valley roads and low hills, with views of vineyards and the river, and the German border is only a few hundred metres away, so the road sometimes slips across and back.

Parking is simple in the area, with plenty of space for bikes beside the falls. Try to come in the morning or late in the afternoon when the crowds thin, and take waterproofs if you plan to go on a boat. Fuel is plentiful in Neuhausen and Schaffhausen. The Swiss motorway vignette is needed for the motorways, and speed cameras are common.
t.fluela pass@46.8,9.9:
The Flüela pass, at 2,383 metres, links Davos with the Lower Engadin, and it is one of the more austere roads in the Swiss Alps: bare rock, small dark lakes and a feeling of height without the crowds of some of its neighbours. The road climbs from the Davos side in a series of broad curves through spruce forest and then through scree and stone, and on the top you find a small lake, the Schottensee, which is at the summit and reflects the surrounding peaks on calm days. A hospice building has stood at the summit for centuries to shelter travellers caught by storms.

On the east side the descent to Susch is quick and has a number of tight hairpins between steep rock walls and then drops into the Inn valley, with Zernez, a village of about a thousand people and the entrance to the Swiss National Park, a short way along. Susch itself has an old church and fortified buildings, a reminder that this was a trade route to the south. The Swiss National Park, founded in 1914, is the oldest in the Alps, and has ibex, chamois and, on rare occasions, bearded vultures; there are no vehicle roads within it, so visitors walk.

The riding is a pleasure. The Flüela road is generally good, with fast, open bends on the lower sections and more demanding ones near the top, and traffic is lighter than on Julier or Albula. Low sun on the western side makes for dazzling light in the afternoon, and the air is cold and clear.

The pass is closed by snow in winter, usually from around November until late spring, and early-season snow showers can make the top slippery well into June. Even in August the temperature at the summit can be close to freezing in the morning, so carry gloves and a warm layer. Thunderstorms in the afternoon are common, and the best time to cross is in the morning.
t.julierpass high road@46.5,9.7:
The Julier is one of the oldest crossings in the Alps, and the summit at 2,284 metres still carries two stumps of stone columns beside the road, thought to be the remains of a Roman shrine. The Romans pushed a road over the pass in the first century, and ever since the route has linked the Oberhalbstein valley with the Engadin, carrying merchants and pilgrims between Chur and the Bergell and the passes south. A small lake sits near the top and a handful of buildings, but there is not much else, and it can be bleak and windy.

On the south side, the road drops to Silvaplana, a village of under a thousand people on the shore of the lake of the same name, which is known for its wind. The Maloja wind, a steady afternoon breeze from the south-west, draws windsurfers and kitesurfers from across Europe, and gives the lake its choppy blue surface. St Moritz, a few kilometres further and still a place of grand hotels and dear coffee, is the larger town for fuel and food, though a fill-up and a sandwich in the valley are cheaper than at the resort. The north side, going down to Bivio and Savognin, is quieter and more rural, with old farmhouses and walnut-brown barns.

For riders the Julier is a flowing road more than a technical one: wide and well surfaced, with long sweeping gradients and just a few tight turns, and it is popular with sports bikes in the early morning. The upper part above the tree line is open and exposed, and weather can shift quickly, with cold rain or snow possible in any month. The pass is generally kept open for much of the year, though winter conditions can close it briefly.

The usual loop on this Graubünden triangle links the Julier with the Albula and the Flüela, a tidy day of high passes and valleys. Light in the early morning is lovely on the lake, with larches turning in autumn. Watch for cyclists on the climb and for the occasional marmot on the verge, and respect the speed limits in the villages.
t.aosta@45.7,7.3:
Aosta is a Roman town with the Alps standing around it like a stage set. The Romans founded it in 25 BC as Augusta Praetoria, after subduing the local Salassi tribe, and they laid it out on a neat grid that still shapes the old centre. The Arch of Augustus, the Porta Praetoria gate, and the remains of a theatre with a surviving wall nearly twenty metres high stand among cafes and shops, and snow-capped peaks rise at the end of every street. It has been called the Rome of the Alps.

The reason for all this is the pass. The Great St Bernard, at about 2,470 metres, is one of the oldest crossings of the Alps, used by Celts, Romans, medieval pilgrims and, famously, by Napoleon's army in 1800. At the top, on the Swiss border, the hospice founded in the eleventh century by Bernard of Menthon has sheltered travellers ever since, and its monks kept the large rescue dogs that took the saint's name. The road from Aosta climbs the valley past old stone villages and the new tunnel entrance, then leaves the tunnel traffic to wind up through hairpins to the pass, with stone avalanche galleries and steep meadows. The old road is only open in summer, usually from June to October, and weather can bring snow even in July, so check conditions. Surface quality is generally good but narrow, with tight corners and occasional rough patches.

Valle d'Aosta is a small, autonomous region where French is an official language alongside Italian, and the food reflects the double heritage. Fontina, a soft, nutty cheese made from the milk of cows grazed on high pastures, is the signature, and it appears melted in fonduta, baked in soups and stuffed into cutlets. Local rye bread, cured lard from Arnad and sturdy red wines from steep terraced vineyards fill out the table. Castles crown many of the nearby hills, and those at Fénis and Aymavilles are especially fine.

Aosta is a town of thirty thousand with fuel, restaurants and hotels, and plenty of parking near the centre. Fill up here before heading into the mountains, because the stations get sparser the higher you go, and prices in Switzerland are higher. Carry your passport for the border and check whether you need a Swiss motorway vignette if you plan to continue on motorways. Warm clothes are a must for the pass, even on a sunny day.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@45.3,5.5:
Beaucroissant and Renage lie in the green hill country of the Bas-Dauphiné, between Grenoble and Lyon, near the little town of Rives, and not far from the Lac de Paladru, which is why the point is tagged for swimming. The lake is a glacial one, about five kilometres long, with clear water, a few beaches and shallows that warm up quickly in July and August, and the water and woodland setting make it a favourite with the people of Grenoble and Lyon. Entrance to some of the beaches is charged in season.

Voiron, a town of about twenty thousand a short distance to the east, is the larger place for fuel and supplies, and it is the home of the Chartreuse liqueur. The monks of the Grande Chartreuse monastery, high in the mountains beyond, make the green and yellow liqueur from a secret recipe of 130 herbs, and the distillery cellars in Voiron, said to be the largest liqueur cellars in the world, offer tours and tastings. The Chartreuse massif, a block of limestone cliffs and forests, forms the skyline to the east, and the road toward the monastery is a lovely ride.

Around Renage and Beaucroissant the country is gentler: rolling fields, walnut orchards, ponds and small villages with stone houses and tiled roofs. The Dauphiné is known for its walnuts, which have their own appellation, and for gratin dauphinois, a potato dish baked with cream. Roads wander along the valley floors and over low ridges, with easy corners, light traffic, and a surface that is mostly smooth, with the occasional patch of gravel on country lanes.

The Alpe d'Huez and the Oisans, the destination of this long ride, lie further south, beyond Grenoble, so treat this spot as a warm-up or a cool-down. A swim after a day on the road is a fine thing, so pack a towel. Summers are hot and thundery, and early autumn gives the best light. Watch for tractors and slow vehicles, especially at harvest time, and for school traffic near the villages.
t.thonon les bains@46.4,6.5:
Thonon-les-Bains sits on the southern shore of Lake Geneva, facing Switzerland across about ten kilometres of water, and it is where the Route des Grandes Alpes officially starts. This was the first great tourist road of France, planned in the early twentieth century by the Touring Club de France to link the lake with the Mediterranean via the highest passes of the French Alps, and the road runs for about seven hundred kilometres over a series of cols, ending in Menton. The fine promenade along the lake, with its views of the Swiss shore and the Jura, and the fish restaurants serving perch fillets, are a gentle prelude.

The old town stands on a bluff above the port, linked to the lakeside by a funicular opened in the late nineteenth century, and nearby the Château de Ripaille, a former residence of the dukes of Savoy, stands in a park beside the water. Thonon was a spa town, and the neighbouring Évian, a few kilometres east, still sells its mineral water around the world. This region, Savoy, belonged to the House of Savoy until it was ceded to France in 1860, and its mountain culture, cheeses and dialect set it a little apart.

The ride proper begins when the road turns south and climbs into the Alps. The first passes are modest, in forests and pastures with Alpine chalets and cow bells, but the route builds toward the giants: the Col de l'Iseran, at 2,764 metres the highest pass in the Alps that is crossed by a through road, the Col du Galibier, at about 2,640 metres, and finally the Col de la Bonette, near 2,715 metres. The road surface is generally good, but bends are tight, there are drops without guard rails in places, and the weather at altitude can switch from sun to snow in minutes. The high passes are only open in summer, typically from June until October, so check status before planning. Early starts avoid the afternoon storms.

At the beginning, everything is easy. Thonon is a town of over thirty thousand, with fuel stations on the main roads and plenty of cafes, hotels and supermarkets, so fill up and eat well. Higher up, villages are small and stations rarer, so top up whenever you pass one. Alpine cheeses, such as reblochon and beaufort, and a savoyard dish of potatoes baked with cheese and bacon, called tartiflette, are the natural fuel for the road. Pack warm layers, rain gear and gloves, whatever the weather at the lake.
t.col des gets@46.2,6.7:
The Col des Gets is a gentle pass of 1,172 metres between the Giffre and Dranse valleys in the Haute-Savoie, linking the villages of Les Gets and Morzine, and it sits on the old Route des Grandes Alpes, the long road from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean. It is not a high or wild pass, but it is a handsome one, with rolling meadows, fir forests and wooden chalets, and the crest of the hills above it holds ski lifts that turn into mountain bike routes in summer.

Les Gets, a village of 1,300 residents, is pretty and a bit more relaxed than its neighbours, and holds a surprising attraction: a museum of mechanical music, with a collection of music boxes, automatons, barrel organs and fairground pieces, housed in an old building. Morzine, a larger resort town of about three thousand, has a lively centre, a variety of restaurants and fuel stations. The Portes du Soleil ski area, which spreads across the French and Swiss border, begins here, and in July and August mountain bikers fill the area, so do not be surprised to share the road with them.

The road from Cluses, which approaches from the valley, climbs through gorges and then onto open pastures with views of the Mont Blanc range in the distance, with a steady gradient and a number of bends. From Thonon-les-Bains, the start of the Grandes Alpes route on Lake Geneva, you climb gradually along the Dranse valley, through the Gorges du Pont du Diable, a deep and rocky cut with a roaring river beneath. The roads are well surfaced and marked, and the bends are open and easy, making it a pleasant ride rather than a challenging one.

The region is dairy country, famous for Abondance cows, with their reddish-brown coats and white faces, and for the cheeses made from their milk, notably Abondance, Reblochon and Tomme. Farm shops sell them directly, and a fondue or tartiflette is the natural lunch. The pass is open throughout the year in most conditions, though snow can cause delays in winter, and chains may be needed. Summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms, so start early and be prepared for a drop in temperature.
t.col des aravis@45.9,6.5:
The Col des Aravis, at 1,486 metres, joins the Arve and Thônes valleys across the Aravis range, and it is one of the most scenic of the middle-height passes in the northern French Alps. The view from the pass looks across to the Mont Blanc massif, dominating the skyline on a clear day, with the white dome and glaciers above dark forests, and in front of it stretch the green pastures of the Aravis. A handful of chalets and a small café stand near the summit, and several farms sell cheese directly from their barns.

La Clusaz, a village of 2,200 permanent residents on the Thônes side, is a ski resort with old stone and wooden buildings, restaurants and shops, and it is the nearest place for fuel and a proper meal. Saint-Jean-de-Sixt, a small village a few kilometres below, is more modest. This is the country of Reblochon, a soft washed-rind cheese with a long history, said to have been made by farmers who withheld part of the milk from the landlord's count and skimmed the rich second milking afterwards, which is the origin of the name. It is the main ingredient of tartiflette, with potatoes, bacon and onions, which is hard to beat after a cold ride.

The climb is easy by Alpine standards, with an even gradient and a broad road, and long stretches of gentle bends through meadows and forest. On the descent towards Flumet, the views open towards the Beaufortain, with rows of peaks to the south. The surface is generally good, and traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with campervans and cyclists as well as bikes. Early morning is best, when the light is soft and the cows are out on the high pastures, with bells ringing.

Snow can close the pass in winter, though it is usually kept open, and chains or winter tyres may be required, so check local conditions. Summer brings hay-making and flowers, with meadows full of gentians, orchids and buttercups in June. The climate is cooler and wetter than the nearby lakes, and fog can come down quickly. Keep a layer in the pannier and drink water, and take your time over the descent.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@46.4,5.7:
Moirans-en-Montagne is a small town of about two thousand in the Jura, where the mountains of Franche-Comté are laid out in long, parallel ridges, and it has a surprise for the visitor: a museum of toys, one of the best in France, in an old convent, which celebrates the local tradition of toy-making in wood and plastic. The Jura has a history of small workshops using local timber, producing clocks, pipes, toys and spectacles, and that heritage is part of the area's character. Arinthod, a village of about thirteen hundred, is a handsome little market place with an arcaded square and a scattering of old houses.

The reason this point is tagged for swimming is the Lac de Vouglans, which lies just to the east. It is an artificial lake, formed by a dam on the river Ain in 1968, and about thirty-five kilometres long and winding like a fjord, it is one of the largest reservoirs in France. The water is clear and deep, and the beaches and bays attract swimmers, sailors and kayakers in summer, with several supervised swimming areas and lakeside cafés. The lake is surrounded by wooded cliffs and has a real mountain flavour.

For motorcyclists, the Jura is one of the best-kept secrets in France: roads that curve through forest, over passes and through the gorges of the Ain, the Valouse and the Bienne, with long, smooth bends and little traffic. The Cascades du Hérisson, a series of waterfalls in a wooded valley a short ride away, are a famous sight, with a path along the stream that takes an hour or two to walk. The Chartreuse, named in the ride, is far to the south-east, so this place is more of a northern neighbour.

For fuel and supplies, Moirans, Saint-Claude and Lons-le-Saunier are the places to head for, and the area's food is another reason to come: Comté cheese, aged for months in caves, smoked sausage from Morteau, and the yellow wine, vin jaune, which is made in a way found nowhere else. Winters are cold and snowy, and the higher roads may be closed. Summer is warm, though storms are common, and autumn light is golden. Watch for cattle on the road and for cyclists.
t.jeju city@33.5,126.5:
Jeju is a volcanic island off the southern tip of Korea, and Jeju City is its biggest town, the gateway for most visitors who arrive by air. Behind it stands Hallasan, a shield volcano reaching just under two thousand metres, and its slopes give the whole island a gentle, tilted shape. UNESCO has recognised the lava tubes and the volcanic landscape here, and a sense of dark basalt is everywhere, in the stone walls that divide the fields, in the statues called dol hareubang that stand guard in villages, and in the black rocks of the shoreline.

The island has a distinct culture from the mainland. The haenyeo, the female divers who gather seafood without breathing equipment, have worked these waters for generations, and their tradition is also protected as cultural heritage. Tangerines grow everywhere, and the island is known for black pork, abalone porridge and fresh raw fish. The wind is a regular feature, and legend says Jeju is known for three things: wind, stones and women.

For riders, the coastal road around the island is the draw, a loop of roughly two hundred kilometres that stays close to the sea and passes beaches, lava cliffs, small harbours and fields of rapeseed in spring. The surface is generally good and traffic is moderate outside holiday seasons, though tourist coaches and rental cars driven by newcomers can be unpredictable. Crosswinds on exposed sections can be strong, and rain squalls arrive quickly. Spring and autumn are the best times, and summer can be humid and typhoon-prone.

Jeju City is large enough to supply everything you need, with fuel stations, repair shops, cafes and hotels. Away from the city, villages and stations are spaced evenly around the loop, so fuel is rarely a problem, though it is wise to fill the tank before the quieter southern and western stretches. Seogwipo, on the south coast, is the other main town, about twenty-five kilometres away across the island's interior.

Speed cameras are common in Korea, including on rural roads, and the limits are marked clearly, so watch the signs. A walk through the fish market near the harbour in the evening is a good way to end the day.
t.bludenz@47.2,9.8:
Bludenz sits at the meeting of several valleys, and that is its whole story. The Walgau runs northwest toward the Rhine, the Klostertal heads east to the Arlberg, the Brandnertal climbs south to the Lünersee, and the Montafon carries the Ill river up to the Silvretta. At 588 metres, the town is a low point in a landscape of high peaks, with the Rätikon walls rising behind the old centre and a compact medieval core of arcades and painted houses. It is an ideal place to begin a ride into the mountains.

Bludenz also has an unexpected sweet side. The Milka chocolate factory operated here for decades, and the town is also the home of Fohrenburg, a respected brewery. The mix of chocolate and beer gives it a pleasant, practical personality. With over thirteen thousand people, it has every sort of fuel station, supermarket, cafe and restaurant that you could need, which makes it a good place for breakfast, a last cash machine and a check of the bike before heading up the valley.

The Silvretta High Alpine Road starts at the head of the Montafon, beyond Partenen, and climbs to the Bielerhöhe at 2,032 metres, near the Silvretta reservoir. It is a toll road, normally open from roughly early summer to autumn depending on snow, so check conditions before you set out. The road from Bludenz to the start is about forty kilometres of gentle valley riding, passing villages with wooden barns, chapels and gardens full of geraniums.

Notice the Alpine light as you go. In the morning the valley is cool and shadowed, and the first sunlight catches the high peaks while the roads below remain in shade. By midday the heat rises and the afternoon storms are common in summer. Eat well in Bludenz, because this is a ride in which you will want to be properly fed. A coffee under the arcades, a pastry, and you are ready.
t.st moritz@46.6,9.9:
St. Moritz sits at 1,822 metres in the Engadin, a high, wide valley of larches, lakes and light that people have been praising for centuries. The town's reputation began in 1864, when a hotelier named Johannes Badrutt is said to have bet his English summer guests that they would enjoy the winter in the mountains, and if they did not, he would pay their travel costs. They stayed until Easter, brown from the sun, and winter tourism was born. The Olympic Games came here in 1928 and again in 1948, and the Cresta Run, an ice-cold toboggan track dug into the hillside, has been in use since 1884.

The valley is the real draw. The Inn river starts nearby and runs north-east, linking a chain of lakes, and the water is dazzling on a clear day. Snow-covered peaks hang above the larch forests, and in autumn the larches turn gold, a few weeks of the year when the whole Engadin glows. The sun shines on more than three hundred days a year, according to the local claim, and the air at this height is dry, thin and sharp. Evening light on the lake, with the long shadows of the pines, is something a rider remembers.

Riding here is a matter of choice, with famous passes in all directions. The Julier road climbs north towards Savognin, the Bernina Pass leads south into Italy through glacier country, and the Maloja Pass drops dramatically from the valley floor towards Lake Como in a series of tight hairpins. All are paved, steep in places and open from late spring to autumn, though snow can close the higher ones at any time. The valley road itself is busy in summer, and the town centre is congested, with expensive parking and strict speed limits, so don't expect a quiet pull-in near the lake.

For fuel, St. Moritz has stations, and the neighbouring villages of Samedan and Celerina, both a few minutes away, are cheaper and quieter. Prices here are among the highest in Switzerland, and a coffee on the lakefront will cost you dearly, but a bakery in Celerina sells the Engadiner Nusstorte, a rich walnut and caramel pastry that is a local classic. Mornings are crisp even in July, so keep your gloves handy, and thunderstorms in the afternoon can build quickly over the ridges.
t.gotthard@46.5,8.6:
Every road across the Alps has a character, and the Gotthard's is that of a main street. For centuries it has been the shortest route between northern Europe and Italy, the pass that built Switzerland's early alliances and that every army, merchant and pilgrim wanted. The summit lies at 2,106 metres, in a bare, grey landscape of granite and small lakes, with a hospice, a museum and little else. From here the water goes four ways: the Reuss flows north to the Rhine, the Ticino south to the Po, and the Rhône and the Rhine begin close by.

Three roads cross the mountain. The first is the old Tremola, a stretch of cobbled road on the Ticino side, a ribbon of tight hairpins with granite setts, built in the nineteenth century and now one of the great motorcycling experiences in Europe. The second is the modern pass road, wide and fast, and the third is the Gotthard road tunnel, nearly seventeen kilometres long, which opened in 1980 and carries the heavy traffic under the mountain. Since 2016 the rail base tunnel, at fifty-seven kilometres the longest in the world, has carried the trains. The pass road is the one you want.

The cobbles of the Tremola need respect. They are broad and generally smooth, but they are slippery when wet and the hairpins are tight and steep, with a stone parapet on the outside, and in summer the road is busy with other riders and cyclists. Take it in dry weather and keep a steady pace, and use the pull-ins to let faster traffic by. Going up the south side from Airolo, the views open slowly, and then at the top you are suddenly in the high, windswept bowl. The road is closed by snow from about late October to May or June, and the weather at the summit can change from sun to hail in an hour.

Fuel is available at Airolo, a village of about fifteen hundred people on the south side, and at Andermatt on the north. There is none at the summit. A bowl of soup in the hospice, a short walk around the lakes, and a look at the museum make a good stop. Take warm clothes, because even in August the temperature at 2,100 metres can drop close to freezing at dawn, and the wind is sharp.
t.neuchatel@46.6,6.5:
The label says Neuchâtel, but you are not at the lake. Neuchâtel, with its castle and its long, pale blue lake, is a good forty kilometres to the north-east, past the first folds of the Jura. This is the landscape on the way, a rolling plateau of farms, orchards and beech woods, where the road to Neuchâtel begins.

Cossonay is the one worth a look. The old town sits on a rise above the river, with a Grand-Rue of old houses, a square with a fountain and a medieval church that overlooks the valley. It has been a settlement for centuries, a minor seat of local lords on the road from the Jura passes to the lake. The valley below is a patchwork of crops, with big skies and a feeling of room that surprises people who think Switzerland is all peaks. In spring the fruit trees blossom, and in summer the wheat turns gold.

From here the riding turns serious.
