The roads climb gently into the Jura Vaudois, a range of long, forested ridges, with passes such as the Col du Mollendruz, at about 1,180 metres, easing up through pasture and spruce to a high plateau. The curves are broad and flowing, the surface is typically excellent, and the traffic is light. Then you drop towards the Vallée de Joux and beyond to the lake of Neuchâtel. Mist often clings to the ridges in the morning, and in winter these roads are icy and closed to bikes.

Penthalaz and Cossonay both have fuel, and Bussigny, a larger place to the south, has more shops and services. In a Vaudois bakery or cafe, you might find a saucisson vaudois, a smoked pork sausage, or a papet vaudois, leeks and potatoes in a creamy mix, both served with local white wine. On Swiss motorways you need the annual vignette, but these minor roads do not, and speed cameras are common, so keep to the limits through the villages. The best time is May to October, when the roads are dry and the days are long.
t.schaffhausen@47.7,8.6:
Schaffhausen is the little Swiss city that wanders north of the Rhine, in a canton that pokes into Germany like a thumb, and from the border post you can hear the language change within a few kilometres. At about four hundred metres it is low country, with gentle hills, vineyards, and fields rolling towards the Black Forest.

The old town is one of the best preserved in Switzerland, with rows of medieval houses carrying painted facades and elaborate oriel windows, the Erker, that stick out from the upper floors like glassed-in balconies. Above it, the round fortress of the Munot dominates the hill, a sixteenth-century circular bastion that you can walk right around, and the view over the Rhine and the red roofs justifies the climb. Down in the lanes there is a watch-making tradition, and the famous IWC company is based here, though you will not find a shop window as plain as the ones in Zurich.

Just downstream, at Neuhausen, the Rhine drops over the Rheinfall, the largest plain waterfall in Europe by volume. It is not tall, only about twenty-three metres, but the sheer weight of water and the spray that rolls up in summer make a deafening, delightful show. The viewing platforms below the Laufen castle get you close enough to feel the mist, and the whole thing is a short walk from the road. It is touristy, and you should go early or late to avoid the coach parties.

For riding, the real draw is the country north and west of the city: the road to the Wutach gorge and the Black Forest in Germany, with its curving climbs through dark spruce, and the Swiss Jura to the south and west, where quieter roads lead to Passwang. The border here is usually quick to cross, but bring a passport and remember that Switzerland needs a motorway vignette if you use the autobahn, which costs a flat annual fee and is sold at the border and at petrol stations.

Weather swings here are mild, though fog hangs over the Rhine valley on autumn mornings, and the sun burns through by lunchtime.
t.bremgarten old bridge@47.4,8.3:
Bremgarten is a medieval town on a bend, and the bend is the whole point. The river Reuss, fast, green and cold from the Alps, loops in a tight horseshoe here, and the old town is built inside the loop, on a spur of land that makes it nearly an island. Its medieval lords chose the site for its defensibility and built walls, gates and towers around it. Some of the towers still stand, and steep lanes run from them down to the water.

The old bridge is the place to start. It is a covered wooden structure, roofed and enclosed, of the kind Switzerland is famous for, and it crosses the Reuss in a few wooden spans, with the pale green water below. Swiss covered bridges were roofed to protect the timbers from rain and snow, which extended their life by decades, and this one is one of the most photogenic. The view back from the far bank, with the old town stacked above the river, is the one on the postcards.

The ride here lies in the low hills of the Freiamt, a gentle region of farms, orchards and beech woods on the edge of the Swiss Plateau, a country of cherry trees in April and a patchwork of crops in summer. Roads are quiet, curving and well maintained, and the main hazard is farm machinery. The Reuss valley has a wetland reserve of floodplain forest where kingfishers and beavers live, and a cycle path runs along the river. At 386 metres, the climate is mild, and fog often fills the valley on autumn mornings.

Bremgarten has fuel and shops, being a town of about six and a half thousand, and the old town has bakeries and cafes. The classic Aargau treat is the Rüeblitorte, a carrot cake with almonds and marzipan carrots on top, and it goes perfectly with a coffee on a terrace by the river. Visit on a weekday if you can, since weekends bring cyclists and walkers. The bridge itself is closed to motor traffic, so leave the bike in the parking areas outside the old walls and walk across.
t.sustenpass west ramp@46.7,8.4:
The west ramp of the Sustenpass starts in the Haslital near Innertkirchen and climbs through the Gadmertal, a deep, quiet, wooded valley that most day-trippers never see. Fuel is down in the valley at Innertkirchen or Meiringen, and the nearest big town is Altdorf, well over twenty kilometres away, so fill up before you go.

The Susten is one of the finest-engineered mountain roads in Switzerland. Built in the late 1930s and early 1940s, partly as a defence project during the war and partly to link the Bernese Oberland with Uri, it climbs steadily on a constant gradient, with wide, flowing bends that are easy to read and a surface that is generally in very good shape. Rock walls rise on one side, and on the other the valley drops away in a drift of glacier-polished slabs and thin waterfalls. Tunnels and galleries protect the road from avalanches, and they can be dark and damp, so lift your visor and let your eyes adjust.

On the way up you pass the Stein glacier, a tongue of ice that once reached almost to the road and has been retreating for decades. A lake of milky meltwater has formed below the ice, and there is a hotel and a car park at the foot of the walk. Sustenhorn and Gwächtenhorn raise their white heads above the pass, and in early summer the snow banks beside the road can stand taller than a rider. The pass closes in winter, usually from late autumn until late spring, so check the opening notices before planning a trip.

Combine it with its neighbours, Grimsel and Furka, and you have the classic Swiss triple, a tour of high passes that one day can barely hold. The best time is early in the morning, when the air is cold and clean and the tourist coaches have not yet begun. At the summit, the thin air makes tea taste better than it has any right to. Watch for cattle on the road, and for cyclists on the long climb.
t.furkapass glacier road@46.6,8.4:
Furka is the pass everybody has seen without knowing it: the Goldfinger car chase of 1964 was filmed on these hairpins, and the hotel at the Rhône glacier still trades on the association. At 2,429 metres it is the highest pass of the classic Swiss trio, linking Uri to the canton of Valais through the Urseren valley and down to Gletsch.

The road itself is a joy. On the Uri side it runs up from Realp in a sequence of tight bends and long straights, with views back along the Urseren valley, while the Valais side drops away in generous hairpins towards Gletsch. The gradients are steady, the surface decent and the barriers sturdy, though a stretch or two is patched and rough after the winter. At the summit, the old Hotel Belvédère sits above the Rhône glacier, whose ice grotto has been cut into the glacier each summer for visitors. A century ago the ice nearly reached the hotel terrace, and a line of photographs shows how far it has retreated. Visitors now see a tongue covered by protective blankets in summer to slow the melting.

The Furka also has a famous railway. The old Furka mountain line, a cogwheel steam railway, used to cross under the pass in a high tunnel before a long base tunnel was opened in the early 1980s and left the summit section unused. Volunteers restored it, and in summer steam trains again climb the route between Realp and Oberwald, a nostalgic sight you may catch from the road. The Swiss love a good railway, and the Furka line is a firm favourite.

The pass closes in the snow season, typically from about late October to early June, and it can close temporarily after a summer storm. It is also exposed to wind and cloud, so even on a fine day, bring a windproof layer. Go early, and you will have the hairpins almost to yourself.
t.chur eastbound@46.9,9.5:
Chur likes to call itself the oldest town in Switzerland, and the claim holds up better than most: people have lived on this spot, where the Plessur meets the Rhine, for several thousand years. It became the seat of a bishop in late Roman times, and the cathedral on the hill still keeps that tradition alive. Today the city has around thirty thousand residents and sits at 593 metres, the gateway to Graubünden, with fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants everywhere a rider could want. As a start point it is practical and charming at once.

The old town is largely car-free, a tight tangle of lanes with fountains, medieval towers and painted house fronts, and a good place for a walk after the ride. The local speciality is Bündnerfleisch, air-dried beef sliced thin, and you will find it on most menus. Capuns, little parcels of dough wrapped in chard leaves, are another regional dish worth ordering. A slice of Engadiner nusstorte, with caramel and walnuts, will carry you through the afternoon.

From Chur the roads fan out in every direction. To the west, the Rhine runs along the Vorderrhein valley towards Ilanz, Disentis and the Oberalp. To the south, the road climbs to Lenzerheide and the Julier. East lies Landquart and the Prättigau, with Davos and the Flüela beyond. The Rhine valley itself is broad and fast, with modern road and heavy trucks, so riders tend to leave it as quickly as possible. The valley is also prone to the Föhn, a warm, dry wind that sweeps down from the south and can make the air feel odd and energetic.

Felsberg, on the far side of the river, sits under a mountain that famously collapsed in the nineteenth century, and rock-fall risks are still monitored on the slopes above. The high peaks of Calanda loom behind it. If you are leaving Chur at dawn to catch the mountain passes, the early light on the cathedral and the quiet streets make a good way to begin. Park in one of the central car parks, or ask your hotel about secure spots for the bike.
t.glarus valley@47.0,9.1:
Glarus is a town that was burned down and rebuilt on a grid, and the grid is why the centre feels so unlike other Swiss towns. On 10 May 1861, a fire driven by the Föhn wind destroyed about a third of the town in a single night, and the rebuilding followed a plan of straight streets and regular blocks, an unusual layout for a mountain town. Today Glarus has just under six thousand people and serves as the capital of its small canton, in the narrow valley of the Linth, where steep limestone walls rise on both sides.

The canton has some curious traditions. Every year, on the first Sunday in May, citizens meet in the open air in the Zaunplatz and vote on laws by a show of hands, in an assembly called the Landsgemeinde. The ritual goes back centuries and survives in only a couple of places today. The valley also makes Schabziger, a hard, green, sharply flavoured cheese, shaped like a cone and flavoured with blue fenugreek, produced here for centuries and exported around Europe, which you grate over potatoes or spread on bread.

For a rider, Glarus is the way into some of the least visited roads in the central Alps. The Linth valley leads north towards the Walensee and the Zurich lakes, and south the road climbs towards Linthal and the Klausen Pass, a famous route over to Uri with hairpins and sheer drops. A third option is the Pragel Pass, at 1,550 metres, reached from Glarus over a narrow, steep road with wooden chalets and grazing cattle, which leads into the Muotathal. Traffic is light, and the sense of space and quiet is a contrast with the better-known passes.

Fuel is straightforward in Glarus, with several stations, and the town has bakeries and cafes. Its position at the foot of the Glärnisch massif, a huge wall of rock and ice, makes for dramatic views from the road, and a long glacier tongue gleams above on clear days. Check the weather before the passes, since the Klausen closes in winter, normally from about November until late spring, and the Pragel is usually closed from late autumn. Foehn winds can be strong here, and the valley is quick to catch fog in the autumn.
t.landquart@47.0,9.6:
Landquart is a railway junction that turned into a town, and a good place to understand how Graubünden ties together. The village lies on the floor of the Rhine valley, a few kilometres north of Chur, at the mouth of the Landquart river, which comes down from the Prättigau and the high passes of the east. It is the point where the Rhaetian Railway, the narrow-gauge line that climbs to Davos and St. Moritz, leaves the main line, and the red trains wait at the platform beside the big Swiss ones. At 523 metres, it is low, mild and often warm, a contrast to the high Alps that lie ahead.

The countryside around is wine country, and surprisingly good wine country. The Bündner Herrschaft, the stretch of vineyards between Fläsch, Maienfeld, Jenins and Malans, is one of the best places in Switzerland for Pinot Noir, which the locals call Blauburgunder. The Föhn wind warms the slopes in autumn and gives long, mild ripening. Maienfeld is also the setting of Johanna Spyri's Heidi, written in 1880, and the village keeps a Heidi house and a Heidi trail, and busloads of visitors from Japan make the pilgrimage.

For the rider, Landquart is the end of the Graubünden triangle and the start of the road home. After the Julier, Albula and Flüela passes, the road along the Prättigau drops through forest to the Rhine valley, and the gradient eases, with the last curves under pine and beech, then the A13 motorway with its steady stream of traffic. The vineyard lanes around Malans and Zizers are an agreeable alternative, narrow and quiet, with walls and stone houses, and mornings in October are especially fine.

Fuel is easy here, with stations in Landquart, Igis and Zizers, and Landquart has a large outlet shopping centre that attracts a lot of traffic. For a meal, try a Bündner Gerstensuppe, the thick barley soup of the region, and a glass of the local Pinot Noir if you are not riding. The vignette is required on the motorway, and speed cameras are frequent in villages. The Flüela and Albula passes close in winter, usually from around November, so check the status before you set out.
t.airolo@46.5,8.6:
Airolo sits at the southern mouth of the Gotthard, the point where northern and southern Europe seem to hand over to each other in a single valley. At 1,175 metres it is a small town of about fifteen hundred people, and the first sign of Italian Switzerland if you come from Andermatt: the roofs turn to stone, the stucco gets warmer, and the language changes to Italian. It has fuel, cafes, a couple of bakeries and a railway station, and it is a natural place to start or finish a day among the passes.

The big story here is the Gotthard itself. The railway tunnel, completed in 1882 after years of painful work, ended at Airolo, and the cost in lives was heavy; hundreds of workers died, and the memorials in the town are a reminder. The road tunnel, opened in 1980, runs for about seventeen kilometres to Göschenen, and the new base tunnel, finished in 2016, is the longest railway tunnel in the world at fifty-seven kilometres. Most of the traffic now goes beneath the mountain, which is exactly why the old road is so peaceful.

That old road is the Tremola, which climbs from Airolo to the Gotthard Pass at 2,106 metres in a series of tight hairpins on cobblestones. The Tremola is a Swiss classic, and the stones give a rattle and a wobble that demand attention, especially in the wet. Ride it slowly, in a low gear, and the views of the Leventina valley are wonderful. The road is closed in winter, usually until late spring, and the cobbles can be treacherous if there is frost in the shade.

Airolo is also the entry to the Bedretto valley, which leads to the Nufenen Pass, the highest paved pass entirely in Switzerland. Fuel is easy here, and the nearest bigger town to the south is Biasca. If you can, wander down to the old station and the church before you leave, and try a plate of polenta with braised beef in a Ticinese restaurant, which will taste better than anything on the motorway.
t.lukmanier pass road@46.6,8.8:
The Lukmanier Pass is the gentlest of the great crossings between the Rhine valley and Ticino, and at 1,915 metres it is also one of the lowest, which explains why it has been used for so long. Its lack of steepness made it a trade and pilgrim route well before the Gotthard became passable, and the monastery of Disentis on the north side owed much of its influence to the traffic.

For a rider, the pass is a relief after the Gotthard. The road is wide and the surface good, with long, easy bends and a gradient that never gets sharp. On the northern side it follows the Medelser Rhine through the Medel gorge, a narrow canyon where the road clings to the rock and tunnels through short galleries. At the top it passes the reservoir of Santa Maria, a long blue lake held back by a big dam, with a small hospice and a chapel beside the water. On the southern side the road drops through the Val Blenio towards Biasca, with the vegetation turning from alpine to chestnut and fig as you lose height.

It is a quiet road compared with its famous neighbours, which makes it good for a slow, thoughtful ride. Traffic can be thick in summer, but it tends to flow, and locals use the road all year round. The pass is normally closed in winter, usually from about November until May, because of heavy snow and avalanche risk. Check the road status if you are out in the shoulder seasons.

Biasca, at the end of the Blenio valley, is the biggest town nearby. In late afternoon the light drops over the lake, and the mountains turn gold; it is a fine place to stop for ten minutes and listen to the quiet, broken only by cow bells.
t.oberalppass high road@46.7,8.7:
The Oberalp is the pass that links Andermatt in the Urseren valley with Disentis in the Surselva, and at 2,044 metres it is the road's high point and a historic watershed. Just above the summit, the little Lake Toma is regarded as the source of the Rhine, the river that eventually runs through Germany and the Netherlands and into the North Sea. A short walk up from the car park gets you to the lakeshore, where a plaque marks the spot.

The riding is smooth and enjoyable, with the road swinging up from Andermatt in wide hairpins, then crossing a high plateau where the wind can be fierce. The red trains of the Matterhorn Gotthard Railway run alongside the road for much of the way, part of the Glacier Express line, and the sight of a train snaking through snow sheds or across a stone bridge is a fine bonus. On the Graubünden side the road drops towards Sedrun and Disentis in graceful sweeps, with views of the Vorderrhein valley opening below.

The area is an important one for the history of the Alps. Andermatt was a garrison town with a military past, and the fortifications still hide in the mountain. The valley was settled by the Walser people and others in the Middle Ages, and the Oberalp route was in use long before the road was paved. The weather can change fast, and a cheerful morning can turn into rain and low cloud by lunchtime, with snow possible even in summer at this altitude.

The road closes in winter, and the railway takes over, running all year, so the pass is usually shut from late autumn until late spring. In early summer there can still be walls of snow beside the road. Late summer, when the air is clear and the days are still long, is a particularly good time.
t.disentis@46.7,8.9:
Disentis is the monastery town of the upper Rhine valley, and the Benedictine abbey that dominates it is one of the oldest in Switzerland, founded, according to tradition, around the year 700 by a wandering monk called Sigisbert with help from a local landowner. The current buildings are mostly baroque, with a huge church and an extensive cloister, and the monks still teach at the school attached to it. The village sits at 1,130 metres where the Medelser Rhine meets the Vorderrhein, and it has the compact feel of a place that was important long before the tourist trade arrived.

For a rider, Disentis is a natural lunch stop between the Oberalp and Lukmanier passes. There are cafes and restaurants along the main street, serving Graubünden dishes such as barley soup, Capuns and dried meats, and a little bakery will usually have a Nusstorte. Fuel is available in the village, and it is a good place to stop for a break before heading up either pass or down the valley to Ilanz. The road from the west follows the Rhine through forests and fields, with long straight stretches and occasional gentle bends.

The language here is Romansh, the fourth national language of Switzerland, spoken by only a small fraction of the population, and you will see it on street signs and shop fronts. Disentis, or Mustér in Romansh, is one of the strongholds of the language, and the abbey played a part in keeping it alive. The valley is also known for its cheese, its snow in winter and its quiet in summer.

Behind the village the mountains rise to glaciers and peaks over three thousand metres, and in winter the area is a popular ski resort. In summer the slopes are covered in meadow flowers and dotted with cows. A visit to the abbey church is worth fifteen minutes, with its white interior and rich decoration, and visitors are generally welcome outside the services. Walk a little further, and you might hear the monks sing the evening office in the half-light.
t.vorderrhein valley flow@46.8,9.2:
Ilanz calls itself the first town on the Rhine, and in a river that runs a thousand kilometres to the North Sea that is a neat claim to hold. It sits in the Surselva at 650 metres, a small, practical place of about two thousand people, where the Vorderrhein valley widens and the Lugnez valley comes in from the south. Fuel, bakeries and a supermarket are all here. Laax, the ski resort village, is a few kilometres up the slope, and Flims lies beyond it.

The riding along the Vorderrhein is relaxed, a flowing run of moderate bends beside a green river, with the Rhaetian Railway's little red trains tracing the opposite bank. Traffic is local, not touristic, and the road is wide enough to be taken at a sensible pace. The valley is a mix of villages and farms, with church towers that have the onion-dome look of the Catholic Alps, and the Romansh language is still heard in shops and on street signs.

Below Ilanz begins the Ruinaulta, the Rhine Gorge, sometimes called the Swiss Grand Canyon. It was carved through the debris of the Flims rockslide, one of the biggest landslides in the Alps, which tumbled off the mountain after the last Ice Age and dammed the river. The river has since cut a gorge of pale limestone cliffs, forested terraces and green water, and rafters and walkers explore it in summer. The main road keeps above the gorge, with viewpoints near Flims where you can look down into the canyon. It is worth the detour even if you only manage a quick look.

Ilanz was an important town of the Grey League, one of the Three Leagues that governed Graubünden before it joined Switzerland, and the old town has a few narrow streets and a fine church. The surrounding hills are rich with legends and small chapels, and there are good walks up to the high villages. A coffee on the main square is a good way to watch the day pass.

The river is the chief character here, and if you stop at a bridge, you can hear the water run, glacial and cold. In spring, melt makes the Rhine brown and high, while by late summer it settles to a gentler green. Early morning light is best on the cliffs.
t.lucerne lake@47.1,8.3:
Lucerne sits where the lake narrows into the Reuss, with the Alps stacked up behind it, and at 436 metres it is one of the most visited cities in Switzerland. The best way to see the old town is on foot, so find a car park and leave the bike.

The Chapel Bridge, a covered wooden footbridge across the Reuss, dates from the fourteenth century and is the city's emblem, with painted panels under the roof showing local history. Much of it burned in a fire in 1993 and was rebuilt, and the octagonal Water Tower beside it survived. A short walk takes you to the Lion Monument, a huge relief carved into a sandstone cliff in the early nineteenth century to honour Swiss guards killed in Paris in 1792. Mark Twain called it the saddest and most moving piece of stone in the world, and it still moves visitors today.

For riders, Lucerne is the lake city that opens the way into central Switzerland. The shoreline roads wind round Lake Lucerne, with its odd shape of fingers and bays, towards Küssnacht, Weggis and Vitznau, with Rigi and Pilatus rising above them. Pilatus gets its name from a legend that Pontius Pilate's body was thrown into a lake on its slopes, and the mountain was long considered haunted. The roads around the lake are scenic but crowded in summer, so use early mornings and late evenings for the best rides.

The lake is one of the cradles of Switzerland. Around its shores lie the original cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, and the Rütli meadow, where the oath of the confederates is said to have been sworn in 1291, is reachable by boat. Steamers still ply the lake, and some are paddle-wheelers more than a century old. If you have time, take one to Flüelen or Vitznau and ride back, or simply watch them from the quay.

Lucerne is dense with tourists in July and August, and parking is expensive, but the lake light in the evening is something special. It is also a city of music, with a famous summer festival and a modern concert hall right by the water.
t.lenzerheide balcony road@46.7,9.6:
Lenzerheide is a high, wide valley south of Chur, a broad saddle of meadow, forest and small lakes at about 1,475 metres. The twin villages of Lenzerheide and Valbella have fuel, cafes and shops, and Chur, a little more than fourteen kilometres north, has everything else.

The road from Chur climbs through Churwalden in a series of generous hairpins, with long views down the Rhine valley, then crosses the low watershed above the Heidsee, the lake at the heart of the resort. This pass is not high, just over fifteen hundred metres, but it feels like a proper mountain crossing. The bends are broad and well banked, the surface is smooth and the gradient is comfortable. On the southern side the road drops through Parpan and Lantsch towards Tiefencastel, the junction of the Julier and Albula routes.

The valley was once a quiet farming district, and its Romansh and German names sit side by side. Tourism arrived with the railways and the first hotels in the nineteenth century, and now Lenzerheide is a big ski resort, with lifts rising on both sides of the valley. In summer the slopes are full of mountain bikers, and the roads can be busy with cyclists as well as cars. The Heidsee is good for a swim on a warm day, though the water stays cold, and a path runs round its shore.

Weather in the high valley can be fickle, with morning mist, afternoon showers and sudden sunshine, and even in summer you should have a jacket within reach. The best time for a ride is early in the day, when the bends are clear and the light is soft. Autumn is lovely, with larches turning gold along the slopes, and the air smells of woodsmoke and cut grass.
t.albula pass railway country@46.6,9.8:
The Albula Pass is the road, but the railway is the star. At 2,315 metres the pass links the Engadine with the Albula valley and Chur, and it is shadowed by the Rhaetian Railway's Albula line, which climbs through spiral tunnels, over viaducts and under the mountain in the Albula tunnel. UNESCO put this line and the Bernina line on the World Heritage list in 2008, and on a clear day you can watch the red trains from the road.

The road is a pleasure, and not too frightening. From Bergün on the northern side it climbs through forest and open pasture, passing the old Albula hospice. The gradients are moderate, the bends are well drawn and the surface is generally smooth, though some stretches are narrow and have no barrier. At the summit the landscape turns bare and stony, with small lakes and patches of snow, and the road slips down towards La Punt and the Upper Engadine through a landscape of larch and spruce.

The Landwasser Viaduct, a graceful curved stone bridge that emerges from a cliff tunnel, is a short distance down the valley and is one of the most photographed railway sights in Switzerland. Bergün itself has a railway museum and a fine old centre, and the lanes of the Engadine villages have the sgraffito-decorated houses typical of the region. The air is thin and clear, and the light in the Engadine is famously bright.

The Albula is normally closed in winter, with snow lingering well into late spring, so check road conditions for opening dates. Fuel is available in Samedan and La Punt, and in Bergün and Filisur on the other side. Traffic is generally light compared with the nearby Julier, and the road is a good choice for a quiet, thoughtful ride.
t.bern@47.0,7.5:
Bern looks like a city drawn by a medieval cartographer who never doubted his own plan. It sits on a high, narrow peninsula inside a tight loop of the Aare river, with the old town packed along the ridge and steep green banks falling to the water on three sides. It was founded in 1191 by Berchtold V, Duke of Zähringen, and the legend says that he named it after the first animal he killed on a hunt, a bear. Bears are still everywhere: on the flag, on fountains, in a park beside the river where several of them live.

The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and it is worth the entry for the arcades alone. About six kilometres of sandstone arcades run along the main streets, so that shoppers walk under cover in all weather, and the streets are lined with sixteenth-century fountains, each topped by a painted figure. The Zytglogge, the clock tower, performs its mechanical show a few minutes before each hour. Albert Einstein lived in a flat on the Kramgasse while working at the patent office, and it was here in 1905 that he wrote the papers that changed physics.

Bern is Switzerland's capital but acts like a small provincial town, with about 120,000 people, a relaxed air and a river you can swim in. On summer evenings, residents float down the Aare in the cool green water. For riders, the city is a convenient base with good roads in every direction: the Gurten hill to the south, the Emmental to the east, the Seeland and Lake Biel to the north-west. The old town centre is mostly pedestrianised and cobbled, so park outside and walk in, and watch the tram tracks, which are treacherous in the wet.

Fuel and food are easy. Bern has stations on all approach roads, and the Marktgasse and its side streets are full of cafes and bakeries. Try a Zopf, the braided Sunday bread, or the Berner Platte, a heavy plate of boiled meats and sauerkraut, if you are hungry. Switzerland requires a motorway vignette, speed limits are strictly enforced, and fines are steep. The best months to ride are May to October, and the view from the Rosengarten across the roofs to the Alps is worth a stop.
t.zermatt@46.0,7.8:
The Matterhorn has the most recognisable shape of any mountain on Earth, and Zermatt sits at its feet, gazing up. It is a village of about six and a half thousand in the upper Mattertal, at 1,600 metres, hemmed in by 4,000-metre peaks, and it is the one resort in Switzerland where the main streets are quiet because petrol vehicles are banned. Small electric taxis and carts hum along the lanes, and the air smells of woodsmoke, pine and horses.

The mountain itself is a pyramid of grey and rust-coloured rock, 4,478 metres high, a steep and unmistakable fang. The first ascent, in July 1865, was by a party led by Edward Whymper, and on the way down four of the seven climbers fell to their deaths, a disaster that shocked Victorian Britain and ended the first golden age of alpinism. Their story is told in a small museum in the village. A cemetery by the church holds the graves of many climbers, and a walk through it is a quiet lesson in what the mountains cost.

For a rider, Zermatt is a destination rather than a road, because you cannot ride in. The road ends at Täsch, a few kilometres short, where a large terminal car park and a shuttle train take visitors the last stretch. Leave the bike at Täsch and take the train, a short ride, then walk up through the village. The Mattertal itself is a spectacular approach, a narrow valley road from Visp with tunnels, galleries and steep rock walls, and the lower Rhône valley around Visp has the nearest main fuel stations. Check the Täsch parking rules for motorcycles before you go.

Once in Zermatt, take the Gornergrat railway, a rack line opened in 1898 that climbs to 3,089 metres in half an hour for views over the Gorner glacier and the whole ring of 4,000-metre summits. Eat Älplermagronen, the Swiss mountain version of macaroni and cheese, or raclette melted from the wheel. Mornings are clearest, since cloud often builds around the Matterhorn by afternoon, and in autumn the larches turn gold. Summer is crowded, and prices are high.
t.lindau@47.5,9.7:
Lindau is an island that behaves like a postcard, and the amusing thing is that it knows it. The old town sits on a small island in the eastern end of Lake Constance, the Bodensee, linked to the mainland by a causeway and a railway embankment, and the harbour at its south side is guarded by two monuments: a tall lighthouse and a stone lion of Bavaria on a pillar. The lighthouse was built in the nineteenth century, and from its top you see the whole lake, with the Austrian and Swiss Alps behind. About twenty-four thousand people live in the municipality, and most of them are on the mainland.

For centuries Lindau was a free imperial city, trading in grain and linen across the lake, and the old streets keep that confidence. Tall gabled houses with painted fronts stand along the Maximilianstrasse, a pedestrian street, and the town hall has a facade covered in frescoes. Every summer, Nobel laureates in medicine, physics and chemistry gather in Lindau to meet young researchers, a tradition that has run since 1951. The lake itself is a mild place: the water holds the heat, vines grow on the slopes above, and palms stand along the waterfront in sheltered spots.

This is the western end of the German Alpine Road, which runs from here to Berchtesgaden, about four hundred and fifty kilometres along the northern edge of the Alps. The first leg to Walchensee goes through the Allgäu, a region of green hills, dairy farms, onion-domed churches and a skyline of limestone peaks, with winding roads, gentle gradients and cheese dairies on every hill. The first miles from Lindau, though, are busy with lake traffic, and the road climbs quickly into the foothills.

Lindau has fuel, mostly on the mainland, and food is excellent. Order Bodensee Felchen, whitefish from the lake, grilled or fried in butter, and drink a glass of the local Müller-Thurgau. Austria is five kilometres away, and the border at Hörbranz is quick, but you need a vignette for motorways there. Summer weekends are crowded, and the best time is May, June or September, when the light on the lake is soft, the ferries are running and the foothills are bright and green.
t.mannheim@49.5,8.5:
Mannheim is a city laid out like a chessboard, and that tells you most of what you need to know about it. The old centre was planned in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by the Electors Palatine, who built a vast baroque palace on the flat ground where the Neckar meets the Rhine and then arranged the streets in squares with letters and numbers instead of names. Locals call it the Quadratestadt. You will find that nobody needs a satnav to cross the middle of town, which is a rare luxury for a rider starting a long day.

The palace still dominates the centre and now houses the university, so on a weekday morning the forecourt is full of students on bicycles. It is one of the largest baroque palaces in Europe, and it is worth a slow roll past before you leave. The city has a quietly mechanical past, too. Karl Drais is said to have ridden his wooden running machine here in 1817, an ancestor of every two-wheeler you have ever owned, and Bertha Benz drove the first long journey by motor car out of this region in 1888, famously stopping at a pharmacy for fuel. Starting a motorcycle ride here feels oddly like paying respects.

The Rhine plain around Mannheim is as flat as a table, and the traffic can be heavy, with Ludwigshafen and its giant chemical works just across the river. Do not expect corners yet. The reward comes once you turn east and follow the Neckar into the hills of the Odenwald, where the Castle Road begins to earn its name, with Heidelberg only a short run away and ruins appearing above the river bends. Leave early on a weekend to get ahead of the commuter belt and the day trippers heading the same way.

Practical matters are easy. This is a city of more than three hundred thousand people, so fuel stations, cafes and bakeries are everywhere, and you can top up the tank and eat properly before the road narrows. Parking a bike near the palace or the water tower area is usually simple, though watch the signs in the central grid. If you want a coffee with some history, the baroque quarters around the palace are a good bet. The smell of the place on a warm morning is river water, hot asphalt and, depending on the wind, a faint chemical tang from the industry across the Rhine. Then you turn the key and leave all of that behind you.
t.konstanz@47.7,9.2:
Konstanz sits right where the Rhine leaves Lake Constance, and so close to Switzerland that Kreuzlingen's streets seem to flow into its own. The border runs through the built-up area with only a fence in places, and because the Germans built the old centre on the northern bank and the Swiss on the south, the two towns are practically one. This closeness is the first thing to know. The second is that the old city was never bombed in the Second World War, spared partly because of its position next to a neutral country, and as a result the medieval streets and merchants' houses survive intact.

The town's great moment came in 1414 to 1418, when the Council of Constance gathered here to end a split in the Catholic church that had left three men all claiming to be pope. It also condemned the reformer Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake outside the walls in 1415, and a memorial stone marks the spot. The harbour is guarded by a nine-metre statue called Imperia, a rotating figure of a woman holding two small men in her hands, installed in 1993 and a good conversation starter. Walk a little along the shore and you will see the Rheintorturm and the old harbour, which still sees ferries to Meersburg and boat trips to the Mainau flower island.

The riding from Konstanz is the real attraction. Roads wind west along the Untersee, past orchards, vineyards and small ports, and the pretty islands of Reichenau and the Swiss shore are close by. The surface is excellent, the corners are mild, and the views over the lake to the Alps in clear weather are the sort that make you slow down without being asked. Traffic can be thick in summer, especially at weekends, and the border crossing can slow things down. Carry your passport or ID card and check whether a Swiss motorway vignette applies if you plan to use motorways there.

Fuel is easy in a city of eighty thousand, and prices on the Swiss side differ from those in Germany, so it pays to check which way is cheaper before you cross. Cafes line the waterfront and the old town, and lake fish such as Felchen are a local speciality. Mornings are calm on the water, with a thin mist, and the light is best in autumn when the orchards turn gold. The air smells of fresh water, damp stone and coffee.
t.stuttgart@48.8,9.2:
Stuttgart lies in a bowl, and everyone who lives there knows it. The city climbs out of the Neckar valley into steep hillsides covered with vineyards, so that you can ride from a central square and be among grapevines within ten minutes. The cauldron shape, known locally as the Talkessel, traps heat and air in summer, but it also gives the city its distinct character, with staircases called Stäffele running up the slopes and villas hanging on the hillsides. It is also, for motorcyclists, a place with unusual pedigree: this is where Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built an early motorcycle in 1885, a wooden contraption with a petrol engine often called the first of its kind.

The city's identity is bound up with engineering. Mercedes-Benz and Porsche both have their headquarters here, and each has a museum that draws rather serious pilgrims. The Mercedes museum, near the Neckar stadium, is a spiral of vehicle history from steam wagons to modern racing cars, and the Porsche museum in Zuffenhausen is a gleaming white block full of sports cars. Both are worth an hour on a wet day. The city also has the Schlossplatz, with the New Palace and the pleasant gardens, and Swabian cooking that includes Maultaschen, a kind of large filled pasta, and Spätzle.

The ride out of town is more demanding than it looks on the map. Steep roads climb out of the valley toward the Schönbuch forest and the Swabian Alb, and the suburbs spread a long way in places, with a lot of traffic lights and a slow-moving flow in the rush hour. Speed limits are tight, and cameras are common. Once you clear the edge of the city the roads open into rolling farmland and wooded valleys, with mild bends and a good surface. Spring and autumn are lovely, when the vineyards are fresh green or golden red and the air is clear.

Fuel is no problem in a city of nearly six hundred thousand people, with stations on all the main roads, and cafes and bakeries are at every corner. Mornings tend to be best, with traffic lower and the air cooler. Be prepared for local environmental zones that restrict older vehicles in the city centre, though modern motorcycles are normally fine. A good start here is a coffee in the old town, a look at the hills, and then the first climb.
t.val trebbia@45.4,9.7:
Crema is the town to know here, a walled little city of about thirty thousand people on the Serio river, a short hop east of Milan's commuter sprawl and quite unlike it. The stop sits just outside, among fields and villages such as Capergnanica and Bagnolo Cremasco, in flat Lombard farmland where the horizon is a line of poplars and the Alps show only on very clear winter days.

Do not expect the Val Trebbia itself, which lies well south, in the Apennines toward Bobbio. This is the lowland end of the ride, where the day's altitude has long since drained away and the road is a matter of straight farm lanes, bridges over irrigation canals and the odd roundabout. Surfaces are generally fine, though heavy farm traffic leaves grooves, and after rain the verges carry mud from the beet and maize harvest. Mornings in autumn bring a fog that sits on the plain like cotton wool.

Crema deserves an hour more than most finish points. Its old centre was fortified by Venice, whose border with Milan ran close by for centuries, and the Venetian walls and bastions still shape the town. Piazza Duomo is a tidy square of brick and white stone, the cathedral mixing Lombard Gothic with later changes. The area is known for tortelli cremaschi, a stuffed pasta with a curious sweet filling of amaretti and raisins that surprises anyone expecting plain cheese, and it is worth ordering once for the story alone.

Fuel is no problem in Crema, and the smaller villages around have pumps too, though self-service machines are common outside daytime hours, so carry a note or a card that works with them. Parking in the centre is limited-access in places, so leave the bike on the outer streets if you want to walk the old town. After the Apennine curves, the flatness can feel like a stiff drink after a long meal, but it is a gentle way to let the day settle.
Underneath the black volcanic soil of Jeju's north-east lies a hidden world. The Geomunoreum lava tube system, a group of caves that carry names such as Manjanggul and Gimnyeong, was formed when rivers of molten rock from the Geomun volcano drained away and left hollow tunnels behind them. UNESCO listed the area together with Hallasan and Seongsan Ilchulbong as the Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes site in 2007, and the tubes are reckoned to be among the finest in the world.

Manjanggul, the best known, runs for several kilometres, though only the first kilometre or so is open to visitors. Inside the air is cool and damp whatever the weather outside, so bring a jacket, and the floor is uneven in places. You walk beneath arched walls streaked with lava ridges, past ropy flow patterns, to a lava column about seven metres tall at the end of the open section. Bats live deeper in, and you will hear water dripping.

The area is wooded in a way the rest of the island is not. These are gotjawal, rough forests grown on jagged lava where nothing could be farmed, a place of ferns, vines and tangled trees that works like a sponge for rainwater and feeds the island's springs. Roads here cross low, quiet country, past stone walls, tangerine orchards and small farms, with Jeju City about twenty kilometres to the west and Seogwipo further south. The wind can be fierce, and fog and rain move in quickly.

The caves have a ticket office and a small museum, with fixed seasonal hours that are worth checking, and some tubes close for conservation. Wear shoes with grip. Fill the tank in Jeju City or the larger villages on the main roads, since the forest lanes have none. Local black pork, grilled over charcoal, and abalone porridge are the island's prized dishes, and small restaurants near the caves serve them. Go in a quiet season if you can, and enjoy the rare feeling of walking inside a volcano's old plumbing.
t.jeju@33.5,126.5:
Jeju is a volcanic island off the south coast of Korea, and everything on it is shaped by that fact. Hallasan, the central cone and the highest mountain in South Korea, rises to about 1,950 metres and is visible from nearly every corner of the island on a clear day, and the whole land slopes from it to the sea in long, easy lines. Jeju City, on the north coast, is the main gateway, with an airport that ranks among the busiest in the world and a harbour with ferry links to the mainland.

The people and traditions are distinct. Jeju has its own dialect, its own customs, and the haenyeo, women divers who plunge without breathing equipment to gather abalone, conch and seaweed, and who are recognised by UNESCO for their tradition. Walls of black volcanic stone divide the fields and shelter the crops from wind, and the stone grandfather figures called dolhareubang stand at gates and in tourist shops. Tangerines are grown everywhere and sold from roadside stalls.

The roads around the island are a joy to ride, with a coastal ring road circling the shore past beaches, cliffs and fishing harbours. The sea is a deep blue-green, and the land is covered in rapeseed flowers in spring and white-tipped silver grass in autumn. Wind is the main factor, sometimes strong enough to push a bike sideways on exposed stretches, and the weather changes fast. Typhoons can cause cancellations in late summer. The mountain roads that cross toward Seogwipo climb through forest and are cooler and misty.

Jeju City has fuel in abundance and plenty of restaurants. Try the island's black pork, raw fish, abalone and the sea urchin soup, or a bowl of noodles with pork bone broth. The old market near the harbour is lively in the evening, and Yongduam, a dragon-head rock on the shore near the airport, is a good place for sunset. Rent or ride early, avoid holiday weekends, and take your time.
t.jackson@43.5,-110.8:
Jackson sits in a valley that the old trappers called a hole, a high, flat basin ringed by mountains, and the Teton Range rises straight from its western edge without any foothills to soften the view. The town stands at about nineteen hundred metres, with the National Elk Refuge just to the north, where thousands of elk spend the winter. The town square is marked by four arches made of shed elk antlers, which locals gather each spring, and it is a good place for a photo before you start the day.

Riders come for Grand Teton and Yellowstone, and both are within reach. The road north runs beside the refuge and enters Grand Teton National Park, passing Jackson Lake and giving some of the best mountain views in the American West. Yellowstone's south entrance lies about a hundred and twenty kilometres from town, and the road runs through forest, along the Snake River and beside open meadows where bison and moose are regular visitors. Surfaces are generally good, with speed limits that match the wildlife, and long stretches at fifty-five miles an hour. Wildlife on the road is a real hazard, especially at dawn and dusk.

West of town, Teton Pass climbs steeply to over 2,500 metres on the way to Idaho, with sharp bends and steep grades, and it can be treacherous in wet or icy conditions. For most of the year it is an exciting ride, and the views to the east over the valley are lovely. Summer afternoons bring storms that build over the peaks, and even in July the nights can be near freezing.

Jackson has about ten thousand people, with fuel, restaurants and motels in good supply, though prices are high, especially in summer and during ski season. Book a room early. Local bars still keep the cowboy tradition, with saddle stools at the counter, and elk burgers and bison steaks appear on many menus. Services between Jackson and Yellowstone are thin, so start with a full tank and some water, and carry warm layers even on a hot afternoon.
t.ticino lakes@45.3,8.9:
Morimondo is the quietest place on this map, with only a few hundred residents, but its abbey is among the finest in Lombardy. The abbey, a Cistercian foundation of the twelfth century, was established by monks from Morimond in Burgundy, and its brick church, with a plain, severe interior, is still in use.

For a ride that explored the Ticino lakes and passes, the end is a gentle one. The roads here run straight across rice fields and meadows, with sudden bends where a canal or a hedge intervenes, and the surface is generally good, though narrow and sometimes bumpy. In autumn, mist hangs over the fields and visibility can drop to a few metres, and in spring, the paddies are flooded and reflect the sky. Mosquitoes are a feature of summer evenings. The Ticino Park, a large protected area along the river, has woods, marshes and cycle paths, and is rich in birds.

Rice is the main crop, and the local risotto, made with Carnaroli or Arborio, is a staple. The monks who built the abbey helped to drain and cultivate this land, and the network of canals, the Navigli, was used to carry goods and water. The Certosa di Pavia, a vast Carthusian monastery founded by the Visconti in 1396, lies about twenty kilometres to the south, and it is one of the great monuments of Lombardy.

Fuel is available at Motta Visconti, with a station and supermarket, and the tiny villages around the abbey have a bar or trattoria. A bowl of risotto in a local trattoria, perhaps with frog or saffron, is a good way to end the day.

Walk through the cloister if the abbey is open. The quiet, the brick and the long shadows have a gentle effect after a day on the road.
t.seogwipo@33.3,126.6:
Seogwipo is the main town on the south coast of Jeju Island, with about a hundred and fifty thousand people, and it faces the open ocean with Mount Halla behind. Jeju is a volcanic island, and the southern coast has some of its finest scenery, with black basalt cliffs, waterfalls and small islands. The town itself is relaxed and pleasant, with a lively harbour, seafood restaurants and an old-fashioned market, the Maeil Olle, where you can buy tangerines, fish and snacks.

The island is famous for its tangerines, which are grown on terraced orchards across the south, and you often see the fruit stacked in baskets at the roadside in winter. Another symbol of Jeju is the haenyeo, women divers who plunge into the sea without breathing equipment to collect abalone, sea urchins and seaweed, a tradition that has been recognised by UNESCO. You can sometimes see them at work near the shore, and some restaurants serve their catch fresh from the sea.

Close to town are several sights. Jeongbang Falls drops straight into the ocean, an extraordinary sight, and Cheonjiyeon Falls lies in a lush forest with a path from the car park. Further west, the Jusangjeolli cliffs, a row of hexagonal basalt columns that look like stacked logs, rise from the shore, battered by the waves. Oedolgae, a sea stack of rock that stands alone in the water, is another landmark.

The riding on Jeju is delightful. The coastal road circles the island, with open views, gentle curves and little traffic outside the holiday season. In summer and on weekends, tourist traffic can be heavy, particularly around the popular sights, and rental scooters and cars share the road. Wind blows hard on the coast, and weather can change fast, with sudden fog or rain.

Fuel stations are common in Seogwipo and across the island, so there is no problem. Jeju City, almost thirty kilometres away, is the other main centre. A fresh seafood meal by the harbour is the best end to the day.
t.la paz@24.1,-110.3:
La Paz is the capital of Baja California Sur, a city of over two hundred thousand people on the shore of a wide bay that gave it a pearl fishing industry for centuries. Cortés landed here in 1535, the pearl oysters made the place famous, and John Steinbeck set his novella The Pearl on this coast after sailing the Sea of Cortez with his friend Ed Ricketts in 1940. The oyster beds failed in the early twentieth century, but the city has kept its easy, coastal character, and the seafront walk, the malecón, is where everybody goes in the evening to eat ice cream and look at the sunset.

After the long run down Highway 1 the arrival is almost shocking. You have been riding for days through desert, mission towns and empty coast, and now there are traffic lights, supermarkets, taxis and a proper urban grid. Slow down and use the extra patience, since city traffic here is brisk and speed bumps are placed everywhere, often without much warning. Fuel is easy, and so are repairs and a laundry, which will be welcome if you have been camping. From La Paz the road continues south to Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo, or you can drop the bike at one of the ferry terminals at Pichilingue, a few kilometres north of the city, where boats cross to the mainland at Mazatlán and Topolobampo.

The bay itself is shallow and calm, and from about October to April you can go out on a boat to snorkel with whale sharks, which feed in the bay in those months. Sea lions haul out on a rock off Isla Espíritu Santo, a short boat trip away. Both are worth the time if you have a spare day.

Summer here is hot and sticky, and the city is quieter then, with cyclone season running through September and October. In winter the days are clear and mild, which is the better time. Finish the ride at the water, with a plate of fish tacos or a cold beer, and let the Baja miles settle.
t.dornbirn@47.4,9.7:
Dornbirn is the biggest town in Vorarlberg, with nearly fifty thousand people, and it sits at a hinge in the landscape. To the west lies the flat floor of the Rhine valley and, beyond it, Lake Constance and the Swiss hills. To the east the land rises abruptly into the green, steep country of the Bregenzerwald, with the Karren, a hill above the town reached by a cable car, giving a view of the lake and the Alps. The town lies at about 437 metres.

It is a prosperous, practical place, with an old textile industry and a modern trade-fair centre, and the centre has a pleasant pedestrian zone with cafes and bakeries. Nearby, the Rappenlochschlucht, a narrow gorge carved by the Dornbirner Ach, has a path with wooden walkways, and is a favourite walk. The town's market square is lively on Saturday mornings, and local cheeses and sausages are worth buying.

For a rider, Dornbirn is an excellent finishing point, with fuel stations on every approach and the motorway close by. The A14 Rhine valley motorway runs along the valley, and in Austria a vignette is required for motorways, so make sure you have one if you plan to use it. The best riding is on the roads up into the Bregenzerwald, which twist through steep meadows and woods, with views of farms and the occasional waterfall. Traffic is light, but cyclists are common, and the weather can change quickly in the mountains.

The evening light over the Rhine valley is lovely, and in autumn, a warm southerly wind called the Föhn can bring remarkable clarity to the air, with the mountains seeming close enough to touch. On the other hand, it can make the weather unsettled, so watch the sky.

If you are ending a ride here, try a Kaspressknödel, a cheese dumpling in broth, or a plate of Käsespätzle, cheese noodles with fried onions. They are the right food for a day in the mountains, and the cafes and inns around the old centre serve both.
t.splugen@46.6,9.3:
Splügen is where the Rhine, still a young and rather modest river, runs through the high Rheinwald valley in Graubünden, and the village has been a waystation for as long as people have wanted to get over the Alps. Two passes leave from here: the Splügen itself, 2,113 metres, which drops to Italy and the Valle San Giacomo, and the San Bernardino, 2,066 metres, which heads south into Ticino. Choosing between them at the village fountain is one of the nicer decisions in the Alps.

The village is compact and handsome. Tall stone houses, some with painted fronts, crowd narrow lanes, and the old merchants' warehouses recall the days when mule trains and wagons carried goods over the pass and the village earned its living by feeding and housing the carriers. The Splügen road itself was rebuilt as a proper carriage route in the early nineteenth century, an Austrian-era engineering effort to keep trade flowing toward Milan, and you can still sense that ambition in the tidy masonry of the hairpins above the Italian border. The valley above is Walser country, settled by German-speaking migrants from the Valais centuries ago, and place names and farmhouses carry that story.

Riding up the Splügen from here is a steady build rather than a rush. The first stretch climbs through meadow and larch to the dam at Sufers, then the road ramps up to the Italian side, where a run of tightly stacked hairpins drops toward Chiavenna and the first palms and chestnut trees of the south. It is a pass for riders who like precision: narrow in places, with short sight lines and stone walls close to the edge. The San Bernardino is the easier sibling, faster and smoother, and a tunnel carries the motorway beneath it, which keeps the old road quiet.

Practically, Splügen is small, so do not count on a petrol station at the moment you need one. Thusis, down the valley, is the more reliable bet northbound, and Chiavenna waits on the Italian side. Both passes close in winter, usually from around November to May, and snow can linger on shaded bends well into June. Bring a layer even in July; the Rheinwald sits high and the air cools quickly when the sun goes behind the ridge.
t.wutach gorge scenic area@47.8,8.3:
The Wutach is a river with an identity crisis, and that is why the gorge it cut is so spectacular. Once a headwater of the Danube, it was captured, in geological terms quite recently, by a short, steep tributary of the Rhine, and since then it has been tearing a deep trench through the limestone and granite of the southern Black Forest. The result is a gorge well over a hundred metres deep, wild and wooded, and the longest and deepest in the region. Geologists come to study the river capture; walkers come for the moss, the ferns and the sound of water.

The gorge is a nature reserve, and the best way to see it is on foot, on a trail that winds along the river for many kilometres. The best sections have narrow ledges, wooden walkways and short ladders, and the terrain is wet and slippery. Because the walls are steep and shaded, the microclimate is cool, and rare plants and orchids grow in the damp. Dippers and grey wagtails are among the birds on the water, though you will be lucky to see them.

The roads around the gorge are another matter. The B315 and the lanes around Bonndorf, Löffingen and Lenzkirch pass through open plateau, forest and farmland, with long curves, easy gradients and good views, and they are among the better secondary roads in the Black Forest. The area is quiet outside summer weekends, and in autumn the larches and beeches turn gold. Watch for walkers and cyclists, and for tractors in the farming season. Near Blumberg, the Sauschwänzlebahn, a steam railway known as the Pig's Tail Railway for its looping route, runs on summer weekends over viaducts and through tunnels.

Bonndorf, less than two kilometres away, has about seven thousand people, with petrol stations, bakeries and inns, and it is the natural base. The gorge's car parks are small and fill early in the day on sunny weekends, so arrive early. At around six hundred and fifty metres above sea level, the air is fresh, and spring can arrive late.

Black Forest cake and a plate of smoked ham are the local rewards, and a cold beer at the end of the day is hard to resist.
t.todtnau forest roads@47.8,7.9:
Todtnau sits in the Wiese valley in the southern Black Forest, and the forest roads around it are the reason people ride here. At about 650 metres, the town is tucked below the Feldberg, the highest mountain in the whole range, and the lanes that thread up through the spruce on either side belong to a landscape of steep pastures, deep side valleys and old farmsteads with their huge, low-hanging roofs.

The riding is the best sort of Black Forest riding: not about speed but about rhythm. Roads here were laid down along streams and ridges, so they pitch, bend and twist, tight hairpins followed by long straight bits where the trees close overhead and the light turns green. The surface is generally good, but patched in places after winter, and in shaded corners you may find damp or pine needles even in July. Traffic is mostly local, plus cyclists, who are numerous and often climbing slowly, and tourists. Weekends are busy, and the best hours are early morning or early evening, when the valleys are quiet and the smell of cut grass and resin hangs in the air.

Todtnau is a proper town of about five thousand, so fuel and food are easy. It built its name on winter sports as much as anything: skiing in the Black Forest has a long history, and the area claims some of the earliest ski clubs and lifts in Germany. Nearby, the Todtnau waterfall tumbles down a rock face and is among the taller falls in the country, a short walk from the road. In the town itself, the cafes serve Black Forest cake, which here is not a tourist gimmick but a point of local pride, made with kirsch from the valley's orchards.

The forest also carries older history. Silver and other ores were mined on these slopes in the Middle Ages, and the scattered hamlets and chapels grew from that wealth and from the work of farmers who lived on poor, steep land. If you stop on a quiet lane, listen: cowbells, running water, and the odd chainsaw, a reminder that forestry is still the economy.
t.st blasien@47.8,8.1:
St. Blasien is the kind of town that surprises you from a distance. You come down through spruce forest, round a bend, and there is a green copper dome of tremendous size standing over a small Black Forest town as if someone had mislaid a cathedral from a much bigger city. The dome belongs to the former Benedictine abbey church, and at roughly thirty-six metres across it is one of the largest church domes in Europe north of the Alps.

The abbey itself goes back to the early Middle Ages, a monastery founded in the Albtal in a clearing so remote that the monks had to make everything themselves. Over the centuries it became rich and powerful, and in 1768 a fire destroyed most of it. The abbot of the time chose to rebuild on a grand scale, with a French architect designing a neoclassical rotunda that was completed in 1783. Today the buildings house a well-known boarding school run by Jesuits, and the church is open to visitors; the interior is plain white and calm, which is a relief after the busy Baroque of so many Alpine churches.

The town sits at around 770 metres in a high valley, and it has long been a health resort, valued for its clean air and quiet. With about four thousand people it has enough shops, bakeries and cafes to make a proper coffee stop, and the square in front of the dome is a pleasant place to sit with a bike in sight.

The roads in and out are what you hope for in this region: climbing through dark forest, passing small reservoirs and meadows, with fast sweepers on the open stretches and tighter work near the valley floor. In winter they are often snowy, and ice lingers in the shade. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, when the forest is bright and the tourists are fewer.
t.koblenz@47.6,8.2:
Koblenz is a small Swiss town on the Rhine, and its job on this ride is simple: it is where you cross back. Across the river lies Waldshut, the German side, and the pair are connected by an old bridge that has seen centuries of toll collectors and, later, customs officers. Today the border is open and relaxed, but the habit remains of stopping here to sort out the practical things before the road home.

The setting is flatter and gentler than the Black Forest you have just left. The Rhine here is wide and green and moves with a quiet weight, and not far upstream the Aare joins it, bringing the waters of half of central Switzerland to the party; the rivers meet near Koblenz in a confluence that does not look like much from the road but is among the most important in the country. Downstream, the Klingnau reservoir is an internationally recognised bird reserve, where herons, ducks and, in winter, huge flocks of migrants gather on the shallows.

For riders the point is fuel. Waldshut-Tiengen, a town of twenty thousand, has everything, and Klingnau, a few minutes down the valley, has a pretty little old town with a medieval look. Switzerland requires a vignette to use its motorways, so if you plan to take the fast road home rather than the lanes, check that you have one.

The roads around Koblenz are mostly practical rather than thrilling: river roads, commuter lanes, the occasional slow farm vehicle. But the evening light on the Rhine can be lovely, and in the late afternoon the quiet water and the old bridge make a good pause before the final run home. Keep your passport or ID with you, because spot checks still happen.
t.staffelegg ridge road@47.4,8.1:
The Staffelegg is a modest pass, 621 metres, but it deserves more credit than the number suggests. It crosses the folded ridges of the Jura between the Aare valley at Aarau and the Fricktal beyond, and the road that climbs it from Küttigen is one of those quiet Swiss crossings that locals use daily and visitors rarely notice. That is its charm.

The Jura here is a landscape of long, tilted limestone ridges, like waves frozen on their way to shore, with beech and pine woods on the slopes and neat farms in the folds between. The Staffelegg road follows one of those folds. Climbing from Aarau, it winds through woodland, with corners that tighten gradually and then relax into flowing bends along the ridge. The surface is generally excellent, the signage clear, and the gradient gentle enough that even a loaded tourer feels no strain. On the far side the road dips toward Densbüren and then down into the Fricktal, a region of orchards and cherry trees that explode into white blossom in April.

Traffic can be heavy at commuting hours, as the pass is a practical shortcut, and some drivers take it fast, so ride with some patience on weekday mornings and evenings. Weekend afternoons are easier, and the best light is in the evening, when low sun picks out the ridges and the fields glow. In winter, expect frost and occasionally snow, but the road is cleared quickly.

Küttigen, with its five thousand residents, makes a good base for fuel and a quick coffee, and Aarau, just down the road, is a proper city with all services. Aarau is worth a short walk if you have time: its old town has painted gables and wide eaves, and it was briefly the capital of the Helvetic Republic in 1798, a footnote of history that most visitors miss. Between the city and the pass there is also a good chance of seeing red kites circling over the fields, a bird that has made a notable comeback in Switzerland.
t.passwang road@47.4,7.7:
Passwang is a Jura crossing at 943 metres between Balsthal in the Solothurn canton and the Baselland valleys to the north. It is a proper mountain road in miniature, and for many riders it is the highlight of this part of Switzerland, because it packs good bends, long views and quiet forest into a short distance. The road leaves Balsthal through the Gäu and the gorge of the Klus, then climbs through Mümliswil in a series of rising bends toward the saddle.

The northern side drops toward Reigoldswil and the Waldenburg valley, where a narrow-gauge railway, one of the oldest of its kind in the country, runs beside the road and sometimes crosses it. The grade is moderate, the bends are well engineered, and the surface is generally smooth, though the occasional patch of frost heave appears after a hard winter. In summer, cattle graze the high pastures near the top, and on clear days the view reaches over the folded Jura toward the Black Forest, with the Alps visible further off as a pale line on the southern horizon.

Passwang is usually open all year, but snow and ice can close it briefly in winter, and early mornings in spring can be treacherous in the shade. Fuel is better planned for Balsthal, a town of nearly six thousand at the foot of the south side, or for the larger centres on the plain.

Geologically, the Jura is the product of the same pressure that raised the Alps, but felt at a distance. The rocks here were pushed into folds like a rug crumpled against a wall, and the ridges you cross follow the pleats. Limestone gives the region its caves, springs and bright, dry-stone character, and also its wildflowers: orchids and gentians on the high meadows in early summer. A slow pass and a quiet morning will get you the most out of it.
t.solothurn@47.2,7.5:
Solothurn has a habit of making visitors ask why they have not come sooner. It sits on the Aare at the foot of the Jura, about fifteen thousand people living in what is probably the best-preserved Baroque town in Switzerland, and for a couple of centuries it was the seat of the French ambassador to the Confederation. That gave the place a refinement out of proportion to its size: grand townhouses, fountains in every square, and a cathedral built in the eighteenth century in pale Ticinese style, dedicated to Saint Ursus.

The town has a thing about the number eleven. There are eleven churches and chapels, eleven fountains, eleven museums, and the cathedral's steps are laid out in groups of eleven. Locals will tell you the story with a straight face, and whether or not it is quite exact, it adds to the charm. The old town is compact and walkable, with arcades and painted shutters, and the river path, lined with plane trees, is a lovely place to eat a sandwich while the Aare slides past.

For a food stop it is ideal. There are bakeries, cafes with outdoor tables on the square, and a Saturday market that fills the streets with cheese, bread and vegetables. Fuel is plentiful on the ring roads around the centre, and parking for bikes is easier than in bigger cities, though in the old town itself you will want to leave the machine on the edge and walk.

The riding around Solothurn is a pleasant mix. To the north the Weissenstein ridge climbs into the Jura, with a road that gains height quickly and offers views over the Mittelland and, on a clear day, a long line of Alpine summits from the Eiger to Mont Blanc. To the south the landscape is gentler, farmland with the Aare carving lazy loops. Traffic in the centre can be slow, and the morning commute clogs the bridges, so aim for mid-morning or the quiet afternoon. The film festival in January and the farmers' markets give the town a lively rhythm all year, but late spring, when the lime trees bloom, is when it looks its best.
t.hallwilersee@47.3,8.2:
Hallwilersee is one of the quieter lakes of the Swiss Plateau, a long, narrow stretch of water in the Aargau hills some forty kilometres south-west of Zürich, lying in the Seetal valley at roughly four hundred and fifty metres. It lacks the drama of the lakes near the Alps, but it has a gentle beauty that appeals to those who prefer a slower pace: green meadows, orchards, small harbours and a swimming beach on each shore. In summer, rowing boats and paddle boards dot the surface.

At the northern end stands Schloss Hallwyl, a moated castle that is one of the best-preserved water castles in Switzerland. The Hallwyl family held it for centuries, and the buildings, which date from the twelfth century onward, are set on two islands in a pond and surrounded by gardens. Inside, a museum shows how the nobility lived. The area is also home to some of the oldest lake dwellings in the region, with prehistoric pile settlements around the shore that form part of a UNESCO listing of the Alps' pile-dwellings.

For a rider, the ride around the lake is a pleasant interlude between more ambitious roads. Minor lanes follow the shore through villages such as Meisterschwanden, Beinwil and Seengen, with good surfaces and gentle bends, and the climb to the ridge above the lake gives wide views. The Seetal is a favourite with cyclists, so take care on weekends, and speed cameras are common. It makes a good water stop on the way to the Jura, with plenty of cafés and lakeside restaurants where you can sit with a drink.

Meisterschwanden has about two and a half thousand people, with a few shops and places to eat, and Reinach, a few kilometres away, has fuel and larger supermarkets. Regional roads here are well signed, and motorcyclists will find parking easy at the lakeside.

Try fresh lake fish, such as perch fillets, if you see them on the menu, and a glass of local white wine from the Seetal hills. The evening light on the water makes it hard to leave.
t.schwyz@47.0,8.7:
Schwyz is the village that gave Switzerland its name. The country's flag grew from the banner of this canton, and the oldest surviving federal charter, dated to 1291, is kept in a museum in town, written on parchment with seals that have survived seven centuries. If history is the thing for you, this is as close to the source as you can get, and a short walk in the old centre shows how modest the beginnings were.

The town itself is lively without being busy: a broad square with a baroque church, a town hall with painted facades showing a battle scene, and stately patrician houses built by men who had made fortunes as mercenary officers in foreign armies. Behind it all rise the Mythen, two sharp limestone peaks that look from the village like a pair of horns and dominate every photograph. The cloud sits on them often, and on a clear morning they are a fine sight with coffee in hand.

With fourteen thousand people, Schwyz has fuel, bakeries and sit-down restaurants, so as a start or a food stop it is easy. The start of the loop is the main reason to be here: from Schwyz the road climbs south and east into the hills, toward the Ibergeregg and the Pragel, a pair of passes that make a rewarding day. The first miles run through meadows dotted with fruit trees and farmhouses with deep-eaved wooden roofs, and the gradient builds gradually, so there is time to warm up the tyres and your rhythm.

Weather can be unpredictable here, because the Alps' northern edge catches the moist air coming from the lowlands, and a bright start can become grey by lunchtime. Plan accordingly, with a waterproof near the top of the luggage. The Föhn wind also blows through this region, warm and dry from the south, and on those days the air is incredibly clear but the gusts can be strong on the open stretches. In winter, the high passes close, but the town stays lively, and a bowl of something hot in a Gasthaus makes a fair reward for the effort.
t.jura@47.0,7.1:
The real Jura mountains rise on the far northern shore as a long, wooded wall, and the whole scene has the unhurried look of a place where wine, boats and long lunches are taken seriously.

Erlach, called Cerlier in French, is one of the oldest settlements on the lake, a cluster of gabled houses climbing to a small castle, with a stone harbour and a lakeside promenade. It lies at the edge of the language border, so signs are in both German and French, and people code-switch without noticing. Offshore, the St. Peter's Island, which is really a peninsula now, was the refuge of the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau in 1765, who spent just two months there and later called them the happiest of his life. A path through the woods and meadows leads to the old monastery that stands on the island, which is now an inn.

The vineyards on the north shore, around Twann, La Neuveville and Le Landeron, produce light, crisp whites from the Chasselas grape, and the wine villages are a pleasure to explore, with narrow lanes, cellar doors and taverns. The ride around the lake is gentle: the road on the north shore threads between vines and the water with easy bends and good views, while the south shore road is flatter and a little busier. Weekends bring cyclists, walkers and visitors from Bern and Neuchâtel, so aim for a weekday or an early morning start.

The lake sits at about four hundred and thirty metres, and the mild microclimate allows vines, fruit trees and even a few fig trees to flourish. Fog sometimes lies on the water on autumn mornings, lifting by late morning to reveal the Alps on the southern horizon on a clear day.

Fuel and shops are best found in Le Landeron, where there are about four thousand people, or in Murten, twelve kilometres away, which has a perfectly preserved medieval wall that you can walk on. Erlach itself has small restaurants, and the fish from the lake, usually perch or whitefish, is the thing to order.
t.basel@47.1,7.2:
Despite the label, this is Biel, or Bienne in French, a bilingual city of nearly fifty thousand at the northern tip of Lake Biel, and one of the most underrated towns in Switzerland.
