It sits where the lake meets the first long ridge of the Jura, and its centre is a mixture of a medieval old town, with a fountain-filled square and half-timbered houses, and the clean, grid-like modernism of the twentieth-century town that grew up around the watch factories.

Watches are the thing. Biel is the home of Swatch and Omega, and the Swatch Group headquarters, a long timber-clad building by Shigeru Ban, sits on the edge of the old centre. For generations the town's economy has been tied to precision manufacturing, and the old workers' quarters have been slowly turned into galleries and cafés. A walk in the Neustadt, the planned town with its straight streets and 1930s buildings, shows a version of Swiss modernism that is a world away from the chalets and cows on the postcards.

The geography is dramatic for a small city. A funicular runs from the lakeside up to Magglingen, on a ridge about four hundred metres higher, where the Swiss federal sports school stands among meadows, and the view over the lake and the Alps on a clear day is superb. Behind the town, the Taubenloch gorge cuts into the limestone. On the roads, the climb to Magglingen and the long ridge above the lake give excellent riding, with good surfaces, smooth bends and views to the south. The hills above the town are well known to Swiss riders, and on sunny weekends you will find plenty of company, so keep the pace sensible, because speed cameras and police checks are routine.

Biel has all the services of a regional city: fuel, repair shops, supermarkets and a wide choice of restaurants, with Italian and Portuguese places that reflect the communities who came to work in the factories. A perch fillet from the lake, with a glass of local white wine, is the traditional lunch.

Sit by the lake in the late afternoon, and watch the sailboats. The long summer evenings make it easy to linger.
t.aarau@47.6,7.6:
Again the label misleads: this is Basel, the Swiss city where the Rhine turns north, and its position at the meeting of three countries makes it feel more European than most. France and Germany both begin within a few kilometres of the city centre, and the river carries barges, tourists and swimmers through the heart of town. In summer, Baslers float down the river in the current with their clothes in waterproof bags, and the riverbanks fill with picnics and music.

The old town stands on a hill above the Rhine, crowned by the red sandstone Münster, a cathedral that was first built in the eleventh century and later became a Protestant church after the Reformation reached Basel in 1529. The scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam spent his last years here and is buried in the cathedral. Below, the narrow lanes lead past the Rathaus, whose bright red walls and painted façade are the city's most recognisable building, and down to the river, where small cable ferries cross the water, powered only by the current, as they have for centuries. In February, the city's carnival, the Fasnacht, begins at four in the morning in February or March with drums and piccolos, a tradition so beloved that people plan the year around it.

Basel is also a capital of art and science. It is home to some of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, and the city has an unusual number of museums for its size. The Kunstmuseum holds a major collection from the Renaissance to the present, and the Fondation Beyeler, just across the border in Riehen, sits in a beautiful building by Renzo Piano in a green park. Each June, Art Basel brings the art world to town.

For riders, Basel is the gateway to the Jura and to the Black Forest and the Vosges, which are close. City traffic is dense, with trams that need respect: rails and wet cobbles are slippery on a motorcycle, so cross them at a right angle. Parking for bikes is available in many places and is cheaper than for cars.

Fuel and food are everywhere, and nearby Germany and France have different prices, so many people cross the border to fill up. Order a Basler Läckerli, a spiced honey biscuit, for the road.
t.brig@46.3,8.0:
Brig is a small town with a big palace, and its position at the foot of the Simplon Pass gives it a significance out of proportion to its size. It sits in the upper Rhône valley in the canton of Valais, where the river runs west to Lake Geneva, and a route over the mountains to Italy has existed here since Roman times. The Stockalperschloss, the biggest private residence in Switzerland when it was completed in the late seventeenth century, was built by Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper, a merchant who controlled the Simplon trade and became the richest man in the country. With its three onion-domed towers, named for the Three Kings, it dominates the old town and is open to visitors.

The Simplon Pass road is the reason riders come. Napoleon had a carriage road built over it between 1801 and 1805, so that his armies could cross to Italy, and it is still one of the great engineering works of the age. The road climbs in broad curves out of the Rhône valley, passes through galleries and over a famous bridge at the Ganter gorge, and crosses the top at about two thousand metres. The surface is good, the bends are open and consistent, and the views toward the Bernese and Valais Alps are huge. The pass is usually open from about May to October, and sections can be icy in the shoulder seasons, so check road conditions before you go.

South of the border lies the Italian valley of the Ossola, and Domodossola is a pleasant place for lunch. The Simplon Tunnel, a railway tunnel opened in 1906, runs far beneath the pass and was the longest tunnel in the world for much of the twentieth century. Naters, just across the river from Brig, is the starting point for the Aletsch Glacier region, the largest ice stream in the Alps.

Brig and Naters together have fuel, supermarkets and plenty of restaurants, and the town is a handy base. The Rhône valley can be hot in summer and windy in the afternoon, so start the pass early.

Raclette, melted local cheese scraped onto potatoes, is the Valais speciality, and a glass of Fendant, a crisp white wine, goes with it.
t.grimselpass reservoirs@46.6,8.3:
The Grimsel is one of the great Alpine passes, and it is also one of the least wild. At 2,164 metres it joins the Bernese Oberland and the upper Valais, and the landscape it crosses is a bare, glaciated bowl of grey granite, scoured smooth by ice and then dammed by engineers. There are three reservoirs in the immediate area, and the water in them is a startling turquoise or slate depending on the sky.

The lakes are the key to the place. They belong to a huge hydropower system, built mostly in the twentieth century, which uses the water from glaciers and snowmelt to run turbines far below in the Haslital. The Grimsel lake sits right beside the road, held by a long curved dam, and a smaller lake at the summit, the Totesee, lies in a hollow where the mountain seems to have given up.

The ride is excellent from either side. From the north the road climbs out of Innertkirchen past the roaring gorge at Handegg, then through a series of long galleries and bends carved into the rock. From the south the climb out of Gletsch is a set of tight hairpins that give you views back toward the Rhône glacier, which is retreating year after year. At the top the air is thin and cold, even in August, and the wind can take your breath.

Fill the tank at Meiringen or Innertkirchen on the north side, or at Brig and Naters in the south. The pass is open from about June to October, depending on snow, and the closing dates vary by the year. Mornings are best: the road is quiet, the light is sharp, and the reservoirs are glassy before the wind comes up.
t.gotthard tremola cobbles@46.6,8.6:
The Tremola is the old road over the Gotthard, and riding it is a bit like walking into a museum that is still in use. It climbs from Airolo on the Ticino side up to the pass at 2,106 metres in a staircase of tight hairpins, all of them paved with granite cobbles, laid by hand in the nineteenth century and restored in recent decades. The tarmac road runs alongside for those who prefer it, but the cobbles are the point.

Riding the cobbles takes patience. Stay relaxed, keep your weight low and let the bike find its own line; the stones are smooth from centuries of wheels and rain, and in the wet they turn slick and treacherous. Brake gently before the bends, not in them. The corners are hairpins, tight and steep, with the uphill side usually giving the better line, and the surface vibrates through the bars in a way that is hard to forget. Cyclists labour up the same road, and in summer the traffic includes coaches and slow cars, so overtaking takes thought.

Around you the landscape changes quickly. The lower slopes of Ticino carry chestnut trees and stone houses, then the road crosses into alpine meadows and finally into bare rock and low scrub near the top. The air cools, and on a clear day the views look south across the Leventina valley, the road you have climbed snaking below you like a ribbon dropped on a rug.

At the summit you will find the old hospice, a stone building that has offered shelter to travellers for hundreds of years, and a small museum about the pass. The lakes are cold and grey, and on a cloudy day the whole place has a severe beauty. Fuel is not available at the top; fill in Airolo, which lies some twelve kilometres below, or in Andermatt on the northern side. The Tremola is closed in winter, usually from late October until late spring, so check before you plan a trip around it.
t.airolo fuel and water@46.5,8.6:
Airolo is a small town with a big job. It sits at 1,175 metres at the southern end of the Gotthard, where the Leventina valley begins, and for centuries anyone coming south from the pass has funnelled through it. Today much of that traffic disappears underground: the railway tunnel, opened in 1882, and the road tunnel, opened in 1980, both come out near here, and the village is the place where the north-south corridor changes from German to Italian speech, from larch to chestnut.

For a rider it is an honest, practical stop. There is fuel, as you would expect in a place that sees so many vehicles, and there are fountains where you can fill a bottle with cold mountain water. The cafes and bakeries serve good espresso and the kind of simple Ticinese food that comes without fuss: polenta, cured meats, cheese from the high pastures. The language is Italian, the pace is a little slower, and the afternoon light has a warmer tone than north of the pass.

Airolo's surroundings are rich in history. The Gotthard was a fortress area in the twentieth century, and mountains around the town hide old military installations, some of which are now open as museums. Avalanches are a fact of life on these slopes, which is why the mountainsides above the village are dotted with protective barriers. The village was also a staging post for the stagecoaches that carried mail and passengers over the old pass before the railway made them redundant.

The riding starts right at the village: the Tremola climbs steeply to the north, while the main road swings through the Val Bedretto toward the Nufenen. Both are stunning, and it is worth thinking through what you want before you leave town. In the other direction, the road drops down the Leventina in a long, easy descent past gorges and waterfalls. Summer mornings are cool and clear, and afternoons can bring thunderstorms that roll quickly across the high ground, so keep an eye on the sky when you are filling up.
t.nufenenpass high point@46.5,8.4:
The Nufenen is the highest pass entirely within Switzerland, at 2,478 metres, and it earns the superlative with a bleak, windswept summit that feels more like the moon than the Alps. There is no pretty village at the top, no hotel, only a small car park, a few marker stones and a wide view of bare rock and snow patches. The pass links the Goms in the Valais with the Val Bedretto in Ticino, joining Ulrichen and Airolo, and it was built only in the 1960s, which makes it one of the youngest major roads in the Alps.

That youth shows in the engineering. The surface is smooth, the curves are open and well banked, and the road climbs in big, confident loops rather than the knotted hairpins of the older passes. On the Valais side, the road leaves Ulrichen and rises through meadows and scattered larches, with the long green trough of the Goms below. On the Ticino side, a descent of generous bends carries you into the Val Bedretto, steep-sided and quiet, where the Ticino river begins its run to Lake Maggiore.

The wind is the thing to remember. At the top it can blow hard from any direction, and temperatures are low even on a sunny day, so you will want a warm layer and gloves for the stop. The air is thin enough to feel in your lungs on the walk to the viewpoint. Snow lingers late and arrives early, and the pass is usually open only from June to October; in a bad year it can be shut well into the summer.

Plan from Airolo on the south side, or from the Brig area on the north. If you enjoy a wild landscape, though, the top is hard to beat: the Nufenen is the watershed between the Rhône and the Ticino, and a little stream nearby will end up in the Mediterranean. Stop for a minute and listen to how quiet it is.
t.furka west ramp@46.6,8.4:
The western approach to the Furka starts in the Goms and ends on the shoulder of one of the most famous glaciers in the Alps. At 2,429 metres the pass joins the Valais and Uri, and on this side the road climbs from the hamlet of Gletsch, where the Rhône begins its journey, through a staircase of hairpins that give increasingly grand views of the ice behind.

The Rhône glacier used to fill the valley floor here, and a hundred and fifty years ago it came down almost to the old hotels at Gletsch. It has been shrinking steadily since, and the stone-built Belvédère hotel on the road once looked straight at the ice front, which has since pulled back a long way. White blankets are laid on parts of the glacier each summer to slow the melt, and a tunnel carved into the ice, open in season, lets you walk inside. The source of one of Europe's great rivers is a grey, milky stream pouring from the foot of the glacier, and it is humbling to stand over it.

The riding is a pleasure. The ramp has tight corners at first, then settles into longer curves with good views and a reasonably smooth surface. There are no guardrails in places, so concentration matters, especially in traffic, since the road is popular with coaches and cyclists as well as bikes. Wind and cold are the usual company at the top. Fuel is not available on the pass, so fill in Oberwald or in the Brig area before you start, and in Andermatt if you are heading east.

The Furka also has film history: a car chase in the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger was shot on its hairpins, and the Belvédère hotel stands in the background. Whether or not you care about Bond, the road is worth the effort, and the pass is open roughly from June to October, depending on the snow.
t.klausenpass@46.9,8.9:
The Klausenpass is a road that you only really understand once you are on it. It runs for nearly fifty kilometres between Altdorf in Uri and Linthal in Glarus, crossing a ridge at 1,948 metres, and unlike many Alpine passes it feels like a real journey from one world to another, from the green terraces of the Schächental to the broad, high pastures of the Urnerboden and then down into the Linth valley.

In the 1920s and early 1930s the Klausen was the site of one of Europe's best-known hillclimb races, the Klausenrennen, in which the leading drivers of the day raced up the road in cars of terrifying power and little safety. The races ended before the war, but the hairpins and rock cuttings that crowded the spectators still feel dramatic. Today the speed limits are modest, and the road is mostly shared with cyclists and cattle, particularly on the high plateau, where cows wander across with no concern for traffic.

The Urnerboden, near the top on the Glarus side, is said to be the largest alpine pasture in Switzerland, a broad flat valley bottom where hundreds of cows spend the summer and a few farmhouses cluster along the road. It belongs to the canton of Uri even though it lies over the ridge on the Glarus side, a quirk that tells you how old pasture rights count for more than the lines on a map. The bends on the Linthal side are numerous and tight, with good views of the waterfalls that pour off the steep cliffs.

The pass is closed through winter and normally opens in late spring, so check the dates. Mornings are quieter than afternoons, and the light on the Schächental in the early sun is lovely. A coffee at one of the small restaurants near the summit is a good way to pause before dropping toward Glarus.
t.altdorf lunch window@46.9,8.6:
Altdorf is where the legend of William Tell lives, and the town has the statue to prove it. In the main square, a bronze figure of the archer stands with his crossbow and his son, put up in the nineteenth century, and the whole place has a theatrical sense of being on a stage for a story that every Swiss child knows. Whether Tell existed or not, the tale of an apple, an arrow and a tyrant has become part of the way the country imagines itself.

For riders the town is more simply a convenient place at the foot of the Gotthard route. It lies on the flat floor of the Reuss valley, with steep mountain walls rising on both sides, and the lake of Lucerne a few minutes to the north. With nearly nine thousand people, Altdorf has fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, and it is the last big town before the climb to Göschenen and the Gotthard, or the turn up to the Klausen and the Susten, so topping up here is sensible.

The valley is a funnel for traffic. The main road and the motorway run along it, and the railway is not far away, so the area hums with trucks and commuters. There is a calm side too: the old centre has a few lanes of painted houses, a Capuchin monastery from the sixteenth century, and quiet courtyards that tell of a more modest past. Not far away, in the village of Bürglen, there is a museum and chapel associated with Tell's legend, a gentle detour on a hot afternoon.

Lunch here is easy and unpretentious: a plate of rösti, a sausage, a coffee with a slice of cake. The weather is changeable, with sudden showers coming in off the lake or down the valley, and the Föhn can make the air very warm in autumn. If you are hurrying toward the passes, aim to start early; if you are coming down, the long afternoon shadows in the valley make for a restful end to the day.
t.pragelpass high road@47.0,8.9:
The Pragel is one of the narrowest and least known of the central Swiss passes, and for those who like their riding small-scale and quiet, it has a charm of its own. It climbs out of the Muotatal at Muotathal and crosses a ridge at 1,550 metres before dropping toward the Klöntal and the town of Glarus. The road is mostly a single lane wide with passing places, and that fact shapes the whole experience: you ride slowly, with attention, and you wave to oncoming drivers who pull in for you.

The landscape is alpine in character but gentle in form. Meadows run up to the edge of dark spruce forest, small wooden chalets stand scattered across the slopes, and cattle graze with bells that clank through the whole valley. On the Muotatal side, the surroundings include the Hölloch, a vast cave system that ranks among the longest in the world, with hundreds of kilometres of passages explored beneath the meadows. You will not see it from the road, but it is a reminder that the limestone below your wheels is hollow.

The Klöntal beyond is a quiet glacial valley with a lovely lake, the Klöntalersee, where the water takes on a deep green in the shade of steep cliffs. It is a fine place for a rest, with paths along the shore and a few modest inns. Fuel is not available on the pass or in the small villages; the sensible places are Glarus and Schwyz, and it is wise to fill up before you start.

Because the road is narrow, there are limits on larger vehicles, and traffic is usually light, but on a sunny summer weekend you may meet cyclists, hikers and the odd tour group. The pass is closed in winter, normally opening in late spring, and rockfall or damp patches may linger after storms. Gravel can lie on the bends, so ride carefully, especially in the morning when the shade holds moisture. With a clear sky and no hurry, it is an unforgettable little crossing.
t.walensee view@47.1,9.2:
The Walensee is a long, deep, intensely green lake wedged between steep mountains, and a stop above it is one of the best views on the road between Zürich and Chur. On the northern side, the seven peaks of the Churfirsten rise like a jagged wall nearly two thousand metres above the water, their limestone faces catching the light in the late afternoon. Behind you, the slopes of the Flumserberg drop to the shore, and the lake lies between the two walls like a fjord, with the wind whipping up whitecaps on a stormy day.

The lanes here are quiet and winding, climbing from the shore through meadows and forest toward the Flumserberg. The surface is generally good but narrow, with tight bends and some steep sections, and in winter it can be icy. The best time to come is on a weekday in spring or autumn, when the air is clear and there are few other visitors.

The lake is famous for its microclimate. Because the mountains shelter it, the north shore is mild enough to support figs, almonds and even a few palm trees at Quinten, a tiny village that can only be reached by boat or on foot, with no road. Visitors can take a ferry from Murg or Unterterzen and eat a long lunch in one of its two restaurants, with a view across the water, and the isolation means that the village has an air of being cut off from the modern world. The lake's colour can turn from emerald to slate in minutes as the weather shifts.

For services, Walenstadt, at the eastern end of the lake, has about five thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and cafés. The motorway on the southern shore carries most of the traffic, and the old road, beside the water, is quieter and offers better views. Cameras monitor the main routes, so watch your speed.

Stop at the viewpoint for a few minutes and look across the lake. The peaks are best in the late afternoon, when the low sun turns the cliffs a warm gold.
t.sainte marie aux mines@48.2,7.2:
Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines sits in a narrow valley on the Alsace side of the Vosges, with steep wooded slopes rising on both flanks and a small river running through the middle. The name gives away its story. This was silver country, and from the Middle Ages until the sixteenth century miners dug galleries into the hills here, making the valley, the Val d'Argent, one of the richest in the region. Later, textiles took over, and tall old mill buildings still line the town's main street. Visitors can still go underground in an old mine to see the tunnels.

Every September the town fills with colour for a big European patchwork festival, which draws quilters from many countries, and the shops and halls fill with fabric. The rest of the year it is quieter, a small town of around six thousand people with good bakeries, a market and bars where the Alsatian dialect is still heard. Look for a slice of kugelhopf, the local yeasted cake, or a plate of tarte flambée with a glass of Riesling.

This is the start of a classic mountain ride. The Route des Crêtes, the Crest Road, was built by the French army during the First World War to move troops and supplies along the Vosges front, and it now runs along the high ridges for about eighty kilometres, with views across the Alsace plain to the Rhine and, on a clear day, the Black Forest and the Alps. It climbs by way of the Col des Bagenelles and then rolls along the tops, past lakes and high farms where munster cheese is made. Corners are wide and easy, and the surface is generally good, though the road is busy on summer weekends, so aim for a weekday or an early start. Sections close in winter because of snow, usually from late autumn until spring, so check before you go.

Fuel is available in town, and it is wise to fill up here because the ridge itself has none. Bring a warm layer even in July, since the summits can be cool and windy, and fog can come down fast. Start in the clear morning and you will have the best of the views.
t.cernay@47.8,7.2:
Cernay marks the southern end of the Vosges ridge road, a town of around eleven thousand people on the Thur river, where the mountains drop to the Alsace plain. The old centre has a fortified gate, the Tour de l'Horloge, and a few half-timbered houses, and the town has the practical air of a place that serves a valley. It is also the gateway to a part of the Vosges with a serious past.

A few kilometres to the north-west, the summit of the Hartmannswillerkopf, known to French soldiers as the Vieil Armand, was fought over bitterly in the First World War. Both sides dug trenches and tunnels into the rocky ridge, and the death toll was huge. Today a national monument and cemetery stand on the slope, and the trenches, bunkers and barbed wire have been preserved among the trees. It is a sombre and moving place, and a short ride from Cernay for anyone who wants to understand why the Route des Crêtes was built.

At the other end, Cernay is where the ride becomes ordinary again. The descent from the high ridge, past the Grand Ballon, the highest summit in the Vosges at about 1,424 metres, brings you down through steep woods and then out onto the flat vineyards of the plain. On a motorcycle, the last stretch is a fine run, with long bends and a clear view over the Rhine valley, though it can be crowded at weekends with cyclists and day trippers. Surfaces are good and corners are open, so it is an easy, flowing ride.

Practicalities are simple. Fuel, food and coffee are all easy to find in a town of this size, and there are supermarkets on the edge of town as well as bakeries in the centre. If you stay for dinner, try a choucroute, the Alsatian sauerkraut with sausage and pork, washed down with a local white wine. Evening light comes late in summer, and the sun on the hills as you finish the ride is a satisfying end.
t.loire gorges@45.4,5.1:
This corner of the Isère département lies between Lyon and Grenoble, in a broad, gentle valley called the Bièvre, the work of glaciers that once poured out of the Alps and left a plain of gravel and clay. Saint-Jean-de-Bournay, Beaurepaire and Eyzin-Pinet are market villages of two to four thousand people, with stone churches, farmhouses and fields of maize, orchards and pasture. It is a rural, unhurried landscape, rarely visited by outsiders, and the roads are quiet.

The area has its place in French folklore. The smuggler Louis Mandrin, a sort of Robin Hood of the eighteenth century, was born in the region, and for years ran a gang that carried contraband salt and tobacco across the Alpine borders, taking on the tax collectors of the king. He was captured and executed in Valence in 1755, but his legend lives on in songs and local stories. Many of the old farmhouses here have walls of rounded river stones set in lime mortar, a style typical of the region.

For a rider returning from the gorges of the Loire, the Bièvre makes a restful end. The roads are mostly straight and fast, with a few gentle bends, and the surfaces are good. Heavy lorries use the main roads, so choose the smaller lanes if you can. Fuel is available in Saint-Jean-de-Bournay and Beaurepaire, both about four thousand people, so you will not be stranded. Cafés and bakeries are in the centre of each village, and a market day brings stalls of cheese, vegetables and cured meats. Late in the afternoon, the light slants across the fields and the Alps are sometimes visible on the horizon, a pale blue line.

The only real difficulty is the occasional dense fog that can lie on the plain in autumn and winter, which can make the roads treacherous. In spring, orchards bloom and the hedgerows are bright. Stop for a coffee and a pastry, and let your legs recover. The long journey from the Loire is over, and the evening is yours.
t.marlenheim@48.6,7.5:
Marlenheim is where the Alsace Wine Route begins, or at least its northern end, and a sign on the edge of the village announces it. From here, a signposted trail of about a hundred and seventy kilometres winds south along the foothills of the Vosges, linking over a hundred villages built among the vines. The first impression is of low hills in ordered rows, half-timbered houses with flower boxes at every window, and storks nesting on chimneys and church towers. In spring, the white blossom on the cherry trees brings a sudden, brief brightness.

The village has an old story. In the early Middle Ages, it was a royal estate of the Merovingian kings, and tradition says that Dagobert held court here, but little of that survives beyond the name. What it does have is wine. Marlenheim is known for its red wine, rare in a region famous for whites, made from Pinot Noir on the slopes around, and for a delicate pink version, so this is one of the few places in Alsace where a bottle of red is the natural choice with lunch. Neighbouring Wasselonne, a few kilometres up the road, has a hilltop castle ruin and a pleasant market.

As a start, this is a gentle, rolling landscape. The road follows a line of villages on the lower slopes of the Vosges, with vines to one side and farmland to the other, and the gradients are mild, the bends easy and the surface good. It is not a mountain road, but it makes a lovely warm-up, and the rhythm of village after village, each with its own fountain and church, is soothing. Traffic can be busy in harvest season and on summer weekends, with tractors and sightseers, so take your time. Fuel is available in Wasselonne, which has nearly six thousand people, as well as in nearby Strasbourg, about twenty-five kilometres east, and in the larger roadside stations on the main road.

Stop for coffee and a slice of kugelhopf in a village bakery. In autumn, the vineyards turn gold and crimson, and grapes are carried in tubs through the narrow streets, which smell sweetly of fermenting must. It is an extraordinary time to be here, as long as you are patient with the tractors.
t.ribeauville@48.2,7.3:
Three ruined castles stare down at Ribeauvillé from the first slopes of the Vosges, and each belonged to the same family. The lords of Ribeaupierre ruled this corner of Alsace for centuries, building the Saint-Ulrich, Girsberg and Haut-Ribeaupierre castles one above the other on the ridge, and from the town's main street you can see all three on a clear day, like a set of broken teeth. A footpath climbs to them, and the view from the top, over a sea of vineyards to the Rhine plain and the Black Forest beyond, is the best reward.

The town itself is a handsome, brightly painted place of about five thousand people, with half-timbered houses in pastel shades, a Butchers' Tower with a bell, a long main street and fountains at every turn. It lies on the Route des Vins d'Alsace, and the surrounding slopes produce some of the best Riesling and Gewurztraminer in the region, from grand cru sites such as the Osterberg and Geisberg. The vintners' cellars along the street offer tastings, and a glass of dry Riesling with a slice of flammekueche, the thin Alsatian tarte with cream, onions and bacon, is hard to beat.

A curious tradition marks the first Sunday of September. The Pfifferdaj, the day of the pipers, commemorates the medieval minstrels who were given special rights by the Ribeaupierre lords, and a procession in historic costume, with music and wine, fills the streets. It is a lively time to be here, though crowded.

For the rider, the Route des Vins is a gentle, winding road that threads between the vineyards, with views across the plain and the Vosges rising on the other side. The surface is smooth, the bends are easy, and the speed limits in the villages are low, so this is a road for savouring rather than racing. At harvest, in late September and October, tractors and workers fill the lanes, and in summer the heat and tourist traffic can be heavy. Spring, with its fresh green vines, and October, with the golden leaves, are the best seasons.

Riquewihr and Bergheim, a few kilometres away, are other lovely wine villages worth a visit. For fuel, check in town or at the edge of it, and the larger Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, twelve kilometres west, is the next real centre. Parking in the old town is limited, so use the car parks near the entrance.
t.colmar@48.1,7.4:
Colmar is the driest city in France, and the Vosges are the reason. The mountains to the west catch the rain coming in from the Atlantic, leaving the Alsace plain in their shadow with some of the lowest rainfall of any French city, and the sunny, dry climate is the secret of the wines and the orchards that surround it. It is a small city of about sixty-five thousand people, the capital of the Alsace wine country, and it has a charm that has made it one of the most visited towns in eastern France.

The old town is a maze of cobbled streets lined with timbered houses in ochre, pink and blue, with flower boxes at every window, and a quarter called Petite Venise, where the Lauch river runs between gabled houses and flat-bottomed boats drift past. The Maison Pfister, a Renaissance house with a painted facade and a wooden balcony, and the Koïfhus, a medieval customs house, are among the finest buildings.

Colmar's great cultural treasure is the Unterlinden Museum, housed in a former convent, which holds the Isenheim Altarpiece, painted by Matthias Grünewald in the early sixteenth century. Its images of the Crucifixion and the Resurrection, intensely emotional and disturbing, are among the masterpieces of German Renaissance art, and the altarpiece was made for a hospital where patients suffered from skin diseases, so that the tortured body of Christ would give them comfort. It is a place to give an hour. The town is also the birthplace of Auguste Bartholdi, the sculptor of the Statue of Liberty, and a small version of the statue stands at a roundabout on the edge of town.

For the rider, Colmar is a base and a break. The roads leading to it from the Route des Vins are easy and scenic, but the old town is largely pedestrian, and parking is the challenge, so use one of the underground car parks near the centre and walk. Traffic on the ring roads can be heavy, particularly in the summer and at Christmas, when the markets draw huge crowds.

Fuel, supermarkets, cafes and restaurants are all easy to find. A winstub, a traditional Alsatian wine tavern, is the place for choucroute, baeckeoffe and a glass of crisp white.
t.thann@47.8,7.1:
Thann marks the southern end of the Alsace Wine Route, where the vineyards run out and the Vosges close in on the river Thur. It is a small industrial and market town of about eight thousand people, with a Gothic church whose slender spire is one of the finest in Alsace. The Collégiale Saint-Thiébaut, built in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, has a richly carved west portal and a roof of glazed coloured tiles, and it was built to house a relic of Saint Theobald, a bishop whose thumb, according to legend, was brought here in the Middle Ages. Legend also says that three small lights appeared in the fir trees above his resting place, and to this day, on the evening of 30 June, the town burns three fir trees in a fire ceremony to remember it.

Above the town stand the remains of the Engelbourg castle, of which only a round tower survives, with a gaping hole in the wall that locals call the Witch's Eye. The slope beyond holds the Rangen, the southernmost grand cru vineyard in Alsace and probably the steepest, a volcanic hillside terraced with dry-stone walls where the grapes ripen in the heat of the dark rock. Wine from the Rangen is concentrated and smoky, and the vineyard is a spectacular sight in autumn, when the leaves flare orange against the black stone.

At the end of the wine route, Thann is a fine place to finish a ride. The last miles from the north run through vineyards and villages, and the road finishes with a gentle climb into the valley. There is a pleasant buzz in the town, with cafés and brasseries around the main square, and the old centre is compact enough to explore on foot. Fuel is available in town and in Vieux-Thann next door, which has several stations and a large supermarket, so a long day is easy to end here.

Behind the town, a road leads up into the Vosges toward the Route des Crêtes and the Grand Ballon, a classic mountain ride for those with energy left, but keep in mind that it can be closed by snow outside summer. The light is lovely in the evening, when the hills turn blue and the spire catches the last sun. Order a tarte flambée and a glass of the local wine, and let the day end gently.
t.pont en royans village@45.1,5.3:
Pont-en-Royans is one of the odd, brilliant sights of the Vercors: a row of old houses hanging out over the river Bourne on wooden balconies, supported by nothing but stone and optimism. The village sits where the gorge opens a little, with cliffs above, the water running green and fast beneath, and a stone bridge crossing the stream. The coloured houses, red, ochre and yellow, lean out from the rock face, and in the morning, when the sun lights the façades, they seem to float. It is a village of barely a thousand people, but it is one of the most photographed in the Alps.

The valley's history is tied to water and wood. For centuries, the Bourne was a transport route for timber, which was floated downstream from the high plateau, and the village grew as a hub for the trade. The rock walls around have caves, and the nearby Choranche cave, a few kilometres up the valley, is known for its forest of thin, hollow stalactites, which are among the rarest in Europe. A little further, the Grands Goulets road, blasted through a narrow gorge in the nineteenth century, climbs into the high plateau with tunnels cut straight through the cliff.

For a rider, this is a place to slow down. The roads in the Royans are narrow, winding and spectacular, with deep drops and short tunnels, and in many places the road is carved into the rock face, so surface water, rockfall and gravel are real hazards. The best time is a weekday morning in spring or early autumn, when traffic is light. Leave the bike at the edge of the village and walk across the bridge for the view. The nearest large town is Saint-Marcellin, about ten kilometres west, which has several stations, supermarkets and a good market, and it is wise to fill up there before heading into the mountains.

Saint-Marcellin gives its name to a soft, creamy cow's milk cheese, often sold in a little terracotta dish, and it appears on menus throughout the area. Eat some, with bread and a glass of Drôme white wine, at a table near the river. The mountain plateau of Vassieux, the next stop on the ride, is cooler, and a warm layer is useful even in summer.
t.combe laval balcony road@45.0,5.3:
The Combe Laval road is a ledge cut into a cliff, and it feels like it. The D76 leaves Saint-Jean-en-Royans and climbs into a deep, narrow valley on the western edge of the Vercors, a great gash in the limestone with walls hundreds of metres high, and then runs along the side of the cliff on a shelf blasted out of the rock. It was built over a long period, beginning in the late nineteenth century, to bring timber down from the forest of Lente on the plateau above, and the tunnels and rock overhangs are the marks of that labour.

The result is a road that grants views no engineer would call sensible. On one side is a wall of grey stone, sometimes overhanging; on the other, a drop of several hundred metres to the bed of the valley, with only a low parapet or, in places, a few stones at the edge. The curves are tight, the road is narrow, and in some places two vehicles cannot pass without one backing up. Take it slowly, and use the pull-ins to look, rather than looking while riding.

The surface is generally good, but the road can be wet and slippery in the shade, and rocks sometimes fall from the cliff above. In winter, the road is often closed because of snow and ice, and in busy periods there may be traffic restrictions, so check the local situation before you go.

Below, the villages of the Royans are a different world: Saint-Jean-en-Royans is a quiet market town of three thousand people, with stations and shops, and Pont-en-Royans, a few kilometres away, is famous for its houses that hang over the gorge of the Bourne on wooden beams. The local specialities are walnuts, ravioles, tiny cheese-filled pasta parcels, and Saint-Marcellin, the small, creamy cow's-milk cheese named for the town to the west.

Fuel is available in Saint-Jean-en-Royans, and there is none on the road itself, so fill up before you begin. The smell of wet rock and pine mingles with the cold air that rises from the valley, and the experience stays with you long after the ride.
t.freiburg@48.0,7.9:
Freiburg is where the Rhine plain meets the western edge of the Black Forest, and the transition is abrupt: one minute you are on a flat road past vineyards, the next the hills climb into dark spruce and the road begins to wind. The city of just over two hundred thousand has a long reputation for sunshine, one of the sunniest big cities in Germany, and its students, cyclists and solar panels give it an easy, green character.

The old town is worth wandering on foot. The Münster, with its lace-like openwork spire, is a Gothic masterpiece that took centuries to build and escaped the worst of the wartime bombing that flattened most of the centre in November 1944. In front of it, the market stalls sell sausages and fruit every morning, and in the cobbled lanes little streams called Bächle run in gutters along the pavement. Local legend says that if you step into one by accident, you will marry a Freiburger. Locals are kind enough not to laugh when tourists try it.

For riding, this city is a perfect launchpad. To the east, the Höllental, the valley of Hell, cuts through gorge scenery up to Hinterzarten and the high plateau. To the south-east, the roads climb toward the Schauinsland and the Belchen, with hairpins and long views over the Alsace plain to the Vosges. Some Black Forest roads have weekend restrictions or noise limits for motorcycles, so heed the signs and ride considerately; the locals notice. West of town, the Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano covered in vineyards, offers gentle lanes and excellent white and Pinot wine.

The best times are late spring and September, when the forest is bright and the roads are drier. Winter brings ice on the heights, and summer weekends can be crowded around the lakes.

Fuel stations are plentiful around the ring road, and parking in the old town is limited, so use one of the garages at the edge. Try a Black Forest ham sandwich or a flammkuchen at a student tavern before heading up into the trees.
t.saarbrucken@49.2,7.0:
Saarbrücken lies on the river Saar, close enough to the French border that some of its suburbs are across it, and the town carries both cultures in its stride. You can hear French in the market, find tarte flambée next to sausage on the menu, and watch locals switch between languages mid-sentence. It is the capital of Germany's smallest area state, the Saarland, and the region's history has been tugged back and forth between Paris and Berlin more than once.

After the Second World War the Saarland was placed under French protection, with its own currency and stamps, until in 1955 its people voted against a European statute and in effect chose to return to West Germany, which happened in 1957. Older Saarlanders remember it clearly. The industrial history is just as strong: coal and steel shaped the valleys, and the vast ironworks at nearby Völklingen, now a UNESCO World Heritage site, stands as a rusting cathedral to that era.

The most elegant sight in the city itself is the Ludwigskirche, an eighteenth-century Protestant church by the architect Friedrich Joachim Stengel, a baroque jewel whose pale stone glows at dusk. The old Saar bridges and riverside paths make a good short walk.

As a riding base the city is less thrilling than its surroundings. Heavy traffic clogs the motorway entries at rush hour, so leave early. But within half an hour you reach rolling forested hills, and further north the Hunsrück offers beautiful quiet roads with bends and views. Upstream near Mettlach, the Saar makes a dramatic loop around a wooded spur, the Saarschleife, a classic viewpoint reached by minor roads that suit a relaxed afternoon.

Fuel is easy and cheaper than in France on most days. Try a local dish like Dibbelabbes, a potato casserole, or Schwenker, grilled marinated pork turned over a beech fire, before you cross the line. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.ettelbruck@49.8,6.1:
Ettelbruck sits where the rivers Alzette and Sûre meet, in the middle of northern Luxembourg, and it has been a junction town for as long as there have been roads. People here call it the capital of the north, which is a bit of a stretch for a place of six thousand souls, but it does have the feel of a working crossroads: a railway station, a market, and a good number of cafes where farmers and commuters mix.

The town's big moment in the history books came in December 1944, when the Battle of the Bulge swirled through the valley. General George Patton, who commanded the American Third Army that fought to relieve Bastogne, is remembered with a museum and a monument here, and his statue stands in a small park. His grave is not far away in the American cemetery at Hamm, outside Luxembourg City.

For a rider, Ettelbruck is the gateway to the Ardennes, or the Luxembourg Ösling as the northern part is called. Pick the roads along the Sûre to the north-west and you find forested hills, little villages with slate roofs, and a kinked river lined with cliffs and castles. Vianden, with its great fortress above the Our valley, is about twenty-five minutes away and is a good lunch or photo stop. Diekirch, next door, has a brewing tradition worth a pint if you are not riding on. Roads are smooth, signs are in French and German, and the tarmac is generally kept in good repair.

Fuel is a pleasant surprise here: Luxembourg taxes it less than its neighbours, so many riders cross the border specifically to fill up. Expect a station or two close to the roundabouts on the main road. Late spring and early autumn give you the best weather, while winter fog can pool in the valleys and frost lasts long in the shady hollows.

A day among the hills, a coffee at a river terrace and a fill-up before the border is a very Luxembourg way to spend a ride.
t.bouillon@49.8,5.1:
Bouillon is squeezed into a tight loop of the river Semois, with a castle that seems to grow out of the rock above the town. The crags force the river into a hairpin, and the town huddles on the neck of land below. It is a small place, barely five thousand people, yet it is one of the most memorable in the Belgian Ardennes, and the bend of the Semois here is the kind of scene that makes people take out their phones without being asked.

The castle is the star. Its origins reach back to the eighth century, and in the late eleventh century it belonged to Godfrey of Bouillon, who sold or mortgaged his lands to help fund the First Crusade and went on to become the first ruler of Jerusalem under Latin control. A statue of him stands in the square. The fortress was later reshaped by Vauban, Louis XIV's great military engineer, and you can walk its long ramparts and dungeons. In summer there are falconry displays.

The riding around Bouillon is some of the best in southern Belgium. The roads follow the Semois through steep, wooded meanders, with tight bends, a short climb and a drop around each spur, and the tobacco-drying barns in the villages are a sign that this was once a tobacco-growing valley. The surface varies from excellent to patchy, and in autumn the leaf litter and morning mist make the shady corners treacherous. Weekends are busy with canoeists, cyclists and motorbikes alike, so a weekday ride is calmer.

There are fuel stations on the approaches, though in the smaller villages upriver you will not find any, so top up in town. Cafes around the bridge serve waffles and Ardennes ham, and local trout is on many menus. Give yourself time to walk across the old bridge for the view of the castle, then take the road towards Corbion or Sedan for the best bends.

Bring a jacket: the valley holds cool air even in summer, and rain arrives quickly off the high plateau.
t.bregenzerwald villages@47.4,9.9:
Above the town of Egg, the Bregenzerwald opens out into a landscape of green slopes and wooden farmhouses that looks like a picture-book version of Austria, and the villages along the Bregenzer Ach are among the best in the Alps. Andelsbuch, Egg and Großdorf are small places, each with a church spire and a cluster of houses, set in a wide valley at about seven hundred metres. The Bregenzerwald is part of Vorarlberg, Austria's westernmost state, and it has its own dialect, its own costumes, and a strong sense of itself.

The architecture is the first thing you notice. The old farmhouses are covered in dark wooden shingles, and the modern buildings, many of them designed by local architects, carry on the tradition with clean lines and carefully chosen wood. In Andelsbuch, the Werkraum Haus, designed by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, is a showcase for local craftsmen, and it is worth a stop even if you only look at the building. The valley takes its craft seriously, and carpenters, cabinet makers and joiners have built a reputation across Europe.

Cheese is the other pride. The Bregenzerwald has a Cheese Route, a network of dairies and farms that sell Bergkäse, a hard mountain cheese, along with Alpkäse made on the high pastures in summer. Cows are driven up to the alps in early summer and brought back down in September, and when the herds return, decked with flowers, the villages celebrate with a festival. You can taste the product in almost any inn, with Käsknöpfle, a dish of small cheese dumplings with fried onions, a local staple.

The roads here are a pleasure. The L200 follows the valley through villages and meadows, with easy bends and good surfaces, and it is a fine way to begin a day. Side roads climb to the high pastures and viewpoints, and they get narrow, so watch for tractors and farm vehicles. Wet weather can come down quickly, and the clouds sit on the hills in a way that adds to the atmosphere, but cold mornings and showers are common, so carry a layer.

For fuel, Egg and Andelsbuch have stations in the valley, but Dornbirn, about twelve kilometres west, is much bigger, and has everything. Cafes and inns are plentiful, and a slice of cake with coffee is never hard to find.
t.faschinajoch high road@47.3,9.9:
At 1,486 metres, the Faschinajoch is a gentle pass, and it manages to be one of the prettiest in Vorarlberg. The road links the Bregenzerwald with the Großes Walsertal, climbing from Au through meadows and spruce woods to a broad saddle with a handful of hotels and a ski lift or two. From the top, the views open up toward the Lechquellen mountains, a pale limestone massif with a few snowfields that linger deep into summer.

The village just below, Damüls, makes the claim of being among the snowiest places in the Alps, and the winter snowfall here is indeed enormous. In the cold months, the road is often lined with drifts, and the whole region becomes a ski area. In summer, the same meadows are full of wildflowers and cowbells. Damüls is also known for its tiny church, which has medieval frescoes inside, a rare treasure for a place so remote.

These valleys were settled by the Walser, a people who moved from the Valais in Switzerland in the Middle Ages, taking their language and customs with them to the high Alpine slopes. They were skilled at farming at altitude, and settled places that others avoided. The Großes Walsertal, on the far side of the pass, keeps that heritage, and the Walser dialect still lives in the villages. The valley is a biosphere reserve, protected by UNESCO for its landscape and culture.

For a rider, the Faschinajoch is a relaxed climb with open bends, good tarmac and long sightlines, and it is also a link in a loop with the Furkajoch, which makes a satisfying day. The road gets busy at weekends, with cyclists in particular working their way up, so share the road. In rain or low cloud, the visibility can fall suddenly, and in winter, snow and ice make the road a matter for chains and winter tyres. Check the conditions before setting off outside the summer months.

Fuel is not available on the pass, so fill up in the valley. Au has a small supply, and Bludenz, about fourteen kilometres away, and Dornbirn are the larger towns with proper stations. The hotels near the summit serve coffee and cake, and the terraces make a fine place to rest.
t.furkajoch pass road@47.3,9.8:
The Furkajoch is the highest paved pass in Vorarlberg, at 1,761 metres, and it is quiet in a way few Alpine passes are. The road, number L193, runs from Damüls on the east to Laterns on the west, a narrow, winding strip of tarmac that follows the contours of the mountain. It rises through spruce forest and then through open alpine pasture, with steep drops on one side and rock on the other. On the western side, the view stretches out across the Rhine Valley toward Switzerland, and on a clear day, you can see the peaks of the Säntis.

This is a road that demands attention. It is narrow, with tight hairpins, short straights and few barriers, and it is only open in the warmer months, usually from late spring until the first snow in autumn. A winter closure is standard, so check before heading up in early or late season. Surfaces are generally good, but there are patches of gravel after rain, and cattle sometimes wander across the road. Meet a bus at a hairpin and you will quickly learn the value of a patient mind.

The pass is called Furka after the Latin for fork, a common name in the Alps for a place where paths divide. For centuries, it was a route for herders and traders, who moved cattle and cheese between the valleys. Today, the pastures at the top are still grazed in summer, and the tinkle of cowbells is the usual soundtrack. In the alpine meadows, you may spot marmots, chamois and, with luck, an eagle overhead.

In late June, the meadows are full of gentians, orchids and alpine roses, and in September the air is clean and crisp, with sharp light on the peaks. Fog, however, can roll over the pass in minutes, so be ready to slow down and use your lights.

Nothing at all is sold on the summit itself beyond a small alpine hut or two that may serve a drink in season, so fill up before the ascent. Laterns and Damüls have a few guesthouses, but the nearest proper fuel stops are in Hohenems and the Rhine Valley, some fourteen kilometres away, or in the villages of the Bregenzerwald. Pack a jacket and take it easy on the descent.
t.rankweil@47.3,9.6:
Rankweil is the practical, friendly town that sits where the Walgau meets the Rhine Valley, about ten kilometres from the Swiss border, and it is a place riders pass through more often than they stop. With about twelve thousand people, it has the services you want, including fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes, and it makes a good place to rest and refuel before heading up into the hills. The town lies at about 470 metres, in a wide valley between the Vorarlberg mountains and the Rhine, and it is easy to reach from the motorway.

What sets Rankweil apart is the church on the hill. The Basilica of Our Lady, known as the Liebfrauenberg, stands on a rocky outcrop above the town, a fortified church with a tall tower and thick walls that have watched over the valley for centuries. It has been a pilgrimage site since the Middle Ages, and the view from the top, across the rooftops to the mountains, is lovely. A covered stairway leads up from the centre, lined with the stations of the cross, and the climb takes only a few minutes.

Food is the pleasant part of a stop here. Vorarlberg has a proper cuisine, and the signature dish is Käsknöpfle, little dumplings of dough covered in melted mountain cheese and topped with crisp fried onions, usually served with apple sauce and a green salad. It is the kind of lunch that makes the afternoon ride feel slow. Local bakeries make good bread and pastries, and a coffee and a slice of cake in a cafe is easy to arrange.

The surrounding roads are a gateway to better riding. To the east, the roads climb into the Laternsertal and up to the Furkajoch, while to the west, the valley road leads toward Feldkirch, an attractive medieval town with a castle and old arcades. The Rhine Valley itself is flat and busy, but turn off into the side valleys, and the roads become narrow, quiet and winding.

In summer, the valley can be hot and humid, with thunderstorms building over the mountains in the afternoon. Spring and autumn are more comfortable, with sharp, clear light on the peaks. Traffic around Rankweil is heavy at commuting times, so if you can, start your day early.
t.bouillon castle bend@49.8,5.1:
From the bend below the castle, Bouillon seems to hang between the rock and the river. The Semois, a slow, green stream, loops round the town in a tight horseshoe, and the old fortress stands on the ridge above, grey and square against the dark forest behind it. The bend is the sort of place where you cut the engine, because the sound of the water below and the smell of damp leaves and woodsmoke are part of the view.

The valley is a product of old geology. The Ardennes are the worn-down roots of a mountain range that was raised some three hundred million years ago, folded and compressed, and the Semois has cut through the hard schist and slate to make its meanders, leaving steep wooded flanks on one bank and gentler slopes on the other. The thin soil carries oak, beech and hazel, with wild boar and roe deer in the woods and kingfishers over the water. The valley is also known for its tobacco, grown here since the seventeenth century, and old drying sheds with slatted sides can be seen in the villages.

Riding in this area is a fine experience. The roads follow the river, rising and dropping across the spurs, with tight bends and steep little climbs, and each ridge brings a view of the next loop. The tarmac varies, and after wet weather the shaded stretches stay slippery with mud and leaves. In summer the villages are busy with canoeists and campers, and in autumn mist fills the valley in the morning. The border with France is only about a dozen kilometres away, and the old fortress town of Sedan, where Napoleon III surrendered in 1870 and where German armour broke through in 1940, is within easy reach.

Fuel is available in Bouillon, and it is wise to fill up in town, since the smaller villages along the river have no pumps. A cafe by the bridge is a pleasant place to look back at the castle. Come in May or October for the best colour and light, and bring a warm layer, as the valley holds the chill.
t.semois valley roads@49.8,5.2:
The Semois is one of the most winding rivers in Europe, and it spends its time in the southern Belgian Ardennes carving deep, looping meanders through a forested plateau of slate and sandstone. The roads here follow the loops, climbing out of the valley and dropping back to the water, so that in a single morning you cross and recross the river and look down on the same bend from several angles. Bertrix is the nearest sizeable town, and Herbeumont, with its ruined castle on a rocky spur above the river, is the prettiest of the villages.

The valley has a character of its own. The houses are built from local grey slate, with roofs of the same stone, and the villages sit tight against the hillsides. The Semois is also known for tobacco, one of the few places in Belgium where it is grown, a tradition that goes back a long way, and you may still see tobacco leaves drying in barns in late summer. Walkers, canoeists and cyclists all come here, and the river is a favourite for kayaks in warm weather.

For a rider, it is a serious pleasure. The corners are tight and frequent, the road surface is generally good, and the forest closes in on both sides so that the light flickers through the trees. The viewpoints over the river meanders, such as the one at Rochehaut, are among the most famous in Belgium, and are worth a stop. Take it steadily, because the roads are narrow, and there is local traffic, tractors and logging trucks. Belgium is strict with speed cameras, so keep an eye on the limits in villages.

The Ardennes forest is dense and old, with beech, oak and spruce, and it is home to red deer, roe deer and wild boar. They cross the roads at dawn and dusk, so slow down in those hours. In autumn, the forest smells of damp leaves and mushrooms, and mist hangs in the valley in the mornings. Winters here can be cold and foggy, with ice on the roads, and many places close for the season.

Bertrix has fuel, supermarkets and a few places to eat, about four kilometres away, and Chiny, further along the river, has more. Smaller villages have a bakery or a cafe, but it pays to plan lunch. Local specialities include ham from the Ardennes, game in season and a fine local beer.
t.col du bonhomme@48.2,7.1:
The Col du Bonhomme is a quiet pass in the Vosges, nine hundred and forty-nine metres up on the border between Alsace and Lorraine, where the D415 crosses the main range between Le Bonhomme on the Alsace side and Plainfaing on the Lorraine side. It is not a dramatic pass, with no bare rock or snowfields, but it has the long, steady, forested feel that gives the Vosges their character: dark firs, damp meadows and a wind that smells of resin. The ridge here marked the French border from 1871 until 1918.

That history is easy to forget in the sunshine, but it is written into the land. During the First World War the front line ran along these mountains, and French and German troops fought for the high ground and the passes. The Route des Crêtes, the long ridge road that runs south from here toward Cernay, was built by the French army to supply the front, and today it is a scenic road rather than a military one. Memorials and old trench lines are still found in the woods nearby, and respect for the dead is worth remembering as you ride.

The riding is a pleasure. On the Alsace side the road drops through Lapoutroie in long, open bends, with views down the valley to vineyards, while to the west it winds through forest and meadow. The surface is generally good, there are plenty of tidy hairpins, and traffic is light outside summer weekends. Weather can change quickly, with fog on the ridge when the valleys are clear. Early autumn is lovely, with the beeches turning gold, and the road may be snowy or icy in winter, so check conditions before setting out in the cold months.

This is also a country of distillers and cheesemakers. Lapoutroie is known for its eaux-de-vie, spirits made from plums, raspberries and other fruit, and the munster, a strong washed-rind cheese, is made in the high farms. Farm inns, called marcairies, serve hearty meals of potatoes, smoked meat and cheese. There are few services at the col itself, so the nearest reliable fuel is at Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, about ten kilometres away, or in the larger towns of the valley below. Bring a warm layer even in summer.
t.col de la schlucht@48.1,7.0:
The word Schlucht means gorge in German, and the pass takes its name from the deep valley on the Alsace side, a steep, craggy defile that drops away from the col in the direction of Munster. At eleven hundred and thirty-nine metres, it is among the best-known crossings of the Vosges, and it is also the point where the Route des Crêtes, the ridge road that runs along the main crest, meets the road between Gérardmer in the west and Munster in the east. It is a junction, a viewpoint, and a place where nearly every rider on this route pauses.

You arrive by the D417 from either side. From the Alsace side the climb is dramatic: a ribbon of tarmac climbing the side of the valley in broad hairpins, with the rock wall above and the drop below. From Gérardmer, the approach is gentler, passing lakes and forest. The surface is good, the bends are open and flowing, and the whole thing makes for superb riding when the weather is clear. In summer weekends the road is crowded with motorcyclists, cyclists and families, and in autumn the fog can roll in and chill everything. The Route des Crêtes is often closed in winter because of snow, so check before you go in the cold months.

The col stands near the summit of the Hohneck, at over thirteen hundred metres the second-highest peak in the Vosges, and the area has a special flora. Close by, the Jardin d'altitude du Haut-Chitelet, a botanical garden at about twelve hundred metres, shows mountain plants from many parts of the world. Chamois, which were introduced to the Vosges in the twentieth century, live on the rocky slopes. The frontier between France and Germany once ran along this ridge, and the pass saw heavy fighting in the First World War.

At the col itself you will find a few cafés, restaurants and shops, which makes it a handy place for coffee or a hot meal, though prices are tourist ones. Fuel is not available at the pass. The nearest source is Munster, nine kilometres down the valley, which has stations, supermarkets and the cheese that bears its name. A slice of munster with a few cumin seeds, bread and a glass of Alsace wine is a fine lunch.
t.grand ballon@47.9,7.1:
The Grand Ballon is the highest summit in the Vosges, at 1,424 metres, and it looks nothing like a ballon in the way you would expect. The name comes from the rounded, treeless shape of the upper slopes, a smooth dome of grass and heather that stands above the forest like the back of a sleeping animal. A radar dome and a few masts sit on top, which spoil the symmetry, but the view makes up for that. On a clear day you can see over the Rhine plain to the Black Forest in Germany and, on the very best days, the white line of the Alps, including Mont Blanc, far to the south-east.

The road to the top is a short spur from the Route des Crêtes, a narrow, well-kept road with a handful of bends. The Route des Crêtes itself is one of the best ridge roads in Europe, running along the crest of the range with views alternating between Alsace and Lorraine. On the Grand Ballon, a monument to the Chasseurs Alpins, the French mountain infantry known as the Blue Devils, recalls the fighting that took place on these slopes. The mountains were hard-fought, and the peaks changed hands.

Weather here is serious. The summit is exposed, and the wind can be strong and cold even in summer, while fog can reduce visibility to a few metres in minutes. In winter the road is closed by snow and ice, and in spring and autumn it may be affected as well, so check before you set off. The best conditions are on settled, clear days in late spring, early summer or early autumn, and the best light is in the morning or toward evening. The upper slopes are covered in short mountain grass, bilberry and heather, with patches of beech and fir below. Chamois are sometimes seen on the slopes.

There are no facilities directly on the summit, though a hotel-restaurant near the top has historically served visitors, and the farm inns of the region, the marcairies, serve hearty food: smoked pork, potatoes and munster cheese. Guebwiller, about eight kilometres away in the valley, is the nearest large town for fuel, shops and cafés, and its vineyards produce Alsace wine, including grand cru wines from the slopes. Take a windproof layer and enjoy the height.
t.obernai@48.5,7.5:
Obernai is the town where the Alsace wine route really begins to feel like itself, a handsome walled place of twelve thousand people at the foot of the Vosges, just south-west of Strasbourg. The old centre is a pleasing jumble of half-timbered houses, painted in cream, red and ochre, set around a market square with a Renaissance well, the Puits aux Six-Seaux, whose six buckets once hung from a wheel. The Kappelturm, a medieval tower that was once part of a chapel, rises above the square, with a fine view from the top.

It is also a town with a saint. Odile, the patron saint of Alsace, is said to have been born here in the seventh century, the daughter of a local duke. According to the legend she was born blind and gained her sight when she was baptised. She later founded the convent on Mont Sainte-Odile, a sacred hill about thirteen kilometres to the west, which is still a place of pilgrimage and a fine destination for a ride, with views over the Rhine plain.

The Route des Vins d'Alsace, established in 1953, was the first of France's wine routes, and it runs south from here for about a hundred and seventy kilometres, through villages that look as though they have been taken straight from a storybook. The riding is relaxed rather than sporty. The roads weave between vineyards and villages in easy curves, and the surface is generally good, but there are plenty of cyclists, tractors and tourists, and the speed limits in villages are strictly observed. In harvest time, from September to October, trailers loaded with grapes slow the traffic, and the air smells sweet. Spring is lovely with green vines, and the Christmas markets in winter draw huge crowds.

Alsace food is hearty and delicious: choucroute with sausage and pork, tarte flambée, a thin crisp pizza-like flatbread with cream, onions and bacon, and the sweet and savoury baeckeoffe, a stew baked in an earthenware pot. The local wines are mostly white, Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer, and the dry, floral Crémant d'Alsace is a good sparkling choice. Cafés and restaurants line the market square and the lanes around it, and a stop for a coffee and a slice of kugelhopf is easy to justify.

Obernai is a proper town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and all the services a rider might need. It is also a good place to fill up before heading into the quieter villages. Parking in the centre can be tight in the season, so look for the car parks just outside the walls.
t.riquewihr@48.2,7.3:
Riquewihr was once the property of a distant German dynasty, and some say that explains why the town looks so well preserved. It belonged to the counts, later dukes, of Württemberg from the fourteenth century until the French Revolution, and during all that time it grew rich on wine and trade, building tall half-timbered houses with carved doorways, oriel windows and courtyards. The Thirty Years War and later conflicts largely passed it by, and the old walled core survived largely as it was built, which is why people now come in their thousands to walk its main street, the Rue du Général de Gaulle, under hanging signs and baskets of flowers.

The Dolder, a tall gate tower from the thirteenth century, stands in the middle of the town and looks down the main street, and the high walls and smaller gates still enclose the old part of the village. Inside, wine merchants' cellars open directly to the street, with barrels and bottles on display, and the signs of the wine houses, such as Hugel, one of the great family names of Alsace, are everywhere. A walk through the courtyards and down the side alleys, away from the main street, reveals quieter corners with storks' nests on the rooftops, a symbol of Alsace.

The wines are the point. Riquewihr is surrounded by vineyards on the slopes of the Vosges foothills, and its best-known sites, such as the Schoenenbourg grand cru, produce excellent Riesling, a dry, mineral white wine, and Gewurztraminer, a richly aromatic one. Late harvest wines, such as vendange tardive, are sweeter and made from grapes left on the vine. If you are tasting, do it sensibly, with a small sip and a spittoon, and save any serious drinking for the evening.

The riding on the Route des Vins around Riquewihr is gentle and pleasant, with the village roads, vineyard tracks and small lanes weaving between the villages of Ribeauvillé, Hunawihr and Bergheim. It is not a road for speed, as the lanes are narrow and the speed limits are low, and in high season the town is packed, so a weekday visit in spring or autumn is much better. Park outside the walls and walk in. The Christmas market in December is famous and very crowded.

Fuel and supermarkets are best found in Colmar, about twelve kilometres south, or in Wintzenheim and Ribeauvillé. In the village itself, cafés, bakeries and restaurants serve Alsace specialities, and the wine shops are everywhere.
t.eguisheim@48.0,7.3:
The streets of Eguisheim run in circles. Houses were built in concentric rings around the old castle at the centre, and the lanes follow the curve of the oldest fortification, so you can walk round the village like the rings of a tree, passing half-timbered houses in pastel colours, flower boxes and wrought-iron signs. It is a layout found in very few places, and it makes the village feel like a small, perfect machine. It has been voted among the favourite villages of the French, and on a sunny day you can see why.

The castle at the heart of it was the home of the counts of Eguisheim, and one of them, Bruno, born here around the year 1002, became Pope Leo IX, one of the great reforming popes of the eleventh century. A chapel in the village commemorates him, and a statue of the pope stands in the square. The castle itself was rebuilt in the Middle Ages, and the present building is a modest one, but the wall and its towers give the village its shape. Above the vineyards on the hill, the ruins of three medieval castles, the Trois Châteaux, can be seen on a spur of the Vosges, an easy detour for the curious.

Wine is the beating heart of the village. Eguisheim claims to be the cradle of Alsace wine, and its slopes, such as the Eichberg and Pfersigberg grand crus, produce Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer of high quality. Many growers have their cellars right on the streets, and a sign outside invites you in to taste. Remember that tasting and riding make poor partners, and buy a bottle for later rather than draining the glass. In September and October the harvest brings the smell of fermenting grapes, and in winter the village is dressed for Christmas.

On a bike, Eguisheim is a gentle stop on the Route des Vins, not a destination for the sporting rider. The approach roads are narrow and the village streets tight, with signs asking visitors to park outside the centre. Early morning and evening are quiet, and the light on the pale stone is lovely. Spring brings fresh green vineyards, and autumn turns them gold and red. In summer, tour groups fill the streets at midday.

Wintzenheim, about three kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and the services of a small town, and Colmar, a bigger and more famous city, is a few kilometres further north. In the village, cafés and winstubs, the traditional Alsace wine taverns, serve onion tart, sausages with sauerkraut and plates of local cheese.
t.gevrey chambertin@47.2,5.0:
Napoleon is said to have drunk Chambertin on campaign, and whether or not the story is true, the wine has had a reputation as a king among Burgundies for centuries. Gevrey-Chambertin is its home, a wine village of about three thousand people at the northern end of the Côte de Nuits, a few kilometres south of Dijon. The name has two parts: Gevrey is the village, and Chambertin, supposedly from the field of Bertin, is the vineyard that gave the village fame, to the point that it added the name in the nineteenth century.

The wine route here is the Route des Grands Crus, and it follows the D974, the old main road from Dijon to Beaune. It runs along the foot of the limestone slope, with the vineyards climbing above to the right and the plain stretching away to the left, and is a pleasure at a moderate speed, with gentle curves and little gradient. Traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends and harvest, and the road passes through a series of villages with speed limits that are checked. If you prefer a quieter ride, the lanes that wind through the vineyards are narrow and slow, but they let you see the walled clos, the famous small plots, at close range.

Gevrey has nine grand cru vineyards, among the most famous in Burgundy, all planted with Pinot Noir, the single red grape of the region. The soil is limestone and marl, and the slope faces east, catching the morning sun. The idea that a few metres of ground can change the taste of a wine is called terroir, and here it is taken very seriously: the local winegrowers have mapped and named every small parcel, which they call climats, and the Climats of the Burgundy vineyards were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2015.

The village also has a medieval castle, built by the monks of Cluny in the tenth century and rebuilt later, standing in the middle of the village, and a church with a Romanesque tower. The little streets are lined with cellars and tasting rooms, though the great estates are often by appointment. Burgundy food is rich and satisfying: boeuf bourguignon, eggs poached in red wine sauce, snails baked in garlic butter and, to finish, a plate of Époisses, a strong washed-rind cheese. Gougères, light cheese puffs, are the classic nibble with a glass.

Fuel and supermarkets are best found at Marsannay-la-Côte, about five kilometres to the north, or in Dijon. There are cafés and restaurants in the village, but as always in France, many close between lunch and dinner and on Mondays.
t.nuits saint georges@47.1,5.0:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the working capital of the Côte de Nuits, a town of about five thousand people that has made its living from wine for centuries, and it feels less like a museum than the pretty villages around it. Behind the main street, the old streets are full of cellars, wine merchants and négociants, the firms that buy grapes and ferment, blend and bottle them. The wines are mostly red, made from Pinot Noir, and are known for being structured, earthy and long-lived, with a firm backbone that rewards patience. There are no grands crus in the appellation, but there are many outstanding premiers crus, such as Les Saint-Georges, regarded by many as the equal of a grand cru.

The town also holds a charity auction of its wines every spring, the Hospices de Nuits sale, a smaller sibling of the famous Hospices de Beaune event in November. The proceeds fund the care of the sick, as they have since the eighteenth century. In a more modern turn, Nuits is also the centre of the Burgundy blackcurrant trade, and a visitor centre called the Cassissium explains how the fruit is turned into crème de cassis, the liqueur that, mixed with white wine, gives the drink called kir.

The Route des Grands Crus runs through the town on the D974, and on a bike it is a calm, scenic ride rather than a technical one. The road follows the slope of the Côte, with vineyards rising to the west and the plain of the Saône to the east, and the traffic in summer can be heavy and slow. Early mornings in May, June, September and October are the best times, with soft light and cool air. In the harvest, from September, tractors and trailers fill the lanes, and the smell of fermenting must hangs in the air.
