Vineyard tracks lead up into the combes, the little valleys that cut into the limestone escarpment, where oak and box woods give way to scrub and rocky outcrops. Above the vines, the plateau is mostly forest and farmland, and the hills are riddled with caves.

As a proper town, Nuits-Saint-Georges has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, bakeries, and a good range of restaurants and cafés. It is also a convenient overnight stop, with a selection of small hotels and guesthouses. Try local specialities such as jambon persillé, ham in parsley jelly, and a glass of Aligoté or a local Crémant de Bourgogne.
t.bellagio@46.0,9.3:
Bellagio sits at the end of a long peninsula where Lake Como splits into two arms, in a spot so well placed that the Romans and then the Milanese noble families all wanted a villa here. It is a town of steep stone lanes, stepped alleys lined with shops and cafes, and houses in warm yellow and ochre with green shutters. The waterfront is a line of arcades and terraces, with boats coming and going and a view across the water to the mountains. It is often called the pearl of the lake, and for once the cliche is not too far off.

The two grand attractions are the villas. Villa Melzi, with its landscaped gardens by the water, was built in the early nineteenth century for an official of Napoleon's Italian republic, and the Villa Serbelloni on the headland above the town has terraced gardens with views over both arms of the lake. The silk industry was important in the region for centuries, and the town still has shops selling silk scarves and ties, as well as wood carvings and local honey.

Getting here by bike is half the fun. The road from Lecco or Como up the peninsula, the SP583, is narrow, twisting and in places very steep, with a couple of tight stretches where buses and cars have to squeeze past each other. The surface is generally good but the road is busy, particularly on summer weekends, and the lake views come in glimpses between the trees and walls. Early morning is best, and a weekday in spring or autumn is a joy. From Bellagio you can also take a car ferry across to Varenna, Menaggio or Cadenabbia, which makes it a natural hub for loops around the lake.

Services are plentiful but expensive. There are restaurants of every kind, from simple trattorie serving fried lake fish, perch and risotto, to very formal dining rooms. For fuel, it is better to plan ahead, since the town is small and on a narrow peninsula. The larger town of Mandello del Lario, across the water on the eastern shore and famous for the Moto Guzzi factory, is the reference point in the data, and the roads around Lecco and Como have more stations.

Parking in Bellagio is tight and mostly paid, so arrive early or park at the edge of the town and walk down. The best time to see the town is in the evening, when the crowds on the waterfront thin out and the lights on the lake begin to come on.
t.varenna@46.0,9.3:
Varenna is a small, tidy village on the eastern shore of Lake Como that looks like a set designer's idea of an Italian lake town. Houses in orange, yellow and rose crowd down to a little harbour, a lakeside path runs along the water, and steep stepped lanes climb between them with flowers on every windowsill. Above the village, the ruins of Castello di Vezio look down from a hill, and the best views across the lake to Bellagio are from its walls.

There are two grand villas open to the public. Villa Monastero, built on the site of an old convent, has long gardens along the water with palms, cypresses and citrus trees, and Villa Cipressi, now a hotel, has a terraced garden with views over the lake. The village also has a small curiosity, the Fiumelatte, the Milk River, which is reputed to be one of the shortest rivers in Italy. It runs for only a few hundred metres, from a spring in the mountainside to the lake, in a white, foaming torrent, and appears only in the warm half of the year. It was mentioned by Leonardo da Vinci, who was fascinated by its disappearing act.

The riding in the area needs some patience. The main road along the eastern shore, the SS36, runs through a series of long tunnels and is busy with traffic going to Lecco and the Valtellina, while the old lakeside road is narrow and twisting. Neither is a place for speed, but both give views of the water and mountains. The village itself is a pedestrian zone and the streets are too narrow for cars and bikes, so park on the edge and walk in. Parking can be expensive.

The ferries are the real transport. A short ride on the water takes you to Bellagio, Menaggio and Cadenabbia, and a car ferry crosses regularly, so Varenna is a natural place to cross the lake and switch sides. The crossing is a pleasant break from the saddle and gives you views of the villages from the water.

Varenna has restaurants and cafes along the waterfront, serving the usual lake fare of perch, missoltini, which are dried and salted shad, and polenta. Fuel is not sold in the village, so fill on the main road before you get here. Mandello del Lario, about ten kilometres to the south, is a larger town with stations and shops.

Visit in the evening if you can, when the day-trippers have gone and the light on the water is soft. The village is at its best when it is nearly empty.
t.colico@46.1,9.4:
Colico lies at the very top of Lake Como, on the flat plain where the Adda river arrives from the Valtellina, and it is a place that works for a living rather than for the camera. The mountains here are higher and closer than anywhere else on the lake, with Monte Legnone rising to almost 2,600 metres directly above the town, and the lake itself narrows and turns north into a wider, windier stretch. The wind is the local gift. In summer, a steady breeze blows up the lake from the south, the Breva, and the northern end is one of the best places in Italy for windsurfers and kitesurfers, who fill the beaches on warm afternoons.

History is visible in the landscape. On a rocky hill above the town stands the Forte di Fuentes, a Spanish fortress built in 1603 by the governor of Milan, Count of Fuentes, to control the routes into the Valtellina and the passes to the north and protect the Spanish possessions from the Grisons and the Swiss. It was a strategic place, since whoever held it controlled the way between Italy and northern Europe. The fort fell into ruin but has been partly restored and can be visited, and the view from it over the lake and plain is wide.

Colico is a junction. Roads lead east into the Valtellina toward Sondrio, Tirano and the Stelvio or Bernina routes, and north towards Chiavenna and the Splügen Pass into Switzerland. The roads are generally good, with a mix of straights and bends, and the traffic is a mixture of local and long-distance vehicles. The valley floor roads can be busy and dull, and the interest picks up as the roads climb. Be wary of strong winds on exposed stretches and the occasional fog in the plain in autumn and winter.

Services are practical. The town has fuel stations, supermarkets, a train station and plenty of places to eat, and the prices are lower than in the famous lake resorts. It is a good place to refuel the bike and the rider before heading into the mountains or down the lake. Colico Piano, the flat part of the town, has most of the facilities, and the old village of Colico is on the slopes above. There is also a nature reserve at the Pian di Spagna, a wetland with reeds, birds and quiet paths, a short ride from the town.

If you want a taste of the local cuisine, try pizzoccheri, the buckwheat pasta of the Valtellina, with cheese and cabbage, or missoltini, dried lake fish. Both are honest food made for cold winters.
t.menaggio@46.0,9.2:
Menaggio is the western door of the lake, a handsome small town with a ferry quay, a lakefront of cafes and a population that doubles with visitors in summer. It sits at the foot of the mountains on the western shore of Lake Como, opposite Bellagio and Varenna, and its position is the reason for its life: the road from Switzerland through Porlezza and Lake Lugano reaches the water here, and so does the old route along the shore from Como to Colico. Behind the town, the steep slopes rise to a ridge where the mountain paths of the Via dei Monti Lariani run along the top, giving views of the lake from above.

The story of the region is one of crossing places and borders. In the Middle Ages, this shore was part of the lands of Como, and the road along the lake, the Via Regina, was a Roman and then medieval route used by merchants and pilgrims and soldiers. Parts of it are still walkable as a path, a pleasant alternative on a rest day. The nearby Villa Carlotta, on the shore south of town, is a fine example of the lake's villas, with its famous gardens of azaleas and rhododendrons that bloom in spring.

For riders, Menaggio is an excellent base. The ride up the western shore from Como is a series of bends, tunnels and villages, with the lake glittering through the trees, but it can be slow in summer when the traffic is heavy. Northwards towards Colico the road is quieter, and the stretch past Gravedona and Domaso gives wide views over the northern end of the lake. West over the hills, the road to Porlezza and Lugano is a pleasing and twisty route, with fewer cars and good scenery. Watch for cyclists on all of these, since the lake is a favourite training ground.

The town has all the services you would expect. There are fuel stations on the main road, a supermarket, a small golf course nearby and a lively square with restaurants and gelaterie. Lunch by the lake, with a plate of risotto with perch fillets and a glass of cold white wine, is one of the pleasures of the region, and it goes down well on a hot day. The ferry service is frequent, so you can hop over to Bellagio or Varenna without much effort.

The best months are May, June and September, when the weather is warm but the lake is not crowded. In the evening, the mountains above turn pink as the sun goes down, and the water is calm.
t.seongsan ilchulbong@33.5,126.9:
Seongsan Ilchulbong rises from the eastern tip of Jeju like a crown set on the sea. It is a volcanic cone about a hundred and eighty metres high, formed some five thousand years ago when magma erupted through shallow water and exploded into ash, building a huge bowl-shaped crater with steep green walls and jagged rim. The name means the sunrise peak, and the tradition of watching the sun come up over the Pacific from the summit is the main reason people come. The crater is a bowl of grass and wildflowers, about six hundred metres across, and cattle and horses once grazed on its floor. The site is part of Jeju's UNESCO World Heritage listing for its volcanic landscape.

The climb to the rim takes about twenty to thirty minutes up a staircase, and it is steep enough to make you breathe but not so hard that you cannot manage it in motorcycle boots. Crowds arrive before dawn on clear mornings, and the top can feel like a party in the half-light. A fee is charged for entry. Down at the shore beside the cone, local women divers, the haenyeo, who dive without oxygen tanks to collect shellfish and seaweed, give demonstrations in the afternoon. Their tradition, passed down through generations, is also recognised by UNESCO, and it is a wonderful thing to watch, though they are getting fewer as the older women retire.

The riding on Jeju is relaxed rather than technical. The coast road circles the island, mostly flat or gently rolling, with black basalt walls, tangerine orchards and bright ocean views, and the stretch around Seongsan is open and breezy, with long, easy bends. The wind can be strong and sudden, and the road is busy with rental cars and tour buses, so patience is needed. Speed cameras are common and limits are low. Rain and fog arrive without much warning, and the surface can be slick when wet. Helmets are required, and riders should check local rules for foreign licences.

Seongsan has the full range of services you would expect near a tourist attraction. There are petrol stations on the main roads nearby, cafes, seafood restaurants and guesthouses, and Jeju specialities include grilled black pork, abalone porridge and fresh tangerines. Jeju City, about thirty-nine kilometres to the north-west, is the main city with an airport and ferry port.

If you plan to see the sunrise, check the weather and tide, and stay in the village the night before. Sunrise here, on a clear morning, is something you do not forget.
t.jungmun@33.3,126.4:
Jungmun is the resort coast of southern Jeju, a strip of beaches, hotels and cliffs on the sheltered side of the island, and it holds some of the island's most unusual scenery. The beach at Jungmun is known for its sand, which is a mixture of black, white, grey and reddish grains, made of crushed basalt and shell, and gives the shore a coloured, speckled look. The sea beyond is a popular spot for surfers when the swell comes in from the south. Behind the beach, lines of palms and manicured resort grounds run up the slope, and the whole thing has a faintly Hawaiian feel.

The geological highlight is a short walk away. The Jusangjeolli Cliff, a wall of hexagonal basalt columns that stand like stacked pillars along the shore, was formed when a lava flow cooled and cracked into regular shapes, and the waves crash against it in great sprays. It looks like the work of masons, but it is nature's. Nearby, the Cheonjeyeon Falls tumble in three stages through a green gorge, and other waterfalls on the south coast, fed by water that filters through the volcanic rock, are a pleasant break from the heat. Mount Halla, the great volcano that forms the spine of Jeju at nearly two thousand metres, stands over the island, and on a clear day its summit is visible from the coast.

The ride along the south coast is a pleasure. The roads run through tangerine orchards, past stone walls and beside the sea, with views of the ocean and small islands, and the surface is good. Traffic is steadier than in the north, because of the resorts, and tour buses and rental cars can slow things, but it is still easy riding. Wind and sudden showers are common, so a waterproof layer helps. In summer the humidity can be high.

Seogwipo, the second city of the island about fourteen kilometres away, has the nearest large stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and a famous open-air market. Local food includes grilled black pork, raw fish, sea urchin and the sweet tangerines, and hot noodles in the cooler months. Hotels and guesthouses are plentiful, though prices peak in July and August.

Jeju is known as the island of three abundances, which are stones, wind and women, and a ride along this coast shows the first two within minutes. For the third, watch for the divers.
t.hyeopjae@33.4,126.2:
Hyeopjae is the beach that makes people on Jeju stop talking. It lies on the west coast, a crescent of pale sand with palms standing along its edge and water that goes from clear green to turquoise in the shallows, and across the bay the small volcanic island of Biyangdo sits like a green hat on the horizon. The sand is white because it is made largely of crushed shell, rather than the black basalt that dominates elsewhere, and the contrast with the dark volcanic rocks at the ends of the beach is striking. The water is shallow and calm, which makes it popular with families, and at low tide the sand flats stretch far out.

Behind the beach is a landscape of lava. Jeju is a volcanic island, and under the surface are long tunnels left behind by flowing lava, some of which can be visited. The caves near Hyeopjae, in a nearby park, have a ceiling hung with calcite formations that are unusual in lava tubes, and they are lit for visitors. The park also has gardens with subtropical plants and a collection of stone sculptures, a pleasant place to spend a morning when the weather is dull.

The riding along this coast is relaxed, with open views and ocean light. The coast road runs along the shore past fishing villages and farm fields, with black stone walls, windmills and, in spring, fields of yellow rapeseed flowers. The wind is a constant on this side of the island, and it can be strong enough to push a bike sideways on exposed stretches, so a firm grip is wise. Rain arrives in sudden showers, and the sunsets over the sea are spectacular on clear evenings. Traffic is moderate and slower than on the main highways, with plenty of rental cars and tourists who are not sure of the route. Speed cameras are common.

For practicalities, the beach has a car park, cafes and small restaurants, and food ranges from seafood noodles to fried chicken and ice cream, and a refreshing local drink made from Jeju oranges. There are petrol stations on the main road nearby, and the town of Hallim, a short ride away, has stores and restaurants. Jeju City, about twenty-nine kilometres to the north-east, is the main base for services.

Come at sunset if you can. The light on the sand, the dark rocks and the silhouette of the island is one of the best on Jeju.
t.luxembourg city@49.6,6.1:
Luxembourg City is built on a rock, or rather on several rocks, split by deep gorges cut by the Alzette and Pétrusse rivers. The old fortress, one of the most formidable in Europe, was dismantled after 1867, but the casemates, long tunnels cut into the cliff, survive and can be visited. The old town and fortifications are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the viewpoint along the Chemin de la Corniche, which has been called the most beautiful balcony in Europe, looks down on the valley and the old quarter of Grund. About seventy-seven thousand people live in the city proper, and it is a wealthy, multilingual, slightly formal place with a large banking sector.

For a rider, this is an easy and civilised start. Fuel is cheaper than in most neighbouring countries, which is why you will see queues of cross-border drivers at the pumps, and the roads out of the city are very well kept. The Grand Duchy is small, and within half an hour you can be among forests, fields and villages. Traffic in the city is heavy at rush hour, with commuters flowing in from France, Belgium and Germany, so leave outside those times.

The route heads northeast toward the Mullerthal, the area known as Little Switzerland, a landscape of sandstone cliffs, moss-covered boulders and beech forest. The roads here are narrow and winding, with good surfaces, gentle gradients and numerous bends that follow valleys. Luxembourg's speed enforcement is firm, with fixed cameras and patrols, and limits are lower than you might expect. In autumn, the forests turn gold and copper and the road surface can be wet with leaves.

Before you go, eat something. Luxembourg cuisine reflects its neighbours: judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, is the national dish, and Bouneschlupp, a bean soup, is typical. Wine from the Moselle, particularly Riesling and crémant, is excellent and underrated. The city is a delight for walking, so give the Corniche and the old town an hour before heading out. A clear spring morning is ideal.
t.larochette@49.8,6.2:
Larochette sits in a narrow, wooded valley in the middle of Luxembourg, under a huge sandstone crag with a ruined castle perched on top. The Luxembourgish name is Fiels, meaning rock, and the rock is the point. The castle was built in the Middle Ages and developed over the centuries by local lords, then abandoned in the sixteenth century and left to the ivy, and its walls still stand, with a few towers and halls open to visitors. The town below is small and pleasant, with a main square, old houses along the White Ernz stream, cafes and a long history of textile making.

The surrounding area is called Little Switzerland, a name given by 19th-century visitors who thought the sandstone gorges and forests resembled the Alps, though the scale is much smaller. The rock is soft, pale sandstone, shaped by water and weather into canyons, caves, towers and narrow passages, and covered in beech forest. It is a wonderful place for walking, and the long-distance Mullerthal Trail passes through the area. From the castle, the view across the roofs and the forest is a pleasant one.

For riders, the roads around Larochette are a treat, a web of narrow, twisting lanes through woods and valleys, with good surfaces and light traffic outside holidays. The bends are smooth, the gradients gentle and the scenery changes around every corner, with sandstone cliffs, meadows and half-timbered villages. Luxembourg is small, so everything is close, and the whole region can be explored in a day. Speed limits are enforced, and cameras are not uncommon, so keep an eye on the signs. In autumn, the leaves turn the forest red and gold, which is the best time to visit, but spring is lovely too.

The town has restaurants and cafes serving local dishes such as judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, and Luxembourg sausages, along with regional beers and Moselle wines. It is a good lunch stop, and in summer the terraces are full. For fuel, remember that Luxembourg has lower fuel taxes than its neighbours, so petrol is cheaper than in Germany, France or Belgium, and it is worth filling the tank. The bigger town of Diekirch, about ten kilometres away, has stations and supermarkets, and there are others on the main roads.

Parking in the village is easy, and the castle is a short walk from the centre. Visit on a weekday if you can, since weekends in summer bring day-trippers from across the border.
t.mullerthal@49.8,6.3:
The Mullerthal is the green heart of what Luxembourgers call Little Switzerland, a region of deep, narrow valleys cut into pale sandstone, where the forest grows right down into the gorges and the streams tumble over mossy rocks. The name means mill valley, because the Black Ernz stream once powered a string of mills, and a few still stand along the water. The landscape is dominated by sandstone formations, with walls of rock, huge boulders, narrow passages between cliffs and caves where legend says smugglers and outlaws once hid. It is a gentle, mysterious sort of country, damp, green and quiet.

The rock is the story. Millions of years ago this area was under a warm sea, and the sand that settled on the bottom hardened into the sandstone that is now being slowly carved by wind and rain, producing strange shapes and tight gorges that visitors have compared to a miniature Alps. Waterfalls such as the Schiessentümpel, a small cascade beneath a footbridge, are popular, and the walks along the trails are short but rewarding. The Mullerthal Trail, a long-distance walking route of over a hundred kilometres, runs through the region, and many shorter circuits start from small car parks.

The riding is lovely. Narrow roads wind through the forest and along the valleys, with smooth tarmac, easy bends and light traffic, and every village has a bakery or a cafe. The speed limits are low and enforced, with cameras in places, and the roads are used by cyclists and walkers, so keep alert. Weather is mild and changeable, and rain can fall at any time, so a waterproof is useful. Leaf fall in autumn makes the roads slippery, and in winter, frost can linger in the shaded gorges.

Close to the region is Echternach, the oldest town in Luxembourg, which grew around an abbey founded by the missionary Willibrord in the seventh century. Each year at Whitsun, the town holds a dancing procession, in which thousands of people hop through the streets in rows, a tradition recognised by UNESCO. It is a fascinating event and the town is worth a visit at any time, with a handsome market square and a basilica.

For services, small villages such as Consdorf and Waldbillig have cafes and small shops, and there are petrol stations in larger towns such as Diekirch and Echternach. Fuel is cheaper in Luxembourg than in neighbouring countries, so it is worth filling here. Hotels and guesthouses are easy to find, and the region is well set up for walkers and cyclists.
t.shoshone idaho@42.9,-114.4:
Shoshone sits on the Snake River Plain in south-central Idaho, a flat, dry, lava-floored country of sagebrush, irrigated fields and enormous skies, and it is the county seat of Lincoln County, with about fifteen hundred people. Its stone buildings date from the days when the railroad arrived, in the 1880s, and the town was a junction where cattle and sheep were shipped. The courthouse and the old storefronts have a worn, dignified look, and the whole place has the unhurried air of a town that has seen a lot and seen it go by.

The ground beneath is volcanic. The plain is a vast sheet of basalt laid down by eruptions over millions of years, and it is full of lava tubes, caves and cracks, some of which hold ice year-round. Not far away, Craters of the Moon National Monument shows the landscape in its rawest form, a field of black lava, cinder cones and spatter cinders. To the south, near Twin Falls, the Snake River drops over Shoshone Falls, a waterfall higher than Niagara, often called the Niagara of the West, which is at its best in spring.

The Sawtooth Scenic Byway begins here and heads north on US 93 and then Highway 75, through the Wood River valley and the resort towns of Hailey and Ketchum, then up over Galena Summit, at about eighty-seven hundred feet. The country changes from desert to mountains as you ride, with the road gaining height through sage, then aspen and pine, until the pass opens a view of the Sawtooth Valley, with its jagged ridge above. The surface is good, with long straight sections early on and winding bends after Ketchum.

Fuel and supplies are available in Shoshone, so fill up before the ride, since there are few services on the long road across the plain. Jerome, about twenty-five kilometres to the south, is a larger town with more choices. Summers are hot and dry, with thunderstorms, and winters are cold. Wind can be strong, and dust blows across the flats. The best seasons for the ride are late spring and early autumn, when the weather is milder and the light is clear.
t.ketchum@43.7,-114.4:
Ketchum is the small town below the big ski mountain, at about 1,800 metres in the Wood River Valley of central Idaho, and it is best known for two things: skiing, and Ernest Hemingway. The writer first came in the late 1930s as a guest of the new Sun Valley resort, returned often, and settled here in his last years. He died in Ketchum in 1961 and is buried in the town cemetery, under a simple slab that visitors still leave pennies and bottles on. A memorial to him stands nearby in the woods beside Trail Creek.

Skiing came earlier than the writers. In 1936 the Union Pacific Railroad, searching for a place to build an American answer to the Alpine resorts, sent an Austrian count to scout the West, and he picked the valley behind Ketchum. The result was Sun Valley, which opened that winter with the world's first chairlifts, adapted from the contraptions used to load bananas onto ships. The town that grew beside it took its own name from David Ketchum, a trapper who had a cabin in the area in the 1860s. Today Ketchum has the feel of a place that is half mining town, half resort, with log lodges and low brick shops on the main street, expensive boutiques, cheerful bars and mountain bikes everywhere.

The roads here are some of the best in Idaho. Highway 75, the Sawtooth Scenic Byway, runs north from Ketchum up the Big Wood River to Galena Summit and then down into the Sawtooth Valley, and it is a beautiful, easy ride of long, smooth curves through lodgepole forest, with the jagged Sawtooth Mountains appearing ahead. South toward Hailey, the road follows the valley through a broad landscape of aspen and sagebrush. Summer is warm and dry with cool evenings, autumn brings golden aspen, and winter is for skiers, with snow and ice on the roads. Tourist traffic is heavy at weekends.

Ketchum has petrol, supermarkets, coffee shops, restaurants and every kind of lodging, from hostels to grand hotels, though prices are not low. Hailey, about eighteen kilometres to the south, is bigger and a little cheaper. Stock up here before heading north, because the next services are at Stanley, a long way off. Allow time to wander the main street, and if you are in town in September, the light on the hills is lovely.
t.galena summit@43.9,-114.7:
Galena Summit is a broad, quiet notch in the Smoky Mountains at 2,652 metres, and it is the high point of the Sawtooth Scenic Byway, but the reason people stop is the view from the overlook just to the north. From a wide pull-out on the rim you look north across the Sawtooth Valley, a vast, flat-bottomed basin of sagebrush and meadow with the Salmon River winding through it, and beyond it the long, jagged wall of the Sawtooth Mountains, grey and white against the sky. It is one of those views that feels like a map suddenly turned into land.

Highway 75 climbs to the summit from Ketchum along the Big Wood River, through lodgepole pine and open slopes, in a series of long bends and gradual climbs. On the north side, the road drops in a handful of tight switchbacks and long, curving descents into the valley, with the mountains growing ahead. The surface is generally good, and the road is wide, but the descent is steep enough to demand engine braking. Traffic is heaviest in July and August, and when the weather turns, the pass gets cold, with snow possible even in early summer. The summit is rarely closed for long, and the road is kept open all winter, though chains can be needed.

The country takes its name from galena, the lead ore that was mined near here in the 1880s, and a town of the same name flourished briefly as a silver camp before fading away. A little to the north, the Salmon River begins its long journey, running north and then west through the largest wilderness area in the lower forty-eight, the Frank Church River of No Return, and eventually joining the Snake. The valley below is the home of elk, pronghorn and, in the lakes, sockeye salmon that make an astonishing journey of some nine hundred miles from the Pacific to Redfish Lake.

There are no services at the summit, only the overlook, a car park, a few interpretive signs and toilets. Ketchum, about thirty-five kilometres south, has fuel and everything else, and Stanley, to the north, has a small selection of shops, a few motels and, in season, fuel. Fill up in Ketchum before you set out. Bring layers, because the wind at the overlook can be sharp, and take time to look at the peaks, which change with the hour.
t.stanley idaho@44.2,-114.9:
Stanley is a tiny town of a hundred or so people at about sixty-two hundred feet in the Sawtooth Valley of central Idaho, and it is one of the best-situated villages in the American West. The jagged granite wall of the Sawtooth Range stands directly behind it, tall and sharp, with snow in most months, while the infant Salmon River, the River of No Return, runs past the edge of the town. There are log buildings, a few lodges and cafes, a rodeo ground, and a sky so clear that the whole range seems to hang in the air.

The Salmon River is a historic route and a natural wonder. It rises in these mountains and runs over four hundred miles through the largest roadless wilderness in the lower forty-eight, before joining the Snake, and its salmon runs once reached all the way up to here. Sockeye salmon still make a long journey of about nine hundred miles from the Pacific to Redfish Lake, a few miles from town, climbing over a thousand miles of dams and rivers in the process, though their numbers are small and endangered. In 2017, the area was designated an International Dark Sky Reserve, the first in the United States, and at night the Milky Way is overwhelming.

The ride up here from the south crosses Galena Summit, from which the Sawtooth Valley appears below in a single sweep, and the descent into the valley is one of the great moments of the byway. The road is smooth and flowing, with gentle bends and long views, and it runs along the river through meadows and lodgepole pine. Traffic is light, and the pace is slow. In summer, thunderstorms can build quickly over the peaks, and mornings are often frosty even in July, since Stanley is one of the coldest places in the lower states.

Stanley has fuel and a small market, plus a handful of restaurants, but services are limited and close early outside summer, so plan ahead. The nearest large town, Ketchum, is a long way south. Hot springs along the Salmon River offer a soak, and the lakes, such as Redfish and Alturas, are good for a swim in July. Late September is often glorious, with crisp air, golden aspens and a clear blue sky. In winter, the road can be closed by snow and avalanches.
t.caves and ice age art in the swabian jur:
Forty thousand years ago, someone sitting in a cave above the Ach valley carved a tiny woman out of mammoth ivory, and someone else made a flute from the wing bone of a griffon vulture. Both were found in the Hohle Fels near Schelklingen, a few kilometres from where you are standing, and they rank among the oldest figurative art and musical instruments ever found. The caves of the Ach and Lone valleys were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2017 as the Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura, and they changed how archaeologists think about the first modern humans in Europe.

The Ach valley is short and steep-sided, a dry limestone gorge between Schelklingen and Blaubeuren where the cliffs are pocked with caves and the river has long since sunk underground. The Hohle Fels can be visited in season, and the finds themselves are shown at the Urgeschichtliches Museum in Blaubeuren, where the little Venus sits in a case so small you have to bend to see her properly. It is worth it.

Blaubeuren has another marvel. The Blautopf is a spring that wells up from the karst into a funnel-shaped pool of an almost unreal blue, the outflow of a vast cave system that divers are still mapping. Legend says a water nymph named Schöne Lau lived in it, and the town's former monastery stands right beside it, with a carved high altar inside.

For riding, the Swabian Jura is excellent and underestimated. Roads climb out of the valleys onto the Alb plateau in short, twisting ramps, then run across open farmland with junipers, beech woods and long views. The Blau and Ach valley roads are pleasant but busy with commuter traffic toward Ulm, and police keep an eye on popular bike routes at weekends. Schelklingen and Blaubeuren both have fuel, bakeries and inns serving Swabian food, so order Maultaschen or Linsen mit Spätzle and look up at the cliffs while you eat.
t.sacro monte o nuova gerusalemme di varal:
Varallo is a small town at the point where the Valsesia stops being a wide valley and starts becoming a mountain one, and above it, on a rocky spur reached by a winding road or a short cable car, is the oldest and most ambitious of the Sacri Monti. In 1491 a Franciscan friar called Bernardino Caimi, back from the Holy Land, set out to recreate Jerusalem here for pilgrims who could never make the journey. The result is a hilltop village of more than forty chapels filled with life-size painted terracotta and wooden figures, hundreds of them, telling the life of Christ like a frozen theatre. Gaudenzio Ferrari, the great Renaissance painter of this valley, worked on many of them.

It is a strange, moving and slightly overwhelming place, and the figures are often disarmingly real, with glass eyes and real hair. Together with eight other devotional mountains in Piedmont and Lombardy, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it remains a pilgrimage site today.

Riding the Valsesia is a joy. The road up from Varallo follows the Sesia river toward Alagna, at the foot of Monte Rosa, through a valley of stone villages with Walser wooden houses, and the river below is clear, fast and famous for rafting and kayaking. Side valleys, like the Val Mastallone toward Fobello and the climb over to Lake Orta at the Colle della Colma, offer narrow, twisting roads with little traffic. The main valley road is good but busy on summer Sundays.

Varallo has fuel, a pleasant old centre with arcaded streets, and cafés. The local food is mountain fare: polenta, cheeses like toma, and miacce, thin crêpes cooked on hot irons. Come in late spring or early autumn, when the light is clear and the chestnut woods are fresh or golden, and ride up to the holy mountain in the morning before the coach parties arrive.
t.exhibition grounds 1904@49.9,8.7:
In 1899, Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse invited a group of young artists and architects to Darmstadt and gave them a hill to build on. The Mathildenhöhe became an artists' colony and a showcase for Jugendstil, the German Art Nouveau, with studios, houses and exhibitions designed as total works of art, down to the cutlery. Behind it lay a simple idea: that art should shape everyday life, from the house to the chair to the wallpaper. The exhibitions of 1901, 1904, 1908 and 1914 drew visitors from all over Europe, and the ensemble was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2021.

The skyline of the hill is unmistakable: the Wedding Tower, built by Joseph Maria Olbrich in 1908 to commemorate the grand duke's second marriage, with its five rounded fingers at the top, and the golden onion domes of the Russian chapel, built for the grand duke's sister, the last tsarina of Russia. The exhibition building, the artists' houses and the Platanenhain, a square of plane trees with sculptures, are all within a short walk.

Darmstadt itself is a university city of around one hundred and forty thousand people, known for science, technology and research. It was badly damaged in the Second World War, and much of the centre was rebuilt in a modern style, but the Mathildenhöhe survived largely intact. Fuel, food and everything else are easy to find.

For riders, the Odenwald, just south and east of Darmstadt, is one of the best motorcycle regions in Germany, with winding roads through forests and valleys, small villages and castles. Popular routes can be busy at weekends, and some roads have motorcycle restrictions or speed limits due to noise and accidents, so check the signs. The Bergstraße, along the edge of the Rhine plain to the south, is famous for its early blossom and wine, and the Abbey of Lorsch, a Carolingian monastery with a famous gatehouse, is a short ride away.
t.rutte@47.1,7.2:
Rütte sits on the gentle southern slope above Lake Biel, a scatter of farms and orchards between the village of Bellmund and the lakeshore, with the long blue ridge of the Jura filling the view across the water. Nidau and the city of Biel are a few minutes away, yet up here it feels thoroughly rural: cows, cherry trees, a sharp smell of cut grass in early summer and the clank of a tractor somewhere below.

The reason it appears on a heritage map lies under the water and the peat along the shore. Around five to seven thousand years ago, Neolithic and Bronze Age farmers built villages on piles at the edges of the Swiss lakes, and Lake Biel is one of the richest places for their remains. The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps were listed by UNESCO in 2011, and finds from this shore, from pottery to wooden posts preserved in the mud, have helped archaeologists date these settlements almost to the year. There is nothing dramatic to see at the site itself; the story is told in the museums of Biel, but knowing what lies just offshore changes how you look at the reeds.

The riding is short and sweet. The lanes above the lake loop through Bellmund, Ipsach and Sutz with gentle curves, good tarmac and views opening up between the farmhouses, and you can ride on along the south shore towards Erlach and its old castle. Across the lake, the vineyard road through Twann and Ligerz clings to the Jura foot, and above it the climbs to the Chasseral or over the Jura passes give real corners. Swiss rules apply: motorway vignette required, speed limits enforced strictly and expensively, and village speed zones that change without much warning.

For fuel and food, Nidau and Biel have everything you need. On a summer evening, take a boat out to St Peter's Island, where Jean-Jacques Rousseau spent a few happy weeks in 1765 and later wrote that he had never been so content. With a glass of local Chasselas in hand and the sun setting behind the Jura, you might understand him.
t.vi 1 emissario@45.4,8.0:
Lago di Viverone is a small, warm lake in northern Piedmont, cupped inside one of the most remarkable glacial landforms in Europe. Ice flowing out of the Aosta Valley during the last glaciations dumped a vast ring of moraine here, the Morainic Amphitheatre of Ivrea, and its eastern wall, the Serra, runs for many kilometres as an almost perfectly straight wooded ridge. The lake sits at the foot of it, with the villages of Viverone and Azeglio on its shores and Ivrea around a quarter of an hour's ride to the northwest.

The label refers to the lake's outlet stream and to the prehistoric site nearby. Bronze Age people built pile dwellings in the shallows here, and their remains are part of the UNESCO listing that covers similar sites around the Alps. Underwater surveys have mapped thousands of wooden posts, though there is nothing to walk around on land; the lake is the monument. In summer it is a local swimming and boating spot, ringed by campsites and lidos, and in the evening the light over the water turns soft and gold behind the hills.

The riding around here is better than many realise. The road along the Serra crest and the lanes through the moraine hills twist through vineyards, chestnut woods and small villages with castle towers, and the Erbaluce di Caluso, a crisp local white wine, comes from these slopes. Northwest, the Aosta Valley opens towards the big passes, while to the south the plain flattens out towards the rice fields of Vercelli, where you trade corners for long straights and mosquitoes. Traffic is light outside weekend afternoons, though tractors and cyclists are common.

Ivrea, a town of over twenty thousand, is the obvious place for fuel, food and a break. It is famous for Olivetti, whose modernist factory town is itself a World Heritage site, and for the Battle of the Oranges at carnival, when teams pelt each other with fruit in the squares. Closer by, the small villages around the lake have bars and pizzerias, and fuel stations are spread along the main roads.
t.watchtowers wp 12 40 to 12 59@48.8,9.9:
The Romans called it the edge of the world they cared about, and in the Rems valley east of Schwäbisch Gmünd you can still trace where they drew the line. A string of watchtower sites, numbered by archaeologists along the stretch between Mögglingen, Heuchlingen and Böbingen, marks the course of the Raetian Limes, the frontier that guarded the province of Raetia in the second and third centuries. Here the frontier was a stone wall, which later locals, puzzled by the long ruined bank, called the Teufelsmauer, the Devil's Wall.

Do not expect towers standing tall. What survives is mostly a low ridge through fields and woods, occasional foundations and reconstructed outlines, and information boards along the Limes walking and cycling route. The satisfaction is in the idea: an empire stretching from Scotland to Syria, and here, in a quiet Swabian valley, men from far-off provinces stood watch over farmland that looks almost exactly the same today. The wall formed part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site together with the Upper German Limes, which joins it a little to the west near Lorch.

The countryside makes for very pleasant riding. To the south rises the escarpment of the Swabian Jura, and just above Heubach the ruin of Rosenstein castle perches on a cliff with caves beneath it and a view right across the valley. The three conical hills known as the Kaiserberge, Hohenstaufen, Rechberg and Stuifen, stand to the west, and the minor roads that weave between them are full of short climbs, open bends and orchard views. The B29 along the valley floor is fast but busy, so use the side roads whenever you can. Weekends bring plenty of fellow riders and cyclists, and some Jura roads have speed limits or noise restrictions for motorbikes.

Heubach, a town of around ten thousand, is the closest place with a full range of services, and Mögglingen and Böbingen have bakeries and inns. Heubach is also, perhaps surprisingly, where the lingerie company Triumph was founded in the nineteenth century. Order Maultaschen or Linsen mit Spätzle and a local beer, and you have the whole Swabian experience in one meal.
t.watchtowers wp 9 36 to 9 68@49.1,9.5:
Between Öhringen and Mainhardt, the Upper German Limes does something a Roman engineer must have been proud of: it runs dead straight for many kilometres, up hill and down dale, ignoring the terrain as if drawn with a ruler on a map. The watchtower sites numbered along this section lie on that line, in the Hohenlohe country of northern Württemberg, between the open farmland around Pfedelbach and the dark wooded hills of the Swabian-Franconian Forest.

On the ground, you will find the bank and ditch of the frontier running through woods, the foundations of some towers, and in places reconstructed timber towers that give a sense of how the line worked. Soldiers in each post could signal to the next, and behind them lay forts such as those at Öhringen, where two garrisons were stationed, and at Mainhardt, where a small museum tells the story. The Limes here was a palisade with a bank and ditch rather than a wall, and when the frontier was abandoned in the third century the forest slowly took it back.

The riding is the kind that sneaks up on you. North of the forest, Hohenlohe is a gently rolling plateau of wheat fields, vineyards on south-facing slopes and small towns with castles, the land of the princely Hohenlohe family. Climb south into the Swabian-Franconian Forest and the roads narrow, twist and dive through dense spruce and beech, past mills, ponds and tiny hamlets. Surfaces are generally good, though leaves, mud from logging and the odd deer demand attention, particularly in autumn and at dusk.

Öhringen has more than twenty thousand residents and Pfedelbach several thousand, so fuel and food are close at hand. The region is proud of its cuisine: Hohenlohe beef and the local Schwäbisch-Hällisch pig, a dark-headed breed brought back from near extinction, turn up on many menus. A glass of Lemberger or Trollinger from the Hohenlohe vineyards rounds things off, though perhaps save that for the end of the day.
t.speyer cathedral@49.3,8.4:
Some buildings impress you with height, others with mass. Speyer Cathedral does it with both, rising from the left bank of the Rhine with six towers and a long, rhythmic nave of red sandstone. It was begun around 1030 by the emperor Conrad II, the first of the Salian dynasty, and is generally considered the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world. Its crypt, a forest of sturdy columns and striped arches, holds the tombs of several emperors and kings, which tells you how central this town once was to the Holy Roman Empire.

Speyer itself is a lively, walkable city of around fifty thousand people. The broad Maximilianstraße runs from the cathedral to the old gate tower, lined with cafés, ice cream parlours and stalls selling the city's giant pretzels. Speyer hosted many imperial diets, including the 1529 assembly where Lutheran princes issued the protest that gave Protestants their name. The Jewish community of medieval Speyer was one of the most important in Europe, and the remains of its synagogue and ritual bath, the mikveh, are part of a separate World Heritage listing.

For riders, the Technik Museum Speyer is a magnet, with aircraft, a space shuttle prototype, locomotives and a respectable collection of motorcycles. The riding in the area is flat on the Rhine plain, with river-meadow lanes and the occasional small car ferry across the Rhine, but the Palatinate Forest begins just west of Neustadt and offers fine winding roads through sandstone hills. The German Wine Route along the foot of those hills is pretty but slow, packed with villages and wine festivals in summer and autumn.

Speyer is an easy town for a break: pumps on the main roads, food on every corner. Park near the cathedral on the edge of the old town; the centre is compact and pleasant on foot. In the Palatinate, try Saumagen, a stuffed pork stomach that sounds worse than it tastes, or simply sit in the cathedral garden by the old stone basin, the Domnapf, which by tradition was filled with wine for the people whenever a new bishop took office.
t.baie de clendy@46.8,6.7:
At the southern tip of Lake Neuchâtel, just east of Yverdon-les-Bains, the shore curves into a shallow bay fringed with reeds, poplars and a beach where local families swim in summer. Behind it, in a meadow, stands a double row of tall grey stones. These are the menhirs of Clendy, raised by Neolithic farmers more than five thousand years ago and re-erected in the twentieth century after they were found toppled in the ground. Offshore and along the bay lie the remains of lakeside settlements of the same era, part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

The lake level was lowered in the nineteenth century during the great Jura water correction, which exposed many of these old villages and made Lake Neuchâtel one of the cradles of pile-dwelling archaeology. Today the bay is a gentle place of walkers, dogs and birdwatchers, and the reedbeds of the southern shore, the Grande Cariçaie, form one of the largest lakeside wetlands in Switzerland, alive with herons, grebes and reed warblers. On a calm evening the lake turns silver and the Jura ridge darkens behind it.

Yverdon is a spa town with thermal baths that have been used since Roman times, a castle in the centre and a link to the educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi, who ran a famous school here. Just up the shore, the castle of Grandson looks over the lake; it was near here in 1476 that the Swiss Confederates defeated Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, capturing his treasure and his pride.

The riding in this corner of Switzerland is varied. The lakeshore roads are easy and scenic, while the Jura rises steeply to the west with excellent climbs towards Sainte-Croix and the plateaus beyond, through forests and wide pastures with stone walls. Expect Swiss speed limits and strict enforcement, as well as the motorway vignette requirement. Yverdon has plenty of fuel stations, restaurants and cafés. Try a plate of perch fillets from the lake with fries and tartare sauce, or in colder months a vacherin Mont-d'Or, a soft cheese from the Jura baked in its own wooden box.
t.watchtowers wp 12 39@48.8,9.9:
Iggingen is a small village on the plateau above the Rems valley, a few kilometres east of Schwäbisch Gmünd, and like many villages in this part of Württemberg it has a Roman frontier running through its fields. The site labelled Watchtower WP 12/39 sits on the Raetian Limes, the stone wall that marked the edge of Roman Raetia, and from here the line runs eastwards towards Aalen, the largest Roman cavalry fort north of the Alps, now home to an excellent Limes museum.

The wall here has mostly disappeared into fields and woods, surviving as a low bank in places and marked by signs along the Limes hiking and cycling trail. In Roman times, soldiers in the watchtowers would have looked north across forests and hills towards the lands of the Germanic tribes, and you can still get a sense of that outward gaze from the higher ground. Nearby, at Böbingen an der Rems, the site of a Roman fort is marked out on the ground, and Schwäbisch Gmünd, the oldest Staufer town, has a fine cathedral and a long tradition of gold and silversmithing.

The riding around here is a lovely mix of gentle valleys, plateaus and sudden steep climbs onto the edge of the Swabian Jura. Minor roads link small villages and farms, with good surfaces and little traffic, though tractors and cyclists are common. The Jura edge to the south offers excellent routes, with climbs up to viewpoints such as the Rosenstein and down into hidden valleys. The main valley road is busy, so it pays to explore the back roads on either side. Some popular motorcycle routes in Baden-Württemberg have speed limits or seasonal restrictions, so watch the signs.

Iggingen itself is tiny, so for fuel and services head to Schwäbisch Gmünd, Heubach or one of the larger villages along the valley. Look for a traditional Gasthaus serving Schwäbischer Rostbraten, roast beef with crispy onions and Spätzle, or Kässpätzle, cheese noodles with fried onions, and in summer, a cold beer from one of the small local breweries.
t.fort site and civil settlement of lorsch:
Lorch, in the Rems valley east of Stuttgart, sits on a historic seam. Just outside town, the Upper German Limes, which ran as a palisade and ditch from the Rhine, met the Raetian Limes, the stone wall running east to the Danube, and the Romans built a fort here to watch over that junction and the valley road. The fort lay beneath what is now the old town centre, and its outline, together with traces of the civilian settlement that grew around it, is marked in places in the streets. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site, and a reconstructed watchtower stands on a hill nearby.

Lorch has a second claim to fame. On the hill above town stands Lorch Abbey, a Benedictine monastery founded in the early twelfth century by the Staufer family, who went on to rule the Holy Roman Empire. Several members of the dynasty are buried here, and the abbey church, with its Romanesque core, a large painted genealogy of the Staufers and walls that still enclose the complex, has a quiet, dignified atmosphere. The family's ancestral castle stood on the Hohenstaufen, one of the three conical hills visible to the east.

The riding around Lorch is pleasant and varied. The B29 along the Rems valley is fast and busy, linking Stuttgart with Aalen, but the minor roads on either side are much more fun, climbing onto the wooded plateau of the Schurwald to the north or the Welzheim Forest, with tight bends, steep climbs and dense woods. To the south, roads lead towards the Kaiserberge and the edge of the Swabian Jura, one of the finest riding areas in southern Germany. Weekends bring crowds of riders, and police checks are common.

Lorch is a town of around eleven thousand, with fuel stations, cafés and restaurants. The abbey has a café and a garden with views over the valley, perfect for a break. Look for local dishes like Zwiebelrostbraten, beef with crispy onions, or Gaisburger Marsch, a hearty stew of beef, potatoes and Spätzle, and taste local wines from the Rems valley.
t.abbey of st gall@47.4,9.4:
In the centre of St Gallen, a city in north-eastern Switzerland between Lake Constance and the Appenzell hills, the twin towers of a baroque cathedral rise above a wide square, and beside them stands one of the oldest and most beautiful libraries in the world. The Abbey of St Gall was founded in the eighth century on the site where the Irish monk Gallus had settled in the early seventh century, and it became one of the great centres of learning in medieval Europe. The abbey precinct was listed by UNESCO in 1983.

The abbey library, the Stiftsbibliothek, is a baroque hall of carved wood, inlaid floors and painted ceilings, housing thousands of manuscripts and early printed books, some more than a thousand years old. Visitors must wear felt slippers to protect the floor, and the atmosphere is hushed and reverent. Among its treasures is the Plan of St Gall, a ninth-century drawing of an ideal monastery, the only surviving architectural plan of its kind from the early Middle Ages. The cathedral itself is a masterpiece of late baroque, with a bright, ornate interior of stucco and frescoes.

St Gallen is a lively city with a university and a long tradition of textile production, especially embroidery and lace, which made it rich in the nineteenth century. The old town has elegant houses with painted oriel windows, shops and cafés. Around the city, the landscape is green and hilly, with farms, forests and views of the Alpstein massif and its highest peak, the Säntis. The roads into the Appenzell hills are a joy to ride, winding through villages with painted wooden houses and meadows, and the climb to the Schwägalp at the foot of the Säntis is one of the classic rides of eastern Switzerland.

St Gallen has plenty of fuel, food and parking. Swiss traffic rules are strict, with speed cameras and high fines, and you need a vignette for motorways. Try the St Gallen bratwurst, made from veal and traditionally eaten without mustard, and the local Appenzeller cheese. In the city, the Stiftsbezirk is best visited on foot, so park nearby and walk in.
t.hurden rosshorn@47.2,8.8:
Where Lake Zurich narrows to a waist between Rapperswil and Hurden, a low peninsula runs out from the Schwyz shore, and at its tip, the Rosshorn, the remains of prehistoric lakeside villages lie beneath the shallow water. People lived here in the Neolithic and Bronze Ages, in houses built on wooden piles, and they also built some of the earliest known bridges across the narrows. The site is one of the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011, a group of sites that has given archaeologists a remarkably detailed view of everyday life thousands of years ago, preserved in the mud of lakes and moors.

The crossing here has been important ever since. In the Middle Ages, a wooden bridge carried pilgrims on their way to the monastery of Einsiedeln, and in 2001 a new wooden footbridge was built on the same line, running for about eight hundred metres across the water from Rapperswil to Hurden. Walking across it on a calm evening, with the lake turning gold and the mountains rising to the south, is a lovely way to end a ride. The Seedamm, the causeway that carries the road and railway between the two shores, runs alongside.

From Hurden, the obvious ride is up to the Etzel pass, a short, steep climb from Pfäffikon through meadows and forests, with tight bends and fine views back over the lake, before descending towards the Sihlsee and Einsiedeln, where the great baroque abbey and its Black Madonna have drawn pilgrims for a thousand years. The roads are narrow and busy at weekends, with cyclists, cars and tractors. The lakeside roads are pleasant but slow, with plenty of traffic and speed limits that are strictly enforced, as anywhere in Switzerland.

Hurden is a small village with a few restaurants, known for fish from the lake, while Rapperswil, just across the water, and Pfäffikon, a short ride away, have fuel and all the services you could need. Swiss motorways require a vignette, and speed cameras are common, with high fines. The weather is changeable, with fog on the lake in autumn and winter, and summer thunderstorms that can arrive quickly from the mountains. On a sunny day, though, the lake is at its best, with boats, swimmers and the view of the Glarus Alps in the distance.
t.technikum@47.2,8.8:
Students at the technical university in Rapperswil study engineering on a lakeside campus, and beneath the shoreline in front of their buildings lie the remains of villages that people built on piles thousands of years ago. The site, named after the old Technikum, as the college was long known, is one of the prehistoric pile dwelling sites around Lake Zurich included in the UNESCO listing of 2011. Nothing is visible, but the idea that this shore has been home to people for so long gives a different perspective to a stroll along the promenade.

Rapperswil is one of the most charming towns on Lake Zurich. Its old town sits on a small peninsula, with narrow streets, arcades and colourful houses climbing towards the castle, a stout medieval fortress with three towers that looks out over the lake. It is known as the town of roses, with rose gardens planted around the old town, including one in the grounds of a Capuchin monastery. The castle long housed a museum dedicated to Polish history and culture, founded in the nineteenth century by Polish exiles, which tells a surprising story of the links between Switzerland and Poland. The town is also the winter quarters of the Knie family's Swiss National Circus, and its children's zoo is a favourite with families.

For riders, Rapperswil is a good base. The lakeside roads are slow and often busy, but the hills behind the town, in the Zurich Oberland and the Toggenburg, offer quiet roads with plenty of bends, wide views over the lake and the Alps, and villages with good restaurants. To the south, across the Seedamm, the roads climb into the canton of Schwyz, towards the Etzel, the Sihlsee and the passes beyond. The Ricken pass, linking the Linth plain with the Toggenburg, is a pleasant ride, with long, flowing bends.

Rapperswil and Jona, which merged into a single town, have fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants, many of them with terraces overlooking the lake. The harbour is busy with boats, and in summer, the lake steamers stop here on their way to and from Zurich. Remember the Swiss rules: strict speed limits, high fines and a vignette for the motorways. The weather can be changeable, with fog in autumn and winter, but on a clear day the views over the lake to the mountains are superb.
t.il sabbione o settentrionale@45.8,8.6:
Lake Monate is small, round and remarkably clean, set in the gentle hills of the Varese province between Lake Maggiore and Lake Varese. It has no river flowing into it, being fed by springs, and its water is among the clearest of any lake in Lombardy, which makes it a favourite with swimmers on hot summer days. On its northern shore, near Cadrezzate, the site known as Il Sabbione preserves the remains of a prehistoric village built on piles at the water's edge, part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. The Varese area is rich in such sites, and the finds from them, including pottery, tools and the remains of wooden canoes, are displayed in local museums.

The landscape is a patchwork of small lakes, low hills, woods and villages, shaped by the glaciers that once flowed down from the Alps. Lake Varese, just to the east, has an island, Isolino Virginia, which was also a pile dwelling site and has a small museum. Lake Maggiore, to the west, is much larger, with grand villas, gardens and islands, including the Borromean Islands off Stresa.

The riding is varied and enjoyable. The roads around the lakes are winding and scenic, with views over the water and the hills, though they can be busy with traffic, especially at weekends. North of Varese, the road climbs to the Sacro Monte, a mountain sanctuary approached by a cobbled pilgrim path lined with fourteen chapels, part of the UNESCO listing of the Sacri Monti of Piedmont and Lombardy. Beyond it, the Campo dei Fiori offers twisting roads through forests, with views over the lakes and the Alps. Further north, the Valcuvia and the valleys towards the Swiss border have quiet roads with plenty of bends.

Besozzo, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel and shops, and Varese, the provincial capital, is a larger city with everything you could need. The beaches on Lake Monate, with their clear water, are perfect for a swim after a ride, and the local restaurants serve lake fish, risotto and polenta. The weather is warm in summer, with occasional thunderstorms, and the hills can be foggy in autumn and winter.
t.volklingen ironworks@49.2,6.8:
Rust, soot and colossal machinery: the Völklingen Ironworks is a cathedral of heavy industry, and walking through it is an overwhelming experience. Founded in 1873 and developed by the Röchling family into one of the largest iron producers in Europe, the works produced pig iron from 1883 until 1986, when the blast furnaces were shut down. Instead of being demolished, the complex was preserved, and in 1994 it became the first industrial monument from the heyday of heavy industry to be listed by UNESCO. Today visitors can climb the blast furnaces, walk through the huge blowing engine hall, and explore the coking plant and the ore storage, much of which has been taken over by nature, with birch trees and wild plants growing among the steel.

The history of the ironworks is not only one of technical achievement. During both world wars, the works relied on forced labour, including prisoners of war and civilians from occupied countries, and the conditions were brutal. The site does not hide this history, and exhibitions explain it alongside the story of the workers, the technology and the region. The ironworks also hosts art exhibitions and cultural events, and the illuminated blast furnaces at night are a striking sight.

The Saarland is a small region with a complex history, passed back and forth between France and Germany, and its culture reflects both. The riding is surprisingly good, with rolling hills, forests and river valleys, and quiet roads away from the industrial towns. The highlight is the Saarschleife, near Mettlach, where the river Saar makes a dramatic hairpin bend through a wooded gorge, best seen from the viewpoint at Cloef, where a treetop walkway offers a view over the loop. The roads along the Saar and into the hills of the Hunsrück to the north are winding and scenic, with good surfaces and little traffic.

Völklingen, a town of about forty thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Saarbrücken, the capital of the Saarland, is a short ride away, and France is just across the river. The local food is hearty, with Dibbelabbes, a potato dish cooked with bacon and leeks, and Lyoner sausage, and the local beers are good. The weather is mild, with warm summers and cool, damp winters, and fog can settle in the river valleys in autumn.
t.la place forte de longwy@49.5,5.8:
In 1678, after Louis XIV won Longwy from the Spanish Netherlands in the Treaty of Nijmegen, he sent his great military engineer Vauban to make sure nobody took it back. Vauban did not just fortify the old town; he built a new one, Longwy-Haut, on the plateau, designing a star-shaped stronghold with bastions, ditches and a geometric grid of streets around a central square with a well and church. It is one of the twelve sites grouped as the Fortifications of Vauban on the World Heritage list, and walking the ramparts you can still read the logic of seventeenth-century siege warfare in the earth and stone.

Longwy's later history belongs to iron and steel. The nearby ore fields fed great blast furnaces from the nineteenth century, and the whole corner where France, Belgium and Luxembourg meet became one of Europe's industrial heartlands, until the crisis of the late 1970s and 1980s closed the works and left deep scars. The town is also famous for enamels: the émaux de Longwy, brightly coloured decorative ceramics in a cloisonné style, have been made here since the late eighteenth century and still are.

The riding around Longwy is more about borders than about bends. In a few minutes you can be in Belgium or Luxembourg, and the landscape is a mix of old industrial towns, farmland, woods and rolling hills. The roads are good, traffic can be heavy with cross-border commuters at rush hour, and the more interesting riding lies to the north in the Belgian Ardennes and to the east in the Moselle valley. Winters here are often grey and damp; May and September are kinder.

There is fuel in Longwy, but the locals know better: Luxembourg's lower fuel taxes have made the stations just across the border famous, and the queues at Pétange or Rodange show it. Longwy-Haut has cafés around its square, and Lorraine food is solid and filling, from quiche to mirabelle plum tart. Take a moment at the ramparts to look out over the valley and the three countries that meet just beyond it.
t.strandboden@47.0,7.1:
Erlach sits at the south-western tip of Lake Biel, a little Bernese town of one steep street climbing to a castle, with vineyards on the slope behind and reed beds and beaches along the shore below. The flat ground by the water, the Strandboden, is where archaeologists have found traces of prehistoric lakeside villages, part of the network of pile dwelling sites around the Alps inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. Five or six thousand years ago farmers built their houses here on posts at the water's edge, and the waterlogged mud preserved timbers, tools, seeds and even textiles in astonishing detail.

From Erlach a long, narrow strip of land, the Heidenweg, runs out across the lake to the St. Petersinsel, which stopped being an island when the Jura water correction of the nineteenth century lowered the lake. Jean-Jacques Rousseau spent a few blissful weeks there in 1765 after being driven out of his previous refuge, and later wrote that they were the happiest of his life. On the north shore, the wine villages of Ligerz, Twann and La Neuveville line the water beneath steep terraces of Chasselas vines, and the language border runs straight through the region, French on one side, German on the other.

Riding here offers the best of both worlds. The roads along the lake are gentle and scenic, with vineyards and villages and constant views of the water, although the north shore road is busy, squeezed between the railway and the cliffs. Above it, the Jura rises like a wall, and the climb to the Chasseral, with its hairpins, open pastures and enormous views across the Swiss plateau to the Alps, is one of the finest rides in western Switzerland. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced and fines are steep, so keep an eye on the speedometer.

Le Landeron and La Neuveville, three or so kilometres away, have fuel and shops, and Murten, twelve kilometres away, is a lovely walled town on its own lake. Erlach has a few restaurants and cafés, and the beach is a pleasant place for a swim on a hot day. Try the local white wine with a plate of lake fish, perch or whitefish, in one of the restaurants along the shore.
t.oterswil insel eielen@47.1,8.5:
Lake Zug is the quiet one among the central Swiss lakes, long and slender, with the Rigi rising steeply from its southern end and gentle farmland and orchards rolling down to its northern shores. Around its edges, as around many Alpine lakes, people built villages on the shore in prehistoric times, and the remains of these settlements at places like Oterswil and the little island of Eielen are among the sites of the transnational pile dwelling listing inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. Under water and mud, wooden piles, pottery and tools have survived for thousands of years.

Zug itself, the cantonal capital, is a small, wealthy town with a charming old centre on the lake, a clock tower, narrow lanes and a lakeside promenade famous for its sunsets. The canton's low taxes have attracted many international companies, but the old town and the countryside around it have kept their calm. Zug is also famous for cherries, and its cherry kirsch and the Zuger Kirschtorte, a layered cake soaked in kirsch, are local specialities. The orchards around the lake are a sea of white blossom in spring.

The roads around Lake Zug are a pleasure. The eastern shore road, from Zug through Walchwil to Arth, is narrow and winding, squeezed between the lake and the steep slopes, with constant views over the water and the Rigi. On the western side, the roads through Risch, Buonas and Immensee are quieter, through farmland and orchards. From Arth or Küssnacht, roads climb towards the Rigi and the Lake Lucerne region. Swiss speed limits are enforced strictly, and traffic can be heavy at peak times.

Rotkreuz, five kilometres to the west, takes care of petrol and groceries, and Zug covers everything else. The lakeside restaurants serve fish from the lake, often perch or whitefish, and their terraces face west for the famous sunsets. A slice of Zuger Kirschtorte, nutty meringue layers soaked in cherry kirsch, with a coffee, is the local ritual, and in May the orchards around the lake are worth the trip on their own. On hot summer days the lido areas along the shore are an easy, cool way to end a ride.
t.rorenhaab@47.3,8.7:
The winter of 1853 to 1854 was so dry that the water in Lake Zurich fell to an unusually low level, and at Obermeilen, on the eastern shore, villagers extending their land into the lake found rows of wooden piles sticking out of the mud, along with pottery, bone tools and stone axes. The antiquarian Ferdinand Keller studied the finds and concluded that they came from prehistoric villages built on platforms over the water, and his reports launched the pile dwelling craze that swept through Europe in the nineteenth century. Rorenhaab, at Obermeilen, is that very site, and it is part of the pile dwellings around the Alps listing inscribed by UNESCO in 2011.

Today the shore here is lined with gardens, villas and boat houses, and it takes imagination to picture the Neolithic village that once stood on the water. Meilen is one of the villages of the so-called Gold Coast, the sunny eastern shore of Lake Zurich, which gets the afternoon and evening sun and has long been a favourite place for wealthy Zurich families to live. Vineyards climb the slopes behind the villages, and the Pfannenstiel, a wooded ridge above, offers walking trails and views over the lake to the Alps.

The Seestrasse, the lakeside road from Zurich to Rapperswil, runs through Meilen, and it is busy, with traffic lights, speed limits and plenty of cars. The roads up into the hills behind, through vineyards and villages towards the Pfannenstiel and the Zurich Oberland, are quieter and more interesting, with curves and views over the lake. A car ferry links Meilen with Horgen on the opposite shore, a handy shortcut and a pleasant break. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced.

Meilen has fuel and a range of shops, and Männedorf, three kilometres along the shore, has more. In summer, the public lake baths along this coast, the Seebäder, are one of the great pleasures of Zurich life, with wooden decks and clean, cool water. The vineyards above Meilen produce Räuschling and Pinot Noir, and a glass on a terrace in the evening sun is the reward the Gold Coast is named for. The car ferry to Horgen runs frequently and turns a crossing of the lake into a ten-minute break with a view of the Alps.
t.crespi d adda@45.6,9.5:
Crespi d'Adda is a whole company town, built from 1878 by the Crespi family of cotton manufacturers on a bend of the Adda river where the water could turn their turbines. Around the mill they laid out rows of neat houses with gardens for the workers, larger villas for the managers, a school, a church that copies the Renaissance church of Santa Maria di Piazza in Busto Arsizio, a washhouse, a hospital, and, on a slight rise at the end of the main street, a cemetery with a strange, almost Mayan-looking mausoleum for the family. It was a paternalistic utopia in which the company looked after its workers from cradle to grave, and UNESCO listed it in 1995 as one of the best-preserved examples of its kind in Europe.

The mill closed in 2003, but the village is still lived in, and the houses with their little gardens, the straight avenues and the giant chimney give the place a quiet, orderly feel that is quite unlike the towns around it. You can walk the whole thing in an hour.

The Adda is a lovely river, deep green and fast here, flowing between wooded banks with old canals and towpaths running alongside. Leonardo da Vinci spent time in this valley and studied its rapids; some believe the landscapes in his paintings echo its scenery, and the ferry crossing at Imbersago upstream is said to follow his design. The towpath along the Martesana canal and the river is a favourite cycle route, but not for bikes with engines.

As a ride start or finish, Crespi is close to the motorway network around Bergamo and Milan, and the roads out are suburban at first, with traffic, roundabouts and industry. Head north, though, and within half an hour you are into the foothills, climbing towards Lecco and the lakes or into the valleys above Bergamo. Brembate, Canonica d'Adda and Vaprio d'Adda all have fuel stations, bars and pastry shops, so you will not go short of an espresso. Bergamo's upper town, Città Alta, inside its Venetian walls, is a perfect evening destination.
t.igel column@49.7,6.5:
The Igel Column is one of those Roman monuments that seems to have survived by a happy accident. It stands in the village of Igel, on the Moselle a few kilometres upstream from Trier, a sandstone pillar some twenty-three metres high, covered with carved scenes. It was built in the third century as a funerary monument for the Secundinii, a family of wealthy cloth merchants, and the reliefs show them at work: bales of cloth being loaded and transported, customers being received, and a family meal, as well as mythological scenes on the upper sections. In the Middle Ages, people came to believe it showed the marriage of Constantine's mother, St Helena, which probably saved it from being broken up for building stone.

Goethe saw it and admired it, and today it is grouped with Trier's World Heritage Roman monuments, alongside the Porta Nigra, the imperial baths and the amphitheatre in the city. A copy at the Rheinisches Landesmuseum in Trier shows the column with its original painted colours, which gives a vivid sense of how gaudy Roman art could be.

The Moselle valley here is lovely riding, with vineyards on the steep slopes, river barges, small wine villages and the long curves of the river. The road along the river, the B49 on the German side and the corresponding roads in Luxembourg, are easy and scenic, though busy at weekends with tourists and cyclists. Igel is right on the border with Luxembourg, across the river at Wasserbillig, where fuel is cheaper and stations crowd the road for exactly that reason; it is a ritual for German riders to fill up there.

Konz, a couple of kilometres downstream where the Saar comes in, covers everything else. A short ride up the Saar takes you to the famous Saarschleife, a dramatic hairpin bend of the river best seen from the viewpoint at Cloef. Moselle wine, especially riesling, is excellent, and the wine taverns in the villages serve it with local dishes like Teerdisch, a potato and sauerkraut mash with bacon. In autumn, the vineyards turn gold and the grape harvest brings busy roads and wine festivals.
t.bleiche 2 3@47.5,9.4:
Arbon sits on the Swiss shore of Lake Constance, in the canton of Thurgau, and just outside the town, on land that was once lake shore, lies one of the most remarkable prehistoric sites in Europe. At Arbon-Bleiche, archaeologists excavated a Neolithic village of wooden houses built on the edge of the lake around 3400 BC. Because the wood was preserved in waterlogged ground, tree rings allowed the village to be dated almost to the year: it was built, lived in for about fifteen years and then destroyed by fire. The finds, from pottery and tools to textiles and food remains, gave a detailed picture of how these early farmers lived, and Arbon counts among the Swiss sites in the Alpine pile-dwelling inscription of 2011. There is nothing to see at the site itself, which is now under buildings and fields; the finds are displayed in the Thurgau archaeological museum in Frauenfeld.

Arbon has had a long life since then. The Romans built a fort here called Arbor Felix, and the remains of its walls lie under the castle and church in the old town.
