In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the town became an industrial centre, home to Saurer, a company that made embroidery machines and later trucks and buses famous throughout Switzerland; a museum near the lake shows off its machines.

The riding along Lake Constance is pleasant rather than challenging. The lakeside road runs through towns and villages, past orchards and vineyards, with views across the water to Germany and Austria and, on clear days, the snowy peaks of the Vorarlberg and Swiss Alps. It is often busy, especially in summer, with cars, cyclists and tourists, and Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced with plenty of cameras; fines are notoriously steep. Better riding lies inland, in the hills of the Appenzell and the Toggenburg, just a short ride south, with winding roads and small farming villages.

Arbon, a town of thirteen thousand people, has everything you need: fuel, shops, cafes and restaurants on the lake front. Lake fish such as perch and whitefish are local specialities, served at many restaurants. The lakeside promenade is a pleasant place to relax, and on hot days a swim in the lake is welcome. Bregenz is a short ride east across the Austrian border.
t.from the great saltworks of salins les b:
Salins-les-Bains lies at the bottom of a deep, narrow valley in the Jura, squeezed between two forested ridges, each crowned by a fort, and its wealth for most of history came from beneath its streets. Deep underground, salty water flows through layers of rock salt, and for over a thousand years the people of Salins pumped it up and boiled it in great pans to make salt, a precious commodity before refrigeration, used to preserve food and taxed heavily by the crown. The Grande Saline, the great saltworks, is now a museum, and you can walk through its underground galleries, where a huge hydraulic wheel and pump from the nineteenth century still turn, lifting brine from the depths.

By the eighteenth century, the forests around Salins were exhausted from feeding the fires under the salt pans. The solution was to bring the brine to the wood instead: a pipeline, made of hollowed tree trunks, carried the brine some twenty kilometres through the valley to Arc-et-Senans, on the edge of the great forest of Chaux, where the architect Claude-Nicolas Ledoux built the Royal Saltworks in the 1770s, a semicircular complex designed as an ideal industrial city. Arc-et-Senans was listed by UNESCO in 1982, and Salins was added in 2009, linked by their shared history and the pipeline.

The riding around Salins is superb. The roads climb out of the valley in steep, twisting stretches onto the Jura plateaus, with forests, meadows, small villages and wide views, and continue south towards Champagnole and the lakes, or east into the higher Jura towards Switzerland. The surfaces are generally good, traffic light, and the scenery changes with every bend. Watch for cows on the road, logging trucks and, in winter, ice and snow.

Arbois, a few kilometres to the southwest, is the wine capital of the Jura and the town where Louis Pasteur grew up; his house is a museum. The Jura produces unusual wines, notably the nutty vin jaune, aged under a film of yeast for over six years. Comté cheese is the other local treasure, made in village dairies called fruitières. Salins itself can supply petrol and lunch; for a larger choice, Champagnole, twenty-two kilometres away, has everything. Try poulet au vin jaune with morels.
t.enge alpenquai@47.4,8.5:
Zurich's lakefront is one of the most pleasant urban shorelines in Europe, and the Alpenquai, in the district of Enge, is a stretch of it where the city opens up to views across the water to the Alps. On a clear day, especially when the föhn blows from the south, the peaks of the Glarus Alps seem close enough to touch. Under the water off this shore, archaeologists have found the remains of prehistoric villages built on piles along the lake edge, and several of Zurich's shore sites were inscribed in 2011 among the prehistoric pile dwellings of the Alpine lakes. You will see nothing of them from the promenade; they lie in the mud of the lake bed, preserved by the water.

The lakefront from Enge south is a ribbon of parks, bathing places, sailing clubs and promenades, busy with joggers, walkers and swimmers on summer evenings. The arboretum is a quiet park with old trees, and the Mythenquai continues south towards the Rote Fabrik, an old factory turned cultural centre. The Enge district itself is a mix of offices, villas and apartment buildings, with the Rieterpark and the Museum Rietberg, which houses one of the best collections of non-European art in Europe, on the hill above.

Riding in Zurich is not a pleasure. Traffic is dense, speed limits are low, and there are many cameras and strict enforcement; Swiss fines are very high, and serious speeding can lead to licence loss or worse. Trams and cyclists add to the complexity. The good news is that motorcycle parking is generally easy in designated areas. To use Swiss motorways, you need a vignette, which covers a full calendar year.

The real riding starts outside the city. South along the lake, roads lead to the Sihl valley, the Zug lake and the hills above, and further to the passes of central Switzerland. East, the Pfannenstiel ridge has nice curves and views over the lake. Zurich has fuel stations everywhere, but they are often small and crowded. Food is expensive but excellent: try Zürcher Geschnetzeltes, sliced veal in a cream sauce with rösti, or a sausage from a stand. On a hot day, a swim in the lake from one of the public baths is a fine way to cool off.
t.seematte@47.2,8.3:
Lake Baldegg lies in the Seetal, the lake valley north of Lucerne, a gentle, green landscape of meadows, orchards and woods, with the lake in the middle and the hills rising on either side. Seematte, on the shore near Hitzkirch, is the site of prehistoric lakeside villages, built on piles over the water's edge thousands of years ago, and it was inscribed in the same 2011 listing that covers lakeside villages from France to Slovenia. As with most such sites, there is nothing to see above ground, but the setting is lovely, and standing on the reedy shore you can imagine the wooden houses and dugout canoes.

The lake itself has an interesting recent history. In the twentieth century, runoff from intensive farming filled it with nutrients, and the water became starved of oxygen. Since the early 1980s, the lake has been artificially aerated, with oxygen pumped into the depths, one of the longest-running lake restoration projects in Switzerland. The lake is protected, and its shores are largely undeveloped, with reed beds and meadows that attract birds.

The Seetal also has Hallwil, the next lake to the north, with the water castle of Hallwyl, a beautiful medieval moated castle on two islands, now a museum. Beromünster, a few kilometres west, has a medieval collegiate church and was once home to the national radio transmitter, whose tall mast was a landmark across the region. Hitzkirch has a former Commandery of the Teutonic Order.

The riding here is relaxed and scenic, on quiet country roads through villages and farmland, with gentle curves and small hills. The road along the eastern shore of the lake is particularly pretty, with views across the water to the hills. Traffic is light, but watch for tractors, cyclists and the strict Swiss speed limits, enforced by cameras. Hitzkirch has basic shops and cafes; Menziken, six kilometres away, is a slightly larger town with fuel and services. Lucerne, about twenty-five kilometres south, has everything. Try the local Luzerner Chügelipastete, a puff-pastry vol-au-vent filled with veal, mushrooms and cream, and the apple and pear products of the Seetal orchards.
t.le locle@47.1,6.7:
Le Locle, high in the Swiss Jura near the French border, is a town built for making watches. After a series of fires in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it was rebuilt on a grid of parallel streets, with houses and workshops designed to let maximum light into the rooms where watchmakers worked at their benches. The town, with neighbouring La Chaux-de-Fonds, was listed by UNESCO in 2009 as an example of urban planning shaped entirely by a single industry. Tissot was founded here in 1853, Zenith in 1865, and many smaller firms continue the tradition. Daniel JeanRichard, a goldsmith who is said to have founded the Jura watch industry, worked here in the eighteenth century.

The Château des Monts, a manor on the hill above the town, houses a fine museum of watches and automata. On the edge of town, the underground mills of Col-des-Roches are a remarkable sight: water mills built in caves, where the river disappears into the rock, used for centuries to grind grain and power machinery. The Doubs river forms the border with France just a few kilometres away, and at Les Brenets it widens into a lake before plunging over the Saut du Doubs, a waterfall about twenty-seven metres high, reached by boat or on foot.

The landscape is the high Jura: wide valleys and ridges of limestone, pastures, pine forests and farmhouses with huge roofs. At around nine hundred metres above sea level, Le Locle has long, cold winters, and the valley of La Brévine, nearby, is known as the Swiss Siberia for its record low temperatures. Summers are fresh and green, perfect for riding.

The roads here are quiet and flowing, with long curves through the valleys and climbs over the ridges, and views across to France and the Alps on clear days. The road down to the Doubs at Les Brenets and Villers-le-Lac is narrow and twisty. Traffic is light, but watch for cattle, cyclists and Swiss speed cameras. Le Locle covers the basics comfortably; fuel is often cheaper across the border in France. Try absinthe, which was born in the Val-de-Travers nearby, and local cheeses such as Tête de Moine and Gruyère.
t.kehrsiten@47.0,8.4:
Kehrsiten is a small settlement on the southern shore of Lake Lucerne, at the foot of the Bürgenstock, a steep, forested ridge that juts out into the lake, and it feels almost cut off from the rest of Switzerland. A narrow road follows the shore from Stansstad, squeezed between the rocks and the water, and ends here; beyond, the cliffs of the Bürgenstock drop straight into the lake. For most visitors, Kehrsiten is the place where the boat from Lucerne stops and the Bürgenstock funicular begins, climbing steeply through the forest to the resort on top, which has been welcoming guests since the late nineteenth century.

Along the shore at Kehrsiten, archaeologists have found the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, which UNESCO also counts in its group of Alpine lake villages. Like other such sites, they lie underwater or under the ground, invisible to visitors, but they show that people were drawn to this sheltered shore thousands of years ago.

The Bürgenstock itself is famous for its views over the lake to Lucerne, Pilatus and the Rigi, and for the Hammetschwand lift, an outdoor elevator built into the cliff, which rises over a hundred metres to a viewpoint at the top of the ridge. The cliff path to the lift, cut into the rock face, is spectacular. The resort, rebuilt in recent years, has hotels, restaurants and spas, popular with wealthy guests from around the world.

The road to Kehrsiten from Stansstad is narrow, with tight bends and sections where two cars can barely pass, so take it slowly, especially in summer when it is busy. The road up to the Bürgenstock from Stansstad is better, climbing in hairpins through the forest. The wider area of Nidwalden and Lucerne has excellent riding, from the lakeshore roads to the passes of central Switzerland. Kehrsiten itself has few services; Stansstad, about four kilometres away, and Horw, across the lake, have fuel and shops, and Lucerne has everything. A swim in the lake, followed by a coffee on the terrace at the boat station, is a pleasant way to spend an afternoon.
t.messel pit fossil site@49.9,8.8:
Forty-seven million years ago, in a warm, subtropical world, a deep volcanic lake lay where the forest near Messel now stands, a few kilometres northeast of Darmstadt. The lake's depths were starved of oxygen, and animals that fell or sank into it were preserved in fine layers of mud with extraordinary detail: not just skeletons, but skin, feathers, fur, the contents of stomachs and even the colours of beetles' wings. Over time the mud turned into oil shale, which was mined here from the nineteenth century until 1971. After mining ended, there were plans to turn the pit into a rubbish dump; scientists and local people fought the plan, and in 1995 the pit became Germany's first natural World Heritage site.

The finds are astonishing. There are early horses no bigger than a fox, with their last meals of leaves and grapes preserved; bats with their wing membranes intact; birds, crocodiles, turtles, insects and the primate known as Darwinius masonae, nicknamed Ida, unveiled in 2009 with great fanfare as a possible ancestor of humans, a claim most scientists later dismissed. Every year, excavations bring up new species. A visitor centre explains the science, and guided tours take visitors down into the pit itself, a deep, scarred hole surrounded by forest, where you can see the dark layers of shale.

The landscape around Messel is wooded and gently rolling, at the northern edge of the Odenwald and the southern edge of the Rhine-Main area, so it is a mix of forest, villages, suburbs and roads. The riding nearby is pleasant but not spectacular; the real riding starts in the Odenwald to the south, where roads like the Nibelungenstraße wind through hills, forests and villages, with many curves and popular biker cafes. Weekend traffic around Frankfurt and Darmstadt is heavy, and speed cameras are common.

Messel itself is a small village with basic shops; Roßdorf, about six kilometres away, and Dieburg have fuel and more services, and Darmstadt, with its Art Nouveau artists' colony on the Mathildenhöhe, also a World Heritage site, has everything. Try Handkäse mit Musik, a tangy sour-milk cheese with onions and vinegar, and a glass of Ebbelwoi, the local cider, in a traditional tavern.
t.fort site and civil settlement of worth@:
For a stretch of about fifty kilometres, the Roman frontier of Upper Germany did not need a wall at all. Between Großkrotzenburg and Miltenberg, the Main river itself served as the border, and the Romans lined its western bank with forts and watchtowers to watch over the water and the forested hills of the Spessart on the other side. Wörth am Main had one of these forts, with a civil settlement where soldiers' families, traders and craftsmen lived. Very little remains above ground, but this wet frontier is inscribed as part of the Upper German Limes, and standing on the riverbank you can see why the Romans thought the river was enough.

Wörth is a small, attractive town of about five thousand people, with half-timbered houses and a riverside promenade. It has a museum of shipping and shipbuilding, a reminder that the Main has long been a busy waterway, with barges carrying sand, stone and timber. The red sandstone of the region, quarried along the river, was used to build much of the town, as well as churches and castles far and wide.

Across the river and up the valley, Klingenberg is known for its red wines grown on steep terraces above the town, some of the best Spätburgunder in Franconia, and Miltenberg, a little further upstream, is one of the most beautiful small towns in Germany, with a market square of half-timbered houses and a castle above. Erlenbach am Main, right next door, is the nearest larger town, with fuel and shops.

The riding here is excellent. The Main valley road follows the river through vineyards, forests and towns, with gentle curves and lovely views, though it can be busy at weekends. On either side, the Spessart and the Odenwald offer some of the best riding in central Germany: quiet roads through dense forests, climbing and descending through small villages, with plenty of curves. Watch for cyclists, deer at dusk and speed cameras. In autumn, when the forests turn gold and the grape harvest is in full swing, the region is at its most beautiful. Try Franconian wine served in its traditional round bottle, the Bocksbeutel, and local sausages and roasts in a riverside inn.
t.murrhardt civil settlement northern part:
Murrhardt lies in the valley of the Murr, deep in the Swabian-Franconian Forest northeast of Stuttgart, a hilly, densely wooded region of streams, mills and small villages that feels a long way from the industrial heartland just to the west. The Romans built a fort here on the Limes, the frontier that ran through these forests from north to south, and a civil settlement grew up around it. The northern part of that settlement lies under parts of the modern town, and while there is little to see, the town's museum displays Roman finds, and the frontier through these woods is protected by its World Heritage status.

The Middle Ages left a stronger mark. A Benedictine monastery was founded here in the ninth century, and the Walterichskirche, on a hill above the town, is named after Walterich, the founder of the monastery, whose grave became a place of pilgrimage. The tiny Romanesque Walterich chapel, attached to the monastery church, is a jewel of twelfth-century stone carving. Murrhardt is also known for its old town and the many mills along the river.

The Swabian-Franconian Forest is a nature park, with deep valleys, sandstone cliffs, waterfalls and lakes such as the Ebnisee, a popular spot for swimming and walking. The forest is mostly spruce and beech, with clearings of meadows and farms, and the villages have half-timbered houses and old inns. The riding here is excellent: winding roads through the forest, up and down the valleys, with little traffic outside the weekends and plenty of curves. The roads around Murrhardt, Welzheim, Kaisersbach and the Ebnisee are particularly popular with riders. Watch for cyclists, walkers, deer and wet leaves in autumn.

Murrhardt has filling stations, bakeries and inns, everything a rider needs. Sulzbach an der Murr and Kaisersbach are smaller villages nearby. Welzheim, to the south, also had a Roman fort, with a reconstructed gate. Swabian food is hearty and delicious: try Maultaschen, large pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, Käsespätzle, cheese noodles with fried onions, and a glass of Trollinger, the light red wine of Württemberg. In autumn, the forest roads are at their most beautiful.
t.takashima coal mine hashima coal mine@32:
From the sea, Hashima looks like a battleship: a small rocky island off Nagasaki surrounded by high concrete walls, crowded with tall, empty apartment blocks. The Japanese call it Gunkanjima, battleship island, and it is the most famous ruin of Japan's industrial age. Mitsubishi mined coal here from undersea seams from the late nineteenth century, and as the mine grew the island was extended with land reclaimed from the sea and built up with concrete housing, schools, a hospital and shops. At its peak it was one of the most densely populated places on Earth. When the mine closed in 1974, everyone left within weeks, and the island has been slowly crumbling ever since.

Takashima, the larger island nearby, was where it all started. In 1869 the Scottish merchant Thomas Glover, working with the Saga domain, introduced Western steam-powered mining technology here, one of the first in Japan. Both islands are part of the World Heritage site of the Meiji industrial revolution, and both carry a darker history too: during the war, Korean and Chinese labourers were brought in to work in the mines under harsh conditions, and Japan has committed to telling that part of the story as well.

You cannot ride to the islands, of course. Tour boats leave from Nagasaki harbour, and landings on Hashima depend on the weather, often cancelled when the sea is rough. But the ride along the Nagasaki Peninsula is a fine consolation. The coast road heads south from the city towards Nomozaki, winding along the shore with views out to Hashima and the scattered islands, and there is a small museum and viewpoint on the cape. North of Nagasaki, the Sotome coast offers another beautiful road, with sunset views over the East China Sea and the village where the novelist Shusaku Endo set Silence, his book about the persecuted Christians.

Nagasaki is a big city with fuel, accommodation and everything else. It is a steep, complex place, built around a deep harbour, so careful navigation pays. Try champon, a noodle soup loaded with seafood and vegetables that was invented here for Chinese students, and visit the Peace Park and the atomic bomb museum, a sobering and essential stop.
t.winkel@47.3,8.6:
Under the calm surface of Lake Zurich, just off the shore at Erlenbach, lie the remains of villages that people built here more than five thousand years ago. The site called Winkel is one of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, a UNESCO site of more than a hundred settlements, and here, as elsewhere on the lake, archaeologists diving in the shallow water have found wooden piles, pottery, tools and food remains preserved in the mud. There is nothing to see from the shore, only the water and the reeds, but it is fascinating to think that the people who farmed and fished here in the Neolithic chose the same sunny slope that, thousands of years later, would become known as the Gold Coast.

The eastern shore of Lake Zurich, between Zurich and Rapperswil, gets its nickname from the evening sun that shines on it and, many would say, from the wealth of those who live there. Villages like Küsnacht, Erlenbach, Herrliberg and Meilen climb from the lake up the slopes of the Pfannenstiel, with vineyards, orchards and villas, and the views across the water to the Albis and the Alps on a clear day are wonderful. In summer, the lake is warm enough for swimming, and there are public bathing places along the shore.

The Seestrasse along the lake is the obvious route, but it is busy, with low speed limits, many traffic lights and villages one after another, so it is better suited to a relaxed ride than a sporty one. The real fun is up the hill. The roads that climb from the lake up to the Pfannenstiel ridge and the Forch, through vineyards, orchards and woods, offer bends, views and much less traffic, and from the ridge you can continue towards the Zürcher Oberland and the hills of the Tösstal. Swiss traffic rules are strictly enforced, with speed cameras everywhere and very high fines, so keep an eye on the speed. A vignette is required for motorways.

Erlenbach has a few cafés and shops, and Herrliberg and Küsnacht have fuel. There are restaurants with lake views along the shore, and up on the Pfannenstiel, inns with terraces serve hearty Swiss food, such as rösti and sausages. A boat trip on the lake, with the bike parked for an afternoon, is a pleasant way to enjoy the view from the water.
t.halbinsel@47.2,8.1:
At the northern tip of Lake Sempach, near the little town of Sursee in the canton of Lucerne, a small peninsula pushes into the water, and on and around it lie the remains of prehistoric lakeside settlements, part of the World Heritage site of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps. Nothing remains visible above ground, but under the water and in the wet soil of the shore, piles and objects have survived for thousands of years, telling the story of farmers and fishermen who lived here long before the Romans. Today, the shore is a quiet area of reeds, meadows and paths, popular with walkers and cyclists.

Lake Sempach is best known in Swiss history for the battle of 1386, when the troops of the Swiss Confederation defeated the army of Duke Leopold III of Austria near the town of Sempach, at the southern end of the lake. According to legend, the battle was won thanks to the sacrifice of Arnold von Winkelried, who threw himself onto the enemy lances to open a breach in their ranks. A chapel and a monument mark the site. The town of Sempach is also home to the Swiss Ornithological Institute, the Vogelwarte, with an interesting visitor centre, and the lake is a good place for watching birds.

Sursee itself is a charming small town with a well-preserved old centre, a handsome late Gothic town hall, and a few old gates and houses. The countryside around is the gentle hill country of the Lucerne plateau, with farms, orchards and woods, and the roads are winding and pleasant, with views of the Alps on clear days. To the south-west, the Napf area offers steeper, twistier roads through narrow valleys and over ridges, and to the south, Lucerne and Lake Lucerne open the way into the mountains, including the Bürgenstock, a cliff-top resort above the lake reached by a narrow road from Stansstad with views over Kehrsiten and the water. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, and cameras are common.

Sursee has fuel, shops, restaurants and a railway station. In the old town, cafés and inns offer local dishes, such as the Luzerner Chügelipastete, a puff pastry filled with veal and mushrooms in cream sauce, a speciality of the region. On a hot day, a swim in Lake Sempach is a pleasant way to end the ride.
t.valli di lodano@46.3,8.7:
Halfway up the Maggia valley in Ticino, a narrow side valley climbs steeply west from the village of Lodano into a forest that has been left almost untouched for decades. The Valli di Lodano, together with the neighbouring valleys of Busai and Soladino, form a forest reserve in which beech trees grow from the valley floor up to the tree line, and in 2021 they were added to the World Heritage site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of Europe, a series of forests spread across eighteen countries. Walking up into the reserve, you pass through old chestnut groves, then into the beech forest, with moss-covered boulders, streams and the sound of falling water everywhere.

The Maggia valley is one of the most beautiful in southern Switzerland. The river flows over smooth granite slabs and boulders, forming pools of green and turquoise water, and the villages, such as Lodano, Maggia and Cevio, are built of grey stone, with stone roofs, narrow lanes and small churches, some with frescoes. Higher up, the Val Bavona is even more remarkable, with hamlets of stone houses squeezed between huge boulders that fell from the mountains, and no mains electricity. The river is tempting in summer, but beware: water levels can rise suddenly when hydroelectric dams upstream release water or after storms in the mountains, and every year there are accidents.

The road up the Maggia valley from Locarno and Ponte Brolla is a pleasant ride, with smooth surfaces and gentle curves along the river in the lower part, and narrower, steeper sections as you climb towards Bignasco and the side valleys. Above Bignasco, roads lead up to Fusio and the Lago del Sambuco, and into the Val Bavona, with hairpins and narrow passages. Traffic is light during the week but can be busy at weekends in summer, with cyclists and campers. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced.

Losone, near Locarno, and the village of Cevio have fuel and shops, and the larger villages of the valley have grotti, traditional restaurants with stone tables in the shade of chestnut trees, where you can enjoy polenta, cold meats, cheese and a glass of Merlot from Ticino. On a hot summer day, a dip in one of the river pools, in a safe place and with care, is irresistible.
t.le cret de chatillon@45.9,6.2:
The Crêt de Châtillon is the summit of the Semnoz, the long wooded mountain that rises above the western shore of Lake Annecy, and from the top, at around 1,700 metres, the view on a clear day is one of the finest in the French Alps: the whole lake below, the Bauges and the Aravis around, and, to the east, Mont Blanc in all its glory. Sites with names like Châtillon and Les Mongets along this shore preserve the remains of villages built on the edge of the lake thousands of years ago.

Lake Annecy is often said to be one of the cleanest lakes in Europe, thanks to a sewage system built around it in the 1960s, and the water is a startling turquoise. In summer, it is warm enough for swimming, and the beaches along the shore are busy. Annecy, at the northern end, is a beautiful old town with canals, flowers and the island prison of the Palais de l'Isle.

For riders, the Semnoz is the attraction. The road up from Annecy or from Leschaux climbs through forest to the open summit, a climb sometimes used by the Tour de France, with good surfaces and steady gradients, and the descent towards Leschaux and the Bauges offers more bends and views. On the other side of the lake, the Col de la Forclaz de Montmin climbs steeply from the lakeside, with a famous viewpoint over the water, popular with paragliders. Around the lake, the roads can be very busy in summer, with cars, cyclists and campervans, so the early morning is the best time to ride.

Saint-Jorioz and Sevrier have fuel, shops and restaurants, and there are many lakeside cafés where you can stop for a drink. Try a tartiflette, the Savoyard dish of potatoes, bacon and reblochon cheese, or fresh lake fish, such as féra, the local whitefish, served with butter. At the summit of the Semnoz, there are a few restaurants and an alpine garden, but the weather can change quickly, so bring warm clothes.
t.insel werd@47.7,8.9:
Where the Rhine leaves Lake Constance at Stein am Rhein, a group of small islands sits in the river, connected to the shore by a wooden footbridge, and on the largest, Werd, stands a small chapel surrounded by trees and water. It was here, in 759, that Saint Otmar, the first abbot of St Gallen, died in exile after falling foul of powerful local nobles, and the island has been a place of pilgrimage ever since. Long before Otmar, people lived here too: the islands and the surrounding shores are among the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, a World Heritage site, and excavations have found traces of settlements from the Neolithic onwards.

Stein am Rhein, just across the water, is one of the most beautiful small towns in Switzerland. Its main square is lined with medieval houses whose façades are covered with colourful paintings from the sixteenth century, showing biblical scenes, historical events and allegories. The former monastery of St George, on the riverbank, is a well-preserved medieval complex, and on the hill above the town, the castle of Hohenklingen offers views over the Rhine, the Untersee and the hills of the Hegau in Germany, with their old volcanic peaks.

The roads around Stein am Rhein cross the border constantly, as the town sits on a narrow strip of Swiss land surrounded by Germany. To the west, the road along the Rhine towards Diessenhofen and Schaffhausen follows the river through vineyards and woods, and to the north, the roads of the Hegau climb towards the volcanic hills, with the castle ruins of Hohentwiel near Singen standing out on the horizon. The road along the Untersee towards Konstanz passes through charming villages, with views across the water to the island of Reichenau. Note that Swiss and German traffic rules differ, and fuel is often cheaper on the German side.

Stein am Rhein has cafés, restaurants and shops, and fuel is available in the nearby villages and in Rielasingen-Worblingen across the border in Germany. Try the local fish, such as perch or whitefish from the lake, and a glass of white wine from the vineyards of the region. On a summer evening, a stroll along the Rhine and across the footbridge to Werd, with the swans gliding on the river, is a perfect end to the day.
t.chateau de sasso corbaro@46.2,9.0:
Bellinzona sits at the point where the valleys of the southern Alps converge before opening towards Lake Maggiore and Italy, and whoever held it controlled the routes over the Gotthard, the Lukmanier and the San Bernardino passes. In the fifteenth century the Dukes of Milan built a formidable system of defences here: three castles and a wall that ran across the whole valley floor. Castelgrande, on a rocky hill above the old town, Montebello, on the slope above it, and Sasso Corbaro, highest of all on a wooded spur, together form a World Heritage site. Sasso Corbaro was built in 1479, in a matter of months, after the Swiss Confederates defeated the Milanese at the Battle of Giornico, a short way up the Leventina valley, and the Duke wanted to plug the gap in his defences.

The castle is a compact square fortress with a massive tower, and from its walls the view over Bellinzona, the Ticino valley and the mountains is superb. Inside, there are exhibitions and a small restaurant. Down in the town, the Saturday market fills the old streets with stalls selling cheese, bread, sausages and vegetables, and the atmosphere is distinctly Italian.

For motorcyclists, Bellinzona is a crossroads of great rides. To the north, the road up the Leventina leads to the Gotthard Pass, including the old cobbled Tremola road with its many hairpins, and to the north-east, the San Bernardino pass road climbs through the Mesolcina valley. To the west, the Centovalli and the Maggia valley lie beyond Locarno, and to the south, the road over the Monte Ceneri pass leads to Lugano and on to Monte San Giorgio, a World Heritage site famous for its fossils of marine reptiles. High passes such as the Gotthard and San Bernardino are closed in winter, usually from late autumn until late spring. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, and a vignette is required for motorways.

Bellinzona has fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants. Try risotto, the classic dish of Ticino, often made with saffron or mushrooms, and the polenta and braised meat served in the grotti, the rustic restaurants of the region, with a glass of Ticino Merlot. The road up to Sasso Corbaro is narrow and steep, but there is parking near the castle.
t.secteur des mongets@45.9,6.2:
Sevrier, on the western shore of Lake Annecy, is home to an unusual industry: bells. The Paccard foundry, which has been casting bells since the late eighteenth century and moved to Sevrier in the 1980s, has made bells for churches and carillons all over the world, and its museum explains how they are designed, cast and tuned. It is a curious contrast to the quiet lakeshore just below the village, where the Secteur des Mongets marks the remains of a prehistoric village built on the edge of the lake, now under water. It is one of the sites included in the World Heritage listing of the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps, and divers have found wooden piles, pottery and tools in the lake bed.

The western shore of the lake is gentler than the eastern one, with a cycle path running along the old railway line, beaches, campsites and reed beds, and views across the water to the steep cliffs of the Dents de Lanfon and the Tournette, the highest mountain around the lake. The lake is known for its clear, turquoise water and is a popular place for swimming, sailing and paddleboarding in summer. In winter, the shore is quiet, with mist often hanging over the water.

From Geneva, the ride to Annecy takes you through the Genevois countryside and over the mountains, and an alternative to the motorway is the road through Cruseilles, which crosses the deep gorge of Les Usses on the Pont de la Caille, a suspension bridge from the nineteenth century that stands next to the newer road bridge. Around the lake, the road along the western shore through Sevrier and Saint-Jorioz is often busy, especially in summer, but the roads that climb into the hills, towards the Semnoz or the Col de Leschaux and the Bauges, are much more rewarding, with forests, meadows and fine views. The eastern shore, through Menthon-Saint-Bernard and Talloires, is narrower and more winding.

Saint-Jorioz, about two and a half kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Sevrier has cafés and shops. Try fondue or raclette, made with local cheeses, in one of the restaurants around the lake, and a glass of white wine from Savoie. If the weather is warm, a swim from one of the public beaches is the best way to cool down after a ride.
t.watchtowers wp 9 2 to 9 13@49.3,9.5:
Götz von Berlichingen, the knight with the iron hand, was born at Jagsthausen castle in about 1480, and he would probably be amused to know that he is best remembered today for a rude phrase. In Goethe's play about him, Götz tells an imperial messenger exactly what the emperor can do, a line that every German knows. The castle still stands in the village, now a hotel, and in summer the Burgfestspiele, an open-air theatre festival, stages the play in the castle courtyard. Long before Götz, the Romans were here too: a fort stood at Jagsthausen on the line of the Upper Germanic Limes, and in the hills around, a series of watchtowers, numbered by archaeologists as WP 9/2 to 9/13, kept watch along the frontier.

The Limes in this region is remarkable for one thing: between Walldürn and Welzheim, it ran in an almost perfectly straight line for about eighty kilometres, regardless of hills, valleys and rivers, a feat of Roman surveying that still astonishes. The towers were placed so that they could see each other and pass signals, and today, the sites are mostly marked by small mounds, foundations or reconstructions in the woods and fields. The World Heritage site includes the whole line from the Rhine to the Danube.

The landscape is the Hohenlohe region, a plateau of fields, woods and small villages cut by the deep, winding valleys of the Jagst and the Kocher. The roads along the valleys follow the rivers in long, gentle curves past mills, castles and vineyards, and the roads that climb out of the valleys onto the plateau offer short, twisty sections with good surfaces. It is a popular area with motorcyclists, especially at weekends, but traffic is generally light. The towns of Schöntal, with its baroque monastery, and Langenburg, with its castle above the Jagst, are well worth a detour.

Forchtenberg, about six kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Jagsthausen has a few inns and cafés. The food of Hohenlohe is hearty: try Maultaschen, large stuffed pasta squares, Schäufele, roast pork shoulder, and Spätzle with plenty of sauce, washed down with a local beer or a glass of wine from the Kocher valley.
t.building remains south of gotzingen@49.5:
Between the Odenwald and the Tauber country lies the Bauland, a high, open plateau of limestone, cornfields and small villages that most travellers cross without slowing down. Just south of Götzingen, among fields and woodland edges between Buchen and Osterburken, are the remains of a Roman building on the line of the Upper Germanic Limes. It is not a grand ruin, more a footprint in the ground, but it belongs to one of the best documented stretches of the frontier, the section that runs straight as a ruler through this part of northern Baden-Württemberg.

Osterburken, six kilometres away, is the place to put it in context. The town had a substantial Roman fort with a later annexe, and its Roman museum displays finds from the frontier and the military bath house, preserved under a protective hall. The famous Mithras relief found at Osterburken in the nineteenth century, one of the most complete ever unearthed, now lives in the state museum in Karlsruhe, but the town makes good use of its Roman past. Buchen, a bit further, has a compact old centre with a gate tower and a strong Carnival tradition.

The landscape tells its own story. This is Grünkern country: spelt harvested half ripe and dried over beech smoke, a local speciality you will find in soups and patties in village inns. The fields roll in long waves, there are small chapels and wayside crosses at junctions, and in early summer the poppies and cornflowers run along the verges. Red kites hang over the stubble after harvest.

On a bike, the Bauland rewards anyone who likes flowing, empty B-roads. The roads between Seckach, Osterburken and Buchen are smooth and open, with long sighted bends over gentle crests where the next village church tower guides you in. Wind can be a factor on the exposed plateau, and in autumn early morning fog lies in the hollows until late, which also makes for lovely light once it lifts. Agricultural traffic and mud near field entrances are the main hazards. The Kirnau and Seckach valleys drop off the plateau with tighter corners for some variety.

For fuel, coffee and food go to Osterburken or Buchen; both are proper small towns with filling stations and bakeries. Seckach is a little closer and has the basics. There is nothing at the remains themselves, so treat it as a short walk from the road, a moment to look across the plateau and picture the line of towers and palisade running over the horizon.
t.grand ventron@48.0,6.9:
At around 1,200 metres, the Grand Ventron is one of the high rounded summits on the main crest of the southern Vosges, where Lorraine meets Alsace. To the west lie the valleys of La Bresse and Ventron; to the east the ground falls steeply into the Thur valley above Kruth. The top is open, grassy and wind combed, a classic Vosges hautes-chaumes landscape of summer pastures, bilberry and granite boulders, with beech and fir forest closing in below. On a clear day the view runs across the Alsace plain to the Black Forest, and on rare exceptional days the Alps show as a pale line far to the south.

The road up is the experience. From the Ventron side a narrow lane climbs past the small ski area of the Ermitage du Frère Joseph and on through forest to the high ground; from Alsace the climb to the Col d'Oderen links in from the Thur valley. Expect single track tarmac in places, broken edges, gravel on the bends after rain, and cattle or walkers round blind corners. It is a ride for patience and low gears, not speed, and it is at its best on a weekday morning in June or September. Snow can linger up here well into spring, and the upper lanes are not cleared in winter.

The high farms of the Vosges have an old tradition of the ferme-auberge, summer farm inns serving the repas marcaire: meat pie, smoked pork, potatoes cooked with onions and bacon, Munster cheese and a slice of tart. There has long been one near the summit of the Grand Ventron, and in season it is the reason many riders make the climb; check before relying on it, as farm inns keep their own hours. The Munster cheese itself comes from these pastures.

Below the crest, the Lac de Kruth-Wildenstein fills the head of the Thur valley, with the ruined Wildenstein castle on its rock. The valley road toward Thann and Mulhouse is a pleasant fast ride with good surfaces. Westward, La Bresse is the main town, a resort of about five thousand people with fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and it is the safest bet for a fill. Kruth and Oderen on the Alsace side are smaller villages. All of this sits inside the Ballons des Vosges regional nature park, so watch for chamois on the steeper slopes and keep noise down near the farms.
t.fort site and civil settlement of welzhe:
Welzheim had not one but two Roman forts, and that alone tells you how seriously the frontier was taken in the Swabian Forest. The larger west fort held a cavalry unit, while the smaller east fort, now an archaeological park on the edge of town, housed an auxiliary infantry detachment. At the east fort the west gate has been rebuilt to its full height, and standing in front of it you get a rare sense of scale that low foundations never give. Around both forts lay the civil settlement, the vicus, with workshops, taverns and homes.

The town sits on the high ground of the Welzheimer Wald, part of the Swabian-Franconian Forest east of Stuttgart. Just north of here the Upper Germanic Limes runs in an astonishingly straight line, roughly eighty kilometres from near Walldürn down to the Haghof near Welzheim, ignoring hills and valleys as if drawn with a ruler. Surveyors still argue over how the Romans achieved it. South of Welzheim the frontier turned east along the line of the Raetian Limes.

This is lovely riding country, and the locals know it. The roads around Welzheim twist through spruce and beech forest, drop into narrow valleys like the Wieslauftal and climb back up in tight sequences of bends, with sawmills, old mills and small hamlets along the way. Surfaces are generally decent, but shaded corners stay damp and leaves pile up in autumn. On sunny weekends there are many bikes and plenty of cyclists, and noise complaints have led to restrictions on some routes in the region, so ride with some courtesy.

The Schwäbische Waldbahn, a restored railway line from Schorndorf up to Welzheim, crosses tall viaducts in the Wieslauf valley, and when steam specials run you may see a plume of smoke drifting over the trees. The Laufenmühle on the valley floor is a well known stop for walkers and riders alike. Further north, Murrhardt has its own Roman fort site and a lovely old monastery church.

Welzheim, with around eleven thousand people, is right next to the fort and has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and a few restaurants. Alfdorf and Kaisersbach are smaller villages nearby. The east fort park is open ground with information boards and a short walk from the town centre, so leave the bike in town and stroll over.
t.sacro monte di s maria assunta di serral:
On a wooded hill above the vineyards of the Monferrato, between Casale and Asti, stands the Sacro Monte di Crea, one of the nine Sacred Mountains of Piedmont and Lombardy that are listed together as a World Heritage Site. The sanctuary of Santa Maria Assunta, a pilgrimage church, sits on the slope, and above it a path climbs through the woods past a series of chapels, each with terracotta statues and painted scenes from the life of the Virgin, to the Chapel of Paradise at the summit, with a crowd of figures depicting her coronation.

The Monferrato is a landscape of rolling hills, vineyards, castles and villages, known for its wines: Barbera, Grignolino and Freisa, and for truffles in autumn. Moncalvo, a few kilometres away, is often called the smallest town in Italy to hold the formal title of città, and it has a well known truffle fair in autumn. Casale Monferrato, on the Po, is the historic capital of the area.

The riding here is wonderful. The roads twist through the hills, climbing and descending through vineyards, with views across the Monferrato and on clear days to the Alps in the distance. Surfaces are generally good, traffic is light outside the towns, and there are plenty of places to stop for coffee or a meal. Autumn is the best time, when the vineyards turn gold and red, and the truffle season begins.

The Sacred Mountains were born in the years after the Council of Trent, when the Church wanted pilgrims to experience the stories of faith almost physically, walking from scene to scene as if on a real path to Jerusalem. Crea, with its oak and chestnut woods, is the highest point in this part of the Monferrato, and the summit chapel has a view over a sea of hills toward the rice fields of the Po plain. In spring the slopes are full of birdsong and wildflowers, and the whole hill is a natural park.

Fuel is available in Moncalvo and in Trino, eleven kilometres away, and Casale Monferrato has everything. The restaurants of the Monferrato serve excellent local food, including agnolotti, bagna cauda and bollito misto, and the wines are superb. The sanctuary of Crea has a restaurant and a café, and parking is available near the church.
t.lac d aiguebelette@45.5,5.8:
Motorboats are banned on the Lac d'Aiguebelette, and on a calm summer morning you notice the difference straight away: rowers sliding across water so still it mirrors the wooded slopes above, swimmers heading out from small beaches, and no engine noise beyond the occasional car on the shore road. The lake, in Savoie just west of Chambéry, is one of the largest natural lakes in France, and its clean water is among the warmest of the alpine lakes in summer. It hosted the World Rowing Championships in 2015.

The lake lies at the foot of the Montagne de l'Épine, a limestone ridge that separates it from Chambéry, and the A43 motorway passes beneath through a tunnel. The old road over the Col de l'Épine, from Chambéry, climbs in tight bends through forest to the pass and then drops toward the lake, with superb views across the water and the hills to the west. The Col du Mont du Chat, further north, is another climb, steep and narrow, with views over the Lac du Bourget.

The shore road around the lake is narrow and busy in summer, with cyclists, walkers and parking cars, so take it slowly. The surrounding country of the Avant-Pays Savoyard is a gentle landscape of hills, villages and farms, with quiet roads and pleasant views. Spring and autumn are lovely, when the crowds are gone and the light is soft.

The lake has two islands, one with the ruins of a chapel, and the shores are partly protected as a nature reserve, home to birds and plants. Swimming is possible at several beaches, some with an entrance fee in summer. Fuel and services are available in Cognin, seven kilometres away, and Chambéry, a little further, has everything. Le Pont-de-Beauvoisin, to the west, is another option. Lakeside restaurants serve fish from the lake, including perch, and Savoyard dishes such as tartiflette.
t.ono village in sotome@32.9,129.7:
For more than two centuries Christianity was banned in Japan, and in the villages along the Sotome coast north of Nagasaki, communities practised their faith in secret, disguising prayers as Buddhist chants and hiding images of the Virgin as the bodhisattva Kannon. These were the Hidden Christians, the Kakure Kirishitan, and their villages, including Ono, are part of the World Heritage listing of Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region, inscribed in 2018. At Ono the small Ono church, built by the French missionary Marc Marie de Rotz in the late nineteenth century after the ban was lifted, has thick walls built in a local technique of stones bound with mortar, known as de Rotz walls.

Father de Rotz did much more than build churches. He set up workshops to teach local women to make bread, macaroni and textiles, and a museum in Sotome tells his story. The novelist Shusaku Endo set his novel Silence in this area, and a memorial museum dedicated to him stands on the coast with views over the sea.

The Sotome coast faces west over the East China Sea, with steep hills, terraced fields and fishing villages, and the sunsets are famous. National Route 202 runs along the coast from Nagasaki, with curves, views and light traffic, a lovely ride. The hills behind are covered with forest and cut by narrow roads.

The weather here is mild, with hot, humid summers and the rainy season in June and July; typhoons can hit in late summer and autumn. Spring and autumn are the best times to ride. Japanese roads are well maintained, traffic is orderly, and speed limits are low.

Fuel is available along Route 202 and in Nagasaki, twenty two kilometres away, and Togitsu and Obita are nearer towns. Local food includes de Rotz's somen noodles, still made in the area, and fresh fish. The Ono church is small and open on some days only, so check before visiting.
t.sipplingen osthafen@47.8,9.1:
At Sipplingen the north shore of Lake Constance changes character. The Überlinger See, the long north-western arm of the lake, is hemmed in here by steep molasse cliffs and wooded slopes rising to the Sipplinger Berg, and the village sits on a narrow strip between the hill and the water. Below the surface off the eastern harbour lie the remains of prehistoric pile dwellings, villages of wooden houses built on stilts along the shore some five to six thousand years ago. They are part of the World Heritage site of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

You will not see much of the pile dwellings from the shore, as they are underwater and protected. To get a sense of them, visit the open-air museum at Unteruhldingen, a few kilometres east, where reconstructed houses stand in the water. The finds from Sipplingen, including pottery, tools and food remains, have helped archaeologists understand how people lived on the lake in the Neolithic and Bronze Age.

The riding around here is varied. The B31 along the north shore is busy and often congested, especially in summer, so it is better to take the smaller roads that climb into the hills behind the lake. From the heights above Sipplingen, you get fantastic views across the water to the Swiss Alps on a clear day. The roads are well-maintained, with plenty of curves and changes in elevation. In the hinterland, the Linzgau and Hegau regions offer quiet country roads through orchards, forests and farmland.

Lake Constance is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe, bordered by Germany, Switzerland and Austria. The Überlinger See is deep and clear, popular for swimming and sailing. The hills above Sipplingen are covered with orchards, and in spring the blossom is spectacular. In autumn, the vineyards turn gold and red, and the lake is often shrouded in mist in the morning.

Sipplingen is a small village with a few restaurants, a café and a beach. For fuel, head to Überlingen, about six kilometres away, a lovely old town with a promenade, Gothic minster and plenty of places to eat. Try local fish such as Felchen, a whitefish from the lake, often served fried or smoked, and wash it down with a glass of wine from the slopes above the shore.
t.inkwilersee insel@47.2,7.7:
You could ride past the Inkwilersee a dozen times without noticing it. It is a small, shallow lake tucked into a fold of farmland right on the line between the cantons of Bern and Solothurn, ringed with reeds and alders, with a tiny wooded island near its middle. That island is the reason for the label: beneath its trees and in the mud around it lie traces of prehistoric lakeside settlement, enough to earn the Inkwilersee a place among the Alpine pile-dwelling sites on the World Heritage list.

There is nothing to see of the old villages, so do not come expecting stilts and thatch. What you get is a quiet, slightly secret lake, the kind of place locals cycle to on a summer evening for a swim. Because it is shallow it warms up early in the season, and on a hot July afternoon the water feels more like a bath than a Swiss lake. Herons stalk the reed beds, coots fuss about near the shore, and in spring the frogs are loud enough to hear over an idling engine.

The riding is classic Swiss Mittelland: smooth, narrow country roads looping between farms, orchards and woods, with gentle rises and the long blue line of the Jura to the north. It is not dramatic, but it is relaxing, and there are plenty of ways to string together villages without touching the motorway. Watch your speed in the villages, where limits drop sharply and cameras are common, and keep an eye out for tractors and cyclists on the narrow lanes.

Within a few minutes are some good stops. Wangen an der Aare has a covered wooden bridge across the river and a compact little old town. Herzogenbuchsee is a market town with a handsome church on its hill. Further afield, Solothurn, the baroque city on the Aare, is one of the most beautiful small towns in the country and has a strange obsession with the number eleven, which shows up in its churches, fountains and clocks.

Herzogenbuchsee, about three and a half kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, cafés and shops. Subingen and Wangen also have the basics. There is a small parking area by the lake and a path around the shore that takes perhaps half an hour on foot, a good way to work the stiffness out of your legs before the next leg.
t.la chaux de fonds le locle@47.1,6.8:
At about a thousand metres up in the Jura, in a long, high valley where winter arrives early and leaves late, two towns spent two centuries making most of the world's watches. La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are strange, fascinating places: not pretty old towns, but industrial cities laid out on a grid, with long parallel streets of apartment blocks designed to let maximum light into workshops where generations of craftsmen assembled tiny gears by the window. Their urban planning, built entirely around one industry, is on the World Heritage list.

La Chaux-de-Fonds was rebuilt after a fire in 1794 according to a rational plan, and the result is a town that feels more like a small American city than a Swiss village. Le Corbusier was born here in 1887, and several of his early villas still stand on the hillside, including the Maison Blanche he designed for his parents. Louis Chevrolet, who co-founded the car company that still bears his name, was also born in La Chaux-de-Fonds. The International Museum of Horology is outstanding even for people who think they are not interested in watches.

The ride up is half the fun. From Neuchâtel the road climbs over the Vue des Alpes pass, at a little under 1,300 metres, with wide curves, good surface and, on a clear day, the entire chain of the Alps lined up across the horizon from Mont Blanc to the Bernese Oberland. On the other side you drop into the high valley with its dry stone walls, wood-pastures and spruce. North of Le Locle the land falls away to the Doubs, which forms the border with France, and the road to Les Brenets and the Saut du Doubs waterfall is a beautiful winding descent.

Le Locle has its own odd treasure: the underground mills of Col-des-Roches, where millers in the seventeenth century carved out caves to harness an underground river. The whole region also has a long and slightly furtive history with absinthe, which was banned in Switzerland for most of the twentieth century and distilled in secret in the Val-de-Travers next door.

Both towns have fuel, cafés, restaurants and hotels. Come prepared for weather: even in summer, the high Jura can be cool and wet, and in winter snow is reliable. The Neuchâtel wines from the lake shore below are worth sampling in the evening, once the bike is parked.
t.swiss alps jungfrau aletsch@46.5,8.0:
No road comes anywhere near. This is a landscape of ice, rock and sky, the first Alpine area to be listed as a World Heritage site, and the riding is all around it rather than through it.

What makes this region special for a rider is that you can circle it on some of the finest pass roads in Europe. From Innertkirchen the Grimsel climbs past granite slabs and dammed lakes to 2,164 metres. On the Valais side you drop to Gletsch and can take the Furka towards Andermatt, where the old Rhône glacier hotel stands by the hairpins. Further east, the Susten links the Bernese Oberland to Uri through tunnels and galleries, and the Nufenen runs south into Ticino. These roads are generally in excellent condition, with well-engineered hairpins, but they are busy in summer and closed from late autumn to late spring. Morning is the time to be on them, before the camper vans and tour buses.

The Aletsch glacier is the longest in the Alps, a smooth river of ice more than twenty kilometres long, striped with dark moraines. It has been shrinking fast, and the change over just a few decades is visible to anyone who compares old postcards. From the cable car stations above Fiesch, Bettmeralp and Riederalp you can look down on its great curve. On the north side, the famous trio of Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau looms over Grindelwald and Lauterbrunnen, and the railway to the Jungfraujoch climbs right through the Eiger.

The surrounding valleys are a mix of old wooden villages, steep meadows, waterfalls and larch forests. In autumn the larches turn gold, and the air in the high valleys has that clean smell of snow and stone. Above the Aletsch, the Aletsch forest holds some very old Arolla pines.

Practically, fuel is easy in the main valleys: Fiesch, Naters and Brig on the south side, Meiringen and Innertkirchen on the north. Switzerland requires a motorway vignette for motorway use, and the speed limits are strictly enforced, so leave your enthusiasm for the bends rather than the straights.
t.castel grande@46.2,9.0:
Coming down from the Gotthard or the San Bernardino, the Ticino valley narrows into a bottleneck at Bellinzona, and right in the middle of it, on a rocky hill above the old town, sits Castel Grande. Its two square towers and long crenellated walls are the oldest and largest of the three castles of Bellinzona, which together with the defensive wall across the valley make up a World Heritage site.

The site has been fortified since at least Roman times, but most of what you see dates from the fifteenth century, when the Dukes of Milan, first the Visconti and then the Sforza, made Bellinzona the northern bolt of their territory. Their enemies were the Swiss confederates pushing south over the Alps, and for decades the castles stood in the way. In the end the Swiss took the town in 1500 and kept it, which is why Ticino is Swiss today rather than Italian. The two smaller castles, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro, climb the hillside to the east, each higher than the last.

You can walk up to Castel Grande or take a lift that runs inside the rock from the old town, a pleasantly surreal entrance. At the top, the grassy courtyard is wide and calm, the walls offer views up and down the valley, and the small museum covers the history of the castle and the region. In the late afternoon, when the stone turns honey-coloured and the swifts scream around the towers, it is one of the most atmospheric places in Switzerland.

For riders, Bellinzona is a natural hub. The A2 motorway runs through, but the old cantonal road up the Leventina towards the Gotthard and the road up the Mesolcina towards the San Bernardino are more fun if you have the time. South, the roads lead to Lake Maggiore and Lake Lugano, and into the side valleys like the Valle Verzasca, with its emerald water and stone bridges. Summer can be hot in the valley, so plan your passes for the morning.

Bellinzona has plenty of fuel, restaurants and accommodation. The Saturday market in the old town is lively, with cheese, salami and local wines. Try a plate of polenta with brasato, or a glass of Ticino Merlot on a terrace below the castle walls.
t.stations de concise@46.8,6.7:
In the late 1990s, engineers working on a new stretch of railway along the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel ran into something unexpected near the village of Concise: layer upon layer of prehistoric settlement, preserved in the waterlogged ground. Over several years, archaeologists uncovered thousands of wooden piles, pottery, tools and food remains from villages that had been built and rebuilt on the shore over many centuries in the Neolithic and Bronze Age. The site is now part of the World Heritage list of pile dwellings around the Alps, though there is little to see above ground today.

What you can see is the lake, long and silvery, with the Jura rising steeply behind the shore and the plain of the Broye and the Alps on the far side. The road along the northern shore between Yverdon and Neuchâtel passes through Concise, Saint-Aubin and Bevaix, with vineyards climbing the slopes above. It is a gentle, scenic route with lake views most of the way, though traffic can be heavy, especially around the towns. For more interesting riding, head up into the Jura: the roads to Mauborget, Provence and Sainte-Croix climb through forest and pasture with fine views back over the lake.

The area has a rich history beyond the prehistoric. Just down the shore, Grandson is famous for its castle and for the battle of 1476, when the Swiss confederates defeated Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, capturing a vast treasure that is still partly on display in Swiss museums. Yverdon-les-Bains, at the southern end of the lake, has been a spa since Roman times and was home to the educational reformer Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi, who ran a famous school in the castle.

The lake and its shores are rich in birdlife, especially in the reed beds and marshes. The vineyards of the Bonvillars and Neuchâtel appellations produce crisp white wines from Chasselas and some fine Pinot Noir. In spring and autumn, the light on the lake can be stunning, with mist rising off the water in the morning.

Yverdon-les-Bains, about nine kilometres away, has fuel, food and accommodation. Grandson and Saint-Aubin are smaller but have basic services. Concise itself has a small station and a few cafés, a quiet place for a pause by the water.
t.rempart du bourg@46.2,9.0:
Most people who stop in Bellinzona look up at the castles. Spend a little time at street level instead and you will find the other half of the story: the walls of the old borgo, the medieval town that grew up beneath Castel Grande. Stretches of these ramparts still enclose the old centre, linking the castles to each other and to the great Murata, the wall that once ran right across the floor of the Ticino valley to the river, so that nothing could pass north or south without the Duke of Milan's permission.

Inside the walls, Bellinzona feels thoroughly Italian. The Piazza Collegiata is dominated by the Renaissance church of Saints Peter and Stephen, its pale façade facing a square of arcades and cafés. Narrow streets lead to the Piazza Nosetto and the town hall, whose courtyard is painted with frescoes of old Bellinzona. In February the whole town goes slightly mad for Rabadan, one of the biggest carnivals in Switzerland, with parades, masks, music and risotto served in the streets.

For a rider, the walls are a good reminder of why this town matters. Bellinzona sits where the routes from two of the great Alpine passes come together, the Gotthard via the Leventina and the San Bernardino via the Mesolcina, before carrying on towards Lugano, Locarno and Milan. That geography makes the town a natural pause on almost any tour through southern Switzerland. The roads out of town are a mix: motorway and busy main roads in the valley, but within minutes you can be climbing into the hills on narrow, twisting lanes with stone villages and chestnut forests.

Look around at the hillsides: chestnut trees everywhere, the old staple food of these valleys, ground into flour in hard times. In autumn the woods are full of people gathering them, and you can buy roasted chestnuts from street vendors. Higher up, the forests turn to larch and pine, and the side valleys are full of waterfalls and granite.

Bellinzona has all the services you could want: fuel, restaurants, hotels and mechanics. Park outside the old town and walk in, since the centre has restricted traffic. Find a seat in the Piazza Collegiata, order a coffee or a glass of Merlot, and watch the town go by under the walls that once decided who could cross the Alps.
t.corcelettes les violes@46.8,6.7:
Corcelettes is a little lakeside hamlet just north of Grandson, near the southern tip of Lake Neuchâtel, and Les Violes is the stretch of shallow shore where Bronze Age people built a village of wooden houses on piles, some three thousand years ago. The site was one of the first in the region to attract attention in the nineteenth century, when low water levels after the correction of the Jura waters exposed forests of ancient posts in the mud. It is now listed among the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

Today it is a quiet, reedy shore with a few houses, a campsite and paths along the water. The real highlight in this corner is Grandson, a short ride up the road, with its heavy, five-towered castle standing right above the lake. It was here in 1476 that Charles the Bold of Burgundy hanged the Swiss garrison, only to be routed by the Confederates a few days later, abandoning his tents, artillery and treasure as he fled. Some of the loot, including tapestries and jewels, survives in Swiss museums.

The riding is gentle along the shore and becomes much more interesting as you head into the Jura. From Grandson, the road climbs steeply to Sainte-Croix, a town that made its fortune with music boxes and automata, and now has a museum full of them. Beyond lies the Col des Etroits and the Chasseron, with views over the lake and the Alps. The roads are winding and well-maintained, with some tight hairpins and steep gradients, and they are often less busy than the main routes.

On the opposite, south-eastern shore of the lake lies the Grande Cariçaie, the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland, a long ribbon of reed beds, marsh and woodland that is a haven for birds. From Corcelettes you can see it across the water, a soft green line against the hills of the Broye. In spring and autumn the area is busy with migrating birds, and in summer the lake is warm enough for a swim.

Grandson has fuel, restaurants and shops. Yverdon-les-Bains, about five kilometres away, is the main town of the area, with a thermal spa that is a good place to ease tired muscles after a long day in the saddle. The local Chasselas, crisp and mineral, pairs perfectly with perch fillets from the lake.
t.riesi@47.3,8.2:
Riesi is a stretch of shoreline at the northern end of the Hallwilersee, a long, narrow lake in the Aargau Seetal, between the villages of Seengen and Boniswil. It is a peaceful place of reeds, meadows and walking paths, and below the water and in the marshy ground lie the remains of prehistoric pile-dwelling settlements, part of the World Heritage list of such sites around the Alps.

The Hallwilersee is one of the cleaner and calmer lakes in the Swiss Mittelland, with a ring of villages, orchards and wooded hills around it. At its northern end, just outside Seengen, stands Schloss Hallwyl, one of the most beautiful moated castles in Switzerland, built on two islands in the stream that flows out of the lake. It was the seat of the Hallwyl family for centuries, and today it is a museum that brings their history to life, from medieval knights to nineteenth-century aristocrats.

The riding here is gentle and scenic. Roads run around both sides of the lake and into the surrounding hills, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. The routes towards the Lindenberg ridge, between the Seetal and the Freiamt, offer some nice curves and views of the Alps on clear days. This is farming country, so expect tractors, cyclists and the occasional herd of cows. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and villages often have traffic calming measures.

The lake is a nature reserve in parts, with reed beds that shelter birds such as great crested grebes, reed warblers and kingfishers. In summer, the water is warm enough for swimming, and there are several public bathing areas around the lake. Passenger boats cross between the villages in summer, a lazy way to see the shore from the water.

Seengen, about a kilometre away, is the nearest village with basic services, including a petrol station and restaurants. Villmergen, about five kilometres away, is the nearest town with more facilities. Lenzburg, with its imposing castle on a hill, is also nearby and worth a visit. Try a slice of Aargauer Rüeblitorte, a moist carrot cake that is a regional specialty, or local fish from the lake.
t.watchtowers wp 9 132 to 12 38 including:
Lorch is where two Roman frontiers shook hands. The Upper Germanic Limes, a line of wooden palisade and watchtowers running down from the Rhine, met the Raetian Limes, a stone wall stretching east towards the Danube, in the hills near this small town in the Rems valley. The watchtower numbers jump here from series 9, the end of the Upper Germanic stretch, to 12, the start of the Raetian, and the whole system is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

Lorch has more than Roman history. Above the town, on a hill, sits Kloster Lorch, a Benedictine monastery founded in the early twelfth century by the Staufer, the dynasty that produced Frederick Barbarossa and other emperors. The Staufer had their burial place here, and the monastery now houses a huge circular painting of the family's story. The Hohenstaufen hill, from which they took their name, rises as a perfect cone a short ride to the south-east, and from the top you can see far across the Swabian Alb.

The riding is very good. The Rems valley is busy, but the roads that climb north into the Schwäbischer Wald, the Swabian Forest, are narrow and twisting, with quick changes in direction, steep descents into stream valleys and long stretches through deep forest. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for damp patches and leaves in the shade. Traffic is light on weekdays, though weekends bring many fellow riders. South of the valley, the roads towards the Hohenstaufen and the edge of the Alb offer more open views.

The Swabian Forest is a landscape of deep, narrow valleys, clear streams and dense woodland, with old watermills and small villages. In spring the forest floor is covered with wild garlic and wood anemones, and in autumn the beech leaves turn gold. The area is also known for its fruit orchards, and in late summer the trees are heavy with apples and pears.

Lorch, about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Schwäbisch Gmünd, a few kilometres east, is a larger town with a fine old centre and a famous Gothic minster. Stop for Maultaschen, the Swabian pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, or a slice of plum cake if you are passing in late summer.
t.fort altheimer strasse@49.5,9.4:
Walldürn is a small town on the eastern edge of the Odenwald, where the hills of the forest give way to the open plateau of the Bauland, and the Roman frontier ran right through it. The Upper Germanic Limes followed a straight line here, and the town had a fort and a bathhouse, whose remains have been excavated and partly reconstructed. Fort Altheimer Strasse, named after the road where it was found, was one of the smaller installations along the line, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site.

Walldürn is better known today as a pilgrimage town. Since the Middle Ages, pilgrims have come to its basilica to venerate a relic known as the Holy Blood, connected with a legend of a priest who spilled consecrated wine onto a cloth that then showed an image of Christ. The main pilgrimage takes place in the weeks after Pentecost, when the town fills with processions and visitors. The basilica, a large baroque church, dominates the town centre.

The riding in this area is very good, especially in the Odenwald. The roads that wind through the forests and valleys between Walldürn, Amorbach, Miltenberg and the Neckar are narrow, twisting and often hilly, with excellent surfaces and little traffic outside weekends. The Main valley to the north and the Neckar valley to the south offer different landscapes, with vineyards, castles and old towns. In autumn, the Odenwald is particularly beautiful, with the forests turning gold and red.

The Odenwald is a low mountain range with dense forests of beech, oak and spruce, and many legends, including that of the Nibelungs, are set here. The Bauland to the east is a more open landscape of farmland and villages, with fields of grain and orchards. The area is known for its Grünkern, green spelt harvested before it is fully ripe and then dried over a fire, used in soups and patties.

Walldürn, about four and a half kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Buchen, a little further west, is a larger town with a charming old centre. Amorbach, to the north, has a beautiful abbey church with a famous organ. A bowl of Grünkern soup is a fitting local lunch.
t.ehrenstein@48.4,9.9:
Ehrenstein is a small district on the western edge of Ulm, in the Blau valley, where the little Blau river flows from its spring at Blaubeuren towards the Danube. In the 1950s and 60s, archaeologists found here the remains of a Neolithic village, built on the damp ground of the valley floor around six thousand years ago, with wooden houses, hearths and remarkably well-preserved organic material. The site is part of the World Heritage list of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, though there is nothing to see above ground today.

The Blau valley is a narrow, winding valley cut into the limestone of the Swabian Alb, with steep slopes, cliffs and caves. At Blaubeuren, about fifteen kilometres upstream, the river emerges from the Blautopf, a deep, intensely blue spring that is one of the most beautiful natural sights in Germany. The colour comes from the way light is scattered in the deep, clear water, and legend has it that a water nymph lives at the bottom. Nearby, the caves of the Ach and Lone valleys have yielded some of the oldest works of art in the world, including the Venus of Hohle Fels and the Lion Man, carved from mammoth ivory around forty thousand years ago.

The riding here is good. The roads through the Blau valley and up onto the Swabian Alb are winding and scenic, with climbs and descents through forests and limestone cliffs. The Alb itself is a high plateau with juniper heaths, pastures and small villages, crossed by quiet country roads. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is moderate. In winter, the Alb can be snowy and cold, while summer is pleasant.

Ulm, just next door, is a city with a long history. Its minster has the tallest church spire in the world, at 161.5 metres, and you can climb its stairs for a view over the city and, on clear days, to the Alps. Albert Einstein was born in Ulm in 1879. The old town, with its half-timbered houses and the fishermen's quarter along the Blau, is charming and full of restaurants.

Klingenstein, a district of Blaustein about a kilometre away, has fuel and basic services. Ulm has everything you need. Stop for a plate of Käsespätzle, Swabian egg noodles with cheese and crispy onions, the classic dish of this region.
t.bourg@46.3,6.2:
Geneva's lake shore is not the only place where Switzerland feels close at hand, and the stretch north of the city, around Versoix, is one of the quietest. Versoix itself is a calm, lakeside town with a little harbour, a long promenade and a medieval-looking centre, and it is easy to forget how close the French border is.

The history of this region is a mix of French, Savoyard and Swiss influences. Geneva was the city of Calvin, and the Reformation shaped its character, and the French writer Voltaire lived just across the border at Ferney from 1758, welcoming visitors and writing his pamphlets in safety from both the French and the Swiss authorities. The label also mentions Lac de Chalain, which lies in the French Jura, a lake known for the traces of prehistoric villages built on piles along its shores.

For the ride, the Jura is the attraction. A short run from here takes you up to the Col de la Faucille, at around thirteen hundred metres, through a series of bends and hairpins with views back over Lake Geneva and, on a clear day, to Mont Blanc. The roads in the Jura are quieter than the Alps, with long forested ridges, alpine pastures and dairy farms that produce Gruyère and Comté cheese. Switzerland requires a motorway vignette, a sticker you buy at the border or at a service station, if you plan to use the motorways, and speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras common.

Versoix has fuel, cafes and bakeries, and Geneva is within easy reach for anything more. Prices in Switzerland are high, particularly for food and drink, so a picnic with bread, cheese and sausages can be a good idea. The best months for riding in the Jura are May to October, and the lake shore is pleasant all year, with the bise, a cold north wind, sometimes sweeping across the water in winter.
t.fort site and civil settlement of obernb:
