Obernburg stands on the Main, in the bend where the river leaves the Spessart forest and turns north, and for a time in the second century it was the frontier of the Roman world. The Odenwald Limes, the earlier version of the frontier, ran along the hills to the south and reached the river near here, and a fort was built on the bank to guard the crossing. A civil settlement grew beside it, and finds from both are shown in the town's small Roman museum, which stands on the site and has a collection of tombstones, tools and pottery.

The Limes was abandoned in the middle of the third century, when pressure from the Alemanni forced the Romans back to the Rhine, and the fort fell into ruin. The Roman line is listed by UNESCO as part of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, and the section along the Main is among the quieter parts. Obernburg itself is a small town with a well-kept old centre of half-timbered houses, and Elsenfeld, a neighbour, has a more industrial character.

For a rider, the Main valley and the forested hills on either side are a good combination. The Spessart, a large wooded upland, has roads with long bends, mixed beech and oak, and few cars, and the Odenwald across the river is similar. The wine villages along the Main, the Churfranken region, grow Silvaner and Spätburgunder on steep slopes, and they have terraces where you can stop for a glass of wine and a plate of ham and bread. Miltenberg, a half-timbered town with a famous old inn, is a short ride south, and Aschaffenburg, with its Pompeian-style villa, lies to the north.

Fuel stations and supermarkets are available in Obernburg and Elsenfeld, and the area has plenty of guesthouses and cafes. The Main cycle path runs along the river, and in summer the road can be busy with cyclists. Late spring and September, when the vineyards are heavy, are the best times to ride, and a stop for local wine is best taken on foot, not before the road home.
t.rosenbach park@49.8,9.9:
Würzburg sits on the Main in lower Franconia, and the Rosenbach label puts you on its northern edge of green space, a few minutes from the old centre rather than out in open country. Take it as what it is, a pleasant city stop among the trams and one-way streets, and the real interest lies in the town around it.

The river is the reason for everything here. The Main loops through a narrow valley whose south-facing slopes are covered in vines, and Würzburg has made wine on them for well over a thousand years. The local drink is Silvaner, dry and slightly earthy, and it comes in the flat green bottle called a Bocksbeutel, which you will see in every shop window. The hill above the old bridge carries the Marienberg fortress, for centuries the seat of the prince-bishops, who also built the Residenz in the town below. That palace, with its Tiepolo ceiling fresco over the staircase, is the grandest baroque building in Bavaria's north and it was rebuilt with some stubbornness after the bombing of March 1945 flattened most of the city in a single night.

For a rider, the city itself is slow going. Trams, one-way streets and plenty of cyclists mean you walk the centre rather than ride it, and the best plan is to park somewhere sensible, cross the old bridge on foot with a glass of wine from the vendors who set up there in the evenings, and look up at the fortress. Fuel is no issue, since Würzburg is a city of well over a hundred thousand and Höchberg and Gerbrunn on either side have their own stations. Coffee and a proper meal are easy to find; the town has a long habit of feeding students and tourists at the same time.

The roads beyond are the reward. West along the Main towards Karlstadt and Marktheidenfeld the valley road is gentle and the vineyards crowd in; to the south the Romantic Road begins here and rolls towards Tauberbischofsheim and Rothenburg, gentle farmland with the occasional long straight. Go on a weekday morning in September or early October when the grapes are in and the light comes low and gold across the slopes. Summer weekends bring tour buses and slow convoys, and in winter the hills hold fog for days.
t.fort site and civil settlement of unterb:
The Rems valley runs east from Stuttgart towards the edge of the Swabian Jura, and Unterböbingen lies just outside the village of Böbingen, with Heubach three kilometres on and the long wooded wall of the Alb rising behind. The ground here is gently rolling farmland, orchards, small fields and the occasional church spire, the kind of country that looks entirely ordinary until you remember who once held it.

The Romans did, and they held it with care. A Roman fort stood at Unterböbingen on the Raetian frontier, and beside it grew a civil settlement, the vicus, where traders, craftsmen and soldiers' families lived under the protection of the garrison. That pairing, fort and village, is how the empire built almost everywhere on its edges. The frontier line itself, the Limes, was listed by UNESCO in 2005 together with its German sections, and it is easy to follow by road if you like quiet, unglamorous history.

On the bike this is a gentle, almost pastoral area. The B29 follows the Rems and carries commuters, so avoid it at rush hour; the smaller roads that climb out towards Heubach and the Rosenstein are far better, tight little bends through beech woods with the escarpment looming. The Rosenstein above Heubach has a ruined castle site and caves, and from the Albtrauf the view drops all the way to the Hohenstaufen, the hill that gave the medieval Staufer dynasty its name. Schwäbisch Gmünd and Aalen are the bigger towns either side, and both have fuel and a decent meal.

Heubach, with just over ten thousand people, is the practical stop for fuel, bakeries and cafes, and Böbingen itself has a few shops. Spring brings blossom over the orchards, autumn the colour on the Alb, and the road surfaces in the valley are good almost everywhere. Winter can bring ice on the shaded climbs, so be wary before ten in the morning.
t.reggia di venaria reale@45.1,7.6:
The Reggia di Venaria Reale lies ten kilometres north-west of the centre of Turin, at the edge of the Piedmontese plain, with the white wall of the Alps visible on a clear day behind the Lanzo valleys. The Savoy dukes built it as a hunting lodge, and it grew into one of the largest palaces in Europe, now at the centre of a town of thirty-three thousand people that carries its name.

Duke Charles Emmanuel II began the work in 1658, with the architect Amedeo di Castellamonte, who also laid out the town around it as a service area for the court. The building was damaged in the French wars and later used as a barracks, and it fell into serious decay. In the early eighteenth century the Sicilian architect Filippo Juvarra added the great gallery, a hall of white stone flooded with light, and the church of Sant'Uberto, named for the patron saint of hunters. After a long and expensive restoration the palace reopened to the public in 2007, with the gardens following later. It belongs to the group of Savoy residences inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1997.

Beside the palace lies the park of La Mandria, a huge walled royal hunting estate with woods, meadows and an old farm complex, now open to walkers and cyclists, where deer and boar still roam. Behind the palace, the Alpine foothills begin, and the roads into the valleys of Lanzo reward a rider with a series of bends. The Colle del Lys, a pass to the north-west, is a modest climb with a pleasant surface, though traffic around Turin on weekdays is heavy and the ring roads are fast and confusing, so plan the exit carefully.

Venaria Reale itself has everything: fuel, parking, cafes and restaurants in the old town streets, and a daily pace that feels more provincial than the nearby city. The Savoy kitchen was rich in game, truffles, hazelnuts and the creamy chocolate, gianduja, invented in Turin, and a glass of Barbera or Nebbiolo goes well with the local salami. The palace has a lot of rooms and walking inside takes a couple of hours, so go in the morning, and choose spring or autumn for the best light on the gardens. In August the plain is hot and humid, and the city is half empty.
t.borgo castello nel parco della mandria@4:
The Parco La Mandria, north-west of Turin, is the largest remnant of the royal hunting estates of the House of Savoy, and the Borgo Castello at its centre was once the heart of the estate. The word mandria means a herd, and the park began as a stud and breeding farm for horses and cattle on the plain, with the woods kept for the hunt. Today the park is a protected area of about three thousand hectares, surrounded by a wall, where visitors walk or cycle between oaks, hornbeams and meadows, and where deer and wild boar still live.

The Savoy kings came here to hunt, and the best-known resident is Vittorio Emanuele II, the first king of a united Italy. He is said to have loved the park above all his other estates, and he lived at the Borgo Castello with Rosa Vercellana, known as Bela Rosin, his companion for many years and later his wife in a morganatic marriage. The buildings of the borgo include a small castle, stables, a church and the long courtyards of a working farm, and parts have been restored and opened. Check the opening days before you go, as access varies through the year.

The park is a pleasant place to leave the bike and walk, and the nearby roads are good for quiet riding. Northwards, the plain gives way to the Lanzo valleys, and eastwards the hills of the Turin side rise to the basilica of Superga, a splendid baroque church on a ridge with a view over the city and the Alps. The Villa della Regina and the Sacro Monte di Belmonte, also on your ride, show a different side of the region's history, a royal summer house and a pilgrimage route with chapels. The ring roads around Turin are heavy with traffic on weekdays, so pick the weekends or the early mornings.

Druento, with eight thousand people, is the closest place for fuel and a coffee, and Venaria Reale is a bigger town a few kilometres east. Piedmont is a good country for the table, with agnolotti, bagna cauda, vitello tonnato and hazelnut cakes, and the wine of the nearby hills is Barbera and Dolcetto. Spring is lovely in the park, with new leaves and wildflowers, and October brings amber foliage. In midsummer the plain is humid and the mosquitoes are persistent.
t.monferrato of the inferot@45.1,8.4:
The low hills of the Monferrato, in Piedmont, roll between the Po to the north and the Tanaro to the south, and the Inferot label points at the part of them near Cella Monte, Rosignano and Frassinello, ten kilometres from Casale Monferrato. This is soft country, sandstone ridges clothed in vines, with brick villages on the crests and fog in the valleys on autumn mornings.

The word Inferot is the Piedmontese form of infernot, the small cellars cut by hand into the soft local sandstone, the Pietra da Cantoni, beneath village houses. They are tiny, cool rooms, sometimes with niches for bottles, shelves and a stone table, and the family would go down to taste its wine or hide it from tax collectors. The tradition is nineteenth-century and mostly local, and the infernot cellars, together with the vineyards, are part of the landscape listed by UNESCO in 2014 as the Vineyard Landscape of Piedmont, Langhe-Roero and Monferrato. Cella Monte has a small museum and several of the cellars can be visited, though many are private and open only by arrangement.

The riding is delightful if you like steady, curving small roads and are happy with low speed. The provincial roads between Rosignano, Ozzano and Casale follow the ridges, climbing and dropping with views over the vineyards, and there is almost no traffic apart from tractors at harvest. The surface is variable, with patches and some gravel on the farm tracks, and the best time is September and October, when the grape harvest is in progress and the air smells of must. Summer is hot and slightly hazy, and winter fog makes the roads slippery in the early hours.

Local flavours are Barbera and Grignolino, a pale, peppery red that is made almost nowhere else, together with Freisa. Food is hearty: agnolotti, bagna cauda in the cold months, and bollito misto. Frassinello and Cella Monte are tiny villages, so do not rely on them for fuel. Casale Monferrato, ten kilometres away and with some thirty thousand people, has stations, bakeries and good restaurants, and it also has a fine synagogue and a lively market. Book a table ahead on autumn weekends, because the wine country fills with visitors.
t.les argilliez@46.9,6.8:
Around the shores of Lake Neuchâtel, the water level once sat lower than it does now, and prehistoric farmers built villages on pilings along the edge. Les Argilliez, near Gorgier on the northwest shore, preserves traces of one of them. The wet mud at the bottom of the lake kept wood, textiles and tools in astonishing condition, which is why the pile dwellings around the Alps were inscribed by UNESCO in 2011. There is little to see above the waterline, but the idea of a village standing on stilts in these waters, with the Jura mountains behind it, is a strong one.

The shoreline here is lovely. Vineyards climb the slopes behind the lake, and the villages of Gorgier, Saint-Aubin-Sauges and Bevaix are lined with winegrowers' houses, many with cellars open for tasting. The local specialities are Chasselas, a crisp white wine, and the pale rosé known as Œil-de-Perdrix, the eye of the partridge. The Castle of Gorgier stands above the village, and the lake itself, long and calm, is often busy with sailboats from the marina.

Riding the lake road is easy and civilised. The N5 runs along the shore between Neuchâtel and Yverdon, with views of the water and the Alps on a clear day, though it can be busy with commuters. Smaller roads climb into the vineyards and the Jura foothills, with tighter bends, stone walls and farms with large, low roofs. In autumn the vines turn red and gold, and a sea of fog sometimes fills the lowlands while the hills stand clear in sunshine.

Fuel and supplies are available in Saint-Aubin-Sauges and Bevaix, and Estavayer-le-Lac, across the water, is a handsome medieval town with a castle and a lakeside promenade. Swiss prices are high, so budget accordingly. Spring is pretty, with blossom and fresh green, summer is warm enough for a swim, and winter brings grey skies and the smell of woodsmoke. A glass of local white and a cheese plate on the quay at sunset is hard to beat.
t.le grand lac de clairvaux@46.6,5.7:
The Jura plateau behind Clairvaux-les-Lacs is a country of limestone, cows and lakes, and the Grand Lac de Clairvaux is the largest of the lakes that give the town its name. Prehistoric people lived on its shore on pilings, in villages that rose and fell for centuries, and the waterlogged mud preserved their wood and tools. The sites on Clairvaux's lakes are among the pile-dwelling places inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2011. The lake today is a quiet blue sheet, ringed by reeds and low wooded hills, with a beach where families swim in July.

It is a gentle stop but the country around it is far from flat. The Jura here rolls in long folded ridges, and the roads cross them in loops and climbs: the D678 and its neighbours twist between pastures, spruce forest and villages with stone farmhouses and broad roofs. Surfaces are generally good, and the bends are the right kind, open enough to carry speed and tight enough to keep you awake. Cowbells ring from the meadows in summer, and the farms smell of hay and cheese.

Food is half the point of the region. This is Comté country, where the great wheels of cheese ripen in cellars for months or years, and the Jura also makes vin jaune, a nutty, oxidised yellow wine aged under a veil of yeast, best served with chicken in cream and morels. Château-Chalon, a hilltop village not far away, is the home of that wine. Clairvaux-les-Lacs itself is a small town of about fifteen hundred, with shops, restaurants and a fuel stop, and Lons-le-Saunier to the north is the bigger place to fill the tank properly.

Within an easy ride lies the Saline Royale at Arc-et-Senans, the great semicircular salt works designed by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux in the 1770s, another World Heritage Site, and the waterfalls of the Hérisson valley, just east. Spring and early autumn are lovely, with clear light and fewer visitors. Winters are cold and snowy at altitude, and roads over the higher ridges can ice up, so choose your season with care.
t.grosse stadt kleiner hafner@47.4,8.5:
Zürich's lake has been a home for much longer than the city's banks suggest. The names Grosse Stadt and Kleiner Hafner belong to prehistoric settlement sites in the shallows of the Seebecken, the lake basin where the water meets the old town, and they are part of the UNESCO listing of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps. Farmers and fishers built villages on stilts here between roughly 4,000 and 800 BC, and the lake mud kept their traces. The site is underwater, so you cannot see it, but you can stand on the Utoquai or the Alpenquai promenade and imagine it.

Swiss pile-dwelling research started up the lake in Meilen in 1854, when an unusually dry winter dropped the water and exposed rows of wooden posts. Ferdinand Keller, a Zürich antiquarian, recognised what they were and set off the first wave of lake-dwelling enthusiasm across Europe. Many of the finds ended up in the Swiss National Museum beside the main station. It is satisfying to know that the sparkling lake you are looking at is a kind of archive.

For a rider this is simply Zürich, which means orderly, expensive and well signposted. Trams run in the middle of the streets, and their rails are treacherous when wet, so cross them squarely. Speed limits are enforced with a vengeance, and cameras are everywhere, so stay under the limit. Parking for motorcycles is generally available on marked spaces in the centre. Fuel is plentiful, though pricey, and the lakeside has cafés, ice-cream kiosks and bathing platforms where people swim in the summer.

Beyond the city, the lakeshore roads on both sides are pleasant but busy at weekends, and the best riding lies in the hills behind, around the Pfannenstiel on the east shore, where roads climb through orchards and woods with views down to the water. On a clear day the Alps line the southern horizon. A morning stroll along the quay, followed by a coffee at a lakeside kiosk, makes a calm start to a ride, and the autumn light, low and golden, is excellent.
t.nussbaumersee@47.6,8.8:
Out in the Thurgau countryside, between Frauenfeld and the Rhine, a chain of small lakes lies in a glacial hollow: the Nussbaumersee, the Hüttwilersee and the Hasensee, with the wetland of the Seebachtal around them. It is a place of reeds and still water, where herons stand in the shallows and dragonflies hang over the surface. The Nussbaumersee is the biggest of them, a modest lake with a wooded shore, and a footpath circles it.

Prehistoric people liked it too. The sites at Nussbaumersee and the neighbouring lakes, such as Weier and Bleiche, preserve remains of lake-shore villages from the Neolithic and Bronze Age, and a few of them belong to the Alpine pile-dwelling UNESCO listing. As with most such sites, the evidence is buried, so the pleasure is in the setting: a quiet shore where people once lived in houses on stilts, farming and fishing under the same hills.

The riding is soft Swiss countryside at its best. Narrow, smooth roads wander between orchards, maize fields and farms with big timber barns, and the corners are gentle. Thurgau is apple country, so cider and fresh juice are sold at farm gates, and in spring the blossom is dazzling. Hüttwilen, the nearest village, is small, with about fourteen hundred people. Frauenfeld, nine kilometres away, is the bigger town, with stations, supermarkets and a castle, the largest in the canton, standing on a rock above the old town.

To the north, the Rhine flows out of the Untersee at Stein am Rhein, one of the prettiest old towns in the region, with painted facades. Eschenz and the little island of Werd, with its chapel, are close by. Mornings in late spring or early autumn are best, when mist lies on the water and the light is soft. Bring swimming gear in summer, since the lakes are clean, and avoid weekends in July, when families fill the shore. In winter the lakes sometimes freeze, and the surrounding roads can be icy.
t.mathildenhohe darmstadt@49.9,8.7:
On a low hill above Darmstadt, at the very end of the nineteenth century, the young Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse decided to gather artists and let them build a new way of living. The Mathildenhöhe became an artists' colony from 1899, and its buildings are some of the best Jugendstil, the German Art Nouveau, anywhere. UNESCO listed the ensemble in 2021. Joseph Maria Olbrich designed most of the first generation, including the exhibition hall and the tall Wedding Tower, with its fingers of brick at the top, finished in 1908 as a gift for the Grand Duke's marriage.

Walking the hill is a pleasure. A grove of plane trees shades the square, the Lily Basin glitters with tiles, and the Russian Chapel, with its golden onion domes, stands a little apart, built for the Tsar's family, who had links to the Hessian court. Peter Behrens, later the architect of industrial Berlin and a teacher of Le Corbusier and Mies, built his own house here in 1901, a statement of modern design. Details are everywhere: carved doorways, mosaic panels, flowing ironwork and exuberant gables.

Darmstadt is a city of around 140,000 people, with fuel, cafés and workshops at every turn, so supplies are easy. Parking for a motorbike on the hill is simple outside busy weekends, and a walk through the plane trees is a nice change from the saddle. The city itself is known as a science town, with a large technical university and the European Space Operations Centre, which gives it an energetic, youthful feel.

The riding around is superb. The Odenwald, a gentle, forested range to the east, offers smooth roads with long bends through beech and oak woods, and the Bergstrasse, along the western foot of the hills, is known for its early spring blossom and wine villages. Both are busy on sunny weekends, so go midweek if you can. A visit to Worms, with its medieval synagogue and cathedral, makes an excellent companion trip. Autumn light on the brick of the Wedding Tower is hard to beat.
t.castello di rivoli@45.1,7.5:
Rivoli stands on a ridge at the mouth of the Susa valley, where the Alps give way to the plain of Turin, and the Savoy dukes liked it for exactly that reason: from the castle terrace, you can see the city to the east and the wall of mountains to the west. A fortress stood here in the Middle Ages, and in the eighteenth century the architect Filippo Juvarra began to rebuild it as a grand residence for Victor Amadeus II. The duke, who had become King of Sardinia, ended his days here in 1732, reportedly confined by his own son, and the great project was never finished.

The castle now houses the Castello di Rivoli Museum of Contemporary Art, which opened in 1984, an unexpected union of baroque shell and modern installations. The unfinished wing of the building, which Juvarra intended to be much larger, stands as a raw, brick-built mass, and the contrast with the sleek white gallery spaces inside is striking. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy, inscribed in 1997. The terrace, with the Alps ranged behind, is lovely at sunset.

The geology around is a gift. Rivoli sits on the edge of a morainic amphitheatre, a ring of low hills left by the great Alpine glacier that once spilled out of the Susa valley, and the area is full of ponds, woods and vineyards. Rivoli itself has forty-six thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and plenty of restaurants, and Alpignano is nearby. Local food leans toward Piedmontese classics, with agnolotti, bagna cauda and a glass of Barbera or Freisa.

For a rider, the pleasure is in the choice. Turin's ring roads and the Susa valley highway are fast and busy, but a few minutes away the lanes of the morainic hills are quiet and winding. Further up the valley, the road climbs toward the Sacra di San Michele, the dramatic abbey on its mountaintop, and the Mont Cenis pass. Spring and autumn offer clear air and fine views, while winter fog can fill the plain for days.
t.limessection between watchtowers wp 9 68:
Mainhardt is a small town in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, a long ridge of wooded hills east of Stuttgart and north of Schwäbisch Hall, and the Romans chose to drop their frontier straight through here. The Upper Germanic Limes runs dead straight for many kilometres in this region, up and down hills without regard to the terrain, because the surveyors drew the line first and let the army follow it. At Mainhardt there was a fort with a garrison of auxiliary soldiers, and the outline can be traced in the ground east of the town. The numbers on the label refer to the watchtowers, small timber and then stone posts that stood at intervals along the line within sight of one another.

Like most of the frontier, it is rarely spectacular. Most of the pleasure here is in the forest. The ridges are covered in spruce, fir and beech, the valleys cut sharply into the sandstone, and the paths are carpeted with needles. In the morning the mist lies in the hollows. Streams run fast in spring, and the air has a faint smell of resin and wet soil. The old Limes route is signed for walkers, and a short stroll along it to find the faint bank of a tower platform makes a good break from the saddle.

For motorcyclists the area is very well liked. The roads around Mainhardt and Wüstenrot twist up and down the forested slopes, with a series of tight bends, short steep climbs and quick descents that reward a steady rhythm. The surface is generally good, though forest roads are shaded and slow to dry, and leaf litter and cut timber can be treacherous in the shoulders. Weekends see many other riders and cyclists, and the local police have been known to keep an eye on the popular stretches, so keep the speed civil.

Mainhardt has fuel and a bakery, and Wüstenrot, a few kilometres away, is the village where the first German building society was founded in the 1920s. Both are fine for a coffee. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, because the forest is cool in midsummer but the weekend traffic is heavy.
t.fortlet holderbusch@49.5,9.4:
Holderbusch is a small piece of woodland above the Odenwald plateau, close to Buchen, where the Romans placed a fortlet on the Odenwald Limes about the middle of the second century. This part of the Upper Germanic frontier was, for much of its length, a simple palisade and ditch, running in an astonishingly straight line across hills and valleys from the Main to the Neckar. A fortlet was a small post, a few dozen soldiers behind a bank and ditch, and from here the watchtowers on each side could be reached on foot within minutes. The ground is marked by gentle swellings in the forest floor and a path with explanatory signs, and the walk takes less than half an hour.

The country around Buchen is called the Bauland, a plateau of farm fields and low woods between the Odenwald and the Tauber valley, with long views and occasional deep stream cuts. Buchen is a neat little town with a half-timbered centre and a regional museum, and Walldürn, a few kilometres further, is a pilgrimage place whose basilica holds a relic known as the Blood Miracle, drawing processions every year in the summer. The festivals of the region are old and devout, with brass bands and flower carpets laid in the streets.

For a motorcyclist, the area is quietly appealing. Roads follow the ridge and then slide down into sheltered valleys, with gentle bends, crests that open sudden views, and long straights where a tractor may be crawling. The surface is mostly decent, and traffic is light outside the main towns. The Neckar valley to the south is livelier, with castles at almost every corner, and the Main to the north offers wine villages and broad river roads.

Buchen has fuel, supermarkets and several cafés, and Walldürn and Seckach can fill in the gaps. The nearest museum devoted to the Limes is at Osterburken, a short drive away, where a good Roman fort bath complex survives in the town. Spring is fresh and green and a little damp, summer is warm, and autumn gives clear, golden days when the beech forest is at its best. In winter, the plateau is cold, with frost on the road in the mornings.
t.fortlet of freimuhle@48.8,9.8:
Schwäbisch Gmünd sits in the Rems valley below the Swabian Jura, at the foot of the hill where the Staufer dynasty built their castle, and the Roman frontier ran through the same country. The Upper Germanic Limes crosses the Rems valley near here, and at Freimühle a small fortlet was set on the slope above the river to watch the line, a modest square of earth bank that archaeologists have traced and the town has marked. It is a quiet and easily missed spot, but a nice reminder that the Romans knew a good viewpoint.

Gmünd itself is a pretty town, one of the oldest in Swabia, with a market square, a lively old centre and the Holy Cross Minster, an early example of the hall church style in which aisles and nave rise to the same height, designed by the Parler family of builders who went on to work in Prague. The town was a free imperial city for centuries and is still known for its jewellery and silverware. Just beyond, the Hohenstaufen mountain rises out of the plain like a loaf of bread, and the castle that once crowned it has long been ruined. The Staufer emperors, including Frederick Barbarossa, came from this family.

Mutlangen, a few kilometres from here, has a different claim to history. In the 1980s it hosted American Pershing missiles, and the gates of the base became a focus of peaceful demonstrations that drew thousands of people, including a number of prominent writers and politicians. It is a reminder that the Cold War was fought here too.

The riding around Gmünd is a pleasure. The Rems valley road is easy and open, and the roads up onto the Swabian Jura are tight, steep and full of tight bends through beech woods, with views over the Remstal vineyards. Weekends bring many other motorcyclists, and the local police keep watch on the hairpins, so ride accordingly. The surface is generally good, but frost can linger on shaded bends in the shoulder seasons.

Schwäbisch Gmünd has all the services of a town of sixty thousand: fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants serving Spätzle and Maultaschen. Waldstetten and Mutlangen have petrol as well. Come in spring, when the orchards flower, or in early autumn, when the light on the Hohenstaufen is gold.
t.kasuga village and sacred places in hira:
Hirado is an island at the far northwest of Kyushu, joined to the mainland by a bridge, and it has a stranger history than most. In 1609 the Dutch East India Company opened a trading post here, and for a while Hirado was the only place in Japan where Europeans traded openly, before the shogunate shifted them to the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki in 1641. The town still has a harbour and a castle on the hill, and the sea is never far from any road.

Kasuga village, a few kilometres from the town, is something else entirely. It is part of the group of sites recognised by UNESCO in 2018 as relics of Japan's hidden Christians, the communities who kept their faith alive in secret through more than two centuries of persecution after Christianity was banned in the early seventeenth century. In places like this, believers disguised their devotions as Buddhist or Shinto customs and venerated mountains, including the sacred mountain of Yasumandake, whose peak rises behind the village. Rice terraces climb the slopes in small steps, and the old fields and stone walls feel unchanged.

The riding is slow and attentive. The coastal road around Hirado is narrow in places, with farms, small harbours and frequent bends, and in the village itself the lanes are tight, so go quietly. This is a working farming community, and the polite approach is a quiet engine and a wave to anyone you meet. Light traffic, good views over the water to the islets, and a feeling of rural calm make for a rewarding day, though one that rewards patience more than speed.

For fuel and meals, Hirado town, about eight kilometres away, has what you need, and it is a small but proper town with seafood restaurants and the sort of coffee shops where you can sit for an hour. Sasebo, a larger port and naval city, lies some thirty kilometres further south and has everything a rider could want, including the famous Sasebo burger.

Spring brings fresh green on the terraces and autumn gives clear, soft light; the summer is hot and humid, and typhoon season can disrupt things. If you can, visit on a weekday morning when the village is quiet.
t.seongsan ilchulbong tuff cone@33.5,126.9:
Seongsan Ilchulbong rises from the eastern tip of Jeju like a stone crown that someone dropped into the sea. It is a tuff cone, formed in a single explosive eruption when magma hit shallow water, roughly five thousand years ago, and the crater at the top is a wide, grassy bowl about six hundred metres across, ringed by jagged rocky teeth. The name means sunrise peak, and the Koreans take the idea seriously: on New Year's morning thousands climb the steps to watch the sun come up out of the East Sea.

The climb itself takes about twenty minutes on a stepped path and is steeper than it looks. From the rim you see the green fields of the island on one side, the open sea on the other, and, on a clear day, the little island of Udo, which you reach by short ferry from the port below. Along the shore the haenyeo, the women divers of Jeju, still work the shallows for sea urchins, abalone and conch, holding their breath for minutes at a time, and their small stalls sell the day's catch right at the water's edge.

Riding on Jeju is among the happiest in Korea. The coastal roads follow the shoreline past black basalt walls, tangerine orchards and fields of rapeseed in spring, with the great cone of Hallasan floating in the middle of the island. Winds can be strong, especially in winter and at the exposed eastern end, and the weather changes quickly, so a waterproof layer is wise. Traffic builds around the cone in the middle of the day with tour buses, so early morning or late afternoon is calmer.

Jeju City is about forty kilometres away, and that is where you will find the larger fuel stations and the choice of food, though the local villages around Seongsan have small stations, cafes and restaurants for the immediate needs. Try a bowl of the black pork that the island is known for, or a hot seafood stew after a windy morning. The light at the end of the day, with the cone in silhouette, is worth waiting for, though it is also busy, so be patient with the car park.
Geomunoreum is a quiet, forested volcanic cone on the north-east side of Jeju, and the real attraction is underground. Thousands of years ago lava poured from this cone down towards the sea, and as the outside of the flow cooled and hardened, the molten rock inside kept draining out, leaving long tunnels. Together they form the Geomunoreum lava tube system, which is part of the UNESCO listing for Jeju's volcanic island and its lava tubes. Manjanggul, the most famous tube, runs for several kilometres, with only a section open to visitors, and it has a lava column rising several metres from the cave floor, a remarkable sight.

Inside, the air is cool all year, so a light jacket feels good in August and the walk is surprisingly easy: wide passage, damp walls, dripping ceilings and the faint blue-black sheen of old lava. The caves are home to bats and, in their deeper parts, small cave-adapted creatures. Above ground the same volcanic soil supports gotjawal, the tangled forest that grows over rough lava ground, where ferns, vines and evergreen trees mix in a way found almost nowhere else.

For riding, this corner of Jeju is calm and green. The roads here run between farms and woods, with occasional views of the sea to the north. Weather can be damp and foggy in the early summer rainy season and windy in the winter. Spring brings yellow fields of canola, autumn gives silver grass on the slopes, and mid-week visits mean far fewer buses. Do not expect twisting mountain roads; this is easy riding with a gentle pulse.

Jeju City is about twenty-five kilometres to the west and is the main place to fill the tank and have a proper meal. Seogwipo on the south coast is farther. Small villages along the way have bakeries and cafes, and the stalls around the lava tube entrance often sell tangerine products and snacks. The ride heads on to Hallasan, whose massive crater lake stands about two thousand metres above sea level, and which is the highest point in all of South Korea, so you will be watching the cone grow larger on the horizon as you go.
t.andermatt@46.6,8.6:
Andermatt sits at 1,444 metres in the Urseren valley, a high, wide, treeless hollow in the heart of the Swiss Alps, and it has been a crossroads for centuries. Three great passes meet here: the Gotthard, which runs south to Italy and Ticino at 2,106 metres, the Furka, which climbs west over 2,429 metres toward the Valais, and the Oberalp, which leads east at 2,044 metres into Graubünden. For a motorcyclist it is a kind of Mecca, since the three roads are among the most famous in the Alps, and the town fills with bikes on any fine summer weekend.

The history is dramatic. North of the town, the Schöllenen gorge is a narrow, steep cut in the granite, and the Devil's Bridge, which crosses the roaring Reuss river, has been a symbol of the Gotthard route since the thirteenth century, when a first bridge opened the pass to trade. In 1799 a Russian army under General Suvorov fought its way through the gorge against the French, an episode remembered with a huge monument carved into the rock. The Swiss army also used the area as a fortress, with tunnels and artillery positions hidden in the mountains. Today, a base tunnel of 57 kilometres runs beneath the Gotthard for trains, the longest railway tunnel in the world, and most traffic passes below the mountain.

The old Gotthard road, the Tremola, is the part many riders remember: a cobbled road of tight hairpins zigzagging up the south side from Airolo, closed to heavy traffic and thrilling in dry weather. The passes are closed by snow in winter, usually from late autumn until around June, so check before you go. In summer, traffic and weather can change quickly, with fog on the passes and thunderstorms in the afternoon. A Swiss motorway vignette is needed for the motorways.

Andermatt itself is a modest village with a few hotels, cafes and shops, recently expanded by a large resort development and linked to a ski area. It has a fuel station, though prices are higher than in the lowlands. Try the Älplermagronen, a dish of macaroni, potatoes, cheese and onions with apple sauce, or a hearty rösti after a long day of hairpins. Early mornings are best, before the crowds, when the light on the peaks is golden and the air smells of cut grass.
t.three castles@46.2,9.0:
Bellinzona is a small city in a very big position. It stands where the Ticino valley opens into the Magadino plain, at the point where the roads from the San Gottardo and San Bernardino passes both come down from the Alps, and whoever held it controlled the way between Milan and the north. That is why three castles crown the rocky hills above the town, linked by a long wall that once barred the whole valley. Castelgrande, the oldest, stands on a rock in the centre, Montebello on a spur above, and Sasso Corbaro on a high hill farther back, and together they were listed by UNESCO in 2000 as outstanding examples of medieval fortification.

The fortresses were built mostly by the Visconti and Sforza dukes of Milan in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, although the site had been defended since Roman times. Swiss cantons took Bellinzona in 1500, and for three centuries the castles were seats of the bailiffs sent from Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden. Ticino became a canton of the Swiss Confederation only in 1803. You can walk along the walls and through the keeps, and the view from the battlements over the red roofs and the green valley, with snow on the high peaks, is wonderful.

The old town below has arcades, pastel facades and a Saturday market that fills the main square with vegetables, cheeses and cured meats. Food is Ticinese and decidedly Italian in flavour, with polenta, risotto, mushrooms, and a glass of Merlot, the red wine that grows well on the sunny slopes of the canton. The climate is milder than north of the Alps, and in spring camellias and magnolias flower early in the gardens.

The riding from Bellinzona is excellent. North, the road over the San Bernardino pass, at 2,065 metres, winds through green valleys and tunnels, while the Gotthard route heads for Airolo and Andermatt. East and south, lanes lead along the shores of Lake Maggiore and over the hills of the Ceneri to Lugano. Monte San Giorgio, near the Lake of Lugano, is another UNESCO site, famed for fossils of marine reptiles from the Triassic, some two hundred and forty million years old. Snow shuts the high passes for the winter months, yet the valley roads stay open all year.

Bellinzona has sixteen thousand residents, petrol stations, cafes and parking near the castle. In summer it is hot, and in the evening the castle walls are floodlit, with a lovely glow over the valley. A Swiss motorway vignette is required for the A2 and other motorways.
t.grundwiesen@48.1,9.6:
The Federsee is what remains of a much larger lake that filled the basin after the last ice age, and over thousands of years it silted up into a vast moor, one of the most important wetlands in southern Germany. Wet ground preserves things well, which is why this corner is a treasure chest for archaeology. People settled around the lake from the Stone Age on, building houses on timber foundations or on stilts, and the waterlogged soil has kept their wood, tools and even textiles in remarkable condition.

Bad Buchau has a museum of the pile dwellers, with reconstructed houses outdoors, and the Federsee area belongs to the UNESCO group of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, recognised in 2011. The best way to feel the moor is to walk the long boardwalk that leads across the reeds to the open water, where you can watch herons, grebes, marsh harriers and, in spring and autumn, cranes and other migrating birds.

Upper Swabia has its own cultural identity, with onion-domed baroque churches in every village, rich monasteries and a countryside of orchards and farms. The Upper Swabian Baroque Road passes close, and the abbey at Ochsenhausen and the pilgrimage church of Steinhausen, a short way off, are masterpieces of the style. Schreckensee, the other point on the ride, is a small, dark lake in a forest farther south, and the Ach valley is a gentle, green river landscape.

The riding is relaxed. Roads run among fields, small woods and farming villages, with gentle bends, light traffic and long views, though tractors and cyclists share the lanes in summer. Mist often hangs over the moor in the early morning, and autumn brings golden light. Winter can be cold and foggy. It is a region for slow riding, with pauses for cake and coffee.

Bad Buchau, Uttenweiler and Attenweiler are small, with fuel stations, bakeries and inns, and the larger town of Biberach is not far away. Look for Swabian dishes such as Maultaschen, stuffed pasta pockets, and Spätzle, the soft egg noodles served with cheese or lentils, and a glass of local cider or beer.
t.wurzburg residence with the court garden:
Balthasar Neumann was a military engineer before he was an architect, and it shows in the Würzburg Residence, a palace so confidently engineered that its great staircase vault, with no central support, was said to be impossible. It was built for the prince-bishops of Würzburg in the early eighteenth century, with the main construction running from about 1720 to the mid-1740s. The ceiling above the stairs carries a fresco by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, which is among the largest in the world and depicts the four continents. UNESCO listed the whole ensemble in 1981, court gardens included.

The city around it sits on the Main river in Franconia, wine country in every sense. The slopes just outside town are terraced with vines, and the local speciality is Franken wine poured into a flat, rounded bottle called the Bocksbeutel. A glass of Silvaner on the Old Main Bridge, with the fortress looking down from across the water, is the kind of evening that should be on every rider's list. Würzburg was heavily bombed in March 1945 and the Residence was badly damaged, yet it was patiently restored, which is part of why it feels so lived-in today.

Practically, this is a proper city of well over a hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and parking are not a problem, although the centre is busy and tram-ridden. The Residence stands on the edge of the old town, so you can leave the bike in a nearby car park and walk. Allow time for the gardens at the back, which are quieter than the palace and good for shade on a hot afternoon.

The riding nearby is excellent in an unhurried way. The Main valley opens out in long loops with vineyards on one side and river on the other, and the roads that climb the hills toward the Steigerwald or Spessart turn properly curvy. Spring blossom and autumn harvest are the best months, and a weekday keeps the traffic down. Start early, because the town fills with tour groups by mid-morning.
t.shum sites of speyer@49.3,8.4:
Speyer was one of the great Jewish centres of medieval Europe, and the evidence is still standing in the Judenhof, the old Jewish courtyard just behind the cathedral. In the early twelfth century a synagogue was built here, and beside it a ritual bath, the mikveh, reached by a narrow stair down into the cool, damp earth. Together with the sister communities of Worms and Mainz, the three towns formed a league known by the initials of their Hebrew names, ShUM, and UNESCO listed the sites in 2021. The bath is among the oldest and best preserved in Europe, and descending into it is a quiet, slightly chilling experience.

Speyer sits on the Rhine, in the flat Palatinate plain, and the ride here from Heidelberg is gentle rather than exciting. You cross the river country on straight, well-surfaced roads between asparagus fields and orchards, with the Palatinate hills visible to the west and the Kraichgau to the east. It is an easy hour or so, good for a relaxed afternoon, and the Rhine ferries and bridges add a bit of variety. Ride in spring or autumn, when the light on the plain is soft and the traffic gentler, and plan on walking the old town rather than riding it.

The city has fifty thousand people and everything you need, from fuel on the outskirts to cafes around the Maximilianstrasse. The cathedral, a vast Romanesque basilica begun under the Salian emperors in the eleventh century, was also listed by UNESCO, in 1981, and holds the tombs of several emperors and kings. The Technik Museum on the edge of town is a different kind of attraction, with a Concorde and a Soviet space shuttle on display, which might appeal to anyone who rides for the pleasure of machinery.

If you eat here, try the Palatinate specialities, such as Saumagen, a stuffed pig's stomach beloved of the region and of Helmut Kohl, or a glass of dry Riesling from the nearby Weinstrasse. It is the kind of town where history is underfoot and lunch is serious.
t.ach valley@48.4,9.8:
Below the village of Schelklingen the Swabian Jura gives up some of the oldest art in the world. In the caves of the Ach and Lone valleys, early modern humans carved ivory and bone about forty thousand years ago, among them a small female figure found in the Hohle Fels cave in 2008, which is among the oldest known sculptures of the human form. Flutes made from bird bone and mammoth ivory turned up too. UNESCO listed six of these caves in 2017 under the title of Caves and Ice Age Art of the Swabian Jura, and a museum in nearby Blaubeuren tells the story well.

The Ach is a short river, but it carves a lovely valley. The road runs beside it between steep limestone slopes, with beech woods overhead and white cliffs showing through the trees. At Blaubeuren the river meets the Blautopf, a spring pool of an astonishing deep blue, fed from a cave system and the subject of local legend. Climb out of the valley and the plateau opens into fields and juniper heath, with curving roads that make for relaxed, rhythmic riding. In spring the meadows are dotted with flowers, and in autumn the beech woods blaze.

Schelklingen has about seven thousand people and Blaubeuren nearly twelve thousand, so fuel and a decent meal are both easy to come by. Blaubeuren has an attractive old monastery with a late Gothic altar, and its half-timbered lanes make a fine place for a stroll. Ulm, the city with the tallest church spire in the world, lies a short ride to the east, and Ulm is a good choice if you want a real town for the evening.

Weather on the Alb can change quickly, and mornings are often cool even in summer, so a light layer is worth packing. The caves themselves are small and some require guided visits, so check ahead before you go. Even if you never go underground, the valley carries the feel of an ancient place, and the cliffs and cool air do the rest.
t.palazzo madama@45.1,7.7:
Turin was Italy's first capital, and the Palazzo Madama in the middle of Piazza Castello was its first parliament. When the kingdom was proclaimed in 1861, the Senate met in a room inside this strange building, a medieval castle with a baroque facade added in the early eighteenth century by the architect Filippo Juvarra. The name comes from the royal widows, the Madama Reali, who lived here in the seventeenth century, among them Christine of France. Today it houses the city's museum of ancient art, and the staircase and facade are among the most beautiful in Italy. The whole ensemble of Savoy residences in and around Turin is listed by UNESCO.

Turin itself is a ride-in, park-and-walk city. The centre is a grid of broad arcaded streets, with a limited traffic zone that bikes cannot ignore, so find a garage or a car park outside the core and walk. The city has more than eight hundred thousand people, with fuel and every service, but traffic is heavy and tram lines and cobbles can be tricky in wet weather. The best riding lies outside, in the hills across the Po, where roads climb through woods to the Basilica of Superga, with a sweeping view of the Alps on a clear day.

The food and drink here are a pleasure. Turin invented the aperitivo culture around vermouth in the eighteenth century and gave the world gianduja, the hazelnut chocolate, and the bicerin, a layered drink of coffee, chocolate and cream served in small glasses. The old cafes along the arcades have preserved their nineteenth-century interiors, and a morning coffee and pastry at one of them is a ritual worth keeping. Lesna, a small village on the western edge of the metropolitan area, is the other nearby town on the list.

Piazza Castello is at its best in the early evening, when the light turns the stone gold and the cafe terraces fill. Wander the arcades, glance up at the facade and consider that this unlikely castle sheltered a parliament, a court and a library at different times. The mountains, white-topped in winter, close the view to the north.
t.castello di moncalieri@45.0,7.7:
The Savoy dynasty liked a country house with a view, and Moncalieri Castle, perched on a hill above the Po, was one of their favourites. Built on older foundations, it was remodelled by the family over several centuries and served as a royal residence, hosting kings, queens and a number of historic decisions. In 1849, after the defeat at Novara, King Victor Emmanuel II issued from here the Proclamation of Moncalieri, addressed to the voters, which helped steady the kingdom in a dangerous moment. The castle is part of the group of Savoy residences around Turin that UNESCO listed in 1997, and part of it is still used by the Carabinieri.

Moncalieri is a town of almost fifty thousand people on the southern edge of Turin, with a medieval centre of narrow streets climbing a hill. The riding here divides into two kinds. On the plain, you are in the commuter belt, with heavy traffic and a lot of roundabouts. On the hill behind, the roads turn into twisting lanes among vineyards, villas and chestnut woods, with views over the city and the Alps beyond. The best time is a clear morning in spring or autumn, when the mountains sit on the horizon like a white wall, and the Piedmontese light is clean and soft.

Nichelino, next door, is another large town with nearly the same population, so fuel and food are everywhere, and Turin itself is a short ride away. The area has a rich food culture, with agnolotti, bagna cauda in winter, grissini breadsticks, and local red wines like Barbera and Freisa. Sunday lunch in a trattoria on the hill is a full affair, and you should not plan to ride far afterwards. Piedmontese cooking is generous, and the portions are not meant for tourists.

The Sacro Monte di Belmonte, listed among the sacred mountains of Piedmont and Lombardy, lies a good distance north, and the pilgrim route up to its chapels is a pleasant detour for riders heading toward the foothills. Back in Moncalieri, take a short walk around the castle grounds and look back at the city. From up here, Turin lies spread out below, a grid of avenues and rooftops, with the Mole Antonelliana poking up above the haze.
t.lucerne@47.1,8.3:
Lucerne is where central Switzerland likes to show off. The town sits at the end of its lake, with the Reuss river sliding out through the middle, old houses with painted gables along the quay, and mountains on every side, Pilatus to the south and the Rigi to the east. The best-known sight is the Kapellbrücke, the Chapel Bridge, a covered wooden footbridge from the fourteenth century with a stone water tower beside it, and painted panels under the roof. A fire in 1993 burned much of it, and the bridge was rebuilt, so the paintings you see are mostly reconstructions, but the shape is old. Nearby the Lion Monument, carved into a sandstone cliff in 1821, commemorates Swiss guards who died in Paris in 1792, and Mark Twain called it the saddest piece of stone in the world.

For a motorcyclist, Lucerne is both a hub and a reward. From here the roads fan out toward the Brünig, the Susten, the Furka, the Grimsel and the Gotthard, and in the other direction toward the Entlebuch and the Emmental. The town itself is not for riding, with a dense one-way system, many bus lanes and fines that are issued without sympathy, so park in one of the garages and walk. Speed limits are strictly enforced across Switzerland, and cameras are plentiful.

The best time is late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and tour buses are fewer. In July and August the lakefront is full and the Alpine passes are open, with the highest ones usually closed from late autumn into early summer. Lake fog in winter can be thick, though the mountains above are often sunny. The air smells of water and woodsmoke when you arrive by the lake road in the evening.

At a little over four hundred metres above sea level, the town has everything, with fuel stations on every approach, workshops, hotels and restaurants. Try a Luzerner Chügelipastete, the local pastry filled with veal and mushrooms, or just a coffee at the lakeside. Prices are high, and a vignette is needed on motorways, though you will rarely use them in the mountains. Walk the old town in the evening, cross both bridges, and leave the bike for a ferry ride across the lake.
t.bellinzona@46.2,9.0:
Bellinzona is the town that guarded the Alps. It lies on a flat piece of the Ticino valley where the routes from the Gotthard, San Bernardino and Lukmanier passes come together, and whoever held it controlled the way between northern Europe and Italy. Three castles, Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro, stand on rocky hills over the old town, linked by walls, and they form a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Milanese Visconti and Sforza dukes strengthened them in the fifteenth century, before the Swiss cantons took control, and Bellinzona stayed with them ever since. The oldest, Castelgrande, rises from a rocky outcrop right in the middle of town, and you can wander its courtyards and ramparts.

Under the castles, the town has a distinctly Lombard feel, with arcades, piazzas, cafés and a Saturday market that has been drawing people from the surrounding valleys for centuries. The cooking is Ticinese, with polenta, risotto, braised meat and cheeses, and the local Merlot is dry and gentle. Italian is the language of the street, with dialect behind it.

Riding here, you are at the junction of some of the best roads in Switzerland. North lies the Gotthard and the San Bernardino, to the east Val Mesolcina, and to the west the climb toward Locarno and Lago Maggiore, while a short run south takes you over Monte Ceneri to Lugano. Roads are in excellent condition, with well-banked bends, tunnels and strict enforcement of limits. The Alpine passes are closed in winter, but the Ticino valley itself is mild, with palm trees and camellias, and spring comes early. Autumn is gentle and golden, with chestnuts falling.

Bellinzona has fuel in the town and on the approach roads, plenty of eating places, and parking near the old centre, though free spaces are scarce on market days. The motorway vignette applies to the A2 through the valley, and the road tunnels can be busy with holiday traffic at weekends in summer. Climb up to Castelgrande in the morning, when the town is quiet, have lunch in a grotto, one of those rustic stone-built restaurants with long tables, and leave time for a coffee on the piazza before riding on.
t.la saunerie@47.0,6.9:
The shore of Lake Neuchâtel, on the Swiss side, is lined with vineyards, and at the foot of them sits a thin strip of beach and reeds called La Saunerie, near the village of Auvernier. Four or five thousand years ago people lived here in houses raised on piles over the shallows, fishing, hunting, farming and keeping cattle, and the waterlogged mud preserved the timbers, tools, textiles, seeds and even bread that most archaeological sites would have lost. Together with more than a hundred similar places around the Alps, La Saunerie is part of the UNESCO listing of Prehistoric Pile Dwellings, and the underwater site is not meant to be visited, only protected, though the shore and the museum nearby tell the story.

Today the lake is a postcard of a different kind. The water is calm and green, the Jura mountains lie behind, and on a clear day the Alps are visible across the water, from the Bernese Oberland to Mont Blanc. Auvernier itself is a winegrowers' village of stone houses, fountains and cellars, and it produces the white Neuchâtel Chasselas, light, dry and often a little prickly with carbon dioxide, along with the rosé called Oeil-de-Perdrix, partridge-eye, made from Pinot Noir. Tasting rooms open to the public at weekends, and a cheese fondue in autumn is considered a duty.

The riding is delicate and rewarding. The lakeside road from Neuchâtel toward Boudry and the vineyard lanes above are smooth, narrow and full of curves, with stone walls on either side, while higher up the Chaumont road climbs through forest to a ridge with views over the lake. The Val-de-Travers and the Creux du Van, a great natural amphitheatre, lie a short ride away to the west. Traffic can be heavy at commuter hours, speed cameras are plentiful, and Swiss limits are enforced with real severity. Spring blossom and autumn harvest are the best moments, and in winter the lake often wears a layer of fog.

Auvernier is small, but Peseux, about two kilometres away, has fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, and Neuchâtel is a short ride to the east. Parking along the shore is limited, so arrive early, particularly on summer weekends when swimmers fill the beaches. Bring some Swiss francs for cellar tastings and the village cafés, which do not always accept cards. A vignette is required for the motorways, though you will not need them for this ride.
t.le marais@46.8,6.8:
At the south end of Lake Neuchâtel, below the old Roman and medieval town of Yverdon, the shore turns into a wide, flat belt of reed beds and meadow, one of the biggest areas of shoreline marsh in Switzerland. Le Marais, near the village of Yvonand, belongs to this landscape, and like many places along the lake it also belongs to the Prehistoric Pile Dwellings that UNESCO lists, because the shallows hold timbers and artefacts from villages built on stilts thousands of years ago. The remains lie under water or mud, so there is nothing to see at the spot but reeds, willows and the glinting lake, but a visit to the museum in Yverdon or Neuchâtel brings the finds to life.

Birdlife is the real draw. The reed beds shelter herons, great crested grebes, reed warblers, marsh harriers and, in winter, large flocks of ducks and coots, and the lake attracts migrating birds in spring and autumn. Yvonand's beach, the Grèves, is a long strip of sand and shingle popular with swimmers and windsurfers in summer, and quiet in other seasons. The area was drained and farmed in the nineteenth century as part of a major project that lowered the Jura lakes, which is why there is so much flat, fertile ground.

For a rider it is a gentle, enjoyable corner. The road along the south shore is flat and fast, with lakeside views in places, and small lanes lead to farms and fields. Further inland the Vaud countryside rises in rolling hills of orchards, with plenty of quiet curves. Rain falls often in the area, and fog and bise, the cold north-east wind, can make winter rides unpleasant. Weekends in summer bring crowds to the beaches, so aim for weekday mornings.

Yvonand is a village of some two thousand people with a bakery, shops and a few restaurants, and fuel is available at Yverdon-les-Bains, a town of over twenty thousand people about nine kilometres away, which also has a thermal spa, a castle built by the Savoy family and a lively market. The local specialities are perch fillets from the lake, eaten with fries, and Vaud sausage with leek, papet vaudois. Swiss traffic rules apply, with limits strictly enforced by cameras. Keep some small change for parking at the beach.
t.petite villa au bord du lac leman@46.5,6:
In the 1920s Le Corbusier built a house for his parents on the shore of Lake Geneva, and he called it, a little ruefully, the little house, la petite maison. It stands at Corseaux, just east of Vevey, and it is tiny, only about sixty square metres of living space on a strip of garden between the railway and the water. The design is a manifesto in small. A single long window frames the lake and the mountains of Savoy like a painting, the garden wall has a table and a window cut into it, and every cupboard and corner has a purpose. His mother lived there into her nineties, and he wrote a little book about it. The house is part of the UNESCO listing of his works, and it can be visited in the season, with timed guided tours.

The setting matters as much as the house. Above it, the terraces of Lavaux, a UNESCO landscape in its own right, climb the slope in steps of stone-walled vineyards, producing the Chasselas that locals drink with fondue. The lake lies wide and silver in front, and the French Alps stand across the water, with the Dents du Midi at the end. Charlie Chaplin lived in Corseaux for his last decades, in a manor house a few minutes away, and is remembered with a museum and a statue in Vevey.

The ride along the lakeshore is one of the loveliest short rides in Switzerland. The road from Vevey toward Lausanne passes through Lavaux, with the vineyard terraces on one side and the lake on the other, narrow, curving, with stone walls and tiny villages like Chexbres, Cully and Epesses. In autumn the vine leaves turn gold and red. Traffic can be thick on weekends, and the road is narrow in places, with parking at a premium. A short climb to the Rochers-de-Naye or the Jaman pass gives alpine views and a change of scene.

Chardonne, one kilometre away, is a village with a few cafés and good views, and Vevey, a lively town with a market, cafés and fuel, is a short distance away. The Alimentarium food museum and the statue of Chaplin are worth a stop. Tasting rooms in the vineyards open for walk-in visitors in summer and autumn, and a glass of wine on a terrace is hard to resist, so plan a place for the bike. Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced.
t.fortlet mainhardt herrenwiesen@49.1,9.6:
The Swabian-Franconian Forest is a country of ridges and ravines northeast of Stuttgart, and the Mainhardt area lies on its northern edge, where the hills drop to wide clearings of meadow. The Romans pushed their frontier through here in the second century, building a line of watchtowers, small forts and a wooden palisade, and at Mainhardt they placed a larger fort, with smaller fortlets such as the one at Herrenwiesen along the frontier line. A fortlet was a compact post for a handful of soldiers who watched the forest, signalled to the next tower and checked travellers at the border.

Little shows above ground, so the experience is mostly one of landscape, the straight line through the trees, a faint bank and ditch in the moss. Mainhardt itself, a village of nearly six thousand, has a local museum with Roman finds and a small archaeological park with reconstructed pieces of the frontier, and the Limes path runs through the woods for walkers and cyclists. The whole line from the Rhine to the Danube, the Upper German-Raetian Limes, is a UNESCO site.

For riders, this is among the best terrain in Baden-Württemberg. The roads through the Mainhardt Forest and over to the Löwenstein hills climb and dive through beech and spruce, with long, flowing bends, little traffic during the week and good surfaces. On sunny weekends in summer many motorcyclists come, and the local authorities have been strict on noise and speed, with cameras and sometimes random checks. Mist lingers in the valleys in the morning, and in winter ice can be a problem, particularly on shaded north-facing slopes.

Mainhardt has a petrol station, a bakery, a few inns and some small shops, and Schwäbisch Hall, a handsome medieval salt town about twenty-five kilometres away, offers more of everything, including a great open-air staircase in front of St Michael's church. Heilbronn is the larger city to the west. Try the Swabian specialities, Maultaschen, a kind of large stuffed pasta, or Spätzle with lentils, and a glass of Trollinger wine. Please respect the signs prohibiting motor vehicles on forest tracks, and keep to the public roads.
t.watchtowers wp 7 38 to 8 10 including fo:
The Odenwald Limes is famous for its stubborn straightness. For about eighty kilometres, from the Main near Miltenberg south to the Neckar near Neckarburken, the Romans drew their frontier almost as a ruler line across the wooded hills, ignoring valleys and ridges, and surveyors today still marvel at it. The watchtowers numbered 7/38 to 8/10 belong to this stretch, including a small fort, and the line here passes through the countryside around Buchen, in the Neckar-Odenwald district of Baden-Württemberg, a quiet region of beech forest, meadows and farms. The wooden towers of the first phase were later replaced by stone, and the palisade was supported by a bank and ditch that survive in the woods as a long, shallow trough.

A waymarked Limes trail follows the line for walkers and cyclists, with information boards at several points. A short distance away the pilgrimage town of Walldürn is known for the Holy Blood pilgrimage, which draws many people every year, and its great baroque basilica stands out in the landscape. The frontier here is part of the UNESCO Upper German-Raetian Limes.

For riders the Odenwald is one of the favourite regions in southern Germany. The roads climb and fall over forested ridges, with long bends and good surfaces, and the traffic is moderate on weekdays. Weekends in summer bring many motorcyclists, and there are speed limits and noise restrictions on some stretches, with cameras at the usual trouble spots. The winter brings cold, and the hills can have ice and snow. Spring and early autumn are the best times, with clear air and green or golden woods.

Buchen is a small town with nearly nineteen thousand people across its villages, with fuel stations, supermarkets, inns and bakeries, about six kilometres away, and the larger towns of Mosbach and Miltenberg are within a short ride. The local dishes include Bauland produce, with spelt, known there as Grünkern, the unripe dried spelt that is used in soups and patties. Keep to the public roads, since many forest tracks along the Limes are closed to vehicles, and bring a map for the walks. Shade is plentiful in summer, but so are flies.
t.strasbourg@48.6,7.7:
Strasbourg sits where the Rhine, France and Germany come together, and the city has been passed back and forth between them for centuries. It was a free imperial city, then French from 1681, German from 1871 to 1918, French again, German again in the Second World War, and French since 1944. The history is written into the city, in the half-timbered houses of the Petite France quarter with their steep roofs, in the German-built Neustadt and the Palais du Rhin, in the language, Alsatian, which is a Germanic dialect still spoken by older residents, and in the food, with sauerkraut, tarte flambée and Riesling. Today the city is also the seat of the Council of Europe and the European Parliament.

Over everything stands the cathedral, a Gothic mass of rose-pink Vosges sandstone with a single tall spire, which was the highest building in the world for more than two centuries. Its astronomical clock, a Renaissance machine with a parade of figures at midday, is a delight. Gutenberg worked in Strasbourg in the fifteenth century, before printing his Bible in Mainz. The historic island, the Grande Île, with the cathedral and the canal-lined quarters, is listed by UNESCO.

For riders, Strasbourg is a gateway to some very good country. To the west the Vosges rise in forested ridges, with roads like the Col du Donon and the Route des Crêtes offering long, flowing bends and views, and to the south the Route des Vins d'Alsace links wine villages with half-timbered houses and flower boxes. Across the Rhine, the Black Forest High Road above Baden-Baden is one of the great German motorcycle roads. The city centre is a different matter, with trams, cycle lanes, a pedestrian zone and a low-emission zone that requires a Crit'Air sticker for vehicles, including foreign-registered ones.

The city has all services, including many fuel stations on the outskirts and plenty of workshops. Try a choucroute garnie, a pile of sauerkraut with sausages, or a flammekueche, the Alsatian thin-crust pizza with cream and bacon, and a glass of Gewürztraminer. Parking is easiest at the car parks on the edge, with trams into the centre. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with festive Christmas markets in December that draw huge crowds, and a hot summer sun in July and August.
t.villa della regina@45.1,7.7:
Turin looks up at its hills, and on the slope above the Po stands a villa built for those who wanted the view. The Villa della Regina, the Queen's Villa, was begun in the early seventeenth century for Cardinal Maurizio of Savoy and later passed to the queens of the House of Savoy. It stands on the hillside above the city, with a baroque garden descending in terraces, a fountain and a nymphaeum, and a vineyard that still produces wine.

It was part of the circle of royal residences built around Turin by the Savoy dynasty, which UNESCO listed in 1997. The dukes of Savoy had moved their capital to Turin in the sixteenth century and set about making it a worthy capital, with grand palaces and country retreats linked by avenues. The villa had a rough time over the centuries: it was bombed in the Second World War and neglected for years, and its restoration has taken decades. Its interiors, with their Chinese-style rooms and painted ceilings, are slowly regaining their colour.

For a rider, the hill of Turin is one of the city's great pleasures. The roads that climb from the Po bank through villas and gardens are twisty and shaded, with fine views across the river toward the Alps. The road continues up toward the Basilica of Superga, a baroque church on a ridge that is the burial place of the Savoy family, with a panorama that takes in the whole plain and the snow-capped mountains beyond. On a clear winter day, with the air sharp and the Alps standing like a wall, it takes your breath for real.

The hills are also wine country. The vineyards of Turin produce Freisa and other local reds, and Piedmont is the home of Barolo, Barbaresco and the sparkling Asti. The vermouth that Turin invented in the eighteenth century is still a favourite aperitivo, and a glass on ice with a slice of orange is a fine reward.

Turin has nearly nine hundred thousand people, so fuel is everywhere, though the city centre has restricted traffic zones. Check parking before you go, and visit the villa when it is open, as hours vary.
t.palazzo carignano@45.1,7.7:
Turin has a palace whose front is bent like a sail, and it is the sort of building that makes architecture students go quiet. Palazzo Carignano was designed by Guarino Guarini, a priest, mathematician and architect, and completed in the late seventeenth century. Its brick facade swells outward in a great curve, with decoration pressed into the clay in patterns, and the building seems to breathe. Guarini was one of the great figures of the baroque, and his work in Turin, including the chapel that holds the Holy Shroud, is some of the most daring in Italy.

The palace is also important for what happened inside. The Carignano branch of the House of Savoy lived here, and in 1820 Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of a unified Italy, was born in its rooms. In 1848 the building housed the parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia, and in 1861 it hosted the first parliament of the newly united Italy, when Turin was the capital of the new state. Today it holds the National Museum of the Risorgimento, which tells the story of Italian unification, in rooms that are as much part of the exhibit as the objects.

The palace stands in the middle of Turin, a city of arcades, long straight avenues and cafés that have been serving coffee since the eighteenth century. At the Consolata, a short walk away, you can try a bicerin, a layered drink of espresso, chocolate and cream that is a local institution. Turin is also the city of vermouth, of the Egyptian Museum, which holds the biggest collection of Egyptian antiquities outside Cairo, and of football.

For motorcyclists the city centre is a place to park and walk. Turin has restricted traffic zones, called ZTL, which may fine you if you enter without permission, and the arcaded streets are lovely on foot. The best rides start at the edge of the city, up the hills toward Superga or out toward the Alps, only half an hour away.

Fuel is easy to find on the ring road and the outskirts. Book parking for the day if you plan to linger.
t.villages on hisaka island@32.8,128.9:
Hisaka is a small island just across a narrow strait from Fukue, in the Goto archipelago far out in the East China Sea west of Nagasaki, and it has a quiet, particular history. Christianity arrived in Japan in the sixteenth century, was banned by the shogunate in the early seventeenth, and ruthlessly suppressed. Yet in the countryside around Nagasaki, communities went on practising in secret for more than two hundred years, mixing Catholic prayers with Buddhist and Shinto forms in order to avoid detection. They are known as the Hidden Christians, or Kakure Kirishitan. In the late eighteenth century, the lord of the Goto islands asked for farmers from the mainland to settle his empty land, and many of those who came were secret Christians, glad to move to a remote place where they might be left alone.

The villages they founded on islands like Hisaka were deliberately modest and tucked in hollows by the sea, and UNESCO included the sites in its 2018 listing of the Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region. After the ban was lifted in 1873, many of the island Christians built churches, and the Goto islands are now dotted with white chapels with a dramatic sense of simplicity.

Reaching Hisaka takes planning. You ride your bike around Fukue, the main island, which has good roads along a rugged coast, and then make the crossing by boat from a small port. Ferry and boat schedules depend on weather, and the sea in the Goto channel can be rough, so check times locally and be prepared for changes. On Fukue itself, the riding is lovely, with grassy volcanic hills, long beaches and camellia forests, and the traffic is light. Spring brings camellias in bloom, while typhoon season in late summer and autumn can close ferries.

Fuel should be filled at Fukue, where the town of Fukue, with more than twenty-five thousand people, has stations, because smaller islands have little or none. Bring cash, since small places do not always take cards, and expect to find simple food such as fresh fish and noodles made in the island style.

When you stand on the quiet slope above the water, with a small church tucked in the trees, the story feels very close, and it is respectful to keep voices low near places of worship.
t.nagasaki shipyard mitsubishi no 3 dry do:
Nagasaki spills down its hills towards the harbour in a way that makes every drive feel like a lesson in gravity, and the Mitsubishi shipyard sits right at the water's edge, a wall of cranes and dry docks that has shaped the city for a century and a half. The Number Three Dry Dock, finished in the early twentieth century, is one of the pieces of Japan's Meiji-era industrial heritage that were added to the World Heritage list in 2015. It is stone-lined, deep and surprisingly beautiful, like a rectangular canyon cut for ships. Mitsubishi took over the yard in the 1880s, and from here came warships and liners that helped turn a closed, feudal country into an industrial power in a startlingly short time.

Industrial history here has a darker side, and Nagasaki is honest about it. The shipyard was a prime target, and the city was hit by the atomic bomb in August 1945, and many of the people who built and repaired the ships in these yards suffered through the war years. The Takashima coal mine, which the ride also visits, was part of the same story, an island whose coal fed the furnaces and whose workers included forced labourers at the time of the war. Visit with that in mind.

Your day carries on from the city to the Sotome region on the north-west coast, where the hillsides are covered in terraces and small hamlets look out over the East China Sea.
