The Sotome district is famous for the hidden Christian communities, farmers and fishermen who kept their faith alive in secret during more than two centuries of persecution, and for the elegant church built at Shitsu by the French missionary Marc Marie de Rotz in the 1880s. The road out is a good one, mostly the coast route, with views across inlets and a rhythm of gentle bends that give you time to look around.

Within Nagasaki there are fuel stations and convenience stores in plenty, and the city's food is a pleasure: champon noodles, castella sponge cake and the Chinese influence that comes from centuries as Japan's single window on the outside world. Traffic around the harbour is heavy at rush hour, and the trams, narrow lanes and steep hills reward patience. Once you are out on the Sotome coast, stations get fewer, so fill up before you leave the city.
t.hallasan natural reserve@33.4,126.5:
Hallasan rises from the middle of Jeju like a shield laid face-up on the sea. At 1,947 metres it is the highest mountain in South Korea, a massive shield volcano with a crater lake at the top, called Baengnokdam, and a ring of smaller cones on its flanks, perhaps three hundred in all, which the islanders call oreum. The upper slopes were declared a nature reserve and are part of the World Heritage listing of the island's volcanoes and lava tubes. Camellias, Korean fir, azaleas and a great variety of mosses grow in layers by altitude, and in winter the summit is under snow, a surprise on an island with palm trees at its coast.

Two roads cross the mountain and make Jeju a serious destination for riders. The 1100 Road, which reaches the pass at about 1,100 metres above sea level, links Jeju City's side to the south coast near Seogwipo, with wide bends through cedar and oak forest and a high wetland. The 516 Road runs further east and also cuts through mountain woods. Both are well surfaced, with tidy gradients, and both can be foggy and slippery at the wrong moment, and in winter they can ice up and be closed to vehicles without chains. In clear weather you look out across a green sea of trees to the ocean.

Jeju is a place with its own character. The island has its own dialect, its volcanic stone walls round the fields, and its dol hareubang, the squat stone grandfather statues that stand guard. The haenyeo, the women divers who harvest shellfish without breathing apparatus, are a local legend, and their tradition has UNESCO recognition. Tangerines grow all over the lower slopes, and you will see small roadside stands, while the local black pork and fresh fish are among the best meals in Korea.

Seogwipo is a town of about a hundred and fifty thousand people, twelve kilometres from the reserve, so fuel and lodging are plentiful, and the road network makes it easy to get everywhere. The best seasons are spring, when the canola flowers turn the roads yellow, and autumn, when the pampas grass on the oreum waves in silver. Summer brings typhoons and the monsoon, and heavy fog on the mountain. Remember that Jeju's wind is strong, so be careful on exposed coastal sections.
t.moselle bridge@49.8,6.6:
A Roman bridge still carries traffic across the Moselle at Trier, and that is not a figure of speech. The stone piers of the Romerbrucke, the old bridge in the centre of town, date to the second century AD, which makes it the oldest bridge north of the Alps, and cars, cyclists and pedestrians cross it every day on a road deck rebuilt many times over. Trier itself was founded as Augusta Treverorum in the reign of Augustus, grew into one of the great cities of the western empire, and served for a time as an imperial residence. The Emperor Constantine had a basilica built here, still standing with its great hall, and a monumental gate made of dark sandstone, the Porta Nigra, has dominated the northern entrance of the town for eighteen centuries.

These Roman monuments make up a World Heritage property with the nearby cathedral and the Church of Our Lady, and the Luxembourg day ride that uses the bridge as a stop is a straightforward one: you cross to the left bank, then follow the river valley to the border and on to the city of Luxembourg, about fifty kilometres to the west. Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818, and his birthplace on the Brueckenstrasse is a small museum, a reminder that the town has produced more than emperors.

The Moselle valley is a rider's pleasure. South and north of Trier, the river meanders in tight loops between steep vineyards, with roads that follow the water and now and then climb to a ridge for a view back. The road is mostly smooth, with gentle bends, small villages with half-timbered houses, and signs for wine estates every few kilometres. In summer the terraces are green, in autumn they turn gold and red, and at harvest the new cloudy wine, federweisser, is sold from roadside stalls. Riesling is the grape of the valley, and the slate soil gives it a mineral edge.

Trier is a city of more than a hundred thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and hotels are all easy to find. The town centre is largely pedestrianised, so park outside it and walk. Luxembourg is cheaper for fuel than Germany, a well-known habit among local drivers, so many riders cross the border with a nearly empty tank. Traffic on the autobahn and on the Luxembourg motorway is fast, so keep to the right and stay alert.
t.interlaken@46.7,7.9:
Interlaken means between the lakes, which is exactly where it sits: a flat strip of land on the Aare, wedged between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the Bernese Oberland piled up behind. On a clear day the Jungfrau fills the end of the main avenue, and visitors line up to take pictures of that view across the green lawn of the Höhematte, where paragliders land.

The town grew out of an Augustinian monastery founded in the twelfth century, and from the early nineteenth century it became one of the first mass tourist towns in Europe, attracting English visitors, artists and poets. The grand hotels along the Höheweg date from that period. Today it is the springboard for the Jungfrau region and the base for every kind of mountain activity, and it can be crowded in July and August.

For a rider, arriving here after the Grand Tour is a gentle ending. The road along Lake Thun or Lake Brienz is smooth and scenic, with lake water on one side and steep hills on the other, and it is slower than it looks because of traffic, speed cameras and tour buses. Good riding starts as soon as you leave, up the Lauterbrunnen valley with its waterfalls, or over the Brünig toward Lucerne, or up the Grimsel from Meiringen. The mountain passes in this area are open from roughly June to October.

All services are here: fuel at several stations around the edge of town, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants with every price. A population of about five thousand makes it small, but it feels bigger because of all the visitors. Parking for a motorcycle is easier than for a car, and the train station is the centre of everything. Take an evening walk by the river when the day-trippers have gone, and the town becomes much quieter.
t.appenzell@47.3,9.4:
Every year on the last Sunday in April, the people of Appenzell Innerrhoden gather in the main square, men and women, many with a ceremonial sword or a bayonet at the hip, and vote with raised hands. The Landsgemeinde is one of the last open-air assemblies of its kind in Switzerland, and it takes place in the middle of this small town, which has been the capital of the half-canton for centuries. Women only gained a vote at the cantonal level here in 1990, after a federal court ruling, which tells you something about how conservative the valley is, and also how proud.

The town is compact and pretty in a plain way. The Hauptgasse is lined with painted wooden houses with bright facades, bakeries selling Biberli, the local spiced pastries, and cheese shops. Appenzeller cheese, made with a herb brine whose recipe is jealously kept, has a strong smell and a stronger taste, and a piece in your tank bag is a fair souvenir. Tucked around the edges are meadows, dotted with farmhouses and neat stacks of wood.

Behind the town rises the Alpstein massif, with the Säntis at 2,502 metres as its summit. The riding here is some of the most enjoyable in eastern Switzerland: green hills, gentle gradients, and a web of narrow, well-surfaced roads that run up and down the valleys. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and cars are numerous, so patience is rewarded. Towards the Schwägalp, the road climbs more seriously, with proper bends and a view of the mountain.

At about 780 metres, the town sits in a mild valley. Fuel and food are easy to find, and a population around five and a half thousand supports a good range of cafes. On a fine Saturday it fills with visitors, so come early or on a weekday, and give yourself an hour to walk the old streets.
t.andermatt base@46.6,8.6:
Andermatt sits in a high, flat valley called the Urseren, at 1,444 metres, where four of the great Swiss passes meet. The Gotthard heads south to Ticino, the Oberalp runs east toward Graubünden, the Furka climbs west to the Valais, and the road north follows the Reuss down through a gorge to Lake Lucerne. People have crossed here for at least eight hundred years, ever since the Devil's Bridge was thrown across the gorge to make the Gotthard route practical, and the village has served travellers and soldiers ever since.

In 1799, the Russian general Suvorov fought his way through the gorge here with an army, losing many men, an episode remembered in a monument carved into the rock. The Swiss army has a long presence in the valley, and the barracks and fortifications are part of the scene. More recently, Andermatt has been remade with new hotels and apartments and a golf course, which sits oddly with the plain old village centre. It is still a quiet place, with a population of just over a thousand, and a good base.

For motorcyclists, this is an obvious starting point. In a single day you can do Furka at 2,429 metres, Grimsel at 2,164, Susten at 2,224 and Nufenen at 2,478, if the weather and the traffic allow, and all four are open only from about June until October, depending on snow. Starting early is important, because by ten the roads are busy and by noon the tour buses arrive. The old Tremola road, paved with cobbles, drops down the south side of the Gotthard and is a different experience, slower and bumpier.

There is fuel in the village, along with bakeries and restaurants, though prices are higher than in the lowlands. Weather changes fast at this altitude, so a warm layer and a rain jacket belong in the luggage even in July.
t.davos@46.8,9.8:
At about 1,560 metres, Davos is often called the highest town in Europe, and it is certainly one of the most unusual. It lies in a long, broad valley of Graubünden, with ski slopes on both sides, a lake, a main street that looks like a motorway, and a mix of grand old sanatoria, apartment blocks and hotels that tells the story of the town.

That story begins with air. In the nineteenth century, doctors began to send patients with tuberculosis to Davos, convinced that the thin, dry, sunny mountain air would help, and sanatoria sprang up along the valley. Thomas Mann stayed here while visiting his wife and went on to write The Magic Mountain, set in a sanatorium very much like these. The painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner also settled nearby after the First World War and painted the mountains. Skiing, and then the World Economic Forum, which meets here each January, turned a health resort into a name known around the world.

For riders, Davos is a good stop at the end of a day over the passes. The Flüela Pass, which climbs from the town toward the Engadin to a height of about 2,383 metres, is one of the finest rides in the area, and the road over the Landwasser valley toward Filisur, with its famous viaduct, is a few minutes away in the opposite direction. Roads near Davos are well surfaced, and traffic can be heavy on summer weekends. Passes are normally open from around June.

The town has about eleven thousand residents and every service you might want: fuel, supermarkets, repair shops, and a large selection of restaurants. Rooms are costly in January and in the high summer. Take a walk by the Davoser See in the evening, when the light turns the slopes pink and the town goes quiet, and you will understand why people kept coming.
t.lugano@46.0,9.0:
Lugano belongs to Switzerland by history and to Italy by temperament. It sits on the northern shore of a lake of the same name, in the canton of Ticino, with mountains, Monte San Salvatore and Monte Brè, rising straight from the water on either side. Italian is the language, the coffee is Italian, and the pace of life slows by a visible notch compared with Zurich. Ticino joined the Swiss Confederation only at the start of the nineteenth century, after centuries as subject territory of the Swiss cantons, and the town still has the atmosphere of a place with its own story.

It is the third financial centre of Switzerland, and you notice the banks along the lakefront. The old centre is much more charming than that suggests. Arcades, stone-paved lanes, the Piazza della Riforma with its cafes, and the cathedral of San Lorenzo with its Renaissance facade make a pleasant hour on foot. The Parco Ciani, along the lake, is the right place to sit in the afternoon.

Riding into Lugano can be slow, as traffic is dense and parking is hard, but once you leave, the surroundings are among the best in southern Switzerland. The roads around the lake wind through villages, with palms and chestnuts, and the road to Monte Generoso or to Morcote on the peninsula is narrow, twisting and beautiful. Spring and autumn are lovely, and in summer it can be hot and humid, with violent thunderstorms. Be careful on the mountain roads, which often have little protection at the edges.

With a population around sixty thousand, Lugano has all services: fuel at stations on the edge of town, a wide range of food, from a quick panino to a serious dinner, and hotels in every price range. If you are crossing the border to Italy, note that border queues can be long at certain times, so plan around them. Evenings by the lake are the real reward.
t.heidelberg@49.4,8.7:
Heidelberg is the place that German Romantics made famous and Mark Twain made funny. The Neckar comes out of its wooded valley here and slips past a steep old town, a stone bridge with a gate, and above everything the red sandstone ruins of the castle. Visitors have been climbing up to look at it since the early nineteenth century, when poets and painters arrived and decided it was the most beautiful ruin in Germany. The damage was done by French troops in the 1680s and 1690s, in a war of succession, and a lightning strike finished the job later, so it was never a romantic wreck by design.

The university, founded in 1386, is the oldest in Germany, and students are still part of the street life. You can see the old student prison, where unruly undergraduates were locked up as a punishment and scribbled on the walls, and in the castle cellar is the Great Tun, an enormous wine barrel. The Philosophers' Walk on the north bank gives the classic view across the river, and is worth the short climb at the end of the day.

For motorcyclists, Heidelberg is the start of the Castle Road, which runs from Mannheim to Nuremberg through the Neckar valley and the hills of the Odenwald and Franconia. Leaving town along the Neckar to the east, you pass castles on hilltops, half-timbered villages and stretches of bendy road, with the river on one side and forested slopes on the other. Weekends are busy, and speed cameras are common, so ride sensibly. Traffic inside the city is heavy, and parking is awkward, so it is better to leave the bike at a garage and walk.

The population is around 145,000, so every service is available, with fuel stations on the main approach roads and every sort of food in the old town, from student cafes to restaurants with white tablecloths. Spring, when the blossom is out, and autumn, with the colours in the Odenwald, are the best seasons.
t.siedlung forschner@48.1,9.6:
Long before the Federsee became a moor, it was a lake with villages along its edge, and the villagers built on wet ground. In the Bronze Age, people here set their houses on timber platforms and foundations at the water's edge, and as the lake slowly silted up, the waterlogged peat sealed their remains. Wooden posts, tools and pottery survived in astonishing condition. The Siedlung Forschner, named for the farmer on whose land it lay, is one of the excavated settlements, and it belongs to the group of prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps that UNESCO listed in 2011.

The landscape is gentle and a bit mysterious. The Federsee is the largest moor in Upper Swabia, a patchwork of reed beds, alder woods, wet meadows and open water, with a boardwalk that leads far into the reeds. Birds are abundant, particularly in spring and autumn, when cranes, herons and many migrants stop to feed. Mist hangs over the water in the mornings, and the whole moor smells of damp earth and plants.

In Bad Buchau, the small town at the edge of the moor, the Federsee Museum has reconstructions of Bronze Age houses and finds from the digs. Another part of the story is the Schreckensee, a lake nearby that shares the same glacial origins. The town itself is quiet, with a palace and an old convent, and the pace is slow.

The roads in Upper Swabia are a pleasure for a relaxed ride. They wander over low hills and past dairy farms, orchards and onion-domed churches, with long gentle bends and little traffic on weekdays. Many of the lanes are narrow, and tractors are common, so keep speed modest. The surface is generally good but can be muddy near fields. Bad Buchau, with about four thousand people, has fuel, a bakery and a few inns. Spring and early autumn are lovely, and the museum is open daily in season, with shorter hours in winter. A short walk on the boardwalk is worth the time, whatever the weather.
t.fort site and civil settlement of mainha:
Mainhardt sits on a plateau in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, a wooded upland east of Heilbronn, and in the second century, a Roman army unit was stationed here. The fort was built around the middle of the second century, as part of the forward movement of the frontier, to guard the Limes that ran just to the east. It held a unit of around five hundred soldiers, and a civil settlement grew up beside it, with houses, workshops, baths and inns, where families, craftsmen and traders lived.

Much of the fort is buried under fields and modern houses, but the outline can be traced, and a small museum in the village has finds from the dig, including pottery, tools and inscriptions. A stretch of the Limes with a reconstructed tower is a short walk away, and the information centre explains how the frontier worked. The site is part of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, which UNESCO listed in 2005.

The landscape is quiet and hilly, with fir and beech forests, small streams, meadows and orchards, in the region called Hohenlohe, famous for its pork, its dairy and its castles. In autumn, the leaves turn and mist lingers in the valleys. The area is rural and unhurried, and locals are friendly and keen to talk about their home.

The riding is a delight, with winding country roads through forest and over ridges, gentle bends and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays, though tractors and cyclists are common. Take care on shaded sections after rain, where damp patches and leaves can be slippery. Mainhardt is a village of about five and a half thousand, with fuel, a bakery, a few inns and a supermarket, and the larger towns of Schwabisch Hall and Murrhardt are within reach. Local food is hearty, with dumplings, roast pork and good beer. Spring brings blossom and green fields, and autumn brings colour. Take time to walk the stretch of Limes, and bring a layer in case the weather changes.
t.connecting ditch system@49.0,8.8:
The monks who founded Maulbronn were Cistercians, and they believed that a monastery should be a self-sufficient world, with its own mill, workshops, fields and, above all, its own water. The abbey, founded in 1147, is today the best-preserved medieval monastery north of the Alps, and a large part of its genius lies in the network of ponds, canals and ditches that the monks dug to collect water from the surrounding hills, drive mills and flush drains. The connecting ditch system is part of that story, a quiet piece of engineering that has lasted for nearly nine hundred years. UNESCO inscribed the monastery complex in 1993.

The abbey church and cloister are a masterpiece of the transition from Romanesque to Gothic, with a graceful fountain house, and the complex is walled like a small town. Famous residents have included the astronomer Johannes Kepler, who studied at the monastery school, and the writer Hermann Hesse, who was sent to the seminary here in 1891 at the age of fourteen. He ran away after a few months, and later used the experience in his novel Beneath the Wheel. A local legend says that Doctor Faustus performed alchemy in the tower, and the Faust tower is a popular stop.

The countryside is the Stromberg and Kraichgau, a gentle landscape of orchards, vineyards, low wooded hills and half-timbered villages. In spring, the cherry and apple blossom is lovely, and in autumn, the vineyards turn red and gold. The ditches and ponds are quiet places, with reeds, frogs and dragonflies.

Riding is easy and enjoyable. Maulbronn is close to the motorway, but the back roads around it are quiet, winding and well surfaced, and a short ride brings you to wine villages and castles. Fuel is available in town and at several stations nearby, and Maulbronn, with about seven thousand people, has bakeries, cafes and inns. Wine from the region, particularly Trollinger and Riesling, is worth a taste when you are off the bike. Visit on a weekday, and give yourself time to walk around the walls.
t.billensbacher pond@49.0,8.8:
The monks of Maulbronn did not just build a monastery. They built a waterworks. In the twelfth century the Cistercians who settled in this wooded fold of the Stromberg hills dammed the streams, dug channels and created a chain of ponds to supply the monastery with fish, to power mills and to keep the buildings dry. Billensbach Pond, a few hundred metres from the abbey walls, is one of that series of lakes, and a reminder that the beauty of the place is the product of planning.

The system was so complete that it has been recognised as part of the monastery's World Heritage status, which gives the water as much importance as the stone. Fish were a daily need for monks who avoided meat for much of the year, and the ponds could be drained, cleaned and refilled in sequence. Walking along the water today, you see reeds, ducks and the odd heron, and the surface reflects the trees that crowd the banks.

Maulbronn lies in the north-west corner of Baden-Württemberg, between Karlsruhe and Stuttgart, in a country of vineyards, orchards and small half-timbered towns. The riding around here is pleasant and calm. Roads climb gently through woodland and fall again into valleys, with enough bends to keep things interesting but nothing demanding, and the surface is generally excellent. This is wine country, so tractors are common during the harvest, and on sunny weekends you will share the road with cyclists.

The town of Maulbronn has about seven thousand people, and that is enough for fuel, shops and a few good places to eat, with Swabian dishes like Maultaschen, a sort of large ravioli, and spaetzle on many menus. The local wine is mostly Riesling, Trollinger and Lemberger. Parking near the monastery is easy, and the walk to the pond takes only a few minutes.

Early morning, with mist rising from the water, is the best moment. The ride pairs the monastery with the Jewish cemetery in Worms, which is another quiet, layered place of memory.
t.pond ro weiher@49.0,8.8:
Roßweiher simply means horse pond, which sounds humble, but the pond is part of a much grander story. It belongs to the water system created by the Cistercian monks of Maulbronn, a network of lakes and canals that fed the monastery, turned its mill wheels and kept its fish stocks full. The pond lies a little over a kilometre and a half from the abbey, on the edge of the forest, where the ground starts to rise.

The monks picked this valley in the twelfth century because it had water and shelter, and because the Cistercians liked remote, workable places. They were great engineers, and the ponds, with their dams and sluices, show how they turned a muddy valley into a productive landscape. Today the shore is quiet and green, with willows and reeds, and the surface often holds a pair of swans or a scatter of coots.

The ride that uses this stop links it with a series of watchtowers on the Roman frontier, the Limes, whose posts were scattered across this part of Germany. That gives a nice contrast, since the Romans controlled the land by watching it, and the monks transformed it by working it. The roads between are rolling and wooded, with moderate traffic, good surface and easy curves, and the wine villages along the way invite a pause.

Maulbronn is a small town, about seven thousand people, but it has a petrol station, bakeries and restaurants, so there is no problem with the basics. Regional food is hearty, with Swabian specialities such as Maultaschen, onion roast beef and spaetzle, and the wine is mostly local. If you need larger shops or a wider choice of fuel, you will find them in Mühlacker or Bretten, a short ride away.

Come in spring or autumn if you can. The woods are at their best, the water is full, and the monastery is quieter than in high summer. A morning walk around the pond before the day's ride makes a fine start.
t.large reut pond@49.0,8.8:
The Große Reutteich is one of the ponds that the monks of Maulbronn created in the folds of the hills around their abbey, and at three kilometres from the monastery it is among the more distant ones. That distance makes it quieter, with less foot traffic and more sense of being in the woods. The pond sits in a shallow valley with trees on its banks, and the surface is calm and dark under the canopy.

The Cistercians arrived here in the middle of the twelfth century, and the system of dams and ditches they built over the next generations ranks as one of the best examples of medieval water engineering in Europe. Without it the monastery could not have fed itself, and it could not have powered its mills or its workshops. The word Reut comes from a root meaning to clear land, a clue that these ponds were carved out of the forest by hand, and that clearing was part of the monks' daily work.

The countryside around is a mosaic of woods, orchards and vineyards, with the ridges of the Stromberg rising to the south and west. The riding is calm and enjoyable, with winding roads through woodland and gentle gradients, a good surface and little traffic away from the main roads. In autumn the beech and oak turn bronze and gold and the ponds reflect them, and in spring wild garlic carpets the woodland floor.

Maulbronn, with nearly seven thousand people, is the place for fuel, bread and lunch, and the town's old streets are worth a short walk after the ride. This is a part of Swabia where good food is taken seriously, so look for regional dishes such as Maultaschen in broth or lentils with spaetzle and sausage, and a glass of the local red.

The ride pairs this pond with the nearby Ödenahlen, a smaller quiet spot in the same woods, so it makes a gentle half-day loop with the monastery as its centre. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the water is full and the light is kind.
t.garten pond@49.0,8.8:
Garten means garden, and this small pond lies a few hundred metres from the abbey wall, on ground that, going by the name, belonged to the monastery's gardens. A Cistercian house was meant to be self-sufficient, so its brothers and lay helpers tilled their own ground, kept bees, grew medicinal plants and managed their orchards, and the ponds supplied water for irrigation as well as for fish.

Maulbronn was founded in the middle of the twelfth century and prospered for nearly four hundred years before the Reformation. When the Duke of Württemberg took it over in the sixteenth century, it became a Protestant school, and the building continued in use for teaching until modern times. Poets and thinkers passed through its classrooms, among them the astronomer Johannes Kepler, the poet Friedrich Hölderlin and, later, Hermann Hesse, who ran away from the seminary after a few months and turned the experience into the novel Beneath the Wheel.

The surrounding country is the kind of place that rewards slow riding. Roads climb out of Maulbronn through woods and vineyards, pass farmhouses and small hamlets, and drop again into pretty valleys, with good surface and gentle corners. Traffic is light on weekdays, and autumn brings the smell of crushed grapes and wood smoke. Spring is lovely too, with blossom in the orchards.

Maulbronn itself, with about seven thousand people, has fuel, bakeries and a good choice of restaurants, many in old half-timbered houses. The local cooking is Swabian, with sturdy dishes like Maultaschen and roast beef with onions and a plate of spaetzle on the side, and the wine, which is mostly red, is very drinkable. For anything bigger, such as a large supermarket or a choice of petrol stations, the nearby towns have more.

Walk the path along the water and look back at the abbey roofs, which give a sense of how the monks fitted their buildings to the shape of the land. It is a short, restful stroll.
t.tiefer pond@49.0,8.8:
Tiefer See sounds like a deep lake, and the Tiefer Teich beside Maulbronn takes its name from the same idea: it was one of the deeper ponds in the monks' water system, and so a place for holding fish through the winter. Medieval fish farming was a clever business. Carp and other freshwater fish were kept in successive ponds, from spawning to rearing to storage, and the monks could drain and harvest each one in turn. Since the Church forbade meat on many days of the year, a reliable fish supply was essential.

The pond lies about a kilometre from the monastery, in the wooded valley that the Cistercians chose for its water and its seclusion. They were organised, quiet and highly practical builders, and the dams, ditches and sluices they left are now part of the World Heritage Site that includes the abbey. A walk here lets you see the other half of the monastery, the working landscape that fed the brothers, rather than the stone church and cloister that visitors usually come for.

Around the water you find willows, alders and reed fringes, with dragonflies skimming the surface in summer and herons standing at the edges. In winter the trees are bare and the sky is the colour of pewter, and the pond often freezes, which has a stark beauty of its own. The ride there is gentle, through woodland and past vineyards, on quiet lanes with good surface and easy corners.

Maulbronn has fuel, a bakery and a handful of restaurants, and it is only a few minutes away. A large Swabian lunch is hard to resist: try the local Maultaschen, or a plate of Zwiebelrostbraten, roast beef with fried onions, with a glass of the red from the surrounding hills. For anything more specialised, Mühlacker and Bretten are not far.

Early morning is best, when mist still lies on the water and the village is quiet. This pond is paired with Ödenahlen, a nearby hamlet in the same wooded hills, so it works nicely as the first stop on a short loop.
t.binsen pond@49.0,8.8:
Binsen means rushes, and the Binsenteich is named for the plants that line its edges. It is one of the smaller ponds in the system that the monks of Maulbronn created, about one and a third kilometres from the abbey, and it is one of the best for watching wildlife. Reeds and rushes, with their pale green stems, create a thick fringe, and behind them the water is full of life, with ducks, coots and moorhens in the open, and in summer dragonflies of several kinds.

The monks managed these ponds for fish and water, and the fringing plants are part of how such a pond looks and works. The Cistercian order came to this valley in the twelfth century and turned a boggy forest into a working landscape, and their water engineering is one of the reasons the abbey is a World Heritage Site. What strikes you on a quiet morning is how natural it all looks, though everything here was planned.

The ride to the pond leads through wooded hills, with a gently winding road, little traffic, and a good surface. This corner of Baden-Württemberg is soft country, with the Stromberg ridge close by, vineyards on the sunny slopes and small villages with half-timbered houses. Bends are easy and there are few steep gradients, so it suits a relaxed pace, and in late summer the hedgerows are full of blackberries.

Maulbronn offers the usual services: a petrol station, bakeries, a few cafés and restaurants, and a small supermarket. Try the local pastries and the dark Swabian bread, and a cup of coffee on the monastery square is a pleasure. The old town is a good place to wander, with half-timbered houses, a fountain and the great abbey walls around it, and a visit to the monastery itself is a must on any day in the area.

For birds, early morning or evening is best. Bring binoculars if you have them, and keep to the paths, since the shores are soft and the plants are fragile. The ride links the pond with the Old Jewish Cemetery at Worms, a place of a very different kind of memory.
t.lower pond hilsenbeuertal@49.0,8.8:
Valleys in this part of Swabia often have names that end in -tal, and the Hilsenbeuertal is one of them, a small wooded valley next to Maulbronn through which a stream runs down toward the town. The Lower Pond, as its name admits, has an upper sister further up the valley, and the two work as a pair. It lies only three hundred metres from the abbey, and it is close enough that you can see the church roof through the trees.

This was how the monks planned things: ponds placed one above another on a stream, each with a dam and a sluice, so that the flow could be controlled, the water cleaned and the fish harvested in order. Such a system needs constant maintenance, and keeping the dams sound would have been a regular chore. Water drove mills and filled fishponds, and it was part of the daily rhythm of work and prayer.

In the twelfth century the Cistercians founded Maulbronn, and its buildings are among the best-preserved medieval monastery complex north of the Alps, with a church, cloister, refectory and fortified walls all surviving. UNESCO listed the abbey in 1993, and the water system is part of the story. A walk along the stream is a good way to see the setting without the crowds.

Riding here is relaxed. The roads wind through woods and fields, with small climbs and descents, a smooth surface and light traffic. In spring the orchards bloom white and pink, in autumn the vineyards are red and gold, and the air smells of leaves and wine. It is not a ride for speed, but it is a pleasure for anyone who likes to look around.

With around seven thousand people, Maulbronn has everything a rider needs: fuel, food, a bakery and a place to sit with a coffee. The speciality of the region is Maultaschen, large pasta pockets filled with meat and spinach, which are served in broth or fried with egg, and they are a good meal after a morning in the damp air.

The ride that includes this pond ends at the Old Jewish Cemetery in Worms, so you pass from a Christian monastery to one of Europe's oldest Jewish burial grounds, which is a striking pairing.
t.sickinger pond@49.0,8.8:
The ponds around Maulbronn outlived the monks who dug them, and the Sickinger pond, about a kilometre from the abbey, is a good place to think about that. When the Reformation reached Württemberg, the monastery's story changed, but the water and the woods stayed, and the ponds went on serving whoever held the land.

The abbey itself changed hands in the sixteenth century. The Dukes of Württemberg took over the monastery in 1534 as they introduced the Reformation, and in 1556 it became a Protestant monastery school, training pastors and teachers. The buildings stayed in use rather than falling into ruin, which is a big reason why Maulbronn is so well preserved today. The ponds, too, remained in use for fish and water supply for centuries.

The pond lies in woodland, with a calm surface and a ring of old trees. It is a good place to sit for a few minutes with a thermos, and to listen to the sounds of the wood: wind, birds, perhaps a woodpecker. The road to it is a quiet lane with a good surface, gentle corners and little traffic. The hills around are covered in forest and vineyards, with several viewpoints and small villages nearby.

For fuel and food, the town of Maulbronn is only a few minutes away, with about seven thousand people and the usual services. The region is wine country, so a glass of Trollinger or Lemberger with a plate of Swabian food is a natural end to the day. The monastery itself is a short ride from the pond and well worth the entry fee, particularly the cloister and the fountain house.

The ride pairs this pond with the Old Jewish Cemetery in Worms. Late spring and early autumn are the most comfortable seasons for the ride, with mild air and soft light.
t.maulbronn monastery complex@49.0,8.8:
Maulbronn is what a medieval monastery looks like when nobody has knocked it down. Cistercian monks founded the abbey in the middle of the twelfth century, in a damp, wooded hollow of the Stromberg hills that no one else wanted, and the church, cloister, refectory, fountain house and encircling wall have survived to an extent that is rare north of the Alps. UNESCO listed it in 1993, calling it the most complete and best-preserved medieval monastic complex in Europe, and a walk through its courtyards shows why.

The church began as Romanesque and was finished in an early Gothic style, and the porch at the entrance, known as the Paradise, is an elegant piece of transitional architecture. The cloister and its fountain house, where the monks washed before meals, are among the finest of their kind, with vaults that spring from slender columns. Behind the walls stands a tower associated with the legend of Doctor Faust, the alchemist said to have worked here, and local lore has made the most of it.

For a rider, Maulbronn is a pleasant place to arrive. The approach roads climb through vineyards and woodland, with gentle bends and a good surface, and the town is small enough to feel intimate. Parking is available near the monastery, and you walk in through a gate in the old wall. The countryside around, the Stromberg-Heuchelberg nature park, is mild, green and unhurried, and it rewards a slow ride along the lanes between villages.

The town has about seven thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and a number of restaurants in half-timbered houses, and its wine, mostly red, is good. A Swabian lunch of Maultaschen or roast beef and onions on the square outside the abbey is a pleasure on a fine day. For larger shops and more petrol stations, the nearby towns of Mühlacker and Bretten are only a short ride away.

The visit takes a couple of hours, and the abbey is quietest in the morning or late afternoon. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and in winter the interior can be cold, so wear something warm under your riding gear. The ride pairs the monastery with the nearby ponds and the quiet woods of the Ödenahlen.
t.monastery@49.0,8.8:
The refectory at Maulbronn is the room that shows what the monks' life was like, a long, vaulted hall where the brothers ate in silence while one of them read aloud. It is just one room in a monastery whose buildings run from the twelfth to the sixteenth century, and the whole thing is enclosed by a high wall with towers and a gatehouse, like a small fortified town. This is the best-preserved medieval monastery north of the Alps, and when you walk through the gate you step into a world that is very nearly intact.

The Cistercians were an order of reformers who wanted a stricter and simpler life than the older Benedictine houses, and they chose remote valleys for their foundations. Maulbronn's founders arrived in the 1140s, and they brought with them a style of building that was plain, rational and beautiful. The order spread across Europe, and the layout of its monasteries, with church, cloister, dormitory and refectory arranged in a standard plan, is repeated from Spain to Poland.

After the Reformation, the monastery became a school, and the dormitories and classrooms are still in use as a seminary, which means that students walk the cloister to this day. Hermann Hesse spent a few months here as a boy and ran away, and Hölderlin and Kepler studied here in earlier centuries. It is a place where learning has been practised for nearly a thousand years.

The ride out here is a pleasure. The lanes climb through vineyards and woods, the villages are tidy and the surface is good. On a weekday morning you share the roads with tractors and cyclists. The town of Maulbronn, with a bit under seven thousand people, has fuel, food and a few small hotels, and the cafés around the monastery wall are a good place for a pause. Try the local Riesling or a glass of red.

The ride combines this monastery with Ödenahlen, a quiet corner of woodland nearby. Come early to beat the tour groups, and allow time to linger in the cloister, where the stone seems to hold the cool air even on a hot day.
t.small reut pond@49.0,8.8:
Small as it is, the Kleiner Reutteich is the smallest of the Maulbronn ponds on these rides, and at three kilometres from the monastery it sits well out in the woods. The pond has a quiet, secluded air, with trees reaching over the water and a soft, muddy margin. It belongs to the same water system as the other ponds, and like them it was created by the Cistercians in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, but its smaller size gives it a more private feel.

Few people come this far, so you are likely to have it to yourself. In spring the woods around it are full of birdsong, and in summer dragonflies patrol the surface. In autumn the leaves float on the surface, gold and brown, and the air smells of damp earth and mushrooms.

The ride that includes this pond goes on to the Roman fort site and civilian settlement at Welzheim, on the Limes, the frontier of the Roman Empire, so you pass from medieval monks to Roman soldiers. Welzheim lies to the east, in the Swabian-Franconian Forest, and it has a reconstructed fort gate and the remains of a bathhouse. The road between runs through woodland and farmland, with long easy bends and little traffic, and it makes a pleasant afternoon ride.

Near the pond, the roads are quiet lanes with good surface, and you may meet cyclists and walkers, so go slowly. The nearest services are in Maulbronn, with about seven thousand people, where you will find fuel, bakeries and restaurants, and the Swabian specialities of Maultaschen and spaetzle. A coffee and a slice of cake near the monastery is a good reward after a woodland walk.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the morning is better than the afternoon, with softer light and fewer people. Wear shoes you do not mind getting muddy, because the path to the shore is not always dry.
t.col du galibier@45.1,6.4:
The Galibier is the big one, and it knows it. At 2,642 metres this is one of the high gates of the French Alps, the saddle where the Maurienne valley to the north hands you over to the Guisane and the Briançonnais to the south, and the road crosses it by way of a short tunnel under the actual crest, or, for those who want the proper view, by the final few hundred metres of open hairpin that go over the top. The summit marker stands on the old crest, with a monument to Henri Desgrange, the founder of the Tour de France, who first sent the race over this pass in 1911. Cyclists still turn up in swarms to touch the sign, so expect lycra and an unhurried pace.

From the north you climb from Valloire, past the Col du Télégraphe, a gentle warm-up through forest, and then the landscape strips off its trees and turns to bare scree, rock and sky. From the south you rise out of the Guisane valley through Le Monêtier-les-Bains and the stunted larch above the village, then across the broad bowl below the Lautaret. The south side is the more open and fast, the north the more intimate, but both are well graded, wide enough for a big bike and rewarded with views toward the Meije and the glaciers of the Écrins when the cloud allows.

Do not treat it as an all-year road. The Galibier closes with the winter snow and typically only opens around early summer, then shuts again around October, so check before planning anything near the edges of the season. The weather can change in twenty minutes at this height, so put on a layer at the top even if you rode up in a T-shirt, and watch for wet patches in the shaded hairpins where snow lingers into July.

Valloire and Le Monêtier are small villages, so if the tank is anywhere near half, fill up in the valley before you start; the nearest bigger town to the north is Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, with Briançon beyond the Lautaret on the other side. At the top there is usually a seasonal café or refreshment stand in the warm months, which does the job for a hot drink and a sandwich, but do not count on it being open early in the day.

Stay a few minutes. The air is thin, the colours are chalk, rust and green, and the marmots near the road whistle at you like annoyed neighbours.
t.grenoble@45.2,5.7:
Grenoble is the capital of the French Alps in everything but title, a big, studenty, slightly industrial city set in a flat basin where three valleys meet, the Isère, the Drac and the Grésivaudan. The mountains here are not a backdrop but a wall: the Vercors on one side, Chartreuse on another, Belledonne on the third, so that wherever you look in the city there is rock rising above the rooftops. It is the end of the Route Napoléon in this case, the road Napoleon took in March 1815 when he landed from Elba and marched north to reclaim power, and the story goes that the people of Grenoble opened the gates to him and the army simply melted into his ranks.

Arriving from Sisteron by that route is the best part of the day. The road comes down through the Alpine foothills, over the Col Bayard near Gap and then down the Valbonnais and the Matheysine, a landscape of plateaus and lakes and quiet farms, before you reach the Drac and the first of the city's outskirts. The final miles are far less romantic: ring roads, dual carriageways and a lot of cars. Grenoble has a reputation for traffic jams at rush hour and for trams that cross your path without warning, so keep your eyes open and avoid the western ring road on a Friday evening.

For a rider this is a place for services, not for corners. Petrol, food and a bed are all easy here, with a large old town of pedestrian streets and café terraces around the Place Grenette and the Isère quays. The cable-car bubbles to the Bastille fort rise above the river and give the best view of the whole basin, with the Vercors and Belledonne lit up in the late afternoon, though check the opening times of the cable car before planning around it.

Grenoble was also the city of the 1968 Winter Olympics, and bits of that era survive in the concrete architecture and the sports facilities. It has a strong tradition of science and technology, with research institutes and a university that bring in a young, international crowd, and the food scene reflects it, with Savoyard cheese dishes alongside everything else. Walnuts from the surrounding hills are a local pride, and a walnut tart or a gratin dauphinois is a decent excuse for a longer stop than you planned.
t.fortified city of bergamo@45.7,9.7:
Bergamo has two cities stacked on one hill. The Città Alta, the upper town, sits inside a ring of sixteenth-century walls built by the Republic of Venice, which ruled here for more than three centuries and wanted a stronghold against Milan. The walls run for about six kilometres and are pierced by gates, and UNESCO recognised them in 2017 as part of the Venetian Works of Defence between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Below lies the Città Bassa, the modern town of broad avenues and shopping streets, and a funicular links the two, a short, steep ride worth taking for its own sake.

The old town is a delight. Cobbled lanes lead to the Piazza Vecchia, a handsome square surrounded by medieval and Renaissance buildings, including a tall civic tower whose bell still rings in the evening. Next door, the Colleoni Chapel, a lavish Renaissance mausoleum with a pink and white marble facade, was built for a Venetian mercenary captain and is among the finest in Lombardy. The composer Gaetano Donizetti was born in Bergamo, and the dialect, food and humour are more earthy than those of Milan, which is only an hour's drive away.

For a motorcyclist the city is an excellent start or finish. The old town has a limited traffic zone, so park at the bottom or in the designated areas and take the funicular or walk up. From the lower town, riding north takes you quickly into the Bergamo Alps, with the Val Brembana, the Val Seriana and the roads toward the Lake Iseo and Lake Como shores within an hour. The passes, such as San Marco and Presolana, give long, well-surfaced climbs with plenty of bends and views of limestone peaks, and in summer they are popular with riders from across Lombardy. In spring and autumn the foothills are quieter.

Bergamo is a city of over a hundred thousand, so fuel, food and coffee are never an issue, and the ring road has supermarkets and petrol stations at every junction. Ponteranica, on the edge, is a small town with a few bars. The food is hearty: polenta with game or cheese, casoncelli, a stuffed pasta with butter and sage, and stracciatella, an ice cream flavour said to have been invented here. For a sweet, try a polenta e osei, a sponge cake covered in marzipan and chocolate birds.

Come on a clear day for the view from the walls across the plain to the Alps.
t.church of our lady@49.8,6.6:
Trier's Liebfrauenkirche stands right beside the cathedral, and from the outside it looks as if two churches had been squeezed onto a plot that was too small. It is one of the earliest Gothic churches in Germany, built in the thirteenth century, and its plan is startling: not a long nave but a Greek cross set inside a circle, with twelve rounded recesses, so that from above it looks like a flower with twelve petals. The French influence is clear, as the builders borrowed from the cathedrals of Champagne and the Île-de-France, and the result is a light, airy interior with slender columns and tall windows that feel far from the dark Romanesque of the neighbouring cathedral.

The twelve petals are sometimes read as the twelve apostles, and the cross at the centre as Christ, a nice symbolic design that has made the church a landmark of medieval architecture. It forms part of the UNESCO listing of the Roman monuments, Cathedral and Liebfrauenkirche of Trier. Inside, the effect is of calm and balance, and the stained glass casts coloured patches on the stone floor on a bright day. Opening times follow church services, and it is a good idea to check them.

Trier is the oldest city in Germany, founded by the Romans in the first century BC, and sits in the Moselle valley near the border with Luxembourg. The old centre is compact and mostly pedestrian, so parking the bike near the edge and walking is easiest. Fuel, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants are plentiful, since Trier has a hundred thousand people, with a university and a young population. The Hauptmarkt, with its market cross and colourful houses, is just a few steps from the church.

The best riding begins just outside the city. The Moselle valley winds in great loops between steep vineyards, with slate terraces climbing the hillsides, and roads run along both banks. The surfaces are good, the bends gentle, the scenery lovely, and the main hazards are camper vans, cyclists on the riverside path and slow tractors during the harvest. The Hunsrück and Eifel uplands on either side offer more demanding roads, with tight forest bends and farmland views.

Taste a glass of Riesling from the slate slopes, as the Moselle wines are among the most refined in Germany, then ride on.
t.porta nigra@49.8,6.6:
The Porta Nigra is the largest Roman city gate north of the Alps, and it has been standing, in one form or another, for roughly eighteen centuries. Built in the second century from huge blocks of sandstone cut so precisely that they were held together with iron clamps instead of mortar, it once formed the northern entrance to Augusta Treverorum, the Roman city on the Moselle. The stone has weathered to a dark grey, almost black, which gave rise to the medieval name, the black gate, though the Romans themselves would have seen a pale, honey-coloured building.

It survived because of a hermit. In the eleventh century a Greek monk, Simeon, walled himself into the east tower and lived there until his death, and after he was made a saint, the gate was turned into a church, which saved it from being dismantled for building stone like so many other Roman buildings. Napoleon had the church fittings removed in the early nineteenth century, restoring something closer to the original look. You can climb the towers and walk through the upper galleries, which give views across the old town, and a small admission fee is charged.

The gate sits in a pedestrian zone, and Trier's centre is best seen on foot. Leave the bike at one of the parking areas near the edge of the old town and walk along the Simeonstrasse, where cafés and bakeries line the way to the main market. With over a hundred thousand inhabitants, Trier has no shortage of fuel, shops and places to eat, and a university keeps the evenings lively.

The surroundings are a draw for riders. Vineyards cover the steep hillsides of the Moselle, and roads wind along the river toward Bernkastel-Kues and Cochem, with views at every bend. In autumn the vines turn gold and red, and the hillsides glow. Spring brings blossom, and summer is warm, though weekends see heavy traffic.

Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818, and a house on the Brückenstrasse, now a museum, is a short walk from the gate. The city makes a good base for a few days, especially if you also want to cross into Luxembourg, which is only a short ride away.
t.ampitheatre@49.7,6.6:
On a hillside on the eastern edge of Trier, a great oval bowl cut into the slope was once the place where the Roman city went to watch gladiators and wild animals. The amphitheatre was built around the end of the first century or the early second century AD, and could hold roughly twenty thousand spectators, which was probably more than the population of the town at the time. Its arena is about seventy metres long, and beneath the sand floor ran a cellar with machinery and cages used to raise animals and scenery into view.

The Emperor Constantine is said to have had captured Frankish chieftains thrown to wild beasts here after a victory in the early fourth century, a story told in the sources and probably true in outline. In the Middle Ages, the amphitheatre, like many Roman ruins, was used as a quarry, and only the earth banks and the vaulted passages survived. Today you can walk into the arena, descend into the cellars, and sit on the grassy slopes, while concerts and a gladiator show are held there in the summer. A modest entrance fee is charged, and the site is closed on certain days in winter.

It is a place that feels more atmospheric than monumental. You enter through a stone tunnel and emerge into a green hollow with a view of vineyards on the hills above, and the quiet is a surprise after the town. From here, a short ride leads up through the vineyards to a viewpoint overlooking Trier and the Moselle, with the city's towers laid out beneath you.

For riding, the hills around Trier are ideal. The roads wind through the vineyards of the Ruwer and Saar valleys, which produce some of the best Riesling in Germany, and farther south the roads climb into the quiet forests of the Hunsrück. Irsch, a small village a few kilometres away, has little in the way of services, so the city is the best place for fuel, food and coffee.

The weather can be changeable, with fog in the valley in the autumn mornings, and warm, sunny days in summer. Spring blossom in the orchards is a bonus. Try a plate of regional food, such as Viez, an apple cider, or Saarland-style sausages, in a Trier tavern near the market.
t.place stanislas@48.7,6.2:
Place Stanislas in Nancy is the work of a king without a kingdom. Stanislas Leszczyński, twice king of Poland and father-in-law of Louis XV, was given the Duchy of Lorraine in 1737 as a consolation prize, and he spent the rest of his life rebuilding its capital. The great square that bears his name, laid out in the 1750s by the architect Emmanuel Héré, links the old medieval town with the newer quarter, and it is one of the most harmonious public spaces in Europe. Pale stone buildings with curved corners stand around a wide cobbled space, and a statue of the duke stands in the middle.

The glory of the square is its ironwork. Gilded wrought iron gates and railings, made by the master smith Jean Lamour, enclose the fountains in the corners and gleam in the sun, with elaborate scrolls and flowers and tiny details that reward close inspection. The town hall, the opera and the fine arts museum surround the square, and an arch at one end leads on to the Place de la Carrière, a tree-lined promenade that leads to the ducal palace. UNESCO listed the three squares in 1983.

Nancy is also a centre of Art Nouveau, as the Nancy School, led by glassmaker Émile Gallé, became a force in the decorative arts around 1900. The city is full of curving balconies, floral windows and ironwork, and a museum devoted to the school is housed in a villa on the edge of town. In the evenings the square is lit and cafés spill out onto the terraces.

Practically, Nancy is a city of over a hundred thousand, so fuel, supermarkets and parking for motorcycles are all easy, though the centre is largely pedestrian and the underground car parks are the best option. Malzéville, on the hill across the canal, has quieter streets. Lorraine's food is distinct: quiche lorraine, macarons, the sweet bergamot candies of Nancy, and spirits made of the golden mirabelle plum.

The roads of Lorraine offer fine riding. To the south-east, the Vosges mountains begin, with wooded hills, lakes and passes, while to the west the rolling plain of the Meuse gives quiet country roads. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, since winters are cold and damp.
t.aula palatina@49.8,6.6:
Constantine built big. The Aula Palatina, which the Romans called the basilica, was the throne hall of the emperor's palace in Trier in the early fourth century, and it is still the largest single-room space to survive from antiquity. It is a plain brick box nearly seventy metres long, about twenty-seven wide and thirty-three high, with a huge apse at the end and tall windows set in two rows, and when it was finished it must have been dazzling, with marble on the walls, mosaics on the floor and heating under the floor. An emperor sitting at one end would have appeared tiny to petitioners entering from the far end, which was the idea.

Trier was at that time one of the capitals of the Roman Empire, a residence of emperors in the fourth century, and Constantine himself lived here in the years before he became sole ruler. The city had a palace, baths, a circus, an amphitheatre and a vast wall, and the remains are among the finest outside Italy. UNESCO listed the Roman monuments of Trier in 1986. The basilica was later used as a palace by the archbishops, and in the nineteenth century it was restored as a Protestant church, the Church of the Redeemer, which is why the interior is so plain and bright, with just a modern altar and a large organ.

The acoustics are good and concerts are held there regularly, and the whitewashed walls give the space a clean, severe beauty. Entry is usually free outside services, and it can be quiet and still. Next door, the Electoral Palace, a pink rococo building with a formal garden, offers a pleasing contrast.

In practical terms, you are in the heart of the old city, so leave the bike at an edge car park and walk. Trier has all services, and a wide choice of cafés near the Konstantinplatz, with a hundred thousand people to support them. Beyond the city, the Moselle valley and the Eifel provide excellent riding, with winding roads, vineyards and forests.

Visit in spring or autumn, when the light on the brick is warm and the tourists are fewer, and try a glass of local Riesling.
t.cathedral@49.8,6.6:
Trier's cathedral is the oldest church in Germany, and the walls prove it. At its heart stand the bricks of a Roman building, a great hall from the early fourth century, which Constantine's mother, Helena, is said to have given to the Christian community. Around that core, bishops and archbishops added, rebuilt and altered over sixteen centuries, so that the cathedral today is a patchwork of Romanesque towers, a Gothic cloister, baroque chapels and a Roman brick outer wall in places. From outside the mix looks puzzling, and from inside it is magnificent.

The cathedral's great treasure is the Holy Robe, the garment said to have been worn by Christ at his crucifixion, which is kept in a case and shown to the public only on rare occasions, drawing large crowds of pilgrims. Whatever one thinks of the relic, the tradition behind it is old, and the cathedral has been a place of pilgrimage for centuries. The archbishops of Trier were also prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire, which means they helped choose the emperor, and their tombs fill the aisles.

The Liebfrauenkirche, the neighbouring Gothic church, shares the UNESCO listing, and the two buildings stand together. The cathedral treasury and museum hold gold, ivory and manuscripts, but opening hours vary and are worth checking.

The old city centre is largely pedestrianised, so find a place for the bike on the edge and walk the short distance. Fuel, food and coffee are easy in Trier, which has a hundred thousand people and the usual array of supermarkets and bakeries. The Moselle riverbank is a pleasant place to walk and the old Roman bridge, which still carries traffic on its Roman piers, crosses the river a few minutes away.

For riding, take a day to follow the Moselle upstream or downstream, or climb into the Eifel, where winding roads cross wide plateaus and drop into wooded valleys. Fog can fill the valleys in autumn and winter. Spring and summer are best, though weekends bring more traffic. Local bakeries sell rich cakes and pretzels, and a late afternoon coffee in the cloister garden of a nearby café is a good break.
t.roman monuments@49.8,6.6:
When people say Trier is the Rome of the north, they mean it more literally than you might think. For about a century, from the late third to the late fourth century, the city was one of the seats of the Western Roman Empire, a place where emperors lived and ruled, and the Romans left a collection of monuments that is among the best north of the Alps. UNESCO listed them in 1986, and the group includes the Porta Nigra, the amphitheatre, the imperial baths, the barbarathermen, the Aula Palatina, the Roman bridge, and the cathedral's Roman core. Some stand in the centre, others on the edge, and a good plan is to walk between them with a map.

The Roman bridge is a favourite of mine. Its stone piers date from the second century, and although the upper parts have been rebuilt, it still carries traffic across the Moselle, which makes it the oldest bridge in Germany still in use. Upstream, at Igel, a tall sandstone column covered in carved reliefs, the Igel Column, was set up by a family of wealthy cloth merchants as a family tomb monument, with scenes of trade, farming and banquets that give a picture of daily life in a Roman province.

For a motorcyclist, Trier's old city has restrictions, so the bike is best left at a car park at the edge. The Moselle valley road is a classic, running along the water between vineyards, with castles on the ridges and villages of half-timbered houses, and the surface is generally good. Be careful on the narrow sections in towns, where parked cars and delivery vans can block the way, and watch for slippery wine-slate on the verges in autumn.

All the services of a hundred-thousand-strong city are on hand, with fuel on the ring roads and supermarkets close to the centre. The best lunch is a plate of local sausage, Riesling and a pretzel in a courtyard in the old town.

Spring and autumn are the finest seasons, and in December the Christmas market under the Porta Nigra draws crowds.
t.imperial baths@49.7,6.6:
The Kaiserthermen were meant to be the grandest bathhouse in Roman Gaul, and the builders ran out of steam before they finished. Begun in the early fourth century, probably under Constantine, as part of the imperial palace quarter, the complex was never completed as a bath, and instead was converted into a barracks, then a fort, and later part of the medieval town wall. What remains is a set of enormous brick walls, apses and arches that rise high above the surrounding lawns, with a facade that is unmistakably Roman in its scale.

The best part is underground. Beneath the bath halls a network of service tunnels, built to let slaves feed the furnaces and carry fuel and water without being seen by the bathers, still survives, and you can walk through them, bending your head in the dim light under arched brick ceilings. It gives a rare sense of the machinery behind Roman luxury, where heat from wood fires flowed through hollow floors and walls to warm the rooms above. The baths belong to the UNESCO group of Roman monuments in Trier, and a small entrance fee is charged, with opening hours that vary by season.

A short walk away lie the older Barbarathermen, which were larger still in the second century but were largely dismantled for building stone, so the Kaiserthermen are the better place to appreciate the scale.

For the rider, Trier is a place to park and walk. The centre is compact, the old streets are busy and partly closed to traffic, and the best approach is to leave the bike in a car park near the Moselle and stroll. The city has everything a traveller might need, from fuel to supermarkets to cafés, with a hundred thousand inhabitants. The ride out is rewarding, whether along the Moselle toward Luxembourg, with vines on one side and the river on the other, or into the Saar valley, where quieter roads lead past small wine villages.

Summer weekends fill the Moselle road with cyclists and camper vans, so a weekday morning is a better choice. Autumn brings the grape harvest and golden light. If you have an hour to spare, the Rheinisches Landesmuseum, close by, holds mosaics, tombstones and a famous carved relief of a wine ship, which captures the spirit of the Roman Moselle better than any guidebook.
t.col du cormet de roselend@45.7,6.7:
The Cormet de Roselend is the pass of cheese and water. It lies in the Beaufortain massif, between the town of Beaufort and the valley of the Isère, and for much of the climb you are riding through the pastures where the cows that make Beaufort cheese spend their summers, wearing bells and grazing on alpine flowers. The cheese, which is aged in the valley, is one of the most prized in France, and it is the reason this valley is prosperous and well kept. A wheel, with its distinctive concave edge, is sold in nearly every village.

The other half of the story is the artificial lake. Below the pass, at about 1,550 metres, the Roselend dam, built in the early 1960s, flooded a whole valley and turned it into a vast turquoise reservoir, and the old village disappeared under the water. A tiny stone chapel, the Chapelle Notre-Dame de la Visitation, was moved to the shore and now sits on the edge, with the mountains in the background, one of the most photographed little buildings in the French Alps. The road runs along the shore for several kilometres before the final climb to the pass at 1,967 metres.

On a motorcycle, this is a big, open and generous road. From Beaufort, the climb is gradual, with wide bends and good visibility, then there is a series of hairpins up toward the col. On the other side, toward Bourg-Saint-Maurice, the descent runs down the Isère valley with views of Mont Blanc on a clear day, and the road gets narrower and more twisting. The surface is generally good, though the cold winters take their toll, and the pass is closed from about late October to early June. Cyclists climb this in large numbers, so be ready for them around the bends.

Beaufort has fuel and a couple of shops, and Bourg-Saint-Maurice, thirteen kilometres from the pass, is the nearest larger town with all the services. The best time is June, when the meadows are in flower and the cows are just being driven up, or September, when the air is clear and cold, and the light on the lake is a pale gold.
t.col de l iseran@45.4,7.0:
The Iseran is the roof of the Alps, as far as paved passes go. At 2,764 metres, it is the highest of the great Alpine passes, a shade above the Stelvio, and the road over it was opened in 1937 to link the Tarentaise valley with the Maurienne, a feat of engineering that took years of work in short summers. It goes through the heart of the Vanoise National Park, France's first, created in 1963 to protect the ibex, which had been almost wiped out by hunters, and the park's work has been a success, as there are thousands now.

From Val-d'Isère, the road climbs through bare, glacier-carved terrain in big, open hairpins, with the peaks of the Vanoise glittering above, and the grass gives way to rock and old snow. The summit is a small, windy plateau with a stone chapel and a monument, and a marker to pose with. Beyond it, the south side drops towards Bonneval-sur-Arc, one of the loveliest villages in France, with stone houses and slate roofs. The surface is variable, and even in summer, you can find snow, ice or cold fog at the top. In June and often in autumn, the road may be closed by snow, and it is generally shut from about November until June.

Weather at this altitude is no joke. Temperatures can be ten degrees below those in the valley, and storms form quickly in the afternoon. A windproof layer and warm gloves are essential. On a clear day, however, the visibility is spectacular, with the Grande Casse, the highest point entirely within the Vanoise, and the glaciers of the Haute Maurienne visible on the south. You may well see marmots, and if you are lucky, ibex on the rocks.

Fuel is available in Val-d'Isère and Tignes on the northern side, and Bourg-Saint-Maurice, thirty kilometres away, has the full range of services. On the southern side, the villages are tiny, so make sure you have enough fuel for the descent to Lanslebourg. In season, a small stand near the top may sell hot drinks, but do not rely on it. Ride early, avoid weekend crowds, and remember that on this one, the point is the height.
t.voiron@45.4,5.6:
Voiron sits where the Isère valley meets the foothills of the Chartreuse, a manufacturing town of twenty-two thousand people about twenty-five kilometres north-west of Grenoble, and it makes things that matter to riders and to anyone who likes a drink. The monks of the Grande Chartreuse monastery, hidden in the mountains above, have made their herbal liqueur since the eighteenth century, and the cellars where it is aged and bottled are in Voiron, said to be the longest liqueur cellar in the world. The town is also where the Rossignol ski company began in 1907, a reminder that these valleys feed the Alps with both hardware and thirst.

As a start and finish, Voiron is very useful. It has fuel stations on every approach, supermarkets, bakeries and a long main street with cafés, and the suburbs of Coublevie and Saint-Jean-de-Moirans run into it. Grenoble's traffic is close enough to cause delays on the roads at commuting time, so leave early or wait until after nine. From here the roads head toward the Vercors balcony roads and the Ardèche gorges, and the first hour is a gradual shift from industrial valley to mountain air.

To the east, the Chartreuse massif rises in vertical limestone cliffs, grey and cream, with forest on the shelves and meadows above. Its roads, which include famous passes like the Col de Porte and the Col du Cucheron, are among the best in the French Alps, but they lie behind the ridge, and on the way out from Voiron you only get the sense of their scale. To the north lies the Lac de Paladru, a glacial lake with clear water and a long public beach, which makes a good swim stop in summer.

Food in Voiron leans toward the Dauphiné and Savoie, with gratin dauphinois, walnut tarts and local cheeses such as Saint-Marcellin. A coffee on the main street before setting off is the right way to begin, and the same coffee in the evening is a fair reward for coming back. Winter mornings can be icy on the valley roads, so check the temperature before you leave.
t.schluchsee@47.8,8.2:
The biggest lake in the Black Forest is not natural. The Schluchsee was created in the 1930s, when the valley was dammed to supply a hydroelectric scheme, flooding farms and hamlets and lifting the water level to form a long, slim lake in the high country at about 930 metres. It looks as though it has always been there, with forested hills on every side, and the older people in the villages can still remember the old landscape.

The town of Schluchsee, with about twenty-six hundred people, sits at the northern end and is a resort in every season. In summer people swim, sail, windsurf and paddle on the lake, with sandy beaches and a boat service across the water; in winter, it can freeze, and in the cold months the nearby ski lifts operate. Lenzkirch, a few kilometres away, is larger, with about five thousand people and the fuel, groceries and bakeries you will need.

The roads around the lake are among the nicest in the southern Black Forest. They twist through spruce and fir forest, up and down the hills, with views of the water through the trees, and the surface is generally good. Traffic can be heavy at weekends, particularly in summer, and some roads have motorcycle restrictions at weekends in parts of the region, so check the signs. The Feldberg, the highest peak in the Black Forest at nearly 1,500 metres, is a short ride away.

Cake is a serious matter here. The Black Forest cherry gateau, Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte, is served in every cafe, along with smoked ham and the sharp local cherry brandy, kirsch. A slice and a coffee on the lake shore is a classic way to end a day. The water stays cool even in August, but swimmers are rewarded with clean water and a lovely setting. Early autumn, when the beeches colour and the mist hangs over the lake, is a particularly good season.
t.grimsel pass@46.6,8.3:
The Grimsel is a road made of granite. At 2,164 metres, the pass sits at the junction of the Bernese Alps and the Valais, in a bare, polished landscape of rounded boulders, tiny lakes and big reservoirs, where the ice of the last glaciation scraped the rock smooth. There is almost nothing growing at the top, and the sky seems close enough to touch.

The road is a classic. Coming from Innertkirchen on the Bernese side, it climbs the Haslital in long straights and hairpins, passes the dam of the Räterichsbodensee, and then reaches the summit with a lake on each side. On the south side it drops in a series of tight hairpins to Gletsch, with the Rhône glacier appearing ahead. The surface is good, the corners are well signed, and the views are huge. It is also very popular, so expect cars, buses and other bikes on fine summer weekends. Start early, and you will have the best of it.

The pass has been used since the Middle Ages by traders and pilgrims, and a hospice on the summit has sheltered travellers for centuries. Much of the surrounding country is part of a huge hydroelectric system, with tunnels and power stations buried in the mountain, and the water that powers it is the melt of the surrounding ice. Alpine choughs wheel on the thermals, and marmots whistle from the grass on the lower slopes.

The pass is closed in winter, usually from about November to late May, depending on snow. A cafe and restaurant at the hospiz offer coffee, soup and cake, with high prices that you will forgive when you see the view. It can be cold and windy, even in July, so keep a layer in the top box.
t.gletsch@46.6,8.4:
Gletsch is where a Bond car drove around a hairpin. The 1964 film Goldfinger used the road near here for its famous chase, with Sean Connery's Aston Martin DB5 winding along the Furka pass, and the old Hotel Belvédère, a big, handsome building from the age of grand Alpine tourism, stands at the foot of the climb. It has the look of a place that has been waiting for travellers for more than a century.

The hamlet sits where the Grimsel and Furka roads meet, at the head of the Goms valley, at an altitude well above 1,700 metres. It is a tiny place, with a hotel, a station and a few buildings, but the setting is superb. The Rhône glacier, from which the great river starts its journey to the Mediterranean, once reached right down to the hamlet, and now has retreated far up the valley, so the ice that tourists once visited by carriage is a long way off. A cave carved into the ice is open in summer.

The riding here is the great attraction. The road to the Furka climbs in a long sequence of hairpins with the glacier in view, then crosses the pass at about 2,430 metres. The surface is good, the barriers are solid, and the corners are generous, but at weekends the traffic is dense. In summer a steam railway runs on the old Furka line between Oberwald and Realp, a lovely thing to see puffing across the hillside.

Come in the morning, when the light is clear and the roads are quiet. Cold wind comes off the glacier even in August, and snow can fall in any month at this height. Passes in this region close in winter, typically from late October to late May, so check before you go. A cup of coffee on the terrace of the old hotel, looking up at the ice, is one of the best small pleasures of the Alps.
t.chur fuel and status@46.9,9.5:
Chur likes to say that it is the oldest town in Switzerland, and the evidence is on its side. People have lived on this spot, where the Plessur river meets the Rhine valley, for around five thousand years, and the Romans put a settlement here, and a bishop's seat followed in late antiquity. Today the city, with about thirty-two thousand people, is the capital of Graubünden, the biggest canton in the country, and the gateway to the great passes and valleys of the east.

The old town is a delight, with narrow lanes, stepped alleys, fountains and a cathedral that rises above the rooftops on a terrace. The Rhaetian Railway, with its red trains, runs from here to St. Moritz and Davos through some of the most spectacular country in the Alps.
