The mountains close in on every side, with the Calanda looming to the west, and in autumn you can smell woodsmoke and wet leaves in the streets.

For a rider, the city is practical. It has fuel stations, bike dealers, supermarkets and every kind of food, and it sits on the main roads: the A13 south to the San Bernardino, the road west toward the Oberalp and Lukmanier passes, and the road east to Davos, Klosters and the Flüela. The Splügen and Albula routes both start nearby. Before a big day in the mountains, this is the place to fill the tank, check your tyres and have a proper breakfast.

The city is warm in summer and the evenings are lively, with outdoor terraces and cafes. The speciality is Bündner Gerstensuppe, a barley soup with ham and vegetables, and the local air-dried beef, Bündnerfleisch, is thin, dark and delicious. Morning traffic on the main roads can be heavy, so start early, and check the passes for closures or roadworks before you set out. Winter ice and snow can affect even the lower roads, so bring warm gear if you travel out of season.
t.san bernardino pass road@46.5,9.2:
Before the tunnel, everyone went over the top. The San Bernardino pass, at 2,066 metres, links the upper Rhine valley of Graubünden with Ticino, and has done for centuries, when mule trains carried goods between the north and the south. Since the opening of the road tunnel in 1967, most traffic goes underneath, and the old road is left for those who prefer the view.

The old road is a beauty. From the north it climbs through the Hinterrhein valley, the source of the Rhine, and then a series of hairpins to the summit, where a small lake, the Lago Moesola, sits beside the road, with a few buildings. On the south side, the road drops through a series of tight, well-marked hairpins to Mesocco, with the castle ruins perched on a rock above the village, and the chestnut woods and stone villages of the Italian-speaking valley below.

The riding is good but not demanding, with smooth tarmac and gentle gradients. In places the road is narrow, but the traffic is light, since most drivers take the tunnel. The pass is open from about June to October, depending on snow, and is closed in winter. The weather can change in an hour, from sun to cloud, and the temperature at the top can be low even in summer.

There are no big towns near the top, and fuel is a practical concern. Mesocco and the villages on the south side have small stations, and the nearest town of any size is Biasca, in the Ticino valley, with about six thousand people, while on the north side Splügen and Thusis have more services. Fill up before you begin. A coffee at the pass restaurant, if it is open, is a fine way to enjoy the quiet, and the lake is a good place to walk for ten minutes. Come on a weekday morning for the best light and the emptiest road.
t.splugenpass hairpins@46.5,9.3:
The Italian side of the Splügen is the one that makes people swear with happiness. From Campodolcino the road climbs the Valle Spluga in a rapid string of tight hairpins, stacked one above another up the valley wall, past waterfalls and a gorge that the old road builders had to blast through. At the top, at about 2,114 metres, you arrive at the border, a modest customs building and the long, cold Lago di Montespluga, held back by a dam and glinting in a bare landscape of grass and stone.

The road you are riding was built in the 1820s by the engineer Carlo Donegani for the Austrian government, which then ruled Lombardy and wanted a better link to the north, and the route is far older than that. Merchants, armies and mule trains have crossed this gap for two thousand years, and the Roman and medieval trade routes ran very much along the same line. The Swiss side drops into the Rheinwald and the old village of Splügen, with stone houses and a small square that has hardly changed in centuries.

On a bike the Italian hairpins are tight and require patience, with some narrow tunnels and gallery sections that are damp and echoing. The surface is generally good but can be patched, and in early summer there may be gravel from rockfall. Traffic is moderate, and the road is closed in winter, usually from about November to May. At the top, expect a stiff wind, snow patches into June, and temperatures that can be low even on a bright day.

Fuel is a real issue. There is none at the top, and Montespluga has only a few buildings. Chiavenna, on the Italian side, is the nearest large town, about twenty kilometres down the valley, with all the services, and Splügen on the Swiss side has some. Fill up beforehand, and enjoy a coffee at the little cafe by the lake if it is open. The best light is in the morning, when the valley is still in shade and the lake is calm.
t.entlebuch@47.0,8.1:
Entlebuch gave the world a dog. The Entlebucher Sennenhund, a small, sturdy, tricolour herding breed, was developed in these valleys to drive cattle on the steep pastures, and the village is proud of it. The surrounding region is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, recognised in 2001, a landscape of moors, wooded ridges and green pasture, where the Kleine Emme river runs down from the Alps toward Lucerne.

The village itself has about three thousand people, and stands at 723 metres on the road between Bern and Lucerne, a crossing that has been important since medieval times. It has a good selection of practical stops: fuel, bakeries, a couple of restaurants and the kind of friendly village guesthouses that serve a hearty plate of rösti or a slice of something sweet with thick cream. This is the end of a long ride for many, a place to finish the day with a beer on a terrace.

The roads around are lovely. The valley road follows the river through farms and forest, with gentle bends, wooden barns and cows with bells on the slopes, and the side roads climb up to the high ridges, with wide views of the Pilatus and the Alps. The surface is generally excellent, and traffic is light outside the commuting hours. Hasle and Schüpfheim, the next villages, are similar, and the road toward Marbach and the Schangnau is a fine piece of riding, with a bit more climbing and some tighter bends.

The biosphere is notable for its moors, which are protected, and the area has a distinctive feel, damp and green, with mist on the hills in the morning. Spring brings blossom and autumn, golden beech woods. Rain is frequent, and fog can sit in the valley, so check the forecast. If you want more services, Malters, a few kilometres down the valley, is larger, with about six thousand people, and Lucerne is a short ride beyond it.
t.giswil@46.8,8.2:
Giswil sits at the bottom of the Brünig road, and so it is a place where riders gather. The village, with about three and a half thousand people, lies in the valley of the Sarner Aa, at 485 metres, south of Lake Sarnen, between wooded hills and steep slopes. It is a quiet farming community in the canton of Obwalden, the heart of central Switzerland, and the main road runs through it on the way up to Lungern and the Brünig pass.

For the practical rider, Giswil is a gift. There are fuel stations, a bakery, small shops and a couple of inns, and it is the last easy place to fill up before the road climbs. Sarnen, the cantonal capital, is the nearest larger town, about eight kilometres north, with about nine thousand people and more choice. The lake at Sarnen is a good place to rest, with a lakeside walk and a shady park.

The riding begins at once. The road to Lungern climbs in a series of smooth bends beside the Lungerersee, a long, narrow lake with water of a deep green, then crosses the Brünig pass at around a thousand metres and drops into the Haslital near Meiringen. It is a gentle pass, wide and easy, but its corners are lovely, and in the early morning, with mist on the lake, it is one of the most pleasant rides in the Alps. The railway, a narrow-gauge line that climbs the pass with a cog section, runs alongside, and sometimes the trains and bikes share the same ridge.

Further afield, the Glaubenbielen road, the other half of the route, climbs west from Giswil through steep forest to a high pass, with narrow lanes, tight bends and a strong sense of being alone in the mountains. It closes in winter and can be icy until late spring. Giswil itself is a good base, and the evening light on the surrounding peaks is excellent.
t.martigny@46.1,7.1:
Martigny stands at the elbow of the Rhône, the place where the river turns from a westward run through the Valais to a northward one toward Lake Geneva, and it has been a crossroads since the Romans. They called it Octodurum, built a town, a temple and an amphitheatre here, and the road over the Great St Bernard, which starts at the edge of town, was one of the main routes over the Alps. You can still visit the amphitheatre, and a museum on the Roman site has a collection that is unusual for a town this size.

Today it is a bustling small city of about fifteen thousand people, with all the services of a larger place. There are fuel stations, bike shops, supermarkets, and a good choice of cafes and restaurants, plus a proper old town with wine bars where you can taste the local Valais wines. The Valais is Switzerland's largest wine region, and its white Fendant and red Dôle are often on the menu, along with raclette, the melted cheese scraped onto potatoes, which is the proper food of the region.

From here, a number of great roads begin. The road to the Great St Bernard climbs south to the Italian border at 2,469 metres, with the old hospice, famous for its dogs, at the top, and the road tunnel below it spares the winter traffic. To the west, the Col de la Forclaz leads to Chamonix and the Mont Blanc massif. Eastward, the Rhône valley road leads to Sion, Sierre and the vineyards of the Valais.

Martigny is warm in summer, protected by the mountains, and the valley can be hot and still, so start early. The Great St Bernard pass is open from about June to October. Fill up here, since the climb has few services, and check conditions before you go. The St Bernard dog kennel in town is an easy visit for a short break.
t.tauberbischofsheim@49.6,9.7:
Tauberbischofsheim has produced more Olympic fencers than most countries. The town in the Tauber valley is Germany's fencing capital, with a club and training centre that has trained generations of champions, among them Thomas Bach, who won gold in the team foil at the 1976 Olympics and later became president of the International Olympic Committee. In a quiet place, the occasional clink of blades from a training hall is a surprise.

The Tauber is a small river that winds through a green valley of orchards, vineyards and meadows, and the whole valley is a rider's delight. The Romantic Road, the Romantische Straße, follows its course for some distance, linking the old towns of Franconia, Tauberbischofsheim, Bad Mergentheim, Weikersheim and the walled city of Rothenburg ob der Tauber, with castles, church towers and half-timbered houses. The roads along the valley are smooth and winding, with gentle bends and a feeling of being in a model landscape.

The town itself has about thirteen thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets, cafes and restaurants, and a small old centre dominated by the castle of the electors of Mainz, with a tall tower and a moat. The wines of the Tauber valley, light and fruity, are well worth trying, and the local inns serve them with roast pork, sausage and dumplings. The Tauber is a pleasant place for a walk, with a promenade along the water.

Spring is lovely, with blossom in the orchards, and autumn brings the wine harvest and the colours of the vines. Summer weekends are busy with cyclists on the Tauber cycle path, so ride with care. The valley can be misty in the early morning, and the afternoon light on the old walls is warm. A relaxed evening here, with a glass of local wine, is a good way to end a day on the road.
t.wassen@46.7,8.6:
Wassen is a village you have probably seen without knowing it, because it is the star of one of the most photographed railway curiosities in Europe. The Gotthard line climbs the narrow Reuss valley in a series of spiral tunnels, and the little church of Wassen, perched on a mound, appears three times from the train window at three different heights and angles. Riders get the same trick on the road, where the old Gotthard route zigzags up the valley and the church tower comes round again and again.

The village sits at around a thousand metres in a tight, steep-sided valley, where the Reuss has cut a deep gorge between granite walls. This is the beginning of the real mountain, and the character of the road changes here: it narrows, bends sharply and gains height quickly, passing small chapels, waterfalls and avalanche galleries. Just above, at Göschenen, the gorge of the Schöllenen opens, and the famous Devil's Bridge leads over the river. A legend says the devil built the original in exchange for the first soul to cross, and was cheated when the villagers sent a goat across instead.

Wassen is also the junction for the Susten road, which turns off to the north-west and climbs steeply toward the pass of the same name. That makes the village a natural place to regroup, check the sky and decide on the day's route. There are a couple of cafes and a small shop, but fuel is not something to count on here; the bigger towns of Altdorf in the north and Andermatt in the south are safer, and Erstfeld lies in between.

Weather in the Reuss valley changes quickly. Cloud gathers on the cliffs, and rain can fall in one side valley while the next is bright. In winter the valley is prone to avalanches, and the road and rail are carefully protected. Spring and early autumn, when the rock is warm and the tourists have thinned out, give the best light, and the sound of the river below the road is the soundtrack.
t.susten pass@46.7,8.4:
Susten is a pass built for driving, and that is rare. Where most Alpine crossings follow old mule tracks or trade routes, this one was planned in the 1930s and finished in the 1940s as a modern road, with smooth gradients, wide curves and sturdy retaining walls, and the result is a ride that flows in a way few others do. It connects Wassen in Uri with Innertkirchen in the Bernese Oberland, crossing the ridge at 2,224 metres through a short tunnel.

The northern side is the more dramatic. Beyond the tunnel the road drops past the Steingletscher, a glacier that spills into a high cirque and ends in a small lake. The ice has shrunk dramatically, but the rock around it is polished and streaked and the mountains stand around you in a ring. Moraines, rushing meltwater and the smell of cold stone give the place a raw feel, and a stop at the glacier car park is almost compulsory. From there the road continues in a series of long bends, then plunges into the Gadmertal, a quiet valley of meadows and old wooden houses.

On the Uri side, the road rises more gradually from Wassen through the Meiental, with a string of hairpins and views back toward the Fünffingerstock and the Sustenhorn. It is a pass with lots of room and lots of long corners, and the surface is usually excellent. Wind can be fierce at the top, and the temperature drops several degrees as the road climbs, so a warm layer helps.

Fuel is the main practical point. There is none on the pass, and the villages near it are small, so fill at Altdorf or Meiringen before you climb. Susten is closed in winter, generally from late autumn until late spring, and snow patches may still lie at the edges in June. If you can choose, ride it on a weekday morning when the light is clear and the traffic is thin.
t.rapperswil lake bridge@47.2,8.8:
The wooden bridge at Rapperswil is the kind of crossing that makes you slow down on purpose. It stretches across the upper end of Lake Zurich, a footbridge of oak planks on piles, rebuilt in the early 2000s on the line of a medieval predecessor, and it joins the old town of Rapperswil on the north shore to the village of Hurden on the south. Pilgrims on the Way of St James have walked across it for centuries, and the modern version makes no attempt to be anything but simple and beautiful.

Rapperswil itself is called the town of roses, a title that comes from the rose gardens on the hill below the castle and the roses on the town's coat of arms. The castle, a rugged thing of towers and ramparts, rises above the harbour, and in the nineteenth century it became a home for Polish exiles, who set up a museum there that still tells the story of their country's struggle. The old town is a maze of cobbled lanes and arcades, with a long lakeside promenade where swans glide beside the walls.

As a start or photo stop, it is hard to beat. Park the bike by the harbour and walk out on the bridge for the view: the lake spreading east and west, the Glarus Alps sharp in the distance on clear days, and the castle watching over the town. Sunrise and sunset are the best times, when the water turns copper and the light picks out the church spires. Rapperswil-Jona, with more than thirty thousand people in the joined municipalities, has plenty of fuel and food, so supplies are not a problem.

The roads that leave from here head south over the Seedamm, a causeway with a long history as a crossing point, and then into the hills toward the Zürichsee's southern shore. Traffic in town can be heavy at weekends, especially in fine weather, when half of Zurich seems to head to the lake, so an early start gives you quiet streets and still water.
t.appenzell old town@47.3,9.4:
Appenzell is a town that has kept hold of itself, and that is the first thing you notice when you ride in. Houses are painted in bright colours, with decorated gables and flower boxes, and the main street feels more like a village than a town of five and a half thousand. The canton it governs, Appenzell Innerrhoden, is the smallest in Switzerland by population, and it clings to traditions that others have dropped.

The best known of them is the Landsgemeinde, held on the last Sunday in April, when citizens gather in the open square and vote by raising their hands. Men once wore swords to the meeting, and some still do as a ceremonial item. It is one of the last places in Europe where this form of direct democracy is practised in public, and there is something moving about a square full of people voting in the open air. Women gained the right to vote in the canton only in 1990, after a federal court ruling, a reminder that tradition can be a mixed blessing.

For lunch, the local cheese is the thing. Appenzeller is a firm, aromatic cheese washed in a herbal brine whose recipe is a closely guarded secret, and it appears in everything from a sandwich to a baked dish with potatoes and onions. The sweet side is the Biberli, a gingerbread-like pastry filled with almond paste. The cafes in the old town serve both, and the pace is leisurely.

Behind the town rises the Alpstein, a compact limestone massif with the Säntis as its high point, and the roads leading into it are rewarding: green hills dotted with farms, little villages with wooden shingled houses, and now and then a view of cliffs. Fuel is available in the town, which is large enough to have stations, and parking is easy at the edge of the pedestrian area. The weather can turn quickly, with cloud wrapping the peaks by early afternoon, so go early if you want the views.
t.schwagalp santis road@47.3,9.3:
The Säntis is the high point of the Alpstein, 2,502 metres of limestone that rises almost out of nowhere above the rolling hills of eastern Switzerland. The road that gets you to its foot is the Schwägalp pass, which climbs from Urnäsch in Appenzell Ausserrhoden to a high saddle at 1,278 metres and then drops toward the Toggenburg. At the saddle, a cable car carries people up the last steep stretch to the summit in a few minutes, and a famous weather station sits at the top.

That weather station has a long record and a short temper. The summit is exposed to everything the north can throw, and winter storms have buffeted the building and the tower for generations. On clear days, the view takes in six countries, according to the local boast: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Liechtenstein, France and Italy. You do not need to go to the top to feel the mountain's presence, though, because from the pass the north face looms above the meadows like a wall.

The ride is the main event for many. Coming from Urnäsch, the road climbs steadily through pasture and spruce, with a mix of tight bends and relaxed stretches, and the surface is generally good. Cattle roam in the high meadows, and the clank of their bells carries on the wind. Plan on Appenzell or Urnäsch, and fill up before the climb.

In summer the pass is busy on weekends, with cyclists, motorbikes and sightseers, and the car park by the cable car fills early. Weather is the other variable. The Säntis creates its own, and a morning of sun can turn to cloud by noon. In winter the road is generally kept open, but snow and ice can make it tricky, and the north-facing hairpins stay in shadow. A clear autumn morning, with the first snow on the summit and the meadows still green, is the best of all.
t.toggenburg flow road@47.2,9.3:
Toggenburg is a long valley in eastern Switzerland, carved by the young Thur river, and it is a landscape of soft green hills with steep stone walls above. The road here runs from Wildhaus, high up at the head of the valley, toward Gams and the Rhine plain, and it has a flowing quality that has earned it a name among riders: long, open bends, gentle gradients and hardly any need to touch the brakes.

On one side, the Churfirsten range stands like a row of teeth, seven peaks with sheer faces to the south, rising above a rolling skirt of pasture. On the other, the Alpstein and the Säntis fill the horizon. The road passes between them, and it is the sort of place where every curve opens a new composition of grass, cliff and cloud. In May, the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the cows come down from the high pastures wearing garlands, in a tradition that draws crowds to nearby villages.

Wildhaus is best known as the birthplace of Huldrych Zwingli, the reformer who preached in Zurich and shaped the Swiss Protestant church; he was born there on New Year's Day in 1484, in a wooden farmhouse that still stands. The valley has a strong musical tradition too: yodelling, folk dance and a distinctive local sound that is celebrated in a themed walking trail. It is a place that likes to sing.

Practical matters are simple. Walenstadt, with about five thousand people, is the closest town of size, and it has fuel and food. Wildhaus itself has small shops and cafes, and there are a few modest hotels. Winters are cold and snowy, with a ski season, and the road is kept open, but ice can linger at the bends. Summer mornings are the best, when the air is clear, the grass is wet and the light touches the Churfirsten face by face.
t.walensee photo line@47.1,9.2:
The Walensee is one of the most dramatic lakes in Switzerland, and one of the least visited. It lies in a trench between the Churfirsten range to the north and the Glarus Alps to the south, a long narrow lake of intense green, with cliffs that fall almost vertically into the water. The photograph is the Churfirsten wall reflected in the surface on a still morning, seven jagged peaks mirrored in the lake.

The lake is about fifteen kilometres long and around a hundred and fifty metres deep at its deepest, and the cliffs on the northern shore are so steep that for a long stretch no road runs there at all. The hamlet of Quinten, on the north shore, can only be reached by boat or on foot, which gives it an air of seclusion, and a mild microclimate that allows figs and grapes to grow. Along the southern shore runs the busy motorway and the railway, tucked into tunnels and ledges, with the old road beside them.

For riders, the good road is the one that climbs from Walenstadt toward Amden, a village on a terrace high above the lake, with outstanding views down to the water. The corners are tight at first and then open out, and the lookout points come up quickly, so slow down and pick your stop. Another approach is from the Weesen end, on the western side, where the road sits close to the water and the cliffs hang overhead.

Fuel and food are in Walenstadt, a town of five thousand at the eastern end, which has a lakeside promenade and a few good cafes. The weather on the lake is changeable, with strong winds funnelling along the trench, and the Föhn can blow hard in spring and autumn, making the air startlingly clear and the water choppy. Early morning and the evening are the best times to photograph, before the haze builds or when the sun has dropped behind the ridge.
t.glaubenbielen high road@46.9,8.1:
Glaubenbielen is a pass for people who like their mountains empty. It crosses a green saddle at 1,611 metres between Giswil in Obwalden and the Entlebuch valley in Lucerne, and the road is narrow, steep and often quiet, with long stretches where you will meet nothing but cows and the occasional cyclist. The scenery is gentle but big, with moorland, scattered spruce and an open sky.

The pass lies inside the Entlebuch biosphere reserve, a UNESCO-recognised landscape where high moors, forests and traditional farming have been protected together. The moors here are among the most important in Switzerland, wet, spongy places full of rare plants and insects, and the walking paths across them are carefully marked. It is not a landscape that shouts, and that is its appeal.

On the Giswil side, the road climbs from the shore of Lake Sarnen in a series of hairpins through forest, with views opening gradually over the lake and the mountains of Obwalden. It is steep in places, and the corners are tight, so take care on a loaded bike. At the top, the land opens into meadows and the road eases into a wide, rolling descent toward Sörenberg, a ski village that is quiet in summer. The surface is generally good but patched, and the shade can hold moisture late into the morning.

Giswil is a village of several thousand and the best place to fill up before you start, and Sarnen, a short ride away, is the bigger option. The pass is closed in winter, normally opening in late spring, and it is worth checking the conditions, because snow lingers at this altitude. Summer weekends bring more traffic, but early in the day the road is still your own. Take a warm layer and a camera.
t.brunigpass sweepers@46.8,8.1:
Brünig is the easy pass, and it is more fun than that makes it sound. At 1,008 metres it is one of the lowest of the main Alpine crossings in central Switzerland, joining Lungern in Obwalden with the shore of Lake Brienz and the Haslital, and it is open all year. The road is fast and well made, with long sweepers that let you lean the bike and keep the revs up, a kind of riding that is rare in the high mountains.

The Obwalden side climbs from Lungern, a village beside a green lake, up the steep slope in a series of wide bends with views over the water. At the top, the road runs along a wooded saddle with a few small hotels and the old railway nearby. The Brünig railway, a narrow-gauge line with a cog section, has crossed this saddle since the 1880s and still runs scenic trains. From the summit the descent toward Brienz is quick and open, with views over the lake and the Bernese Alps beyond.

The valley below is a place of old wood and new water. Brienz is known for woodcarving, and the village has a school where the craft is still taught, so the shops sell carved bears, cowbells and music boxes. The Aare river runs through Meiringen, a town famous for inventing the meringue, according to local tradition, and for the nearby Reichenbach Falls, where Sherlock Holmes met his end in a Conan Doyle story.

Traffic is heavier than on the higher passes because the Brünig is a main road, and trucks and caravans slow things down at times, but the road is wide enough to make passing easy. In winter the road is cleared and gritted, but the shaded bends can be icy.
t.zug lake@47.2,8.5:
Zug is a small city with a big lake and a reputation for money. The lake, the Zugersee, lies in a bowl of low hills at the northern edge of the Alps, a calm, blue sheet of water with the Rigi rising across on the south side and the Pilatus further off. The old town sits on the northeastern shore, with a medieval clock tower, pastel houses and a promenade where boats bob in the harbour.

The canton has long been known for low taxes, which has drawn companies and residents from around the world, but the city has kept a personal scale. There are narrow lanes with small shops, cafes with views of the water, and a lake path that is busy with runners and families. The local speciality is Zuger Kirschtorte, a cake made of layers of almond meringue and sponge, flavoured with cherry brandy, and it is on the menu in nearly every pastry shop. The cherries behind the brandy come from the orchards on the slopes around the lake, which bloom in April.

The riding here is gentle, and it works well as a return leg at the end of a day. The roads along the lake are smooth and flat, and the traffic can be heavy, especially at commuting hours. If you want something more lively, the road toward the Zugerberg climbs through woods to a ridge with views over the city and the lake. Parking is easy near the harbour, and the lakeside is a pleasant place for a last coffee before the final run home.

Zug has more than twenty thousand people, along with Baar next door and a ring of suburbs, so fuel and food are everywhere. The weather here is mild by Swiss standards, with fog common in autumn and winter when the lake traps cold air, and the sun comes out late in the morning. In summer, the lake is warm enough for swimming, and the public baths fill with locals, which is a good sign.
t.gotthard tremola cobbled road@46.6,8.6:
Long before anyone dreamed of a tunnel, the Gotthard was a rumour of a route: a way through the central Alps that, once the Devil's Bridge was thrown across the gorge of the Schöllenen in the thirteenth century, turned a remote valley into the shortest link between northern Europe and Italy. Merchants, pilgrims, soldiers and mule trains all used it, and the hospice at the top gave them a bed. The Tremola, the cobbled stair on the southern side, is the nineteenth-century answer to the same problem.

Ticino built it in the 1820s and early 1830s, when the canton was young and keen to bind itself to the north, and the engineers laid the road in a zigzag of stone-walled hairpins up the steep face above Airolo. Coaches with six horses made the climb, and the passes were crowded with mail, travellers and the odd famous name. When the railway tunnel opened in 1882 the traffic dried up almost overnight, and the road fell into a long sleep. It was revived in the last few decades, the cobbles relaid, and it now carries riders, cyclists and anyone with an appetite for old engineering.

The setting changes as you climb. At the bottom the slopes are wooded and warm, with the voices of the south. In the middle the road cuts across bare slabs of gneiss, polished by ice and streaked by seepage. Near the top the air thins and the vegetation shrinks to grass and lichen, and the lake beside the hospice reflects a pale sky. In spring the snow lies in the hollows long after the road has opened, and in autumn the first dusting arrives early.

The surface needs respect, especially when wet. If you are riding the old road, go on a dry day, keep your speed low and your steering relaxed, and enjoy being part of something that has been going on for two centuries.
t.lukmanier return option@46.6,8.8:
Lukmanier is the quiet sister of the great Gotthard, and for most of its history it was the more important of the two. At 1,915 metres it links Disentis in Graubünden with the Blenio valley in Ticino, and Romans, monks and emperors used it long before the Gotthard became practical. For a rider looking for an easy way back toward the north or south, it offers a long, calm descent without the cobbles and queues.

The northern approach starts at Disentis, where a large Benedictine abbey stands on a terrace above the Rhine valley, founded in the early Middle Ages and still home to a community of monks. The abbey church is a Baroque confection that rises over the village, and a visit is a calm interlude. From there the road climbs up the Val Medel, past old Romansh villages with stone houses and small chapels, and then breaks out onto the pass through a landscape of lakes and low peaks.

At the top is the Lai da Sontga Maria, a reservoir with a small chapel on its shore, and the road follows the water for several kilometres. The view is open and quiet, with wind-bent larches and rock slabs. The southern descent takes you down through Olivone and the Val Blenio, a green, steep valley where chestnut woods give way to vineyards and old stone villages, with the road dropping quickly and the air growing warmer with every bend.

The riding is easy and the surface is good, with long bends and few hairpins, and the traffic is light compared with the main passes. The pass is closed in winter, from around November until late spring, and in early summer snow lines the road. It is an ideal late-afternoon pass, when the light turns the slopes gold and the day-trippers have gone home.
t.furka glacier road@46.6,8.4:
The Furka is the pass where you can ride up to a glacier and see the beginning of a river, and few roads in Europe offer that. At 2,429 metres it links Realp in Uri with Gletsch and Oberwald in the Valais, and on the Valais side the road passes right beside the Rhône glacier, whose grey ice tongue spills from the high snowfields above the Belvédère hotel. A trickle of milky meltwater at its foot is the source of the Rhône, which will travel through Lake Geneva and across France to the Mediterranean.

The glacier has been a tourist attraction since the nineteenth century, when visitors came by coach to see it, and the old hotels at Gletsch were built to house them. Photographs from that time show the ice reaching almost to the buildings, and the contrast with the present is stark. Every summer parts of the glacier are covered with white fleece to slow the melting, and an ice grotto is cut into the tongue so that people can walk inside. It is a slightly eerie sight, a mountain trying to hold on.

The road itself has all the elements: hairpins, open sweepers, long climbs and a descent that tests the brakes. The east side from Realp is steeper and more twisted, winding up the valley past an old steam railway whose volunteers have restored a line abandoned after the construction of a new tunnel. The railway runs trains on summer days, and the sight of white steam against the green hills is a treat.

The pass is open from about June to October, with the dates depending on the snow, and the wind and cold at the top are real. Mornings are generally clear, with cloud building by the afternoon, and the light on the ice is best before ten.
t.grimsel reservoirs@46.6,8.3:
The Grimsel looks like a landscape that nature made, but most of what you see was made by engineers. The three big lakes around the pass, the Grimselsee, the Räterichsbodensee and the Oberaarsee, hold water that spins turbines in power stations deep inside the mountain, and the dams that hold them in place were built from the 1920s onward by men working at altitude through harsh winters. The Spitallamm, a curved wall of concrete, closes the Grimselsee, and the road runs along its crest.

The hospice beside the dam gets its name from the old shelter that stood here, a place where travellers were fed and housed on the long crossing between the Haslital and the Goms. The earlier hospice was drowned when the lake was raised, and a new building went up on the shore. That sense of overlapping layers, medieval trade route, nineteenth-century carriage road and twentieth-century power scheme, is what makes the place interesting.

The rock itself is the star. The granite that forms the Grimsel is smooth and pale, polished by glaciers that once filled the valley, and in places the slabs are so clean they look like paving. Visitors can see the glacial polish on the roadside, and below the pass, in the Haslital, waterfalls and gorges cut through the same stone. The Handeck fall drops a good forty metres or so into a mist-filled gorge, and there is a gondola nearby that climbs to the Gelmersee for those who want to walk.

On a bike the ride is a delight, with big, open bends, fast approaches and views of water and rock. The weather is changeable and the temperature low, so layer up. Fuel is not available at the pass itself; Innertkirchen and Meiringen on the north, and Oberwald or Brig on the south, are the dependable places. The road is open in summer and early autumn only, and a clear, calm day in September is hard to beat.
t.brig food and@46.3,8.0:
Brig is a town that has always lived off other people's journeys. It sits in the upper Rhône valley in the Valais, at the northern foot of the Simplon, and for centuries merchants hauling goods over the pass to Italy needed somewhere to rest, change animals and pay their bills. One of them, a seventeenth-century trader named Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper, grew so rich on salt, mining and transport that he built the palace that still dominates the town, with three towers topped by gilded domes. It is among the grandest private houses in the Alps, and a short walk from the station.

The setting is sunny and dry. The Valais sits in the rain shadow of high mountains, and Brig basks under a sky that is often clear when the north side of the Alps is under cloud. Vineyards climb the valley slopes further down, and apricots are a local pride. The town is a pleasant mixture of old lanes and modern shops, with the Simplon road, the railway and the roads to Goms and Zermatt all meeting here.

For riders it is the practical hinge of the Valais. Fuel is plentiful, with Brig, Naters across the river, and Visp not far down the valley together giving the area real size. Restaurants serve raclette, the melted cheese scraped over potatoes, and dried meat from the mountains; for a quick lunch, the bakeries and cafes around the main square do just fine. The traffic can be dense, particularly in summer when holiday traffic funnels toward the passes, so patience helps.

From here a rider can go almost anywhere: up the Furka and Grimsel to the north-east, over the Simplon to Italy, or down the valley toward Lake Geneva. The Simplon road, which Napoleon had built in the early nineteenth century to move troops, is one of the great engineering achievements of its time, and it climbs from the edge of town in a long series of sweeping bends. It is a good place to be at the start of a mountain day.
t.silvaplana@46.5,9.8:
Silvaplana is where the Upper Engadine opens out into water and wind. The village sits on the edge of a lake of the same name, at around 1,800 metres, between the larger resort of St. Moritz and the little village of Sils, and above it the high peaks of the Bernina and Albula ranges hold glaciers in their cirques. The light here is famously clear, an effect of altitude and dry air that has drawn painters and thinkers for generations.

The lake is the thing. A steady wind blows up the valley most summer afternoons, known as the Maloja wind, and it has made Silvaplana one of the best places in Europe for windsurfing and kitesurfing. The water is cold and a deep blue, and the colourful sails on a clear day make a striking sight against the white of the mountains. Nietzsche spent summers in nearby Sils Maria and wrote some of his best-known work walking the lakeshore; a stone with a quotation still marks the place.

The road that ends the ride here is the Julier, one of the old Roman crossings, that climbs from the Surses valley to a pass of 2,284 metres and drops to the Engadine. The riding is wonderful: long, open bends, rocky slopes, and a wide view as you drop toward the lakes. The surface is generally good, and traffic is moderate, though summer weekends bring more. Wind and cold can make the top feel wintry even in July.

Silvaplana itself is small, with a handful of hotels, cafes and a few shops, and the nearby town of St. Moritz, with nearly five thousand people, is the place for fuel and larger services. Prices in the area are high, so it is worth knowing in advance. The Engadine is a place where Romansh is still spoken, and where houses have thick walls with small windows and the decorative sgraffito patterns typical of the valley. Evenings are cool even in summer, and a warm drink beside the lake is an ideal way to end the ride.
t.glaubenberg pass road@46.9,8.1:
The Glaubenberg is one of those passes that rewards you for taking the less obvious option. At 1,543 metres, it crosses the ridge between Sarnen in Obwalden and the Entlebuch valley in the canton of Lucerne, through a landscape of open moor and scattered spruce that feels remote even though it lies in the middle of Switzerland. Much of the high ground is a military training area, and the road can be closed on days when firing is scheduled, so it is wise to check before you plan around it.

The moorland is the highlight. The Glaubenberg lies within the Entlebuch biosphere reserve, where raised bogs, wet meadows and traditional alpine farming have been preserved together. The peat is deep, the plants are specialised, and in early summer the cotton grass makes white patches across the dark ground. Dragonflies, curlews and, with luck, black grouse live in the quiet corners. It is a landscape that asks for slow riding.

The road climbs from Sarnen through forest in a series of tight bends, then emerges onto the moor, where the gradients ease and the corners become longer and more relaxed. Much of the surface is narrow, and there are a few rough patches, especially after winter, so a steady speed is sensible. The descent toward Flühli and Sörenberg is open and fast, with views toward the Schrattenfluh, a wall of limestone cliffs that stands guard over the valley.

In winter the road is closed, and in a snowy spring it may open late. Summer mornings give the best conditions, when the mist lifts off the moor and the air smells of wet grass and resin. A warm layer is wise, because the moor is open and the wind can be cold.
t.sarnen@46.9,8.2:
Sarnen is the capital of Obwalden, and it wears the title lightly. The town sits at the northern end of Lake Sarnen, a long blue lake in the middle of Switzerland, with the Pilatus above and a line of wooded hills on the other side. About nine thousand people live here, and the main street has the usual arrangement of bakeries, banks and cafes, with a large parish church that stands on a rise above the old centre.

What gives the town its identity is the Landsgemeinde, the open-air assembly where citizens once voted by raised hand. Obwalden held its last in 1998, and the stone ring on the Landenberg hill, where the assembly met, is still a place that people visit. The hill is named after a legendary bailiff in the William Tell story, and a path leads to the top, with views over the lake and the old town. Nearby, the village of Flüeli-Ranft is the home of Nicholas of Flüe, known as Brother Klaus, the fifteenth-century hermit who is revered as Switzerland's patron saint and credited with helping to hold the Confederation together.

As a food stop it is easy and pleasant. There are cafes on the lakeside, where you can sit with a view of the water, and restaurants serving local specialities such as cheese, sausages and dishes with potatoes and cream. Fuel is available, and the town is large enough to have everything a rider needs, from a tyre shop to a supermarket. Parking is straightforward near the lake.

The roads that leave Sarnen head in several directions: north toward Lucerne, east over the Glaubenberg, south along the lake to Giswil and the Brünig, or up toward Melchtal and the old pilgrimage valley. It is a hub, and in summer it is busy with traffic. Early mornings are calm, and in the late afternoon the light comes across the lake and turns the water gold, which is a good moment for a last coffee.
t.grimselpass high point@46.6,8.3:
At the top of the Grimsel the world feels stripped to essentials: grey granite, a patch of black water, a pale sky and the wind. The pass reaches 2,164 metres on the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais, and the high point itself is a modest saddle with a small lake, the Totesee, and a handful of buildings. The bigger picture, with its glaciers and peaks, is spread out around you in every direction.

What is surprising is how much history is packed into this bare place. The route has been used since at least the Middle Ages, and for centuries it was a trade path between the Bernese Oberland and the Valais, with mule trains carrying cheese, wine and salt. Armies crossed it too, and in 1799 French and Austrian forces fought around the pass during the Napoleonic wars, which is the source of the name of the small lake, according to local tradition. Today the traffic is bikes, cars and cyclists, and the air smells of cold stone and diesel.

Looking south, the road begins its descent toward Gletsch in a series of tight hairpins, and at the bottom the Rhône glacier gleams in the distance. Looking north, the road runs along the Grimselsee and down the Haslital, a steep glacial valley with waterfalls and old wooden villages. The sensation of being on the roof of the region is strong, and the sound of running water follows you down either side.

For a rider coming from the Innertkirchen direction, this is the high point of the day. There is nothing for fuel here, so fill up at Innertkirchen or Meiringen if you are coming from the north, and at Oberwald or Brig from the south. Bring warm gloves, since even a summer morning can be close to freezing at this altitude, and check the pass is open before you start. Spring snow can linger into June, and the first autumn storms can shut the pass in October.
t.realp fuel and@46.6,8.5:
Realp is a village that most people drive through on the way to somewhere more famous, and that is reason enough to stop. It lies at about 1,540 metres in the Urseren valley, a high, treeless trough between the Furka and the Oberalp passes, with the Reuss river wandering through meadows. The surrounding mountains are bare and wide, and the valley has the open, windswept feeling of high Alpine country.

The village is the home of the Furka steam railway, a volunteer operation that has restored the old Furka line, abandoned in the early 1980s when a new tunnel replaced the mountain route. The volunteers rebuilt the track, locomotives and stations by hand over several decades, and in summer the steam trains run between Realp and Oberwald, climbing over the pass. The workshops at Realp are a fine place for anyone who loves old machinery, and the smell of coal smoke and hot oil is unforgettable.

For fuel the sensible plan is Andermatt, a few kilometres east, which has stations and shops and is much bigger than Realp. Andermatt has also grown in recent years with new hotels and apartments, but the old centre remains a pleasant spot for lunch, with a church and a garrison history that stretches back to the nineteenth century. For a bigger town with every service, Altdorf is a good half hour to the north.

A descent check is good advice here. Coming down from the Furka or the Gotthard, the brakes get hard work, and a stop here lets you cool them and look over the bike. The road down toward Andermatt and the Schöllenen gorge is steep and busy, with trucks and tourists, and the wind in the valley can be fierce. In summer the afternoons bring storms that build over the ridges and break quickly, so keep an eye on the clouds. In winter the valley is deeply snowed in, and the Furka is closed.
t.rorschach lakefront@47.5,9.5:
Rorschach is where Switzerland meets the Bodensee, and it is the sort of port town that rewards a slow walk before the engine starts. It sits on the southern shore of Lake Constance, the big shared lake of Switzerland, Germany and Austria, with the Austrian shore and its mountains low and blue across the water on a clear day. Boats come and go from the harbour, gulls argue on the breakwater, and the promenade is lined with plane trees and benches.

The town grew rich on grain and linen. In the eighteenth century the Prince-Abbot of St. Gallen built the Kornhaus, a handsome granary on the waterfront, to store the grain that came across the lake from Swabia, and it still stands as the town's landmark with its balconies and clock. Rorschach was also an important railway junction, and the old lakeside station is a reminder of the days when steamers connected with trains for the run to Zurich and beyond. Above the town on a hill stands the abbey of Mariaberg, a former monastery of the abbey of St. Gallen.

For a rider the lakefront is a good place to begin. There are cafes and bakeries along the front, and nine thousand residents, together with the neighbouring town of Goldach, give the area all the fuel and food you need. The road out heads east or west along the shore, flat and fast, and then turns uphill into the hills of Appenzell, where the character of the riding changes completely, from lakeside cruising to green hills and tight bends.

The weather on the lake is changeable, with morning mist and strong afternoon winds, and the light can be wonderful just after sunrise. In summer the town is busy with day trippers, and parking near the water fills up, though bikes can usually squeeze in. Fruit orchards cover the slopes behind, and in spring the blossom, with the lake behind it, is a fine sight.
t.santis view road@47.2,9.3:
Above the Toggenburg, on a shoulder of hillside around 1,200 metres, there is a stretch of road where the whole Säntis massif comes into view at once. The Alpstein is a compact mountain range, but from here it appears huge: a wall of pale limestone with steep faces, folded strata and a summit that wears a cap of cloud on most days. The pull-off for photographs is one of the better ones in eastern Switzerland.

The geology is the story. The Säntis and its neighbours are made of layers of limestone that were once the floor of a warm sea and have been pushed into great folds by the collision of continents. In the cliffs you can see those layers curving in giant waves, and the effect is of a mountain made of stacked paper. Beneath the cliffs, smooth green pasture slopes down into the valley, scattered with wooden farms and chalets with deep roofs.

The road here is the kind that gives you time to look. Corners are wide, the gradient is gentle, and the surface is good, with some patching. Traffic is light outside weekends, and on a weekday morning you might share the road with nothing but a milk truck. Cattle graze right to the edge of the tarmac, and in summer the sound of bells rises from the slopes, so keep your speed down and watch for animals.

Wildhaus, a small village in the Toggenburg with a ski lift, has cafes and a couple of shops, and it is a pleasant place to stop for a coffee. For fuel, the best choice is Appenzell or one of the larger towns in the valley, because small villages here may not have a station. Light is best in the early morning, when low sun rakes across the limestone and brings out every fold, and again in the evening, when the cliffs glow pink. Weather changes fast, so keep a rain layer handy.
t.schwagalp road@47.3,9.3:
Schwägalp is a saddle rather than a summit, and it has something of the feel of a clearing in the woods. At 1,278 metres it lies between Urnäsch, on the Appenzell side, and Neu St. Johann in the Toggenburg, and the pass road runs beside a mountain stream and the upper reaches of the Sitter river, through meadows grazed by brown cattle. Behind the hotel at the top rises the massive northern face of the Säntis, which seems close enough to touch.

The Urnäsch side of the climb gives you the character of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. The village of Urnäsch is known for its traditions, particularly the Silvesterchläuse, men dressed in elaborate costumes and huge bell-hung hats who walk through the countryside on the old New Year, in mid-January, driving out the evil spirits of winter. There is a museum in the village where the costumes are displayed, and the strange, beautiful masks are worth seeing. It is one of the surviving rituals of rural Switzerland, and the area still keeps it alive with great seriousness.

On the road, the climb is steady and smooth, with moderate bends and good visibility. The surface is generally good, and the gradient is never harsh, so the pass is a relaxed ride for most machines. The descent into the Toggenburg is a little steeper and more twisting, with views opening over a green valley that stretches toward the Churfirsten. Cold air gathers in the hollow at the top, so expect it to feel fresher than the valley towns.

Fuel is not available at the pass, although there is a hotel and a restaurant with a large terrace. Urnäsch has limited services, so the dependable choice is Appenzell, a quarter of an hour away. In winter the road is cleared and normally open, but snow and ice can make conditions difficult. A clear day in early autumn, with new snow on the summit and the larch turning, is one of the finest times to be there.
t.brunnen@47.0,8.6:
Brunnen sits on a bend in Lake Lucerne where the water turns the corner toward the Urner arm, and from the promenade you can look straight across to the meadow of the Rütli, the spot where the founders of Switzerland are said to have sworn their oath in 1291. The town has a place in the story itself: in 1315, after the victory at Morgarten, the confederates met in Brunnen to renew their alliance, and a stone on the shore commemorates the writer Friedrich Schiller, whose play on William Tell made the legend famous.

The lake is the star. The water is cold, clear and a deep green, and the surrounding mountains drop steeply into it, so the atmosphere is almost fjord-like. The Föhn wind, when it blows from the south, sweeps down the Urner arm with dramatic force and turns the surface white, and the sky takes on a dazzling clarity. Brunnen has a lively waterfront, with boats, ferries and paddle steamers calling at the quay, and a long walkway with benches where it is pleasant to sit and eat a sandwich.

Swimming is a local pastime in summer, and there are public bathing places along the shore where the water is bracing even in August. A short dip is a good way to cool off after a long day in leathers.

Riding out of Brunnen on the Axenstrasse is among the great short drives in Switzerland. The road clings to the cliffs above Lake Uri, passing through tunnels and galleries blasted into the rock, with windows that open onto the water. It was built in the nineteenth century as a link between the cantons, and the engineering is still impressive. Be aware that rockfall can close sections of the road, so check conditions, and expect heavy traffic on summer weekends. Brunnen and the neighbouring municipalities have fuel and food in abundance, and the town is a convenient base before the climb or the run toward Altdorf.
t.bernkastel kues@49.9,7.1:
Bernkastel-Kues is two towns glued together by a bridge across the Moselle. Bernkastel, on the right bank, is the one that appears on postcards, with a market square of leaning half-timbered houses, including one narrow gabled building from the early fifteenth century that looks like it was drawn by a child with a wicked sense of humour. Kues, on the other bank, is where the philosopher and cardinal Nikolaus von Kues, better known as Cusanus, was born in the early fifteenth century, and his old hospital foundation still stands, with a library of manuscripts that he collected.

Above Bernkastel the ruin of Burg Landshut clings to the slope, and the vineyards run up beyond it in terraces so steep that the workers use cable rigs. This is Riesling country, and the steep slate slopes hold the heat and give the wines their mineral edge. The most celebrated slope above the town makes a wine called Doctor, the story being that a sick medieval archbishop was cured by a glass of it. Whether you believe that or not, the local sellers will tell you the story with admirable gravity. A tasting is a fair idea if you are staying the night, and a poor idea if you are riding on.

The riding here is the Moselle in its classic form. The river winds in great loops between slate hillsides, and the road follows it, with vineyards on one side and water on the other, passing village after village of pointed church towers. Tight bends and gentle curves come in a calm, regular rhythm, which makes it a very comfortable road for relaxed touring, though tractors and tourist coaches can slow things in the season. Early autumn, when the leaves turn and the harvest begins, is spectacular, and it is also crowded. Spring is quieter.

Practically, the town has everything: fuel, supermarkets, a long line of cafés and restaurants and a riverside promenade for resting. The market square cobbles are rough but short. If you want a view, walk or ride up towards the castle ruin, and look back down on the river bend. Then come down and eat something with Riesling in it.
t.bad durkheim@49.5,8.2:
The Palatinate has a way of making you hungry and thirsty at the same time, and Bad Dürkheim is where the effect is strongest. The town lies at the foot of the Haardt, the eastern edge of the Palatinate Forest, with vineyards climbing the slope behind it and the Rhine plain stretching flat to the east. It is one of the main stops on the German Wine Route, and it takes its wine very seriously, with a sense of humour attached.

The humour has a shape and a size. Just outside the centre stands the Dürkheimer Riesenfass, a giant wooden barrel from the 1930s that holds well over a million litres and has a tavern inside it, which is exactly as silly as it sounds and makes a fine lunch spot. Each September the town hosts the Wurstmarkt, which claims to be the biggest wine festival in the world and which started as a market for sausages. Locals drink their wine as Schorle, mixed with sparkling water, from the Dubbeglas, a half-litre glass with dimples that you will see on every table. The classic food is Saumagen, a stuffed pig's stomach that tastes much better than its description, and Leberknödel with sauerkraut.

For a rider the pleasure is in the roads that wrap around the town. Along the foot of the hills runs a succession of small wine villages, Wachenheim, Kallstadt, Ungstein, each with a gate, a church and a row of courtyards, and the road between them is flat, narrow and often quite slow. Up the slope, a few lanes climb into the Palatinate Forest in tight hairpins through chestnut and beech. Above town you can find the ruins of Limburg, an old Benedictine abbey on a spur, which gives a view across the plain to the Odenwald on a clear day.

Bad Dürkheim has nearly nineteen thousand people, so fuel, shops and a spa town's worth of cafés are all easy. The old centre and its car-free squares are pleasant on foot, but weekends in autumn fill the place with coach tours and wine tourists. Early spring, with almond blossom out, is the most underrated time to come.
t.triberg@48.1,8.2:
Triberg is built in a steep, narrow fold of the Black Forest, a town that seems to have been poured down a gorge and set hard. Houses climb both sides of the Gutach valley, rooftops overlap, and the main street runs steeply uphill past shops full of cuckoo clocks, carved wooden bears and cherry schnapps. It is touristy, no question, but the tourists come because the place is the real thing, the heartland of the Black Forest clock trade, where families have been making timepieces in workshops since the eighteenth century.

The town's other big draw is the waterfall. The Gutach drops through a series of cascades in a wooded ravine just above the centre, a total fall of well over a hundred metres in seven stages, and it counts among the highest in Germany. A path with steps and bridges climbs beside it, and squirrels, who have learned that visitors carry nuts, will race along the rails to meet you. The spray, the smell of wet rock and spruce, and the roar of water make it a satisfying walk of an hour or so, best in spring, when snowmelt swells the flow, or after heavy rain.

Nearby Schonach claims one of the largest cuckoo clocks in the world, and rival towns argue with some energy about which one is biggest. The claim that the Black Forest cake was invented here is made by several places, and the argument has never been settled, but the cake itself, made with cherries, cream and kirsch, is easy to find in any café and generally excellent.

For riders, the approach is the reason to come. The B33 and the side roads that climb out of the Kinzig and Elz valleys wind through spruce forest in a long series of bends and hairpins, with the road gaining height steadily to over seven hundred metres around Triberg. Surfaces are good, the corners are smooth and well banked, and it is one of the classic bike roads of southwest Germany. That also means it is busy on fine weekends, with riders, cars and the occasional coach, and the police do monitor speed.

Triberg has about five thousand people and enough services for a stop: fuel, a supermarket, many cafés and restaurants. Parking is tight in high season, so arrive early or park low and walk up. Dress for cool weather, as it can be damp and cold even in summer.
t.echternach@49.8,6.4:
Echternach claims to be the oldest town in Luxembourg, and its story begins in the year 698, when the Northumbrian missionary Willibrord received land here from a local noblewoman and founded an abbey beside the river Sure. He had come from England to convert the Frisians, and the abbey that grew up around his tomb became one of the great centres of learning of the early Middle Ages, famous for its illuminated manuscripts. The basilica, rebuilt after heavy damage in the Second World War, still holds his sarcophagus in the crypt, and pilgrims come to it every year.

The pilgrimage has a curious ritual. On Whit Tuesday, thousands of people join the dancing procession, a long line of walkers who hop and skip through the streets to the sound of a polka tune, linked by handkerchiefs, in honour of the saint. It is recognised by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible heritage, and it is among the oddest and most cheerful religious events in Europe. Outside that day, the town is calm, with a market square, a fine town hall and a medieval feel.

The town lies on the German border, with the river Sure marking the frontier, and the footbridge across leads to a village on the German bank. Behind Echternach rises the Mullerthal, called Little Switzerland by the Luxembourgers, a country of sandstone gorges, mossy boulders, beech woods and narrow clefts where the air is cool even in July. Walking trails thread through the rocks, and on a summer weekend, the car parks fill with hikers. The roads that lead into the area are narrow and winding, with sudden bends and steep drops.

Echternach has nearly five thousand people, and fuel is not a problem. In fact, Luxembourg is known for lower fuel prices than its neighbours, and fill-ups here are usually cheaper than in Germany, France or Belgium, so riders often top up before crossing the border. Bars and restaurants in the market square serve Luxembourgish food, a hearty mix of smoked pork with broad beans, river fish and freshly baked bread, and a light white wine from the Moselle, an easy drive to the south. The nearest bigger town is Konz, in Germany, seventeen kilometres away. Early morning, with mist rising from the Sure, is the best time to see the old town, before the coach parties arrive.
t.ratenpass warm up@47.1,8.7:
The Raten Pass, at 1,077 metres, links the Ägerital with the country around Sattel and Biberbrugg, and for a Swiss pass it is quiet and modest, which makes it a very good warm-up. The road climbs from Unterägeri and Oberägeri, villages on the shores of Lake Aegeri in canton Zug, up through meadows and farms, with a view back over the lake and the hills beyond. It is a short climb, but the corners come at a steady pace, with a few well-judged hairpins, and the farmland is as neat as a model railway layout.

Near the lake is a place that matters a great deal in Swiss history. At Morgarten, on the shore, in 1315, a force of Swiss confederates ambushed an Austrian army under Duke Leopold, using the narrow ground between the lake and the slopes to their advantage. The victory is counted among the founding moments of the old Confederacy, and a monument stands by the road. Every November, a shooting contest, the Morgartenschiessen, recalls the battle. The lake itself is clear and quiet, with a swimming beach, a ring of old farmhouses and, on a calm morning, mirror reflections of the mountains.

The road is well maintained, and on a dry day it is one of the most relaxed rides in central Switzerland, with moderate traffic, pleasant gradients and some very good views. Early in the season or in autumn, patches of ice or damp can linger in shaded bends, and heavy rain brings cow slurry onto the tarmac, so be alert. On warm weekends, cyclists climb the pass in numbers, so keep to your side and take the corners wide with care. The best light is in the morning, when the lake lies smooth and mist drifts off the fields.

Fuel is easy at Unterägeri, a town of nearly eight thousand people, and also in Einsiedeln and Zug. Cafés along the lake serve coffee and cake, and are good places to watch the weather. After the warm-up, the higher passes, such as Ibergeregg, await.
t.einsiedeln@47.1,8.8:
Einsiedeln is a town built around a single building, the Benedictine abbey, whose white baroque towers rise above the rooftops from every approach. The monastery grew from a hermit's cell. Meinrad, a monk from Reichenau, settled in the forest here in the ninth century and was murdered by thieves in 861, and in 934 a community was founded at the site. For a thousand years since, pilgrims have come to the Black Madonna, a dark wooden statue in the Chapel of Grace within the church, and the town sits on the old pilgrim road toward Santiago de Compostela, with a yellow shell on a blue sign marking the way.

The present church, finished in the 1730s, is a riot of stucco, gilt and ceiling frescoes, one of the great baroque interiors of Switzerland. Outside, the huge curved forecourt, the Klosterplatz, is used every few years in summer for the Einsiedeln World Theatre, an open-air performance of Calderón's play that has been staged since 1924. The abbey also keeps a stud farm, and the monks have bred horses on the meadows nearby for centuries, a feature that explains the horse tradition in the area.

For a rider, Einsiedeln is a handy and agreeable stop on the way between the Sihlsee, the Ibergeregg pass and the lakes of Zurich and Zug. At 882 metres, the air is fresh and clear, and the town has a lively main street of cafés and pastry shops. Many riders stop for a coffee and a pastry on the street facing the abbey, and the bike can be parked in the town's squares. The roads in and out are smooth, with gentle gradients and broad curves, although traffic through the town centre can be busy, and coaches fill the pilgrim season.

Fuel is easy in town, and there are plenty of places to eat, from simple cafés to gasthofs with Swiss specialities. In winter, snow and ice may linger on the pass roads, and the town can be cold and foggy. Take ten minutes to step inside the abbey, since the interior is worth it.
t.zug lakeside@47.2,8.5:
Zug sits on the northeast corner of its lake with the Alps behind it, and the first thing you notice is how neat everything is. The town has an old centre of lanes and arcades, a clock tower painted in blue and gold, the Zytturm, and a lakeside promenade that looks across the water to the long, green bulk of the Rigi. The town has become famous in recent decades as a corporate and financial centre, drawn by some of the lowest taxes in Switzerland, and a number of cryptocurrency firms have given the area the nickname of Crypto Valley. Yet the old streets still feel local and calm.

Zug is also known for its cherry cake, the Zuger Kirschtorte, a layered sponge of almond meringue, buttercream and cherry brandy that is a local pride, and for the Röteli, a small char that lives in the deep, cold lake. Restaurants along the shore serve it fried or grilled, with a glass of white wine and a view of the sunset. The lake is clean enough to swim in during the summer, and the lakefront has pontoons, diving boards and shaded lawns.

Across the lake, the Rigi, known as the queen of mountains, can be glimpsed on most clear days. In 1871 the first mountain railway in Europe opened on its slopes, at Vitznau, and trains still climb to the summit. The ride toward it from Zug runs along the lake and through orchards and farms, with views of the water and the peaks, and the roads bend gently between villages. Traffic can be busy near the town, particularly at commuting hours and on summer weekends, so aim for a quiet window.

As the exit of a day's ride, Zug is a pleasure. At 413 metres it is warm and sheltered, and fuel stations and parking are easy to find. A coffee on the lakefront, with the sun low over the water and the Rigi in silhouette, is hard to beat. Locals stroll the promenade at dusk, and the evening feels slow and civilised.
t.pavia@45.2,9.2:
Pavia lies on the Ticino River in the flat, fertile Po plain south of Milan, and it has a long and surprising past. The Lombards made it their capital in the sixth century, and for two hundred years it was the seat of their kingdom. The University of Pavia, founded in 1361, is among the oldest in Europe, and its students have given the city a youthful, bicycle-filled atmosphere. In 1525 a battle outside the walls ended with the capture of King Francis I of France by the troops of Emperor Charles V, a defeat that changed the balance of power in Europe.

The old centre has red-brick towers, medieval churches and a covered bridge across the river, the Ponte Coperto. The present bridge is a reconstruction, rebuilt after the Second World War when its predecessor, dating from the fourteenth century, was bombed. A few kilometres north, the Certosa di Pavia, a Carthusian monastery begun in 1396, has a spectacular marble facade, one of the finest works of the Lombard Renaissance. The surrounding country is rice land, with flooded paddies in spring that mirror the sky, and risotto is the local staple.

For a rider heading south toward the Ligurian Apennines and Portofino, Pavia is the practical gate. Fuel is plentiful, and coffee and a brioche are easily found. The Oltrepò Pavese, the hills beyond the Po, offer vineyards, small castles and winding roads that climb toward passes such as Penice, where the plain is left behind. In winter, fog can lie thick over the plains, reducing visibility, while summer days can be hot and hazy.

Check traffic around the city in the early morning, since lorries and commuters fill the roads. Cross the Po on the long bridge and enjoy the first folds of the hills. Pavia is lively in the evening, with students gathering at the cafés, and a stop here is a cheerful way to start a long day.
t.como lake@45.8,9.1:
Como sits at the southern tip of the western arm of Lake Como, with steep mountains rising straight from the water, and the town has been a place of passage for two thousand years. The Romans founded it, and Pliny the Younger was born here. Alessandro Volta, who invented the electric battery, was born in Como in 1745, and a temple on the lakeshore holds his instruments. The city's silk industry, which once supplied much of Europe, gave it a wealth that shows in the grand villas along the shore.

At the heart of town stands the cathedral, built over four centuries, with a marble facade in Gothic and Renaissance style. A funicular opened in 1894 climbs steeply from the lakeside to Brunate, a hill village with views across the lake to the Alps. The lakefront promenade is a favourite for evening strolls, with boats arriving and leaving and the water shimmering in the late light. Lake Como itself is shaped like an upside-down Y, and the arm to the east, around Lecco, is quieter and wilder.

The day's gate leads to the Ghisallo ridge, a gentle rise above the lake with a small chapel, the Madonna del Ghisallo, adopted as the patron of cyclists, and a museum of cycling history beside it. On a weekend you will see lines of cyclists, and motorcyclists gather as well. The roads climbing from the lake wind through woodland and old villages, with narrow bends and good views, though the surface can be patchy, and traffic on the lake road toward Bellagio is heavy in summer, with buses and delivery vans. Go early or on a weekday.

Fuel is available around Como, and the town has cafés and gelaterias in good number, with restricted traffic zones in the centre that you should avoid on a bike. Parking is easier outside the old town. Autumn is lovely, with clear light and fewer visitors, though the mountains can hold mist.
t.egg@47.4,9.9:
Egg is the sort of village where the first thing you notice is the wood. Houses, barns, bus shelters and cafes are all clad in timber, in an elegant, modern way that has made the Bregenzerwald one of the most admired regions in Europe for contemporary country architecture. The older farmhouses have shingled facades that have weathered to silver, and the newer ones echo the style so faithfully that you can hardly tell where one era stops.

The village lies on the Bregenzerach river in a broad, green valley in the westernmost part of Austria, within sight of Lake Constance on a clear day but a world away from its holiday crowds. Egg is the main centre of the lower valley, with a fair-sized church, a few hotels and a high street with shops, bakeries and a bank. The region is famous for its cheese, which the locals take very seriously. The Käsestraße, the cheese road, links dairies, farms and mountain huts, and the valley's Alpkäse and Bergkäse are protected products, made in copper vats over wood fires in summer pastures.

The riding here is relaxed and rewarding. The road through the valley rises and falls over gentle hills, with long, open bends that suit an easy pace. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is moderate except on summer weekends. You might come across cows being driven down from the mountain pastures in September, in the old Alpabtrieb custom, with garlands of flowers on their horns and bells that can be heard from a kilometre away. It is a wonderful sight, and a good reason to be flexible with your timing.

Practically, Egg is a good stop. It is a real village with real shops, and fuel is available in or close to the village. If you need a larger town, Wolfurt, about twelve kilometres away, is close to the motorway, and Dornbirn is a short ride beyond. Cafes in Egg serve Kässpätzle, the cheese noodles topped with fried onions, which is the valley's comfort food and perfectly judged after a day in the saddle. Local apple juice, pressed from the valley's orchards, is a good non-alcoholic companion.

Spend a little time walking the village, and you will see why people who come to ride often end up staying longer.
t.bezau@47.4,9.9:
Bezau is a handsome valley village, with a church tower, a few grand hotels from the age of early summer tourism and a pleasant, slightly sleepy main street. It stands on the Bregenzerach in the middle of the Bregenzerwald, at the foot of the Bezauer Wanne, the hollow in the mountain wall behind the village, and a cable car climbs to the pastures above if you have time for a walk with a view.

What gives Bezau a particular charm is its railway. A narrow-gauge line once ran up the valley from Bregenz, closed in the 1980s, and a short section of it has been preserved. The Wälderbähnle, a little steam train, chuffs between Bezau and Schwarzenberg on summer weekends, with an open carriage, a whistle and the authentic smell of coal smoke. Railway enthusiasts come from Germany and Switzerland to see it, and even if you only watch it pass, the sight of a narrow-gauge locomotive in a green valley is worth the pause.

The valley's cultural identity is strong. The women's traditional dress, the Juppe, is still worn on holidays, with intricate pleating and dark colours, and the local dialect is thick enough that other Austrians struggle with it. Farming still shapes the economy, with dairies and cheese shops in every village, and there are craft workshops making furniture, ceramics and textiles in a modern, simple way. The valley invested in design and craftsmanship long before those words became fashionable.

On the road, the ride from Bezau is a mixture of valley run and small climbs. The main road runs through villages, with enough bends to keep you alert and enough straight sections to enjoy the scenery. For more of a challenge, side roads climb to hamlets and viewpoints, narrow and sometimes rough, with farm traffic. Weekdays are quiet. The best time of day is before ten in the morning, when mist still sits in the hollows and the light picks out the hay meadows.

Bezau is a good place to stop, with cafes, bakeries and a fuel station in the village or nearby. Dornbirn, about thirteen kilometres away as the crow flies, is the largest town and the best option if you need a workshop or a big supermarket. A coffee and a slice of cake on a terrace here is a very civilised way of passing half an hour.
t.san bernardino pass@46.5,9.2:
The San Bernardino Pass is a high, bare saddle at 2,066 metres on the Swiss side of the Alps, and it is one of the oldest crossings between the Rhine valley and Italy. Travellers, muleteers and armies have used it since Roman times, and the pass is named, according to local tradition, after the Franciscan preacher Bernardino of Siena, who is said to have crossed it in the fifteenth century. It sits in the canton of Graubünden, between the German-speaking village of Hinterrhein, where the Rhine begins, and the Italian-speaking valley of Mesolcina, which drops south toward Bellinzona.

The pass has been bypassed since 1967 by the motorway tunnel that passes beneath it, so the old road has turned into a quiet, pleasant motorcycle route, with little traffic and some of the finest scenery in the Alps. On the north side the road climbs from Hinterrhein in a series of broad bends, crosses open meadow and arrives at the summit, where a small lake, the Lago Moesola, sits beside the road. On the south side, a flight of hairpins drops through larch and spruce toward the village of San Bernardino, and then down the long valley to Mesocco, where a ruined castle stands on a rock above the road.

The riding is excellent. The surface is generally smooth, the bends are well engineered, and the views from the hairpins are wide and clear. The north side is bare and stony, with cold air and sparse pastures, while the south side quickly turns green, with chestnut and walnut trees in the lower valley. The climate difference is strong, and the temperature rises many degrees in a short descent. The pass is closed in winter, normally from about November until May, depending on snow, so check before you go.
