The weather can be harsh. Cloud sits on the pass often, and the wind is cold, even in summer. Bring a warm layer, and be careful with fog, which can reduce visibility to a few metres. Marmots whistle from the rocks, and if you are lucky you may see a bearded vulture in the sky, a bird that has been reintroduced to the Alps.

The nearest services are at San Bernardino village and Mesocco on the south, and at Splügen on the north, and Biasca, further down the valley toward the Ticino plain, is the larger town. Fill the tank before you climb.
t.ibergeregg@47.0,8.7:
Ibergeregg is a green saddle at 1,406 metres in the central Swiss Prealps, and it is one of those passes that locals ride on a whim rather than a mission. It connects Schwyz, the old town that gave the country its name, with the valley of the Minster river and the village of Oberiberg, and it forms the western half of the loop with the Pragel Pass. The road is not high enough to be a major crossing, but it is wild enough to feel like it, with alpine pasture, fir forest and the rocky ridges of the Mythen above.

The two Mythen peaks, the Grosser and Kleiner Mythen, are the landmark of the area. They rise as sharp, pale limestone teeth over Schwyz, easily recognisable from many parts of central Switzerland, and a path climbs the larger one to a summit with a view across several lakes. From the pass, the shape of the mountains can be seen to best effect on a clear morning, when the air is cool and the light is sharp. The slopes are grazed by cattle in summer, and in autumn the animals descend to the valley in a parade with bells and flowers.

The road has all the character of a good Swiss pass. From Schwyz it climbs in a long series of bends through meadow and beech forest, passes the village of Rickenbach, and enters the open pastureland near the summit. The surface is generally excellent, the gradients are moderate, and the corners are easy to read. On the far side, the road drops toward Oberiberg and the Alpthal. It is a popular road with riders, particularly on sunny weekends, when traffic may be heavy and the cafes at the top fill with leather and helmets.

There is a mountain restaurant at the pass, which does solid Swiss food, including rösti, sausage and cake. The cheese of the region, produced in summer in the alpine huts, is worth a look at farm shops along the road. The pass is generally open throughout the year, but the road is snowy in winter, and ice can persist on shady stretches into April. Check conditions and carry a layer, because the weather can turn quickly.

Muotathal, about five kilometres from the summit on one side, and Schwyz, about six kilometres away on the other, both have services. Fill the tank before the climb, and plan your loop so that you are not caught short in the quiet valleys.
t.muotathal@47.0,8.8:
Muotathal is a long valley village in canton Schwyz, strung along the Muota river in a deep cleft between steep, wooded mountains. It has a population of about three and a half thousand, most of them spread out over small farms and hamlets, and the place has a reputation for being slightly mysterious. The valley is known across Switzerland for its weather prophets, the Wetterschmöcker, a group of local men who claim to predict the weather by watching nature, and whose forecasts for the coming winter are reported in the national newspapers each year.

Beneath the valley is the Hölloch, one of the longest cave systems in the world, with well over a hundred and fifty kilometres of explored passages, all of it carved by water in the limestone. Guided tours take visitors into a section of the cave, in helmets and boots, and tell of the explorers who have spent days underground mapping it. Above it, the Bödmerenwald is the largest natural spruce forest in the Alps, a primeval-looking stand of ancient trees, left largely untouched, where the trunks are covered in lichen and the forest floor is thick with moss.

History arrived here in an unexpected form in 1799, when the Russian general Alexander Suvorov, leading an army out of Italy to join allied forces in Switzerland, found that the allies had already been defeated. He marched his exhausted troops over the Pragel Pass into the Muotathal, fought a series of battles against the French in the valley, and then retreated eastward over the mountains in a campaign of extraordinary hardship. A memorial in the valley remembers the Russian soldiers.

For a rider, Muotathal is the heart of the Pragel and Ibergeregg loop, a good place to stop for a coffee and to check the tank. The road along the valley is narrow in places, with tight bends, tunnels and sheer rock walls, and the surface is patchy. The climb to the Pragel Pass begins here, with a narrow road that can be slow in summer when the cars are many. In the early morning the valley is cool and quiet, and the river is a deep green.

The village has fuel, a few shops, bakeries and restaurants serving Swiss mountain food, including cheese dishes and Älplermagronen, the macaroni and potato dish served with apple sauce. Schwyz, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with more services. The valley can be dark and cold in winter, when the sun barely reaches the valley floor.
t.pragel pass@47.0,8.9:
Pragel is the pass that Swiss riders mention in a slightly lowered voice, because it is narrow. The road between the Muotathal and the Klöntal lake in canton Glarus tops out at 1,548 metres, and long stretches of it are barely one car wide, with passing places cut into the verge and a rule, understood by everyone, that the vehicle with the easier retreat backs up. It is a bike road more than a car road, and on a quiet weekday morning it is also one of the most rewarding in central Switzerland.

The climb from the Muotathal side goes up through damp forest and then steep meadow, with bends that tighten as the valley narrows and the Muota drops far below. At the top, the landscape changes into a bare, rocky plateau, with limestone cut into strange furrows by rainwater. This is karst country, a rock that water has hollowed out from beneath, and the grass between the boulders is full of small flowers in June. From the summit, the descent toward the Klöntal is steeper and more wooded, and the lake appears at the bottom like a green mirror.

The Klöntal side has a different mood. The lake lies in a glacial trough walled by steep slopes, and a lane runs along its shore past a small mountain inn at Richisau, which is the sort of place where hikers, cyclists and riders end up at the same table. Cheese is made in the huts on the high pastures all summer, and the herdsmen bring their cattle down in a procession each autumn.

Practical matters need respect. The road is closed in winter, usually from about November to May, and the opening dates depend on the snow. Large vehicles and trailers are not suitable, and on busy summer days the narrow sections can make progress slow, with queues of cars waiting at the passing places. Rain makes the surface slick and the verges soft, and cattle may be on the road, with their bells clanking in the mist. The best time is early morning in June, September or October.

Unteriberg and Muotathal are the nearest villages with services, and Glarus is the larger town on the eastern side. A cheese from one of the alpine dairies is a worthwhile thing to carry, if you have space in the luggage.
t.simplon dorf@46.2,8.1:
Simplon village sits at about 1,470 metres on the northern slope of the Simplon Pass, in the Swiss canton of Valais, and it is a place that gets its living from a road. A cluster of stone houses with dark timber upper floors, a church tower and an old inn stands on a green shelf above the Gantertal, and the Alps close in on every side. In winter the snow is deep, in summer the meadows are full of flowers, and at all times there is a faint sense of being on a route to somewhere else.

The road is the story. Traders had crossed the Simplon since the Middle Ages, and in the seventeenth century a merchant named Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper built a trading empire on it, with warehouses, a hospice and a mule track that made the pass practicable. His great palace still stands in the town of Brig, on the northern side. In 1801 Napoleon ordered a carriage road across the pass, and the modern road still follows much of that line.

The ride up from Brig is a long, rhythmic climb, with the road looping up the hillside and crossing the Ganter bridge, a modern concrete viaduct that stretches across a deep gorge. The curves are open, the gradient is moderate, and the surface is generally excellent. In the village, the road slows to a village speed and passes between houses, and then it opens again for the last climb to the summit. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, when cars and buses from northern Europe stream over to Italy, and a quiet morning is better.

Simplon Dorf has a few inns and cafes, a small shop and a post office, and the food is typical Valais cooking, with raclette, dried meats and rye bread. The local Walliser Roggenbrot is a dense, dark loaf made with rye, and it keeps well in a pannier.

For fuel, do not rely on the village, as there is little here. Brig, about fourteen kilometres below on the northern side, is the nearest large town, with several stations, and Domodossola, on the southern side, also offers plenty. Fill the tank before the climb, and bring a warm layer, because the weather at the top can be cold and windy even on a clear day.
t.simplon pass@46.2,8.1:
The Simplon Pass is the grandest of the Swiss crossings to Italy that Napoleon bothered to build. At 2,005 metres, it lies on a broad, grassy saddle between the Valais Alps and the Lepontine range, and the road that crosses it, finished in 1805, was the first carriage road across the Alps. It was built for military reasons, and its engineers were told to make it wide and gentle enough for artillery, so riders benefit from a gradient that never becomes harsh and from generous, well-planned bends.

At the summit stands the Simplon Hospice, a big, plain stone building that was begun by Napoleon's order and completed by the Augustinian canons of the Great St Bernard in the 1830s. The monks still live and work there, with their famous dogs, and the building gives a reassuring sense of shelter in a bare landscape. A short distance away, a huge stone eagle on a pedestal commemorates the Swiss soldiers who guarded the border during the Second World War, and it is a good landmark for photographs, with the peaks of the Bernese and Valais Alps behind.

The ride from the north starts at Brig and climbs through Simplon Dorf. From the summit, the road drops steeply to the south, into the narrow gorge of Gondo, where the road passes through galleries cut into the rock and waterfalls spill onto the roadway. Beyond the border lies Italy, with its different light and quickly warming air, and the road continues to Varzo and Domodossola. The surface is generally good, but the galleries can be damp, with water on the road, and the shadows make the bends harder to read. Traffic is heavy in summer, and trucks use the road, so passing needs patience.

The pass is open for most of the year, although heavy snow can close it for short periods in winter, and chains are required when conditions are bad. The weather at the summit is unpredictable, with cloud, wind and sudden temperature drops common. The best time is from late spring to early autumn, in the morning, when visibility is good and traffic is light. Do not be surprised by a snow shower in June.

Brig, on the northern side, and Domodossola, about seventeen kilometres from the top on the Italian side, are the nearest larger towns, and Varzo is a smaller place between them. Prices in Switzerland are higher than in Italy, so you may want to eat in Italy, and buy fuel there too.
t.splugen pass@46.5,9.3:
The Splügen Pass is the border between the Swiss canton of Graubünden and the Italian province of Sondrio, and at 2,114 metres it is one of the most beautiful ways to move between them. It has been in use since Roman times, and the road that crosses it today follows a route that was important for trade between Lombardy and the Rhine, with wine, grain and iron travelling north and salt and cattle south. Its character is bleak and open, with bare slopes, scattered boulders and a vast sky.

On the Swiss side, the road climbs from the village of Splügen in a long series of broad, easy bends, through meadows and then bare rock, to the border post at the summit. The surface is generally good, and the views are of a wide, empty landscape. The Italian side is wilder. From the pass the road drops in a dramatic series of hairpins through a stepped valley, crossing the river and clinging to the mountainside. In places the road is sheltered by concrete galleries to protect it from avalanches, and the waterfalls come down beside it, spraying the tarmac.

This stretch is part of the Via Spluga, an old mule path that has been restored as a walking route, and sections of the cobbled track can be seen from the road, with stone bridges and old customs houses. The walkers who follow it reach the Cardinello gorge, where the path hangs on the cliff above a deep ravine. The gorge was a major hazard for travellers in the Middle Ages, and the road along it is still a sight to see. On the Italian side, the valley is also known for its chestnut trees and for waterfalls that fall from the cliffs, and the village of Campodolcino is the main settlement.

The pass is closed in winter, usually from about November until the end of May, and the opening depends on snow clearing. Even in summer, the weather can be cold, and mist is common. Check opening dates and the situation at the border before you set out, and carry your passport or identity card, even though checks are usually informal. The air is thin and the wind is sharp, and the light at sunrise is very fine.

There is little at the top, with only a few small stalls and a cafe in summer. The nearest fuel is at Splügen on the Swiss side and Chiavenna, about twenty-one kilometres to the south, on the Italian side, and Campodolcino has limited services. Fill the tank before the climb, and keep some euros and Swiss francs in your pocket.
t.montespluga@46.5,9.3:
Montespluga is a handful of buildings by a reservoir at about 1,900 metres, just below the Splügen Pass on the Italian side, and it feels like the end of the road, even though the road goes on. The village is at the head of the Valle Spluga, and it sits beside the dark blue water of Lake Montespluga, a long reservoir that was dammed in the twentieth century to generate electricity, and which covered part of the old village. The mountains rise from the shore in bare slopes of grey rock and tussock grass, and in the evening the light on the water is clear and cold.

The place has a small number of permanent residents, and most of its buildings are hotels, restaurants and holiday houses, many of them closed in winter. The road to the village, the SS36 from Campodolcino, is one of the great motorcycle roads of the Italian Alps, with a series of hairpins that wind up the side of the valley in tight stacks. Traffic is mostly light, with a surge at weekends in summer, and the surface is generally decent, with a few rough patches where frost and meltwater have worked on it. There are tunnels and galleries along the way, some of them dark and wet.

The history of the Valle Spluga is a history of crossing. The pass above has carried travellers for centuries, and the modern road is a successor to the mule track and the carriage road built in the nineteenth century. In summer, shepherds still bring flocks of sheep and goats to the high pastures, and cheeses made in the huts can be bought at the village or at small farm stalls along the road. The reservoir itself is popular with anglers, and the shore offers a gentle path for walks, with views of the dam, the road and the peaks.

The air is thin, and the weather can change in minutes. Mist rolls over the reservoir, the temperature drops, and a shower of rain or sleet can arrive from nowhere, even in July. Dress warmly and keep your visor clear. In September the larches on the lower slopes turn gold, and the first snow often dusts the tops by October, when the road is about to close.

There are a couple of restaurants and bars in Montespluga that serve hot food, polenta, pizzoccheri and local cheese, and they are welcome after a cold ride. Campodolcino, about ten kilometres down the valley, has limited services, and Chiavenna, about nineteen kilometres further, is the nearest large town with several stations.
t.lutry@46.5,6.7:
Lutry is where the Lavaux begins, if you come from Lausanne, and it announces the fact with vineyards that climb straight up behind the old town. The terraces, held by dry-stone walls that run for kilometres, rise from the shore of Lake Geneva to the ridge above, a staircase of green in summer and gold in autumn. They were first built by monks in the Middle Ages, and in 2007 UNESCO placed the whole landscape on its World Heritage list. Lutry itself is a lakeside town of nearly nine thousand people, with a medieval centre, a harbour and a promenade.

The old town has narrow, cobbled streets, stone houses with wooden shutters and a Romanesque church tower that rises above the roofs. Its priory dates from the Benedictines, who held the land and planted vines, and the traces of their work are everywhere, in the cellars, the walls and the layout of the terraces. Lutry's wine is mostly Chasselas, a white grape that produces a light, dry, mineral wine that tastes of the stone and the lake. It is the standard drink of western Switzerland, and pairs well with cheese fondue or a plate of fish from the lake.

For a rider, Lutry is the start of a gentle, rewarding ride along the Corniche de Lavaux, the narrow road that threads between the vines high above the lake. The bends are tight and the surface is smooth, with walls on both sides and sudden views across the water to the mountains of Savoy. Traffic can be an issue, because the road is narrow and popular with cyclists and walkers, and on weekends in the harvest season it can be very slow. The main road along the lake is faster but busier, with traffic lights and heavy lorries. For a quiet visit, aim for a weekday in spring or autumn, preferably in the morning, when the light is soft on the water.

Lutry is a town, not a village, so there are fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, and Lausanne is only a few kilometres away if you need anything more. Parking can be tight in the old town, and motorcycle bays near the harbour are usually the easiest option. A coffee on the harbour front, with the sailing boats bobbing in the water, is a pleasant way to spend a short while.

In September and October, the grape harvest brings tractors and pickers to the terraces, and the air smells of crushed fruit and wine cellars. Walk up through the vines for a few hundred metres, and the view back across the lake is one of the best in the country.
t.cully@46.5,6.7:
Cully is a wine village on the shore of Lake Geneva, and the whole place seems to be organised around the tasting of Chasselas. Narrow streets run down between old stone houses to a small harbour, a lakeside promenade and a pebble beach, and behind the village the terraced vineyards climb the slope. It is a quiet and civilised little place, and the cellars, or caveaux, that open their doors to visitors are the heart of the social life.

The village is famous for its jazz festival, held each spring, when the streets and cellars fill with musicians and listeners, and when the population swells for a week or so. It began modestly in the 1980s and has grown into one of the best-known festivals in Switzerland, held in the village hall, in bars and in the cellars of the vignerons. Outside festival time, it is quiet, with a few cafes, an excellent bakery and a restaurant or two serving fish from the lake, perch fillets with fries being the classic.

The surrounding landscape is the heart of Lavaux, the long terraced slope that runs for about thirty kilometres along the north shore of the lake. The walls that hold up the terraces were built by monks, from the eleventh century onwards, and are in constant need of repair, as rain and frost loosen the stones. The vineyards face south and receive light three times: from the sun above, from the reflection of the lake, and from the heat stored in the walls. That unusual combination, locals say, is the secret of the wine.

The road above the village, the Corniche, is the best way to ride the region, a tight, winding lane through the vines with lake views at nearly every bend. Parking in the village itself is limited, and it is best to leave the bike near the station or the harbour. In the early morning in May or September, with mist on the lake and the Alps standing across the water, it is magical. In the middle of a summer weekend it is crowded.

Cully has a few shops and a small supermarket but no large fuel station, so it is best to top up in Lutry, about four kilometres to the west, or in Vevey. If you plan to taste wine, remember that the Swiss limit for alcohol is low and enforcement is strict, so a sip and a spit is wiser than a glass, and you can always buy a bottle to take away.
t.rivaz@46.5,6.8:
Rivaz is a small village in the middle of Lavaux, and it is easy to ride past without noticing, which would be a mistake. The houses are old and the lanes are narrow, running down toward the lake between walls of dry stone and rows of vines. A railway line cuts through the village, with a station that serves the little trains that run along the shore, and the whole place feels as if it had been left alone by the modern world.

The village is part of the terraced wine country that UNESCO recognised in 2007, and its position is perfect, with a south-facing slope, sheltering ridge and a clear view over the lake to the mountains of Savoy. A short distance away lies the vineyard of Dézaley, one of the most famous in Switzerland, where the terraces are steepest and the wine is rich and mineral. The wine centre in Rivaz, a modern building that explains the work of the vineyards and offers tastings, makes a good place to learn about the wine of the region before you buy a bottle. Opening hours vary with the season, so check them in advance.

Rivaz is best explored on foot. Footpaths drop through the vines from the ridge to the lake, passing under the railway and between the walls, and signs outside the cellars announce when a grower has opened for tasting. The vineyards are worked by hand because machines cannot manage the slopes, and many growers sell directly from their cellars, so a bottle bought here usually has a story attached, and often is not for sale in any shop.

The riding around Rivaz is among the best short rides in Switzerland. The road above the village, the Corniche, winds through the vines with tight bends and narrow sections, with stone walls on either side. Take it slowly, and give way to cyclists and walkers, who use the lanes in large numbers. The main lake road below is faster, but less attractive. Afternoons in late summer can be hot, with sun reflected from the walls, and a cool drink is welcome.

The village has a handful of cafes and wine bars, and a little shop, but you will not find a fuel station here. Chexbres, about a kilometre away on the ridge, has more services, and Vevey, about five kilometres to the east, is the nearest large town, with plenty of fuel and supermarkets. Plan to visit in the spring or autumn, when the vines are green or golden and the crowds are thinner.
t.wildhaus@47.2,9.4:
Wildhaus is the village where Huldrych Zwingli was born, and that makes it, quietly, one of the cradles of the Swiss Reformation. Zwingli, who became the leader of the Protestant movement in Zürich and died in battle in 1531, was born in 1484 in a farmhouse here, and the small timber building still stands, now a museum. It is a modest place, a wooden house with low ceilings and small windows, and it gives a feel for the mountain farming community from which the reformer came.

The village sits at about 1,090 metres on a broad saddle, the Wildhaus Pass, between the Rhine valley and the Toggenburg, in a landscape of green meadows and wooded slopes. Above it rise the Churfirsten, a line of seven limestone peaks that stand like a wall along the north side of the Walensee, and which are among the most recognisable mountains in eastern Switzerland. From the village, the north face is a tall, sheer escarpment. Further north, the Säntis, the highest peak of the Alpstein, can be seen in the distance.

For a rider, Wildhaus is a lovely stop on the road between Buchs in the Rhine valley and the Toggenburg, with gentle bends, smooth tarmac and moderate gradients. The road is a pleasure at an easy pace, and the scenery is varied, with views of both the Churfirsten and the Alpstein. Traffic is light except in the ski season and on summer weekends. Weather can change quickly, and the pass is occasionally icy in winter, so keep an eye on the forecast.

The village has fuel nearby, small shops and cafes, and a handful of restaurants serving traditional dishes. The Toggenburg region is known for its cheese, its dairy products and a distinctive folk music tradition, the Naturjodel, which uses wordless harmonies, and which you may hear at a festival or in a restaurant on a Sunday. In winter the village is a ski resort, and in summer it is a hiking centre, with lifts that take walkers to the high pastures.

Grabs, about seven kilometres down toward the Rhine, is the nearest sizeable town and has more services. A coffee in the village, with a view of the Churfirsten, is a pleasant way to spend a short stop. Try a slice of Toggenburger Biber, the local gingerbread with almond filling, which is a good snack for the road.
t.schwagalp@47.3,9.3:
Schwägalp is a pass road, a mountain pasture and a cable car station all at once, and the third of those is the reason most people stop. At 1,278 metres, on a high saddle between canton Appenzell and the Toggenburg, it is the lower station for the Säntis cable car, which climbs in a few minutes to the summit of the Säntis at 2,502 metres. The mountain is the highest of the Alpstein range, a compact, craggy massif that rises abruptly out of the Swiss plateau, and on a clear day the view from the top extends across six countries.

The pass road, which runs between Urnäsch and Neu St Johann, is an excellent ride, well graded, with bends that open as the road climbs and then drop gently into the Toggenburg. It passes through pasture, forest and clusters of farmhouses, with views of the Säntis rising to the south. The surface is smooth and the road is kept open all year, though snow and ice can make it difficult in winter. On sunny weekends in summer it is busy with riders and cyclists, so start early and take your time.

Because the Säntis stands alone, it makes its own weather. Clouds gather around the summit even when the surrounding sky is clear, and the temperature at the top can be many degrees colder than at the base. A weather station has operated on the summit since the nineteenth century, and the staff once endured long winters in isolation, a story told in the exhibitions on the mountain. Check the webcams before you commit to the cable car, because the view is the whole point.

The Appenzell region has a strong identity, with its painted farmhouses, its folk music, its conservative politics and its cheese. Appenzeller cheese is made from cow's milk and matured in a brine of herbs and wine, the recipe a closely guarded secret, and it has a strong, nutty flavour that goes well with a hot rösti. A restaurant at Schwägalp serves such dishes, with a view of the mountain from the terrace.

Fuel can be found at the town of Appenzell, about eleven kilometres away, a charming place of painted houses and a pedestrian centre, or in Wildhaus. Fill the tank before you climb, and keep a warm layer in the bag, because even on a bright day the wind at this height can be keen.
t.spiez@46.7,7.7:
Spiez occupies a promontory on the south shore of Lake Thun, and it has the kind of position that makes you think the founders knew exactly what they were doing. A castle stands on a spur above the water, with a Romanesque church beside it, vineyards on the slope behind, and a bay below with sailing boats, a harbour and a lakeside promenade. Beyond the lake, the pyramid of the Niesen rises to the south, and the great white mass of the Bernese Alps fills the horizon to the east.

The castle, Schloss Spiez, dates from the early Middle Ages and was altered many times by noble families, and it is now a museum open to the public. Its tower, its courtyard and its rooms with painted ceilings give a sense of how a Bernese lord lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The church, with its early medieval crypt, is older still, and the walk from the harbour up to the castle is only a few minutes. The vineyards on the slope are small but real, producing a light white wine that is rarely exported.

Spiez is also a railway town. It is the junction where the line from Bern splits, with one branch heading up the Simme valley and the other climbing to the Lötschberg tunnel and the Valais, and trains stop here at all hours. The town is lively, with a sizeable population of nearly thirteen thousand, shops, schools and a few industries, including a Swiss federal laboratory that specialises in protection against nuclear, biological and chemical hazards, which seems an odd neighbour for such a pretty setting.

The riding around Lake Thun is an excellent mix. The road along the south shore passes through villages and under cliffs, with gentle bends and views of the water, and the road to Interlaken and Lauterbrunnen continues along the lake. In summer, traffic is heavy, and parking near the lake is limited, so the early morning is best. The ride from here to the Lauterbrunnen valley is a classic, with the road climbing into the heart of the Bernese Oberland, and the Jungfrau massif looming ahead.

Spiez is a proper town with fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a good choice of restaurants, many with terraces overlooking the lake. Eat fresh lake fish if you like, or a local cheese, and take a short walk along the lakeside to enjoy the light. It is a convenient stop for a break, with no compromise on scenery.
t.tremola lower hairpins@46.5,8.6:
The Tremola is the old road up the south side of the Gotthard, and its lower hairpins are where the cobbles begin. Built between 1827 and 1832, when the Gotthard became a proper carriage route, it climbs out of the Ticino valley above Airolo in a staircase of twenty-four tight bends, laid with granite setts and held up by dry-stone walls. The setts are rounded and worn, and in the morning dew or after rain they are slippery in a way that tarmac riders forget until the front wheel reminds them.

The name is usually explained as the Italian for trembling, and people argue about whether it refers to the shaking of the coaches, the fear of the passengers or the tremor of an avalanche. Whatever the truth, the road was dangerous in its day. Mail coaches crossed here with horses, and in winter the snow fell so heavily that parties were trapped for days. A new road was later built on the other side of the valley, and the Tremola was left as a relic, then restored and reopened as a heritage route, now popular with riders, cyclists and people who want to feel what a crossing felt like in the nineteenth century.

The riding is different from anything else in the region. The bends are very tight, the radius is small, and the gradient steepens on the corners, so first and second gear are your friends, and a light touch on the brakes matters more than speed. The cobbles are bumpy enough to make the handlebars twitch, and there is often fine gravel on the apex. Traffic is usually light but slow, with cars and cyclists, and meeting a coach on a hairpin takes patience. In summer, the road is dry and warm, with the sun on the south-facing slope, and the views back down to Airolo grow with each turn.

The road is closed in winter, normally from about October to June, and its opening depends on snow and rockfall, so check before you go. In early summer there may still be snowbanks beside the road, and the temperature falls as you climb. Mist often gathers by afternoon, so a morning ride has better light and views.

Airolo, a small town at the foot of the climb, has fuel, a few restaurants and a fort that once protected the southern entrance to the tunnel. It lies about two and a half kilometres below. Biasca is the larger town, further down the valley. Top up the tank here, because you will not find anything at the pass itself.
t.tremola upper hairpins@46.6,8.6:
Higher up the Tremola, the hairpins lose their trees. The old Gotthard road climbs out of the last of the stunted spruce and into bare granite and tussock grass, and the walls that hold up the bends rise in neat steps, one above another, with the tiny shapes of other riders and walkers moving along them. This is the part of the road that appears on postcards, and it deserves it. From a bend near the top you can look straight down on three or four hairpins at once, laid out like the folds of a ribbon.

The granite here is the heart of the Alps. The Gotthard massif is made of some of the oldest and hardest rock in Switzerland, and the road builders had to cut and blast it by hand, then fit the setts one by one. You can see the quality of the work in the walls, in the neat drainage channels and in the cobbles themselves, which have survived nearly two centuries of coaches, cars and weather with only occasional repairs. Rock fall and frost still do damage, and each spring the road crews check for loose stones before opening.

Riding the upper section is easier than the lower, because the corners are a little more open and the rhythm builds, but the exposure is greater. The wall is low, the drop is real and the wind can arrive suddenly, catching a rider on the bend. The surface is rough, with gaps between the stones where water collects, and a cold morning can leave patches of ice into June. A relaxed grip, a steady throttle and a wide smile at the camera pointed at you from above are the right approach.

The air at this altitude is thin and fresh, smelling of stone, damp moss and the faint sweetness of alpine plants. Marmots whistle from the rocks, and in the evening the light turns the granite pink. Clouds can come down fast, bringing rain, sleet or snow, and temperatures can drop by ten degrees in an hour. A waterproof layer and warm gloves are sensible, even in July.

Airolo, about four kilometres below, is the nearest village with services, and Altdorf, on the other side of the pass, is the larger town. The summit has a restaurant and a museum, a short ride higher, and a hot chocolate there tastes better than it has any right to.
t.gotthard pass@46.5,8.6:
The Gotthard Pass is the pass that Switzerland is built around. At 2,106 metres, it lies in the middle of the country on the great watershed between the Alps' northern and southern slopes, and four of Europe's major rivers rise within a few kilometres: the Rhine, the Rhône, the Reuss and the Ticino. Armies, merchants, pilgrims and, today, motorcyclists have been crossing it for eight centuries, since the Schöllenen gorge was opened by a daring bridge in the thirteenth century, and the pass became the shortest link between Germany and Italy.

The summit is a bare, windy plateau with small lakes, grey rock and a cluster of buildings. The old hospice, first built in the thirteenth century and rebuilt more than once, now operates as a hotel and restaurant, and a small museum tells the story of the pass in objects, maps and photographs. In 1799 Suvorov's Russian army fought its way over this pass against the French, and the Gotthard saw hard fighting in the Napoleonic wars. The names of the lakes, Lago della Sella, Lago Lucendro, have an Italian ring, and the transition between cultures here is sudden.

The ride from either side is a classic. From the north, from Andermatt, the road climbs in a series of long, open bends through bare country, with the modern road running smoothly on a wide, gentle grade. From the south, you can choose between the modern road and the old Tremola, whose cobbled hairpins make a more dramatic ascent. Both are closed in winter and normally open from about June to October, so check the dates in advance. Even in midsummer, snow can fall, and the pass is often cloudy, with a strong, cold wind.

The Gotthard has also given its name to some of Europe's greatest engineering. The railway tunnel, opened in 1882, was the longest in the world at the time, and the road tunnel, opened in 1980, remains one of the longest. In 2016, the Gotthard Base Tunnel, 57 kilometres of twin tubes deep under the mountains, was opened and made the old pass a purely scenic route. It is a delight to ride the pass knowing that most of the traffic is going through the mountain.

Fuel is available at Airolo, about four and a half kilometres below on the southern side, and at Andermatt on the northern side, but nothing at the summit. Altdorf, on the Reuss, is the larger town on the northern side. A coffee on the terrace of the hospice, with a view over the lakes, is the best way to enjoy the top.
t.locarno@46.2,8.8:
Locarno is a lakeside town on the northern shore of Lake Maggiore, and it has a different climate from the rest of Switzerland, mild enough that palms and camellias grow along the waterfront. It lies at the foot of the Alps, on the edge of the Ticino delta, where the Maggia river reaches the lake, and the mix of mountains, water and Mediterranean light has drawn visitors for centuries. The town is Italian-speaking, and the feel of it, with its arcades, cafes and piazzas, is unmistakably southern.

The Piazza Grande is the centre of life, a long arcaded square running parallel to the lake. Each August it turns into an open-air cinema, when the Locarno Film Festival fills it with thousands of seats and a huge screen, and the winners of the festival's main prize receive a golden leopard. Above the town, on a rocky spur, stands the Madonna del Sasso, a pilgrimage sanctuary founded in 1480, reached by steps, a funicular or a pleasant walk through shaded chapels, with a view over the lake that justifies the effort.

Locarno also has a place in diplomatic history. In 1925, delegates of several European countries met here and signed a series of treaties, the Locarno Pact, which were meant to guarantee peace in western Europe after the First World War, and for a few years they raised hopes of lasting stability. The treaties collapsed in the 1930s, but the name remains attached to the town.

For a rider, Locarno is a gateway to two very different routes. Behind the town, the Vallemaggia and Verzasca valleys cut into the mountains, with deep gorges, rock pools and stone villages, and the road to the Centovalli leads west toward Italy through a wooded landscape of chestnut and granite. Traffic in the town is dense and the lakefront can be slow, especially on summer weekends, so allow time. The best conditions are in spring and autumn, when the days are clear and warm, and the crowds are thin.

Locarno has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants, parking and workshops. Eat a plate of risotto or polenta with braised meat, drink a glass of Ticino merlot, and watch the sun slide down behind the mountains. The ferries across the lake are a pleasant way to spend an hour.
t.ascona@46.2,8.8:
Ascona is the pretty cousin of Locarno, a few minutes along the lakeshore, and the better place to sit down. The old centre is a tangle of narrow lanes, houses painted in ochre and rose and a waterfront promenade lined with cafes, and the whole thing looks out across Lake Maggiore toward the mountains of Italy. Boats bob in the harbour and light dances off the water, and in the evening the terraces fill with people who have no particular plans.

Ascona has an unusual history. At the beginning of the twentieth century, a group of idealists settled on the hill of Monte Verità above the town, and started an experimental community based on vegetarianism, nudism, free love, natural medicine and a general rejection of industrial society. The colony attracted artists, writers, dancers, anarchists and philosophers from across Europe, among them the writer Hermann Hesse, who lived not far away and visited, and the dancer Mary Wigman. The buildings on the hill, which include a Bauhaus-style hotel, are now a museum and a conference centre, and the park with its tea house is open to visitors.

Offshore lie the Brissago Islands, two small islands in the lake that hold a botanical garden filled with subtropical plants from around the world, accessible by boat from the Ascona waterfront. The mild climate of the lake allows palms, citrus and rare plants to thrive, and in spring the gardens bloom spectacularly. The lake itself is cool and calm, a blue so intense that it seems artificial, and a ride out to the islands is a nice change from the saddle.

The road from Locarno to Ascona is short and flat, running past the mouth of the Maggia river, and the real riding begins in the hills above, where narrow roads climb through chestnut woods to stone villages with views of the lake. Surfaces are generally good, but the lanes are narrow and traffic in summer can be heavy with cars looking for parking. Weekdays in spring or autumn are better, and mornings are quietest.

Ascona is a small town of about five thousand people, so it has fuel and the usual services, though Locarno has more. Parking for motorcycles is limited near the promenade, so look for the bays at the edge of the old town. A plate of grilled lake fish, a glass of local wine and a slow walk along the waterfront is as good an end to a day as you will find.
t.centovalli@46.2,8.6:
The Centovalli, the Hundred Valleys, is the name given to the long, wooded cleft that runs from Locarno west to the Italian border and beyond to Domodossola, and the name is not much exaggerated. Streams run down from every side through steep gullies, the slopes are covered in chestnut and beech, and the road follows the main river, the Melezza, through a landscape of rock, water and stone villages that seems a world apart from the polished lakeshore a few minutes away.

The road is narrow, twisting and not always in perfect condition, but the ride is superb. It clings to the hillside, passes through small villages with tight corners and crosses the valley on old stone bridges and modern viaducts. At Intragna, a village on a ledge above the gorge, the tallest church tower in Ticino rises more than sixty metres, and the old houses cluster beneath it. A narrow-gauge railway runs along the same valley, carrying a small red train between Locarno and Domodossola, and you will see it crossing bridges and slipping through tunnels beside the road, a pleasing companion on a day of riding.

The valley has long been a trade and migration route. Its people, poor farmers who could not live on the steep land, left to work as stonemasons, chimney sweeps and plasterers in cities across Europe, and sent money home to rebuild the villages. The stone houses you pass, with their slate roofs and shaded porches, are the product of that labour. Chestnuts were the staple food, ground into flour and baked into bread, and you can still find chestnut cakes and honey in local shops.

Across the border into Italy, the valley continues as the Valle Vigezzo, and the village of Re has a large sanctuary, the Santuario della Madonna del Sangue, which draws pilgrims. It was built after a reported miracle in the late fifteenth century, and its big dome and bell tower dominate the village. The border crossing is informal, but carry your passport or identity card, and be aware that you are leaving Switzerland and its prices.

Fuel can be found in Locarno and in the larger villages in Switzerland, and across the border in Italy, in Santa Maria Maggiore or Domodossola, where it is generally cheaper. In the valley itself, services are few, so fill the tank before you enter. Traffic is light outside the summer weekends, but trucks and buses use the road, and the bends are tight, so ride with care. Autumn, when the chestnuts turn gold, is the best time.
t.klausen pass@46.9,8.8:
The Klausen Pass was built for horse-drawn coaches in the 1890s, and a generation later it was being used for motor racing. Between 1922 and 1934, the Klausenrennen, a hillclimb from Linthal to the summit, was one of the great events of European motor sport, with drivers such as Rudolf Caracciola and Hans Stuck throwing huge cars up the hairpins at average speeds that the road had never been designed for. The race was dropped in the 1930s, but the road has never quite lost the association, and on a quiet morning you can imagine the noise.

The pass, at 1,948 metres, links the canton of Uri with Glarus and is open from about June to October. It is a proper alpine road, with long, sweeping stretches, tight hairpins and views of high peaks, glaciers and waterfalls. From the Uri side, the climb begins in the Schächental, a green valley with farms, and rises through forest and meadow to a series of bends cut into the rock, then to the broad saddle at the top, where a restaurant and a small chapel stand. The surface is smooth and the gradient is moderate, so the road is a pleasure for all kinds of riders.

The geology is striking. The peaks around the pass are folded and tilted limestone and shale, and the Glarus Alps just to the east are famous among geologists for a great thrust fault where older rock lies on top of younger, now part of a World Heritage area. The landscape tells the story of the Alps' formation, though most riders are more interested in the next bend.

Cows are a feature of the pass in summer, and you may find yourself sharing the road with a herd, their bells clanging, calves and all. They have right of way in practice, and you wait, engine off, until they pass. Dairy farmers make cheese in the huts along the route, and the famous Schächentaler cheese can be bought at roadside stalls. Weather at the top is changeable, with cold wind, cloud and rain common, so a waterproof layer is wise.

Altdorf, about fourteen kilometres from the Uri side, is the nearest large town, and Linthal on the Glarus side has services. Fill the tank in Altdorf, and bring cash for the cheese stalls. A hot meal at the summit restaurant, with a view of the Clariden range, makes the climb feel earned.
t.urnerboden@46.9,8.9:
Urnerboden is a long, flat valley floor on the Glarus side of the Klausen Pass, and it is the largest alpine pasture in Switzerland. From June to September, hundreds of cows, calves and goats graze on its meadows, watched by herders and by a handful of farm buildings, and the cowbells drift across the grass like a distant orchestra. Its walls of rock rise on every side, streaked with waterfalls after rain, and the tiny church and the scattered chalets give it a human scale.

The village has a quirk of geography that confuses visitors. Although it lies on the Glarus side of the pass, it belongs politically to canton Uri, the result of a medieval agreement over grazing rights, and the people speak a dialect close to that of Glarus rather than the speech of the rest of Uri. The line was drawn centuries ago, and no one has seen a reason to change it. It is a reminder that Swiss borders were drawn by farmers and cheesemakers rather than by surveyors.

The riding through the valley is a lovely interlude on the Klausen road. After the tight hairpins of the descent, the road runs straight and flat across the pasture for a couple of kilometres, giving a chance to relax and look around, before descending again toward Linthal in a series of bends. In summer the road is busy with cyclists, and the cows often cross it, so slow down, and be prepared to stop. The surface is generally good but marked in places by tractor tracks and cow pats, so keep your eyes open.

The weather here is variable, with cold mornings and warm afternoons, and thunderstorms can arrive quickly in summer. The air smells of hay, cattle and wet grass, and the light is clear and bright. At the end of the season, in September, the herds are decorated with flowers and driven down the valley in the Alpabzug, a celebration that draws many onlookers. The valley is closed with the road in winter, and snow lies deep.

Services are modest, with a couple of restaurants and an inn that serve food, including cheese, sausage and dairy desserts. Linthal, about eight kilometres down the road, is the nearest place with services, and Altdorf is the larger town over the pass. Buy cheese from a farm stall if you see one, and drink the buttermilk, which is the local cure for sweating in leathers.
t.bergun@46.6,9.7:
Bergün sits in the Albula valley in Graubünden, in a landscape so steep that the railway has to loop and spiral to climb it, and the village is where the show begins. A line of the Rhaetian Railway runs through the village on its way up to the Albula tunnel, and on the slope above, trains can be seen passing in several levels, vanishing into tunnels, crossing viaducts and turning around themselves in great loops. The whole line, with its bridges and tunnels, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Bergün is one of its best vantage points.

The village itself is a gem of Engadine-style architecture, with thick-walled houses whose facades are decorated with sgraffito, a technique in which patterns are scratched into plaster, and carved wooden doors. The locals speak Romansh, the fourth national language of Switzerland, which survives in valleys like this one, and the place names have an old, soft sound. A small railway museum in the village tells the story of how the line was built in the early twentieth century, and there is a walking trail along the track, with explanations of the engineering.

The road up the Albula Pass leaves from the village and begins its climb with a series of hairpins through forest, and the road and the railway weave around each other in the valley. The surface is generally good, the bends are tight but well engineered, and the traffic is moderate. In winter, the village is known for its sledge run, a long track that drops from Preda, the high hamlet at the top of the valley, to Bergün, and a ride on it is a favourite activity. In summer, it is the walkers who come, to follow the old rail path.

The weather is changeable, as in all of Graubünden. Mornings are often clear and fresh, with a cold wind off the high slopes, and afternoons can bring cloud and thunder. Look for the tiny stations along the line, the alpine meadows and the glimpses of the great peaks of the Albula range. The air is pure and the water from the fountains in the village is cold and drinkable.

For fuel, the village is small, so check your tank before climbing. Samedan, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable place on the other side of the pass, and Tiefencastel and Davos lie in the other directions. Cafes in Bergün serve Bündner specialties, such as barley soup and the sweet walnut tart called Engadiner Nusstorte, which will keep you warm on the climb.
t.albula pass@46.6,9.9:
The Albula Pass is a quieter and more elegant sibling to the Julier and the Flüela, and at 2,312 metres it sits on a bare, stony plateau between the Albula valley and the Engadin. The road was opened in 1865, making it one of the early Alpine crossings built for coaches, and its surface and gradients still show the sensible hand of a nineteenth-century engineer. It is an open, sweeping road, quiet in the shoulder seasons and delightful when the light is good.

The climb from Bergün goes up in a series of hairpins through spruce forest, past the little hamlet of Preda, and then into open country, where the trees thin out and the landscape becomes bare rock and meadow. A dark small lake near the top reflects the sky. Beneath your wheels, a railway tunnel almost six kilometres long carries the Rhaetian Railway under the pass, opened in 1903, a feat of engineering that took a heavy toll in lives and money. The descent on the Engadin side is more gradual, with long straight stretches and views over the broad valley toward Samedan and the Bernina range.

The Engadin has a distinct character. The sun shines more often than in most of Switzerland, the air is dry and clear, and the light has a special quality that has attracted painters and writers for generations. The valley is the home of the Romansh language and has its own architecture, with deep window recesses and painted facades, and the lakes at St Moritz and Silvaplana lie only a short ride away. Sudden changes in weather are common, and a cold snap with snow in August is by no means unknown.

The pass is closed in winter, and normally opens in late May or June, depending on snow, and closes again in October or November. A thick layer of snow can linger at the top into the summer, and at night the road can freeze. Check conditions before you go, and carry a layer. The surface is generally good but has frost damage in places, and there are few safety barriers on the bends, so keep your speed measured.

Samedan, about six kilometres from the summit, is the nearest town with services, and La Punt, on the Engadin side, is another village. Fill the tank before the climb, and plan time for a pause at the top, where the silence is almost complete.
t.savognin@46.6,9.6:
Savognin is the main village of the Surses, or Oberhalbstein, the high valley that climbs from Tiefencastel toward the Julier Pass. It lies at about 1,200 metres, in a broad green basin with forest on either side, and it has the feel of a place that has lived off the road for a long time. The people speak Romansh, the old Latin-derived language of the Graubünden, and the road signs and village names have a gentle, rolling quality that sets them apart from German-speaking Switzerland.

The valley has been a trade route since Roman times, when a road crossed the Julier and Septimer passes, and traces of that history remain in old stone bridges, mule paths and a pair of Roman columns that once stood on the Julier summit. The Romans built to move soldiers and goods north, and later the route served merchants, pilgrims and herders. In the nineteenth century, the painter Giovanni Segantini lived in Savognin for several years, painting the peasants and the mountain light, and his work from that period is among the most admired of Alpine realism.

The village has a ski area that gives it a lively winter season, and in summer it is a base for walking and riding. The old village centre has big stone houses with painted facades, a church with a tall bell tower and a lively square with cafes. The surrounding hills are dotted with hay barns and small farm chapels, and the streams that run through the village are clear and cold. In the morning, mist lies on the valley floor and the peaks catch the first sunlight.

For a rider, Savognin sits at the foot of the climb to the Julier, and the road up the Surses valley is a delight, with long, fast bends, smooth tarmac and wide views. Past Savognin, the road climbs through the villages of Tinizong, Bivio and the high pastures, and then rises to the pass in a series of gentle sweeps. Traffic is moderate in summer, with coaches and caravans, so a start before ten is rewarded. Frost can linger in the shaded bends into April, and the early morning cold is bitter.

Savognin has a petrol station, a supermarket, a couple of bakeries and several restaurants, and the food is good, with barley soup, air-dried beef and Capuns, the Graubünden dish of spätzle dough wrapped in chard leaves. Lenzerheide, about fourteen kilometres to the north, has more services, and Chur is the nearest city. Eat something warm before the climb, because the pass is cold, even in summer.
t.julier pass@46.5,9.7:
The Julier is the pass that stays open. At 2,284 metres, it carries the main road between Chur and the Upper Engadin, and the cantonal snow crews work to keep it passable through most of the winter, which makes it unusual among Swiss crossings of this height. That reliability is why it has been a trade road since Roman times, when merchants carried goods north and south over the same saddle, and why it was recorded in travellers' accounts for centuries.

The summit is a bare, rounded rise of grey rock and thin grass, with a restaurant close to the road, and it has the particular austerity of the high Alps. The peak that dominates the pass, Piz Julier, stands to the east, and the Romans' old line over the saddle runs close to the modern one. It is easy to feel that the road has been here forever.

The ride is a pleasure at any pace. From the north, the road climbs from Bivio in a series of bends and then passes through open, rolling terrain, and from the summit it descends toward Silvaplana in long, open sweeps, with the Engadin lakes appearing below. The surface is generally smooth, but the road is busy with coaches, lorries and holiday traffic, so you may find yourself in a queue on a sunny Saturday. Mornings are best, when the light is low and the road is empty. Wind and cold are the usual hazards, and even in July a shower of sleet can fall.

The water on the pass divides in an unusual way. A stream on the northern side runs toward the Rhine and the North Sea, while the lakes on the southern side feed the Inn, which flows into the Danube and the Black Sea. The Engadin itself is wide and bright, with larch forests, blue lakes and a dry, clear air. Silvaplana lake is famous for the wind that blows up the valley in the afternoon, which draws windsurfers and kitesurfers in summer.

Services at the pass are limited to the restaurant. Fuel can be found at Silvaplana, about five kilometres down on the Engadin side, and in nearby St Moritz and Sils, and in Savognin or Tiefencastel on the north. Chiavenna lies across the Maloja Pass to the south. Fill the tank before the climb, and carry a warm layer for the top.
t.nufenen pass@46.5,8.4:
The Nufenen is the highest road pass that lies entirely inside Switzerland, at 2,478 metres, and it feels it. The road climbs out of the Goms valley in the canton of Valais and crosses a bleak, rocky crest before dropping into the Ticino, and nothing grows at the top except a few tough mosses and lichens. The wind blows hard across the saddle, the air is thin and cold, and on a clear day the view of the Bernese Alps to the north and the Ticino peaks to the south is vast and sharp.

It is a relative newcomer. The road was opened in 1969, built to link the Goms with the Bedretto valley and the Gotthard route on the south side, and it was designed to be ridden. Its bends are wide and well banked, the surface is smooth and the gradient is regular, so the pass is very popular with motorcyclists and sports car drivers, who come in numbers on summer weekends. On a clear day, the sight of the road sweeping away down the southern slope into the Bedretto valley is hard to forget.

On the Valais side, the road winds up from Ulrichen through meadows and rock, with the Gries glacier and the reservoir at its foot coming into view to the east. The glacier has retreated visibly in recent decades, and the lake it feeds is an intense milky turquoise, vivid against the grey rock and white snow. A separate side road leads to the dam, a short detour from the main route.

The pass is open only in summer, usually from about June to October, depending on snow, and it can close at short notice in bad weather. Snow can fall in any month, and ice may form on the road at night, so check the status before you set out. At the summit there is a small restaurant, which may or may not be open, and a place to park. Do not underestimate the cold, which can be severe even in July, and wear all your layers.

Ulrichen, on the Valais side, has services, and so does Airolo on the Ticino side, though both are some distance away. Naters, near Brig, is the larger town to the north-west, about forty kilometres from the pass. Top up in Ulrichen or Airolo, and bring snacks, since nothing is guaranteed at the top.
t.all acqua@46.5,8.5:
All'Acqua is the last place before the Nufenen on the Ticino side, and the sort of place that makes you want to stop even though there is hardly anything there. A few stone buildings, an inn with a restaurant and a small chapel stand at the head of the Bedretto valley, at about 1,600 metres, with the long slope of the pass rising behind. The air is cold and clear, and the light has a hard brilliance that makes the grey stone look almost white.

The Bedretto valley is one of the least visited in Ticino. It runs north-west from Airolo in a long, narrow trough, and its villages, Bedretto, Ossasco and All'Acqua, are small and mostly seasonal. The people speak Italian, in a dialect that is broad and soft, and the architecture is stone, dark timber and slate, built to withstand heavy snow. In winter the snow is deep and the upper valley is quiet, so it keeps its isolation for most of the year. The Ticino river, which flows south to Lake Maggiore and the Po, begins in the high lakes above, and it is a clear, cold stream beside the road.

The road from Airolo to All'Acqua is a delight, a smooth, gently climbing route through meadows and larch woods, with views of steep valley sides and a stream at the bottom. Beyond the hamlet, the road begins the main climb to the Nufenen, with long, graceful bends that rise above the tree line and into the rock. The surface is excellent, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. For a rider, it is a warm-up for the pass and a good place to check your clothing before the cold of the top.

Wildlife is plentiful. Marmots whistle from the rocks above the village, chamois move along the cliffs and golden eagles circle in the thermals. In June the meadows are bright with flowers, and in autumn the larches turn the slope gold. Cows graze on the pasture, and dairy farmers make a hard mountain cheese in the huts, which you may find on sale at the hotel or in a shop in the lower valley.

The restaurant at All'Acqua serves simple, hearty food, such as polenta, cheese and cured meats, and the coffee is strong. Fuel is not available, and the nearest station is in Airolo, about twelve kilometres below, so fill the tank before the climb. The Nufenen can close at short notice, so ask at the hotel if you are unsure of the conditions.
t.pontresina@46.5,9.9:
Pontresina sits at the mouth of two glacial valleys on the Upper Engadin, and the village has been a mountaineers' base since the nineteenth century. The first ascent of Piz Bernina, the highest peak in the eastern Alps at 4,049 metres, was made in 1850 by a Graubünden surveyor, Johann Coaz, and the village grew rich guiding foreigners up the neighbouring summits. Old photographs of men in woollen coats and hobnailed boots, roped together on a glacier, still hang in the cafes.

The setting is the thing. A small, tidy village of old stone houses and newer hotels lies on a terrace in the sun, in a broad valley of larch and pine, and behind it the Roseg and Morteratsch valleys lead toward the glaciers. A flat road follows the Roseg valley to a restaurant at its head, and in summer horse-drawn carriages carry visitors along it. The Morteratsch glacier, a tongue of ice that has been shrinking for a century, can be reached by a short walk from the railway station, with markers along the path showing where the front stood in earlier years, a sobering sequence.

Pontresina is the foot of the Bernina Pass road, one of the most scenic routes in the Alps, and for riders it is the natural start of the climb. The road leaves the village and rises in broad bends through larch forest, with views back over the valley, before reaching the high lake country, where the Bernina railway runs beside the road for much of the way. The surface is smooth, the bends are open, and traffic is moderate, though it can be heavy in summer. In winter the pass is kept open and the road is a popular route to Italy.

The village is also known for its sun. The Engadin has a dry and bright climate, and Pontresina has a reputation for blue skies, even when other parts of Switzerland are in cloud. The air at this altitude, about 1,800 metres, is thin and clear, and temperatures drop rapidly at night. The Romansh language is spoken here as well as German, and the names on the old houses reflect a long history of bilingual living.

There are plenty of cafes and restaurants in the village, and the local speciality is Bündner Gerstensuppe, a thick barley soup, followed if you can manage it by a slice of Nusstorte. Fuel is not as easy as in a larger town, so check the tank, and consider Samedan, a short ride away, or St Moritz, which has more stations. Parking for motorcycles is available near the station and the old village.
t.burgdorf@47.1,7.6:
Burgdorf looks like what a Swiss town ought to look like, and has the good sense not to make a fuss about it. A hilltop castle of pale stone stands above the old town, rooflines step down the slope, and the river Emme runs below in a green gorge. It is a town of nearly fifteen thousand people, and the gateway to the Emmental, the hill country of canton Bern that gave its name to the most famous Swiss cheese.

The castle was built by the Zähringer dukes in the twelfth century and later passed to Bern, and it has served as a fortress, a residence, a prison and, for a few years around 1800, a school. The educational reformer Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi taught children here, developing methods of learning by observation and doing that influenced schools across Europe, and the town is rightly proud of the connection. Today the castle houses a museum, a youth hostel and a restaurant, and the view from its terrace over the old town and the hills is a good start to a day.

The Emmental itself is a landscape of rolling hills, broad farmhouses with enormous overhanging roofs, and green pastures where brown-and-white cows graze. The farmhouses, built of timber with deep eaves and decorated balconies, are among the most distinctive in Switzerland, and they were the setting for the novels of Jeremias Gotthelf, a pastor who wrote about peasant life in the nineteenth century. The cheese, with its round holes and nutty flavour, is made in village dairies, and visitors can watch the process and buy a wedge to take away.

For a rider, the Emmental Panorama Road is a winding, gentle route over the hills, with long bends through forest and meadow, farmhouses at every turn and wide views over the valleys to the distant Alps. It is not a road for speed, since the villages are frequent and tractors are common, but it is a charming one, especially in the early morning when mist lies in the hollows. The surface is mostly smooth, though some of the narrower lanes are patched and have gravel at the edges. Traffic is light except on sunny Sundays, when families and cyclists come out in numbers.

Burgdorf is a real town with everything you might need: fuel stations, supermarkets, workshops, bakeries and restaurants. The bakery windows are full of dense, buttery cakes, and a slice with a coffee is a worthwhile reward. Bern is the capital, about twenty kilometres to the south-west, and Lucerne is not far to the east.
t.lutzelfluh@47.0,7.7:
Lützelflüh is the sort of Emmental village that would be forgotten by everyone except that a pastor once lived here and wrote about it. Jeremias Gotthelf served as the parish priest from the 1830s until his death in the 1850s, and his novels about farmers, cheesemakers and stubborn families gave the valley its literary identity. You will see his name on the church, the museum and half the brochures, and for once the fuss is deserved: read one of his books and the green, rolling hills around you start to look like a stage set for a very old argument over inheritance.

The Emme river runs through the village, brown after rain and clear in dry weeks, and the road follows it with gentle bends, farmhouses with enormous overhanging roofs, and the occasional tractor you will simply have to accept. This is not a road for attacking corners. It is a road for noticing that the barns here are the size of cathedrals, that the wooden walls are darkened by a century of sun, and that every second yard sells cheese or cream from an honesty box. The traditional Emmental cheese, the one with the holes, is made in the valley, though the big dairies now do most of it.

A couple of kilometres away, Trachselwald castle sits on a wooded hill above the road. It served for centuries as a seat of the Bernese bailiffs and later as a prison, and it features in the story of the Peasants' War of 1653, when Emmental farmers rose against Bern's taxes and debased coinage and lost badly. Their leader, Niklaus Leuenberger, was held at this very castle before being executed in Bern. It is worth remembering when you pass a perfectly peaceful farmyard.

With about four thousand people, Lützelflüh has a shop or two, a bakery and the practical stuff, and Sumiswald, just a few kilometres on, is bigger and has more choice for fuel. If you want a proper meal, a table at one of the traditional inns will usually bring you something with Rösti or a slab of meringue and thick Emmental cream, which is the correct way to end any lunch here. Early morning is the best moment on this road: mist lies in the hollows, the hay smells sweet in June, and the traffic has not yet found you.

Weather moves quickly over the Napf hills to the south, so keep a rain layer handy even when the sky looks innocent. Autumn adds fog, but also gold light that makes the hillsides almost absurdly pretty.
t.langnau im emmental@46.9,7.8:
Langnau is the unofficial capital of the upper Emmental, and it behaves like one. There is a proper town centre, a railway station with trains to Bern and Lucerne, a hockey arena where the SCL Tigers play to a loyal, noisy crowd, and a Friday morning when the cattle market and the shops bring the surrounding farms in to town. With nearly nine thousand residents, it is the largest place on this road, which makes it the obvious spot for fuel, groceries and a sit-down meal before the valley gets more remote.

The town has an old pottery tradition, and the glazed Langnau ceramics, often decorated with slip-trailed flowers and proverbs, turn up in museums and in farm kitchens all over the canton. There is a local museum that gathers a lot of this, along with the story of the Emmental farmers' lives, and it is good for a rainy hour. The covered wooden houses along the main street, some of them very old, hint at how prosperous the cheese and cattle trade once made this place.

The riding around Langnau suits a relaxed pace. The Emme and its small side valleys, the Ilfis and the Trueb, cut through the hills, and the roads follow them in easy, rolling bends between dairy farms and patches of spruce. Gradients are mild, but the surface can be patchy where water has run over it, and agricultural traffic is normal. If a tractor with a manure spreader pulls out, the only winning move is patience and an open window, because the smell is part of the local landscape.

Not far to the east in Trubschachen is the factory of the biscuit maker Kambly, whose shop is a pleasant place for a coffee and a bag of cookies for the tank bag. A bit further, the hills rise towards the Napf, a rounded summit from which streams fan out in every direction, and the country becomes steeper, with isolated farms along ridges and gold-panning in the rivers, a hobby the Emmental is oddly known for.

Come in summer for long light, in September for the smell of cut grass, and avoid the first frosty mornings, when shaded hairpins on the side roads can stay slick until well after nine.
t.glaubenberg pass@46.9,8.1:
At 1,543 metres, the Glaubenberg is a modest pass, but it crosses one of the most unusual stretches of Central Switzerland: a high plateau of raised bogs and wet meadows that was protected as a moorland landscape of national importance. The road climbs from Sarnen on the Obwalden side, passes through spruce forest, and then emerges onto an open upland where the horizon is low, the grass is tussocky, and the wind has a free run. It feels more like Scotland than the Alps for a few kilometres, until Pilatus or the Schratten limestone ridges poke out of the clouds and remind you where you are.

The riding is relaxed and slightly strange. The surface is generally decent but narrow, the bends are mostly gentle, and there are cattle grids and the occasional grazing animal standing in the road with total confidence. Part of the plateau on the Obwalden side serves as a military training ground, so firing days exist and the road can be closed for them. Check ahead before you plan a day around it, and expect a little of that sense of being in a place that belongs mostly to soldiers and sheep. The pass is also shut by snow in winter, usually from late autumn until spring.

On the western side the road drops into the Entlebuch, a region declared a UNESCO biosphere reserve, where the land is rough and wild by Swiss standards: marshes, karst limestone, damp pastures and a culture of dairy farming and wood. The people here have a reputation for being direct and not easily impressed, and the local cheese, made on alpine farms, is among the better souvenirs in the country.

Sarnen, about ten kilometres from the pass, is the nearest sizeable town, with supermarkets and petrol stations, and Schüpfheim and Flühli on the other side also have what you need. The moor can be cold and misty even when Lake Sarnen below is warm, so treat the top as a place for a layer and a flask rather than a picnic. Best light comes in the late afternoon, when the low sun rakes across the bogs and picks out every tuft of cotton grass.
t.sorenberg@46.8,8.0:
Sörenberg sits in a bowl of green slopes beneath the Brienzer Rothorn, a ski and hiking village that wakes up properly in two seasons and dozes in the gaps. It belongs to the municipality of Flühli in the Entlebuch, a district that the UNESCO biosphere programme recognised in the early 2000s, and the label suits it: damp meadows, lonely moorland, jagged limestone teeth on the horizon and almost no industry beyond cows, wood and tourism.

The road to get here from Schüpfheim is a pleasure. It follows the Waldemme river up through a valley that narrows by degrees, past Flühli with its old glassworks heritage, a reminder that this forested corner of Lucerne once melted sand into bottles, and then climbs more steeply to Sörenberg at around 1,100 metres. The bends are open and rhythmic rather than technical, the surface is good, and there are enough long views over the pastures to slow you down without any help from the speed limit. Roadside signs mention walkers and cows with equal weight.

Behind the village, a cable car lifts hikers toward the Rothorn, which has a long ridge walk and a steam rack railway on the Brienz side that climbs from the lake with an almost comic sense of nostalgia. The summit is far above you, but the shape of the mountain sets the mood: heavy, grey limestone with cloud wrapped around the top.

For practical matters, Sörenberg has restaurants, bakeries and a couple of hotels that cater to skiers and walkers, but for fuel you are better off in Flühli, a few kilometres down the valley, or in Schüpfheim. Do not rely on an unmanned pump up here. The village is a good place for a long lunch, with local cheese and something sweet and creamy afterwards, and the table outside is better than any museum.

From here the road continues over the Glaubenbielen toward Giswil, which means the next section gets tighter and steeper. Check the weather and whether the pass is open before you leave the village, because snow arrives early and leaves late, and a closed gate on top is a long detour back.
t.glaubenbielen pass@46.8,8.1:
The Glaubenbielen is the wilder sibling in the family. Reaching 1,611 metres between Sörenberg in the Entlebuch and Giswil in Obwalden, it climbs through open alpine pasture, then drops toward the Sarneraatal in a descent that is steeper and narrower than almost anything you will meet on the more famous passes. This is a road where you want a full tank of patience and a rider who is awake.

On the Sörenberg side the approach is gentle, with big views across rolling grassland and the limestone teeth of the Schrattenfluh away to the west. Then the road lifts to the top, a bare saddle where cloud can descend in seconds, and tips over. The Obwalden side is where the gradient arrives: tight bends, a surface that has seen many winters, and a sense of the valley floor opening far below, with Lungerersee glinting to the south on a clear day and Giswil spread beneath. Use low gears and do not try to be fast. Cows and walkers occupy the verges, and the road is narrow enough that oncoming cars will make you stop.

The pass is closed in winter, normally from late autumn into late spring, depending on snow. If you are early or late in the season, you may find the barrier shut with no particular warning. Locals will tell you it is a matter of weather, not of dates, and they are right.

Giswil, with about three and a half thousand people, is the nearest place to fill the tank on the Obwalden side, and Sarnen is the larger town beyond. In Giswil you can also find a bakery or café, which is welcome after the descent. The Brünig road runs to Lungern and on to Meiringen and the Bernese Oberland, so the valley is a natural link between different routes.

The geology is limestone and flysch, meaning the hills are green and soft in places and savagely steep in others, which is why the road is so twisted. Aim for a dry, clear morning in summer, when the light is soft and the bogs smell of damp earth and wild thyme.
t.st cergue@46.4,6.2:
Above Nyon and Lake Geneva, the Jura rises in long, wooded ridges, and Saint-Cergue sits on the first real shelf of them, about a thousand metres above sea level. The village is small, with just under two thousand people, but it has a surprisingly big view: on a clear day the lake lies below and the Alps are lined up beyond it, with Mont Blanc as the white presence at the end. Those who live in the Geneva basin come up here for cooler air and some snow, and the station at the heart of the village hints at why.

The railway is the story. A narrow-gauge line climbs from Nyon, taking its time through vineyards and woods, and for generations it carried walkers, skiers and day trippers into the Jura. It still runs, and it explains the architecture, a mix of chalets, hotels and villas from the age when Swiss mountains were fashionable for health and air. The stone dairy farms that surround the village are older and plainer, built for cattle that graze these high pastures in summer.

For riding, the approach from Nyon via Arzier or from Gland is a classic climb: the road leaves the lakeside traffic, enters beech and spruce forest, and then winds upward in a sequence of firm, readable bends. The surface is generally good, the speed limit is monitored, and there are plenty of cyclists in good weather, so pace yourself.
