From the village, the road continues toward the Col de la Givrine and the French border, passing quiet meadows and the dark band of the Jura forest.

Fuel is not guaranteed in the village itself. Gland and Nyon below are the safe bets and have everything. A couple of cafés and restaurants in Saint-Cergue serve hearty plates, often with local cheese like Gruyère, and in the colder months a fondue seems nearly obligatory. Tourists from the French side of the Jura drop in too, which gives the place an easy cross-border mood.

Weather up here changes quicker than you expect. A hot lakeside day can turn into a damp, cloudy afternoon at altitude, and spring mornings may bring ice on shaded stretches. Autumn is the best season, when the beeches turn copper and the air is clear enough for the Alps to look close enough to touch.
t.col de la givrine@46.5,6.1:
The Col de la Givrine tops out at 1,228 metres, which is hardly a heroic height, but the pass has a character all its own. It lies on the Jura ridge between Saint-Cergue and the French resort of Les Rousses, and it is one of those places where the border is a few paragraphs of paperwork and a different bakery. Bring your passport or ID card, because the checkpoint is real, even if you are often waved through.

The land around the col is classic high Jura: long, undulating pasture dotted with spruce, dry-stone walls, dark forest on the slopes and the occasional chalet with a sweep of roof covering a farmhouse and barn in one. The name Givrine hints at frost, and with good reason, because cold air collects in the hollows and winter comes early. In snowy months, cross-country skiers glide across these meadows, and the pass is a well-known gateway to the trails that thread through the border area.

The riding is pleasant rather than dramatic. From Saint-Cergue the road rises in smooth bends, crosses the ridge, and then drops along the French side toward Les Rousses and the lake of the same name. The surface changes subtly when you cross, and French speed limits and cameras are not decorative. In summer the road is busy with cyclists and weekend traffic, and on foggy days the dark wall of forest feels close enough to touch.

Do not count on fuel at the col. There are a couple of places to eat and drink nearby, but for petrol you need Saint-Cergue, Gland or Nyon on the Swiss side, or Les Rousses and Morez across the border. Les Rousses is a lively mountain town with shops and restaurants, and has a long tradition of cheese and smoked sausage. The Jura here produces Comté on the French side, and if you pick up a wedge it will survive the ride in a tank bag.

The ridge also marks a subtle change in weather. Clouds often pile up against the Jura from the lake side, so the Swiss slope can be gloomy while the French side is sunny, or vice versa. It is worth stopping at the top for a moment just to let your eyes adjust to the sky, which seems larger here than the trees would suggest.
t.le brassus@46.6,6.2:
Le Brassus is at the quiet top end of the Vallée de Joux, a long glacial trough in the Vaud Jura that holds the Lac de Joux and a handful of villages strung together along its length. It is a hard place to farm, cold and high, and over the centuries the people here turned to winter work indoors. That is how the valley became the home of Swiss watchmaking at its most complicated. Audemars Piguet, founded here in 1875, still has its roots in Le Brassus, and other prestigious names have workshops nearby. The houses look like ordinary farmhouses, but behind some of the windows people are assembling movements with hundreds of parts.

The riding is a pleasure of its own sort. The roads through the valley follow the lake and the long meadows, with forest climbing both sides, and the surface is usually good. From Le Brassus you can climb gently towards the Col du Marchairuz, which links over to the Lake Geneva side and takes you through beech and spruce woods and open pasture, or head toward the French border near Bois-d'Amont. The bends are open and rhythmic, ideal for a steady pace, and the traffic is light outside holiday weekends.

Winter is serious here. The valley is one of the coldest places in Switzerland, and the lake freezes thickly enough in cold spells for skating, ice sailing and even ice fishing. Even in spring and autumn, mornings can be sharp. The cold air also explains the dairy tradition: Vacherin Mont-d'Or, the soft cheese that is baked in its own wooden box, comes from this stretch of the Jura and is a seasonal treat in autumn and winter.

Le Brassus itself has a small centre with a couple of shops and cafés, which is enough for a coffee and a pastry. Le Chenit, the surrounding municipality, has just over four thousand people, and for fuel you will find pumps along the main valley road. If you need something larger, Morez across the border or Nyon on the lake are the bigger options. The valley also holds the Risoux forest, a big stretch of spruce that supplies the wood for violins and other instruments, a quiet claim to fame that suits the place.

Visit in early summer when the meadows are full of wildflowers, or in autumn for sharp light and the first smoke from chimneys.
t.sainte croix@46.8,6.5:
Sainte-Croix lies on a sunny shelf of the Vaud Jura, with the Chasseron ridge rising behind it and the Swiss plateau stretched out far below. The town is about four thousand people, but it punches above its weight in one very specific area: mechanical things that make music. For more than a century this was the capital of Swiss music boxes and automata, and the industry grew into a wider tradition of precision engineering. The Paillard company, makers of Bolex cameras and Hermes typewriters, was founded here, and the town's wealth shows in the solid old buildings along the main street.

Today the heritage is on show at the CIMA museum of mechanical art, where you can hear music boxes, singing birds and little automata perform. Even if you are a rider who does not usually visit museums, this is the right kind of rainy-day stop, because everything in it moves and sounds, and the staff will show you how it works.

The road up to Sainte-Croix is where the riding pleasure comes. From the Orbe side or from Yverdon, you climb through gorges and forest with a handful of firm corners, and the view back toward the plateau opens as you rise. The Col des Étroits, a few kilometres on toward France, offers a gentler route across the border to Les Fourgs. Up on top, the Chasseron has a mountain restaurant and one of the finest panoramas of the Alps in this part of Switzerland, though the road to the very top can be rough and seasonal, so do not assume you can ride all the way.

Sainte-Croix is large enough to have fuel, a couple of supermarkets and cafés, so you can sort practical matters without a detour to Orbe. The place has a quiet confidence, a sense of having made something clever and not minding that few people know it. In summer, the air is cool compared with the lake shore, and in winter, the sea of fog lies below the ridge while the town is bright and cold above it.

Aim for a clear morning after rain, when the Alps are sharp from the ridge, and give yourself time to ride slowly; the Jura rewards patience.
t.orsieres@46.0,7.1:
Orsières is where the Valais valleys split apart. Here the road from Martigny forks: one branch climbs into the Val Ferret toward Champex and the Mont Blanc massif, the other follows the Val d'Entremont up toward the Great St Bernard. The town has a little under three thousand inhabitants, the Dranse river rushing through it, and a small narrow-gauge railway that comes up from Martigny and ends at the station. It is the last real place of any size before the pass, and so everyone who rides the road stops at some point.

That makes it the right place to fill up. Fuel is here, along with supermarkets, bakeries and cafés, and there is no reliable supply for a long way after. The next pumps higher up are scarce, so take the opportunity. The valley road runs from here through Liddes and Bourg-Saint-Pierre, with the climb steadily increasing, and the last section above the tree line is a lot less forgiving than the lower valley.

The road itself has been an artery for two thousand years. The Romans used the pass, calling it the Summus Poeninus, and built a temple on the summit. Charlemagne's armies came this way, as did countless pilgrims heading to Rome, and Napoleon marched his army across in 1800 on his way to Italy, an event so famous that the hospice at the top still sells postcards of it. The hospice, run by Augustinian canons, has looked after travellers for nearly a millennium, and its dogs became world famous.

Today a long tunnel under the mountain carries the heavy traffic, which leaves the pass road quiet in good weather and gloriously empty in the shoulder seasons. Keep in mind that the pass is closed by snow for much of the year, normally from autumn until early summer, while the tunnel stays open for a toll. In good weather the climb from Orsières is a joy: smooth, broad curves in the valley, then a sequence of hairpins above Bourg-Saint-Pierre, with the Combin glaciers visible away to the east.

If you arrive in the evening, linger a while over a meal. The Valais kitchen offers dried meat, raclette made with local cheese and the white wines of the lower valley, and it all tastes better after a long day in the saddle. Mountain weather turns fast, so check conditions before the climb.
t.great st bernard pass@45.9,7.2:
The Great St Bernard is one of the oldest crossings of the Alps, and standing at 2,469 metres, with the Swiss and Italian borders running through the lake and the hospice, it feels like a place where history has been piled up in layers. A small, cold lake sits in the saddle, bare rock rises around it, and the snow lingers here far into summer. The air is thin, the light is hard and bright, and on a clear day you can see for a long way in both directions.

People have been crossing here since the Bronze Age. The Romans built a road and a temple dedicated to Jupiter, and travellers passed over the centuries as merchants, pilgrims and armies. The hospice was founded in the Middle Ages, traditionally in the eleventh century, by Bernard of Menthon, and the canons have sheltered stranded walkers ever since. The famous St Bernard dogs were bred here, and a kennel and museum let you meet them in summer. Napoleon led an army over in 1800, with cannons dragged across the pass on hollowed logs, and the crossing is part of the legend of that campaign.

The ride itself is memorable. From the Swiss side the road climbs from Bourg-Saint-Pierre in a series of broad curves and tight hairpins, and the vegetation gives way to rock and grass. The summit has a modest cluster of buildings, with cafés and souvenir shops, which are very welcome after the cold. On the Italian side, the road drops through the Valle del Gran San Bernardo, past Saint-Rhémy and Etroubles, on a surface that can be rougher, with tight bends and patches of damage from frost.

On the Swiss side the last good pumps are in Orsières and Martigny, and on the Italian side you will find them in Aosta, about nineteen kilometres from the Etroubles area. The pass is closed in winter, usually from October to June, though a tunnel runs beneath it year round. Check the status before you go, and bring your documents because the border is still a border.

Etroubles, a small village on the Italian side, is known for cured ham from the nearby Bosses valley and for the Fontina cheese of the Aosta region. A plate of either, with a coffee, is the right reward for a day on the mountain.
t.viamala gorge@46.7,9.4:
Viamala means bad road, and for centuries that was an understatement. The Hinterrhein river has cut a deep, narrow gorge through the limestone and slate between Thusis and Zillis, with walls rising some hundreds of metres in places and the water roaring far below. Until the road builders arrived in the early nineteenth century, travellers going to the Splügen and San Bernardino passes had to cross it by narrow ledges and rickety bridges, and many mule trains were lost here. The name stuck, a warning that became a brand.

A good modern road runs high above the old line, and the gorge itself is reached through a short visitor centre with a staircase that leads down to the river. It is a brief, damp, impressive descent, and if you can spare twenty minutes you will find the sound and the chill remarkable. The old stone bridges visible from the viewing points show how close to the water people were willing to travel.

The riding through the region is a mix of old and new. The main road is smooth and quick, while the old route winds through villages and hairpins with a modest amount of traffic. Corners are mostly flowing, with some tight tunnels and galleries where the sound of the engine echoes. The mountains close in, and for a few kilometres the world is rock and spruce.

Thusis, at the northern mouth of the gorge, is where you start. It is a solid, practical town with fuel, supermarkets and cafés, and from here the road south runs through the gorge toward the Splügen and San Bernardino passes. The valley once carried busy trade in wine, grain and salt. The village of Zillis has a church famous for a painted ceiling of over a hundred and fifty wooden panels from the twelfth century, a rare survivor and a worthwhile detour for anyone who likes art.

Come in dry weather, since wet limestone makes the surface slick, and aim for midday when the sun reaches into the gorge. Autumn is excellent, the larches golden above the dark rock.
t.flims@46.8,9.3:
Flims sits on a terrace above the Rhine, backed by the jagged wall of the Flimserstein and facing a landscape that, once, was catastrophically rearranged. About nine thousand years ago, a vast chunk of mountain collapsed and slid into the valley in one of the largest landslides known in the Alps. The debris dammed the Rhine and left behind a rolling, forested hill landscape, hummocky and strange, now cut by the river into the dramatic Ruinaulta, the Rhine Gorge, often called the Swiss Grand Canyon. Flims is built on the bones of that event.

The town itself is a resort, with grand old hotels from the nineteenth century and modern chalets, serving ski, bike and hiking crowds. It is not a quiet village, but it has all the practical advantages of one that expects visitors: petrol, supermarkets, bakeries, and plenty of restaurants with terraces. Two turquoise lakes in the forest, the Caumasee and the Cresta Lake, are warm enough for swimming in summer and fed by water filtering through the old landslide, giving them their unreal colour.

The riding approach from Chur or Reichenau follows the Rhine, then climbs to Flims in smooth, open curves with views across the valley. There is little technical difficulty here, but the road is busy in high season, particularly on weekends. A short drive along the plateau toward Laax and Falera gives you some quiet roads and good views of the Surselva, the long valley where Romansh is still spoken. For the best view of the gorge, head to the viewpoint at Conn, reached by a short road and a walk through the forest, where the whole cleft of the Rhine opens beneath you.

The weather is typical of the Grisons: bright, dry air, afternoon thunderstorms in summer, and abundant sun in autumn. Mornings are the best time to ride, before the day-trippers arrive. In spring and early summer the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the larch forests turn gold.

If you want a good meal, look for a place serving Capuns, the Romansh speciality of chard leaves wrapped around dough and baked with cheese, or Pizokel, thick noodles served with cheese and sometimes cabbage. They are filling, plain and exactly what you want after a long day.
t.handeck@46.6,8.3:
Handeck is a stop on the way up to the Grimsel where the road and the water meet in the loudest possible way. The Aare river, born a bit higher in the glacial valley, plunges here from a ledge in a single fall of about forty-six metres, throwing spray across the gorge, and a footbridge lets you stand close enough to be soaked. On a warm day it is cold and pleasant, and in spring snowmelt it is deafening.

The setting is the Haslital, a glacial valley where granite dominates. The rock is pale, smooth and polished by ice, with hanging valleys and thin waterfalls on every side. This is also the heart of one of the Alps' great hydropower systems, with reservoirs high in the mountains feeding turbines in the valley, and you will see the hidden infrastructure in the form of pipes, galleries and small power stations. The Gelmerbahn, a funicular that climbs a slope at an astonishing gradient to the Gelmersee, starts close to the Handeck, and is one of the steepest of its kind in Europe, a short ride that is worth the money if you like heights.

For riders, the road from Innertkirchen climbs in a series of long, steady bends, with views opening to the glacier-carved walls, and the Handeck marks the point where the climb becomes serious. Above, the road tightens and gains height over tunnels and galleries, and the trees thin out. The surface is generally excellent and the corners predictable, although the traffic, especially the coaches, can be heavy in summer. Morning is best, before the buses arrive.

Meiringen, about fifteen kilometres down the valley, is the nearest large town, with supermarkets, petrol and restaurants. There is a small hotel and restaurant at the site, and a car park with a short walk to the fall. The Grimsel Pass above is closed in winter, normally from late October until late spring, so the road ends at the barrier early in the year.

Meiringen is also known as the home of the meringue, according to local legend, and the fictional Sherlock Holmes met his apparent end at the nearby Reichenbach Falls. Both tales add a little flavour to a trip through this part of the Bernese Oberland.
t.grimsel hospiz@46.6,8.3:
Close to the top of the Grimsel, the Hospiz is a stone hotel standing beside a reservoir whose water is the colour of slate. It is a landscape of bare granite, scattered snow and wind, and the dam walls, bridges and cables are as much a part of it as the mountains. The Grimsel region is where the Aare begins its journey to the Rhine, with lakes that supply some of the electricity Switzerland uses, and the place has the quiet, purposeful feel of a working mountain.

The hospice has been a refuge on this route for centuries. The Grimsel was an important trade and pilgrim pass between the Bernese Oberland and the Valais, and a hospice has stood on this line for centuries, giving shelter to merchants and travellers caught by weather. The present building is more modern, and the old one, as with much of the area, was submerged or replaced when the reservoir was built. It is now a comfortable mountain hotel with a restaurant, and the food is hearty and generous.

For riders, the pass road is a feast. From Innertkirchen the road climbs roughly fifteen hundred metres, with a series of hairpins, tunnels and big views across the glacier-polished rock. The top of the pass, at 2,164 metres, is a short ride beyond the Hospiz, and on the far side the road drops to Gletsch, where the Rhône Glacier lies above and the Furka and Nufenen passes branch out. The surface is excellent, the bends are wide, and the corners are an invitation to ride at a controlled, steady pace. Be aware of the cold: even in summer the wind at height can bite.

Plan your tank accordingly. The Grimsel is closed in winter, normally from late October to late May or June, depending on the snow, so check before you set out.

Take a moment at the lake. The wind makes patterns on the surface, and the light changes quickly, from grey to bright and back again. In autumn the larches lower in the valley are gold, and the first snow lies on the peaks.
t.salgesch@46.3,7.6:
Salgesch is the wine village at the end of the German-speaking world, or at least at its edge in the Rhône valley. Just downstream, in Sierre, people speak French. In Salgesch, they speak a Valais German dialect and make some of the best Pinot Noir in Switzerland, and the language border runs between them like an invisible fence that nobody has ever bothered to build. The vines grow on steep south-facing terraces above the village, with the Rhône flat and silvery below and the peaks of the Bernese Alps on the other side.

The valley here is one of the driest in the Alps. Rain clouds struggle to get past the mountains on either side, and the sun beats down on the slopes, which is why the vineyards flourish and why the surrounding hills have a steppe-like look, with dry grassland and rocky outcrops. The Pfynwald, a rare natural forest of Scots pine on a glacial rockslide, lies a short distance upstream and is a quiet detour if you want to see a piece of wild Valais.

For riding, the vineyard roads above Salgesch are a gentle pleasure: narrow, winding lanes between stone walls, with a handful of tight bends and long views. They are not fast, but they are a real alternative to the valley road. You will meet cyclists and walkers on the vineyard tracks, and the surface can be gritty in places. Harvest time in autumn brings tractors and a good deal of activity.

The village has a wine museum and several wine cellars where you can taste, and the locals are proud of their local grape varieties, including Cornalin, Humagne Rouge and Pinot Noir. If you plan to taste, a pause for a meal and a coffee is wise, and the village has a few places for it. A couple of cellars will wrap a bottle in a way that survives a tank bag, though riders should think about weight.

Fuel is easy: Sierre, just a few kilometres away, has pumps and supermarkets, and Salgesch itself is on the main road. Choose September for the colour, when the vineyards turn red and gold and the light is soft.
t.leuk@46.3,7.6:
Leuk sits on a small hill above the Rhône, with a castle at the top, a church with a tall spire, and a street plan that has changed very little since the Middle Ages. In German it is Leuk, in French Loèche, and the double name tells you where you are: on the language border of the Valais, where the French-speaking lower valley gives way to German. For centuries the town was the seat of a regional government, and the old houses along the main street, with their carved wooden balconies and painted shutters, reflect a prosperous past.

Above the town, a side road climbs into the Dala gorge toward Leukerbad, one of the largest thermal bath resorts in the Alps. The hot springs, rich in minerals, have attracted visitors since Roman times and made the village famous in the Middle Ages, when travellers took the waters and crossed the Gemmi Pass to the Bernese Oberland on foot or mule. The climb is a pleasure for a rider, with a tight, twisting road through rock and forest, and a final approach to the high amphitheatre of the village, ringed by cliffs. Watch for rockfall and for the occasional bus on the narrow sections.

On the valley floor, the road between Leuk and Sierre runs beside vineyards and the remnant of the Pfynwald forest, so you can ride a pleasant, easy half hour between the two towns. The riding is more of a gentle ramble than a challenge, but the light is lovely and the pace is relaxed. Wind can be strong in the valley, especially in the afternoon, and the Rhône basin often funnels it up toward the Alps.

Leuk has a few shops and cafés, with a bakery or two for coffee and Valais rye bread, which is dense, dark and keeps well. Fuel is available in the town or at Sierre, about eight kilometres away, where there are more services. For a classic Valais meal, look for raclette or dried meats, and try a glass of Fendant, the local white wine made from the Chasselas grape.

The dry air and strong sun of the valley are reliable from spring to autumn. The best light comes in late afternoon, when the castle and the cliffs turn amber.
t.hotel belvedere@46.6,8.4:
There is a hotel on the Furka Pass that has seen more cameras than most film stars. The Hotel Belvédère clings to the hairpins on the Valais side, a few kilometres below the summit, and for generations it sat at the foot of the Rhône Glacier, whose tongue of ice reached almost to the terrace. The glacier has retreated dramatically since then, leaving bare rock and a grey lake, and in summer it is partly covered with white blankets to slow the melt. The scene is a visible record of a changing climate.

The road itself is famous. The Furka was used in the 1964 film Goldfinger, when Bond's Aston Martin raced along its bends, and ever since riders have come to try the same hairpins. The pass climbs to 2,429 metres, linking Gletsch in the Valais with Realp in Uri, and it is one of the classic high Alpine crossings. The surface is generally good, but the bends are tight and the drops are steep, with minimal barriers in places. A low gear and a steady hand are more useful than speed. On a busy summer weekend, traffic is heavy, so a weekday morning is a better bet.

The nearby ice grotto, cut into the glacier each year, is a popular attraction, and the old steam railway, the Furka Cogwheel Steam Railway, runs on the line that once crossed the pass, and now operates in summer from Realp across a spectacular mountain section. The line was abandoned when the Furka base tunnel opened, and then rescued by volunteers.

The nearest pumps are in Andermatt on the Uri side, or lower down in the Goms valley on the Valais side, so top up before you commit. The hotel serves meals and coffee and is a good place to warm up, with a terrace that looks out toward the glacier and the valley below. The pass is closed in winter, usually from October until June, and reopens as soon as the snow is cleared.

The air is thin and cold even in July, so dress in layers. The light is best in the morning, when the glacier is bright and the shadows are sharp.
t.sisikon@46.9,8.6:
Sisikon is a thin line of houses between a mountain and a lake, which is exactly how most of Lake Uri works. The water, the deepest and most dramatic arm of Lake Lucerne, is squeezed between steep rock walls, and there is barely room for a road, a railway and a village. The Axenstrasse, one of the oldest built mountain roads in Switzerland, was blasted out of the cliff face in the 1860s to link Schwyz with Uri, and it has been clinging to the rock ever since.

The road is a mix of open views and short dark tunnels, with galleries that protect it from rockfall. It is narrow, has no real shoulders, and many motorists treat it as a shortcut, so traffic can be dense. But it is a beautiful piece of riding, with the lake glinting through the openings and the sound of the engine echoing off the rock. Take it slowly. The corners are gentle and the surface is generally good, but the limit is monitored and the road can be closed after rockfalls or storms, so check ahead.

This is the heart of Swiss national mythology. A little to the south is the Tellskapelle, a chapel on the shore at the place where, according to legend, William Tell leapt from the boat of the tyrant Gessler. And across the water is the Rütli meadow, where the first Swiss confederates are said to have sworn their oath in 1291. Friedrich Schiller's play, written in 1804, shaped how people imagine these events, and the whole shore is treated as sacred ground.

Sisikon has a small harbour and a camp site, and a couple of places to eat, often serving fresh lake fish. Fuel is not reliable in the village, so use Brunnen or Ingenbohl, about six kilometres away, or Flüelen at the south end. The föhn wind, a warm dry wind from the south, can arrive suddenly, changing the lake from calm to choppy and making the air uncannily clear. The mountains look closer and the colours deeper.

Early morning is best, before the day trippers and the tour buses. In autumn the light slants low across the water and the rock walls glow.
t.sils@46.4,9.8:
Sils is really two villages, Sils Baselgia and Sils Maria, on a flat shelf between two lakes in the Upper Engadin, and it has the particular glow of a place that artists and thinkers have chosen to retire to. Friedrich Nietzsche spent his summers here from 1881 to 1888, renting a small room in a house that is now a museum, and it was on a walk by the lake that he conceived the idea of eternal return. Thomas Mann and Hermann Hesse came too. The light, high and clear, has something to do with it.

Lake Sils, the largest of the Engadin lakes, is a long, bright sheet of water backed by a mixture of larch forest and peaks. The wind from the Maloja Pass blows up the valley most afternoons, which makes this a famous place for windsurfing and sailing, and the surface turns a deep blue flecked with white. The Fextal, a side valley behind Sils Maria, is closed to ordinary traffic and offers a quiet walk or cycle into the glacier-fed valley beneath the Fex peaks.

For riding, the road along the lakes between Silvaplana and Maloja is open, broad and easy, with long curves and views across the water. It is not a technical road, but it is one of the most beautiful stretches of the Engadin, and the combination of larch and water is hard to beat. At the end, the Maloja Pass, at 1,815 metres, drops into the Val Bregaglia in a famous series of hairpins toward Italy, a sharp contrast with the gentle valley floor. Take care in those bends, especially in wet weather.

Sils has a handful of hotels, including some grand old ones, as well as cafés and bakeries, but it is not a place for cheap petrol or large supermarkets. St. Moritz, about ten kilometres away, has the larger choice, and Silvaplana is nearer if you need something quick. Engadin specialities include Nusstorte, a dense walnut and caramel tart, and Capuns, a Romansh dish of chard parcels.

The valley is cold, and snow can arrive even in early autumn, so ride with layers. The best months are June for flowers and September for gold larches and still water.
t.bad bergzabern@49.1,8.0:
Bad Bergzabern lies close to the French border, at the point where the German Wine Route runs out of road and the hills of the southern Palatinate fold into the Vosges across the frontier. It is a spa town of about seven and a half thousand people, with a castle that once belonged to the Dukes of Zweibrücken, a Renaissance inn called the Gasthaus zum Engel, with an ornate carved facade dating from the sixteenth century, and a calm, tidy centre built around a market square. The Palatinate Forest, a large area of woodland, begins just behind it.

The region has a mild climate, with warmth that allows figs, almonds and chestnuts to grow, and the Palatinate is often described as Germany's Tuscany. In late winter and early spring, the almond trees bloom along the foot of the hills, giving the landscape a soft pink glow that draws visitors from across the region, and in autumn the chestnut harvest is celebrated with local dishes. The town's spa tradition comes from mineral springs, and the thermal baths are a relaxing way to spend an afternoon after a long ride.

A few kilometres away, the village of Dörrenbach has a Renaissance town hall and a fortified church, and is considered one of the prettiest villages in the Palatinate. Oberotterbach, another wine village, has good estates and pleasant lanes. Roads between them wind through vineyards and chestnut woods, with gentle bends and almost no traffic. The surface is generally good, though some small roads are narrow and rough, and farm vehicles are common during the harvest. For more of a challenge, head into the forest, where roads climb to hilltop castles such as the Berwartstein in a series of tighter bends.

With a population of over seven thousand, Bad Bergzabern has fuel, supermarkets and many places to eat, so it is a sensible stop before you tackle the more remote roads. Regional cooking is hearty, with Saumagen, a stuffed pig's stomach, the dish that made the Palatinate famous, and Flammkuchen, a thin crust with onions and bacon, both pair well with local white wines. Wine is often served in a large half-litre glass called a Dubbeglas.

The best times are early spring for the almond blossom and autumn for the harvest. In summer the heat can be strong, and a rest in the shade is welcome.
t.landau@49.2,8.1:
A carriage took its name from Landau, which tells you something about the town's old self-importance. The Landauer, with its folding two-part roof, is said to have first been built here in the early eighteenth century, around the time the French and the Habsburgs were scrapping over the fortress. Landau was French for long stretches, and the great military engineer Vauban gave it a star-shaped citadel in the 1680s. Most of the walls have gone, but the street plan and some of the gates remain, and the town still feels more ordered than its winegrowing neighbours.

Today it is the cheerful, slightly academic capital of the southern Palatinate, with about forty thousand people, students, a big covered market and a pedestrian centre full of cafés. The vineyards begin a few hundred metres beyond the last houses. The Pfalz is Germany's second-largest wine region, and the grapes around here are mostly Riesling and Burgundy varieties, plus a lot of Dornfelder, a dark red that locals drink in half-litre glasses without any fuss.

For a rider, Landau is a base more than a destination. The Wine Route rolls south from here through villages like Siebeldingen and Birkweiler, on narrow roads between vines, with the dark wall of the Palatinate Forest to the west. Traffic is thick on weekends in autumn, when every second tractor is hauling grapes and every second car is looking for a parking space. You will do better on a weekday or at breakfast time, when the hills are quiet and smell of damp earth. For something with more bend in it, turn west up the valley toward Annweiler, where the road climbs into red sandstone country and the castle of Trifels sits on its crag. Richard the Lionheart was held there in 1193, a fact the locals take as a kind of personal compliment.

There is no shortage of fuel or food in Landau, which makes it the right place to sort out the bike, find a hotel and sit down to a plate of Saumagen, the stuffed pig's stomach that the Palatinate loves and outsiders approach cautiously. If that is too bold, ask for Flammkuchen, which the French side of the border claims too.

The weather is mild, among the warmest in Germany. Almond and peach trees flower in March, wine festivals fill the summer and the vines turn copper in October.
t.neustadt an der weinstrasse@49.4,8.1:
Here is the one place on the Wine Route where Germany argued about its own future. In May 1832, some thirty thousand people walked up to the ruined Hambach Castle above Neustadt, waving black, red and gold flags and demanding freedom of the press, national unity and constitutional government. The Hambacher Fest was the first great political rally in German history, and the castle is still called the cradle of German democracy. The colours on the flags are the ones on the modern national flag. The castle is a stiff climb above the town and looks out across the whole Rhine plain, which on a clear day stretches to the Odenwald and beyond.

Neustadt itself is a big, handsome town of more than fifty thousand, with half-timbered houses, a collegiate church shared by two denominations for generations, and a market square that is busiest at the time of the German Wine Harvest Festival each October, when the town crowns a wine queen and a good many people stop counting their glasses. Wine here is Riesling first, with Silvaner and Scheurebe pushing in from the side, and a handful of grand estates have their cellars in the old town.

The riding is the real draw. The B39 and the minor roads that run along the foot of the Haardt, the eastern escarpment of the Palatinate Forest, thread through one wine village after another, a few kilometres apart, each with a church spire, a vintner's yard and a sign promising wine by the glass. The road is flat and gentle, so the pleasure is not in the bends but in the pace and the views, with the forested slope on one side and the plain on the other. If you want more corners, take a side road west into the forest, where the surface is generally good and the bends tighten between pines and old sandstone quarries.

Neustadt is large enough to have fuel on the edge of town, plenty of food and places to leave a bike overnight. A glass of Federweisser, the young half-fermented wine sold in early autumn, goes well with onion tart. Be careful with it, because it tastes like juice and does not behave like juice.

Spring mornings, with blossom on the hillside, are the most gentle time to be here.
t.deidesheim@49.4,8.2:
Deidesheim is what a wine town looks like when it has been rich for five hundred years and has kept the receipts. The cobbled centre is a short walk around a Gothic church, a Renaissance town hall with an outside staircase, and half-timbered houses painted in warm colours, with a few of the big estates, Bassermann-Jordan, Bürklin-Wolf and others, tucked into old courtyards. These families made Riesling famous well before Germany had a wine law, and their cellars have grown a fine reputation.

The town's most delightful ritual happens on the Tuesday after Whitsun, when the neighbouring town of Lambrecht hands over a live billy goat and Deidesheim auctions it off in public, a custom that goes back to an old dispute over grazing rights. It is the sort of local tradition that survives because nobody can bear to end it. The villages around Deidesheim, including Forst and Ruppertsberg, have some of the most celebrated vineyards in the country, with a layer of basalt in the soil that holds the heat.

For riders, the Wine Route here is at its most polished. The road between Neustadt and Bad Dürkheim runs flat and gentle through vines and villages, often a single lane of tarmac between rows of Riesling, and the Haardt hills rise in a green wall to the west. Traffic is heavy at weekends and during the harvest, so choose a weekday if you can. In Bad Dürkheim, a few kilometres north, there is a petrol station on the main road, a huge wine barrel that doubles as a restaurant and, in September, a vast sausage and wine festival that fills the whole town.

Food in Deidesheim can be anything from a glass of wine and bread in a vintner's courtyard to a long and expensive lunch at a table with a tablecloth, since the town has a number of serious restaurants. Fuel is better found in Bad Dürkheim than in the village itself.

Park outside the old town and walk in. The streets are narrow, the stone is smooth, and there is plenty of tarmac around the wall for a bike.
t.grunstadt@49.6,8.2:
Grünstadt does not make the postcards, and it does not seem to mind. It is a working wine town of about thirteen thousand at the northern end of the Palatinate Wine Route, with a pedestrian centre, a Saturday market and a few handsome half-timbered houses that survived the wars. The vineyards start right behind the railway, and beyond them the land rolls westward toward the Donnersberg, the highest hill in the Palatinate at just under seven hundred metres, a dome of forest that you can see from half the region.

The area is called the Leiningerland, after the counts of Leiningen who ruled from the Middle Ages, and their ruined castles still sit on the ridges above the villages. At Altleiningen, a few kilometres to the west, a castle that was rebuilt in the twentieth century now holds a hotel and a restaurant, and from its walls you can look across the wooded Eis valley. The villages in between, with their pointed church towers and long low farmhouses, feel more lived-in than polished, which is exactly what you want after a morning of tourist traffic further south.

Riding here is easy and quiet. The back roads between the vines carry a handful of local cars and a lot of tractors, and the corners are gentle and unhurried. West of town, the road climbs into the hills of the northern Palatinate, with views back across the Rhine plain, and the traffic drops almost to nothing. The surface is generally fine, though farm vehicles can leave mud and clippings on the tarmac at harvest. This part of the route is a good starting point if you are heading south along the full length of the Wine Route, and a decent place to take stock before you commit to the day.

Grünstadt has everything a rider needs: petrol stations, supermarkets, bakeries, a bike shop or two, and enough cafés to make a late breakfast easy. In the village of Kirchheim, just south, you will find the first of the big wine estates that line the route. Try a glass of the local Riesling or the lighter Müller-Thurgau with a plate of Leberknödel, the liver dumpling that is the Palatinate's idea of comfort.

Late September has the best light, when the vineyards glow and the grape lorries rumble down every lane.
t.schonach@48.1,8.2:
Schonach is the Black Forest at its most tightly folded, a village of about four thousand strung along a steep valley, with farms on every ledge and a small ski jump looming over the houses. Winter is its big season: the area is a regular stop for Nordic combined and ski jumping competitions, and the big hill, the Langenwaldschanze, is among the larger in Germany. In summer the same slopes fill with walkers and cyclists, and the church bells carry a long way in the clear air.

The clock story starts here, or near enough. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, farmers in the high Black Forest spent the long winters carving wooden clockwork, and by the eighteenth century the craft had grown into an industry that exported clocks across Europe. The cuckoo clock, with its carved wooden case and its bird that pops out on the hour, became the symbol of the region, and you can still see the old farmhouses with deep eaves where the work was done. Schonach and its neighbour Triberg have museums and workshops that carry on the tradition, and shops that sell everything from traditional pieces to enormous novelty clocks.

Triberg, about three kilometres away, has its waterfall, which tumbles in seven stages through a wooded gorge and is one of the highest in Germany. A path with steps runs alongside it, and at dusk there is lighting. The town also has a museum of Black Forest culture and a good place to try the famous Black Forest cherry cake, which is made with kirsch, cherries and whipped cream and is much better when it is not mass-produced.

For riding, the Clock Route is a pleasure. The roads climb from the Gutach valley through dark spruce forest and past isolated farms, with a lot of curves, steady gradients and reasonable surfaces. Traffic is moderate, though coaches run to Triberg, and cyclists are common. The hairpins above the villages are tight, and the weather can change quickly, with fog in the hollows and snow into April on the higher passes.

Schonach is small but has the basics, including a couple of places to eat. Triberg, with a bit more choice, is the better bet for fuel and supermarkets. After a long day, a plate of smoked ham, dark bread and pickles is a fine reward, and the cold clear days of October are particularly lovely.
t.titisee neustadt@47.9,8.2:
Neustadt in the Black Forest has none of the lakeside bustle of its neighbour Titisee, and it is better for it. This is a working mountain town of about twelve thousand people on the Gutach river, with a solid church, a market square and a railway station where the Höllentalbahn from Freiburg arrives after its long climb. The line was an engineering feat when it was built in the nineteenth century, winding up the Höllental gorge with a steep rack section in its early decades, and the station is a handsome reminder of the days when the railway was the great modern invention.

The town has a long tradition of watchmaking, and the neighbouring village of Lenzkirch was home to one of the largest clock factories in the Black Forest in the nineteenth century. The local museum shows the craft, along with the wider history of the region. Above the town, the Hochfirst ski jump is one of the biggest in Germany, with a hill size that attracts competitors every winter, and a summer tour lets you stand at the top of the in-run and look down, which is dizzying.

For riders, Neustadt is a handy base for exploring the southern Black Forest. The roads leaving the town run in all directions over wooded ridges and past high farms, with a good mix of fast sweeps and tighter sections. Heading west, the B31 drops through the Höllental, a deep, narrow gorge with steep walls and a river far below, with tunnels and bends that need care in the wet. To the south, quieter roads climb toward Lenzkirch, Bonndorf and the Wutach gorge, where the landscape opens into fields and woods. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, particularly on the main roads, so side roads are better if you have time.

Neustadt has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. A bakery counter with a slice of Black Forest cherry cake and a coffee is a good start, and a traditional inn will offer smoked ham, a hunk of dark bread and a glass of local beer. If you want the lake, Titisee is only a couple of kilometres away.

Snow can arrive early here, so check the weather in autumn and spring. In summer, the cool air and shade of the forest are a relief from the heat of the Rhine valley.
t.schwetzingen@49.4,8.6:
Schwetzingen would be a large town with a medium-sized reputation if it were not for the palace garden, which is one of the great surviving Baroque landscape gardens in Europe. Elector Carl Theodor of the Palatinate made it his summer residence in the eighteenth century and spent decades improving it, adding a theatre, a pavilion shaped like a Turkish mosque, a fake Roman aqueduct, a temple to Apollo and long avenues of clipped trees that run out into the Rhine plain. The mosque has no function except to look foreign, and it has been doing so for over two hundred years.

The court's cultural ambitions are part of the story. In 1763, the seven-year-old Mozart played at the palace on a European tour with his family, and the small rococo theatre in the palace still hosts opera, notably in the spring festival. Today the town is also known as the asparagus capital of Germany. Between April and the end of June, the surrounding fields are covered with the plastic-covered ridges where white asparagus grows, and every restaurant offers the stalks with ham, butter, boiled potatoes and a little hollandaise. A local asparagus queen is crowned each year, and the season ends on St John's Day.

Schwetzingen is on the Bertha Benz Memorial Route, which follows the historic first long-distance drive in a motor car. In August 1888, Bertha Benz took her husband's three-wheeled Patent Motor Car from Mannheim to Pforzheim, without his knowledge, with her two teenage sons, to prove it could travel. She is credited with the first long-distance journey by car, and she needed all her resourcefulness along the way. The route is signposted by brown signs showing a small car, and Schwetzingen is on the way south.

For riders, the route here is flat and straightforward, through the Rhine plain, with long avenues of old trees, small towns and fields of tobacco and asparagus. The roads are good and mostly quiet outside commuter hours, and the speed limits matter. It is easy riding, and the bends are few, so the pleasure comes from the history and the light. A handful of side roads through villages offer a more relaxed pace.

Schwetzingen has everything: fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and traditional inns, and the whole town is a good place for a pause. The palace garden has a modest entrance fee, and a café inside. In April the cherry trees bloom, and in autumn the garden is a patchwork of gold.
t.wiesloch@49.3,8.7:
Wiesloch has a plaque, a pharmacy and a very good claim to be the birthplace of the filling station. In August 1888, Bertha Benz, halfway through her pioneering drive from Mannheim to Pforzheim, ran out of fuel and stopped at the town's pharmacy, where she bought ligroin, a petroleum solvent usually sold in small bottles for cleaning. The pharmacist, so the story goes, had no idea what she was planning, and by the time she left the shelves were bare. That makes the Stadt-Apotheke in Wiesloch the world's first petrol station, and the town has not forgotten it.

The rest of Wiesloch lives quietly in the shadow of that story. It is a pleasant town of about twenty-five thousand people at the edge of the Kraichgau, a rolling area of loess hills and orchards between the Rhine plain and the Odenwald. The old town has half-timbered houses, a market square and some good coffee shops. It was once an important mining town, with silver and lead extracted from the nearby hills since the Middle Ages, and the museum covers the local history. Today the vineyards and cherry orchards on the surrounding slopes are the real business.

For riders, Wiesloch is a fine point to leave the flat Rhine plain and start climbing. The road rises through vineyards toward Rauenberg and Dielheim, with long views over the plain, and the bends are gentle and rhythmic. The Kraichgau is not a mountain landscape, but the hills have shape, the traffic is moderate, and the surface is generally good. Be careful in harvest season, when tractors and trailers can cover the road with mud. In winter, mist often lies over the plain below, and the hills stand above it in bright sun.

There is fuel in Wiesloch, as you might hope, and plenty of supermarkets and cafés. Two thousand years of cultivation have left the region full of small wine estates, and you can try a local Riesling or a Spätburgunder. Spring and early summer bring asparagus to the menu, and in autumn there is Zwiebelkuchen, a warm onion tart, served with new wine.

Pause in front of the pharmacy, whose sign recalls the 1888 stop, and raise a glass of whatever you are drinking to a woman who solved the world's first range problem with a hatpin.
t.bruchsal@49.1,8.6:
Bruchsal looks, at first, like an ordinary mid-sized German town, with a railway junction, a shopping street and a lot of postwar buildings. This is because the old centre was largely destroyed in an air raid in March 1945, but one thing survived or was rebuilt with obsessive care: the Baroque palace. The Residenzschloss was built in the early eighteenth century for the prince-bishops of Speyer, who moved their court here from Speyer, and its great staircase, designed with help from the architect Balthasar Neumann, is considered one of the masterpieces of the German Baroque. The building was badly damaged in the war and painstakingly restored, and the staircase now stands again in a pale oval hall full of light.

Inside the palace is a museum of mechanical musical instruments, a collection of player pianos, orchestrions and music boxes that fill the rooms with sound when the guides start them up. It is a delight if you have any liking for machines that do the impossible with a roll of paper. The gardens behind the palace are a pleasant place to walk. The Bruchsal region, like Schwetzingen, grows asparagus, and the sandy soil of the plain produces vegetables in huge quantities.

Bruchsal is also a stop on the Bertha Benz Memorial Route, the road followed by the first long-distance car journey in 1888. The route here passes through the Kraichgau, running between the Rhine plain and the hills, and for riders the interest is the mixture of flat and gently rolling terrain, with views over vineyards and orchards. The roads are quiet and well surfaced, and the corners are gentle. It is a ride for a relaxed pace, with plenty of villages and small towns to explore, and the Black Forest foothills rising to the south and the Odenwald to the north.

At over forty thousand people, Bruchsal is the largest town on this stretch of the route, and everything is here: fuel at several stations, supermarkets, repair shops and restaurants. The town centre is not beautiful, but the palace and its gardens make up for it, and a bakery near the market has a good line in local pastries. Keep an eye out for Kraichgau specialities, including sausage, dumplings and wine.

The palace is at its best in late afternoon, when the low sun comes through the tall windows.
t.titisee@47.9,8.2:
Titisee is the lake that every German knows, and the odd thing is that it is a very small lake. It was carved by a glacier that flowed down from the Feldberg in the last ice age, and it lies in a hollow about two kilometres long, dammed by a moraine, with forested slopes rising on all sides. The water is dark and cool, the shoreline is tidy, and a legend credits the Roman emperor Titus with the name, though most scholars suspect a less glamorous origin. A hundred years ago it was a quiet mountain spot. Today it is a summer playground with a promenade full of shops selling cuckoo clocks, cherry liqueur and Black Forest ham.

You come here partly for the scenery and partly for the show. Boat trips run across the lake in summer, with pedalos, rowing boats and steamers all competing for space, and the beach has a swimming area. In winter, the lake freezes and locals walk or skate across it. The town of Titisee is the stop for people heading to Feldberg, to the Höllental or to the cuckoo clock shops, and on summer weekends the main road clogs with traffic and coaches. Take it as it comes, and enjoy the ice cream.

For riding, the point is not the lake but what surrounds it. Heading east, the road passes through Hinterzarten, home of the Adlerschanze ski jump, and joins the B31 toward Freiburg through the Höllental, a wild gorge with a river and tunnels. To the south the B500 climbs toward Feldberg and Schluchsee, a great arc of forest roads with open, flowing bends and views across the Black Forest. In the early morning or late evening, the roads are almost empty, and the dark spruce and pale mist make a good setting. The surface is generally excellent, and speed limits are real.

Fuel is easily found in neighbouring Neustadt, about three kilometres away, where the stations and supermarkets are better than in the tourist strip. In Titisee itself there are plenty of cafés and restaurants, and the classic order is a slice of Black Forest cherry cake, made with cherries, kirsch and cream.

Come outside the school holidays, and walk around the lake on the shaded path to see how it looked before the souvenir shops arrived.
t.feldberg@47.9,8.0:
The Feldberg is the highest mountain in the Black Forest and in Germany outside the Alps, at 1,493 metres, and it behaves like a real mountain. It is a broad, bald dome of grass and heath rising above the surrounding forest, with a radio mast and an observation tower on the summit and, on its eastern flank, the dark cirque of the Feldsee, a small lake in a glacial bowl. During the last ice age, the Feldberg carried its own ice cap, and the valleys around it still show the carved, U-shaped marks. The climate is rough, with wind, fog and snow lasting well into spring.

On a clear day, usually in autumn or winter, the views are extraordinary. You can see across the Rhine plain to the Vosges in France, and when the air is very dry, to the long line of the Swiss Alps. The cattle on the high pastures are Hinterwälder, a small, hardy local breed, and the heath is full of arnica, gentian and other mountain plants. The summit area is protected, and many paths are closed to cyclists and dogs, so respect the signs.

The roads around the massif give a taste of Black Forest riding at its best. From Todtnau, in the Wiese valley to the west, the B317 climbs through forest in a series of lively bends, above a town known for its waterfall, and then emerges onto the heights, with the pass road topping out around twelve hundred metres. It is steep and sometimes narrow, and fog can make the descent slow. From the east, the road from Titisee through Hinterzarten and along the B500 is quicker and busier. Weekends bring a procession of motorcycles, cars and cyclists, and the police enforce limits, so aim for a weekday.

Todtnau, with about five thousand people, is the nearest town with petrol and supermarkets, and Titisee-Neustadt is the other option. The mountain inns near the top serve soup, sausage and cake, and in winter the car parks fill with skiers. If the weather is poor, ride on and leave the summit for another day, because an hour in cloud is not a good way to spend a mountain.

Early and late in the season, the hills turn amber and the first snow lies on the top.
t.mummelsee@48.6,8.2:
Mummelsee is a small, round, black lake in a hollow beneath the Hornisgrinde, the highest peak in the northern Black Forest at about 1,160 metres, and nearly every German has heard of it because of what lives there. According to the legend, the lake is home to the Mummel, water nymphs who dance on the surface at night, and to a lake king who holds court in a crystal palace on the bottom. Anyone who throws a stone in will cause a storm, and a few unwary visitors are said to have been pulled down. The old stories have given the place a quiet reputation for trouble, and the dark water does nothing to discourage it.

In reality, the lake is a cirque left behind by a glacier in the last ice age, roughly seventeen metres deep and surrounded by spruce. It sits beside the Black Forest High Road, the B500, which runs along the ridge from Baden-Baden to Freudenstadt and dates from the early twentieth century, and a large hotel, a restaurant and a car park crowd the shore. On a sunny weekend, the place is busy with coaches, motorcyclists, families on pedal boats and people photographing the carved wooden Mummel figures near the water. The best time is early morning or a weekday in autumn, when you will have the shore nearly to yourself.

The ride to the lake is a classic. The B500 climbs from the Rhine plain near Bühl or from the Acher valley, through dense forest and past viewpoints, with tight bends and tunnels of trees that give way to open ridge. Up on the heights, the road is a long, rolling line with views over the Rhine plain on one side and the forested Murg valley on the other. The surface is smooth, and the speed limits and the number of other riders mean that a relaxed pace is the most enjoyable. In bad weather, fog can reduce visibility to a few metres and make the lake look even more sinister.

The nearest services are in Kappelrodeck, Achern or Bühl on the plain side, and in Baiersbronn to the south. The restaurant serves hearty food, including the local trout and Black Forest ham, and a slice of cherry cake helps to take the chill off.

Walk to the far shore and look back at the lake, and you will see why the legends took hold.
t.ruhestein@48.6,8.2:
Ruhestein has no village, no church and no permanent population, and yet it is one of the more important places in the northern Black Forest. This is a pass on the B500, at 915 metres, where the High Road meets the road that drops west toward Allerheiligen and Oppenau, and where a junction has drawn a few inns and a car park. Today it is the gateway to the Black Forest National Park, which was founded in 2014, and where the forest is being allowed to grow wild, with fallen trunks left lying and storm damage left to regenerate on its own.

You can see this experiment clearly at Ruhestein. The Lotharpfad, a walkway through the area flattened by the hurricane Lothar in December 1999, shows how nature reclaims the space, with young birch, rowan and fir pushing up between the bleached stumps and a rich bird life. A park centre stands near the pass, a long, modern timber building, with exhibits about the forest, the wildlife and the local history, and it is a good place to wait out the rain. Lynx and wildcats are rare, but capercaillie, a large forest grouse, live in the park, and the rangers ask visitors to keep to the paths.

The riding is good. The B500 here is a flowing, well-surfaced road with sweeping views and a long run of gentle bends, and it carries heavy motorcycle traffic on weekends. There are speed limits in places, and the police do check. The side road down toward Allerheiligen drops steeply through forest to a ruined monastery and a waterfall, with tight hairpins that need attention, especially when wet. It is one of the best short descents in the area, and you will meet fewer vehicles than on the main road.

The nearest stations are in Baiersbronn, Oppenau and Achern, and you should plan to fill up before you commit. A restaurant and kiosk at the pass serve hot food, and the car park fills early on sunny days, so arrive before eleven.

Mist often hangs over the pass in the morning, and the sound of the forest dripping is a pleasure of its own.
t.kniebis@48.5,8.3:
Kniebis is a high, straggling village on the ridge at the southern end of the Black Forest High Road, a place where the forest opens out into heath and old fields. At around nine hundred metres, with open views to the south and the dark ridges of the Black Forest in every other direction, it has a bracing, slightly lonely feel. It belongs administratively to Freudenstadt, and it is best known as a spot for walking and cross-country skiing, with a network of trails across the moorland.

The ridge has seen its share of soldiers. In the eighteenth century, the passes on the Kniebis were fortified with earthworks, called Schanzen, to guard the route into the Rhine plain, and the lines were manned during the wars with revolutionary France. Some of the earth ramparts still run through the woods and can be traced on a walk. The name Kniebis is of uncertain origin, but the place has been a crossing point for centuries, and later became a modest holiday village with guesthouses and a church.

The road here is the tail end of the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse, which comes down from Ruhestein and the Schliffkopf along the ridge, and the riding is relaxed and rolling. It is not a road of tight corners, but of long, open bends through dark forest with occasional views through gaps in the trees. In late spring the heath is brown and wet, and in September the bilberries are ripe along the verges. The surface is generally very good, and the traffic is a mixture of cyclists, motorcyclists and families in cars, particularly in summer. The weather turns quickly, with cold fog on some mornings even when the valley below is warm.

Services are modest. There are guesthouses and inns, and a few places to eat, but for fuel you should go to Baiersbronn, about seven kilometres away, which is a large village with a good range of shops, or to Freudenstadt, which has more of everything. Freudenstadt is worth a stop for its square, one of the largest market squares in Germany, laid out in the early seventeenth century around a plan that was never fully completed.

Autumn brings golden light and the smell of woodsmoke.
t.chamonix mountain town@45.9,6.9:
Chamonix is a town that lives in the shadow of a mountain, and not just any mountain. Mont Blanc rises to just over 4,800 metres directly above it, the highest peak in the Alps, and the great ice-streaked walls and needle-like granite spires of the Aiguilles stand around the valley like a stage set. When the clouds lift in the morning, the effect is so dramatic that the whole street seems to stop and look up.

The town's history is the history of mountaineering. In 1786, two local men, Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard, made the first ascent of Mont Blanc, and in doing so launched alpinism as a sport. The first Winter Olympics were held here in 1924, and the cable car to the Aiguille du Midi, which rises to close to 3,850 metres, remains one of the great mountain rides in the world. Across the valley, the Mer de Glace, France's longest glacier, is retreating year by year, a reminder of how quickly the landscape is changing.

For a rider, Chamonix is a fine rest stop and a bustling one. It is a proper town, with fuel, restaurants, bike shops, and plenty of cafes, and in summer the streets are busy with climbers, walkers, paragliders, and families. Traffic through the valley can be heavy, and parking is a puzzle, so aim to arrive early. The road up the valley from Les Houches is wide and fast, though lorries heading to the Mont Blanc tunnel slow everything on the approach. Beyond the town, the road continues over the Col des Montets toward Switzerland, and each direction rewards patience.

Food is one of the pleasures. Savoyard cooking is rich and warming: tartiflette, with potatoes, reblochon cheese, and bacon, fondue, raclette, and crozets, small buckwheat pasta, are all on the menus. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and the temperature at 1,000 metres can fall quickly after sunset. Les Houches, a smaller village to the south-west, is quieter and has its own services. Take a moment, if the sky is clear, to look at the summit above you, and think about the first people who stood on it.
t.col des montets@46.0,6.9:
The Col des Montets is the quiet pass between Chamonix and Switzerland, and it is easy to underestimate. At about 1,460 metres, it is not high by Alpine standards, and the road climbs gently through larch and spruce from the Chamonix valley, but it lies in one of the most dramatic situations in the Alps, with the Aiguilles Rouges on one side and the Mont Blanc massif on the other. The glaciers of Argentière and Tour hang above the road, and on a clear day the views from the roadside are astonishing.

The pass lies in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve, a high, rocky area of lakes, peaks, and alpine meadows that is home to ibex, chamois, marmots, and golden eagles. Lac Blanc, a famous high lake with a view of Mont Blanc, lies on the slopes above, reached by a long walk or a lift. The hamlet of Vallorcine, on the Swiss side of the watershed, has chalets with stone roofs and a small station on the narrow-gauge railway that links Chamonix with Martigny, an excellent train ride in its own right.

The ride is easy and pleasant, with flowing bends, good tarmac, and generous views. The gradient is gentle, and the traffic is steady, with tourists, lorries, and locals. From the top, the road drops through Vallorcine toward the Swiss border, where it joins the road over the Col de la Forclaz to Martigny. The pass is generally open throughout the year, though snow and ice can occur in winter, and the road is regularly cleared. Early morning is best for clear views, as clouds often gather around the peaks later in the day.

Fuel is in Chamonix, about ten kilometres to the south-west, and in Martigny-Combe and Martigny to the north-east on the Swiss side. There is little at the pass itself, apart from a few cafes and viewpoints. The best time is June to September, when the weather is generally clearer, and the late-summer light on the glaciers is wonderful. If you cross into Switzerland, remember that a motorway vignette is needed for the Swiss motorways, though the mountain road does not require it. Keep a spare layer handy, because the air is cool and the wind can be sharp.
t.grand st bernard approach@45.9,7.2:
The road to the Great St Bernard begins in Aosta, in a valley where Roman roads and mediaeval pilgrim paths have run for two thousand years. This is the oldest crossing of the Western Alps still in use, and the approach from the Italian side follows the Valpelline and the narrow Val du Grand-Saint-Bernard past the village of Etroubles, a stone-built place that has turned itself into an open-air gallery of sculptures and murals. The sense of history is strong, and the road climbs gently at first, through meadows and larch woods, before the real mountain begins.

At the top, 2,469 metres up on the Swiss border, stands the hospice, founded in the eleventh century by Bernard of Menthon to shelter travellers on a dangerous route. Monks still live there, and the famous St Bernard dogs were bred at the hospice to find travellers lost in snow. Napoleon led an army of some forty thousand men across the pass in 1800, hauling cannon on sledges made from hollowed tree trunks, on his way to the battle of Marengo. A road tunnel, opened in the 1960s, now carries most traffic under the mountain, which leaves the old pass road to riders.

The approach is a wonderful ride. From Etroubles the road climbs in a series of bends and short straights, with steep, open slopes above and deep gorges below, and the surface is generally good. The final ramp to the pass is steeper, with hairpins, and the air gets thin and cold. The pass is open only in summer, usually from around June to October, and snow can fall at any time, so check the status before you set out. Traffic is light, except at weekends, and the views are huge.

Aosta, about nineteen kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, restaurants, and Roman ruins, including a theatre and a triumphal arch, and it makes a good base. Etroubles and Valpelline are small villages with a few places to eat. On the pass, the hospice offers a museum, a shop, and a small restaurant, and the Swiss side has a long descent toward Martigny. Wear warm gloves, because the wind at the summit is cold, even in August.
t.jura balcony road@46.5,6.0:
The Haut-Jura is the part of France that tourists tend to overlook, and that suits the people who live here very well. The roads run along high plateaus and wooded ridges north-west of Geneva, with long views across the green rolling hills toward the distant white line of the Alps. On a clear day, the Mont Blanc massif appears above the haze like a mirage, and the road seems to be a balcony from which to watch it. It is a gentle landscape, with dairy farms, tall spruce forests, and a quiet that is easy to enjoy.

The area is famous for its cheese. Comté, the hard, nutty cheese aged in mountain cellars, comes from the cows that graze these pastures, and Morbier, with its dark line through the middle, and Bleu de Gex are made nearby. The craft of the region is also worth noting: Morez, a nearby town, has long been the centre of French spectacle-making, and its workshops once supplied much of the country's eyewear. In winter the area turns to cross-country skiing, with hundreds of kilometres of trails, and the small town of Les Rousses is a hub for it.

The roads are a delight for a rider who likes flow rather than drama. The bends are open, the gradients gentle, and the surface is usually good. Traffic is light outside the summer holidays, and the villages are quiet. The weather can change fast, with fog and low cloud on the plateau, and in winter snow and ice are common from late autumn to spring. Mornings in early summer, when the meadows are full of flowers and the air smells of cut grass, are the best time.

Les Rousses, about six kilometres away, has fuel, cafes, and a lake, and Morez, nine kilometres off, is the bigger town with supermarkets and more services. Longchaumois is a smaller village with a good bakery or two. Pick up some Comté from a local dairy as a souvenir, and take time to taste it with a glass of Jura wine, which can be pale, nutty, and unexpected. It is a place that rewards a slow pace, and the best views come when you stop and look back.
t.nyon lakeside@46.4,6.2:
Nyon is a small Swiss town on the north shore of Lake Geneva, and it carries a surprising amount of history in a very pleasant setting. The old town rises from the lakeside in a tumble of tiled roofs, with a castle of round towers at the top and a promenade along the water at the bottom. Behind it, the vineyards of La Côte slope up toward the Jura, and in front of it the lake stretches across to the French shore and the snowy Alps beyond.

The Romans founded a colony here, Colonia Iulia Equestris, around 45 BC under Julius Caesar, and fragments of columns and a small museum on the site of the old basilica preserve the memory. Centuries later, in the late eighteenth century, the town became known for its fine porcelain, delicate white pieces painted with flowers. Today it is home to the Paléo Festival, one of Europe's largest open-air music events, which takes over the fields on the edge of town for a week each July.

For a rider, Nyon is a convenient and pleasant place to rest. The town has fuel, shops, cafes, and restaurants, and the lakeside is perfect for a coffee or a long lunch. The lake road along the shore is busy and slow, with traffic lights, roundabouts, and speed cameras, and Swiss speed limits are enforced strictly, so keep your eyes open. The higher road through the vineyards is more rewarding, with gentle bends and wide views. Geneva is about twenty-five kilometres to the south-west, and the Jura is the obvious destination for the afternoon.

Food and drink are part of the charm. The local white wine, made from the Chasselas grape, is light and crisp, and it goes well with perch fillets from the lake, a Swiss favourite. A walk along the promenade is a good way to loosen up after a long ride. The lake has a mild climate, and in spring and autumn the light is lovely. In winter the bise, a cold north-east wind, can blow strongly across the water, and the lake road can be icy in the mornings. Remember that motorway driving in Switzerland needs a vignette.
t.col du telegraphe@45.2,6.4:
The Col du Télégraphe is the short, wooded climb that every rider must make before the great ascent of the Galibier, and it is easy to dismiss as a warm-up. At 1,566 metres, it is not high, but it lies in a deep, green valley, the Maurienne, between the town of Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne and the ski village of Valloire, and the road is a steady, enjoyable climb through spruce and beech forest, with a good surface and a regular rhythm of hairpins.

The name comes from the optical telegraph, an early system of semaphore towers designed by Claude Chappe in the late eighteenth century to relay messages across France. A tower stood on this pass, and the name stuck. Just beside the road is the Fort du Télégraphe, built in the 1890s as part of the defences facing Italy, one of a chain of fortresses that guarded the Alpine frontier. The fort stands among the trees above the road, and it is open to visitors in summer.

The Maurienne valley itself has a long history as a trade and military route. Hannibal is said, by some historians, to have crossed the Alps in this region, and Roman, Savoyard, and French armies all marched through. The valley is also a heavily industrial corridor, with factories and the railway to Italy, and the contrast between the grey valley floor and the green slopes above is stark. The pass is a regular on the Tour de France, and in summer the road is full of cyclists, so expect to share it.

For fuel, Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne, about two and a half kilometres below, has stations and supermarkets, and Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, farther down the valley, is the bigger town. Valloire, on the far side of the pass, has more services. At the top, there is a small cafe and a few spots to park. The pass is generally open year-round, though snow can fall in winter, and the Galibier beyond it closes for months. Early mornings are best for quiet riding, and the descent to Valloire is a lovely, gentle run, with views of the Galibier massif opening in front of you.
t.valloire@45.2,6.4:
Valloire sits in a green bowl at about 1,430 metres, at the foot of the Galibier, and it feels like a proper mountain village rather than a purpose-built resort, which is rarer than it should be in the Alps. The old centre is a mix of stone chalets, small shops, and a church with an interior that is a riot of Baroque painting and gilding, a reminder that the Savoyard valleys were once rich in devotion and craft. In summer, cyclists and walkers fill the cafes, and in winter, the village becomes a ski resort.

The setting is lovely. The valley of the Valloirette runs toward the Galibier, with high meadows, scree slopes, and the glacier-tipped peaks of the Écrins beyond. Mountain flowers carpet the meadows in June and July, and marmots whistle from the rocks. The air smells of cut grass and pine, and the nights are cool even in summer. A short walk up a path from the village takes you into silence and big views.

For a rider, Valloire is the gateway to the Galibier, one of the great passes of the Alps. The road climbs from the village in a series of long bends, passing the last farms and then rising above the tree line into a barren landscape of rock and snow patches, and the summit stands at 2,642 metres. The ride is spectacular but demanding, with narrow sections, steep drops, and sudden weather changes, and the pass is usually open only from early summer to autumn. Before setting off, check the status, and keep a warm layer in the bag.

Valloire has fuel, though stations are small, so fill up when you can. Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne, about seven kilometres away down the valley, is the nearest bigger place, and Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne is larger still. The village has plenty of cafes, bakeries, and restaurants, and Savoyard dishes such as tartiflette, diots, and gratin dauphinois are on many menus. A pause here before or after the Galibier is a good idea. The best season is July to September, but late June brings the flowers, and autumn brings the clearest air.
t.col du lautaret@45.0,6.4:
Lautaret is the wide, grassy shoulder of mountains that sits just below the better-known Galibier, and it is a rather different kind of pass. At 2,058 metres, it is gentle in shape, with rolling alpine meadows and a long view across to one of the most dramatic peaks in the French Alps, La Meije, whose glacier-covered summit rises to nearly 4,000 metres above the valley of La Grave. On a clear morning, the view is so good that people simply stand in the car park and stare.

The pass has been a crossing for centuries, linking the Maurienne with the Briançonnais, and the old road, which the French army improved in the nineteenth century, still follows a similar line. At the summit, an alpine botanical garden, opened in the late nineteenth century and run by the University of Grenoble, collects mountain plants from around the world. In June and July the meadows are a spectacular display, with gentians, saxifrages, and edelweiss, and the garden is a lovely place to wander.

The riding is a pleasure. The road from Valloire climbs over the Galibier and then drops to Lautaret in a long, open descent, with wide bends and a good surface. Beyond the pass, the road descends the Romanche valley toward Le Monêtier-les-Bains and Briançon, passing through tunnels and past waterfalls, while the other way leads down to Bourg-d'Oisans through the Gorges of the Romanche. The pass is open much of the year, though avalanches and snow can close it, and the Galibier beyond usually shuts in winter. Wind can be fierce, and the weather can change quickly.

Fuel is not available at the pass, and the nearest large town is Briançon, about twenty-four kilometres away, with stations and shops. Le Monêtier-les-Bains and Valloire are smaller, with limited options. At the top there are cafes selling coffee, crepes, and local cheeses, and they are a fine stop. Bring warm clothing, since it is cold even in July, and sun protection, because the light is strong. Morning is usually the clearest time, and the contrast between the green valleys and the white peaks is memorable.
t.sihlsee water line@47.1,8.8:
The Sihlsee is a reservoir, and it is honest about that, which is part of its charm. The Sihl river once wandered through marshy farmland south of Einsiedeln.
