In the 1930s the Swiss Federal Railways dammed it to store water for hydroelectric power for the railway network, and by 1937 the valley floor had become a long blue lake, with farms moved and a stretch of moorland drowned. The lake still has the job of feeding the Etzel power station, so the water level changes with the seasons, and in late winter you can see the tide-line of bare shore.

Today the setting is as pleasant as any natural lake. The water is surrounded by meadows, small farms and low forested hills, with the Mythen peaks above Schwyz showing sharp on the southern skyline on a clear day. A causeway crosses the lake at Willerzell, where you can pause and look out in both directions. Swimming is possible from the shore in warm months, and the water is cooler and clearer than you might guess, though it never gets properly warm until August.

Riders reach it from the Ibergeregg side or from the lake of Zurich, and the road around the water is open, easy and scenic, with moderate bends and a good surface. After the climb and descent of the pass, the lake feels like a pause. It is also close to Einsiedeln, a short ride away, where the great Benedictine abbey has been a pilgrimage destination since the Middle Ages, famous for its Black Madonna and the baroque church on a broad square. The abbey is believed to have been founded in the tenth century, and the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela passes through town.

Fuel and food are in Einsiedeln, about three kilometres away, and the town has plenty of cafés near the abbey. At the lakeside the facilities are simple, so bring water and a snack if you plan to linger. Parking is easy near the shore, but check signs because some areas are for locals.

Wind picks up in the afternoons, ruffling the surface into small waves, and the lake shows a different colour in each kind of light. Morning is calm and glassy, and evening is soft and golden.
t.muotathal valley@47.0,8.8:
The Muotathal has a character that the grander Swiss valleys lack. It is narrow, steep-sided and slightly damp, with the Muota river running through the bottom and the village of Muotathal strung along the road at about six hundred metres. Mountains rise on both sides, wooded at the base and rocky above, and clouds sometimes sit on the ridges like lids on pots. It is a farming valley where the cheese is made, the cows climb to the high pastures in summer, and people have a reputation for being stubborn and individual.

Two things make it famous. Beneath the hills lies the Hölloch, one of the longest cave systems in the world, with explored passages stretching hundreds of kilometres. And in the village lives a group of so-called weather prophets, the Wetterschmöcker, men who claim to forecast the coming season from signs in nature and who are consulted with half a smile and half respect each year. Whether they are right or not, the tradition is a fine example of Swiss mountain stubbornness.

The valley has a military past too. In 1799 the Russian general Suvorov brought his army through here during the Second Coalition war, crossing the high passes in terrible conditions and fighting French troops in the narrow valley. The campaign ended in retreat, and it is remembered locally more with respect than celebration.

Riding in the Muotathal is slow and rewarding. The road from Schwyz follows the river, with moderate curves, short tunnels and views of waterfalls after rain. It is quiet midweek, though it picks up at weekends. Beyond the village the road continues toward Bisisthal and the Pragel pass, which is closed in winter and needs checking in early or late season.

Schwyz, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town for fuel and shops. The village itself has small shops and a few places for coffee or a meal, and the mountain inns often serve simple food made with local cheese and dairy.

Bring a rain jacket. The valley collects weather, and a sunny morning can turn into a soaking afternoon. But even in rain, the green is almost fluorescent and the waterfalls are at their best.
t.ibergeregg pass road@47.0,8.7:
At 1,406 metres, the Ibergeregg is not one of the great Swiss passes, but it is one of the most enjoyable short ones, and local riders know it well. It links the Schwyz basin, with its two jagged Mythen peaks, to the Alpthal and Oberiberg side, and it climbs through a landscape of cow pastures, scattered chalets and mixed forest. The road is narrow in places, with sharp bends, moderate gradients and sudden long views over the Schwyz valley as it opens up behind you.

Schwyz gives its name to the whole country. The town was among the early members of the Swiss Confederation, and the Swiss flag and the name Switzerland both grew from it. The charter of 1291, often cited as the founding document of the Confederation, is kept in a museum in the town. You do not need to care about history to enjoy the ride, but it adds a bit of weight to the view as you climb.

The road itself rewards a steady rhythm. On the Schwyz side the first hairpins come quickly, and the surface can be patchy after winter. Near the top it eases into a rolling stretch across the pasture, with the ski lifts of the nearby Hoch-Ybrig area visible in summer as lines on the hillside. The descent toward Oberiberg is gentler, with more open views and a calmer feel. Traffic is usually light on weekdays, though sunny weekends bring cyclists and other bikers, and cattle sometimes cross the road or graze beside it.

Weather deserves respect. Cloud collects on the ridge, and fog can appear quickly, reducing visibility to a few metres. The pass can close in heavy snow, usually in winter, so check conditions in shoulder seasons. In summer, afternoon thunderstorms are common, so start early.

Schwyz, about six kilometres from the foot of the climb, is the nearest town of any size, and Einsiedeln is just beyond the other side. There are mountain restaurants near the top that serve simple food in season, and the benches on the pasture are good for a quiet break.

The cow bells are part of the experience. In summer they ring across the slope, and with the wind and the smell of cut grass, you feel properly in the Alps.
t.rigi foothills view@47.1,8.5:
Above Arth, where the lower slopes of the Rigi begin to steepen, the land opens to a balcony over Lake Zug. At around eleven hundred metres you are not on the summit, which sits higher and attracts the crowds, but you are high enough to see the lake lying like a bent blade below, the rooftops of Arth and Immensee, and on a clear day the long line of Jura hills far to the west. The Rigi is a strange mountain, an isolated block of conglomerate rock rising from lowland lakes, so that views fall away on almost every side without any competing peaks.

The Rigi earned the title Queen of the Mountains in the nineteenth century, when it became one of the first mass-tourist summits in Europe. The Vitznau-Rigi railway opened in 1871 as the first mountain rack railway on the continent, and the Arth-Rigi line followed a few years later. Travellers from Britain came in numbers to see the sunrise from the top, and Mark Twain wrote a funny account of climbing it. You can still catch that spirit at the old hotels and the wooden stations, though today the crowd is more likely to be hikers than Victorian gentlemen in boots.

For a rider, the foothill roads above Arth are about tempo and outlook. They climb in steady gradients through orchards and meadows, with good tarmac, wide enough bends and farmhouses with big overhanging roofs. In spring the fruit trees bloom pale and pink, and in late summer the lower slopes smell of cut hay. Traffic is moderate, and walkers sometimes use the verges, so keep the speed sensible on blind corners.

Arth, about three kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, bakeries and places to eat. Goldau and Küssnacht are also close.

The weather on the Rigi can be local and sudden. Low cloud, called the fog sea in autumn, often sits over the lakes while the hill stands in sun. If you wake to grey in the valley, ride up anyway. You may find yourself above the lid, with the whole world white beneath you and the peaks poking through like islands. Bring a layer, because the air at eleven hundred metres is cooler than it looks from the lake.
t.brunnen lake food@47.0,8.6:
Brunnen is a lakeside town on the Urnersee, the southern arm of Lake Lucerne, and it sits where the water bends sharply around the cliffs and the Alps appear in layers. The setting is dramatic. Mountains drop straight into the lake on both sides, the water runs deep green or blue depending on the sky, and the opposite shore with its steep forests and little white villages looks almost too composed. It is also a historic place. In 1315 the early Swiss cantons renewed their alliance here after the battle of Morgarten, an agreement known as the Pact of Brunnen, and the town has a long record of hosting meetings, merchants and, later, tourists.

Today Brunnen is a resort town with a promenade, a harbour with steamers, and a main street of cafés and hotels from the age when visiting the Alps was fashionable. The lake climate is mild, and you will sometimes see palms and other warm-weather plants in gardens, a surprise in a landscape of cold peaks. The föhn wind, a warm dry gust that comes over the Alps, can be strong here, making the lake choppy and bringing sharp clear views of the mountains. Locals often claim to feel the föhn in their heads, and some blame it for bad moods.

For riders, Brunnen is a natural food stop between the Rigi roads and the Axenstrasse. The streets can be busy on summer weekends, with tour buses, cyclists and families, but the lakeside is wide enough to find a bench or a terrace. Order something simple. Lake fish such as perch fillets are a classic in this region, and the cafés here usually have some form of rösti and local sausage if you want something filling.

Fuel is easy, since Brunnen and neighbouring Ingenbohl have stations on the main road, and Schwyz is a few minutes inland. Public parking near the water gets full, so ride a block or two back from the front if you need a space, and keep valuables with you.

It is worth walking to the water's edge even for ten minutes. Across the lake you can see the Rütli meadow, the traditional birthplace of the Swiss Confederation, and steamers cross it in summer. The light gets soft by late afternoon, and the mountains turn from grey to rose as the sun drops.
t.axenstrasse awareness section@47.0,8.6:
The Axenstrasse deserves a little respect before you ride it. It is a narrow road cut along the eastern shore of the Urnersee, between Brunnen and Flüelen, built in the 1860s when the canton of Uri and the canton of Schwyz decided they needed a road that did not depend on boats. Engineers blasted ledges into the cliffs, drove short tunnels through the headlands and added stone galleries wherever rocks threatened to fall. The result is a road that still feels like a piece of nineteenth-century ambition, squeezed between the mountain and the water.

The section marked for awareness is the one where the corridor is tight and the tunnels come in quick succession. Some are lit, some dim, and they change from bright sunlight to near darkness in a second, so sunglasses off before the first one. The surface can be damp near the galleries, and gravel or small rock sometimes washes onto the carriageway after heavy rain. Rockfall is a genuine risk here, and the road has been closed on occasion while crews secure the slopes. Check conditions if the weather has been wild.

It is also shared. Lorries, buses and cars use the same ribbon, though the motorway tunnel through the mountain takes most of the long-distance traffic now. On a summer weekend you can find yourself in a slow procession, and that is not a bad thing, because the views are the real reward. Through gaps in the rock you see the lake spread out below, deep and quiet, with the steep faces of the far shore coming down into it. A few pull-offs allow a stop, but use them with care and keep well clear of the carriageway.

Brunnen and Ingenbohl, two kilometres or so back, are the places for fuel and food. Along the Axenstrasse itself, services are limited, with a few restaurants and viewpoints tucked into the cliffs, so arrive with a full tank and a plan.

Keep to the speed limit, because the road is narrow and the tunnels have no room for error. Ride in the middle of your lane out of the galleries, since the corners tighten without warning, and let faster riders go by if they want to. It is not a place to race, and it repays patience.
t.sattel high road@47.1,8.6:
Sattel is a small village on a saddle of land at about eight hundred metres, between the Rigi to the west and the Mostelberg ridge above. The name means saddle, and the place lives up to it, sitting in a gap between hills with views opening both ways. On a clear day you can look toward the Mythen peaks in one direction and the long shape of the Rigi in the other, with pasture and scattered farms between. It is one of those Swiss places that look as though a very tidy giant arranged them.

The countryside is the heart of old Swiss history. Not far away is the shore of the Ägerisee, where in 1315 a force of Confederates ambushed a larger Habsburg army at Morgarten and won a victory that became a founding story of the nation. A monument marks the site. The battlefield is gentle now, with grass and a small chapel, but the narrowness of the ground helps you understand why a small force on the slope could beat knights on the road.

The riding on the high road toward Sattel is superb for a relaxed afternoon. The route climbs from the lowlands through orchard and forest, with smooth bends and steady gradients that suit a touring pace. It is rarely congested, and the surface is good. In autumn the beech woods turn gold and the mist hangs in the valleys below, which makes the saddle feel like an island. In winter the area has small ski slopes and a cable car at Hochstuckli, so snow can linger on the shaded sections.

Unterägeri, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops, and Steinen and Rothenthurm are close alternatives. In the village itself you can usually find a restaurant or bakery for a break, and the benches along the road make good rest points.

Take a jacket even in summer, because the saddle catches wind and weather from both sides. If the clouds are coming in from the west, you will see them stacking on the Rigi before they reach you, which gives you time to put the rain gear on. It is a quiet, unpretentious stretch, and that is why it works.
t.bauma tosstal@47.4,8.9:
The Tösstal is the quiet valley of the Zürich Oberland, carved by the Töss river as it runs from the hills near the Hörnli toward Winterthur. Bauma sits near the top, at about six hundred and forty metres, where the valley is still narrow and the slopes are close and wooded. It is not a place that features in guidebooks, which is part of the appeal. People here worked in textile mills, and the old factory buildings along the river still show how the water power and cheap labour of the nineteenth century made this a cradle of Swiss industry.

Bauma has one quirk that tempts railway lovers. The local heritage society runs steam trains on a historic line, with old locomotives and carriages chugging through the hills on selected days in the warmer months. If you arrive on the right weekend you may hear a whistle across the valley and smell coal smoke, a fine change from petrol and rubber.

For riders, the Tösstal entry is the start of a gentler kind of fun. The road leads up from Pfäffikon and the Zürich side, with moderate bends and good visibility, then climbs into hills of dairy farms, forest patches and hamlets. It is not wild, but it is varied, and on a weekday you may have long stretches nearly to yourself. The corners tighten as you rise toward the passlets, and the road gets narrower, so keep an eye out for tractors and the occasional walker.

Pfäffikon, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size and the place to find fuel, shops and cafés. Bauma itself is small, though you will find basics such as a bakery or a small restaurant. The Swiss tendency to close early on Sundays is a real issue in villages like this, so do not assume anything will be open late.

The valley has its own weather. Fog gathers in autumn mornings and clings to the river, and the hills above can be bright while the bottom is grey. In winter, snow can fall a little earlier here than in Zürich, and the shaded corners may stay icy. Spring and early summer, when the meadows are green and the flowers are out, are the best time to ride it.
t.hulftegg passlet@47.4,9.0:
The Hulftegg is a pass for people who know where to find it. At 954 metres it is modest, and it sits among rounded forested hills at the meeting point of three cantons, where Zürich, St. Gallen and Thurgau lean toward each other. There are no glaciers, no dramatic cliffs, and the guidebooks say little. But among Zürich riders it has a loyal following, because the road across it is a ribbon of well-judged bends through meadows and spruce, with hardly a straight run between them.

The climb from the Tösstal side starts gently and builds into a sequence of curves that follow the contours of the hill, opening here and there to views of the Hörnli and the Alpstein range to the east on clear days. The surface is generally good, and the radius of the bends rewards a smooth line. On weekends, other bikes and cyclists use the same road, so the pace is rarely wild. On weekdays and early evenings it is calm, with cows grazing right to the edge of the tarmac.

The cultural backdrop is quietly interesting. Down the eastern side lies the Thur valley and Fischingen, where a Benedictine monastery has stood since the Middle Ages and still shapes the village. Its church and buildings sit in a fold of land, and the abbey has long been a centre of pilgrimage and learning in a corner that seems otherwise remote. Farther along are small villages such as Mosnang, where the architecture shifts toward the sturdy timber farmhouses of eastern Switzerland.

Kirchberg, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town with a decent range of services, and Wattwil and Bauma are alternatives on either side. There is usually a farm shop or inn along the way selling simple food and local cheese, but opening hours vary, so carry a snack and some water.

The weather matters more than the altitude suggests. Cloud lingers on these hills and the forest holds damp in the shade, so corners may be slick after rain, with moss and wet leaves on the verge. In winter the road may carry ice for longer than the valley floor. Go on a dry spring morning or an early autumn afternoon, and take your time on the descent.
t.ricken ridge road@47.3,9.0:
The Ricken pass lies between two worlds. On one side is the Linth plain with its flat valley floor, and on the other is the Toggenburg, a region of green hills, farmsteads and a distinct musical tradition. At about 790 metres, the pass is a saddle rather than a peak, but the approach and descent give a great sense of crossing from one valley character to the next. Behind the ridge you will see the long wall of the Churfirsten and, on clear days, the bright mass of the Säntis farther east.

The Toggenburg is known for its natural yodel and for the hackbrett, a Swiss dulcimer played with small hammers, and for farmhouses that look like they have been there forever. Wattwil, the nearest sizeable town on the eastern side, has about eight thousand people and a history in textiles and later in small industry. The railway between the two valleys passes under the ridge in a long tunnel, built in the early twentieth century to avoid the climb. The old road remains for those who prefer the view.

The ride up from Kaltbrunn or Gommiswald is a series of broad bends with moderate gradients, shaded by forest and framed by meadows. Surface quality is typically good, though patches around the hairpins can be rough after winter. It is not a demanding road, and the real pleasure is in rhythm and scenery. Early mornings give you the best light and the fewest vehicles, and in autumn the mist lies in the valley below as you ride along the ridge.

For practical matters, fuel is available in Wattwil, about five kilometres away, and in the larger towns on the Linth side. The ridge itself has a few farm restaurants and small inns, some of which serve simple dishes with local cheese, sausage and bread, though opening times are irregular. Bring water if the day is warm.

Watch for cattle. The upper pastures have grazing animals in summer, and sometimes they stand on or beside the road. Cyclists use the pass heavily at weekends, so take the corners with some margin. The weather changes quickly on the ridge, with a sunny start giving way to cloud by afternoon, so keep a rain layer handy and an eye on the sky behind the Churfirsten.
t.lucerne lakefront@47.1,8.3:
Lucerne works best if you arrive by water, but a motorcycle at the right hour comes close. The city sits where Lake Lucerne narrows into the river Reuss, with the Pilatus massif standing guard on one side and the Rigi on the other, and the old town spills along both banks like a stage set that happens to be real. The wooden Chapel Bridge, first built in 1333, crosses the river at an angle, with painted panels under the roof, and its stone water tower has served as a prison, an archive and a treasury. A fire in 1993 destroyed much of the bridge, and what you walk on today is mostly a careful reconstruction.

The Lion Monument, carved into a sandstone face in the early nineteenth century, commemorates the Swiss Guards who died defending the Tuileries Palace in Paris in 1792. It is a surprisingly moving piece, a dying lion with a spear in its flank, and Mark Twain famously called it the saddest and most moving piece of stone in the world. A short walk from the lake brings you to it, and it is quiet and slightly eerie even in the tourist season.

From a rider's perspective, Lucerne is an arrival rather than a ride. The traffic can be heavy, especially in the summer, and the lakefront is busy with pedestrians, coaches and cyclists. But the setting is superb, and the early evening light on the water and the mountains is spectacular. Park the bike in a designated motorcycle bay, because the city enforces parking, and walk the promenade. The modern concert hall by the station, with its huge floating roof, stands as a counterpoint to the medieval bridges.

Fuel is not a concern in a city of fifty-seven thousand, with large stations on the approach roads, though they can be crowded at peak hours. Coffee and lunch are everywhere, from bakeries to lake terraces. Prices are high, so choose with that in mind.

If you have time, pick a table with a view of the water and watch the paddle steamers pull in. The mountains often wear a cap of cloud, which can lift suddenly and reveal the full scene. That moment, when Pilatus appears from nowhere, is the reason people come back.
t.axenstrasse cliff road@47.0,8.6:
If the Axenstrasse had been built today, it would probably be declared impossible. It runs along the cliffs of the Urnersee, with the lake directly below and rock walls climbing above, and it was cut in the 1860s when engineers still believed in pickaxes and gunpowder. Its main purpose was to link the Gotthard corridor to central Switzerland without relying on lake steamers. The tunnels and galleries along the route were chiselled out by hand, and the carved portals are among the nicest bits of old infrastructure you will see.

This is the stretch where the mountain wins. The road clings to ledges, dips into short tunnels with windows opening onto the water, and bursts out into sunshine with a view straight across to the Uri Alps. Near the northern end the famous chapel dedicated to William Tell sits at the water's edge, which can be reached by boat or on foot. Whether Tell existed is a matter for historians. The scenery here is real and the legend belongs to the place, and in Altdorf, a few minutes down the road, a statue of the archer and his son stands in the square.

The riding is slow and thoughtful. The speed limit is low, the bends are tight, and the tunnels demand attention. Mid-morning sun lights the opposite shore, and evenings give a golden glow on the western cliffs. Winter ice can linger in shaded galleries, and spring rains sometimes loosen stones from the slope above. Treat any warning sign seriously, and expect that the road can close for rock-clearing.

For fuel and supplies, Ingenbohl and Brunnen at the southern end of the lake are the nearest, and the Uri side has stations around Flüelen and Altdorf. There are viewpoints and a few restaurants along the way, though some are seasonal. If you want a quiet moment, look for a lay-by where you can stop out of the traffic, remove your helmet and listen. The lake is so deep and still that sound seems to fall away.

The return is as good as the outward leg. With the sun in a different position, the whole view looks new, and you will catch details you missed on the first pass.
t.sattel return passlet@47.1,8.6:
Coming back over Sattel is a different experience from going out. In the late afternoon the light comes in low from the west, the Rigi is a long dark shape against the glow, and the saddle at about 790 metres feels quieter. The road here winds along gentle slopes with farms dotted across the meadows and the occasional chapel at a bend. Traffic is light, and if you time it right you will share the road mainly with a few cyclists and the odd tractor.

This is also the corner of Switzerland where the old story of the Confederation is told in battlefields. A few kilometres to the south and east lies the Rothenthurm moor, which became an unlikely symbol of Swiss politics in 1987, when voters approved an initiative to protect the moors of the country and stopped a planned army training ground. It was one of the first times environmental protection won in a national referendum in such a striking way. Close to the Ägerisee, the monument at Morgarten marks the 1315 battle, where mountain men from Schwyz ambushed Habsburg troops on a narrow shore path.

For the ride, the return over Sattel is a chance to settle into a rhythm. The corners are open, the surface is generally smooth, and the gradients are steady. Many riders use it as the final climb of the day before descending toward the lake of Zug, so the pace tends to be relaxed. Early evening in September is lovely, with the smell of cut grass and a faint chill that makes the warm tarmac feel kind.

Unterägeri, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town for fuel and food, and the villages of Rothenthurm and Steinen are alternatives. There is often a small restaurant or bakery in Sattel itself, but do not rely on late opening. If you need something to eat, plan it for the valley.

The hills here catch weather from the west, so watch the sky. A shower can sweep in with little warning, and wet leaves on the tarmac get slick in autumn. Take the descent gently, and use the lay-bys if you want to look back at the way you came.
t.ratenpass rhythm@47.1,8.7:
The Ratenpass is a short, quick climb between the Ägerisee valley and the Biberbrugg side, topping out at 1,077 metres. It is not famous like the Gotthard or the Grimsel, and that suits the riders who use it, because the traffic is light and the road is built for fun rather than freight. From the lakeside at Unterägeri the road climbs through forest, then breaks out into open pasture with a broad view toward the Mythen and the Alps beyond. Cows graze right up to the verge, and in summer you can hear the bells from the road.

The word rhythm fits. There are no long straights, no abrupt hairpins, and the bends flow into one another in a way that rewards smooth steering. The surface is usually good, with occasional patches where frost has cracked the asphalt. On the Schwyz side the gradient steepens a little, and the corners tighten as the road drops toward Schindellegi and the lake of Zurich. Local riders use it for after-work blasts, and it tends to be busiest on warm weekday evenings, when you may share the climb with a few like-minded riders and a handful of cyclists.

The landscape is part of a larger story. The ridge lies in the cantonal borderland between Zug and Schwyz, with small farms, moors and woodland. Peat once cut from the bogs fed local stoves, and the traditional farmhouses with wide eaves tell you this is cheese and cattle country. The nearby moors are protected, and in spring the cotton grass and orchids bloom in the wet hollows. If you stop and listen, you can hear the quiet hum of a landscape that has changed little in a hundred years.

Fuel is available in Unterägeri, about six kilometres away, and in Schindellegi on the other side. A few farm restaurants and inns appear near the top, but opening hours depend on the season and the day.

Check the weather before you climb. Fog forms on the ridge, and a bright valley can hide a damp, misty summit. In winter the road can carry snow and ice on the shaded side, and it is usually cleared less promptly than the main roads. On a clear evening in early summer, though, it is one of the loveliest quick climbs in the area.
t.agerisee@47.1,8.6:
The Ägerisee is the sort of lake that locals prefer to keep to themselves. It lies at about 724 metres in the canton of Zug, a small oval of clean water surrounded by meadows, forest and low hills, with the villages of Unterägeri at the northern end and Oberägeri on the eastern shore. The Lorze river drains it toward Zug, and in the south the ground rises to the ridge of Morgarten, where in 1315 the Swiss Confederates won their famous victory over a Habsburg army. The landscape is calm now, and it is hard to imagine knights on the narrow shore path.

Swimming is the main reason for the stop, and the lake is good for it. The water is clear and cool, and because the lake sits a bit higher than the plains below, it never gets as warm as the lowland waters. There are public bathing areas with grass and jetties at Unterägeri, and in summer you will find families, paddleboarders and rowers. In winter, the surface sometimes freezes at the edges, though full ice cover is rare. Fishermen work from small boats, and the local restaurants serve lake fish such as whitefish, which is the usual choice.

For riding, the roads around the lake are gentle, with fine views and a feeling of ease. They lead to the Ratenpass and Sattel, and to the climbs of the Zug mountains. Traffic is moderate, and weekends bring cyclists and walkers, so keep your speed under control near the shore. Evenings are the best time, with long light on the water and the hills turning blue and gold.

Fuel and shops are in Unterägeri, about two kilometres from the water, and Zug is a short ride downhill. There are cafés near the lakefront, and in the village you can find bakeries and small restaurants. Parking for motorcycles is easy near the bathing areas, although it can get busy on hot Sundays, so arrive before midday if you can.

Bring a towel, because the air near the lake can be warm while the water is bracing. A quick swim is enough to wake you up, and the walk back to the bike feels like a small reward for a day on the road.
t.rhine falls photo@47.7,8.6:
You hear the Rhine Falls before you see them, a steady roar rising through the trees as you walk down from the car park at Neuhausen. Then the river appears, wide, green and suddenly frantic, throwing itself over a limestone ledge about twenty-three metres high and roughly a hundred and fifty metres across. By volume it is the largest plain waterfall in Europe, and in early summer, when the Alps send meltwater down the Rhine, the flow is huge, filling the air with spray and a cold, mineral smell.

The falls are young in geological terms. The river took this course after the last ice age pushed it out of its old bed, and it has been cutting through the Jurassic rock ever since. The pillars of stone standing in the middle of the cascade are what remains of harder layers that the water has not yet removed. Goethe came in 1797 and wrote about the spectacle, and painters and poets have been following ever since. Above the falls on the Zürich bank sits Schloss Laufen, a castle with a viewing platform built almost on top of the water, and boats cross in summer to a rock in the middle of the stream.

As a photo stop, this is easy and rewarding. The best light is usually late in the day, when the sun low in the west catches the spray and sometimes throws a rainbow across it. Mornings are quieter and cooler, and in overcast weather the colour of the water deepens. A tripod is overkill, but a steady hand and a wide lens help. Be ready for crowds in summer, especially at weekends, when tour groups arrive in numbers.

Neuhausen, with about ten thousand people, has fuel, cafés and shops, and Schaffhausen, the old town on the Rhine just downstream, is worth a wander for its painted houses and medieval lanes. There are restaurants overlooking the falls, though prices reflect the view. Motorcycle parking is available near the entrance, but check signs and fees.

Mind the spray if you walk the lower platforms, because it soaks quickly. A light jacket with a hood is better than sunglasses and a smile, and your camera will thank you for a lens cloth.
t.lake constance@47.7,9.2:
Kreuzlingen sits right on the Swiss shore of Lake Constance, so close to the German city of Konstanz that the border runs through the streets and you can step from one country to the other without noticing, except for the occasional customs sign. The lake itself is huge, the third largest in Central Europe, shared between Switzerland, Germany and Austria, and the water has a calm, wide-open feeling that the Alpine lakes lack. On a clear day the Säntis and the Austrian mountains show along the far horizon.

Konstanz carries a weighty history. In the early fifteenth century it hosted the Council of Constance, which ended a split in the papacy and condemned the reformer Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake in 1415. A monument and a house in the old town recall the events. Today the city is a lively university town, and its lakeside promenade and old centre are well worth a walk, though if you cross, remember your passport or identity card and be aware of border traffic at busy times.

For a water stop, the Swiss side offers parks and bathing spots right at the shore. The Seeburgpark has lawns that slope to the water and room for a picnic, and you can swim in summer. The lake is shallow near the shore and warms more than the Alpine lakes do, with a gentle shingle bottom. Sailing boats and ferries cross constantly, and in the evening the lights of Konstanz begin to reflect on the water.

The riding in the area is flat and orderly, with roads running between orchards and vineyards, and the occasional glimpse of the lake through the trees. This is not a thrill ride but a pleasant one, with moderate traffic and plenty of cyclists. The best time is a warm late afternoon, when the air smells of water and the light turns gold.

Kreuzlingen has nearly eighteen thousand residents, so fuel and food are straightforward, and the larger Konstanz is on the doorstep. Swiss prices are higher than German ones, so many riders fill up on the German side, though fuel stations on either side are easy to find. If you cross, carry documents and check the rules for vehicles.

Wind can build on the lake in the afternoon, so keep a jacket handy if you plan to sit by the water. In spring and autumn, mist drifts over the surface at dawn, and the whole scene looks like a watercolour.
t.thurgau orchard roads@47.6,9.1:
Thurgau has a nickname that makes it sound like another continent. Locals call it Mostindien, from Most, the cider pressed from apples and pears, and the orchards that cover the hills above Lake Constance justify the joke. In April the blossom turns whole slopes white and pink, and in September the trees hang with fruit, and the air near the farms smells sweet and slightly fermented. It is one of the best quiet-road landscapes in northern Switzerland, and few foreign riders know it.

The area around Weinfelden is the heart of it. The town sits on the Thur river, with a modest old centre and vineyards on the slope of the Ottenberg ridge, where wine grapes ripen in the sun. Between the orchards, small villages cluster around churches and half-timbered farmhouses, and local farm shops sell apples, juice, schnapps and cheese from stands beside the road, often on an honour system with a cash box. If you see one, stop. The produce is good, and buying direct is part of the experience.

The riding is easy and elegant. Roads ripple gently over the low hills, with wide bends, good surfaces and long views across the orchards toward the lake or the distant Alps. It is not a technical challenge, so the pleasure is in rhythm and scenery. Traffic is light on small roads, but tractors and fruit lorries use them in season, so keep your speed reasonable and expect slow vehicles around blind bends. Early autumn is the high point, with golden light and a faint haze, though spring blossom is hard to beat.

Weinfelden has about nine thousand people, so fuel, bakeries and cafés are all available, and smaller villages such as Märstetten and Affeltrangen have basic services. There is no need to carry spare fuel, but do carry something to drink, since the orchard roads have few cafés.

The main caution is dampness. After rain, mud from farm vehicles can coat corners, and in autumn fallen fruit creates slick patches, a hazard not mentioned in many guides. Go slowly through villages, where school and farm traffic is common. If you want a souvenir, a bottle of local cider fits neatly into a pannier, though you may prefer to drink it on arrival.
t.winterthur return food@47.5,8.7:
Winterthur is the city people overlook on the way to Zürich, and that is their loss. It is the sixth largest city in Switzerland, with a compact old town of pastel houses, pedestrian streets and a reputation for being modest, practical and well-fed. The old centre around Marktgasse is car-free, with cafés and bakeries spilling onto the pavement, and a stroll along it is enough to understand why the locals call themselves Winterthurer first and Zürcher a distant second.

Winterthur grew rich on industry. The Sulzer company made diesel engines and locomotives here for over a century, and the engineering heritage shows in the converted factory halls that now hold housing, offices and the Lokremise, a former locomotive depot turned cultural space. The city is also full of museums. The Oskar Reinhart collections hold excellent European art assembled by a local merchant family, and the Technorama science centre on the hill above town lets children and adults play with levers, lightning and sound.

As a return stop, Winterthur is ideal. Riders coming from Lake Constance or the Thurgau hills arrive at the end of the day, and the city offers a proper meal, a seat and a chance to stretch before the final run home. Restaurants range from simple bakeries to better dining rooms, and the Swiss habit of closing the kitchen early means you should aim to eat before eight or nine. Look for places with outdoor seating if the weather is mild.

There is no trouble with fuel, since the city has stations on all the main roads, and the old town has parking for motorcycles at the edges. Inside the centre traffic is restricted, so leave the bike in a designated area and walk. Keep an eye on the weather, because the hills around Winterthur can hold fog in autumn and winter, and the ride in may be cooler than you expect.

The motorway to Zürich is only twenty minutes away, but if you have energy left, take the back roads through the Töss valley or past the Kyburg castle, which stands on a hilltop on the way and is worth a visit. The evening light there is particularly good, and the castle walls glow in the last sun.
t.sihlsee group pause@47.1,8.8:
A group pause needs three things, which are room to park a line of bikes, a flat place to sit and something nearby to eat, and the Sihlsee provides all three without fuss. The reservoir stretches east of Einsiedeln at about 889 metres, and its shores have wide verges, picnic areas and small beaches where a dozen riders can drop gear and take helmets off without blocking anyone. On warm days you will see families, anglers and paddlers, but the lake is big enough to absorb them.

Einsiedeln, three kilometres away, rewards a detour. The town is built around the Benedictine abbey, a huge baroque complex facing a wide curved square with a fountain in front. The church holds the Black Madonna, a medieval statue that has drawn pilgrims for centuries, and the abbey has long been a stop on the Way of St James through Switzerland. The monastery is also known for its stables, where it has bred Einsiedler horses for many generations. The main street leading to the square has cafés, bakeries and souvenir shops, and the pace of life is gentler than the traffic suggests.

The riding around the lake is easy. A road follows the north shore and another crosses the water on the bridge at Willerzell, with wide, flowing bends and a smooth surface. Traffic builds on summer weekends, with cyclists and day visitors, so groups should keep together and leave gaps for overtaking. In the early morning, mist often lies on the lake, and the first light on the Mythen peaks to the south is a worthwhile reward for an early start.

For fuel, Einsiedeln has several stations, and Feusisberg and Schindellegi, on the Zurich side, provide alternatives. There is a mix of lakeside restaurants and small kiosks, though they may be seasonal. If you are leading a group, a quick check of the opening hours in advance is a good idea, because Swiss places often close in the afternoon lull between lunch and dinner.

The lake is artificial and drops in winter, so the shoreline can look bare in spring. By midsummer it is full again, and the water is clean enough for a quick swim. Keep an eye on the weather, because storms form over the hills in the afternoon and can pass quickly.
t.rothenthurm moor road@47.1,8.7:
Rothenthurm looks like an ordinary Swiss village on an open plateau, and then you learn that it changed national law. In 1987 voters approved the so-called Rothenthurm Initiative, which protected the high moors of Switzerland from development and stopped the army from building a training ground on the plain here. It was a surprise victory for conservation and remains a point of local pride. The moor is a raised bog, a spongy landscape of peat, cotton grass and stunted pine, formed over thousands of years after the ice retreated.

The land is flat and wide at around 920 metres, ringed by hills, and the cold air pools here on still nights. Rothenthurm is known as one of the coldest places in inhabited Switzerland, and in winter the plain is a favourite for cross-country skiing, with tracks laid across the open fields. In summer the same landscape is green, quiet and full of the sound of wind in the grasses, and you may see birds such as curlews and lapwings if the season is right.

For riders, the moor road is a change of pace. After the climbs and hairpins of the passes, it is flat and direct, with long straight sections and fast, clear visibility across the open ground. That makes it relaxing, but also exposed. Crosswinds can be strong, especially when a cold front comes in from the west, and the plateau gives no shelter. Early morning mist can lie in the hollows, and frost can persist on the road well into spring.

Einsiedeln, about six kilometres away, is the nearest large town with fuel and food, and Sattel and Biberbrugg are closer for a quick stop. The village itself has a historic bridge and a handful of inns and cafés, but check opening times, since small places often close in the afternoon. A hot drink is welcome on a cool day, and the old inns serve local dishes such as sausage and rösti.

Look out for the old fortified wall that once blocked the valley, a medieval defence line of the Schwyz farmers. It is not the kind of thing you spot at speed, but it adds a layer of meaning to the land. Take your time, and watch for wildlife crossing near the moor edges.
t.rigi foothill view@47.1,8.5:
Not far from Arth lies a piece of ground with a violent story. In September 1806, after weeks of heavy rain, a huge part of the Rossberg mountain slid down onto the valley below, burying the village of Goldau and killing around four hundred and fifty people. The slide covered a wide area in rubble, and the landscape you see today, with its tumbled boulders and rough, uneven fields, is the scar. Nature has reclaimed much of it, and a wildlife park now stands on the debris, though the scale of the event still shows in the shape of the ground.

From the Rigi foothill viewpoint you can read that history in the landscape. Look across the valley and you see the gap on the Rossberg where the rock tore away, the hummocks spread beneath it, and the lakes of Zug and Lauerz, the latter made smaller by the landslide's displacement of water. It is a quiet reminder that the Alps are not fixed, and that the peaceful pasture below once looked very different.

The riding here is straightforward and pleasant. The road climbs gently from Arth through pasture and orchard, with good views opening and closing between the trees. At around nine hundred metres the air feels fresher, and on a clear day the view stretches across the lake to the Albis hills. Corners are open and the surface is generally smooth, so the ride suits a relaxed pace. Traffic is light on weekdays, and walkers use the verge, so stay aware around blind bends.

For the Rigi itself, the summit is a short walk or rack railway ride from the stations, where the famous sunrise draws visitors in good weather. If you want to go up, leave the bike below and take the train, since the summit has no road. Down in Arth, about three kilometres away, you will find fuel, bakeries and cafés, and Küssnacht and Goldau are alternatives.

Weather changes quickly on the Rigi. The mountain catches cloud, and a clear morning can fill with mist by lunchtime. Carry a layer and check the forecast, and if cloud closes in, wait. It often lifts again in an hour, and the view is worth the patience.
t.zug food finish option@47.2,8.5:
Zug is the smallest of the big Swiss business cities, and it carries its wealth lightly. It sits on the northeast corner of Lake Zug, with a compact old town of narrow lanes, a medieval clock tower called the Zytturm with its colourful roof, and a lakeside promenade where swans and joggers share the space. Low taxes have drawn companies and a large share of the world's cryptocurrency firms, so the town is nicknamed Crypto Valley, though you would not know it from the pastel houses and the old town gate.

The food is the draw. Zug is the home of Zuger Kirschtorte, a layered cake of almond meringue, sponge soaked in cherry liqueur and buttercream. You will see it in bakery windows across town, and a slice with coffee is a rite of passage. The lake provides fish, including the local red char, and restaurants along the water serve it fried or poached. For something more hearty, the Swiss classics of rösti, sausage and cheese are on most menus.

As a finish option, the town works well. After a day of hills, the flat lakeside is calm, and you can park the bike near the harbour and walk. In the evening, light hits the water and the mountains behind, with the Rigi and Pilatus standing in the distance, and the old town starts to fill with people leaving work. There are pubs and wine bars, and the cafés spill outdoors on mild nights.

Fuel is no issue in a town of twenty-three thousand, with stations on the main roads and in neighbouring Baar. Parking for motorcycles is available near the lake, though it is limited at peak times, so look for the marked bays and avoid pavements. Public transport is excellent, and if you are heading home by train, the station is close to the old town.

If the weather is warm, the lake invites a swim, and there are public bathing places along the shore. The water is clean, and in summer the town is lively until late. Take a moment on the promenade before you load up, because Zug is one of those places where the end of a ride feels like a small ceremony. Sunset is the best time, with the water turning from blue to pink.
t.sihlsee@47.1,8.8:
Evening is the right hour for the Sihlsee. When the sun drops toward the Zürich side, the light slides along the reservoir and picks out the farmhouses on the far shore, and the hills turn a layered blue. A sunset run from Hirzel or Einsiedeln would end naturally here, with a quiet stop by the water and a long look at a view that fades from gold to grey.

The lake is man-made, finished in the 1930s to store water for the railways, but it has the soft ease of a natural one. To the south the twin peaks of the Mythen rise above Schwyz, and to the north the hill of the Etzel stands over the shore, with an old pilgrim chapel on its flank. The Etzel is part of the Way of St James, and walkers heading for Einsiedeln pass this way carrying shells on their packs. In the evening you may see herons standing at the water's edge and swallows skimming the surface for insects.

Swimming is possible in warm months, and in summer the shore has a few spots where you can wade in from grass or pebbles. After sunset the water holds its warmth for a while, and the surface can be glassy, with reflections of the sky. Fishermen sit patiently at the edge, and the occasional paddleboarder glides by. In late autumn the lake can be steely and cold, with mist rising from the surface at dawn.

The roads around the lake are good riding, with gentle bends and a smooth surface, and at dusk the traffic is light. Keep an eye out for deer, which sometimes cross near the wood edges, and for cyclists without lights on the lakeside track. Shortly after the sun goes down the temperature drops, so a spare layer is worth carrying.

Einsiedeln, about three kilometres away, has the nearest fuel and a good choice of restaurants and bakeries. Feusisberg and Schindellegi on the north side have further services. If you are planning a late meal, check ahead, because Swiss kitchens close early outside the larger towns.

When the last colour leaves the sky, the lake becomes a dark mirror and the lights of villages appear along the shore. That is the moment to pull on your gloves and head home.
t.ratenpass@47.1,8.7:
The return over the Ratenpass in the evening is one of the small pleasures of riding near Zürich. From the Sihlsee side or from Hirzel, the road climbs gradually to 1,077 metres, and the day's heat begins to leave the air as you rise. The forest gives way to open pasture near the top, where cows graze in the late light and the Mythen and the Alps stand in the south as a dark, jagged line. It is a place to feel the day wind down.

The pass sits in the border country between Zug and Schwyz, and the ridge has a quiet, workaday feel. Farms with deep roofs dot the slope, and cheese is made in the old way in some of the huts. Down in the valleys, moors hold wet ground that has been protected for decades, and the lingering smell of cut hay mixes with the cool air from the woods. In summer the evening sky can glow red over the lake of Zurich, and on the descent toward Unterägeri the lake of Ägeri appears below, calm and dark.

On the road, the climb from the Hirzel side is smooth and flowing, with moderate gradients and open bends. The surface is usually good, and speeds are comfortable. As you head down toward Ägeri, the road tightens a little and passes through forest, where shadows can hide damp patches even in summer. Take care at dusk, because deer and foxes cross the road, and cyclists returning from the hills may not have lights.

Fuel is available in Unterägeri, about six kilometres from the pass, and in Schindellegi or Biberbrugg on the other side. A mountain inn sits near the top in the season, but opening hours vary, so do not count on a late meal. A flask of coffee or a bar of chocolate in the pannier is a better plan.

Temperatures drop quickly after sunset, even in summer. At 1,077 metres, the air is a few degrees cooler than at the lake, and a light layer under your jacket makes the descent far more comfortable. On clear nights, you may see stars appear above the ridge before you reach the valley, and that is the best moment of the day.
t.bellagio ferry village@46.0,9.3:
Bellagio sits on the tip of the peninsula that divides Lake Como into its two southern arms, and it has the confident look of a place that has been admired for centuries. Steep stepped lanes run down to the water between old stone houses, and the waterfront is lined with cafés under arcades. Ferries cross from here to Varenna, Menaggio and Cadenabbia, and their horns echo off the mountains. The surrounding hills rise sharply, and on a clear day the Alps stand white at the head of the lake.

The town's grand villas are part of the story. Villa Melzi, with its landscaped gardens by the water, and Villa Serbelloni, on the headland above, were built by wealthy families in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries when Lake Como was fashionable among aristocrats and writers. The gardens are open to visitors at certain times, and the views over the water from the paths are among the best on the lake. Silk was the local industry for generations, and the scarves and ties sold in the shops are a reminder of it.

The ride to Bellagio from Como or Lecco is slow and scenic. The road along the lake, narrow and twisting, passes through villages and tunnels, and traffic can be heavy in summer. A better approach is the ridge road above, which climbs through woods and gives long views over the water. Near the top is the Madonna del Ghisallo, a small chapel that has become the patron shrine of cyclists, filled with racing jerseys and bicycles. It has a small museum and a view of the lake, and motorcyclists are just as at home, with fewer legs to tire.

For practical matters, Bellagio is small and parking is tight, so look for the car parks above the town and walk down. Fuel is available at Mandello del Lario, about nine kilometres by the lake road, and in the bigger towns of Lecco and Como. Cafés and restaurants line the waterfront, with lake fish such as perch and missoltini, dried shad, appearing on local menus. Prices are high on the front, so walk a few streets back for better value.

Evening light is the best. When the day-trippers leave, the town slows down, and the water glows in the low sun. If you can, stay on the lake late and ride back in the dark with the lights of the villages reflecting on the surface.
t.waypoint 2@45.2,6.6:
This spot lies in the Maurienne, the long valley of the river Arc that runs from the high Alps down toward Chambéry, and the town of Modane sits at the heart of it. For centuries this was the way across the mountains to Italy, via the Mont Cenis pass, and in the nineteenth century engineers drove a railway tunnel under the Fréjus massif, which opened in 1871 and gave the town its role as a border station. A road tunnel followed in 1980. Today Modane is quiet and a bit industrial, but its position makes it a natural stopping place.

On the Route des Grandes Alpes, the old tourist road laid out in the early twentieth century from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean, this valley connects two great mountain sections. To the north lies the Col de l'Iseran, over 2,700 metres, among the highest paved passes in the Alps, and to the west the Galibier, which tops 2,600 metres and is the high point of many riders' year. Both are closed by snow for most of the winter and spring, usually reopening in early summer, so check before you plan.

The riding here is a lesson in scale. The valley is steep-sided, with forts clinging to the slopes, avalanche galleries over the road and a scattering of villages with slate roofs. Weather can change quickly: sun in the valley can mean snow above, and thunderstorms build in the afternoon. Start early and keep warm layers handy. In the valley the road is wide and fast, but the passes demand attention, with hairpins and sheer drops.

Modane has about four thousand people and offers fuel, a few cafes and a supermarket. If you are heading up toward the high passes, fill the tank here, because stations become scarce higher up. The nearby ski resorts, such as Val Thorens, are on the other side of the mountains, and in summer they are quiet. Carry a rain jacket, and stop to look at the cliffs when you can.
t.dijon@47.3,5.0:
Dijon was the capital of the Dukes of Burgundy, who in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries were richer than many kings, and the city still carries the marks of that time. The Palais des Ducs, now a town hall and fine arts museum, stands on a wide, curved square, and the narrow streets of the old centre are lined with half-timbered houses and carved doorways. On the wall of the church of Notre-Dame, a small stone owl, the chouette, is worn smooth by the hands of visitors who stroke it with the left hand for luck.

The city is also famous for mustard, which has been made here since the Middle Ages, and for crème de cassis, the blackcurrant liqueur that, mixed with white wine, makes a kir, named after a mayor of the city. You can buy both in shops around the covered market, designed with the help of Gustave Eiffel's workshop, and it is the best place for a lunch of cheese, ham and bread.

For riders, Dijon is the northern gateway to the Route des Grands Crus, the stretch of road, mostly the D974, which runs south along the foot of the Côte d'Or through the most famous vineyards in France: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée, Nuits-Saint-Georges, Beaune. The climats, the small named plots of vines that make Burgundy so particular, were recognised by UNESCO in 2015. The road is gentle, with stone walls, church towers and low sun on the vines, and it is at its best in September and October, when the harvest is under way and the leaves turn red and gold.

Fuel is plentiful in the city and its suburbs, with big stations around the ring roads, and finding food is no challenge. Parking a bike in the centre is usually easy, but note that parts of the old town are pedestrian. Keep a clear head in the evening, since the same road that you ride in the morning leads past dozens of cellars, and a tasting is only polite if you leave the glass half full.
t.como@45.8,9.1:
Lake Como is shaped like an upside-down Y, with the city of Como at the end of one leg, and it is the deepest lake in Italy, plunging to over four hundred metres. The Alps rise straight from the water, with villas and gardens on the shores, and ferries zigzagging between the villages. Como itself is a small and elegant city, with a Duomo that took centuries to build and mixes Gothic and Renaissance styles, a walled old town and a lakefront with a funicular climbing to the hill village of Brunate. It was the birthplace of Alessandro Volta, the inventor of the battery, and the unit of electrical potential carries his name.

For a rider, the lake is a dream and a trial. The roads that follow its shores are narrow, winding and full of tunnels, with stone walls on one side and the drop to the water on the other, and in summer they are crowded with coaches, cars and cyclists. The western shore, with its old road, is slow but beautiful, passing villa gardens and villages of ochre houses. The eastern side has a faster main road with long tunnels and a more modern feel. Go early, avoid the weekends and be patient.

A circuit of the lake takes you through Menaggio, Bellagio at the tip of the central peninsula, Varenna and Lecco, and gives you a good sense of how the shores change from soft southern lakeside to steep northern mountain. The best light is in the morning, when the water is calm and the mountains are clear, and autumn brings colour to the chestnut woods. In summer, afternoon storms build quickly over the mountains.

Como has about eighty thousand people, so fuel is easy in the city, and it is wise to fill the tank before you set off, as stations along the shore are few. Try missoltini, dried and grilled lake fish, or risotto with perch fillets, and an espresso at a lakeside cafe. Silk weaving was the city's trade for centuries, and there are shops selling scarves and ties. Park the bike outside the old town, where the streets are narrow, and walk to the lakefront.
t.turin@45.1,7.7:
Turin looks like a city drawn with a ruler. The old Roman grid, recast by the dukes of Savoy into broad avenues and arcaded streets, gives it a clarity unusual in Italy, and about eighteen kilometres of porticoes shelter pedestrians from the rain. It was the first capital of unified Italy in 1861, and it still has an air of formal elegance, with palaces, royal residences and baroque churches. Beyond the arcades, the Alps seem to stand at the end of every avenue, with Monviso, the pyramid peak, visible on clear days.

The city's quirks are many. The Mole Antonelliana, a tall tower with a spire, houses the national cinema museum, and the Egyptian Museum is the largest of its kind outside Cairo. The Fiat factory at Lingotto, with its rooftop test track, was once the symbol of Italian industry. Cafes in the old centre serve bicerin, a layered drink of coffee, chocolate and cream, and vermouth was perfected here in the late eighteenth century. The chocolate gianduiotto, a little wedge of hazelnut chocolate, was invented here too.

For a rider, the great reward lies south-east of the city, in the hills of Langhe and Roero, where the vineyards of Barolo and Barbaresco climb in neat rows over rolling ground. The road to Govone, with its royal castle, a Savoy residence, passes through this country, with narrow lanes, medieval villages on hilltops and long views to the Alps. In autumn, the vines turn red and gold, mist fills the valleys and the white truffle fair in Alba draws gourmets from around the world.

Fuel is easy in Turin, and the ring roads are straightforward, though the centre has restricted traffic zones, so check before you ride in. The food is rich and serious: agnolotti, a small filled pasta, vitello tonnato, and bollito misto, a stew of boiled meats. Grissini, the thin breadsticks, were born here. Leave early to beat the traffic, and be ready for fog in autumn and winter, when the plain can be thick with mist and the hills rise like islands above it.
t.milan@45.5,9.2:
Milan does not try to charm you, and that is part of its charm. It is Italy's business capital, a city of fashion, finance and design that works hard and dresses well. At the centre stands the Duomo, a Gothic cathedral begun in 1386 and not finished for about five centuries, a forest of white marble spires and statues, and you can climb onto the roof among them. Beside it, the glass-roofed Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II is a nineteenth-century shopping arcade, and beyond it La Scala opera house.

In the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper in the 1490s, and booking is essential if you want to see it. In the south, the Navigli canals, partly designed by Leonardo's era engineers, now line with bars and restaurants, and the city's aperitivo tradition, a drink with a spread of snacks, is at its best here. The yellow trams of the old city rattle along rails that are treacherous for motorbike wheels, especially in the wet.

South of the city lies the abbey of Chiaravalle, a Cistercian foundation from the twelfth century with a tall tower, standing in the fields at the edge of the suburbs, a peaceful contrast. The ride to the Venetian walls of Bergamo, built in the sixteenth century, leads north-east across the Lombard plain, where fog can hang thick in autumn and winter, then up into the foothills of the Alps. The roads are busy, so go early on a weekday, and be ready for a mix of motorway and small country roads.

Fuel is easy across the region, with plenty of stations on the ring roads, and bike parking is common in the centre, though the old core has traffic limits that you need to check. Try risotto alla milanese, golden with saffron, and ossobuco, braised veal shank, and finish with a slice of panettone, which comes from here. The city is quietest in August, when many locals leave for the sea, and liveliest in spring and autumn.
t.nagasaki shipyard mitsubishi senshokaku:
Senshokaku is a surprise in a shipyard city: a wooden Western-style guesthouse of 1904, built by Mitsubishi on the hillside above its Nagasaki shipyard so that foreign clients and dignitaries could stay in comfort while ships were built and launched below. The house, with its verandas and clapboard walls, looks out over the harbour, and from here the owners could watch their vessels take shape. Today it is part of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution, which UNESCO recognised in 2015, and it is a reminder that heavy industry in Japan was as much about hosting and diplomacy as steel plate.

Nagasaki is a city of hills. Houses climb the slopes in terraces and the lanes between them are steep, narrow, and sometimes only wide enough for a scooter. Riding here means low gears, careful braking and plenty of looking around corners. The old streetcars still rattle through the flat parts, and you share the lane with them. Be gentle with a loaded bike: the climb up to Glover Garden or the Oura Church is short but steep, and parking is limited.

The city's history is layered. For over two centuries, when Japan was closed to most foreigners, Dutch traders were confined to the small island of Dejima in the harbour, and this made Nagasaki the country's window on the West. Portuguese missionaries arrived earlier, and a hidden Christian community survived the long ban. The atomic bomb fell on the city on 9 August 1945, and the Peace Park and the museum are quiet, necessary places that deserve a half day.

Nagasaki is also a good place to eat. The local plates are champon, a thick noodle soup, and sara udon, and the Chinese influence from old trade ties is strong. Castella, the sponge cake the Portuguese brought, is sold everywhere. Fuel is plentiful on the roads out of the city, though less so in the centre. Obita and Togitsu, to the north, have easy stations. Come in spring or autumn, when the humid summer has not yet made the hills a trial.
t.nagasaki shipyard mitsubishi giant canti:
The giant cantilever crane stands over the Nagasaki shipyard like a tall green arm, and it was installed in 1909 to lift heavy machinery, boilers and engines into ships being fitted out at the quay. It is among the oldest cranes of its kind in Japan, electric, enormous, and built with the confidence of a country that wanted to build its own steamers. The Mitsubishi yard it served grew into one of the great shipbuilders of Asia, and warships and liners both took form here. The crane is now part of the Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution and is visible, in outline at least, from the water and from some of the roads around the harbour. The yard is still working, so access to the area is limited.

Nagasaki sits at the head of a long narrow bay, with steep green hills on either side and the city crammed into every fold. That shape is why the port is so well sheltered and why the roads are so tight. Riding here is a mix of coastal route, bridge and hill lane. Route 202 follows the bay out to the north and offers good views, and the flat shipyard roads are ordinary city streets with trams and port traffic. If you are on a large bike, prepare to ride slowly and to use the elevated expressway when it helps.

The yard has a dark side, and anyone looking at Nagasaki honestly should know it. The Mitsubishi works were a major target in the bombing of August 1945, and the survivors' accounts of that morning are told in the city's museum and the Peace Park, both a short ride away. The contrast between the cheerful hills and what happened here sits with you for a while.

For a break, head across the harbour to the Dejima reconstruction or walk the Chinese quarter, where the markets sell dumplings and sweet buns. Fuel stops are easy in the suburbs, particularly toward Obita. The best light on the crane is in the evening, when it catches the low sun and turns warm against the water.
t.daeheungsa temple@34.5,126.6:
Daeheungsa sits in a fold of the Duryunsan mountains, near the southern tip of the Korean peninsula, and the approach is half the reward. A long path runs beside a stream through an avenue of old trees, camellias, maples and cedar, and the sound of water follows you all the way up. The temple is among the more important in Korean Buddhism because of a monk named Hyujeong, known as Seosan Daesa, who led a force of warrior monks against the Japanese invasion of 1592. Before he died he asked that his robe and bowl be kept here, and the temple is now treated as the seat of that tradition. It is also tied to the history of Korean tea, since the monk Choui lived at a hermitage in its grounds and wrote on the subject.

The riding around is worth the detour. From Haenam, about eleven kilometres away, the road climbs through the ridge in a series of well-surfaced bends, with forest on one side and the valley falling away on the other. In autumn the colour is intense and the air is cool and clear. On weekends, the temple road fills with visitors, and parking can be difficult, so a weekday morning is gentler. To the west, the road runs on to Ttangkkeut, the Land's End of the peninsula, where the view stretches over islands and fishing boats.

Haenam is the place for fuel and food, a small agricultural town known for its cabbages, sweet potatoes and, more recently, its Korean-style banquet meals. Tteokgalbi, grilled rice-cake beef patties, and a table of local side dishes are standard in the region. At the temple, the shops at the entrance serve tea, noodles and simple vegetarian meals, and the monks run a temple stay programme for visitors who want to try the quiet life.

Etiquette is simple. Dress modestly, speak quietly, keep off the inner halls unless you are invited, and take shoes off where others do. Photography is allowed outside but discouraged inside. The weather can change fast in the mountains, and rain brings out the green on the cedar bark.
t.luxembourg@49.6,6.1:
Luxembourg City is a fortress town built on a rock, and it has the sort of dramatic geography that makes you stop the bike and look. The old town sits on a sandstone promontory surrounded on three sides by the deep gorges of the Alzette and Petrusse rivers, so that the walls rise straight from the valley floor. For centuries it was one of the strongest fortresses in Europe, fought over by Spanish, French, Austrian, Prussian and Dutch armies, and its tangle of tunnels, the Bock Casemates, ran for kilometres inside the cliff. Much of it was dismantled after 1867, but enough survives to be walked. The old quarter and the fortifications are on the UNESCO list.

Riding here is easy and quite agreeable. The roads are wide and well kept, and traffic is orderly, with speed limits strictly watched by cameras. The bridges, including the stone Adolphe Bridge of 1903, with its great arch over the Petrusse, give you views down into the green valleys. The Grund, the old lower town beside the river, is a lovely, quiet quarter of old houses and cafes. For a more open ride, head out of the city to the Moselle valley to the east, with vineyards and white-wine villages along the river, or north into the Ardennes, where roads twist through forests and past small castles.

Fuel is the practical joy of this country. Petrol and diesel have long been taxed more lightly than in the neighbours, so riders from Germany, Belgium and France often fill up here before crossing the border. Stations on the main roads are plentiful and open late. Food in the city runs from cheap Portuguese cafes, a legacy of the large Portuguese community, to dignified French-style restaurants. Try judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork collar with broad beans, the national dish.

The day ahead leads toward the Roman monuments of the region, and the countryside between shows the old border. Luxembourg is tiny, you can cross it in under an hour, but it has a language of its own, Luxembourgish, and an unshowy, prosperous feel. Come in spring or autumn, when the gorges are green or gold and the city is quiet in the early morning.
t.yellowstone national park@44.5,-110.8:
Yellowstone was the world's first national park, set aside by the United States in 1872, and the first thing to understand is that the ground here is alive. The park sits on a huge volcanic caldera left by eruptions that blew out an enormous chunk of the Rockies, and the heat still rising from below drives roughly half of the world's geysers, along with hot springs, mud pots and steaming vents. Old Faithful, in the south-west of the park, is the famous one, going off at fairly regular intervals through the day.

Riding here is a slow business, and gladly so. The Grand Loop road is a figure of eight, and speed limits are low, often around forty-five miles an hour, with good reason: bison walk down the middle of the tarmac, elk graze on the verge, and traffic stops dead whenever somebody spots a bear. Surfaces are decent, though frost heaves and patched sections appear, and the road is much busier in July and August than it looks on a map. Go early, around dawn, and you will often have the best light, the thinnest crowds and the most wildlife. Weather turns fast at over two thousand metres. Snow can fall in any month, and most roads close to cars from late autumn until spring, so check before you set out.

The landscape moves from lodgepole pine forest to open valleys such as Hayden and Lamar, where bison and wolves are the main attraction, to the deep golden canyon of the Yellowstone River with its two waterfalls. The sulphurous smell around the geyser basins is unforgettable, and the colours of Grand Prismatic Spring, which come from heat-loving bacteria, look almost unreal on a bright day. Keep to the boardwalks. Water in these pools can be scalding and acidic, and people have died by stepping off the path.

For fuel, the nearest town outside the park is West Yellowstone, about thirty kilometres from here, and there are a few service stations inside at the major villages, though they cost more and can have queues. Do not rely on them if you are low. Carry water, a warm layer and a rain jacket whatever the forecast, and respect the distance rule for wildlife, which is a good deal longer than most people think.
t.ardeche gorge@45.7,5.3:
The Ardèche Gorge, with its limestone cliffs and the great natural arch of the Pont d'Arc, lies about two hundred kilometres to the south, and the place on the map is somewhere far less dramatic: the flat, farmed country of the Nord-Isère, east of Lyon, around L'Isle-d'Abeau. This is a landscape of fields, ponds, low hills and small towns, in the old province of the Dauphiné. L'Isle-d'Abeau itself is a new town, planned in the 1970s to relieve pressure on Lyon, with housing estates, shopping centres and a business park, while the older villages of Saint-Savin, Trept and Salagnon retain their churches and farms.

The district has more history than first impressions suggest. Bourgoin-Jallieu, a few kilometres away, was a textile town, famous for printed cloth, and the river Bourbre, which runs through the plain, once powered mills. To the north lies Crémieu, a medieval walled town with a covered market hall, and the hills of the Isle Crémieu, a limestone plateau with caves and small lakes. The airport of Lyon-Saint-Exupéry is close, so there is a steady sound of aircraft overhead.

The roads here are not exciting, but they are pleasant, and they make a calm contrast to a day spent among gorges. They run straight and level through fields of maize and sunflowers, with a few gentle bends where a stream cuts across, and the surface is mostly good. Traffic is heavy near the motorway interchanges and the new town, and lighter on the back roads. In summer the sun is strong, and afternoon thunderstorms can roll in. In winter the area is often foggy, with low cloud lingering in the plain.

Fuel is easy here, with stations on the main roads near L'Isle-d'Abeau, and the supermarkets are open late. Bakeries in the villages have good bread and pastries, and a local speciality is the Saint-Marcellin, a soft creamy cheese from the Dauphiné, which you can find in most shops. The air smells of cut maize and wet earth, and the sky is wide. It is a good place to end a long journey, with a full tank, a bed nearby and no more mountains to worry about.
t.jura wine@45.9,5.1:
The Dombes plateau, north-east of Lyon, is the strangest piece of farmland in France. Spread across it are some thousand-odd ponds, made by hand over the centuries, filled in winter, fished in autumn, and then planted with cereals in a rotation that has been going for hundreds of years. Medieval monks and landowners dug them to farm carp, and the system still works, which is why the horizon here is a patchwork of reed, water and sky, full of herons and migrating ducks.

Béligneux and Montluel sit on the southern edge of this wet country. Montluel, with about 6,500 people, has an old town that climbs a small hill, with the remains of a castle, and it is the sensible place to find fuel and a good lunch. Behind the town, the land rises in the escarpment known as the Côtière, a sharp edge above the Rhône plain, and from its upper roads the view stretches across the valley to the Alps on a clear day, a long blue line of peaks.

On the bike it is easygoing country. The roads across the Dombes run straight and flat past ponds and woods, with long views and few cars, and the Côtière gives you short, tight climbs through vineyards and old villages whose houses are built from rounded river stones and pale brick. Surfaces are generally good, although wet autumn weather leaves mud on farm tracks. In the cold months fog gathers over the ponds, and a sunrise through it is memorable, even if you cannot see more than a few hundred metres ahead.

This is the end of a Jura wine ride, which means you have already been up to Arbois and the country of yellow wine, made under a film of yeast, and walked past the limestone cliffs and waterfalls of the Revermont. Coming back through the Dombes is a gentler finish than it might have been: quiet, flat, and full of birds. The nearby Rhône plain is crowded with industry, but here the land still feels old, and the ponds hold the light.
t.annecy@45.9,6.1:
Annecy sits at the northern tip of its lake, with the mountains stacked behind it, and on a clear morning it is one of the prettiest towns in the French Alps. The old centre is a knot of canals, arcaded streets and pastel houses, with a small medieval prison built on an island in the middle of the stream, and the lake beyond is so clean that you can see the bottom a long way out. With around 49,000 people it has everything: fuel, food, repair shops and plenty of places to sleep.

The riding starts at the lake itself.
