The road around its shore runs through Talloires and Menthon-Saint-Bernard, past old châteaux and stone villages, and then climbs gently through woods before dropping again to the water. It is lovely, and very busy in July and August, when cars and cyclists fill every lay-by. In the shoulder seasons it is a different place altogether, quiet and cool, with clear light on the Dents de Lanfon and the snow just visible on the Tournette. East of the lake the roads climb toward the Col de la Forclaz de Montmin, a modest pass of about 1,150 metres with a good view over the water.

The town's history has been shaped by its position, between Geneva, Savoie and the passes to Italy. For centuries it belonged to the counts of Geneva, and later to the dukes of Savoy, and the little château that rises above the old town was theirs. Today it is a place where paragliders gather on the hills and where the lakeside promenade fills each evening with people eating ice cream and watching the light fade.

As a start and finish, Annecy works very well. Early in the morning the town is calm, with delivery vans in the lanes and the smell of bread in the air, and you can be on the mountain roads within twenty minutes. At night the lights of the old town reflect in the canal, and the cafés along the quay stay open late. Book a bed ahead in summer.
t.schaffhausen@47.6,8.6:
The dot lies a few kilometres south of the Rhine in the quiet Unterland of Zurich canton, near the villages of Rorbas and Freienstein, where the Töss river flows through orchards and woods before it meets the larger river. Schaffhausen itself is further north, but this is the stretch of country that leads you to it, with modest farms, half-timbered houses and the Rhine's wide green valley just beyond the ridge.

When you do reach Schaffhausen, the town is a treat. The old centre is one of the best preserved in Switzerland, with painted facades, bay windows called Erker, and a hilltop fortress named the Munot, built in the sixteenth century as a circular citadel, where a watchman still lives and a bell rings in the evening. A short distance downstream from the old town, the Rhine Falls drop about twenty-three metres over a width of about a hundred and fifty, the largest plain waterfall in Europe. Boats take visitors to a rock in the middle of the thundering water, and the spray makes the air feel cold even in July.

The Grand Tour of Switzerland is a route of some 1,600 kilometres that links the country's best-known sights, created in the 2010s as a tourism product, and it works well as a way to see the variety of the landscape, from lakes to glaciers. For a rider, the Swiss rules are strict, and speed cameras are widespread, with heavy fines that scale to income. A motorway vignette is required for the motorway network, and the standard speed limits are 120 on the motorway, 80 outside towns and 50 inside. Obeying them is half of enjoying the country.

The riding here is gentle, with modest hills, smooth tarmac and very little to alarm you. Traffic around Zurich and the airport can be heavy at rush hour. Eglisau, a pretty walled town on the Rhine just to the north, has an old bridge and a view of the river from the terraces of its cafes.

Fuel and food are easy in the villages and towns, though prices are high by European standards. Many riders fill up just across the German border if the route allows.
t.bodensee@47.7,8.8:
Büsingen am Hochrhein is one of Europe's oddities: a German village entirely surrounded by Switzerland, with the Rhine and Swiss fields on every side, and a population of around fourteen hundred. It has its own car plates, uses both euros and Swiss francs in shops, and is part of the Swiss customs area, though it belongs to Germany. Gailingen, next door, has a rich history as the home of the largest Jewish community in Baden, and its old synagogue still stands as a reminder.

The Rhine here is wide and slow, and the landscape is a mix of orchards, vineyards and low hills. To the north, the cone-shaped volcanic hills of the Hegau poke up from the plain, with the ruined fortress on the Hohentwiel mountain dominating the view, and further east lies the Bodensee, the Lake Constance of English maps, shared between Germany, Austria and Switzerland and a major destination for holidaymakers. Stein am Rhein, a few kilometres west on the Swiss side, is a medieval town of painted houses where the river leaves the lake, and it is often called the prettiest in the country.

Riding here is relaxed. The roads pass through farmland and low forest in gentle curves, and the biggest hazard is slow tractor traffic in summer and early autumn. Border crossings between Germany and Switzerland are usually quick, but you should carry a passport or ID card, and check any rules on vehicle documents. In the Hegau, there are good twisty roads with views of the volcanic cones, and a ride through the Randen hills, a forested limestone range to the south, is a nice change.

The Bodensee itself has a gentle climate, which allows apples, pears and even wine to be grown on its shores. Ferries cross from Konstanz to Meersburg, and the island of Mainau, famous for its flower gardens, is a short ride away. In early morning, mist rises from the water, and the light is soft and golden.

Fuel is easy in nearby Singen and Stein am Rhein, and cafes are plentiful. Germany is typically cheaper than Switzerland for fuel and food, so if you are crossing, it makes sense to top up on the German side.
t.st gallen@47.7,9.2:
Konstanz and Kreuzlingen are two towns with one street between them. The border runs between buildings, with Germany to the north and Switzerland to the south, and for most of the day people pass through without a glance, going shopping, to work or to a lakeside cafe. Konstanz has about eighty thousand people and a handsome old town on the shore of the Bodensee, while Kreuzlingen is smaller but is the larger of the two Swiss towns on the lake. The Rhine leaves the lake here, flowing west, and the narrow passage between the Obersee and the Untersee is crossed by an old bridge.

Konstanz has a history that is well worth a pause. From 1414 to 1418, the town hosted the Council of Constance, a gathering of church leaders that ended the papal schism and condemned the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake here in 1415. The huge council building by the harbour still stands, and the statue of Imperia, a large woman holding two tiny figures in her hands, is an ironic modern monument at the harbour mouth. Locals will tell you that the city was spared bombing in the Second World War because it blended with the Swiss lights, a story that is widely repeated though hard to prove.

St Gallen, the label for this stop, lies about thirty kilometres south-east, in the hills above the lake. Its abbey library, with a baroque hall filled with carved wooden shelves and ancient manuscripts, is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the abbey itself goes back to the eighth century, when a monk named Gallus is said to have built a hermitage here.

Riding around the lake is easy, with flat roads, bike paths and ferries, but the traffic at weekends is heavy. On the Swiss side, speed limits are strictly enforced. A motorway vignette is needed to use the Swiss motorways.

Fuel is easy in both towns, though prices are higher in Switzerland, and plenty of Swiss residents cross to Konstanz to shop and fill up. The harbour promenade has cafes and ice cream, and the ferry to Meersburg is a pleasant way to see the lake.
t.vaduz@47.1,9.5:
Liechtenstein is a country you can cross in half an hour, a narrow strip of about twenty-five kilometres between the Rhine and the Austrian border, and Vaduz is its small, tidy capital with just over five thousand people. It sits under a steep hill crowned by the castle of Vaduz, a medieval fortress that is the home of the princely family, and its wide valley is closed in by the high wall of the Rätikon mountains. It is a country of banks, postage stamps, dental products and orderly lawns.

The castle is not open to the public, but the walk up through the vineyards gives a view of the Rhine valley and the Swiss mountains beyond. The prince's own vineyards produce a well-regarded wine in the valley below, and a small number of museums, including one for modern art with a striking black building, make a short visit worthwhile. The main street is pedestrian and lined with sculpture and cafes, and the whole town can be explored in an hour.

Riding in Liechtenstein is a pleasure in a quiet way. The road leads from the valley up to the village of Triesenberg, settled in the thirteenth century by Walser people from the Valais, who still keep their own dialect, and on to the Malbun ski area, with a series of tight bends and fine views of the Rhine plain. The surface is good, and the traffic is light. The roads are narrow and winding, and in winter the upper parts are covered in snow.

Practicalities are easy. The currency is the Swiss franc, and you can use cards almost everywhere. Fuel is available in Vaduz and Schaan, though prices are in line with Switzerland. A passport is no longer checked at the border with Switzerland, but you may be asked for papers at the Austrian side. A Swiss motorway vignette is valid for the motorway that passes along the valley.

The best time to ride is from May to October, though the valley can be hot in July and August. Autumn brings clear air and golden vineyards, and the Rhine valley is often filled with mist in the morning. Spend a little time in a cafe on the main street, and you will understand how a tiny state keeps its character.
t.lugano@46.0,9.7:
Labelled as Lugano, this dot is in fact nowhere near the lake: it lies about sixty kilometres to the east in the Val Brembana, in the Bergamo Alps, among the villages of Piazzatorre and Branzi. This is the Orobie, a range of steep, grassy mountains and rocky summits rising to nearly three thousand metres that most foreign riders never see, and one of the pleasures of looking at it is that nobody seems to be in a hurry.

The valley's history is bound up with a road. In 1593 the Venetian Republic, which then ruled Bergamo, built the Via Priula up the valley and over the Passo San Marco, a route designed to carry Venetian trade north to the Grisons without passing through Milanese territory. It was named after Alvise Priuli, the official who ordered it, and the stretch near the pass is still used today, with tight bends and stone walls. The pass itself, at 1,992 metres, is a good ride, though narrow and often misty, with long views on a clear day, and it drops into the Valtellina on the far side.

Branzi and Carona are cheese country. The local Formai de Mut, a semi-hard cheese made in the high summer pastures, has protected status and a taste that is sweet and slightly nutty, and many dairies sell it directly. The Brembo river runs clear and cold through the valley, with swimming holes in summer, and the woods of beech and fir are full of mushroom pickers in autumn. Tiny hamlets of stone and timber are clustered on the slopes, many of them half-empty in winter.

Roads in the upper valley are narrow, with limited barriers and frequent hairpins. Cyclists and sheep share the tarmac, and in summer the pastures are dotted with cattle, so expect bells and the odd animal in the road. The best season is June to September, because snow lingers late, and the San Marco pass is closed in winter.

Fuel is more of a problem. The upper valley has few stations, so fill your tank in San Pellegrino Terme or Piazza Brembana before heading up, and carry cash, since small shops and bars may not take cards.
t.bellinzona@46.0,9.0:
The dot sits in the heart of Lugano, a bright, steep little city on the shore of its lake, and it is easy to see why the Italian-speaking Swiss canton of Ticino feels like a different country from the German north. Palms grow along the waterfront, the arcades are full of coffee and pastry shops, and the light has an Italian softness, even though the banks are very Swiss. Lugano is the largest city in the canton, with about sixty thousand inhabitants, and one of the main financial centres in the country.

Bellinzona, which names the stop, is about twenty-five kilometres north-east at the foot of the Alpine passes. Its three medieval castles, Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro, rise from the valley floor and are a UNESCO World Heritage site, built by the dukes of Milan to guard the routes over the Gotthard and San Bernardino. They still dominate the old town, and the walls run right across the valley like a stage set.

Lugano itself is hemmed in by steep, wooded mountains: Monte San Salvatore rises directly from the lake, with a funicular to the summit, and Monte Brè on the opposite side has a small village of narrow lanes. A lakeside walk to the village of Gandria, mostly on a path hung above the water, gives a good view of the lake, and the water in summer is clear and warm enough for swimming. Piazza della Riforma, in the centre, is the place to sit with a coffee.

For riders, the roads around the lake are twisty and scenic but busy. Traffic in Lugano can be heavy, parking is limited, and Swiss speed limits are enforced with cameras and fines that sting. In the hills around, the roads climb in tight bends through chestnut woods, and in places the surface is rough. Ticino has a mild climate, with warm summers and a relatively gentle winter, though heavy rain can arrive from the south with force.

Fuel and food are easy, and Ticinese cooking leans toward risotto, polenta and local salami, with Merlot as the local wine. Cross-border shoppers from Italy keep the supermarkets busy on Saturday mornings. A motorway vignette is needed on the A2, which runs past the city.
t.andermatt@46.7,8.4:
The dot falls north-west of Andermatt, in the high Urner Alps near the Susten Pass road, where granite peaks, glaciers and bare slabs of rock dominate the view and the road clings to the mountainside as it climbs. It is country that feels cold even in summer, with snow lingering in the gullies and the air smelling of stone and meltwater. Andermatt itself, the label on the map, lies about fifteen kilometres to the south-east in the Urseren valley, a flat, wide, windy basin at about 1,440 metres.

That valley is a crossroads. Four passes meet here: the Gotthard to the south, the Furka to the west, the Oberalp to the east, and the Susten to the north-west, and the town has long been a garrison for the Swiss army, protecting the route through the mountains. The Devil's Bridge, a short walk down the Schöllenen gorge, is the stuff of legend: the story goes that the devil built the first crossing in return for the first soul to cross it, and was cheated when the villagers sent over a goat. A statue and a gorge, and an old stone bridge next to the modern one, make it an easy stop.

In recent years Andermatt has been transformed by a large resort development with luxury hotels and apartments, but the old centre remains small and quiet. The Gotthard Pass, at 2,106 metres, has a historic cobbled road, the Tremola, with dozens of hairpins climbing the southern side, and the paved modern road next to it is smoother. Both are worth riding, though the cobbles are demanding in the wet and slippery under tyres.

Riders heading for the Susten should note it is a toll-free pass that closes in winter, usually from around November to May, and reaches 2,224 metres. The road is a broad, engineered masterpiece, with tunnels and bends and views of the Stein glacier, and in the morning, the light on the ice is exceptional.

Fuel is available in Andermatt and in Wassen, further down, but not in the high country, so fill up before you go. Cafes in Andermatt serve hearty food, and the Gotthard region is known for its cheese and dried meats. Take a warm layer even in July.
t.furka@46.6,8.3:
Somewhere in the glaciated heart of the Bernese Oberland, close to the Grimsel lakes and a short distance from the Furka Pass, this dot falls in country that belongs more to climbers than to riders. The mountains here are huge and bare, the Finsteraarhorn and its neighbours stand above deep valleys, and the rivers run milky with glacial flour. It is among the wildest parts of the Alps.

Furka itself, at 2,429 metres, connects Uri and Valais and has one of the best-known views in the Alps. On the Valais side, the Rhone glacier, the source of the great river, spills down a rocky slope. Fifty years ago the ice reached nearly to the road, but it has retreated dramatically, and today it is partly covered in white blankets to slow melting during summer. You can walk into an ice grotto cut into the glacier, a short tourist experience that gives a sense of the scale. The hotel at the foot of the glacier is an old Victorian building and a landmark in its own right. The pass was also used in the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger, where Bond's Aston Martin chases through the bends, and the road still draws film fans.

The ride over the Furka is a series of wide hairpins with exposed drops and little barrier, and the weather can change rapidly. Cold wind, fog and snow are possible in any month, and the pass is closed in winter, normally opening in June. An old narrow-gauge steam railway runs nearby on part of the route, preserved by volunteers, and the sight of steam rising against the rock is memorable.

Fuel is the catch. There is none at the top, so tank up at Meiringen, Andermatt or Gletsch before climbing, and note that Gletsch has little more than a hotel and a handful of buildings. Meiringen, the larger town to the north, has plenty of services and is known for the meringue, supposedly invented there, and for Reichenbach Falls, where Sherlock Holmes met his end.

If you can, ride early. The tarmac is cold in the morning, but traffic is light, and the light on the ice is pure.
t.grimsel@46.7,7.9:
The dot is in Interlaken, the old tourist town between two lakes, with the label pointing to the Grimsel Pass that lies some forty kilometres to the east. Interlaken sits on a flat strip of land between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, which is exactly what its name means, and the Aare river runs through it, a bright blue-green ribbon that is wider than you expect. From here, the great white mass of the Jungfrau and its neighbours fills the southern sky, and on a clear morning it seems close enough to touch.

Tourism came early. In the early nineteenth century, English visitors found the Bernese Oberland, and the grand hotels along the Höheweg promenade date from that age, when guests arrived for weeks at a time. The old Augustinian monastery, founded in the twelfth century, gave the town its beginning, and its buildings now house the regional government. Paragliders drift down to a meadow in the middle of town, and the cafes along the promenade are full of people watching them.

For a rider, Interlaken is a base for some of the best roads in Europe. The Grimsel Pass, at 2,164 metres, runs from Innertkirchen and Meiringen through the Haslital, a deep glacial valley, passing the reservoirs of the Oberhasli power company. The road climbs through hairpins, with granite walls and dams on both sides, and the top has a hospice and a lake. From there it connects to the Furka and the Nufenen, forming one of the finest loops in the Alps. Meiringen is the usual place to stop on the way up, and Brienz, on the lake, is known for wood carving.

The town has plenty of fuel and food, with supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants of every kind. Parking is easy, though it can be busy in July and August. Interlaken has two railway stations, and the trains to the Jungfraujoch, the highest station in Europe, leave from here.

The best time to ride is from June to September, when the high passes are open. Rain can set in for days, and morning mist often lingers over the lakes, but evening light on the mountains is superb.
t.interlaken@46.4,7.6:
The label says Interlaken, but the dot is actually high above the Rhône valley in the canton of Valais, at Leukerbad, a small spa village tucked at the head of a steep side valley under the cliffs of the Gemmi. It is a quiet, curious place, about 1,400 metres above sea level, and it is surrounded by a wall of rock on three sides, with waterfalls streaming from the heights after rain.

Leukerbad is built on hot springs. More than three million litres of water, warmed to more than fifty degrees, pour out of the ground here every day, and the village has the largest thermal bathing complex in the Alps. People have been bathing here since Roman times, and the old tradition lives on, with open-air pools where you can sit in the warm water and look at snow-covered peaks. For a rider with stiff shoulders after a long day, there are few better places to end a trip.

The road up from Leuk, in the Rhône valley, is a lively climb with a series of tight bends along the side of the Dala gorge, a deep cleft in the rock, and it takes only a few minutes to reach the village. Above Leukerbad, the old Gemmi pass trail climbs to 2,314 metres and drops to Kandersteg in the Bernese Oberland, though only walkers and a cable car can use it. The cliff path, with ladders and ledges, was an important trade route for centuries, and it still looks improbable.

The Rhône valley below is warm and dry, with vineyards on the sunny slopes producing fendant and other wines, and the landscape feels more Mediterranean than Alpine in summer. The villages of the Valais are built of dark timber and stone, and the people speak German in the upper valley and French in the lower.

Fuel is easy in Leuk, a small town in the valley, and in nearby Susten. Leukerbad itself is largely car-free in the centre, with parking at the edge, and it has restaurants serving raclette, cheese and local wine. The road is open all year, but in winter, snow chains may be needed. Autumn is especially beautiful, with the vines turning gold and the first snow on the peaks.
t.thun@46.2,7.4:
The dot is at Sion, the capital of the Valais, a town of about twenty-eight thousand in the broad, sunny Rhône valley, and nowhere near the lake and castle at Thun that the label suggests. Sion is Switzerland's driest region in many places, protected by the high Alps on both sides, and it grows grapes, apricots and asparagus in a climate that feels almost Mediterranean. Two great rocky hills rise from the town floor, each crowned by a medieval fortress.

The hill of Valère carries a fortified church that contains what is said to be the oldest playable pipe organ in the world, dating to around 1435, and in summer a festival of organ music uses it. The neighbouring hill, Tourbillon, has the ruins of a castle built as a bishop's residence in the thirteenth century and burned in 1788. A climb up to either gives a wide view of the valley, with the Rhône winding below and the glaciers at the head of the side valleys glinting in the distance.

Valais wines have a character of their own. Fendant, made from the Chasselas grape, is light and refreshing, and Cornalin and Humagne are rarer local reds. Many cellars offer tastings, and the vineyards climb in terraces up the slopes. The valley's traditional dish is raclette, melted cheese scraped over potatoes, and it tastes best after a day in the mountains.

For riders, Sion is a base for excellent passes. The road to Col du Sanetsch, a narrow dead-end road above Savièse, climbs to a high lake and a glacier view, and the Grand Saint-Bernard, the Simplon and the Nufenen are all within reach. The Val d'Hérens, east of town, is known for the earth pyramids of Euseigne, strange columns of moraine capped by boulders, and for the Hérens cattle, small black cows that fight each other in friendly contests.

Fuel is easy here, with large stations around the town, and there are cafes and restaurants of all kinds. Sion has an airport used by small planes and military aircraft, and you may hear fighter jets in the valley. Summer is hot, with temperatures above thirty degrees, so an early start suits the mountains. Winter can bring fog to the valley floor, while the passes stay in sun.
t.bern@46.3,6.9:
The label says Bern, but the dot is in the Chablais, at the lower end of the Rhône valley near Aigle and Vionnaz, about a hundred kilometres south-west of the Swiss capital. This is where the great river, having run west through the Valais, turns north toward Lake Geneva, and the landscape is a mix of broad flat farmland, steep vineyards and bare limestone peaks, the Dents du Midi, whose serrated summits dominate the horizon to the south.

Aigle is a wine town with a castle, a pleasant old centre and slopes covered in Chasselas vines, which produce a crisp white wine that sells best in the cafes of the region. The castle, a handsome medieval fortress, now houses a museum of wine and the vine, and its tower has a view across the valley. The town also has an unexpected role in world sport. The headquarters of the international cycling union is here, with a velodrome and training centre, so on any given day you may meet professional cyclists on the roads.

Passes lead out of the valley in several directions. The Col des Mosses and the Col de la Croix, toward Les Diablerets, climb in smooth, wide bends through forest and pasture, with views of the glaciers above. The Col du Pillon, linked to the Glacier 3000 cable car, is another good ride, with good tarmac and gentle gradients. The Rhône valley itself is flat and busy with trucks, so the real riding is up the side valleys.

Bern, the capital, is worth a visit in its own right if you pass through. The old town sits in a bend of the Aare, with arcades, fountains and the famous clock tower, the Zytglogge, and bears are kept in a park by the river. It is a quiet and comfortable city that feels very unlike a capital.

Fuel is easy in Aigle, Monthey and the valley towns. Swiss speed limits are strict, with cameras at many exits. A motorway vignette is required on the A9. The best weather is from May to October, though autumn is lovely, with the vineyards turning golden and the first snow dusting the peaks.
t.montafon overnight base@47.1,9.9:
Schruns sits at about 650 metres in the Montafon, a long valley in Vorarlberg, Austria's westernmost state, where the river Ill runs south between the Rätikon and the Silvretta ranges. It is a small town of under four thousand people, with a pointed church tower, wooden chalets and a feel of quiet prosperity, and its sister village Tschagguns lies just across the river. In winter the area is busy with skiers, and in summer with hikers and cyclists, but outside the high seasons it is peaceful, and a good place to sleep after a long day in the saddle.

Ernest Hemingway spent a winter here in 1925 and 1926, skiing and writing, and some of The Sun Also Rises was revised in the valley. The valley also has its own traditions, including a local sour cheese called Montafoner Sura Kees, which smells strong and tastes sharp and creamy, and a dialect that sounds quite different from standard German. The old mining history of the area is remembered in a small museum, and the narrow-gauge railway that runs along the valley floor is still in use.

The great attraction for riders is the Silvretta High Alpine Road, which starts at Partenen at the head of the valley and climbs in a series of about thirty hairpins to the Bielerhöhe, at 2,032 metres. At the top lies the Silvretta reservoir, with a dam and a view of glaciated peaks, and the road continues down to Galtür and Ischgl in the Paznaun valley. It is a toll road, closed in winter, and normally open from late spring to autumn depending on snow. The surface is good, and the hairpins are wide enough to be enjoyable but demanding in traffic.

The valley road itself, from Bludenz up through Vandans and Schruns, is gentle and pleasant, passing meadows and old farmhouses. Traffic is light apart from peak holiday periods, and the locals are used to motorcycles.

Fuel is easy in Schruns and Tschagguns, and there is a good choice of hotels and guesthouses, many offering secure parking for bikes. Evening meals are generous, with Käsknöpfle, a dish of cheese noodles with fried onions, a common choice. Mornings are cool and clear, so start early for the pass.
t.freudenstadt@48.5,8.4:
Freudenstadt was built to a plan. In 1599, Duke Frederick I of Württemberg laid out the town as a refuge for Protestants fleeing persecution in Austria, and the heart of it is a vast market square, one of the largest in Germany, an almost perfect square about two hundred metres on each side, with covered arcades along its edges. There was meant to be a castle in the middle, but it was never built, and the open space became the town's living room instead. The town, with about twenty-four thousand people, was almost destroyed at the end of the Second World War and rebuilt in a similar style.

It lies at about 700 metres on a high plateau at the southern end of the Black Forest Panorama Route, the B500, also known as the Schwarzwaldhochstraße. Opened in the early 1930s and one of the oldest scenic roads in Germany, it runs about sixty kilometres along the crest of the northern Black Forest from Baden-Baden, passing through dark spruce and fir forest with open views west over the Rhine plain to the Vosges. The road is wide and well surfaced, with long open bends and a series of lay-bys that make good viewpoints. The Mummelsee, a small lake that is said to be home to water sprites, lies just off the road, and the Hornisgrinde, at 1,164 metres, is the highest point on this stretch.

Weather on the ridge can be harsh, with fog, ice and snow possible from autumn to spring, and the road may be closed at times. On a clear summer day, though, it is a delight, and on weekends it fills up with riders, cyclists and tourists. Speed limits are enforced and noise restrictions are in effect on some parts, so keep a steady pace.

Fuel is easy in Freudenstadt, with stations on the main roads and supermarkets in the town. Baiersbronn, a few kilometres away, is known for having an unusually large number of top-rated restaurants for a village, so you can eat very well here if your wallet allows. For something simpler, a slice of Black Forest cherry cake and a coffee at a bakery in the market square will do.

The best time is June to October, with September especially clear.
t.isere valley@45.6,5.3:
Bourgoin-Jallieu and Domarin lie in the Nord-Isère, the broad rolling country between Lyon and Grenoble known as the Bas-Dauphiné, where the landscape is of low hills, maize fields, ponds and small woods. It is an unglamorous corner, a place that most people see only from the motorway, but it has its own quiet pleasures. Bourgoin-Jallieu is a town of about twenty-three thousand that grew rich on textile printing, and old mills and workers' housing still line some of its streets.

Behind you, the day has probably been spent in the Isère valley and the Belledonne range, one of the great mountain walls of the French Alps. The Isère flows from the high Tarentaise toward Grenoble through a broad valley of orchards, poplars and walnut groves, and the Belledonne, to the east, rises to more than 2,900 metres, with a long ridge of jagged rock. The roads that climb into it, through villages like Les Sept Laux, are narrow and steep, and offer views across the valley to the Chartreuse and Vercors.

The Dauphiné has a character of its own. The region is known for walnuts, a protected product called Noix de Grenoble, and for gratin dauphinois, a dish of potatoes baked in cream that is a classic of French cooking. It has also long been a land of independent spirits, and the famous Day of the Tiles, in 1788, when the people of Grenoble threw roof tiles at royal troops, is regarded as a prelude to the Revolution.

The riding in the Nord-Isère is straightforward and relaxed. Roads are quiet, with gentle curves, and run through villages with old stone farmhouses and big barns. Speed cameras are common around larger towns, and traffic is heavy near Bourgoin and the L'Isle-d'Abeau new town. In summer, the maize stands high and the roads feel tunnel-like, so watch for tractors at junctions.

Fuel is easy at Bourgoin-Jallieu, with supermarkets and stations on the ring road, and bakeries and cafes in the centre. A simple lunch in a village restaurant, with the plat du jour and a quarter-litre of wine, is a reliable pleasure.
t.beaujolais dawn@45.9,5.1:
Dagneux and Béligneux are villages on the plateau north-east of Lyon, called the Côtière, a long terrace above the Rhône valley where the land breaks away in a steep slope toward the river. From the edge of the escarpment, the view stretches over the plain and, on a clear day, to the Alps on the horizon. The dot sits above the Rhône, at the edge of the Dombes, a country of ponds and woods that begins just to the north.

The ride is called Beaujolais Dawn, and the name tells you what it is about. The Beaujolais is the wine region north-west of Lyon, on the other side of the Saône, where granite hills are carpeted with Gamay vines, and the villages are built from a soft, golden limestone that gives them a warm glow. The Pierres Dorées, as the area of golden-stone villages is called, are among the prettiest in France, and the wine, made from Gamay, is light, fruity and meant to be drunk young. Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November, is a national ritual.

Starting before sunrise has rewards. The mist lies in the valleys, the vineyards are silver with dew, and the first light turns the stone of the villages to honey. The roads in the Beaujolais are narrow and winding, with tight bends, short climbs and views of the vines, and there is almost no traffic early in the morning. In harvest time, from late August to September, tractors and trailers laden with grapes fill the roads, and the smell of fermenting must hangs in the air.

Coming back toward Lyon, the way crosses the plateau of the Côtière, with straight roads through fields of maize and wheat. Traffic builds up near Lyon, and the roads around Montluel and Miribel can be heavy at commuter hours. Cameras are common.

Fuel is easy here, with stations at the large supermarkets and in the nearby towns, and bakeries open early. A Lyonnais breakfast, with a coffee and a croissant, or a more substantial bouchon lunch with sausage and a glass of local wine, is a good reward after a morning ride.
t.pilat ridge@45.8,5.2:
The Rhône is the main character here. Pilat, the ridge in the ride's name, is on the other side of Lyon altogether, so this is an end of day well away from the hills.

The roads are flat and quiet, and the interest lies in the setting. The river has been tamed here by canals and hydroelectric works, but the old braided channels and wooded islands survive and are a nature reserve, with herons, kingfishers and in winter large flocks of ducks. Beyond the plain, to the east, the escarpment of the Balmes Dauphinoises rises as a low, wooded line, and a few of its little roads make a pleasant detour if you have energy left. The surface is generally good, bends are gentle, and a spring evening here is cool and smells of wet earth and river mud.

History is quietly present. The Rhône was a trade route since Roman times, and the town of Crémieu, a few kilometres east on the edge of the Isle Crémieu plateau, preserves a medieval market hall and ruined fortifications that are worth a look. The villages here have the typical Dauphiné pisé, rammed earth walls, in older farm buildings, a building style that is unusual and unexpectedly beautiful in the late light.

Fuel is the point to plan. These villages are small, so the usual choice is Tignieu, about nine kilometres away, which is a town of over five thousand and has stations and supermarkets. Saint-Maurice-de-Gourdans is large enough to have a bakery and a bar, and is a good place for a coffee or a sandwich. Lyon's eastern ring road and the A42 motorway are not far away, so the final run back to the city is easy.

As an ending, it is an unglamorous, peaceful place, a long way from the ridge in the name but pleasant in its own right. If the weather is clear, it is worth stopping on a riverbank, turning off the engine, and listening to the water.
t.vanoise gateway@45.8,5.2:
This is the Isle Crémieu area, the low limestone plateau that pushes the river into a wide bend east of Lyon, and the landscape of fields, gravel pits, poplars and small villages has an unhurried feel.

After a long day returning from the Vanoise gateway, it is a calm place to arrive. Roads are flat, with long straights and occasional bends where they follow the river or the edge of the plateau. Surfaces are generally decent, and traffic is light except around the main road to Lyon and the autoroute junctions. If you have time, the plateau roads to the east are among the nicest in the area, with farms, stone walls and views across the Rhône valley to the Alps on a clear day. Spring and early autumn have the best light, and morning mist often lies in the river valley.

The Rhône here has a mixed history. It was a Roman and medieval trade route, and the old channels and islands are now a protected nature area, home to beavers, herons and many kinds of dragonfly. Crémieu, a short ride away, is a small medieval town with a market hall, old gates and a ruined priory, and it is worth a short stop for its atmosphere alone. The villages around here have a number of old farms built from rammed earth, which glows a golden brown in the late sun.

For fuel, the choice is Tignieu, which has stations and supermarkets, or the larger service areas along the Lyon road. Loyettes and Saint-Romain have bakeries and a bar or two, and both are small enough to be sleepy in the afternoon, especially on Mondays. The riverbank at Loyettes is a pleasant place for a sit-down, with shade and the sound of water.

When the ride ends on an evening like this, with the sun low over the fields and the Alps a pale shape in the east, there is a quiet satisfaction in it that no pass can match.
t.chartreuse forest@45.5,5.2:
Cattle graze here in a landscape that few tourists see. The hills are low, the villages are small and the sky is big, a very different world from the limestone cliffs of the Chartreuse that gave the ride its name.

The roads are slow, quiet and curvy in a gentle, rural way. They follow ridges and cross shallow valleys, with bends that are tight enough to keep you awake and not so tight as to be dangerous. The surface is usually fine, though farm traffic leaves mud on the road in wet weather. The area is sometimes called the Terres Froides, the cold lands, because of its heavy clay soil and chilly winters, and the mist that lies in the hollows on an October morning explains the name. In spring and early summer, the hedges are full of flowers and the air smells of hay.

Local history is rooted in farming. The old Bonnevaux forest nearby was a medieval monastic estate, and the Cistercians who settled here cleared and managed the land for centuries. Bourgoin-Jallieu, an old textile town, printed cloth for the whole of France in the nineteenth century, and its museum tells the story of the trade. The villages have large stone farms and old churches, and a number of châteaux hidden among the trees.

For fuel, Bourgoin-Jallieu is the nearest town of any size, with stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and the larger village of Saint-Jean-de-Bournay lies closer. Champier and Châtonnay have bakeries and small shops, but you should not rely on them late in the day or on Sundays. A local walnut cake or a plate of cheese from a village shop is a good snack, as the Isère region is known for its walnuts and for Saint-Marcellin cheese.

As a finish, it is gentle and unpretentious, with open skies and quiet lanes that let the day end slowly.
t.rapperswil@47.2,8.8:
Rapperswil sits at the eastern end of Lake Zürich, where a long wooden footbridge crosses the water to Hurden on the far shore, and it calls itself the Rose Town for the thousands of rose bushes that bloom in the gardens beside its castle. The old town climbs a small hill capped by a medieval castle with three towers, and its lanes are a mix of arcaded houses, small squares and lakeside terraces, with a view over the lake to the mountains. The lake here is about four hundred metres above sea level, and the air feels mild and soft.

The castle has a curious history. In the nineteenth century, Polish exiles who had fled their country after the failed uprisings of the 1830s and 1860s made Rapperswil their home, and in 1870 they founded a Polish National Museum in the castle, which housed Poland's treasures during the years when the country did not exist as a state. The collection returned to Warsaw in 1927. A column in the castle courtyard and a small museum still recall the connection, and the town has retained a quiet affection for Poland.

The wooden bridge across the lake, the Holzsteg, is a pilgrim path as well, part of the Way of St James that leads from the east of Europe to Santiago, and the original crossing dates back centuries. In recent times it has been rebuilt for walkers and cyclists, and the stroll across it at sunset is one of the nicest things to do in the area. The Seedamm, an embankment carrying the road and railway, runs alongside it.

For riders, Rapperswil is a gateway to the quiet hills of the Zürich Oberland and the Linth plain. The main roads around the lake are busy, but the lanes up toward Pfäffikon and the Etzel, or north toward Hombrechtikon, offer gentle bends, farmland and views of the lake. Rapperswil-Jona has over thirty thousand people, so fuel, cafés and shops are never far away, and parking for motorcycles is available near the old town.

Visit the Kinderzoo, the zoo founded by the Knie circus family, which keeps elephants and sea lions that spend winters here. A rose-garden stroll in June and a lake-side coffee are all you really need.
t.lago maggiore evening base@46.2,8.8:
Locarno sits at the northern tip of Lake Maggiore, at about two hundred metres above sea level, and the lake itself, at roughly a hundred and ninety metres, is the lowest point in Switzerland. The effect is that the air feels soft and mild, even in winter, and palm trees, camellias and magnolias grow along the promenade, a startling sight for anyone who has just ridden down from the snow of the Gotthard. Ticino is Swiss, but it is also Italian in its language, its food and its pace, and the evening here has a distinctly Mediterranean rhythm.

The Piazza Grande, the long arcaded square in the middle of town, is the centre of life, and in August the huge screen that appears there for the Locarno Film Festival, which began in 1946, draws thousands of people to watch films under the stars. Above the town, the sanctuary of Madonna del Sasso, founded in the late fifteenth century after a vision of the Virgin, clings to a rock with a view over the lake, and can be reached by funicular or a stepped path through chapels. Along the shore, Ascona, a small, pretty town of pastel houses and lakeside cafés, was once a haven for artists, writers and dreamers, and it still has a bohemian charm.

For a rider, the arrival is a pleasure, because after the long climb and descent of the alpine passes the road drops into warmth and a landscape of vines, chestnut woods and stone villages. In the evening, the lake road and the winding lanes of the nearby valleys, such as the Centovalli, are quiet and beautiful. Traffic in the town centre can be slow on summer evenings, with tourists and local traffic crowding the narrow streets, and parking is tight, so plan to leave the bike in a secure place.

Locarno and its neighbours, Muralto and Minusio, have a full range of services, with fuel, repair shops, supermarkets and many hotels, and there is no shortage of choice for the night. Book ahead in July and August and during the film festival.

For supper, find a grotto, a traditional Ticinese restaurant, for polenta, risotto or a plate of local cured meats, with a glass of Merlot, the region's signature red wine.
t.andermatt overnight option@46.6,8.6:
Andermatt is a mountain village at about fourteen hundred metres, in the Urseren valley, a high, wide, treeless basin where several of the great alpine passes meet. The Gotthard heads south to Ticino, the Furka goes west to the Valais, and the Oberalp leads east to Graubünden, and the village sits at the crossing, like a small hub at the centre of a big wheel. The source of the Reuss river is just above, and the water flows north through the dramatic Schöllenen gorge, where the Teufelsbrücke, the Devil's Bridge, crosses the torrent in a spray of mist.

The area has been a transit point for centuries. The Schöllenen gorge, once almost impassable, was opened to traffic by a bridge in the thirteenth century, which made the Gotthard route a major link between northern and southern Europe. A legend says that the devil built the first bridge in return for the soul of the first creature to cross, and that the locals tricked him by sending a goat. In 1799, a Russian army under General Suvorov fought its way through the gorge against the French in one of the most extraordinary episodes of the Napoleonic wars, and a monument carved into the rock commemorates it. The Swiss army has used Andermatt as a fortress for generations, with tunnels and bunkers hidden in the hills, and the village still has a military feel.

More recently, Andermatt has been remade as a luxury resort, with new hotels, apartments and a revived ski area, and the old centre retains its traditional wooden houses. For a rider staying overnight, it is a convenient base for the three passes, with the Tremola, the cobbled old road of the Gotthard, waiting on the Ticino side of the pass. Nights at this height are cold, even in summer, and frost is possible in spring and autumn, so pack warm clothes. The passes are closed in winter, usually from late October to May.

The village has a few shops and restaurants, but fuel can be limited, so arrive with a reasonable tank, and book accommodation ahead in the high season. Altdorf, on the northern side of the gorge, is the nearest larger town, about twenty-seven kilometres away, with a full range of services.

Have a bowl of hot soup and a plate of Alpine cheese at the end of the day, and be glad of the thick blankets.
t.gletsch historic junction@46.6,8.4:
At Gletsch, the Rhône is still a young stream, trickling from the foot of a glacier that once filled the whole basin. The hamlet sits at about seventeen hundred and sixty metres, in a bleak, beautiful hollow where two of Switzerland's great passes diverge: the Furka heads east toward Andermatt, and the Grimsel runs north to Meiringen, while the Rhône valley falls away to the south-west. A grand old hotel from the nineteenth century stands at the junction, its pale façade looking oddly large against the bare mountains, and for a few months each year it is the only sign of human life for miles.

The Rhône Glacier, which gives the river its source, has been retreating for more than a century. In the 1800s, it reached down almost to the hamlet, and visitors came in carriages to admire it. Today it ends high above, and large sections are covered with white fleece blankets in summer to slow the melting. An ice grotto cut into the glacier can be visited by a short walk from the Furka road, and lets you stand inside the blue ice, though the tunnel has to be recut each year as the ice moves.

Film fans will know the place. The Furka Pass was the setting for a car chase in the James Bond film Goldfinger in 1964, with an Aston Martin on the hairpins above the glacier, and the hotel appears in the sequence. Steam railway enthusiasts come too: the Furka Steam Railway, a restored mountain line, runs on summer days between Realp and Oberwald, passing near Gletsch.

The riding is the reason to come. The Furka, at about 2,430 metres, has a long series of hairpins on both sides, with a good surface and big views. The Grimsel, at about 2,160 metres, has wider bends, huge dams and turquoise reservoirs. Both are open only in summer, usually from June to October, and snow can close them at any time, so check before you set off. At this altitude, temperatures can be close to freezing even in July, with wind and sudden storms, so carry warm gear and keep gloves in the top box.

The hotel serves meals, and a cup of coffee on its terrace, with the glacier in sight, is a fine reward.
t.pilatus view road@47.0,8.3:
Pilatus is a mountain with a legend, and the road that skirts its flank gives you a different view of it than the one from Lucerne. The peak, 2,128 metres at its highest, is a jagged limestone ridge with a long, flat top that looks, from the north, like a sleeping dragon. Medieval stories said that the spirit of Pontius Pilate haunted the mountain's lake, and the authorities of Lucerne banned climbing it for centuries, in case the disturbance brought a storm. The name may in fact come from an old word for a cloud-covered mountain, but the legend is better.

Above you, the cogwheel railway that climbs Pilatus from Alpnachstad is the steepest in the world, with a gradient of up to forty-eight per cent, and has been running since 1889. Gondolas and cable cars also run from Kriens, and a visit to the summit gives a vast view over Lake Lucerne and the central Alps. In clear weather the display of peaks and lakes is magnificent.

Riding the lanes around the mountain is a pleasure of a quieter kind. The road toward Glaubenberg climbs from Sarnen and Alpnach through moorland and spruce forest, a landscape of raised bogs and wet meadows that is protected moorland next to the Entlebuch biosphere reserve, with long, open curves, little traffic and a surface that is usually good. The pass at Glaubenberg, at about fifteen hundred metres, is a lovely road to ride on a weekday morning. In spring, the high sections can have snow or mud, and cows wander freely, so keep an eye out.

For fuel, Hergiswil, about four kilometres away, and Alpnach have stations and supermarkets, and the shore of Lake Lucerne has restaurants. Hergiswil is also known for its glass factory, where you can watch glassblowers at work.

Look for the view of Pilatus from the south in the evening, when the setting sun lights the cliffs a deep red.
t.rorschach@47.5,9.5:
Rorschach sits on the south shore of Lake Constance, the big, shallow, sea-like lake where Switzerland, Germany and Austria meet, at about four hundred metres above sea level. It is a small port town with a promenade, a harbour, and the look of a place that was once busier than it is now. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries it was the centre of a linen trade, and later of embroidery, and the grain trade passed through it too. The Kornhaus, a big granary built in the 1740s by the monks of St. Gallen, stands on the waterfront with a baroque gable, and it is the town's emblem.

The lake has its own character. Called the Bodensee in German, it is large enough to have waves, storms and a horizon, and steamers and ferries connect the towns on its shores, so you can cross to Lindau in Germany or Bregenz in Austria in an hour or so. On a fine day the Alps rise behind the Austrian shore, and a long, gentle light lies on the water. In summer, the promenade fills with walkers, cyclists, ice-cream eaters and sailing enthusiasts, and boats bob in the harbour.

For riders, Rorschach is a good place to begin or end a loop through the hills of eastern Switzerland. A rack railway climbs from the town to Heiden, an old spa resort high above the lake, and the road up beside it is a fine ride through orchards and meadows, with views over the water. To the south the Appenzell hills offer wavy farmland, small villages and a chain of lovely roads toward the Säntis. To the east, the roads cross the Rhine plain into Austria and the Bregenzerwald, and from there on to the German Alpine Road.

Rorschach has about nine thousand people, and Goldach next door is the same size again, so there is no shortage of petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés. The lakeside restaurants serve perch and whitefish, which are the local favourites, with a glass of Swiss or Austrian wine.

Cross-border formalities are easy, but carry your passport, and be aware that Austria charges for road use in some places and requires a vignette on motorways. Check the current rules before you ride across.
t.schweigen rechtenbach@49.1,8.0:
The German Wine Road starts at a gateway, and this is the gateway: the Deutsches Weintor, a stone arch built in the 1930s that spans the road at the border between Germany and France. Schweigen-Rechtenbach is the southernmost village in the Palatinate, its vineyards running right up to the frontier, and the French town of Wissembourg, with some nine thousand people, lies less than two kilometres away. The Weinstraße, the first signposted wine route in Germany, was opened in 1935, and its length is about eighty-five kilometres.

The countryside is a long, sunny strip between the Palatinate Forest and the Rhine plain, where the hills fall into a band of warm, sheltered slopes. Vines cover almost everything, with sandstone villages tucked between them and small chestnut woods on the high ground. In March the almond trees blossom pink, early for Germany, and in October the leaves turn red and gold, which many people think is the best time to ride. The sunshine here is among the most reliable in the country, though summer can be hot and the light flat at midday.

The road itself is mostly a gentle, flowing country road, going through villages and over small rises, with the odd hairpin up a vineyard slope. Don't expect adrenaline; expect pleasure, with a pause at every second village for coffee or a glass of Riesling, depending on how serious your riding day is. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and during wine festivals, especially in autumn, when tractors and coaches clog the lanes.

Fuel is easy. Wissembourg has stations and shops, as do the larger Palatinate towns a little further north, though small villages like Schweigen-Rechtenbach itself have little. Local specialities include Saumagen, a kind of stuffed pig stomach that the former chancellor Helmut Kohl famously served to visitors, and a light, sharp new wine called Federweißer in the autumn. Park under the gate, take a photograph, and start the road north.
t.bockenheim@49.6,8.2:
The northern end of the German Wine Road is Bockenheim, a village of around two thousand people in the Leiningerland, where the vineyards slope gently down towards the Rhine plain. It makes sense that it should be the gate, because here the hills of the Palatinate flatten out, and the long, warm ridge that has carried you north finally gives way to broader country. A small gateway and a modest museum mark the start, and the villagers are proud of both.

Wine has been made here for centuries, and the village is a picture of the Palatinate: pastel half-timbered houses, steep-roofed barns, arched courtyards with tables set for wine tasting, and a little church. Local growers make Riesling, white Burgundy varieties and Dornfelder, a dark red grape that is a recent German favourite, and many of them sell directly from the courtyard. In September and October, the grape harvest brings tractors loaded with fruit and the sweet smell of crushing must across the village.

The riding is easy and relaxed after the more winding southern sections. Roads in the area are well-surfaced, with low curves through vineyards and small rises, and you can see long distances over the plain on a clear day, with the Rhine valley a faint line on the horizon. Cyclists share the lanes, especially at weekends, and tractors are common during harvest.

For fuel and larger shops, Grünstadt, a short distance south-west, has the nearest range of services, and the villages of Kindenheim and Obrigheim have bakeries and the usual small shops. Worms, the old Rhine city, lies not far to the east, with a great Romanesque cathedral and a place in the history of Martin Luther, who appeared before the Imperial Diet there in 1521. If you are ending the ride here, find a courtyard, order a glass of local wine if you are not riding again, and let the day settle. Otherwise, ask for a coffee and a slice of onion tart, a seasonal classic in the Palatinate.
t.dolomites sella@45.2,9.6:
This part of southern Lombardy, near Orio Litta and Ospedaletto Lodigiano, lies on the great plain of the Po, a few kilometres short of the river itself. It is a flat, damp, rather secretive landscape of poplar rows, irrigated fields of maize and rice, and long straight lanes, with old farmhouses and church towers breaking the horizon. In winter fog settles over it for days at a time, and in summer the air is thick and hot, buzzing with cicadas and mosquitoes.

What makes the area interesting is that a medieval pilgrim route passes through it. The Via Francigena, the road from Canterbury to Rome, crosses the Po not far from here, and since the Middle Ages, pilgrims have come this way, many of them stopping at the chapels and hospices that dotted the route. At Orio Litta, a baroque villa with a formal garden stands on the edge of the village, and the Po can be crossed by a small ferry at certain points. In the west, a lone hill, San Colombano al Lambro, rises out of the plain to nearly a hundred and fifty metres, the only hill with vineyards in the whole Lombard plain, and its wines have been made since Roman times.

This is the end of a ride from the Dolomites, and its character is as flat as you could imagine. The roads are straight and quiet, with little traffic in the evenings, and the main hazards are tractors, fog and the occasional cyclist. The Via Emilia, the old Roman highway, runs a few kilometres to the south, and the motorway to Piacenza runs along the plain. Ride gently, enjoy the long light and be ready for mist after dark.

San Colombano al Lambro, with nearly seven thousand people, is the nearest sizeable town, about six kilometres away, with fuel and shops. The villages nearby are small, with a bar and a bakery, and a few farm restaurants serve boiled meats and risotto. A glass of San Colombano red is a modest, pleasant local wine, and a plate of salami from the nearby farms goes well with it. Go slowly and look for the herons in the ditches.
t.lake@45.6,9.3:
That park, laid out in the early nineteenth century around the Villa Reale, the royal residence of the Austrian and later Italian rulers, is the largest walled park in Europe, with meadows, woods and the Lambro river running through it. In the middle of it, the Monza racetrack, built in 1922, is known as the Temple of Speed, and the Italian Grand Prix has been held here for most of the history of Formula One.

If the engine is on your mind, you are in the right place. On race weekends, in early September, the whole area shakes with sound, and even on ordinary days you can sometimes hear cars and bikes testing. The town of Monza has a cathedral with the Iron Crown, said to hold a nail from the cross, with which the kings of Italy were crowned, and the whole region has long been home to craftsmen, especially furniture makers, whose workshops line the roads.

The ride from Lake Como ends here, and the way in is classic Lombardy: the road drops from the hills of Lecco through a continuous string of small towns, with traffic lights, roundabouts and warehouses, and the whole thing seems to run together. It is slow, but tolerable, and there are quieter ways, such as the cycle route along the Lambro. In winter, fog hangs in the valley, and on summer evenings the traffic builds as people return from the lakes.

You are among eleven thousand people in Biassono and seven and a half thousand in Sovico, so petrol stations and bars are everywhere. The restaurants nearby serve polenta, risotto and braised meats. If you have time, the park is worth an hour; motorcycles are not allowed on its paths, but you can walk or cycle, and the shade of the old trees is welcome after a long ride. Leave the bike in a car park at the edge, and enjoy the quiet.
t.jeju volcanic island and lava tubes@33.5:
Jeju is a volcano that has decided to be an island. Rising from the sea about ninety kilometres south of the Korean mainland, it is crowned by Hallasan, an extinct volcano of 1,947 metres, the highest peak in South Korea, with a crater lake at the top and a skirt of about three hundred smaller cones scattered across the landscape. UNESCO listed the island's volcanic landscapes and lava tubes in 2007, and the combination of black basalt, green fields and blue sea is the island's signature.

The island has its own culture, and a distinctive look. Walls of black volcanic stone divide the fields and edge the roads, protecting crops from the wind, and stone grandfather statues with bulging eyes stand guard at the roadside. The haenyeo, women divers who plunge into the cold sea without breathing apparatus to gather shellfish, are a living tradition recognised by UNESCO, and some of them sell their catch at small stalls by the shore. The local pork, from black pigs, and the tangerines, grown on every slope, are the island's food. The weather is changeable, windy and often misty.

For a rider, Jeju is a joy. The coastal road circles the island, with views of sea and cliffs, and the mountain roads that climb toward Hallasan run through forests of deciduous and evergreen trees, with long curves and frequent clouds. Traffic can be heavy near the city of Jeju, which has over four hundred thousand people, and tourist buses crowd the main sites, so get an early start. Winds on the coast can be strong, and rain may arrive suddenly, with fog on the higher roads.

Carry a rain jacket, and respect the speed limits, since cameras are common. Spring brings yellow rapeseed flowers, and autumn brings silver grass on the volcanic cones. Take time to look at the stone walls and the way the light changes.
Underneath the green hills on the north side of Jeju run some of the longest lava tubes in the world, and Manjanggul is the best known. When the volcano of Geomunoreum erupted, in the distant past, rivers of molten rock flowed north toward the sea, and as the surface cooled and hardened, the liquid inside drained away, leaving long hollow tunnels. The Manjanggul tube runs for more than seven kilometres, and the section open to visitors, about a kilometre, is vast, wide enough for a bus and as tall as a house.

Inside, the air is cool and damp, around eleven degrees even in summer, so bring a jacket. The floor is uneven, rocky and wet, and the walls are streaked with ridges where the lava once flowed, with stalactites of lava hanging from the ceiling. At the end of the route, a lava column nearly eight metres tall stands in the dark, one of the largest in the world. Bats live in the deeper reaches, and the whole place has a hushed, ancient feeling that is hard to forget. Helmets are sometimes provided, and sturdy shoes are essential.

Outside, the land around the caves is the Gotjawal, a tangled forest growing on rough lava terrain, where ferns, vines and evergreen trees thrive in the cracks and hollows. It is a natural reservoir, since rain seeps through the porous rock and feeds the springs that supply the island with water. The ground is too rough to farm, which is why the forest has survived.

The riding here is easy and pleasant. Minor roads run through farmland and woodland, with stone walls and tangerine orchards, and the surface is generally good. There is little traffic outside the peak season, and the views of the coast and the hills are fine. Jeju City, about nineteen kilometres away, has fuel, food and everything else, so fill up there. Check the cave's opening hours and closure days before you go, since they vary by season, and allow about an hour for the visit.
The fourth stop in the Geomunoreum system is a quiet one, tucked away in the middle of the island, on the slopes below Hallasan. The volcano's name means roughly the dark hill, and its eruption sent lava flowing down the northern flank to the sea, creating a network of tubes that now form part of the UNESCO site. Not all of them are open to the public, and the quieter ones, in the forest, are of most interest to the hardy, since they preserve the strange, damp, silent world of the island's underground.

The mountain above is the other attraction. Hallasan National Park offers trails through zones of vegetation, from broadleaf forest at the bottom to bamboo grass and dwarf conifers near the top, and a crater lake, Baengnokdam, lies at the summit. The hike to the top is long and strenuous, but on a clear day the view over the island and the sea is excellent. In winter, snow covers the upper slopes and attracts people to the sledding hills, and deer roam in the forest.

For motorcyclists, the road known as the 1100 Road, which crosses the island at a height of about eleven hundred metres, is a classic. It climbs from both sides in a series of gentle curves through woodland, and at its highest point there is a wetland that is protected under the Ramsar convention, with a boardwalk and a rest area. In autumn the trees are red and gold, and in winter ice and snow can close the road, so check conditions. Fog is common and visibility can drop quickly.

The nearest large town is Jeju City, twenty-one kilometres away, with fuel and all services, and there are no stations on the mountain roads, so fill before you climb. Carry a warm layer, since the temperature on the high road can be ten degrees lower than on the coast. Try a bowl of noodles in a roadside restaurant, and watch the clouds roll over the cones.
t.vianden@49.9,6.2:
Vianden is one of those towns that looks like a scene from a children's book, and the castle is the reason. It stands on a rocky spur above the Our River, in the north-east of Luxembourg, a pile of towers, halls and chapels that grew over several centuries from the eleventh to the fourteenth, and was once the seat of the counts of Vianden. It fell into ruin in the nineteenth century and was restored from the 1970s, and today you can walk through its great halls, kitchens and armouries with a very good sense of how a medieval noble household worked.

The town below is small, with about sixteen hundred residents, a single steep main street of old houses and cafes, and a bridge over the Our. Victor Hugo spent time here in exile in 1871 and lived in a house beside the bridge, now a small museum, and his drawings of the castle show the romance he felt. A chairlift rises behind the town to a viewpoint, and the view of the castle and the winding river from the top is the most photographed in the country.

For motorcyclists, the surroundings are a delight. The valley of the Our has smooth, flowing roads with gentle curves along the river, with forests and meadows on both sides, and Germany is just across the water. The Mullerthal region to the south, with its sandstone gorges, is called Little Switzerland, and its lanes wind among rocks and beech woods. Weekends bring many riders, and the pace is relaxed. The nearby pumped storage power station, one of Europe's largest, sits inside the hillside, and the reservoir above is a surprising bit of engineering.

Vianden has limited fuel, so the practical choice is Diekirch, a town of about six thousand, eight kilometres away, with stations and shops. Luxembourg is compact, and fuel is usually cheaper than in neighbouring countries. Try judd mat gaardebounen, smoked pork with broad beans, the national dish, and a glass of local Riesling or a Diekirch beer. Spring and early autumn are lovely, and in winter the castle is dusted with snow.
t.saint michel de maurienne@45.2,6.5:
Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne is a working town, with no pretensions, in the bottom of the Maurienne valley, and its great virtue for a rider is its position: it is the foot of the road to the Galibier. The town of just over three thousand people lies at around 700 metres on the river Arc, with train tracks, factories and a long industrial history behind it, and the valley walls rise steeply on both sides. Valloire, the nearest village on the climb, is a pleasant mountain resort a little way beyond the first col.

As a starting point, it is hard to beat. There are petrol stations, bakeries, supermarkets and small hotels, and it is easy to get away. The road climbs first to the Col du Telegraphe, at around 1,566 metres, through forest in a series of regular bends, then dips to Valloire before the long, open climb to the Col du Galibier, at about 2,642 metres, one of the great passes of the Alps. The road is well surfaced, with sweeping views, though wind, cold and sudden weather changes at the top are real hazards. It is closed by snow for much of the year, usually from late autumn to early summer, so check before you go. Early starts are rewarded with cool air and light traffic, since cyclists and campervans crowd the road later.

The valley has a rich and often hard history. For centuries it was a route between France and Italy, used by merchants, armies and pilgrims, and the local people farmed steep pastures and mined in the mountains. Industry arrived in the nineteenth century, with hydroelectric power and aluminium and chemical works, and the railway to Italy through the Frejus tunnel ran through the valley and made Saint-Michel an important junction. Today its role is quieter, but the railway still hums.

The Galibier has become a legend among cyclists, since the Tour de France first crossed it in 1911, and a monument near the summit honours Henri Desgrange, the race's founder. The Telegraphe takes its name from a fort and an optical telegraph station built on the summit in the nineteenth century. Nature changes steadily as you climb, from valley woodland to alpine meadows, rock and snow, with marmots whistling among the stones and choughs wheeling above.

Fill the tank here, pack layers, and enjoy the climb.
t.pfaffikersee warm up@47.3,8.8:
The Pfaffikersee is the quiet one of the Zurich Oberland lakes, a long, narrow stretch of water in a hollow left by a glacier, ringed with reeds and meadows and almost free of the big villas and motorboats that crowd its neighbours. It lies at about 537 metres, between Pfaffikon and Wetzikon, and the lakeshore is largely protected as a nature reserve. As a warm-up for the climb to Hulftegg, it is ideal: flat, gentle and just far enough from Zurich to feel like countryside, with Pfaffikon, a town of about eight thousand people, two kilometres away for fuel, bakeries and coffee.

The riding on the flats is easy and civilised. Narrow roads run between meadows and farm buildings, past the reed beds and the little harbours, and it is a good time to let tyres and engine come up to temperature before the hills. After the lake, the route climbs east into the Tosstal, through forest and farmland, with tighter bends and short, steep ramps toward the Hulftegg, a modest pass with a reputation among Swiss riders for its twisty, narrow road. Traffic is light in the early morning, and weekends bring cyclists, walkers and Sunday drivers. Swiss speed limits are low and radar traps are frequent, so keep an eye on the signs.

The shore has a remarkable history. At Robenhausen, on the south side of the lake, archaeologists have found the remains of prehistoric villages built on wooden piles over the water, some of them more than five thousand years old, and the site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for pile dwellings around the Alps. At Irgenhausen, near Pfaffikon, stand the remains of a late Roman fort, from the late Roman period, built to guard the road, and its walls are visible in a quiet meadow. People have been drawn to this water for thousands of years.

The reserve is rich in wildlife. Reed warblers, grebes and kingfishers nest on the shore, and the wet meadows are home to orchids and dragonflies, while in autumn the mist rising from the lake is magical. The air smells of wet grass and reeds, and on a still morning the water is like glass.

Fill the tank in Pfaffikon, bring a jacket for the early morning, and use the lake as a quiet start.
t.albis ridge warm up@47.3,8.5:
The Albis is the long, wooded ridge that rises between the Sihl valley and the Reppisch valley south of Zurich, and the road over it has been the traditional way from the city toward Zug and central Switzerland for centuries. The ride begins near Langnau am Albis, a town of about seven thousand people on the eastern flank, with the Albis Pass, at about 790 metres, a few kilometres up the hill. It is an excellent warm-up: just enough bends and gradient to get the tyres warm without asking for much, and close enough to the city for an after-work ride.

The road climbs from the valley through beech forest in a series of easy bends, with the ridge close on one side and views over the Sihl valley, the Zurich lake and the Alps on the other. The surface is well maintained, the corners are open, and the traffic can be dense at commuting times, with heavy flows of cars and buses and the occasional cyclist grinding up the slope. After the pass, the road drops toward the Knonauer Amt and the Reuss valley, with farmland, orchards and small villages. Speed limits are strict and cameras are common, so ride accordingly. The best conditions are on dry evenings in late spring and early autumn, when the light is gold on the forest.

The ridge has a history as a frontier. In 1799, during the Napoleonic wars, French and Russian armies fought in the area around Zurich, and the heights around the Albis were part of the lines. The old road over the pass was a major route for merchants and pilgrims. Today the Felsenegg viewpoint, on a spur near Adliswil, is a popular spot for sunset, reached by cable car, and the Uetliberg, at the northern end of the ridge, is Zurich's local mountain, with a lookout tower and a railway.

Nature on the ridge is surprisingly wild. Beyond Langnau, the Sihlwald is a former working forest that has been left to regrow and is now part of a wilderness park, with deer, foxes and a rich bird life, and the old trees there are slowly returning to a natural state. In spring the beech leaves are an unreal fresh green, and in autumn the forest glows copper. The air smells of earth and leaves, and the quiet in the woods is welcome after the city.

Fuel and food are plentiful in Langnau and the villages nearby. Bring a light waterproof, since the weather changes quickly on the ridge, and take care on damp leaves.
t.hirzel sweepers@47.2,8.6:
Hirzel is the village that sits on a shelf above Lake Zurich, between the lakeside town of Horgen and the high country toward Einsiedeln, and the road that climbs there from the water is one of the most popular afternoon rides in the canton. It is a quick succession of wide, open bends through orchards and meadows, with the lake spread out behind you and the Alps on the horizon. The ride starts and ends at these corners, which riders have named the sweepers for their smooth, generous radius. Horgen, a lakeside town of about six thousand people in its centre, lies four kilometres away, and has fuel and cafes.

The surface is excellent and the gradients are modest. This is a road for finding your rhythm, rolling on the throttle out of each bend and sweeping across the hillside, with the odd tractor to remind you that the land is working. It is also popular, so you will share it with cyclists, sports cars and other bikes, especially on sunny weekends. The road continues over the ridge to Biberbrugg and then to the Sihlsee, a long artificial lake created in the 1930s by damming the Sihl river, and one of the largest reservoirs in Switzerland. Speed limits are low and enforcement is regular, so ride with courtesy.

The destination is Einsiedeln, a small town built around its great Benedictine abbey, founded in the tenth century on the site where a hermit named Meinrad had lived. The baroque church, with its twin towers and black Madonna, has drawn pilgrims for a thousand years, and the long square in front is a place to sit and watch the world go by. The town also lies on the Way of St James, the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela. Nearby, the moor country around the Sihlsee shelters rare plants and birds, and the dam is a good spot to watch the sunset.

The landscape is a pretty mix of orchard, farm and forest. Cows with bells graze on steep fields, and in spring the cherry blossom makes the hillside white, while in autumn the beech turns copper. The air smells of grass, hay and, sometimes, woodsmoke from farmhouses. On a clear day you can see the Glarus Alps and the Rigi, and the lake below glints like a mirror.

Bring a light jacket for the evening, since the shaded slopes can be cool, and expect a busy road on summer weekends.
t.bergamo old town@45.7,9.7:
Bergamo is two cities in one: a modern lower town of boulevards, offices and shopping streets spread across the Lombard plain, and above it, on a steep spur of the foothills, the Citta Alta, a walled medieval city of cobbled lanes, towers and piazzas. The upper city is the point of this stop, a place to finish a long day and walk around while the stone cools. The city as a whole has about 114,000 people, and Orio al Serio, home of Milan's third airport, is just to the south.

For a rider, the old town is a place to be careful. The upper city is a restricted traffic zone, with limited access for vehicles, so most visitors leave the bike in a car park in the lower town and ride the funicular up the hill, which is a pleasure in its own right. The lower city is busy, with streams of traffic and plenty of fuel stations, and the approach from Milan is by fast roads across a flat, built-up plain, with the Alps appearing on a clear day as a pale line on the north. Early evening is wonderful in the upper town, when the stone glows and the crowds thin out.

The walls are the most impressive thing. Venice ruled Bergamo for more than three centuries, and its engineers built the great ring of ramparts in the sixteenth century to protect the city's border, work so fine that they are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Venetian defensive works. The city has a rich cultural life: the composer Gaetano Donizetti was born here, and the Colleoni Chapel, a Renaissance gem on the main square, is dazzling with its coloured marble. Piazza Vecchia, the heart of the upper city, is often called one of the loveliest squares in Italy, and a cafe table there is a good place to end a ride.

Food is important. Polenta is the staple of the region, served with game, mushrooms or cheese, and the local pasta, casoncelli, is stuffed with meat and topped with butter and sage. Polenta e osei, a sweet cake decorated with marzipan birds, is the city's signature dessert. A glass of local red goes with all of it.

The surrounding hills, the Bergamo Alps, rise just to the north, which makes this a natural launch point for the Dolomite road. Book a hotel in the lower town if you want easy parking, and carry a lock.
t.bregenz@47.5,9.7:
Bregenz is the Austrian end of Lake Constance, and the lake is the whole point. The Bodensee stretches out in front of the town like a small sea, flat and silver in the early light, with Germany and Switzerland on its far shores and the Alps rising right behind your shoulder. Bregenz is the capital of Vorarlberg, with around thirty thousand people, so you will find every kind of shop, fuel station and café you might need before you set off.
