It is an easy place to begin a ride and an easy place to put off beginning it.

If you have an hour, go up the Pfänder by cable car and look down on the lake and the ring of towns. Or walk the promenade to the floating stage, where the Bregenz Festival stages its opera spectacles on the water each summer, with sets built on a scale that makes a motorcycle look like a toy. The Kunsthaus, a glass box designed by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, is worth a look from the outside even if you do not fancy modern art. The old town, the Oberstadt, sits on a small hill and has the medieval gate and the tower with the onion dome that appears on every postcard.

The ride east into the Bregenzerwald is a gentle climb, which is a good way to start. The valley is the heartland of the region's alpine cheese tradition, with farms and dairies that sell directly to the public, and the roads become quieter and more curved the further in you get. The Bregenzerwald is Austrian green in its purest form: steep meadows, wooden houses with shingled fronts, and mountains that rise suddenly rather than gradually. You will pass villages known for their carpentry and their timber architecture, and stop at least once for a slice of Bergkäse and a coffee.

Traffic around Bregenz itself can be thick on summer weekends, especially when there is a festival performance in the evening, so leave early. The lake can produce its own weather, with fog in autumn and sudden afternoon gusts, so look at the sky as you pull out. Fill the tank before you leave town, since the pricing and choice are better here than in the narrow valleys, and then go and find the cheese.
t.glarus@47.0,9.1:
Glarus is a small town with an outsized sense of its own history, tucked into a narrow valley beneath the pale bulk of the Glarner Alps. It is the capital of a canton of the same name, a tiny mountainous republic where, until recent decades, the citizens met each year in the open air to vote by raised hands on the laws of the land. The town was burned to the ground in a great fire in 1861 and rebuilt on a neat grid, which is why it has a surprisingly orderly layout for a place wedged between cliffs. With about five and a half thousand people, it has fuel, supermarkets and several bakeries.

The most famous local product is Schabziger, or Ziger, a hard, green, herb-flavoured cheese made from skimmed milk and blue fenugreek, which has been exported since the Middle Ages. You grate it onto bread, potatoes or pasta, and its smell is very much an acquired taste. The valley also has a long textile history; cotton printing made the area rich in the nineteenth century, and the big old factory buildings and merchant villas remain. Above everything stands the Tödi, the highest peak in the area at over 3,600 metres, with its glaciers visible on clear days.

The Pragel and Ibergeregg loop is for riders who like their roads narrow and mountain-sized. The Pragel Pass, at about 1,550 metres, links the Klöntal valley to the Muotatal, and the road is single-lane in places, with passing bays and steep stretches, so you need patience and a light hand on the throttle. Ibergeregg, at around 1,400 metres, is wider and quicker, running down toward Schwyz through alpine pastures. Both are closed in winter and sometimes open late in spring, so check before you go.

Along the way you ride beside the Klöntalersee, a green lake that has an almost Scandinavian look, with steep forested slopes plunging into the water. Cows wander the pastures with their bells, and the farms sell cheese and yoghurt from small shelves. Mist often drifts across the passes, and the temperature can drop quickly, so carry rain gear even on a sunny morning. Glarus is where this loop ends and you can finally sit down: pick a café, order something sweet and take your time.
t.domodossola@46.1,8.3:
Domodossola is the Italian doorstep of the Simplon, a town of about eighteen thousand that sits at the junction of several Alpine valleys in the northern Piedmont, at the point where the Ossola valley opens toward Lake Maggiore. For centuries it has been a place of passage, with merchants, pilgrims and armies crossing the mountains by the Simplon road, and its old centre, built around the Piazza Mercato, still has the arcades, wooden balconies and frescoed houses of a market town. The weekly market is lively, and local cheeses, cured meats and the sweet wines of the valley are for sale.

Above the town, the Sacro Monte Calvario climbs a wooded hill in a sequence of chapels and stations, a UNESCO-listed pilgrimage route built in the seventeenth century and still a peaceful walk. The setting is lovely, with views over the rooftops and the surrounding mountains. The town is also the railway gateway to the Simplon Tunnel, which opened in 1906 and, at nearly twenty kilometres, was for decades the longest in the world.

The pass road itself was ordered by Napoleon, who wanted a way to move guns and soldiers into Italy, and was built between 1801 and 1805 by the engineer Nicolas Céard, with a great number of bridges, galleries and cuttings. It is one of the most civilised high passes in the Alps, wide, smoothly graded and well surfaced, which makes it a fine road for a touring bike. From Domodossola you head up through the Gondo gorge, a spectacular, narrow cleft with waterfalls pouring off the cliffs, then cross into Switzerland and climb to the pass at around 2,000 metres, where the old Simplon Hospice stands.

Fuel is easy in Domodossola, and cheaper on the Italian side than in Switzerland, so fill the tank before you cross. Be aware that the pass has seasonal closures, usually from late autumn to spring, though the tunnel remains open for cars on the train. The Italian approach can be warm and humid, while the pass is much cooler and often windy. Eat something local before you go, perhaps a plate of polenta with cheese, and take your time.
t.chiavenna@46.3,9.4:
Chiavenna is a town of about seven thousand people at the head of the Valchiavenna, where two great Alpine roads, the Splügen and the Maloja, split in different directions. The name is believed to come from the Latin clavis, a key, which is just what it was, the key to the passes between Lombardy and the north. Romans, medieval merchants and Habsburg troops all came this way, and the old town still has narrow streets, stone doorways and a small museum in a historic palace. The Mera river runs through the valley, cold and green.

Chiavenna is also known for its crotti, natural cellars dug into the rock where cold air flows out of the mountain through fissures, keeping the wine and cheese cool without electricity. Eating at one on a hot day is one of the best things you can do in northern Italy. The local food is hearty and warming: pizzoccheri, short buckwheat noodles served with cabbage, potato, cheese and butter, and sciatt, little fried cheese fritters, and a glass of red from the Valtellina goes with all of it. The tradition of working soapstone, carved into pots and stoves, is also a long local craft.

For riders, the Splügen road is one of the finest in the Alps, with a spectacular Italian side. From Chiavenna it climbs through the Cardinello gorge, where the old road is carved into the cliff, and the main route rises in a long sequence of hairpins to the pass at about 2,100 metres on the Swiss border. The surface is generally good, the bends are tight and regular, and the views down toward the plain are fine. On the northern side the road drops into Splügen and the Rheinwald, with a gentler pace.

The pass is closed in winter, typically from about November to May, and the weather can change suddenly, with cold, mist and snow in any month. Fuel is plentiful in Chiavenna, so fill up before you climb, and if you finish here, the old town has plenty of cafés and gelato. The air in the valley is warm, almost Mediterranean, and the chestnut trees on the hillsides remind you that this is Italy, even though the Alps tower overhead.
t.vevey@46.5,6.8:
Vevey is a lakeside town where the Alps seem to drop straight into Lake Geneva, and the light on the water can be so clear and bright that the mountains on the far side, in France, look close enough to touch. It is the capital of the Riviera vaudoise, about sixteen thousand people strong, with a long promenade, a market square lined with arcades and an air of calm prosperity. The town is the home of Nestlé, which started here in the nineteenth century, and the company's headquarters and food museum are a fixture on the waterfront.

Charlie Chaplin lived in the hills above Vevey for the last twenty-five years of his life, and a bronze statue of him stands on the lakeshore, with his cane and bowler hat. The great cultural event is the Fête des Vignerons, held roughly once a generation, with a huge pageant celebrating the winegrowers of the region, and the last edition took place in 2019. Look for the giant fork stuck in the lake, a sculpture placed there as a joke about the Alimentarium, and for the many cafés where you can have a coffee with a view.

The ride leading here follows the Lavaux, a steep terraced slope of vineyards that runs for about thirty kilometres along the lake and is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The terraces were built up by medieval monks, mostly Cistercians and Benedictines, over many centuries, and the vines, principally the white Chasselas, soak up three kinds of sun: direct, reflected from the lake and radiated from the stone walls. The roads are narrow, walled and twisting, with villages such as Cully, Lutry and Chexbres perched on the slope, and you need to ride at walking pace in some places.

Fuel, food and rest are no trouble in Vevey. The weather is mild by Swiss standards, though the wind called the bise can blow cold from the northeast in winter. Late September is the grape harvest, when the vineyard roads are busy with tractors and pickers, and a tasting in a winemaker's cellar is a fine way to end the day. Do not drink and ride, but do buy a bottle for later.
t.thun@46.8,7.6:
Thun is a town that looks as if someone designed it for a postcard and then forgot to charge for it. The Aare river flows out of the lake through the middle of town in a fast, clear, turquoise channel, past wooden covered bridges and old mills, and above it all stands the castle, a twelfth-century keep with four corner turrets built by the Zähringen dukes, its tall tower visible from many angles. At the foot of the castle hill is the Obere Hauptgasse, a street with raised pavements above the shops, which gives the town centre a quirky, two-level look. With over forty thousand people, Thun has all the services you could want.

Lake Thun itself is long, cold and deep, ringed by steep slopes, with the snowy giants of the Bernese Oberland, the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau, visible in the distance on clear days. Schadau Castle, a fanciful nineteenth-century château on the shore, sits in a park that is lovely in the evening. Paddle steamers still cross the lake, and you can often see their wake from the road. Thun is also a long-standing army town, with the Swiss military's training facilities, so you may see soldiers in town.

The ride to Lauterbrunnen follows the lake past Spiez and Interlaken, with the water on one side and the mountains rising on the other. It is a scenic road, not a hard one, and the bends are gentle, with villages, vineyards and orchards beside it. Traffic can be heavy in summer, particularly near Interlaken, so leave early if you want the view without the queue. Be aware that speed limits are enforced firmly in Switzerland, with plenty of cameras, and that a fine can be expensive, so keep it relaxed.

Before you go, fill the tank and have a coffee in the old town. Spring brings blossom around the lake and snow-capped mountains behind it, while autumn is clear and crisp. Winter fog can sit on the water for days. In the right light, with the alps pink at the end of the lake, Thun justifies its reputation.
t.lauterbrunnen@46.6,7.9:
The first thing about Lauterbrunnen is the walls. The valley floor is flat and green, a little under a kilometre wide, and on both sides the limestone rises almost vertically for several hundred metres, as if a giant had cut the mountain with a spoon. That is what a glacier does, and this one did it thoroughly. Water falls off the cliffs in dozens of places, which gives the valley its name, meaning loud fountains, and there are said to be some seventy-two waterfalls within its length.

The best known is the Staubbach, which drops nearly three hundred metres from a hanging ledge and turns to mist before it lands. Goethe watched it in 1779 and wrote a poem about it. Inside the mountain, a short ride up the valley, the Trümmelbach falls are glacial meltwater thundering through a series of rock chambers, reached by a lift and walkways, and a good wet-weather alternative. Tolkien walked through here as a young man in 1911, and the valley is often cited as a model for Rivendell, which you will understand the moment you look up.

Riding here is all about arrival. The road from Interlaken passes through Wilderswil and then runs up the valley floor, quite flat and easy, past chalets with window boxes and meadows full of cattle. At the head of the valley, the road ends, and the cable cars and trains rise to Mürren and Wengen, two car-free villages on the terraces above, and onward to the Jungfraujoch. So this is a place to park the bike, walk and look up. Parking in the village can fill on summer days, and the car parks are paid, so arrive early.

The village has about two and a half thousand residents and a handful of cafés, bakeries and a supermarket, but fuel is not reliably on hand, so use Interlaken, eleven kilometres back, or Thun on the way. Rain is common, and cloud can wrap the cliffs for days, though when it clears the effect is spectacular. Base jumpers leap from the cliffs in season, and you may see their parachutes opening against the rock. In the evening, with the light turning gold and cowbells ringing, the valley feels completely out of time, and I have never met a rider who did not stay longer than planned.
t.hospental@46.6,8.6:
Hospental is a small village with a big job: it sits in the Urseren valley, a high, treeless basin between the Furka, the Oberalp and the Gotthard, where the Reuss river begins its journey north. Its name comes from the old hospice, a resting place for travellers on the road over the Gotthard, and the village is still very much a gateway. Above the houses stands a stone tower, often called the Lombard tower, a medieval watchtower from which the lords of the valley could see who was coming. Andermatt, a couple of kilometres away, has more shops and fuel, and the nearest sizeable town is Altdorf, thirty kilometres down the valley.

The Gotthard has been one of the great routes across Europe since the thirteenth century, when the Devil's Bridge was thrown across the wild Schöllenen gorge, making the northern approach practicable. Traders, pilgrims, soldiers and mule trains used it for centuries, and later came the carriage road, the railway and the motorway tunnel. Suvorov's Russian army fought its way through here in 1799. The pass itself is at about 2,100 metres, and from Hospental the road climbs gently across moorland to a bare, stony summit with a small lake and a hospice.

The star of the ride, though, is the Tremola, the old road on the southern side, a cobbled staircase of some twenty-four hairpins dropping into the Ticino. The stones are original, carefully restored, and riding them on a bike is a lesson in humility. In the dry they are grippy but bumpy, in the wet they are slick as glass, and the inside of each bend is tighter than it looks. Take it slowly, keep your weight low, and do not brake on the cobbles in a corner. The new road alongside is smoother if you prefer it. Pass closures are seasonal, usually from October to May, so check ahead.

Weather in this valley is its own thing. The air is thin and bright, the wind sweeps down the open basin, and even in July it can be cold enough for gloves. Snow patches linger beside the road in June. Granite surrounds you, grey and fractured, and the smell is of cold stone and wet grass. A coffee in Hospental, with the tower above and the road ahead, is as good a way as any to start the climb.
t.linthal@46.9,9.0:
Linthal is the last real village at the head of the Linth valley in canton Glarus, a long way into the mountains and a place that the modern world mostly passes by. About a thousand people live here, among steep meadows, old wooden houses and the dark shapes of textile mills from the days when cotton printing ruled the valley. Above the village rises the Tödi, the highest peak of the Glarus Alps, at over 3,600 metres, with ice on its flanks and a long history of mountaineering. From the valley floor, in the right light, the glaciers look like they are poured down the rock.

For riders, Linthal is the start of the Klausen Pass, one of Switzerland's grand classic crossings, climbing to nearly 1,950 metres before dropping into Uri. The road was an official hill-climb race course in the 1920s and early 1930s, the Klausenrennen, when cars and motorcycles flew up the hairpins in front of crowds, and you can see why it was chosen. The surface is smooth, the bends are well engineered, and the views on the way up, with waterfalls pouring from the cliffs, are among the best in the central Alps. It is wide enough for confident riding, but traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, so aim for the morning.

Up the valley beyond Linthal, an aerial cable car and a funicular climb to Braunwald, a car-free village on a terrace, and a dam holds the Limmernsee in a high basin. The Pantenbrücke, a wooden bridge in the gorge, is a favourite with walkers.

Fuel is not available in the upper valley with any reliability, so top up in Glarus, about fourteen kilometres down the road, before setting off. The Klausen is closed in winter, normally from late October to early June, and in the shoulder seasons a sudden storm can bring snow and ice. Temperatures drop quickly, and the wind at the summit can be cutting. Cows grazing near the road are common, so be ready for a slow stretch. When you leave Linthal, the road begins to rise almost immediately, and you will feel the day tighten around you.
t.la punt chamues ch@46.6,9.9:
There are places in the Upper Engadine where the light behaves differently, and La Punt Chamues-ch is one of them. The valley here is high, around 1,700 metres, wide and flat-floored, with the young Inn river meandering through meadows and larch woods, and the air has a dry, thin brightness that makes distant peaks look sharp. The village is a cluster of traditional Engadine houses with thick walls, deep-set windows and sgraffito decoration scratched into pale plaster, and the language spoken here is Romansh, one of Switzerland's four national languages, in its local Puter form.

The road you came on, the Albula Pass, climbs to 2,315 metres from the Bergün side, and its character is quieter and calmer than many other Swiss passes. It is not as busy as the Flüela or the Julier, and its curves are rhythmic, with open views of rock and alpine pasture, and the surface is usually good. On the far side, you descend into the Engadine on a road that opens suddenly into this big, bright valley. Alongside, the Rhaetian Railway runs through the Albula tunnel under the pass, part of a line that is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

La Punt is close to Zuoz, a more elegant village with a boarding school, and to Samedan, the larger town of the valley, six kilometres away, where you can find fuel, supermarkets and a hospital. The valley is also a place for Nusstorte, the walnut and caramel tart of Graubünden, which you should try with a strong coffee. The Engadine's reputation for sunshine is deserved, with more than three hundred days of it each year, though that does not mean warmth, and mornings can be cold even in summer.

The pass is closed in winter, normally from November until late spring, and snow can fall at any time of year at the top, so carry something warm. In autumn the larches turn gold, and the valley glows in a way that is hard to forget. Riders who have come over the Albula often stop here to rest, and an hour at a table outside a café, with the Inn rippling by and the peaks around, is a very good use of an afternoon.
t.tiefencastel@46.7,9.6:
Tiefencastel sits at the bottom of a deep, narrow fold in the Graubünden mountains, at the point where the Albula river meets the Julia, and its name, the deep castle, is accurate in a geographical sense. The village is small, with a little baroque church on a rock above the river, and its importance is mostly as a junction: roads and railways from Chur, Davos, the Engadine and the Surselva meet here. For a motorcyclist, it is the start of the Julier Pass, one of the oldest crossings of the Alps, and the entry to a landscape that rises steadily from woodland to bare rock.

The Julier has been used since Roman times, and at the top, about 2,284 metres up, two stumps of Roman columns once marked the crossing. The modern road is wide and well surfaced, with long bends and gentle gradients, making it an easy pass to ride quickly or slowly. Beyond Savognin, the valley opens into pastureland and the forest thins, then the road climbs through bare terrain toward Bivio, a village where the Italian-speaking influence is visible in the architecture. From the top, the view descends to the Upper Engadine lakes, silver and blue under a wide sky.

At Tiefencastel itself, there are a few cafés and shops, but for fuel and bigger supplies, Lenzerheide is seven kilometres away and Chur, twenty-one kilometres, is the sensible choice. Riders sometimes miss that the pass is high and exposed, so it is wise to be full before you start. The region is Romansh-speaking in parts, and you will see signs in a language that most Swiss cannot read either. The local food leans on barley, cured meat and cheese, and a bowl of Bündner Gerstensuppe, the barley soup, is a comfort in cold weather.

The railway is part of the experience. The Albula line, with its viaducts and spiral tunnels, is a masterpiece of Alpine engineering, and the red trains of the Rhaetian Railway wind through the landscape like toys. If you hear a horn echoing through the valley, you can be fairly sure a train is coming. The pass is open in summer and closed or restricted in winter, so check conditions, and expect weather to change fast above the tree line.
t.ulrichen@46.5,8.3:
Ulrichen is a small Valais village in the Goms, the upper valley of the Rhône, where the river is still a shallow, quick stream running between wide meadows. The valley is long, high and quiet, about 1,350 metres up, and its villages are clusters of dark wooden houses raised on stone stilts, burned black by the sun over centuries. This is a Walser landscape, a place settled by mountain people who lived at the limit of the habitable, and even now there is a sense of space and slow time. Summer visitors come for cycling and walking, winter ones for the long cross-country ski trails that run the length of the valley floor.

The Nufenen Pass starts here, a climb to about 2,478 metres, which makes it the highest fully paved pass lying entirely within Switzerland. The road is a modern one, built in the 1960s, and it is generous, with broad bends, a good surface and spectacular views. The climb takes you through alpine meadow into bare, rocky terrain, with the Gries glacier visible to the east, and the summit is a stark, windy saddle with a small restaurant and a lot of wind. On the other side, hairpins drop into the Val Bedretto, in Ticino, where the language changes to Italian and the air becomes distinctly warmer.

Ulrichen is also close to the junction of the Furka and Grimsel roads, which means that a ride from here can be linked into a grand tour. The village has a church, a few guesthouses and cafés, and not much else, so do not count on a fuel station. Fiesch, some seventeen kilometres down the valley, is the nearest reliable option, and Naters near Brig, thirty-two kilometres off, has larger shops. Top up before you go, because the pass is a long way from anything.

The pass is closed in winter, usually from October to June, and snowfall can come at any time of year. Temperatures at the top can be near freezing even in July, and the wind can be fierce, so a good jacket and gloves are worth carrying. In the clear light of an early morning, with the road empty and the river glinting, Ulrichen is the sort of place where you tend to say little and ride well.
t.nyon@46.4,6.2:
Nyon was a Roman town before most of Europe had names, founded by Julius Caesar around 45 BC as Colonia Iulia Equestris, a settlement for veteran cavalry on the shore of Lake Geneva. Columns from the Roman forum still stand by the lake, and a small museum in the old basilica shows what remains. Today it is a pleasant town of about seventeen thousand people with a castle on the hill, a waterfront promenade and a market, and it has the quiet, wealthy air of a place that has been well looked after for two thousand years.

Nyon has a few modern claims to fame. Its porcelain factory, active from the 1780s to the early nineteenth century, produced delicate pieces now treasured in museums. In July the town hosts the Paléo Festival, one of Switzerland's largest open-air music events, which brings the population of the whole area to a standstill, so book ahead if you are here then. Prangins Castle, close by, houses part of the Swiss National Museum, with exhibits on life in the country in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

For riders, Nyon is the base for the Jura crest road, a ride that climbs the long, forested ridge behind the lake. The Jura is a very different range from the Alps, made of folded limestone, with gentle summits, meadows with cattle and forest of spruce and beech. Roads here are narrow, often twisty, with passes such as the Marchairuz, at about 1,450 metres, and long views across the lake to Mont Blanc on a clear day. The surface can be patchy after winter, and cows may be on the road, so watch your speed.

Practical points are easy in town: fuel, food, a bakery for the road and a range of hotels. Weather behaves differently on the Jura, with cloud banks and mist frequent on the ridge while the lake is bright, and a sea of fog may lie over the lowlands in autumn, with the summit above in sunshine. In winter the high roads can be icy or closed. Come in late spring, when the meadows bloom, or in October, when the beech forests turn copper.
t.creux du van@46.9,6.7:
Creux du Van is a huge natural amphitheatre carved into the limestone of the Neuchâtel Jura, a curved cliff about a kilometre and a half long and well over a hundred metres high, ringing a deep bowl of scree and forest. It looks like a giant's quarry or a collapsed volcano, but it was made by ice and water, which worked away at the soft layers of rock over many thousands of years. From the rim, at about 1,450 metres, you look down onto treetops and across to the Alps on a clear day, and the Mont Blanc range is often visible on the horizon.

The cliff is the home of ibex, which were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s after being hunted out, and chamois, which you may see on the ledges at dawn or dusk. Because the rim has no fence in most places, walkers must keep a respectful distance from the edge, and the same applies to anyone stepping off the bike. The area is a nature reserve, and the gorges of the Areuse river run down below it. The air carries the smell of pine and cold stone.

The valley beneath, the Val-de-Travers, has one very famous export, absinthe, which was born here in the late eighteenth century and made in secret after the drink was banned in Switzerland from 1910 until 2005. The villages of Couvet and Môtiers are the heart of the story. Travers, the nearest village, is also known for its old asphalt mines, which now shelter a museum underground. Local food leans on the dairy, cured sausage and a good fondue, and there are farm restaurants on the high pastures.

The ride up from the valley is steep and narrow, with tight bends, farm gates and patchy tarmac, and the road is only open in the warmer months. Allow time and expect to meet walkers and cyclists, and cows who are not in a hurry. Cold air gathers in the bowl, even in summer, and fog may fill it for hours. A clear morning in September is the best time to come.
t.ruinaulta viewpoint@46.8,9.3:
Nine and a half thousand years ago, give or take, the side of a mountain fell into the Rhine valley. The Flimserstein rockslide, the largest in the Alps, sent some twelve cubic kilometres of limestone down into the valley, dammed the river into a lake and left behind a field of broken boulders that you now ride across without noticing. When the lake finally burst through, the Vorderrhein cut a deep channel through the debris, and the result is the Ruinaulta, the Rhine Gorge, which the Swiss like to call their Grand Canyon. It is an overstatement, but not a ridiculous one: the white cliffs reach some four hundred metres, topped with pine, and the river runs turquoise at the bottom.

From the viewpoint above the gorge, near Flims and Laax, the whole canyon opens beneath your boots. A platform sticks out into the void, and the cliffs fall away on both sides, with the river curving below like a ribbon. In the gorge itself, a red train of the Rhaetian Railway creeps along the bottom, and in summer rafts drift past full of cheerful passengers in helmets. Cars and trucks cannot reach the bottom, so the gorge feels wild, though it lies close to ski resorts and golf courses. Pay attention near the edges, where the drop is real.

The ride that brings you here is the Viamala and Rhine Gorge route, a pairing of two very different canyons. The Viamala, the bad road, is a narrow slot cut by the Hinterrhein south of Thusis, crossed by bridges of different centuries, while the Ruinaulta is wide and open by comparison. Roads are good and the bends are easy, with Flims and Laax offering mountain scenery and bike-friendly hotels. Traffic is moderate, though weekends in summer see more cars and rental bikes around Flims.

Flims and Laax are small resort villages, with about two or three thousand residents, so expect cafés, shops and a few pumps, but for large supermarkets and a wider choice of fuel, Domat/Ems, about twelve kilometres away, is the better bet. The nearby Caumasee, a small, green lake in the forest, is a lovely place to cool off in summer. Mornings are clearest, and autumn is spectacular when the forest turns, while winter closes the access roads.
t.fluelen@46.9,8.6:
Flüelen is the harbour at the southern tip of Lake Uri, the long, dark, steep-sided arm of Lake Lucerne that cuts into the heart of Switzerland, and for hundreds of years it was the starting point of the Gotthard route. Goods and travellers came up the lake by boat, landed here and went on by mule to the pass. Today it is a quiet village of around two thousand people, with a tower, a small harbour and a few cafés, and the old trading importance has dissolved into the calm of the water. The proper town, Altdorf, is three kilometres away and has the fuel, supermarkets and hardware shops.

This is the land of William Tell, the legendary archer who is said to have shot an apple from his son's head and then, after the Habsburg bailiff Gessler arrested him, escaped from a boat on this very lake and killed his captor. The story is almost certainly a legend, but it has been told since the fifteenth century and has become a symbol of Swiss independence. In Altdorf there is a bronze statue of Tell and his son, and along the lake the Tellskapelle stands on the shore at the spot where he is said to have leapt ashore. Schiller's play of 1804 did the rest.

The Axenstrasse, which leads you here, is a road carved out of the cliff on the eastern side of the lake. It was opened in the 1860s, and its tunnels, galleries and sudden windows of view give a mood of drama, with the water of Lake Uri far below and the rocky walls above. The driving is slow and sinuous, with a few tight tunnels and bends, and traffic can be heavy, especially at weekends, because it is the main approach to the Gotthard. Rockfalls sometimes close sections, so check before you set off.

The lake is deep and cold, and the Föhn wind can turn it from calm to choppy in minutes. The best time for the ride is early morning, before the day's traffic, when mist lies on the water and the peaks above are lit. In autumn, the walnut trees along the road turn yellow. As a place to stop, Flüelen is not exciting, but it is peaceful, with a lakeside walk and a good view of the mountains, and a coffee by the harbour is a good way to end the ride.
t.maloja@46.4,9.7:
Maloja is a pass that does two things at once: it sits at the head of the Upper Engadine, where the valley is wide and gentle, and it looks down over a cliff into the Val Bregaglia, where the road suddenly tumbles in a dozen or so hairpins toward Italy. The difference in character is startling. On the Engadine side the village lies by the shore of Lake Sils at around 1,800 metres, among larches and meadows, while a few hundred metres away the Italian side falls steeply, as if the mountain had been sliced.

The hairpins on the south side are among the best in Switzerland, tight, evenly spaced and well surfaced, and the road drops about 400 metres in a very short distance. They make a satisfying descent and a more demanding climb. You come out in the Bregaglia, a green valley with chestnut woods and stone villages like Stampa, the home of the Giacometti family, whose artist sons Alberto and Giovanni were born here. At the bottom lies Chiavenna, in Italy, twenty-five kilometres away.

Maloja has a particular weather phenomenon called the Maloja snake: when moist air from the south pushes up the valley in the morning, it forms a long, winding bank of cloud that curls over the pass, and the effect looks like a snake wriggling across the mountains. Sailors on Lake Sils know the Maloja wind, which blows up the lake on summer afternoons and fills sails across the water. The painter Giovanni Segantini lived in a small chalet above the village and died on the nearby Schafberg in 1899, and his panoramic mountain paintings seem to catch this exact light.

The village itself is small, with a few hotels and a large old palace-hotel, and fuel is not reliably available, so top up in Silvaplana, ten kilometres away, or in St Moritz, fifteen. The pass is open all year, though snow can make the hairpins tricky in winter. Even on a warm day, the air is cool and thin, and the lake can be icy. For the riding, come in the morning, when the road is quiet and the cloud sits on the pass in a long, silent drift.
t.trier@49.7,6.6:
Trier calls itself Germany's oldest city, and nobody in a position to argue has managed to win. The Romans founded Augusta Treverorum around 16 BC, and by the fourth century it was one of the largest cities in the western empire, an imperial residence with palaces, baths and a great amphitheatre. The Porta Nigra, a massive black stone city gate from the second century, still stands on the northern edge of the old centre, grim and perfectly preserved because a hermit and later a church used it in the Middle Ages. A short walk away the Basilica of Constantine, a vast brick hall that was once a throne room, has a ceiling over thirty metres above the floor.

There are baths, an amphitheatre that held perhaps twenty thousand, a Roman bridge pier still carrying traffic in the Moselle, and a medieval cathedral that is among the oldest in Germany. UNESCO listed the whole set in 1986. Karl Marx was born here in 1818, and a small museum in the house tells the story. The Hauptmarkt, a handsome market square with a cross and a fountain, is the place to sit with a coffee, and the Moselle wines are served in the cafés around it.

The Moselle Wine Route comes to an end here, a ride that follows the river through some of the steepest vineyards in the world. The slopes of slate hold some of Germany's best Riesling, with a delicate, mineral, lightly sweet character, and the road weaves along the river with castles, villages and endless rows of vines. It is a slow, scenic ride rather than a fast one, with bends that follow the water, tractors and cyclists in season, and dazzling views from the bends where the river loops tightly. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, though the harvest brings its own traffic.

With about a hundred thousand people, Trier has everything: fuel, restaurants, hotels and bike shops, so you can sort out the practicalities with ease. Traffic in the centre can be slow, and much of the old town is pedestrianised, so leave the bike in a car park and walk. Luxembourg is just across the border, only a short ride away, with cheaper fuel, if you need it. After a long day, a glass of Riesling and a plate of local ham makes a good ending.
t.villingen schwenningen@48.1,8.5:
Villingen-Schwenningen is two towns that were made to share a name in 1972, and they still do not quite agree. Villingen, to the west, is a medieval walled town in the Black Forest, with gates, towers and a minster, once part of Austria and proud of its carnival, the Fasnet, in which masked figures in elaborate wooden masks and painted costumes parade through the streets in a thunder of whips and bells. Schwenningen, to the east, is younger and more industrial, a clockmaking town that grew in the nineteenth century, and it has the source of the Neckar river in a small park, marked with a stone.

That clockmaking is the reason for the ride. The Black Forest developed clocks in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when farmers in long winters carved wooden wheels and built clocks to sell, and the craft grew into a major industry. Schwenningen became a centre for factory-made clocks and watches, with firms such as Kienzle and Mauthe, and the Black Forest cuckoo clock is a more rural cousin. The German Clock Route links museums, workshops and villages in the region, and you can follow the story across the hills.

The town has about eighty thousand people, so everything is available, including large fuel stations and supermarkets, and it is an easy place to begin. The Baar plateau around it is high, open and gentle, with farmland, wind and big skies, and the climate is cold by German standards, so mornings can be frosty even in spring. Riding west toward Furtwangen, the road climbs into the forest, with spruce on the hills and wooden farmhouses with huge roofs coming down almost to the ground, a style that has been used for centuries to shed snow.

The bends in the Black Forest are among the best in Germany, smooth, rhythmic and well surfaced, and weekend traffic of other motorcycles can be heavy. Speed limits are enforced in places, and some roads have noise restrictions for bikes on certain days, so check signs before you go. Autumn is clear and crisp, winter can be snowy, and the pace of life in the villages is slow. Try a slice of Black Forest cake in a village café, and you will understand why the region is famous for more than clocks.
t.furtwangen@48.1,8.2:
Furtwangen is a Black Forest town high on a ridge, at about 850 metres, and it is the place where the story of the cuckoo clock is told. The Deutsches Uhrenmuseum, founded in the 1850s to inspire local craftsmen, holds one of the great clock collections in Europe, from early wooden Black Forest pieces with painted faces to elaborate astronomical machines and cuckoo clocks in every size. A clockmaking school was established here too, and it grew into a university of applied sciences, which is why a town of under ten thousand people has a fair number of students.

The Black Forest clock trade began in the eighteenth century, when farm families made wooden-geared clocks during the winter months and peddlers carried them across Europe on their backs. The cuckoo clock, with its carved wooden case and tiny bellows that imitate the bird's call, became the best-known export. Today craftsmen still make them by hand, and several workshops welcome visitors, though many cheap versions are made elsewhere, so look for the maker's mark if you want the real thing.

The geography is a curiosity as well. Near Furtwangen, in the hills, rises the Breg, which together with the Brigach forms the Danube at Donaueschingen, and the Breg spring is traditionally called the true source of Europe's second-longest river. It is a small stream here, and the idea of it ending up in the Black Sea is hard to believe. The surrounding forest of spruce and fir is dark, tall and quiet, and the air smells of resin.

The ride is a gentle and winding one, through valleys with big farmhouses and small chapels, and the roads climb and drop in long, smooth curves. The Black Forest is popular with riders, so expect company on dry weekends, and slow trucks and tractors on the narrower roads. The winters are cold and snowy, with frost possible into May, and summer thunderstorms can be sudden. Furtwangen has a few petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, so it is a sensible stop for a break. Order a slice of local cake and watch the time pass, as befits a clock town.
t.pforzheim@48.9,8.7:
On a summer morning in August 1888, a woman named Bertha Benz took her two teenage sons, climbed into her husband's new Patent-Motorwagen without telling him, and drove from Mannheim to her mother's house in Pforzheim. It was about a hundred kilometres, the first long-distance journey by motor car, and it was a piece of brilliant publicity as well as a family visit. She bought ligroin, a petroleum solvent, from a pharmacy in Wiesloch, which is considered the world's first filling station, used a hat pin to clear a blocked fuel line and her garter to insulate a wire, and had a cobbler fit leather to the brake blocks, thereby inventing brake lining. The Bertha Benz Memorial Route follows that trip, and here is where it ends.

Pforzheim, called the Golden City, lies at the northern edge of the Black Forest, where three rivers, the Enz, the Nagold and the Würm, meet. It has been a jewellery and watchmaking centre since the eighteenth century, when the Margrave of Baden founded an orphanage that made watches and jewellery to support itself, and the industry grew from there. On 23 February 1945, a British air raid destroyed most of the old city and killed a large share of its people, and the town was rebuilt in the plain postwar style, which means it is not pretty, but it has strong character and good museums. The Jewellery Museum is worth a visit.

With about a hundred and twenty thousand people, Pforzheim has fuel, shops and services in plenty. The ride from Mannheim runs mostly through gentle country, with orchards, vineyards, castles and the half-timbered towns of the Kraichgau, then rises into the northern Black Forest. It is a gentle road, mostly through villages, with slow traffic and many roundabouts, and the pleasure is in the history, not the bends. Look for the signs with the route's emblem, and you can follow it without a map.

For a good night, there are plenty of hotels, and the local Swabian food is filling, with Maultaschen, spätzle and onion roast beef. Spring is lovely in the Enz valley, when the orchards bloom, and autumn is golden. Rain is common, and the northern Black Forest is cool and often misty, so pack a waterproof. A tank of fuel in Pforzheim is a small tribute to a very brave woman.
t.waldshut@47.6,8.2:
Waldshut is a small town on the High Rhine, with Switzerland on the opposite bank, and its character is that of a border place with a long, slightly cantankerous history. The old town, a neat street running between two gates, the Upper Gate and the Lower Gate, is painted in cheerful colours and has the feel of a medieval fortress trimmed for peacetime. Waldshut was part of Habsburg Austria for centuries, and in 1524 it became one of the first towns to join the Peasants' War, led by the preacher Balthasar Hubmaier, who was later burned in Vienna. The twin town of Tiengen, a few kilometres away, has an old castle and its own market.

With more than twenty thousand people in the combined town, you will find fuel, shops and restaurants. A bridge carries the road across the Rhine to Koblenz, in the Swiss canton of Aargau, and the border post is quick. The river is big and green here, flowing out of Lake Constance, and just upstream and downstream are weirs, power stations and the sort of bends that make for fine fishing. Waldshut is also known for its fair, the Chilbi, held in late summer, with fairground rides and a lot of beer.

The Black Forest Panorama Route, the B500, ends here after a long run from Baden-Baden through the highest parts of the range. The southern section is the quieter one, with long, smooth curves, forested ridges and farmhouses with deep roofs, and as you descend toward the Rhine, the air turns warmer and the valley opens. The roads are among the best in the region, but they are heavily used on weekends, and German police enforce speed limits and noise rules for motorcycles on some stretches, so check signs and keep to a sensible pace.

On a clear day, you can see the Swiss Alps from the heights above the town, a faint white line along the southern horizon. The summers are warm and the autumns long, with fog sometimes lying in the Rhine valley. Fuel here is cheaper than in Switzerland, so it is worth filling the tank before crossing, and the cafés in the old town are a pleasant place to finish. Order a plate of Black Forest ham and a glass of local wine, and the day sorts itself out.
t.col de la faucille@46.4,6.0:
The Col de la Faucille is the Jura's front door to Lake Geneva. At about 1,320 metres, this pass on the French side of the border carries the main road from Gex up and over the ridge toward Les Rousses and the Haut-Jura, and the first view from the top is the thing people remember: a long drop through meadows and forest to the lake, a smudge of Geneva beyond it, and on clear days the white dome of Mont Blanc floating above everything. The name means the sickle pass, after the curved shape of the ridge, and it has been used as a route for centuries.

The ride up from Gex is the kind of road that makes you glad to have left the city. It starts among the villages and fields of the Pays de Gex, a flat shelf between the Jura and the lake, then climbs through beech and spruce in a succession of well-banked bends. The surface is generally good, with moderate gradients and enough hairpins to keep things interesting. It is popular with cyclists and sports-car drivers, so on weekends you will want to ride with patience, and winter can bring snow and ice. Early morning, with the mist in the valley below and the sun hitting the ridge, is the best time.

The Jura is limestone country, and the cheese reflects it. This is the area of Bleu de Gex, a mild, creamy blue cheese made in the high pastures, and of Comté and Morbier a little farther north. The pass has a small ski area, with lifts and a hotel or two, and a few places selling hot drinks, crêpes and local specialities. The pastures are grazed by cows with big bells, and in spring the slopes are covered with gentians and narcissi.

Gex, about five kilometres below, has fuel, supermarkets, bakeries and cafes, so top up there before you climb, and stock up on water and snacks. Services at the pass itself are limited and seasonal. Weather can change quickly on the ridge, with fog rolling in from the Swiss side and a wind that can find every gap in a jacket. It is a good place to begin a ride, with a coffee and a map, and the ability to see exactly where you are going.
t.la dole view area@46.4,6.1:
La Dôle is the high point of the Swiss Jura's southern end, a rounded summit of about 1,677 metres above Lake Geneva, topped with a radar dome and a communications mast that you can see from half of western Switzerland. From the ridge, the view is one of the great panoramas of the country: the whole of Lake Geneva, the city at its tip, the Savoy Alps and the long white line of the Mont Blanc massif, with the Bernese Alps on the horizon in clear weather. On a good day you can see for well over a hundred kilometres.

The mountain is mostly reached by walking, from the Col de la Givrine or from the small resort of Saint-Cergue, a few kilometres away, so a motorcycle is usually left at the roadside while you climb a trail through pasture and forest. The summit is not far above, and the walk takes less than a couple of hours for most people. Along the way, you cross high meadows grazed by cattle, with limestone outcrops, gentians and in places the sound of cowbells. The ridge here marks the border with France, with the Jura running southwest into the French Haut-Jura.

The road in is a fine one. From the lakeside town of Nyon, a twisting mountain road climbs through woodland and farmland to Saint-Cergue, with decent surface, medium-radius bends and gradual gradients, and views opening up as you rise. The air is cooler and fresher, and in autumn, the forests turn orange and gold. Weather changes rapidly: you may be riding in clear sun at the lake and find thick fog at the ridge, so choose your day carefully. Winter brings snow, and some of the minor roads are closed.

For services, Saint-Cergue has cafes, a bakery and a few small hotels, and mountain restaurants in the area serve fondue, saucisson and tarte aux myrtilles. Fuel is available at larger towns, and on the French side, Les Rousses has stations and shops. Divonne-les-Bains, a spa town, is the nearest bigger place on the lower slopes. Bring a windproof layer and a bit of patience for hairpins behind slow cars, and make time to sit on the grass and watch the lake shimmer below you.
t.col de la@46.4,6.0:
Coming back to the pass at the end of a ride is a different thing from setting out. The light has changed, the legs are looser, and you notice the small stuff you rushed past in the morning: the cowbells, the smell of cut grass and cold stone, the way beech trees lean over a bend as if they were reading the road. The Col de la Faucille sits at about 1,320 metres on the French side of the Jura, and its best trick is that it hides the lake until the last moment, then lays the whole of Lake Geneva out below you in one go.

Heading down from the col toward Gex, the road drops in a run of broad bends with the Pays de Gex spread beneath like a tablecloth. In the late afternoon, the Alps are lit from the side, and on a clear evening Mont Blanc turns pink while the valley below goes blue. It is the best view of the day and a good reason to stop for a few minutes. Be careful of the gravel that collects on the outside of the hairpins, and of the cyclists who toil up the same road and then come back down faster than you would believe.

The area has odd and interesting neighbours. A short way below, at the foot of the slope, is Ferney-Voltaire, where the writer Voltaire lived for the last two decades of his life, writing, farming and annoying kings from a safe distance across the border. Not much further, on the plain near Geneva, CERN's rings run under the fields, so the quiet pastures sit above one of the largest scientific machines on earth. Both facts feel absurd when a herd of cows is blocking the road in front of you.

For the end of a loop, Gex is the sensible place to finish. It has fuel, bakeries, cafes and supermarkets, and a sense of ordinary life that is welcome after the mountains. If you still have energy, the climb back to the pass for a last look at sunset is worthwhile, though temperatures drop quickly after dark, and fog can roll in from the Swiss side in minutes. Take a layer, and give the cows right of way.
t.rapperswil food@47.2,8.8:
Rapperswil sits on a little promontory on the northern shore of Lake Zurich, joined to the other side by a long causeway and a wooden footbridge, and it has the feel of a town that knows it looks good and does not need to say so. About thirty-five thousand people live in Rapperswil-Jona, though the old town is compact, with a castle above, arcaded lanes below and a harbour full of boats. After the Hulftegg and its farm roads, it is a pleasing place to come down to.

The castle holds an unexpected story. In the nineteenth century, Polish exiles who had fled their country after failed uprisings against Russian rule made Rapperswil their base, and in 1870 they founded a Polish national museum in the castle, preserving documents and relics for a country that did not then exist on the map. The museum eventually moved on, but a Polish connection remains in the town, and a column in the castle square honours Polish heroes. The town is also known as the town of roses, with several rose gardens, and from the promenade on a summer evening you can see the Glarus Alps lined up across the lake.

The ride into Rapperswil from the hills is easy and agreeable, with winding roads through orchards and meadows above the lake, and long views across the water. Surfaces are good, and traffic is moderate, though weekends can be crowded around the lake. Weather can change quickly in the Pre-Alps, and the lake has its own breezes. Early evening is ideal, when the light turns gold, the streets fill with people and the cafes put out their tables.

As a food stop, Rapperswil is an easy choice. There are lakeside restaurants serving fresh perch fillets, called Egli, with fries and sauce, and bakeries selling Zurich-area pastries, and in the old town small cafes serve coffee and cake. Fuel is available at several stations in town and in neighbouring Jona. Parking can be tight in the old town, but motorcycles can usually find a space near the harbour. A short walk along the wooden bridge, over the water, is the best digestif.
t.zug food window@47.2,8.5:
Zug has a reputation as a place for banks, crypto start-ups and low taxes, and the first impression, with modern glass blocks beside the lake, does not argue. But keep walking toward the water and the old town appears, tight and clean, with a medieval clock tower, painted gables and arcaded lanes, all looking over the Zugersee toward the Rigi. It is a town of about twenty-three thousand people that tends to be a lot nicer than its press, and it is especially good for a meal between the mountain roads that surround it.

The riding here is the real attraction. East of town, the climb toward the Raten pass, at about 1,070 metres, runs through the green Ägerital, with the little Ägerisee glinting below, and beyond it the road drops to Biberbrugg and the Sihl. The bends are neat and rhythmic, the surface is good and the gradients friendly, a sort of finishing school for corners. Near the Ägerisee, a memorial marks Morgarten, where in 1315 a force of Swiss confederates ambushed an Austrian army, a battle that became part of the founding story of Switzerland. Cows with bells, orchards and little farm shops sit along the way.

Weather in the Pre-Alps is changeable. Mist often hangs on the lake in the morning, and in summer afternoons can bring a sharp thunderstorm, while on a clear autumn day the whole chain of the Alps from Pilatus to the Glarus peaks appears to stand along the horizon. Weekends bring cyclists and other riders, and the road can bunch up behind slow cars, so a weekday evening is more enjoyable.

As a food window, Zug is hard to beat. Lakeside restaurants serve Egli fillets and other freshwater fish, and the town's famous Kirschtorte, a cake of nut meringue layers, buttercream and local cherry brandy, is sold in every bakery. Fuel is easy to find, with several stations in town and in neighbouring Baar, about three and a half kilometres away. Parking for motorcycles is generally easy, though the old town is partly pedestrian. A coffee in the late afternoon, in the sun on the quay, is the best preparation for the ride home.
t.stein am rhein old town@47.7,8.9:
Stein am Rhein looks like the illustration in a fairy tale about a town: two rows of medieval houses facing each other across a cobbled square, every facade painted with scenes, flowers, coats of arms and carefully rendered shadows. It sits at the point where the Rhine leaves the Untersee, the western arm of Lake Constance, and starts its journey across northern Switzerland. With about three thousand inhabitants, it is tiny, but it has the best-preserved old centre in the region, and the Rathausplatz is one of the prettiest squares in the country.

Many of the paintings date from the sixteenth century and later, and they were often a way for wealthy merchants to show off their taste and their education. The town hall, with its stepped gable, is covered in frescoes of historic scenes. On the hill above stands Hohenklingen castle, a medieval fortress with a long view over the Rhine and the lake, and in the town below, the former Benedictine monastery of St George has a museum with fine interiors and frescoes. The Rhine here is wide and green, and boats, ducks and swans glide past the quay.

For riders, the approach is a pleasure. The roads along the Untersee and the Rhine are quiet and gentle, with long, easy bends through orchards, vineyards and fields, and lake glimpses all the way. Surfaces are good, but speed limits are strictly enforced and fines in Switzerland are high, so keep an eye on the signs. The border with Germany is very close, and back roads cross it frequently, so carry your passport. The best light comes in the morning and late afternoon, and in spring the orchards are in blossom.

Stein am Rhein is busy with day-trippers in summer, especially at weekends, but it empties in the evening. You will find fuel in nearby towns, such as Rielasingen-Worblingen on the German side or Diessenhofen and Schaffhausen on the Swiss side, but few stations in the old town itself. Cafes and restaurants along the main square serve Bodensee fish, coffee and ice cream, and the lanes are pleasant to walk. Leave the bike at the edge of the old town and explore on foot, looking up, always up.
t.rhine@47.7,8.6:
The Rhine Falls are not high, but they are loud. At Neuhausen, near Schaffhausen in northern Switzerland, the young river throws itself over a rocky ledge about twenty-three metres high and a hundred and fifty wide, in a roaring curtain of white water, and it is the largest plain waterfall in Europe by volume. In summer, hundreds of cubic metres of water pass every second, and the spray drifts up on the viewing platforms, soaking anyone who gets too close. The Rhine here is still green and clear from its passage through Lake Constance.

The falls were formed at the end of the last ice age, when the river was diverted from its old course by glacial deposits and forced across a hard limestone ledge. A rock formation stands in the middle, in the middle of the river, and small boats take visitors to a platform on it, which is a wet and thrilling trip. Above the falls on the northern bank stands Laufen castle, a medieval building with a view platform, and on the other side, a path with galleries goes right to the edge of the water. In the nineteenth century, painters, poets and early tourists flocked here, and even Goethe stopped to marvel.

As a finish to a ride, it is a good one. The roads around Neuhausen are quiet and easy, with orchards, vineyards and gentle hills of the Zurich Weinland to the south and the Randen ridge to the north. The last miles run beside the Rhine, which gleams in the late sun, and then the sound of the falls reaches you before you see them. Weekends are busy with coaches, so evenings are better, when the spray catches the light and the crowds thin.

Neuhausen am Rheinfall is a town of around ten thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Schaffhausen is just a few minutes away for a larger choice. Near the falls, cafes and a restaurant at water level serve coffee, cake and simple meals, and the smell of wet rock is surprisingly refreshing. Park the bike where signs allow, and pay attention to parking rules, which Swiss authorities enforce. If you are lucky with the sky, a rainbow often forms in the mist, and you can stand there for a while and let it all roar past.
t.einsiedeln abbey@47.1,8.8:
Einsiedeln is a monastery that grew a town around it. The story goes back to the ninth century, when a hermit named Meinrad settled in the forest here and was murdered in 861 by robbers who coveted the candlesticks of his chapel. A Benedictine community was founded on the spot in 934, and over the centuries it became one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Europe, centred on a statue of the Virgin Mary, the Black Madonna, kept in a chapel inside the church. Pilgrims still arrive from all directions, many on foot, since it lies on a branch of the Way of St James.

The abbey church of today is a great Baroque building from the early eighteenth century, with twin towers, a facade that curves gently forward into the huge square, and an interior where every surface seems to be covered in stucco, gilding and ceiling paintings. In the evening, the monks sing the Salve Regina, a tradition kept for centuries, and visitors may listen in. In the square in front, a fountain with fourteen spouts invites pilgrims to drink and wash. The abbey also runs one of Europe's oldest horse studs, which still breeds horses in its stables.

For a rider, the abbey is the centrepiece of a beautiful loop. The roads around it cross the Rothenthurm moor, a large high peat bog protected after a famous referendum in 1987, and climb and fall gently across wide pastures with views of the Mythen peaks. The surface is generally good, with moderate bends and long, open straights, though weekend traffic can be heavy. The air at around 880 metres is cool and fresh, with mist drifting over the moor in the early morning and snow arriving early in winter.

Einsiedeln is a town of thirteen thousand, so it has fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, as well as many shops selling devotional items, candles and sweets. Try a piece of Schafchäs, or a local pastry, and have a coffee on the square. Parking for motorcycles is available near the abbey, though it can be busy on pilgrimage days. Respect the quiet of the church, take off your helmet, and spend a few minutes looking up at the ceiling.
t.einsiedeln monastery@47.1,8.8:
The monastery at Einsiedeln has seen a great many people pass through, and a few of them became famous. Paracelsus, the Renaissance physician and alchemist, was born in 1493 in a hamlet nearby, the son of a doctor, and spent his early years in the shadow of the abbey. Huldrych Zwingli, who would become the leader of the Reformation in Zurich, served as a priest here for two years from 1516, and it was in Einsiedeln that he began to preach against the sale of indulgences to pilgrims. The abbey he criticised is still working, with Benedictine monks living by the old rule of prayer and work.

Inside the abbey, one of the highlights is the library, a Baroque hall with tall shelves and a ceiling decorated with painted scenes, holding many thousands of volumes and manuscripts, among them medieval texts of great value. The monks also run a school, a publishing house and a farm. The church can be visited freely, with its dazzling interior, but the library and some other areas have limited hours, so check before you set out. A short walk away, the town's main street runs gently uphill from the square, lined with shops and cafes.

The ride from Hirzel to Einsiedeln is a delight on a calm evening. The road crosses the high ground south of Lake Zurich, passing farmland and woods, then runs beside the Sihlsee, a large reservoir built in the 1930s, whose blue water and wooded shores reflect the late sun. Corners are easy and flowing, the surface is good, and there are views of the Mythen peaks to the south. At sunset, the water turns copper and the hills go purple, and the cowbells and church bells drift across the valley.

The Sihlsee has several places to stop, with small beaches and cafes, and sailing boats on the water, and the shoreline road is popular with cyclists and walkers. In Einsiedeln itself, there is fuel, food and parking, and the pace is leisurely, with pilgrims, tourists and locals sitting in the sun. A coffee on the monastery square before the final stretch home is the perfect way to end the day. Wrap up warm if the evening is cool, because the air near the lake can be sharp.
t.zug lakeside food@47.2,8.5:
Zug's real charm is on the water, where the old town ends and a long promenade runs along the Zugersee. In the evening, people stroll, children throw bread to swans, and cafes spread their tables toward the lake, which is the colour of slate and silver and ringed by the green hills of Rigi and Zugerberg. On a clear evening, you can see Pilatus rising beyond the opposite shore. It is a town where life seems to happen outdoors from May to September, and the pace slows accordingly.

There is a darker story under the promenade. In 1887, part of the medieval town, built on soft lake sediment, suddenly collapsed and slid into the water, taking with it several houses and eleven people. The event was one of Switzerland's worst natural disasters of the nineteenth century, and the shoreline you see today was rebuilt afterward with firmer foundations. A small memorial recalls the victims, and it is a reminder that even the prettiest lake can be treacherous.

Coming here on a motorcycle at the end of the Sihlsee ride, you arrive from the east or north along roads that are calm and straightforward. The final approach is flat and easy, mostly through suburbs and fields, with light traffic in the evening. Be aware of trams and bicycles, as well as pedestrians in the town centre, and of the speed cameras on the main roads. The lakeside roads are slow, with limits strictly enforced, but at the right moment the water and the lights are worth the delay.

For food, the lakeside terraces offer fish dishes, salads, pizza and, of course, the Zuger Kirschtorte, a local cake with cherry spirit, which makes a good partner to a late coffee. Fuel is available at several stations in the town and in nearby Baar, with supermarkets and bakeries open until early evening. Motorcycle parking is generally available near the lake and the railway station. Sit by the water, watch the sunset colours spread over the hills, and let the last of the ride settle.
t.grimsel pass point 2@46.6,8.3:
Handeck is a small place where a great river falls over a cliff. The Aare plunges about forty-six metres down a rocky chasm, and a footbridge crosses the gorge close to the water, so that the spray drifts over you and the roar fills your ears. It is a dramatic sight, particularly in early summer, when the snowmelt is at its peak. A short path leads to the viewing platforms, and a few minutes' walk is enough to feel the power of the water.

Handeck is also home to the Gelmerbahn, a funicular railway that climbs to the Gelmer reservoir high above. It was built in the 1920s to carry materials for the dam, and it is one of the steepest funiculars in Europe, with a gradient of more than a hundred per cent, which means the track rises more than a metre for each metre travelled. Today it carries visitors in open cars up the cliff, a short but exciting ride with huge views. The reservoir at the top is a lovely, remote lake in a granite basin.

The rock around here is smooth, pale granite, polished by glaciers over thousands of years. The valley walls are scoured and rounded, with long, shining slabs, and in places, the road passes beneath great domes of stone. It is a landscape of stern beauty, with little vegetation, only a few stunted pines and clumps of alpine flowers clinging to cracks. Waterfalls run down the cliffs after rain.

For the rider, this stretch of the Grimsel road is a classic. The road climbs in long, steady bends along the valley, passing through short galleries and across bridges, with the Aare roaring beside you. The surface is generally good, the corners are open, and the gradient is moderate. The traffic includes buses and campers, and the narrow sections need patience. Rockfall can occur after heavy rain, and the road is closed in winter.

A small restaurant and cafe at Handeck serve food and drink, and the terrace is a pleasant place for a pause. Wear a warm layer, because the air here, in the shadow of the cliffs, is cool and damp. If the weather is clear, take a few moments to listen to the water.
t.grimsel pass point 3@46.6,8.3:
The summit of the Grimsel is at 2,164 metres, and it is a grey, stony place, with the character of a high mountain that has seen everything. The pass lies on the border between the cantons of Bern and Valais, and also on the great European watershed, with water on the north side flowing toward the Rhine and the North Sea and the south side toward the Rhône and the Mediterranean. Around the road, there are no trees, only bare granite, scoured by ice, with small lakes lying in hollows. The Totesee, the Lake of the Dead, sits right beside the road at the top, a cold, dark pool.

The mountains here are among the most stunning in Switzerland. Huge, smooth granite slabs, polished by glaciers, slope down to the lake, and above them, the peaks of the Bernese Alps rise with their caps of snow and ice. A few kilometres to the south-east is the Rhone Glacier, source of the Rhône, reached by the Furka Pass, and another road continues over the Nufenen Pass to Ticino. Together, they form the heart of the Swiss Alpine road network.

The Grimsel Hospiz, a hotel and restaurant on the northern side, has been offering shelter to travellers for centuries, and an old hospice stood here long before the modern road. Today the buildings stand beside a reservoir, the Grimselsee, and the area is dominated by dams and power stations. Despite the engineering, the setting remains wild and impressive.

For the rider, the Grimsel is a joy. The road climbs from the north in long, sweeping bends with a smooth surface, and the gradient is steady, so you can enjoy the rhythm. There is a good deal of traffic in summer, including coaches and campers, and weekends can be busy, so aim for an early start or a weekday. Weather changes fast, with fog and rain in minutes, so wear warm, waterproof clothing.

The pass is open from about June to October, and the exact dates depend on the snow. In the evening, the light on the granite turns warm and golden, and the water of the lakes goes still.
t.grimsel pass point 4@46.6,8.3:
The top of the Grimsel is a bare, grey bowl at 2,164 metres where the Bernese Oberland hands over to the Valais, and the first thing you notice is how little grows here. Granite polished by ice, a few tarns, and the small dark Totesee, the Dead Lake, lying beside the road as if someone had set down a slab of slate. Meiringen is the nearest proper town, a good twenty kilometres of road behind you, and Andermatt is about the same distance the other way.

The approach from the west is one of the great climbs for a motorbike. You leave the Aare valley at Innertkirchen and work up past the reservoirs of the Oberhasli power company, where the water is that unreal milky green, and the hairpins stack up on the last rise to the pass. The surface is good, the bends are wide enough to find a rhythm, and in the early morning there is almost nobody on it. By eleven on a summer Saturday you will be sharing it with every sports car and coach in central Switzerland, so leave early or accept the company.

This is a watershed in the plain sense: rain falling on one side ends up in the North Sea via the Aare and the Rhine, and on the other the Rhone carries it to the Mediterranean. The old mule track over the Grimsel was a trade and pilgrim route for centuries, and the hospice at the western foot was a famous stop long before the road. Walkers still cross by the old paths. Marmots whistle from the scree below the road, and with luck you will see ibex higher up on the crags.

A little restaurant is usually open near the top in season for coffee and a heavy slice of something. The pass is shut by snow from late autumn into early summer, and even in July the wind up here can turn raw within minutes, so keep a warm layer in the bag. Take five minutes at the Totesee before you drop down towards the Rhone glacier.
t.grimsel pass point 5@46.6,8.4:
Below the summit on the Valais side the Grimsel changes character completely. The road leaves the polished granite and drops in a run of tight hairpins toward Gletsch, a tiny cluster of buildings at 1,757 metres where three roads meet: the Grimsel you have just come down, the Furka climbing east, and the long valley of the Rhone heading away south-west. Andermatt and Airolo are each roughly twenty kilometres from here as the crow flies, but the crow does not have to do the Furka.

For a rider this is the more playful side. The descent is short, steep and very twisty, with views opening out across the Goms and, if the light is right, the pale tongue of the Rhone glacier coming into sight as you reach the valley floor. The glacier has retreated a very long way over the last century and a half; the old hotel at Gletsch was built when the ice came down almost to its doorstep, and in summer the surrounding slopes are now covered with tarpaulins to slow the melt of the ice cave tourists walk into. It is a strange thing to see, and a sober one.

Gletsch itself is a place of hotels from the grand age of Alpine travel, when coaches ran between railheads over the passes. Some stand empty, one or two are open in season, and the little steam railway that works the Furka line from nearby Oberwald is a reminder of how the area used to be reached. Cheese and cold meats and strong coffee are what you will find, not fine dining, and that suits a rider with the Furka still ahead.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There are no big towns at this junction, so top up before the Grimsel or in Andermatt on the far side of the Furka, and treat the small villages down the Goms as a fallback rather than a promise. All three passes here close for winter, usually from late October until around June, and snow can still fall at any time in summer on the heights. Take your time on the downhill: the bends are blind in places and cyclists crawl up the other way in numbers.
t.furka grimsel susten pass loop point 2@4:
The Furka Pass tops out at 2,429 metres, and the summit is a bare, windy saddle where the road passes between the Urseren valley and the upper Valais. The point lies right on that ridge, and the experience is as dramatic as the number suggests. On the south side the road drops in long, open switchbacks toward Realp and Andermatt, and on the north-west it falls toward Gletsch and the Rhône valley. Snow banks beside the road well into July are normal.

Many people know this pass as the one in the James Bond film Goldfinger, where Bond's Aston Martin chases an Alfa Romeo along the hairpins in the 1964 film. The scene was filmed on the pass, and the old Hotel Belvédère, just below the summit, was a landmark of it, though it was closed for years and its fortunes have been mixed. The pass is still the same: wide, bare and exposed, with the glacier-carved landscape stretching far in every direction.

The road is narrow in places and has no guardrail at some of the outer edges, so respect the drops. The surface is generally good, but frost damage leaves patches of rough asphalt, and cattle sometimes wander across the road. It is steep and tight enough that you want to be in a low gear on the descent, and the brakes get hot. A good rule is to ride it in the morning, when the road is quiet, rather than at midday, when traffic and heat combine. Weather changes fast: a clear start can end in cloud, rain or even snow within an hour, and the temperature at the top is often ten degrees colder than in the valley.

The Rhône Glacier lies near the western side, and the river that begins from its melt flows all the way to the Mediterranean. Stop, turn off the engine and listen. At this altitude the quiet is broken only by wind and water.
t.furka grimsel susten pass loop point 3@4:
The Grimsel Pass is a notch in the ridge between the Haslital to the north and the upper Rhône valley to the south, at 2,164 metres, and its character is dominated by water. All around are lakes, some natural, some dammed, and the high granite is smooth and grey, polished by ice into long, bare slabs. The Grimsel is among the most beautiful of the Swiss passes, in part because of this stark, rounded shape.

The summit area has a small hospice, a lake and a cluster of buildings, and a little further along is the Totensee, the Lake of the Dead, which takes its name from a battle in 1799 when French and Austrian troops fought across the pass during the Napoleonic wars. Whether or not the name carries all that weight, it makes you think. The pass has long been a trade route, used by traders and pilgrims, and the old stone paving of the mule track can still be seen in places.

Riders will find a good road here. It is wider than the Furka and less hair-raising, with long open bends, and the surface is mostly smooth. On the northern side, the descent goes through a series of fast curves above the Grimsel reservoirs, and the views of the dams and blue water are remarkable. The wind can be strong on the summit, and the cold can bite, so keep a layer in the top box. Fuel is not available at the top, and you need to remember that the last proper stations are in the valleys, Meiringen to the north and the Goms villages to the south.

Hydropower has shaped this landscape; the dams of the Oberhasli are among the largest in Switzerland, and the power lines and cable cars you can see are part of that story. The rock, a hard granite, has also made the region famous among climbers. Late afternoon is lovely, with the low sun lighting the granite a warm gold, and the traffic quieter. Take a few minutes at the lake, just to look. Then ride on, because the descent is a long one.
t.three passes loop susten grimsel furka p:
The Grimsel Pass is one of the great engineering landscapes of the Alps, a high granite country where glaciers, dams and lakes have been fitted together into a kind of outdoor power station. The summit sits at 2,164 metres, and the road climbs to it from Meiringen through the narrow Haslital valley, passing the Handeck waterfall, where the Aare drops some distance in a single leap, and the cable-car and funicular stations that lead to remote reservoirs.

The granite itself is the star. Smoothed and polished by glaciers into rounded humps and shining slabs, the rock lines the road and the shores of the lakes, and its pale grey colour gives the whole landscape an austere, cold beauty. The Grimsel Hospiz, a traditional mountain inn, has stood near the top for centuries, serving travellers on the old mule track that connected the Bernese Oberland to the Valais and Italy. Dams at Räterichsboden and Oberaar hold back turquoise lakes, and the water they release powers turbines deep within the mountain. The nearby Gelmerbahn, an extremely steep funicular, climbs to a small lake in minutes.

The road is a joy to ride. The bends are wide and well banked, the surface is good, and the views of lakes, rock and glaciers open up with each corner.
