Traffic is heavy in summer, with cars, buses and motorcyclists, and the road can become congested at weekends. Mornings are better, and so are weekdays. The weather can change quickly, and cloud often settles on the summit, so carry waterproofs and a warm layer. In late spring and early summer, snow walls may line the road.

The pass is usually open from about June to October, though dates vary with snowfall, and the road is closed in winter. The Hospiz and several restaurants near the dams serve hot food, and a plate of rösti or a bowl of soup is welcome in the thin air.

The vegetation is sparse, with mosses, lichens and hardy alpine flowers growing in cracks between the stones. Marmots are common, and chamois and ibex can sometimes be spotted on the slopes. The air is cold, clean and still, except when the wind rises.

Gletsch is hardly a village at all, but a crossroads in a bleak, windswept bowl where the Grimsel and Furka roads meet, and where, for a long time, the Rhône Glacier filled the valley above it. The glacier gives birth to the Rhône, one of the great rivers of Europe, which begins here as a milky meltwater stream before running through the Valais, Lake Geneva and France to the Mediterranean. The glacier was once so large that it reached almost to the hotel, and photographs from a century ago show a wall of ice where there is now a grey, stony slope.

The retreat of the glacier is one of the most visible effects of climate change in the Alps. Today the ice has pulled back up the valley, and its surface is covered with white blankets during the summer to slow the melt. An ice grotto, carved into the glacier, is open to visitors in summer, and walking through it gives a sense of the ice's blue light and the cold. The old Hotel Glacier du Rhône, a grand building from the days of nineteenth-century tourism, stands at the bottom of the hairpins, and its terrace is a place to sit and watch the traffic.

The riding between Gletsch and the Furka is a series of tight hairpins, climbing the head of the valley in tiers, with the glacier on the other side. The road is narrow in places, and the drop is steep, with limited barriers, so take care. The surface is generally good, though frost heave and patches can occur. Traffic is thick in summer, and weekend crowds can slow progress. Avoid the middle of the day, when tour buses are most frequent, and go early or late.

The area was a stop on the old pilgrim and trade routes between the Valais and the Bernese Oberland, and the Grimsel and Furka passes have been crossed since Roman times. The locals, Walser and Valaisans, built their villages and hospices to serve travellers, and the stone architecture of the area reflects the harsh climate.

Fill up before the climb in Andermatt, Meiringen or Obergoms, and bring warm clothes, because the wind from the glacier is bitter even in summer. Check the pass opening dates, as the roads are closed by snow for much of the year.
t.nufenen pass road point 1@46.5,8.3:
Ulrichen is the first village you meet when the Nufenen Pass road leaves the Rhône valley, and the valley it sits in is one of the quietest and most characterful in Switzerland. This is the Goms, the upper reach of the Valais, a long, flat-bottomed trough just a kilometre or so wide, with the young Rhône winding through it and steep forested slopes on both sides. The villages are clusters of dark larch houses, burnt almost black by the sun, perched on stone stilts to keep the mice from the grain, and the church towers are slender and white.

The Goms is also the home of cross-country skiing in Switzerland. In winter, dozens of kilometres of trails run along the valley floor, and the Goms marathon is among the best known races in the country. In summer the valley is a haven of hay meadows, wildflowers and quiet. The people here are Walser, descended from a medieval group of German-speaking settlers who moved across the Alps and who have a reputation for toughness and independence, and the local dialect is among the oldest forms of Swiss German.

The ride up the valley from Brig or Fiesch is an easy, relaxed run along the Rhône. The road is smooth and well surfaced, with gentle bends, and there is little traffic apart from the occasional tourist or trucker. The mountains close in as you go, and the sky seems larger, and the air gets cooler. The road to the Nufenen leaves the valley at Ulrichen, climbing steeply through a series of hairpins to a high alpine plateau.

Ulrichen is small, with just a few hundred residents, but it has the essentials, including a place to eat and a guesthouse. Fuel may be available in the valley, but options are limited, and the sensible plan is to arrive with a full tank from Brig, the nearest large town, or from the main road. The pass is the highest in Switzerland to lie entirely within its borders, and there are no services on it.

Weather in the Goms is often fine when the weather elsewhere is poor, because the valley lies in a rain shadow, and it is known for its sunny climate. Mornings are crisp, afternoons can bring thunderstorms, and the road to the pass is closed in winter, normally from about October to June, depending on snow.
t.near meiringen@46.7,8.2:
Above Meiringen the Hasli valley opens out, and this spot lies on the slopes between the town and the Brünig, the low pass that carries the road over to Lungern and Obwalden. Below, the Aare runs flat and straight across the valley floor toward Lake Brienz, and above rise the steep walls of the Bernese Oberland, with the Wetterhorn and Engelhörner peering over the ridge to the south. It is a place where several of the great Swiss passes come together.

Meiringen is famous for two things, one real and one fictional. The real one is meringue, which according to local tradition was invented by a pastry cook here, though the claim is disputed, and you can still buy giant meringues with whipped cream in the town's bakeries. The fictional one is Sherlock Holmes, who met his apparent death at the Reichenbach Falls just above town in a struggle with Professor Moriarty in a story by Arthur Conan Doyle. The falls are reached by a funicular, and there is a small Sherlock Holmes museum in town and a statue of the detective.

Also worth seeing is the Aare Gorge, the Aareschlucht, just east of Meiringen, where the river has cut a narrow, deep slot through a limestone barrier, and a walkway clings to the walls above the rushing water.

For riders, Meiringen is a crossroads. To the south, the road climbs past Innertkirchen to the Grimsel Pass at 2,164 metres, a spectacular route past dams and lakes and bare granite. To the east, the Susten Pass climbs to 2,224 metres, with beautiful sweeping curves, tunnels and views of glaciers. To the west, the Brünig is lower and gentler, but has its own pleasant curves and views over Lake Lungern. High passes are generally open only from early summer to autumn, so check before you go.

Meiringen has fuel, supermarkets, cafes and hotels. Sarnen, about twenty kilometres west over the Brünig, is the nearest larger town. In summer, expect plenty of other bikes on the roads and plenty of tourists in town, and an evening coffee in Meiringen, with a meringue, is an easy pleasure.
t.near bouvesse quirieu on the way back@45:
Where the Rhône swings around the northern edge of the Isle Crémieu, the river runs wide and green between limestone cliffs, with the Bugey hills rising on the far bank, and the villages of Bouvesse-Quirieu, Montalieu-Vercieu and Hières-sur-Amby sit along its southern side. It is a quiet corner, an hour from Lyon, that most people never think about, and on a hot day it is exactly where you want to be.

The swimming is real. At Montalieu-Vercieu there is a large leisure area on the Rhône with a supervised beach in summer, set on a broad stretch of slow water held back by the river works, and it is popular with families from Lyon on weekends. Away from managed areas, keep out of the main river: the current is strong and cold, and the hydroelectric works upstream can change levels without warning.

High above the river at Quirieu are the remains of a medieval fortified town that once guarded the crossing and the border between the Dauphiné and Savoy. Little is left except broken walls and a sense of space, but the view from the cliff edge over the Rhône is superb. Not far away, the plateau of Larina above Hières-sur-Amby is an archaeological site with traces of settlement from prehistory to the early Middle Ages, and at La Balme-les-Grottes a cave system has drawn visitors for centuries, including, legend says, the bandit Mandrin, who is supposed to have hidden there.

The Isle Crémieu itself is a limestone plateau of small lakes, marshes, woods and stone villages, crossed by narrow lanes that twist around rocky outcrops, ideal for riding at an easy pace. Crémieu, with its medieval market hall and old gates, is a lovely place for lunch. Across the Rhône, the roads into the Bugey climb steeply in hairpins to viewpoints above the river. The local stone has been quarried here for centuries, and you will see it in walls and farm buildings everywhere.

Montalieu has shops and basic services, and Tignieu, about fourteen kilometres away towards Lyon, is the nearest town of over five thousand people, with fuel and supermarkets. Arrive in late afternoon in summer, swim while the sun is still on the water, and the ride back to Lyon in the evening light will feel like a holiday.
t.near gaggiano@45.4,9.1:
Gaggiano is a canal town, which is not something people expect on the outskirts of Milan. The Naviglio Grande runs straight through it, a broad, slow, green waterway dug in the Middle Ages to bring water and goods from the Ticino river to the city, and along its banks stand old villas with gardens down to the water, a church, a few bars and an iron footbridge. Just under seven thousand people live here, and on a warm evening half of them seem to be walking or cycling along the towpath.

The canal is the story. It was begun in the twelfth century and was one of the first navigable canals in Europe, and for centuries it carried salt, timber, grain and stone into Milan. The marble for the Duomo came this way, floated down from quarries near Lake Maggiore, and barges marked "AUF", for "ad usum fabricae", were allowed through without paying tolls. Wealthy Milanese families built summer villas along the banks in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and you can still see many of them as you ride along the canal road towards Abbiategrasso and Robecco.

Around Gaggiano lies the Parco Agricolo Sud Milano, a huge protected belt of farmland, rice fields, irrigation ditches and old fortified farmhouses called cascine. In late spring, when the paddies are flooded, the land becomes a mirror, reflecting the sky and the poplars, with herons and egrets stalking in the water. About fifteen kilometres south-west, the Cistercian abbey of Morimondo, founded by monks from Burgundy in the twelfth century, stands in this landscape like a brick ship, plain and beautiful.

As a finish to a Dolomites trip, it is a soft landing after a long day on the motorway across the Po plain. The canal road is narrow and slow, with cyclists and pedestrians, so take it easy, and in summer evenings the mosquitoes are relentless near the water. In winter, thick fog often lies over the plain, sometimes for days, and visibility can drop to almost nothing. There is fuel, food and coffee in Gaggiano and in Trezzano sul Naviglio nearby, and the city is only a short ride east. Stop at a bar by the water, order an aperitivo and watch the canal slide by; it is a very Milanese way to end the journey.
t.roasio@45.6,8.3:
Roasio sits on the last low hills before the Alps, between Gattinara and Biella in northern Piedmont, a village of around two and a half thousand people spread across a few hamlets, with vineyards on the slopes above and the flat rice plain of Vercelli stretching south below. On clear days, Monte Rosa rises enormous and white to the north-west, and it is hard to concentrate on anything else.

This is a quiet wine corner with a great grape. The Nebbiolo, the variety behind Barolo and Barbaresco further south, is grown here too, on soils of porphyry and old volcanic rock, and the local wines, Bramaterra, Lessona and above all Gattinara, are elegant, firm and long-lived, though much less famous than their southern cousins. Roasio lies inside the Bramaterra zone, and the small producers in the area often sell from the door. In autumn, during the harvest, the lanes smell of crushed grapes.

The riding is excellent and still under the radar. The roads climbing north from the plain towards the Valsesia and the Biella hills are narrow and twisting, through chestnut woods, vineyards and small villages, with tight bends, short steep climbs and good views back over the plain. The surface is generally fair, with patches and gravel in places. Head west towards Biella and you reach the Ricetto di Candelo, a remarkable medieval fortified village built to store grain and wine, and beyond it the road climbs to the great sanctuary of Oropa in the mountains. Head east and you are soon in Gattinara, a town with a long main street, arcades and a tower on the hill above, the Torre delle Castelle, a landmark visible for miles.

Roasio has a fuel station and small shops, and if you need more, Gattinara is about six kilometres away, with supermarkets, bars, restaurants and wine shops. Coffee in a bar in the village is a simple pleasure, and you may find yourself chatting with old men who have farmed these hills all their lives.

The best times are spring, with wild cherry blossom and fresh green, and autumn, with gold and red leaves and the smell of wine. Summer can be hot and humid on the plain, with sudden thunderstorms in the afternoon, so ride early and keep an eye on the sky over the mountains.
t.neustadt@49.4,8.1:
Neustadt an der Weinstraße sits where the wooded hills of the Palatinate Forest drop down to the wide, sunny plain of the Rhine, and it is the unofficial capital of the German Wine Route, which runs for about eighty-five kilometres along the edge of the hills from the French border to the north. The town has an old centre of half-timbered houses, narrow lanes and wine taverns, and around it vineyards stretch in every direction, with small wine villages like Gimmeldingen and Haardt just above the town.

Above Neustadt, on a wooded hill, stands Hambach Castle, and it holds a special place in German history. In May 1832, about thirty thousand people marched up to the castle to demand freedom, democracy and national unity, waving black, red and gold flags, and the Hambach Festival is remembered as the birth of the German democratic movement. The castle has a museum telling the story, and the view over the plain and the vineyards from the walls is superb.

The town is also the home of German wine celebrations. Every autumn, the German Wine Harvest Festival in Neustadt crowns the German Wine Queen, and the streets fill with stalls, music and wine. The Palatinate is one of Germany's largest wine regions, known for its Riesling, but also for Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir and other varieties, and the climate here is so mild that almonds, figs and even lemons grow in sheltered gardens. Try a glass of wine with Saumagen, a stuffed pig's stomach that is the local speciality.

The riding is varied. The Wine Route itself is a gentle road through vineyards and villages, often busy with cars, cyclists and tourists, especially during harvest season. The roads into the Palatinate Forest are much more exciting, with tight curves, steep climbs and long stretches through beech and pine woods. The Kalmit, at 673 metres the highest peak in the forest, has a winding road to the summit, popular with riders. However, some roads in the area have speed limits and noise restrictions because of complaints from residents, so ride responsibly.

Neustadt has fuel, food and every service, and it is a lively town with plenty of places to eat and drink. Stop at a wine tavern, sit under a vine-covered pergola and enjoy a glass of Riesling with something hearty.
t.sitten@46.2,7.4:
Two hills rise from the floor of the Rhône valley at Sion, and on top of each stands a medieval landmark: the fortified church of Valère on one, the ruined castle of Tourbillon on the other. They give the capital of the Valais one of the most striking skylines in Switzerland, and around them the old town, with its narrow lanes, squares and cafés, has a relaxed, almost southern feel. Sitten is the German name; most locals speak French and call it Sion.

The Valère basilica holds a treasure: an organ that is one of the oldest playable organs in the world, built in the fifteenth century, and concerts are still held on it in summer. The town was the seat of powerful bishops, who ruled the Valais for centuries, and the Tourbillon castle was their stronghold until it burned in the eighteenth century. From the top of either hill, the view over the valley, the vineyards and the mountains is superb.

This is the heart of Swiss wine country. The Rhône valley is one of the sunniest and driest places in Switzerland, and its slopes are covered with vineyards on steep terraces held up by dry stone walls, some of them centuries old. The local wines include Fendant, made from Chasselas, as well as Petite Arvine, Cornalin and Humagne, varieties found almost only here. For centuries, the farmers have brought water from the glaciers through irrigation channels called bisses, which run along the mountainsides, and many of them can be followed on foot.

The riding around Sion is excellent. Roads climb from the valley floor to the villages on the slopes, with tight hairpins and views over the valley, and some continue into the side valleys, such as the Val d'Hérens, with its strange earth pillars, the Pyramides d'Euseigne, or to the Col du Sanetsch, a high road to a dam and a lake. The main valley road is busy, and the motorway requires a vignette, which applies to motorcycles too. Watch for vineyard tractors and cyclists on the narrow roads.

Sion has fuel, food and every service, and the old town has plenty of restaurants. Try raclette, the cheese dish of the Valais, melted and scraped onto potatoes, with a glass of Fendant.
t.wissembourg@49.1,8.0:
The German Wine Road begins, or ends, depending on which way you are pointed, at a gate. In Schweigen-Rechtenbach, a wine village pressed right up against the French border, stands the Deutsches Weintor, a heavy stone arch built in the 1930s to mark the southern terminus of the Weinstrasse. It is a slightly pompous thing, very much of its time, and today it houses a wine bar and a viewing gallery from which you look out over vineyards rolling north toward the Haardt hills. A couple of kilometres south, across a border you will barely notice, lies Wissembourg in Alsace.

Ride down into Wissembourg if you have an hour. It is a small, handsome French town of about nine thousand people with half-timbered houses leaning over the little river Lauter, a big Gothic abbey church dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul, and remnants of the old ramparts. The town has been fought over more than once. In August 1870 the first battle of the Franco-Prussian War was fought on the heights just south of it, and the Lines of Wissembourg, a chain of earthworks, ran along the Lauter in the eighteenth century. Today the only thing that changes at the border is the language on the bakery signs and the price of fuel, which is often worth comparing.

For riders, this end of the Weinstrasse is the gentle overture. The road runs through the vineyards at the foot of the Palatinate Forest, the Pfälzerwald, which rises on your left as a dark wooded wall of red sandstone. If you want proper curves, the forest is where they are: small roads climb west into the trees toward Bad Bergzabern and the castles around Dahn, with crags of red rock and plenty of switchbacks. Back on the wine road, the pace is slow, villages come every few kilometres, and in autumn you will share it with tractors hauling grapes and walkers holding glasses of Federweisser, the cloudy young wine sold in September and October.

The southern Palatinate is one of the warmest corners of Germany, and you see it in the plants: figs, almonds and even the odd lemon tree in a sheltered courtyard. In March the almond blossom turns the hillsides pink. Fuel, food and coffee are easy here, in Wissembourg or in the larger villages along the road, and the local Pfälzer cooking is hearty: Saumagen, a stuffed pig's stomach that sounds worse than it is, and Flammkuchen once you cross into Alsace.
t.landau in der pfalz@49.2,8.1:
Landau is the town the Weinstrasse orbits without ever quite touching. With some forty thousand people it is the largest place in the southern Palatinate, and the wine villages that string along the foot of the hills a few kilometres to the west, Birkweiler, Siebeldingen, Frankweiler, all look to it for shopping, schools and trains. It sits on the flat plain of the Rhine rift, so there is nothing dramatic about the ride in, but it is the obvious place in this stretch to refuel, eat properly and sort out anything the bike needs.

The town has a past bigger than it looks. Landau was a free imperial city, then a French fortress for well over a century after the Thirty Years' War, and Louis XIV's engineer Vauban redesigned it into a star-shaped stronghold. Two of his town gates survive, the French Gate and the German Gate, along with stretches of fortification in the parks. After 1815 it went to Bavaria, which ruled the Palatinate until after the Second World War, and the broad streets and big squares owe something to both French and Bavarian planners. The ring of boulevards where the walls used to stand makes the town easy to cross.

There is also a word in the dictionary that came from here: the landau, the four-wheeled carriage with a folding roof, takes its name from the town. And the town claims a share of the region's wine identity, since it is one of the largest wine-growing municipalities in Germany once its incorporated villages, such as Nussdorf and Arzheim, are counted.

For the riding, Landau is a hub rather than a destination. The wine road proper runs along the Haardt edge a short hop west, and from there the roads into the Pfälzerwald are the real reward: the climb through the Queichtal toward Annweiler and the Trifels castle, where the English king Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in the 1190s, is a fine piece of riding with steady curves through beech and pine. On the plain itself traffic can be heavy at commuting times, and the town has the usual German speed controls, so keep to the limits inside the ring.

Practically, everything is here: fuel stations on the main roads in and out, supermarkets, cafes around the market square and the Rathausplatz, and bakeries selling the pretzel-shaped breakfast that keeps a rider going until lunch. If you are crossing the Palatinate in late summer, look out for the wine festivals that fill almost every weekend in the surrounding villages.
t.near heidesheim@49.6,8.2:
Bockenheim marks the northern end of the Deutsche Weinstrasse, and if you have ridden it from the French border you have come about eighty-five kilometres through almost unbroken vineyards. The village has its own counterpart to the stone gate at the southern end: the Haus der Deutschen Weinstrasse, a building that straddles the road like a gatehouse, so you literally ride through it. It is a quieter monument than the one at Schweigen, and the village around it is a working wine place rather than a showpiece, with farmyards, cellars and a few taverns.

The landscape here is softer and more open than further south. The Palatinate Forest has dwindled to low wooded hills on the western horizon, and the land rolls out in long gentle swells toward Rheinhessen, which begins just across the state line to the north. On a clear day you can see across the Rhine plain to the hills of the Odenwald on the far side. It is wide country, good for light: the evening sun comes in low over the vines and catches the dust kicked up by tractors at harvest. The soils change too, from the sandstone of the south to limestone and loess, and growers will tell you that this shows in the wine.

The riding is calm. Roads are narrow but well surfaced, linking villages such as Kindenheim and Obrigheim through the vineyards, with short climbs and plenty of blind farm junctions. It is not a place for speed, and in September and October you will meet grape harvesters, which are tall, slow and occasionally drop mud on corners. If you want something livelier after the long run up the wine road, the small roads west into the Leininger Land, toward Altleiningen and its castle, give you proper woodland curves and a change of scenery.

There is little in Bockenheim itself beyond wine taverns and a bakery, so look to the larger places around it for fuel, such as Grünstadt a few kilometres south or the towns on the main road. Heidesheim, the name on the label, is a nearby town just over the border in Rheinhessen. The local wines are mostly whites, Riesling, Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau, with a growing number of reds, and the taverns open their doors in the warm months with plain local food. Taste in the evening, not between bends: Germany's alcohol limit is strict for new riders, and nobody should be weaving through vineyards on wine.
t.near baden baden@48.7,8.2:
Baden-Baden is where the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse begins its climb, and this stretch just south-east of the spa town is the moment the road leaves the parks and villas behind and starts to work. The B500 rises out of the valley through mixed woods of beech and fir, gaining height steadily in long, well-cambered bends, with the occasional tighter hairpin and glimpses back over the Rhine plain. Within a few kilometres you have gone from a town of colonnades and casinos to the cool, resin-scented air of the northern Black Forest.

The town below is worth knowing about even if you only pass through. Baden-Baden was built on hot springs, first used by the Romans, and in the nineteenth century it became one of the great resorts of Europe, the place where Russian aristocrats, French writers and German royalty came to take the waters and lose money at the casino. Dostoevsky gambled there and turned the experience into a novel. The Kurhaus, the Friedrichsbad bathhouse and the Lichtentaler Allee, a long avenue of parkland along the little river Oos, still give the place an air of faded grandeur. In 2021 it was listed by UNESCO as one of the Great Spa Towns of Europe.

The road up from here is famous, and that brings its own problems. On sunny weekends from spring to autumn it is busy with motorcycles, sports cars and coaches heading for the viewpoints, and the police take a close interest. Speed checks are common and parts of the route have had weekend restrictions on noise and speed in the past, so ride with a little restraint. The tarmac is good, but the forest keeps some corners damp and shady long after the sun has dried the open stretches, and in early spring and late autumn fog can roll in without warning.

As you climb you pass the old grand hotels on the ridge, Bühlerhöhe and Plättig, which once received guests from all over Europe, and trailheads where walkers set off toward the summits. The views west over the Rhine valley to the Vosges in France are best in the late afternoon. For fuel and food, fill up in Baden-Baden or Bühl before the climb, since the high road itself has hotels and restaurants but no great choice of filling stations. In winter, snow comes early up here, so check conditions if you are riding between November and April.
t.near biberach@48.6,8.2:
This is the high middle of the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse, where the road runs along the crest at more than a thousand metres and the Hornisgrinde, the highest summit of the northern Black Forest, rises just to the north. Right beside the road lies the Mummelsee, a small dark lake of glacial origin set in a hollow of fir trees. It is the stop everyone makes, which is both its charm and its problem: on summer weekends the car park is full, coaches line up, and the lakeside hotel and shop do a roaring trade in Black Forest cake and cuckoo clocks.

The lake has a legend that suits its colour. Local folklore says it is home to water sprites, the Mummeln, and that a king of the lake lives in its depths and punishes anyone who throws stones into it. The stories go back centuries and were picked up by writers of the Romantic era, including the poet Eduard Mörike. Today it is simply cold, clear and pretty, best seen early in the morning before the crowds arrive, when mist lies over the water and the forest is silent.

The Hornisgrinde itself is worth the short walk if you have the time. Its summit is a flat moorland plateau with boardwalks through the heather and bog, an odd and lovely landscape for the Black Forest, with a television tower and an old signal tower, and from the top you look down over the Rhine plain to Strasbourg's cathedral and the Vosges on a clear day. The weather up here changes fast: the crest gets more rain and fog than the valleys below, and the temperature can be ten degrees lower than in Baden-Baden.

For riders this stretch is all about rhythm. The road is broad, well surfaced and fast, with long sweepers through the forest and open views where windthrow and storms have thinned the trees. Its popularity means busy weekends and regular police controls, so keep an eye on the speed. Down the western side, small roads drop steeply to Seebach, Sasbachwalden and the vineyards of the Ortenau, with hairpins and tight wooded bends, a good detour if you want something more technical. There are restaurants and cafes along the crest, but for fuel look to the valley towns such as Kappelrodeck, Achern or Bühl, which are a twenty-minute descent away.
t.near oppenau@48.5,8.2:
South of the Ruhestein the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse runs along the high ground between the Schliffkopf and the Kniebis plateau, and the forest feels wilder here than further north. Much of this ridge lies in the Black Forest National Park, created in 2014, where large areas are being left to grow without forestry. You see the results from the saddle: grey snags of storm-felled trees, dense young growth, open patches of heather and grass on the old high pastures called Grinden, where cattle once grazed. It is not a manicured landscape, and that is the point.

The road is fast and open along the crest, with long curves and good sightlines, and in places the trees fall away to give you views east over the endless wooded ridges of the Black Forest and west toward the Rhine. The Schliffkopf has a hotel and a car park with a fine outlook, and the Kniebis at the southern end has a scattering of guesthouses and was once a fortified pass where armies crossed between the Rhine and the Danube valleys. Old earthworks, the Schwedenschanze, date back to the Thirty Years' War and later conflicts.

Just below the ridge to the west lie the Allerheiligen waterfalls and the ruins of the Allerheiligen monastery, a Premonstratensian house founded around 1200 in a deep side valley. The roofless Gothic walls of the church stand among the trees, and the falls drop through a narrow gorge in a series of cascades with steps and walkways beside them. It is one of the most atmospheric places in the northern Black Forest, and the road down to it is narrow, twisting and steep, a good test of low-speed control. From there the valley continues down to Oppenau, a small town of about five thousand people in the Rench valley.

Weather matters at this height. Fog often sits on the crest when the valleys are clear, and in spring and autumn wet leaves and damp patches linger in the shady bends. The ridge is popular with bikers in summer and the police are a regular presence. For fuel, food and supplies, drop down to Oppenau or further to Oberkirch, a larger town of about twenty thousand known for its fruit brandies, or east to Freudenstadt, whose huge central market square is one of the largest in Germany. Bad Peterstal-Griesbach, a small spa town with mineral springs, is another quiet option for coffee on the way south.
t.near embrach@47.6,8.6:
North of Zurich, in the quiet countryside between the airport and the Rhine, the Töss river runs its last few kilometres through a wooded valley before joining the big river at Tössegg. Around Freienstein and Rorbas the valley is narrow and steep-sided, with mixed forest of beech and spruce, and the ruins of Freienstein Castle sit on a wooded spur above the village. It is a surprisingly wild corner for a place so close to Switzerland's largest city, and it is where many Zurich riders go for a short afternoon loop.

To the west rises the Irchel, a long, wooded ridge with walking trails and a tower on top, and the roads that cross it and run along its flanks are small, twisty and fun, through forest and farmland with views across to the Black Forest on a clear day. The villages here, Freienstein, Rorbas, Teufen and Berg am Irchel, are farming communities with half-timbered houses, orchards and vineyards on the sunny slopes. The Zürcher Weinland, the wine country of the canton, begins just to the north.

The riding is gentle and varied, with plenty of curves and short climbs, but the roads are narrow and you share them with tractors, cyclists and walkers, especially on weekends. The Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, and the fines are high, so keep an eye on the speedometer. The Töss itself is popular for swimming in summer, with pools and gravel banks along the river, and the confluence with the Rhine at Tössegg has a small ferry and a restaurant where boats on the Rhine stop.

Embrach, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Bülach, a little further west, is larger and well stocked, and Winterthur, to the east, is a big city with plenty of culture and good museums. If you have time, ride north to the Rhine and follow it to the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen, the largest waterfall in Europe by volume, which is about twenty kilometres away and makes a spectacular stop on the Grand Tour.
t.near diessenhofen@47.7,8.8:
A covered wooden bridge, a medieval town gate and a river the colour of bottle glass: Diessenhofen is the kind of small Swiss town that makes you wonder why you are in such a hurry. It sits on the south bank of the Rhine in the canton of Thurgau, between Stein am Rhein and Schaffhausen, and the wooden bridge across to Gailingen in Germany is one of the loveliest border crossings anywhere, a long, dim timber gallery where your footsteps or your exhaust echo off the beams. The old town behind it is compact, with painted facades, oriel windows and a clock tower over the main street.

The canton is famous for its apples and pears, and in autumn the roadside stands sell fresh juice and cider. Just upstream from Diessenhofen, on a bend of the Rhine, stands the former Dominican convent of St. Katharinental, founded in the thirteenth century, with a baroque church that is one of the finest in the region. Across the river, the German village of Büsingen is a curiosity: a German exclave entirely surrounded by Swiss territory, where the euro and the Swiss franc are both used and the postcode is Swiss as well as German.

The riding is relaxed. The roads between the villages are small, well surfaced and gently curving, with little traffic, and the route along the Rhine toward Stein am Rhein or Schaffhausen is lovely, with views over the water and the wooded hills on the German side. Speed limits are strictly enforced in Switzerland, and the villages have plenty of 30 km/h zones and cameras. In summer the river is full of swimmers floating downstream in the current, and boats run between Schaffhausen and Kreuzlingen.

Fuel is easy to find: Diessenhofen has a station, and across the border, Gottmadingen and the German towns often have cheaper petrol, though you need to remember the customs rules if you are carrying goods. Stein am Rhein, about ten kilometres east, is one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Switzerland, with painted houses around its main square, and Schaffhausen, ten kilometres west, has the Munot fortress and the Rhine Falls nearby. For a quiet break, the riverside restaurants in Diessenhofen are a good bet, especially for fish from the Rhine.
t.near samedan@46.6,9.9:
The Upper Engadine is the high valley where the Inn begins its long journey to the Danube, and around Samedan and Celerina it is at its most open: a flat valley floor at more than 1,700 metres, broad meadows, the river meandering between larch woods, and mountains on both sides rising to glaciers. The light here is famous. Painters such as Giovanni Segantini came for it in the nineteenth century, and the dry, clear air gives the valley more sunshine than almost anywhere in Switzerland. In autumn the larches turn gold, and the whole valley glows.

Samedan is the administrative centre of the Upper Engadine, a village of about three thousand people with traditional Engadine houses: thick stone walls, deep-set windows and facades decorated with sgraffito, patterns scratched into the plaster. The language here is Romansh, the fourth national language of Switzerland, and you will see it on signs and hear it in the shops. On the valley floor lies the Engadin airport, often called the highest in Europe, used mostly by private planes bringing visitors to St. Moritz. Celerina, a little further south, is the finish of the famous bobsleigh run from St. Moritz, which is rebuilt from natural ice each winter, and the Cresta Run, where riders hurtle head-first down an ice track on toboggans.

St. Moritz, about five kilometres away, needs little introduction: a glamorous ski resort since the nineteenth century, host of two Winter Olympics, with luxury hotels, designer shops and a frozen lake that hosts horse races and polo in winter. In summer it is quieter, and the lake and the walking trails are lovely.

For riders, the Upper Engadine is a crossroads of great passes. The Julier comes in from the north, the Maloja drops to Italy in a spectacular series of hairpins, the Bernina climbs toward Poschiavo and Tirano, and the Albula, one of the most beautiful passes in Switzerland, joins the valley at La Punt. The roads in the valley itself are well surfaced and fairly straight, but they fill up in the high seasons of summer and winter, and the speed limits are strictly enforced. The weather is changeable, and snow can fall at any time of year.

Samedan has fuel, shops, restaurants and cafes, and St. Moritz has everything you could need, at a price. For a cheaper option, try the cafes in the smaller villages, and order a slice of Engadiner Nusstorte, a rich walnut and caramel cake that keeps for weeks and travels well in a tank bag.
t.piazzatorre@46.0,9.7:
High up the Val Brembana, north of Bergamo, the valley narrows and the villages get smaller until you reach Piazzatorre, a little resort of a few hundred people on a sunny slope surrounded by spruce forest and meadows. In winter it has a modest ski area; in summer it is a place for walkers and families from the plains escaping the heat of Bergamo and Milan. For riders, it sits near the start of one of the finest climbs in the Bergamo Alps: the road over the Passo San Marco, which leaves the valley at Mezzoldo and climbs toward the Valtellina.

The San Marco has a long history. In the late sixteenth century the Republic of Venice, which then ruled Bergamo, built a mule road over the pass, the Via Priula, to connect its territory with the Grisons and the Valtellina without passing through Spanish-ruled Milan. It became an important trade route for goods and soldiers, and near the top stands the Ca' San Marco, an old stone inn and customs house that once sheltered travellers and still serves food today. The pass itself is close to 2,000 metres, and on the far side, the road drops in a long series of hairpins toward Morbegno.

The riding is excellent. The road up from Mezzoldo is narrow and steep, with tight hairpins, rough patches and little room for passing, but the scenery is superb, with views back down the valley and up to the rocky peaks of the Orobie. The descent to the Valtellina is longer and more open. It is a seasonal road, normally closed by snow from late autumn to late spring, so check before you go. Traffic is light on weekdays but can be heavy on summer weekends with motorcycles and cyclists. Lower down, the road along the Val Brembana passes through a series of villages and gorges, with tunnels and bridges, and can be busy.

The Val Brembana is known for its cheeses, including Branzi and Formai de Mut, and nearby valleys produce Taleggio. San Pellegrino Terme, further down the valley, is the spa town that gave its name to the famous mineral water, with an Art Nouveau casino and baths. For fuel, Piazzatorre has none of note, so fill up in the larger villages of the lower valley, such as Zogno or San Pellegrino, or in Morbegno on the other side of the pass, about eighteen kilometres away as the crow flies, but much further by road.
t.near airolo@46.5,8.6:
The nearest one climbs up from the Maggia side to Fusio, a stone village at the head of Val Lavizzara, and continues to the Sambuco dam, a curved concrete wall holding back a long reservoir. It is about as far from the bustle of the Gotthard as you can get while staying within a few kilometres of it.

For most riders on the Grand Tour, though, this part of Ticino is about Airolo and the Gotthard. Airolo sits at the southern foot of the pass, where the Tremola, the old cobbled road, comes down the mountain in a series of tight hairpins stacked one above the other. It is one of the most famous stretches of road in the Alps, paved with granite setts in the mid-twentieth century over a nineteenth-century route, and riding it is a rattling, slow and unforgettable experience. The modern road over the pass, wider and smoother, runs alongside, and the road tunnel underneath carries most of the traffic.

The Gotthard has been one of the key routes across the Alps since the thirteenth century, when the Schöllenen gorge on the northern side was made passable. Airolo has a museum dedicated to the history of the pass and the people who built its roads and tunnels, many of them Italian workers who died in accidents and of disease during the construction of the railway tunnel in the 1870s. A monument at the station remembers them.

Back in this high country, the weather is the main concern. Snow lies late on the ridges, storms build quickly on summer afternoons, and the minor roads close in winter. The roads up into the side valleys are narrow, steep and sometimes rough, with little traffic and few places to pass. Wildlife is plentiful: chamois, marmots and the occasional golden eagle. For fuel and food, Airolo is the nearest village with services, and Faido, further down the Leventina, has more. For a bigger town, Biasca is about thirty kilometres away. The Val Lavizzara side has small villages with bars, but plan your fuel carefully if you head that way.
t.near meiringen@46.6,8.3:
Between Innertkirchen and the Grimsel Pass, the Haslital is a narrow, steep valley of granite and forest, and this is where the road starts climbing in earnest. The landscape is raw and powerful, shaped by glaciers that filled the valley during the ice ages and left behind smooth, rounded slabs of granite that gleam in the sun.

The valley has been a route across the Alps for centuries, used by traders carrying goods between the Bernese Oberland and the Valais. Today it is dominated by hydroelectric power: the Grimsel area is home to a series of dams and reservoirs, with tunnels and power stations hidden inside the mountains, and you will see the power lines and the huge walls of the dams as you climb. Guttannen is a small village of stone and wood houses, with a crystal museum that displays the minerals found in the area, including some huge quartz crystals.

The Grimsel road is one of the great Alpine rides, with long, sweeping curves and tight hairpins, smooth tarmac and spectacular scenery. The climb from Guttannen to the top of the pass, at 2,164 metres, passes the Handegg falls, the Räterichsboden and Grimsel reservoirs and the old hospice on its rock in the middle of the lake. On summer weekends you share it with coaches, camper vans, cyclists and half the motorcycles of Switzerland, and the road is closed in winter, typically from October or November to late May or June. The weather can change quickly, and snow can fall at any time of year.

In the valley below, Meiringen is the main town, about thirteen kilometres away, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and it claims to be the birthplace of the meringue. It is also where Sherlock Holmes met his apparent end at the Reichenbach Falls, in Arthur Conan Doyle's story, and the town has a Sherlock Holmes museum. Innertkirchen, at the foot of the climb, has a station and a few restaurants, and is also the start of the Susten pass road. Guttannen has a small shop and a restaurant, but for fuel, fill up in Innertkirchen or Meiringen before you start the climb.
t.near leukerbad@46.4,7.6:
The road up to Leukerbad feels like it is going nowhere, and then it arrives at a wall. From Leuk in the Rhône valley, it climbs north through the Dala gorge, past the village of Inden, in a series of hairpins and tunnels cut into the rock, and finally opens into a high basin at about 1,400 metres, ringed by sheer limestone cliffs that rise more than a thousand metres above the village. The wall of rock is the Gemmi, and the only way over it, unless you take the cable car, is a footpath carved into the face.

Leukerbad is a spa town, and its hot springs have been used since Roman times. Around three million litres of thermal water flow out of the ground every day, at temperatures up to about fifty degrees, and the village has several large public baths, both indoor and outdoor, where you can soak with a view of the cliffs. In the nineteenth century, it became a fashionable resort, visited by writers such as Goethe, Mark Twain and Guy de Maupassant, who crossed the Gemmi on foot or on horseback, and the old village still has some of the wooden houses and grand hotels of that era.

The riding is short but sweet. The road from Leuk is narrow and steep, with tight hairpins and spectacular drops into the gorge, and the asphalt is in good order. Weekends and the ski season bring a steady procession of cars, and buses run up and down regularly. At the top, the road ends in Leukerbad, so you will need to come back the same way. The views from the road over the Rhône valley and toward the peaks of the Valais Alps are superb, especially in the late afternoon, and the Pfyn forest below Leuk is one of the largest pine forests in the Alps.

Leukerbad has fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants, and the baths are a great place to recover after a long day on the bike. Leuk, the medieval town in the valley, has a castle renovated by the Swiss architect Mario Botta. For a larger town, Sierre, about ten kilometres down the valley, covers anything Leukerbad cannot. The region produces some of Switzerland's best wines, especially whites from the Petite Arvine and Fendant grapes, and reds from Cornalin and Pinot Noir.
t.near aigle@46.3,6.9:
Here the Rhône valley is flat, straight and wide, a broad plain between two walls of mountains, and the river runs canalised between high dykes toward Lake Geneva, a few kilometres downstream. On the east side, Aigle sits at the foot of vineyards that climb the slopes in terraces, with its castle, a turreted white fortress surrounded by vines, standing at the edge of town. On the west side, the villages of Vionnaz and Collombey sit at the foot of the Chablais Alps, and the Dents du Midi, a jagged ridge of peaks more than three thousand metres high, dominate the view up the valley.

The castle of Aigle is the symbol of the region, built in the Middle Ages by the Savoyards, then taken over by the Bernese, who ruled Vaud until the late eighteenth century. It now houses a wine museum, which tells the story of winemaking in the region, and the vineyards around it produce Chasselas, the main white grape of the Vaud and Valais. Aigle is also home to the headquarters of the UCI, the international cycling federation, and its world cycling centre, which explains why you might see racing cyclists on the roads.

For riders, the plain itself is a transit zone, with straight roads, roundabouts, industrial estates and traffic. The motorway runs along the valley, and the main roads can be busy with trucks and commuters. The real riding is in the mountains on either side: to the east, the road over the Col des Mosses and the Col du Pillon climbs from Aigle into the Alps, with sweeping curves and lovely views, while to the west, roads climb into the Chablais toward Champéry and the Portes du Soleil, or over the Pas de Morgins into France.

Aigle has everything you need: fuel, shops, restaurants and cafes, and the villages on the plain have fuel stations and supermarkets. Monthey, a larger town a few kilometres south, has more choice. If you want a break, the wine cellars in Aigle and Yvorne offer tastings, but remember that Switzerland has strict drink-driving laws. In summer, the plain can be hot and humid, while in winter fog can settle on the valley for days, so the best riding is often in the mountains above.
t.near bussigny@46.6,6.5:
The Gros-de-Vaud is the breadbasket of western Switzerland, a rolling plateau of wheat and rapeseed between Lausanne and the foot of the Jura, and the Venoge river cuts through it in a winding green valley. Here, around Penthalaz and Cossonay, the river runs in a deep wooded ravine below the hilltop town of Cossonay, an old medieval market town with a church tower that is visible for miles. The landscape is gentle and pastoral, with farms, orchards, small woods and villages of stone houses with big barns.

The Venoge is the subject of a famous song by the Vaudois poet Jean Villard Gilles, which every schoolchild in the canton knows, praising the little river that rises at the foot of the Jura and flows into Lake Geneva. Just north of here, between Eclépens and Orny, lie the remains of the Canal d'Entreroches, an ambitious seventeenth-century project to link Lake Geneva with Lake Neuchâtel and thus the Rhône with the Rhine by water. The canal was partly built and used for barges for more than a century, but the final section was never completed, and today you can walk along its dry bed through a rocky cutting in the forest.

The riding is relaxed and easy, with small roads winding through the fields and villages, gentle climbs and long views across to the Alps and the Jura. Traffic is light on the country roads, but heavier on the main routes near Lausanne and on the motorway. The towns and villages have plenty of 30 and 50 km/h zones, and the Swiss police are strict. For something more challenging, the Jura mountains are close: the roads over the Col du Mollendruz and the Col du Marchairuz, to the west, offer long, sweeping curves through forest and pasture, and are popular with riders from Lausanne and Geneva.

Cossonay has fuel, shops, cafes and restaurants, and Bussigny, about six kilometres south, is a larger town with more choice. Lausanne, just beyond, is a big city with everything you could need. La Sarraz, a few kilometres north, has a castle with a museum of the horse and a park. In summer, the fields are full of colour, with poppies and sunflowers, and the air smells of hay and ripening grain.
t.erlach@47.0,7.1:
Erlach is a one-street town with a castle on top and a lake at the bottom, and that is most of its charm. It sits at the south-western tip of Lake Biel, where the Jura comes down to the water on the far shore, and its old town climbs a short, steep cobbled lane from the harbour up to the castle, a solid medieval fortress that now houses a school. The houses along the lane are of yellowish Jura limestone, with arcades at street level and red-tiled roofs, and from the top you look out over the lake and the vineyards on the slopes of the Jura opposite.

From the harbour, a narrow strip of land runs out into the lake: the Heidenweg, a natural causeway that leads to St. Peter's Island. It only appeared when the lakes of the region were lowered by the great Jura water correction projects of the nineteenth century, which drained the marshes of the Seeland and turned the island into a peninsula. You can walk or cycle along it, about four kilometres through reeds and woods, but not ride a motorbike. On the island stands a former monastery, now a hotel and restaurant, where the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau took refuge for a few weeks in 1765. He later wrote that it was the happiest time of his life.

Erlach sits on the language border. Across the lake, La Neuveville is French-speaking; Erlach itself is German-speaking; and the nearby village of Le Landeron is French again, with one of the prettiest old town squares in the region. The Seeland to the south is flat, fertile land, reclaimed from the marshes, and is now one of the main vegetable-growing areas of Switzerland, with fields of lettuce, carrots and onions stretching to the horizon.

The riding around here is gentle. The roads along the lakeshore are flat and fairly straight, with views over the water, and the roads through the Seeland are dead straight across the fields. For curves, head up into the Jura behind La Neuveville, toward the Chasseral, the highest summit in the Bernese Jura, with a road that climbs through forest and pasture to a viewpoint over the Alps. Erlach has a few restaurants and cafes, and the harbour is a lovely place to sit with a coffee or lunch, but for fuel, head to the larger towns: Ins, Le Landeron, or Murten, about twelve kilometres away.
t.biel bienne@47.1,7.2:
Biel is the only city in Switzerland where you can order a coffee in either German or French and nobody blinks, because it is officially bilingual: street signs come in pairs, schools teach in both languages, and conversations switch mid-sentence. Bienne in French, Biel in German, it is a working city of about fifty thousand people at the north-east end of Lake Biel, and it has a confidence and a grittiness that sets it apart from the polished cities of the Swiss plateau.

The city made its fortune from watches. In the nineteenth century, watchmakers from the Jura settled here, and Biel became one of the centres of the Swiss watch industry, home to Omega, Rolex's movement maker and, since the 1980s, Swatch, whose headquarters is a striking timber building by the Japanese architect Shigeru Ban. The industry nearly collapsed in the 1970s, when cheap quartz watches from Asia flooded the market, and Biel suffered, but the revival brought by the Swatch has helped it bounce back. The old town, on a hill above the modern centre, is small and lovely, with a square called the Ring, fountains and arcaded houses.

From the edge of the city, a funicular climbs to Magglingen, Macolin in French, the home of the Swiss Federal Institute of Sport, on a terrace above the lake with views over the Seeland to the Alps. For riders, the road up there and over the Jura is a good escape: a winding climb through forest with tight hairpins, then onto open pasture. Just north of the city, the Taubenloch gorge is a narrow cleft in the limestone, with a walkway through it beside a rushing stream, and the road through the Vallon de Saint-Imier, toward La Chaux-de-Fonds, follows the watchmaking country deep into the Jura.

Biel is a city, with city traffic, so expect congestion, traffic lights and speed cameras. Once you are out, the lakeshore road toward La Neuveville is pleasant, though often busy. The city covers every practical need, from fuel and workshops to hotels and plenty of restaurants. In summer, the lakeside is lively, and boats run across the lake to St. Peter's Island and along the Aare to Solothurn. The local wines from the vineyards on the north shore of the lake, mostly Chasselas, are light and refreshing, and best enjoyed after the day's riding is done.
t.basel@47.6,7.6:
Basel is the city where Switzerland, France and Germany meet, and you can stand at the point where the three borders converge, on the Rhine in the harbour district, and see all three countries at once. The Rhine is the heart of the city: it sweeps through in a broad curve, dividing the old town of Grossbasel on the south bank from Kleinbasel on the north, and on summer evenings thousands of people float downstream in the current, holding their clothes and phones in waterproof fish-shaped bags called Wickelfisch.

Across the river, four small ferries without engines are pulled across by the current, attached to a cable stretched over the water, a charming way to cross the river. The old town is dominated by the red sandstone Münster, the cathedral, with its two towers and colourful tiled roof, where the humanist scholar Erasmus is buried. Basel was a centre of learning and printing in the Renaissance, with the oldest university in Switzerland, founded in 1460, and it is still a city of culture, with dozens of museums, including the Fondation Beyeler and the Kunstmuseum, and every June it hosts Art Basel, one of the world's leading art fairs.

The city is also the home of the Swiss chemical and pharmaceutical industry, with the huge headquarters of companies such as Novartis and Roche, whose tower is one of the tallest buildings in Switzerland. Carnival, the Fasnacht, is a big event, starting at four in the morning on the Monday after Ash Wednesday, when the lights go out and processions of masked drummers and piccolo players march through the old town for three days.

For riders, Basel is a city, with all that entails: traffic, trams, narrow streets, speed cameras and limited parking. It is best seen on foot. Beyond it, though, the riding is excellent. To the north, the Black Forest is just across the border, with winding roads through forest and valleys, while to the south, the Jura offers curvy roads through limestone gorges and over passes, and to the west, Alsace and the Vosges are within easy reach. Fuel, workshops, hotels and restaurants are all easy to find. The Läckerli, a spiced honey biscuit, is the local speciality, and makes a good snack for the road. Remember that the Swiss motorway vignette is required for the motorways, and that fuel is often cheaper across the border in Germany or France.
t.jeju island coastal loop point 2@33.5,12:
The eastern tip of Jeju is where the island's volcanic origins are most obvious. Seongsan Ilchulbong, the Sunrise Peak, rises straight from the sea here, a huge bowl-shaped tuff cone with steep green walls and a crater wide enough to hold a village. It formed when rising magma met seawater a few thousand years ago and blew itself apart into layers of ash, and the sea has been cutting at its sides ever since. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site that covers Jeju's volcanoes and lava tubes, and the climb to the rim, steep and stepped, takes about twenty minutes.

This corner is also the heartland of the haenyeo, the women divers who have harvested shellfish, sea urchins and seaweed from these waters for generations, holding their breath and diving in all seasons. Their culture is recognised by UNESCO, and at Seongsan you can sometimes watch older divers come ashore with their catch in nets, still in wetsuits, and buy sea urchin or abalone from them. The divers are fewer and older every year, which makes it worth seeing while you can.

The coastal road around here is flat and windy, in both senses: it follows the shoreline in small bends past black basalt rocks, fishing harbours and low stone walls built from the volcanic stone that is everywhere on Jeju. The wind can be strong enough to push a bike sideways, especially in winter, when cold air comes down from the north. Spring brings fields of yellow rapeseed flowers around Seongsan, and early mornings are the best time, before the tour buses arrive and while the low sun lights up the cone.

From the harbour at Seongsan a short ferry runs to Udo, a small island with white sand, peanut ice cream and a quiet coastal road, and many visitors take scooters or small bikes across. The town around the harbour has fuel, convenience stores and many small restaurants serving seafood, as well as Jeju's black pork, a local breed grilled at the table. Jeju City is about forty kilometres away, so fill up here if you are continuing south along the coast towards Seogwipo, where the next large services are.
t.near seogwipo@33.3,126.4:
West of Seogwipo, the southern slopes of Hallasan run down to the sea in long, gentle ramps, and the land here is sheltered, warm and green. Hallasan, the volcano at the heart of the island, is South Korea's highest mountain at 1,947 metres, and on this side its summit often stands clear above the clouds that gather on the northern slopes. Below it are tangerine orchards, greenhouses, small villages and the resort district of Jungmun on the coast, with big hotels and a stretch of beach.

The tangerines are the local signature. Seogwipo is the centre of Jeju's citrus growing, and in late autumn and winter the orchards are bright with fruit, stalls line the roads, and the smell of peel hangs over the villages. The fruit was once sent to the royal court as tribute, and today the island grows many varieties, including the sweet hallabong, named after the mountain and shaped with a little knob on top.

The coast nearby has one of Jeju's most striking sights: Jusangjeolli, a cliff of hexagonal basalt columns where lava flowed into the sea and cooled into vertical pillars. On rough days waves crash against the columns and send spray high into the air. Further east, closer to Seogwipo itself, waterfalls such as Cheonjiyeon and Jeongbang drop over volcanic cliffs, the latter falling straight into the sea.

For riding, the roads here are a mix: the coastal road is busy near the resorts, but the roads that climb towards the mountain, through forest and fields, offer more interesting curves and much less traffic. The mid-mountain roads that cross the island, passing over the shoulders of Hallasan, are popular with riders, with good surfaces and views back to the sea, though fog and rain can come in fast. Summer is hot and humid with occasional typhoons, so spring and autumn are the best seasons. Seogwipo, about fourteen kilometres away, is the town for fuel, food and a bed, and it has a lively market where you can try local snacks, including tangerine everything.
t.near gaigeturi@33.4,126.2:
The north-west coast of Jeju around Hallim faces the open sea and the prevailing wind, and it feels different from the sheltered south. The water off the beaches at Hyeopjae and Geumneung is turquoise over white sand, an unexpected colour against the black lava rocks, and the small island of Biyangdo sits just offshore, a low cone that looks like a hat dropped in the sea. Hallim itself is a working harbour town with fish markets, boats and a scattering of cafes, a little rough around the edges and all the better for it.

Jeju has an old saying that the island has three things in abundance: wind, stones and women. The wind you will feel; the stones are everywhere, in the low walls of black basalt that divide the fields, built with gaps so that the wind can pass through without knocking them down; the women refers to the haenyeo divers and to a history in which men were often lost at sea. The stone grandfather statues called dol hareubang, carved from the same porous rock, stand at village entrances and outside public buildings, and their round eyes and mushroom hats appear on every souvenir.

The coastal road north-east from here towards Aewol is one of the most enjoyable stretches on the island for a relaxed ride. It hugs the shoreline, rising and falling over low headlands, with the sea on one side and fields of cabbage, garlic and onions on the other. The road has become famous for its cafes with big windows over the sea, so expect parked cars on the verges and people crossing to take photographs. In winter the wind is fierce and cold; in spring and autumn it is pleasant; summer brings crowds on the beaches.

Inland are lava tubes and botanical parks, including a garden near Hallim with caves and palms, and further up, the gentle volcanic cones called oreum dot the landscape, many with short paths to their rims. Hallim has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants, and Jeju City, about thirty kilometres away, has everything. Try the local seafood, especially grilled mackerel or a bowl of seafood noodle soup, and keep an eye on the sky, because squalls come in from the sea fast.
t.near thonon les bains@46.4,6.5:
The Route des Grandes Alpes officially begins on the shore of Lake Geneva at Thonon-les-Bains and ends some seven hundred kilometres later on the Mediterranean at Menton. Standing here at the start, with the lake spread out flat and silver in front of you and the Swiss shore hazy on the far side, it is hard to believe that within an hour you will be climbing into proper mountains. That contrast is the whole romance of the thing.

The stop itself is just east of Thonon, towards Publier and Amphion, on the stretch of shore that runs on to Évian, whose spring water ends up in bottles all over the world. Thonon itself is a lively spa town with a funicular linking the upper town to the port, and on its outskirts stands the Château de Ripaille, where Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy, retired in the fifteenth century before being elected antipope as Felix V. Between Thonon and Publier, the Dranse river spreads into a wild delta, now a nature reserve full of birds and willow scrub.

Turning south, the route heads up the Dranse valley through narrow gorges, including the deep cleft at the Pont du Diable, and on towards Morzine and the Col des Gets. The road is good but busy in summer, with trucks and holiday traffic, so the first half hour is more about getting into rhythm than attacking corners. After Cluses come the Colombière, the Aravis and the Saisies, and the ride grows steadily bigger. Most of the high passes further south, the Iseran above all, are only open from roughly June to October, so check the status before committing to the full traverse.

As a start or finish, this lakeside area has everything: fuel, supermarkets, bakeries, cafés by the water and plenty of places to stay in Thonon and Évian. Lake Geneva has its own weather, often calmer and milder than the mountains, and on summer evenings the light over the water turns gold, then pink. Finishing a long day here, after descending out of the Chablais, with a cold drink at a lakeside table and the mountains glowing behind you, is about as good as riding gets.
t.ardesio@45.9,9.9:
High in the Val Seriana, where the valley narrows between steep, wooded mountainsides and the river Serio runs fast and green over grey stones, Ardesio is a mountain village of about two thousand people, with stone houses, a parish church and the Sanctuary of the Madonna delle Grazie, built after a reported apparition of the Virgin in the early seventeenth century. Every June the anniversary is celebrated with a procession and festivities that draw people from all over the valley.

The village has an old mining history. Iron and other metals were extracted from the mountains around Ardesio for centuries, and some of the old mines can now be visited. Further up the valley, at Valbondione, the Serio Falls are among the highest in Italy, a series of cascades dropping more than three hundred metres, but since the river is dammed upstream for hydroelectric power, the falls only flow on a few days each summer, when the water is released for the spectacle. If you happen to be here on one of those days, it is unforgettable.

For riders, the Val Seriana is a gateway to the high mountains. The road up the valley is pleasant, winding along the river through villages and forests, and from Clusone, just down the valley, the road climbs east over the Passo della Presolana, a beautiful pass beneath the limestone walls of the Presolana massif, with tight hairpins and views over the Dolomites of Bergamo. From there, the route continues into the Val Camonica and north towards the Stelvio, the destination of the ride.

Ardesio is small, so services are limited, and if you need fuel, Clusone, about six kilometres away, is the better bet. The village has bars and a few restaurants serving mountain food, including polenta, game and the local cheeses, such as Branzi and Formai de Mut. The roads in the valley can be busy on summer weekends, with day-trippers from Bergamo and Milan, and they can be slippery in the shade after rain.
t.near engelberg@46.7,8.4:
At 2,224 metres, the summit of the Susten Pass sits on the border between the cantons of Bern and Uri, under the glaciated peaks of the Sustenhorn and the Gwächtenhorn. Engelberg, the name on the label, lies on the other side of the Titlis massif, ten kilometres away as the crow flies but a long way round by road, so think of this as the pass itself, the highest point of one of the most beautiful mountain roads in the Alps.

The Susten road was built between 1938 and 1946 and is often described as the first Swiss alpine pass road designed from the outset for motor traffic, rather than adapted from an old mule track. You can feel it: the curves are generous, the gradients steady, the stone walls and tunnels beautifully crafted, and the road flows in a way that the older passes do not. On the Bern side, it climbs from Innertkirchen through the Gadmen valley, with the Steingletscher glacier and the meltwater lake of the Steinsee coming into view below the final hairpins, a scene of ice, rock and turquoise water. On the Uri side, the road descends through the Meiental, with its dark forests and waterfalls, to Wassen, where the church perches above the famous loops of the Gotthard railway.

The summit has a short tunnel and a car park where everyone stops for photos. Food is available at the hotel and restaurant near the Steingletscher on the Bern side, and at small places in the villages.

The Susten is part of the Grand Tour of Switzerland, and it is often combined with the Grimsel and Furka passes in a classic loop. It is typically open from June to October, depending on the snow, and closed in winter. On summer weekends it is busy with motorcycles, cars and cyclists, and Swiss speed limits are strictly enforced, so enjoy the scenery at a sensible pace. The weather can change quickly at this altitude, with cold winds and sudden storms, so carry warm, waterproof layers, even in August.
t.near la tour du pin on the way back@45.6:
The geologist Déodat de Dolomieu, born in 1750 in the village that bears his family name, gave his name to the mineral dolomite and, through it, to the Dolomites, the most spectacular mountains of Italy. The village of Dolomieu lies a couple of kilometres from the point, near La Tour-du-Pin, in the rolling hills of the Bas-Dauphiné, between Lyon and the Alps, and it is a pleasant reminder that even quiet corners have their stories.

The landscape here is gentle and green, a patchwork of meadows, woods, orchards and small villages, with views of the Chartreuse and the Belledonne on clear days. It is the kind of countryside that riders cross on the way to the mountains without paying much attention, but on the way back, tired and hot, it is a welcome sight. La Tour-du-Pin is a small market town on the Bourbre river, with fuel, shops and restaurants.

For a swim, there are two fine lakes within reach. Lac de Paladru, about fifteen kilometres south, is a long, clear lake in a glacial valley, with beaches and bathing spots, and at its southern end, near Charavines, archaeologists have excavated the remains of a lakeside village from around the year 1000, preserved in the mud of the lake. Lac d'Aiguebelette, a little further east in Savoie, is one of the warmest natural lakes in France, and motorboats are banned, so the water is calm and clean, with wooded mountains rising above it.

The roads in the Bas-Dauphiné are quiet and winding, with good surfaces and little traffic, ideal for a relaxed ride back from the Alps. The hills offer gentle curves and changes of gradient, and the villages are pretty, with old stone houses and churches. On the way back from the Alpe d'Huez and the Oisans, the route to Lyon passes through Grenoble or skirts the Chartreuse, before descending to the plains. Summers are warm, and a swim in one of the lakes is the perfect way to cool off.
t.near varennes saint sauveur on the way b:
The Bresse is flat, green and fiercely proud of its chickens. This stop lies deep in it, between Varennes-Saint-Sauveur and Saint-Trivier-de-Courtes, close to the line where Saône-et-Loire meets the Ain. The landscape is a quilt of small fields, hedges, damp meadows and woods, crossed by slow rivers that drain north towards the Seille and the Saône.

Look at the farmhouses. Many are timber-framed with brick infill, low and long, and some still carry the strange cheminée sarrasine, a tall, ornamented chimney with a little roof, a regional speciality that has nothing to do with Saracens despite the name. Saint-Trivier-de-Courtes is known for them, and several are preserved in the area. The other icon is the Bresse chicken, with its white feathers, blue feet and red comb, the first poultry in France to win its own appellation.

Louhans, the nearest larger town, holds a big weekly market under long medieval arcades, with live poultry sold alongside everything else. It is one of those French market scenes that has barely changed in a century.

As for swimming, the Bresse is not a lake country. The rivers are slow and muddy, and most ponds are private fishing waters. Look for designated bathing areas in local leisure parks, which open in summer, or simply accept that this is a rest stop rather than a plunge.

The riding is relaxed. The roads are straight or gently bending, often lined with trees, with good visibility and little traffic. The danger comes from farm machinery, mud at field entrances after rain and the occasional loose dog. Wind can be strong across open ground.

Fuel and shops are in the larger villages and in Louhans. Order chicken if a restaurant offers it, cooked in cream with morels if you are lucky.
t.near peronnas on the way back@46.2,5.2:
Bourg-en-Bresse lies just east of here, and this stop sits on its western edge, between Péronnas, Buellas and Saint-Denis-lès-Bourg. The country is gentle, with fields, hedges, farm buildings and the outskirts of a mid-sized town. To the south the Dombes plateau begins, a region of hundreds of shallow ponds created by monks and lords in the Middle Ages for fish farming.

Bourg's great treasure is the Royal Monastery of Brou, built in the early sixteenth century by Margaret of Austria in memory of her husband, Philibert the Handsome of Savoy. Its church is a riot of late Gothic stone carving, with three magnificent tombs and a colourful glazed tile roof. It is one of the finest buildings of its period in France, and it is worth an hour even if you are in a hurry.

The Dombes ponds are drained and refilled in cycles, alternating between fish and crops. They are rich in birdlife, with herons, egrets and ducks in large numbers, and the bird park at Villars-les-Dombes is one of the largest in Europe. The ponds themselves are private and not for swimming.

For a swim, look to Bourg itself. The leisure area at Bouvent, on the northern side of town, has a lake with a bathing area in summer. Check the season and supervision before you go. Otherwise, the town pools offer a reliable alternative.

The riding is easy and open, with straight roads, roundabouts and some traffic around Bourg. The Revermont hills to the east offer more interesting roads, climbing into the Jura foothills with tight bends and views back over the Bresse.

Péronnas has fuel and a supermarket on the way in, and Bourg has the rest, from bakeries to proper brasseries. If you skipped the chicken in the north of the Bresse, here is your second chance.
t.near miribel@45.8,5.0:
East of Lyon, the Rhône splits into channels and lakes on its way into the city, and the vast Grand Parc de Miribel-Jonage has been made out of that watery landscape. This finish lies just above it, on the edge of the Côtière, the steep slope that separates the river plain from the Dombes plateau, between Thil, Beynost and Saint-Maurice-de-Beynost.

The park is the main reason to linger. It covers more than two thousand hectares of lakes, woods and meadows, with a large lake, the Lac des Eaux Bleues, that has supervised bathing beaches in summer. On hot weekends it is packed with Lyonnais, but on a weekday evening it can be surprisingly calm. It also plays a serious role as a flood plain and drinking water reserve for the city.

Above Miribel, on the Côtière, stands a tall statue of the Virgin on a tower, the Madone du Mas Rillier, built in the mid-twentieth century and visible from miles around. The view from up there takes in the Rhône plain, Lyon, and on clear days the Alps and Mont Blanc.

The riding is a mix of busy and quiet. The A42 and the old national road run along the bottom of the slope, with plenty of traffic, while small roads climb the Côtière in tight bends to the plateau. Up top, the Dombes roads are straight and quiet, with ponds and farms on either side.

On a warm evening the order of events writes itself: a swim in the Eaux Bleues, a slow climb up the Côtière to the Madone as the plain turns orange, then dinner in Miribel, where fuel and supermarkets are also close at hand.
t.soresina on the way back@45.3,9.8:
Soresina is a town of the flat Lombard plain, between Cremona and Crema, and it lives and breathes dairy. The local cooperative, Latteria Soresina, is one of the largest cheese producers in Italy, making Grana Padano, provolone and butter from the milk of the surrounding farms. The landscape around is perfectly flat, criss-crossed by irrigation canals and lines of poplars, with large farmsteads, cascine, standing like fortresses in the fields.

There is no lake or beach near here, and the canals are not for swimming: they are fast, cold and steep-sided, and drownings happen every summer. If you want water, the nearest real river is the Adda, to the west, or the Oglio, to the east. At Pizzighettone, south-west of here, the Adda flows past impressive brick walls, and it was in that fortress that the French king Francis I was held prisoner after his defeat at Pavia in 1525.

Cremona, a short ride south, is the home of violin making. Stradivari, Guarneri and Amati worked there, and the town still has workshops where luthiers carve instruments by hand. The violin museum is world-class, and the cathedral square, with its tall bell tower, the Torrazzo, is one of the finest in Italy.

The riding here is a straight-line affair, with long, flat roads between fields. In summer the heat can be oppressive, and mosquitoes swarm in the evenings. In winter, thick fog settles on the plain, sometimes for days. Watch for tractors, slow trucks and sudden junctions at farm entrances.
