The town has the pumps and bars a place of eight thousand needs. Buy some provolone at the source, and if you reach Cremona, look for mostarda, fruit candied in a syrup sharp with mustard, and torrone, the nougat the city has been making for centuries.
t.near binasco@45.4,9.1:
Leave Milan to the south and within twenty minutes the city gives way to rice. The Parco Agricolo Sud Milano protects a wide belt of farmland around the city, and between Binasco, Zibido San Giacomo and Noviglio the fields are flooded each spring, turning the plain into a vast mirror of sky, laced with canals and lines of poplars. The locals call it the chequered sea.

Binasco is a small town on the Naviglio Pavese, the canal that runs from Milan to Pavia. It has a castle built by the Visconti, and it was there, in 1418, that Beatrice di Tenda, wife of Filippo Maria Visconti, was beheaded on a charge of adultery, a story later turned into an opera by Bellini. South of Binasco, the Certosa di Pavia, a huge Carthusian monastery with a marble facade, is one of the great monuments of Lombardy.

Starting or finishing here gives you a gentle introduction to the plain. The roads are flat and straight, running along canals and between fields, with old farmhouses, cascine, scattered across the landscape. In spring, the flooded rice fields are full of herons, egrets and frogs, and the evenings are loud with croaking. In summer, mosquitoes are a nuisance.

The ride south towards the Trebbia valley crosses the Po and climbs into the Apennines, where the roads become twisty and the scenery more dramatic. The return to Binasco brings you back into the flat calm of the plain, a pleasant way to wind down.

Practicalities are simple in Binasco: pumps on the main road, bars by the canal, trattorias that cook the rice grown in the fields you just rode past. Risotto here is not a menu choice so much as a local obligation.
t.near bareggio@45.5,9.0:
West of Milan, between Bareggio, Cusago and Settimo Milanese, the plain is laced with fontanili, spring-fed ditches where groundwater rises to the surface and keeps the water flowing at a steady temperature year-round. These springs made the land rich, and for centuries the area was a patchwork of meadows, rice fields and farmsteads. Today the city is closing in, but the Parco Agricolo Sud Milano protects much of the countryside.

Cusago has a castle built by the Visconti as a hunting lodge, where the dukes of Milan came to hunt in the woods that then covered this part of the plain. South-west of here, the Cistercian abbey of Morimondo, founded in the twelfth century, is a quiet, beautiful place with a brick church and cloister, surrounded by fields and woods.

On a bike this is connective tissue rather than a destination: roads trace canals and field edges at right angles. Traffic around Milan can be heavy, especially at rush hour, and the tangenziale ring road is often congested. Once you get away from the city, the roads become quieter, with long views across the fields.

The Ticino river, to the west, is lined with woods and is protected as a regional park. The riverside paths are popular with walkers and cyclists, and the river itself, fast and clear, is a pleasant place to sit on a hot day.

After a day of lakes and passes, there is something soothing about ending among ditches and herons. Bareggio's pumps and bars are a minute away, and the trattorias in the surrounding villages still cook for farmers rather than tourists.
t.near lenzburg@47.4,8.2:
Schloss Lenzburg crowns a rounded hill above the town, so prominent that you can see it from miles away on the motorway, and it has been watching over this part of the Aargau since the eleventh century. The castle has passed through the hands of counts, the Habsburgs, the city of Bern and private owners, and today it is a museum, with gardens and views over the Seetal and the Jura.

The Aargau is sometimes called the canton of castles, and with reason. Wildegg, Brunegg and Hallwyl are all nearby, and the Habsburg, the original seat of the dynasty that went on to rule half of Europe, stands on a hill near Brugg. Schloss Hallwyl, at the northern end of the Hallwilersee, is a moated castle on two islands, one of the most beautiful in Switzerland.

Lenzburg itself has an old town with a long main street, fountains and arcades, and it is the home of Hero, the jam and food company founded here in 1886. The smell of fruit sometimes drifts through the town.

The Grand Tour of Switzerland passes through this region on its way between Basel and Zurich, and the roads here are a mix of busy main routes and quiet country lanes. Swiss speed enforcement is strict, with fixed and mobile cameras, and fines are high. Ride within the limits, especially in towns and villages.

On a warm afternoon, drop south to the Hallwilersee for a swim from one of the public lidos; the water is clean and the Alps sometimes show at the far end. Lenzburg itself takes care of fuel and lunch, and its long main street is a calm place to sit while the castle looks down.
t.near cosio valtellino on the way back@46:
The Costiera dei Cech is the sunny, south-facing slope on the north side of the lower Valtellina, and this stop lies at its foot, between Mello, Traona and Cercino. Vines and chestnut trees climb the terraces, and the old villages perch on the slope, catching the sun all day. Across the valley, the shaded north-facing slopes are dark with forest, a contrast that shapes life here.

The Adda flows through the valley floor towards Lake Como, a few kilometres west, where the northern tip of the lake meets the flat wetlands of the Pian di Spagna, a nature reserve full of birds. The Abbey of Piona, on a peninsula near Colico, is a Romanesque monastery where monks still live, with a beautiful cloister and views over the lake.

Val Masino, to the north-east, is a granite valley famous for its climbing, with huge boulders and clean rock faces, and the hot springs of Bagni di Masino at its head. The road up the valley is narrow and winding, with stunning views.

For a swim, Lake Como is the obvious choice, with beaches at Colico and along the shore. The water is cold but clear, and on a hot day it is wonderfully refreshing. The Lago di Mezzola, north of Como, is quieter, with reed beds and calm water.

The food of the Valtellina is hearty: pizzoccheri, buckwheat pasta with cabbage, potatoes and cheese; bresaola, air-dried beef; and Sforzato, a rich red wine made from dried grapes. Cosio and Morbegno have fuel, shops and restaurants.
t.near andermatt@46.7,8.6:
The church of Wassen stands on a terrace above the Reuss, and passengers on the old Gotthard railway see it three times as the line spirals through tunnels to gain height, a famous trick of nineteenth-century engineering that makes travellers think they are going in circles. This stop lies in that village, at the foot of the Susten pass, where the road leaves the Reuss valley and climbs west into the Meiental towards the Bernese Oberland.

The Susten road was built between 1938 and 1946, one of the first Alpine passes designed for motor traffic from the start, and its engineering is a pleasure to ride, with wide, well-banked bends, stone walls and tunnels. The eastern side climbs through the Meiental, a narrow valley of farms and forest, while the western side drops past the Steingletscher, a glacier that hangs above the road near the top, and down the long descent to Innertkirchen.

Andermatt, a few kilometres south, is a mountain village at the crossroads of the Alps, where the Gotthard, Oberalp and Furka roads meet, and it has been transformed in recent years by a large resort development. The Schöllenen gorge, between Andermatt and Göschenen, is crossed by the Devil's Bridge, where legend says the devil built the first bridge in exchange for the first soul to cross it, and the locals sent a goat.

The Susten is usually closed from late autumn to early summer, depending on snow. Weather can change quickly, and the top can be cold and windy even in summer.

Wassen is tiny, so do not count on it for fuel; Altdorf, Erstfeld or Andermatt are the safe bets. The village does have a couple of inns, and a coffee on a terrace here, listening to trains disappear into the mountain on one side and bikes winding up towards the Susten on the other, is a very Swiss pleasure.
t.near montluel@45.9,5.1:
Montluel is the kind of small French town that most people only see as a sign on the A42, which is a shame. It climbs a slope above the little River Sereine, on the escarpment that the locals call the Côtière, the step where the Rhône plain to the south rises up onto the plateau of the Dombes. For centuries this was border country: Montluel belonged to the House of Savoy and only became French with the Treaty of Lyon in 1601, and the old centre still has the narrow, defensive feel of a frontier town.

For a rider leaving Lyon in the early morning, the interest lies just north. Climb out of town and the land flattens into the Dombes, a plateau scattered with hundreds of shallow fish ponds dug by monks and landowners since the Middle Ages. The roads are narrow and straight-ish, linked by right-angle bends at farm corners, and at dawn mist lies on the water and herons stand in the reeds. Carp and pike from these ponds still end up on local menus, and frogs' legs are a regional pride.

The surface is generally good, but watch for tractors, mud at field entrances and the odd cyclist on the quiet departmental roads. The plain south of Montluel, by contrast, is industrial and busy, with lorries heading for the motorway junctions, so it is best treated as a transit.

Montluel itself has fuel, bakeries and cafés, and the larger retail zones along the main road have stations open long hours. Topping up here makes sense before heading into the Dombes or towards the Beaujolais hills, where villages are small and pumps scarcer. On a warm day, a coffee in the old town square and a look at the church tower above the rooftops makes a calm start before the ride proper begins.
t.near la cote saint andre@45.4,5.2:
Hector Berlioz was born in La Côte-Saint-André in 1803, and the town has never let anyone forget it. His family home is now a museum, and every summer a festival in his name fills the courtyard of the château with orchestras. It is a fine reason to linger, but the town has other charms too: a huge medieval covered market hall with a timber roof, steep lanes, and the distillery of Cherry Rocher, which has been making liqueurs here since the early eighteenth century.

The town clings to a slope on the edge of the Bièvre plain, a broad, flat corridor between Lyon and Grenoble, with the wooded Chambaran plateau rising to the south. From the higher streets, the view on a clear morning takes in the long blue line of the Vercors, the Chartreuse and, beyond, the snowy summits of Belledonne. That view is a good tonic before heading towards the Oisans and the hairpins of Alpe d'Huez.

The roads around here are relaxed and rural. The Bièvre itself is flat and straight, but the Chambaran lanes wind through chestnut woods and small valleys with very little traffic, ideal for warming up tyres and minds. Watch for gravel in the forest corners and for farm machinery in summer. The plain can be windy, and in midsummer the heat bounces off the fields.

La Côte-Saint-André has fuel, bakeries, cafés and restaurants around the market hall, and it is a much nicer place to eat than the motorway service areas on the A48. A plate of local walnuts or a gratin dauphinois brings you firmly into Isère territory. Fill up here; once you head into the Chambaran woods the villages get small, and the next big service town is Grenoble or Voiron.
t.near chatillon sur chalaronne@46.1,5.0:
Flowers are Châtillon-sur-Chalaronne's calling card. In summer every bridge over the little River Chalaronne is hung with geraniums, and the town has won national prizes for its displays year after year. Underneath the colour sits a fine old centre: half-timbered houses, a brick Gothic church and a huge covered market hall whose oak roof timbers were rebuilt after a fire centuries ago and still shelter the weekly market.

The town has a saintly connection too. In 1617, a young priest named Vincent de Paul was posted here, and it was in Châtillon that he founded his first charitable confraternity, the seed of the Daughters of Charity and the vast network of works that followed. A small museum and chapel recall his stay.

Around Châtillon spreads the Dombes, a plateau of shallow fishponds, farmland and woods, where the light on still water is soft and silvery in the morning. The roads are mostly flat, crossing between ponds with occasional sharp bends at farm corners, and traffic is light outside the towns. Herons, egrets and grebes are everywhere, and the bird park at Villars-les-Dombes, a short ride south, holds one of the largest collections in France. To the west, the land drops towards the Saône and the vineyards of the Beaujolais rise beyond.

Châtillon has fuel, bakeries, cafés and restaurants, and on market days the hall is full of local produce, including Bresse poultry and Dombes carp. It is a lovely place for coffee or lunch on the way south towards the Alps. Ride gently through the old centre; the streets are narrow, and pedestrians, especially on market mornings, have priority.
t.near biol@45.5,5.4:
North-west of Grenoble, the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné fold into a quiet country of meadows, woods and ponds that the locals call the Terres Froides, the cold lands, because of their damp, clayey soils and frosty winters. Biol is one of its villages, scattered across the slopes with farms and a church, and it gives a good taste of a part of Isère that most visitors drive straight past on the motorway.

The riding here is a lot of fun. The roads curl over little hills and dip into valleys, with constant changes of direction and gradient and very little traffic. The landscape is green and pastoral, with cows in the fields and woods of oak and chestnut, and on clear days the Chartreuse and Vercors massifs appear on the horizon, with the snowy summits of Belledonne beyond. Surfaces are variable, and gravel and mud from farm tracks can appear on corners.

A short ride away lies the Lac de Paladru, a long, clear glacial lake that is a popular swimming spot in summer. Its waters hide archaeological treasures: the remains of a Neolithic settlement and a village from around the year one thousand, preserved in the mud, whose finds are displayed in a museum by the lake. The idea of medieval knights and farmers living on the shore a millennium ago gives the place a special atmosphere.

Biol has few services, so fuel and food are best found in La Tour-du-Pin or Le Grand-Lemps nearby, or in Bourgoin-Jallieu, the largest town in the area. Beyond, the ride continues towards the Route Napoléon and the Vercors, where the roads climb into the mountains and the scenery becomes truly alpine.
t.near l isle d abeau@45.6,5.3:
L'Isle-d'Abeau is a town that was planned on paper. In the 1970s, it was chosen as one of the new towns designed to absorb the growth of big French cities, in this case Lyon, and its neighbourhoods were built around the old village on the hills between Lyon and Grenoble. The result is a mix of modern housing, business parks and green spaces, practical rather than beautiful, but surrounded by countryside that is much more appealing.

The Nord-Isère hills around the town are gentle and green, with woods, meadows and small lakes. The area was once a marshy plain, drained over the centuries, and the remnants of wetlands still attract birds. To the north lies the Isle Crémieu, a limestone plateau with ponds, caves and the medieval town of Crémieu, with its huge covered market and fortified gates. To the east, the land rises towards the Alps, with the Chartreuse and Bugey on the horizon.

The riding here is a mix of busy main roads and quieter rural lanes. The A43 motorway runs past, linking Lyon with Chambéry and the Alps, and the roads around the town can be congested at rush hour. But head north or east, and the roads quickly become quieter and more winding, with views over the hills and the plain.

L'Isle-d'Abeau and neighbouring Bourgoin-Jallieu have plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, making this a convenient stop. Bourgoin is known for its rugby club and its textile heritage. Onward, the way heads towards the Lac du Bourget, the largest natural lake in France, with its balcony roads and views over the water to the mountains.
t.near valmadrera caserta@45.8,9.3:
Lecco, at the foot of the jagged Grigne, is the town where Alessandro Manzoni set the opening of The Betrothed, the great Italian novel, and its famous first lines describe the branch of Lake Como that stretches south towards it. Valmadrera lies just across the water from Lecco, at the meeting point of the lake, the small lakes of Annone and the hills of Brianza, beneath the slopes of Monte Barro and the twin peaks of the Corni di Canzo.

The landscape is dramatic and varied. The lake is deep and narrow, with mountains rising steeply from the water, and the villages along its shores are crowded on narrow strips of land. Monte Barro, a nature park, offers wide views over the lakes and the plain of Lombardy, and the hills of the Triangolo Lariano, between the two southern arms of Lake Como, are laced with roads.

The riding is superb. The road over the Valassina towards Bellagio climbs through valleys and past villages, and the climb to the Madonna del Ghisallo, a chapel dedicated to the patron saint of cyclists, is a classic. The roads along the lake are narrow, winding and often busy, with tunnels, blind corners and traffic. Weekends bring crowds of tourists, cyclists and motorcyclists, so a weekday or an early start is advisable.

Valmadrera and Lecco have fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants. Lecco has a pleasant lakeside promenade with cafés and gelato, perfect for a break. Then the road leads north towards the Ticino lakes and passes, with Lake Lugano, Lake Maggiore and the high Alps ahead.
t.buellas@46.2,5.1:
Buellas is a small village in the Bresse, just west of Bourg-en-Bresse in the Ain department. The Bresse is a flat, fertile region of farms, hedgerows, ponds and woods, known above all for its chickens: the Bresse chicken, with its blue feet, white plumage and red comb, matching the colours of the French flag, is the only poultry in France with its own protected designation of origin. Farmers here raise them in open pastures, and they are prized by chefs across the country.

The region is also known for its traditional farmhouses, with timber frames, brick infill and distinctive Saracen chimneys, tall and ornate, some of which can still be seen in the countryside. The Domaine des Planons, an old farm turned museum near Saint-Cyr-sur-Menthon, is a good place to learn about rural life in the Bresse.

Bourg-en-Bresse, just to the east, is home to the Royal Monastery of Brou, a masterpiece of Flamboyant Gothic architecture built in the early sixteenth century by Margaret of Austria in memory of her husband, Philibert of Savoy. The tombs inside are some of the finest sculptures of the period.

The riding around Buellas is flat and relaxed, with roads running between fields, hedges and small woods, and through villages with brick churches. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light. It is not a place for dramatic corners, but it has a gentle charm. Fuel and food are available in Bourg-en-Bresse. As a start and finish, Buellas offers a calm, rural setting close to a city with plenty of services.
t.near tossiat@46.1,5.3:
Tossiat sits at the foot of the Revermont, the first wrinkle of the Jura rising out of the flat Bresse plain east of Bourg-en-Bresse. Stand at the edge of the village and look west, and the whole Bresse lies spread out below, flat and green to the horizon. Turn around, and the wooded slopes of the Revermont climb steeply behind you, with limestone cliffs breaking through the trees.

The Revermont is a little-known corner of the Ain, and its villages are quiet and old-fashioned. The slopes were once covered with vineyards, and some vines survive, along with orchards and pasture. The limestone gives rise to springs, caves and small gorges. The Gorges du Suran, a little to the east, cut a deep, narrow valley through the hills.

The riding here is excellent and largely unknown outside the region. Roads climb from the plain into the Revermont in a series of steep, twisting sections, with hairpins and blind bends, then run along ridges and through small valleys with views over the Bresse. Surfaces vary, and some roads are narrow, so take care. Traffic is very light, especially on weekdays.

There are few services in Tossiat itself, but fuel and food are available in Bourg-en-Bresse and Pont-d'Ain nearby. As a photo stop, the view from the Revermont over the Bresse plain is the highlight, especially in the late afternoon, when the light softens and the shadows lengthen across the fields.
t.near chalamont@46.0,5.2:
Chalamont stands on the highest ground of the Dombes, the plateau of ponds north-east of Lyon, and from its slopes you look out over a strange, watery landscape. There are well over a thousand ponds in the Dombes, most of them created by monks and landowners in the Middle Ages to raise fish and drain the poor, clay soils. They are still farmed in a rotation that dates back centuries: a pond is filled and stocked with carp for a few years, then drained and planted with cereals, before being flooded again.

The ponds attract an extraordinary variety of birds, and the Dombes is one of the most important wetland areas in France. Herons, egrets, grebes, ducks and many other species can be seen, and the Parc des Oiseaux at Villars-les-Dombes, a short ride away, is one of the largest bird parks in Europe. The village of Chalamont has some old timber-framed houses and a church.

The riding on the Dombes plateau is gentle and relaxing. Roads wind between ponds, woods and fields, with frequent gentle bends and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally good. In autumn and early morning, mist often rises from the ponds, creating an atmospheric scene. Watch for wildlife, including deer, and for wet patches in rainy weather.

Fuel and food are available in Chalamont and nearby towns like Villars-les-Dombes and Meximieux. The local speciality is fried frogs' legs, and carp from the ponds is also on the menu in many restaurants. Pérouges, a perfectly preserved medieval village near Meximieux, makes a superb detour.
t.near la motte servolex@45.6,5.8:
La Motte-Servolex sits at the western edge of Chambéry, at the southern tip of the Lac du Bourget, the largest natural lake entirely in France. Behind it rises the long, wooded ridge of the Mont du Chat and the Chaîne de l'Épine, and on clear days the view over the lake and towards the Alps is magnificent.

The Lac du Bourget is a deep, glacial lake, with clear blue water and steep shores. On its eastern side lies Aix-les-Bains, an elegant spa town with grand hotels and a lakeside promenade. On the western shore, the Abbaye de Hautecombe, a Cistercian abbey founded in the twelfth century, served as the burial place of the princes of Savoy. The poet Lamartine wrote some of his most famous verses about the lake.

For riders, the area is a playground. The road over the Mont du Chat, climbing from Le Bourget-du-Lac, is a steep, narrow, twisting ascent with hairpins and spectacular views over the lake. The Col de l'Épine, just south, offers another fine climb. The roads along the lake shore are scenic, though busy in summer. Surfaces are generally good on the main roads, but the minor passes can be rough.

La Motte-Servolex has full services, including fuel, food and coffee, and Chambéry, the historic capital of Savoy, is just next door, with its château, its elephant fountain and a lively old town. For a photo, head up towards the Mont du Chat for a view over the lake, or stop on the shore near Le Bourget-du-Lac.
t.near bourgoin jallieu@45.6,5.2:
South and west of Bourgoin-Jallieu, the flat valley of the Bourbre gives way to a tangle of low hills, and these are the high points of the Bas-Dauphiné: rounded ridges, small woods of oak and chestnut, walnut orchards and farms with pebble walls. Further south they become the Terres Froides, the cold lands, a name that sounds harsh until you ride there in June and find nothing colder than a breeze across the hay meadows.

None of this is mountain country, but the ridges give honest views. North-east, the Bugey and the first ridges of the Jura line the horizon; east, the Chartreuse and Belledonne stand up sharp and grey; on a really clear morning Mont Blanc itself appears as a pale tooth beyond them. That glimpse of the high Alps from a modest hill is one of the quiet pleasures of riding in Nord-Isère.

The roads are a delight for anyone who likes rhythm. They roll and twist over the crests and down into small valleys, rarely straight for long, with good sightlines on the open ridges and tighter, shaded sections in the woods. Surfaces are mostly fine but patched in places, and farm traffic is common. The main roads around Bourgoin carry commuter traffic towards Lyon, so a mid-morning start is kinder.

Hector Berlioz was born in La Côte-Saint-André, in the Bièvre plain a little to the south, and the house where he grew up is now a museum devoted to him. It is a reminder that this unassuming country produced one of the great romantic composers. Fuel, food and coffee are all a few minutes away in Bourgoin-Jallieu or L'Isle-d'Abeau.
t.near tignieu@45.7,5.2:
Tignieu-Jameyzieu sits on the plain between Lyon's eastern sprawl and the Rhône, where commuter villages have spread over old farmland and gravel terraces. It is not a destination in itself, but a few minutes north-east the scenery changes sharply. The Isle Crémieu, a limestone plateau bounded on three sides by the Rhône, rises above the plain, with cliffs, oak woods, dry meadows, small lakes and villages built of pale stone.

Crémieu, the medieval town at its edge, is the jewel. Its covered market hall, built in the fifteenth century with a huge timber roof, still hosts the market. Fortified gates, an old Augustinian convent and the ruins of a castle above the town tell of its importance as a trading post on the road between Lyon and Savoy. Not far away, the caves at La Balme-les-Grottes have been visited for centuries, and legend links them to the smuggler Louis Mandrin.

For a finishing stretch, the plain around Tignieu is flat and easy, with straight roads and roundabouts. The traffic can be heavy at commuting times, especially towards Lyon and the airport. The plateau of the Isle Crémieu offers more interest, with winding roads through woods and meadows, and the descent to the Rhône at Hières-sur-Amby or La Balme is pleasant. Surfaces are generally good.

Fuel and food are available in Tignieu and Pont-de-Chéruy, and Crémieu has cafés and restaurants. If you finish the day here, a stroll through Crémieu's old streets in the evening light is a fine way to unwind.
t.bourgoin jallieu@45.6,5.3:
Bourgoin-Jallieu is the main town of Nord-Isère, a working place on the old road from Lyon to Chambéry and Grenoble, and it makes a good, unfussy start to a ride. The two old villages of Bourgoin and Jallieu grew together in the nineteenth century around textile mills, and printing on cloth was the town's speciality. The museum in the centre has collections on the history of textile printing, and you can still see old mill buildings along the Bourbre river.

The town has one literary curiosity: Jean-Jacques Rousseau stayed here in 1768, and it was in Bourgoin that he finally married Thérèse Levasseur, his companion of many years, in a simple civil ceremony. Today, the town is better known for rugby. Its club, CS Bourgoin-Jallieu, has a long history in the French top flight, and the sport is a passion here.

As a fuel stop, Bourgoin-Jallieu is easy. There are plenty of service stations on the approaches to town and near the motorway junction, as well as supermarkets, bakeries and cafés. The A43 motorway runs past, providing a quick route east towards Chambéry and the Alps, or west to Lyon. Tolls apply.

From here, the riding options are many. To the south, the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné and the Terres Froides offer winding roads through farmland and woods. To the east, the routes towards the Isère valley and the Belledonne range lead to the high Alps. The roads around town can be busy, but once you are out in the countryside, traffic thins quickly.
t.near artemare@45.9,5.7:
Artemare is a small town in the Valromey, a valley in the Bugey, at the foot of the Grand Colombier, the highest summit at the southern end of the Jura. The town sits where the Séran river emerges from its valley, and the landscape around it is a mix of meadows, forests, limestone cliffs and small villages. Just to the north, the Cascade de Cerveyrieu drops in a spectacular fall over a limestone ledge, especially impressive after rain.

The Bugey is a region of deep valleys, limestone ridges and lakes, and it has a long tradition of good food and wine. Brillat-Savarin, the famous gastronome and author of The Physiology of Taste, was born in Belley, just to the south, and the region takes its culinary heritage seriously. The local wines, under the Bugey name, include sparkling Cerdon, a light, fruity pink wine, and reds and whites from local grape varieties. Cheeses, charcuterie and freshwater fish from the lakes are all excellent.

For riders, Artemare is the gateway to one of the great climbs of the Jura: the Grand Colombier, which can be reached from several sides, with steep gradients, hairpins and spectacular views over the Rhône valley, the Lac du Bourget and the Alps. The Col de la Biche and the Col du Grand Colombier are often used in the Tour de France. The roads are narrow and can be rough, and they are usually closed in winter.

Artemare has a few restaurants and cafés, and food options in the valley are good. Fuel is available in Artemare or in Belley and Culoz. Fill up before heading into the mountains.
t.near peronnas@46.2,5.2:
Péronnas is a suburb on the southern edge of Bourg-en-Bresse, and the high ground near it is little more than a gentle swell where three landscapes meet. North and west lies the Bresse, flat and green; south, the Dombes begins, with its ponds and woods; and east, the abrupt wooded wall of the Revermont rises out of the plain like the edge of a stage set. On a clear day the snowy Alps sometimes appear far beyond, an unexpected bonus.

The area's chief cultural treasure is just next door in Bourg: the Monastery of Brou, a shimmering piece of late Gothic architecture whose glazed tile roof catches the sun. But Péronnas itself has its own quieter history. It was long a farming village before Bourg's growth swallowed much of it, and old farmhouses with deep roofs still stand among the newer houses.

The riding here is mostly about transition. The roads south into the Dombes are gentle and flowing, with ponds glinting through the trees, while the routes east climb steeply into the Revermont, where the fun really begins: switchbacks up to small villages, ridge roads with long views, and descents into limestone valleys. Around Péronnas itself, traffic can be busy with commuters and shoppers, so pick your time.

Fuel, food and coffee are plentiful in Péronnas and Bourg-en-Bresse. Bresse chicken and the creamy dishes of the region are on many menus, and Bourg has a good covered market. This is a good place to regroup before tackling the hills.
t.near saint savin@45.7,5.3:
Saint-Savin is a village in the hills just north of Bourgoin-Jallieu, in the part of Nord-Isère where the land starts to fold up towards the Isle Crémieu and the Rhône. It is quiet, green country: hedges and walnut trees, ponds in the hollows, stone farmhouses, and narrow roads that seem to have been laid down by following the cows.

Just south lies the valley of the Bourbre, once a great marsh that was drained over the centuries to create farmland, with the new town of L'Isle-d'Abeau built in the 1970s on its edge. The old villages on the slopes above it, Saint-Savin among them, kept their rural character, and the views south across the valley to the Terres Froides and the distant Alps are lovely in the early morning.

As a start and fuel stop, the practical side is handled by Bourgoin-Jallieu, a few minutes away, which has plenty of service stations, supermarkets and bakeries. The A43 motorway is close for a quick run east towards the Alps. But the real pleasure is in the minor roads around Saint-Savin, which wind over the hills and through small woods, with short climbs, blind bends and good views.

Surfaces vary from good to patchy, and you will meet tractors, cyclists and the occasional herd crossing. Traffic is light. For a long day towards the Ardèche, this is a calm place to start, with a coffee in Bourgoin and the hills waking up around you.
t.near hauterives@45.3,5.0:
In 1879 a country postman named Ferdinand Cheval tripped over an oddly shaped stone on his delivery round near Hauterives. He picked it up, took it home, and spent the next thirty-three years building a palace out of stones he collected on his rounds, carrying them in his pockets, then in baskets, then in a wheelbarrow. The result, the Palais Idéal du Facteur Cheval, is one of the strangest and most moving buildings in France, a fantastical mass of towers, grottoes, animals and inscriptions, admired by the Surrealists and now a protected monument.

Hauterives itself is a small village in the valley of the Galaure, in the Drôme des Collines, a rolling landscape of low hills, walnut groves, orchards and woods north of Romans. The high ground around it rises gently above the valley, giving views over the hills towards the Vercors in the east and the Rhône valley in the west.

The riding here is pleasant and varied. The roads wind through the hills, with frequent bends, short climbs and descents, and generally good surfaces. Traffic is light away from the main roads. The Galaure valley road is a pleasant run, and the routes into the hills offer more challenge and better views. The Vercors, with its dramatic cliffs and gorges, is not far to the east.

The palace draws many visitors, especially in summer, so expect crowds around Hauterives. The village has cafés and restaurants, and fuel is available in the larger towns nearby. Cheval is buried in the village cemetery, in a tomb he also built himself.
t.near chatonnay@45.5,5.2:
Châtonnay is a farming village in the Bas-Dauphiné, on the gently rolling ground between Bourgoin-Jallieu and the Bièvre plain. Its surroundings are typical of this part of Isère: a mix of maize and wheat fields, pastures, hedges and small woods, with stone farmhouses and church towers on the low ridges.

About twenty-five kilometres to the east lies the Lac de Paladru, a lovely glacial lake surrounded by hills. Its waters have preserved the remains of lake villages from the Neolithic and from around the year 1000, when a community of farmer-knights lived on the shores. The archaeological finds are displayed in a museum at Charavines, and the lake is popular for swimming and boating in summer.

As a start and fuel stop, Châtonnay is close to the A43 and to Bourgoin-Jallieu, where there are plenty of services. The village itself has limited facilities, so it is wise to fill up in Bourgoin or La Côte-Saint-André before setting off into the hills. From here, the roads east towards the Chartreuse are excellent, climbing gradually through the hills before the dramatic limestone cliffs of the massif come into view.

The local roads are winding and pleasant, with short climbs, blind bends and good views. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light. Watch for farm vehicles and gravel at field entrances. In early morning, mist often lies in the hollows, and the light over the hills is beautiful.
t.saint jean de bournay@45.5,5.2:
There is a particular kind of French country town that exists mainly to serve the farms around it, and Saint-Jean-de-Bournay is a good example: a square with plane trees, a church, a café where the same men have been drinking their morning coffee for decades, a pharmacy, a bakery and a weekly market. It sits in a shallow valley in the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné, about twenty-five kilometres east of Vienne, and it does not try to be anything else.

What makes it worth a pause is the country around it. The hills here roll in every direction, low enough to be gentle and high enough to give views: east towards the limestone wall of the Chartreuse and the jagged Belledonne, west towards the dark mass of the Pilat beyond the Rhône. Walnut trees line the lanes, hedges divide pastures from maize, and the farmhouses are built of rounded river stones laid in herringbone patterns, a building style typical of the Dauphiné.

The roads between Saint-Jean, Châtonnay, Artas and Villeneuve-de-Marc are made for unhurried riding. They twist across the hills with no particular logic, climbing over crests and dipping into small valleys, and they rarely carry more than the odd tractor or local car. Surfaces are mostly sound, though there is gravel at field entrances and the odd patch of broken tarmac in the shaded corners. The run west towards Vienne drops gradually towards the Rhône and makes a gentle way to wind the day down.

For a finish, the town has fuel, a supermarket and a couple of places to eat. Sit on the square for a while, watch the light turn gold over the rooftops, and let the engine tick as it cools.
t.saint amour@46.4,5.4:
Saint-Amour sits at the very southern tip of the Jura department, where the first ridges of the Jura mountains meet the flat Bresse plain. The town is old and compact, with narrow streets, a church and a few remnants of its medieval past, and it has the relaxed feel of a place on the border between two worlds: the farms and chicken runs of the Bresse to the west, and the forests and limestone of the Revermont to the east.

Its name has a romantic ring, but it comes from a pair of early Christian martyrs, Amator and Viator, whose relics were brought here, according to tradition. The town's history is tied to the counts of Burgundy and the Franche-Comté, and it changed hands several times before becoming French in the seventeenth century.

As a food stop, Saint-Amour is a good choice. There are a few restaurants and cafés in town, and the food of the region is rich and satisfying: Comté cheese from the Jura mountains, Bresse chicken, morel mushrooms, smoked sausages from Morteau and Montbéliard, and the wines of the Jura, including the distinctive vin jaune. Not every restaurant will have all of these, but you will rarely eat badly.

The riding around Saint-Amour is excellent. The roads east into the Revermont climb through forests and limestone valleys, with plenty of bends and short, steep climbs. To the north, the roads lead towards Lons-le-Saunier and the heart of the Jura. Traffic is light, and surfaces are generally good. Fuel is available in town.
t.moidieu@45.5,5.0:
Moidieu-Détourbe is a quiet village in the hills east of Vienne, in the valley of the Gère, among fields, pastures and woods. It is a typical Bas-Dauphiné village, with a church, a few farms and houses, and a peaceful atmosphere. The surrounding hills offer pleasant views over the countryside.

The great attraction nearby is Vienne, about fifteen kilometres to the west, one of the most important Roman cities in Gaul. Its Temple of Augustus and Livia, built in the first century, is one of the best-preserved Roman temples in France, and the ancient theatre, cut into the hillside above the town, is used every summer for the Jazz à Vienne festival, one of the major jazz festivals in Europe. Across the Rhône, at Saint-Romain-en-Gal, a large archaeological site and museum reveal the remains of Roman houses, workshops and mosaics.

The riding around Moidieu is relaxed and scenic. Roads wind through the hills and along the valley of the Gère, with frequent bends, short climbs and descents. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic is light. The descent into Vienne offers views over the Rhône valley.

Fuel and food are available in Vienne and nearby towns. As a scenic stretch, Moidieu offers a calm, rural interlude on the way to the Alps or the Rhône valley. Vienne itself is well worth a stop, for its Roman heritage and its lively old town.
t.near tignieu@45.8,5.2:
A little north of Tignieu-Jameyzieu, the land runs down to the Rhône, and the river makes a broad, braided sweep across the plain before it reaches Lyon. On the far bank lies the Plaine de l'Ain, a wide gravel terrace of farms and industrial zones, and upstream the hills of the Bugey begin to rise. It is a landscape of crossings: bridges at Loyettes and Lagnieu, gravel pits turned into lakes, and long views towards the mountains.

The area has its own peculiar landmarks. The cooling towers of the Bugey nuclear power station at Saint-Vulbas stand above the river to the north-east, visible for miles. Closer to Tignieu, the medieval town of Crémieu and the limestone plateau of the Isle Crémieu offer a more traditional kind of beauty, with old stone villages, oak woods and small lakes.

As a start and fuel stop, the Tignieu area is practical. There are service stations and supermarkets in Tignieu and Pont-de-Chéruy, and Lyon–Saint-Exupéry airport is close by to the south. The roads east towards the Bugey and the Alps are pleasant, crossing the Rhône and climbing gradually into the hills.

Traffic can be heavy around Tignieu at commuting times, but the roads along the river and into the Bugey are quieter. Surfaces are generally good. For a long day towards the Vanoise or the Jura, this is a convenient place to fill the tank and grab a coffee before the hills start.
t.ceyzeriat@46.2,5.3:
Ceyzériat lies at the foot of the Revermont, just east of Bourg-en-Bresse, where the flat Bresse plain meets the first limestone ridge of the Jura. Behind the village, the wooded slopes rise steeply, and the hill of Mont July above it offers a viewpoint over the Bresse, with the Alps sometimes visible far to the south-east on clear days.

The village has a long history of vine growing on the sunny slopes of the Revermont, and some vineyards survive, though much of the land is now pasture and woodland. The Revermont villages are small and quiet, with stone houses, old churches and fountains, and the area is popular with walkers and cyclists.

As a food stop, Ceyzériat is modest but pleasant, with a few restaurants and cafés. Bourg-en-Bresse, a few minutes away, offers much more choice, including the famous Bresse chicken, cooked in cream and morels or simply roasted. The local markets sell excellent cheeses, charcuterie and fruit.

The riding around Ceyzériat is excellent. The roads east into the Revermont climb steeply, with hairpins and blind bends, then run along ridges and through small valleys with views over the Bresse. The Gorges du Suran and the valley of the Ain are close by. Surfaces vary, and some roads are narrow. Traffic is light. Fuel is available in Ceyzériat and Bourg-en-Bresse.
t.neuville les dames@46.2,5.0:
The name gives away the story. Until the Revolution, Neuville-les-Dames was the seat of a chapter of noble canonesses, a community of aristocratic women who lived here under a religious rule but without the strict vows of nuns. To be admitted, a young woman had to prove several generations of noble ancestry on both sides of the family. They lived in comfortable houses around the church, wore elegant habits and could leave to marry if they wished. The chapter was dissolved in the 1790s, but the dames stayed in the village's name.

Today Neuville is a quiet farming village on the northern edge of the Dombes, beside the little river Chalaronne. The land around it is flat to gently undulating, with fields, hedges, small woods and the first of the ponds that make the Dombes so distinctive. Herons stand motionless in the shallows, and in spring the air rings with frogs.

Calling this a high point is generous; the Dombes is a plateau with barely a hill on it. But the slight rise of the land here gives you long, low views across the fields, and on a clear evening the Beaujolais hills stand out to the west across the Saône valley, with the Jura ridges faint in the east.

The roads are a pleasure to cruise. They wind gently between ponds and farms, with very little traffic and generally decent tarmac, though some lanes are narrow and the edges soft. Watch for mud from farm vehicles and for wildlife at dusk. Fuel is available in Châtillon-sur-Chalaronne, a few minutes away, a lovely little town with a covered timber market hall and flower-decked bridges over the river.
t.sostegno@45.6,8.3:
Sostegno is a small hill village on the eastern side of the province of Biella, in the band of low, wooded hills that runs between the Biellese and the Valsesia in north-west Piedmont. On a clear morning the whole southern face of Monte Rosa stands up white beyond the ridges to the north, so close and so enormous that it seems to belong to a different scale of world.

These hills are wine country, though modestly so. The slopes around Sostegno, Lozzolo and Roasio produce Bramaterra and other Nebbiolo-based reds of the Alto Piemonte, lighter and more mineral than the famous Barolo further south, and grown on soils of volcanic and glacial origin. Vineyards cling to sunny slopes among chestnut woods, and the villages have the slightly faded, stone-and-shutters look of rural Piedmont.

The riding is lovely and very little known. Narrow roads twist over the hills from village to village, with tight bends, short steep climbs and surprise views of the Alps, then drop to the plain where the rice fields of the Baraggia begin. Surfaces are variable, sometimes broken, and you will share the lanes with tractors and the occasional cyclist. Further north, the Panoramica Zegna above Trivero, a scenic road built by the wool industrialist Ermenegildo Zegna in the 1930s, climbs through rhododendrons and beech woods with views over the plain, and it makes a superb extension.

Biella, a wool town with a long textile tradition, is the nearest place with full services, and smaller towns like Gattinara and Cossato have fuel and food. As a start and finish, Sostegno is quiet and atmospheric, best at the beginning or end of the day when the light is low and the mountain glows.
t.near senna lodigiana@45.1,9.6:
Senna Lodigiana is a farming village on the north bank of the Po, opposite Piacenza, in the flat, fertile Lodigiano. Here the great river is wide and slow, flanked by poplar plantations, sandbanks and high flood embankments, the argini, which protect the farmland from the floods that have shaped this landscape for centuries.

Pilgrims on the Via Francigena, the medieval route from Canterbury to Rome, crossed the Po near here. Sigeric, Archbishop of Canterbury, recorded the crossing in the tenth century, and today walkers following his route still cross by boat from Corte Sant'Andrea, a hamlet of Senna Lodigiana, to the south bank, where a small ferry service carries them across. It is one of the most atmospheric moments on the whole route.

The food here is wonderful. The Lodigiano is dairy country, and Grana Padano and other cheeses are made from the milk of its cows. Across the river, Piacenza is famous for its cured meats, coppa, pancetta and salame, all with protected status, and for the red wine Gutturnio from the hills to the south. Risotto, tortelli and boiled meats with mostarda are on every menu.

The riding is flat and peaceful, with roads running along the embankments and through the farmland, with views over the river and the poplar groves. Surfaces vary, and some embankment roads are narrow. Traffic is light. Fuel and food are available in the area, and Piacenza, across the bridge, has full services. As a finish, the Po at sunset, with mist rising from the water, is a memorable sight.
t.near giubiasco@46.1,9.0:
Giubiasco lies at the southern edge of Bellinzona, the capital of the Swiss canton of Ticino, where the valley of the Ticino river opens towards the Magadino plain and Lake Maggiore. For centuries, this was the gateway to the Alpine passes, the Gotthard, San Bernardino and Lukmanier, and whoever controlled Bellinzona controlled the trade routes between Italy and northern Europe.

That is why Bellinzona has three castles, Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro, built by the Dukes of Milan in the fifteenth century and linked by walls that once blocked the entire valley. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the views from their towers over the valley and the mountains are spectacular. Castelgrande, on its rock in the middle of town, is the most impressive.

As a food stop, Giubiasco and Bellinzona have plenty of choice. Ticino's food is Italian in spirit, with Swiss precision: polenta, risotto, game, cured meats and cheeses from the mountain valleys, and the local Merlot, which thrives in the mild climate. The traditional grotti, rustic restaurants in the woods above the towns, often with stone tables under chestnut trees, are a delight in summer.

The riding from here is superb. The roads north lead to the great Alpine passes, while the road south over the Monte Ceneri leads to Lugano and the lakes. Switzerland requires a motorway vignette, motorcycles included, and speed limits are strictly enforced, with heavy fines. Fuel is available in town.
t.near motta visconti@45.3,8.9:
Motta Visconti stands on the edge of the Ticino valley, south-west of Milan, where the land drops from the Lombard plain into the broad, wooded corridor of the river. The Ticino here is wild and braided, flowing in multiple channels between gravel banks and islands, and the valley is protected as the Parco del Ticino, one of the oldest regional parks in Italy and a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

The forests along the river are home to herons, kingfishers and many other birds, and the riverside paths are popular with walkers and cyclists. Just upstream, at Bereguardo, a pontoon bridge made of boats crosses the river, one of the last of its kind in Italy, and riding across it is a memorable experience. A little to the north, the Cistercian Abbey of Morimondo, founded in the twelfth century, stands among the rice fields, its brick church and cloister beautifully preserved.

As a start and fuel stop, Motta Visconti is convenient, with service stations in the area and in nearby Abbiategrasso and Bereguardo. The roads here are flat, running through rice fields and along the river, with long straights and gentle curves. In spring, when the rice fields are flooded, the plain becomes a vast mirror reflecting the sky, and on clear days the Alps appear on the horizon.

Traffic is light away from the main roads, but watch for farm vehicles and mosquitoes in summer. Surfaces vary. From here, the roads north lead to the lakes and the Alps, the start of a great day of riding.
t.cilavegna@45.3,8.8:
Call Cilavegna a high point and anyone from the Lomellina will laugh: this corner of Lombardy, between the Ticino and the Sesia, is about as flat as land gets, a vast chequerboard of rice paddies, irrigation canals and poplar rows. But stand on the bank of a canal in spring, when the paddies are flooded and the whole plain becomes a mirror for the sky, with the snow-covered Alps floating above the horizon, and you will understand why people love it. Locals call it the mare a quadretti, the chequered sea.

Cilavegna itself is a farming town with a church, a square and a reputation for asparagus, celebrated each spring with a festival. The Lomellina is one of Italy's main rice-growing areas, and risotto is the local religion. The rice fields also support huge numbers of herons, egrets and other wading birds, which nest in colonies in the woods.

Just to the east lies Vigevano, home to one of the most beautiful squares in Italy, the Piazza Ducale, designed in the late fifteenth century for Ludovico Sforza, known as il Moro, with arcades on three sides and a castle behind. Leonardo da Vinci worked on irrigation projects in this area for the Sforza court.

The riding is flat and straight, with long views and very little traffic. Surfaces vary, and some farm roads are narrow and rough. Watch for tractors, mud and mosquitoes in summer. Fuel and food are available in Cilavegna, Mortara and Vigevano.
t.near cantu@45.7,9.2:
Cantù is a town in the Brianza, the hilly area between Milan and Lake Como, and it has two claims to fame that may surprise you: furniture and lace. For centuries, the craftsmen of Cantù have made fine furniture, and the town is still full of workshops and showrooms. The lace-making tradition, the pizzo di Cantù, is equally old, and the town hosts exhibitions and a lace school. And in Italy, Cantù is also known for its basketball team, which has won European titles.

On the edge of town, the Basilica of San Vincenzo in Galliano is a gem of early Romanesque architecture, consecrated in the early eleventh century, with frescoes of remarkable quality and a baptistery beside it. It is a quiet, atmospheric place, well worth a short stop.

The Brianza hills are green and rolling, covered with woods, villas and small towns, and they rise gradually towards the Alps. Lake Como is only a short ride to the north, and the roads around its southern end, towards Como and Lecco, are scenic and busy.

The riding around Cantù is a mix of urban roads and hill routes. The Brianza is densely populated, and traffic can be heavy, but the minor roads through the hills offer pleasant curves, short climbs and views of the mountains. Surfaces vary. Fuel and food are plentiful in Cantù and the surrounding towns. As a scenic stretch, the hills above the town offer glimpses of the Alps and the lakes.
t.near andermatt@46.6,8.4:
The church of Wassen stands on a terrace above the Reuss, and passengers on the old Gotthard railway see it three times as the line spirals through tunnels to gain height, a famous trick of nineteenth-century engineering that makes travellers think they are going in circles. This stop lies in that village, at the foot of the Susten pass, where the road leaves the Reuss valley and climbs west into the Meiental towards the Bernese Oberland.

The Susten road was built between 1938 and 1946, one of the first Alpine passes designed for motor traffic from the start, and its engineering is a pleasure to ride, with wide, well-banked bends, stone walls and tunnels. The eastern side climbs through the Meiental, a narrow valley of farms and forest, while the western side drops past the Steingletscher, a glacier that hangs above the road near the top, and down the long descent to Innertkirchen.

Andermatt, a few kilometres south, is a mountain village at the crossroads of the Alps, where the Gotthard, Oberalp and Furka roads meet, and it has been transformed in recent years by a large resort development. The Schöllenen gorge, between Andermatt and Göschenen, is crossed by the Devil's Bridge, where legend says the devil built the first bridge in exchange for the first soul to cross it, and the locals sent a goat.

The Susten is usually closed from late autumn to early summer, depending on snow. Weather can change quickly, and the top can be cold and windy even in summer.

Wassen is tiny, so do not count on it for fuel; Altdorf, Erstfeld or Andermatt are the safe bets. The village does have a couple of inns, and a coffee on a terrace here, listening to trains disappear into the mountain on one side and bikes winding up towards the Susten on the other, is a very Swiss pleasure.
t.near airolo@46.5,8.5:
The nearest one climbs up from the Maggia side to Fusio, a stone village at the head of Val Lavizzara, and continues to the Sambuco dam, a curved concrete wall holding back a long reservoir. It is about as far from the bustle of the Gotthard as you can get while staying within a few kilometres of it.

For most riders on the Grand Tour, though, this part of Ticino is about Airolo and the Gotthard. Airolo sits at the southern foot of the pass, where the Tremola, the old cobbled road, comes down the mountain in a series of tight hairpins stacked one above the other. It is one of the most famous stretches of road in the Alps, paved with granite setts in the mid-twentieth century over a nineteenth-century route, and riding it is a rattling, slow and unforgettable experience. The modern road over the pass, wider and smoother, runs alongside, and the road tunnel underneath carries most of the traffic.

The Gotthard has been one of the key routes across the Alps since the thirteenth century, when the Schöllenen gorge on the northern side was made passable. Airolo has a museum dedicated to the history of the pass and the people who built its roads and tunnels, many of them Italian workers who died in accidents and of disease during the construction of the railway tunnel in the 1870s. A monument at the station remembers them.

Back in this high country, the weather is the main concern. Snow lies late on the ridges, storms build quickly on summer afternoons, and the minor roads close in winter. The roads up into the side valleys are narrow, steep and sometimes rough, with little traffic and few places to pass. Wildlife is plentiful: chamois, marmots and the occasional golden eagle. For fuel and food, Airolo is the nearest village with services, and Faido, further down the Leventina, has more. For a bigger town, Biasca is about thirty kilometres away. The Val Lavizzara side has small villages with bars, but plan your fuel carefully if you head that way.
t.near davos@46.8,9.9:
Flüela tops out at 2,383 metres, a wide, bare saddle between the Schwarzhorn and the Weisshorn, and the first thing you notice when you get there is the silence. The road from Davos has climbed through the Flüela valley, first through pine and larch, then out onto open pasture, and now you are in a stony world of scree, snowfields and two small dark lakes beside the road. The old hospice at the top, a solid stone building, has served travellers for generations and still serves coffee, soup and cake to riders who arrive cold.

The pass links Davos, in the Prättigau and Landwasser valleys, with Susch in the Lower Engadine, and it has been used since the Middle Ages, when mule trains carried goods between the two regions. The modern road was built in the 1860s, and it has always been a seasonal route: in winter heavy snow and avalanches close it, typically from November to May, although the canton tries to keep it open as long as possible, and closures can happen at short notice. Since the Vereina rail tunnel opened in 1999, with a car-carrying train between Klosters and the Engadine, the pass has become a summer road for those who want to ride it for its own sake.

The riding is good rather than technical. On the Davos side, the climb is steady and well surfaced, with long bends and a few hairpins, and the road is wide enough for comfortable overtaking. On the Engadine side, the descent to Susch is steeper and more twisting, with a series of hairpins through the forest and views down into the Lower Engadine. Watch for cyclists, who love this pass, and for cattle and sheep on the open pasture. The weather can change quickly: snow can fall at the top even in July, and fog can roll in from the valleys.

The landscape around the pass is wild and empty, and it is a good place for spotting wildlife: marmots whistle from the rocks, ibex graze on the high slopes, and golden eagles hunt overhead. The Schwarzhorn, to the south, is a popular walk from the top of the pass, with views over the whole of Graubünden. For fuel and food, Davos is about ten kilometres away with every service, and Zernez and Susch, on the Engadine side, have stations and restaurants. Zernez is also the gateway to the Swiss National Park, the oldest in the Alps.
t.near rives on the way back@45.3,5.5:
Beaucroissant and Renage lie in the green hill country of the Bas-Dauphiné, between Grenoble and Lyon, near the little town of Rives, and not far from the Lac de Paladru, which is why the point is tagged for swimming. The lake is a glacial one, about five kilometres long, with clear water, a few beaches and shallows that warm up quickly in July and August, and the water and woodland setting make it a favourite with the people of Grenoble and Lyon. Entrance to some of the beaches is charged in season.

Voiron, a town of about twenty thousand a short distance to the east, is the larger place for fuel and supplies, and it is the home of the Chartreuse liqueur. The monks of the Grande Chartreuse monastery, high in the mountains beyond, make the green and yellow liqueur from a secret recipe of 130 herbs, and the distillery cellars in Voiron, said to be the largest liqueur cellars in the world, offer tours and tastings. The Chartreuse massif, a block of limestone cliffs and forests, forms the skyline to the east, and the road toward the monastery is a lovely ride.

Around Renage and Beaucroissant the country is gentler: rolling fields, walnut orchards, ponds and small villages with stone houses and tiled roofs. The Dauphiné is known for its walnuts, which have their own appellation, and for gratin dauphinois, a potato dish baked with cream. Roads wander along the valley floors and over low ridges, with easy corners, light traffic, and a surface that is mostly smooth, with the occasional patch of gravel on country lanes.

The Alpe d'Huez and the Oisans, the destination of this long ride, lie further south, beyond Grenoble, so treat this spot as a warm-up or a cool-down. A swim after a day on the road is a fine thing, so pack a towel. Summers are hot and thundery, and early autumn gives the best light. Watch for tractors and slow vehicles, especially at harvest time, and for school traffic near the villages.
t.near moirans en montagne on the way back:
Moirans-en-Montagne is a small town of about two thousand in the Jura, where the mountains of Franche-Comté are laid out in long, parallel ridges, and it has a surprise for the visitor: a museum of toys, one of the best in France, in an old convent, which celebrates the local tradition of toy-making in wood and plastic. The Jura has a history of small workshops using local timber, producing clocks, pipes, toys and spectacles, and that heritage is part of the area's character. Arinthod, a village of about thirteen hundred, is a handsome little market place with an arcaded square and a scattering of old houses.

The reason this point is tagged for swimming is the Lac de Vouglans, which lies just to the east. It is an artificial lake, formed by a dam on the river Ain in 1968, and about thirty-five kilometres long and winding like a fjord, it is one of the largest reservoirs in France. The water is clear and deep, and the beaches and bays attract swimmers, sailors and kayakers in summer, with several supervised swimming areas and lakeside cafés. The lake is surrounded by wooded cliffs and has a real mountain flavour.

For motorcyclists, the Jura is one of the best-kept secrets in France: roads that curve through forest, over passes and through the gorges of the Ain, the Valouse and the Bienne, with long, smooth bends and little traffic. The Cascades du Hérisson, a series of waterfalls in a wooded valley a short ride away, are a famous sight, with a path along the stream that takes an hour or two to walk. The Chartreuse, named in the ride, is far to the south-east, so this place is more of a northern neighbour.

For fuel and supplies, Moirans, Saint-Claude and Lons-le-Saunier are the places to head for, and the area's food is another reason to come: Comté cheese, aged for months in caves, smoked sausage from Morteau, and the yellow wine, vin jaune, which is made in a way found nowhere else. Winters are cold and snowy, and the higher roads may be closed. Summer is warm, though storms are common, and autumn light is golden. Watch for cattle on the road and for cyclists.
t.near modane@45.2,6.6:
This spot lies in the Maurienne, the long valley of the river Arc that runs from the high Alps down toward Chambéry, and the town of Modane sits at the heart of it. For centuries this was the way across the mountains to Italy, via the Mont Cenis pass, and in the nineteenth century engineers drove a railway tunnel under the Fréjus massif, which opened in 1871 and gave the town its role as a border station. A road tunnel followed in 1980. Today Modane is quiet and a bit industrial, but its position makes it a natural stopping place.

On the Route des Grandes Alpes, the old tourist road laid out in the early twentieth century from Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean, this valley connects two great mountain sections. To the north lies the Col de l'Iseran, over 2,700 metres, among the highest paved passes in the Alps, and to the west the Galibier, which tops 2,600 metres and is the high point of many riders' year. Both are closed by snow for most of the winter and spring, usually reopening in early summer, so check before you plan.

The riding here is a lesson in scale. The valley is steep-sided, with forts clinging to the slopes, avalanche galleries over the road and a scattering of villages with slate roofs. Weather can change quickly: sun in the valley can mean snow above, and thunderstorms build in the afternoon. Start early and keep warm layers handy. In the valley the road is wide and fast, but the passes demand attention, with hairpins and sheer drops.

Modane has about four thousand people and offers fuel, a few cafes and a supermarket. If you are heading up toward the high passes, fill the tank here, because stations become scarce higher up. The nearby ski resorts, such as Val Thorens, are on the other side of the mountains, and in summer they are quiet. Carry a rain jacket, and stop to look at the cliffs when you can.
t.near saint jean de bournay@45.4,5.1:
There is a particular kind of French country town that exists mainly to serve the farms around it, and Saint-Jean-de-Bournay is a good example: a square with plane trees, a church, a café where the same men have been drinking their morning coffee for decades, a pharmacy, a bakery and a weekly market. It sits in a shallow valley in the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné, about twenty-five kilometres east of Vienne, and it does not try to be anything else.

What makes it worth a pause is the country around it. The hills here roll in every direction, low enough to be gentle and high enough to give views: east towards the limestone wall of the Chartreuse and the jagged Belledonne, west towards the dark mass of the Pilat beyond the Rhône. Walnut trees line the lanes, hedges divide pastures from maize, and the farmhouses are built of rounded river stones laid in herringbone patterns, a building style typical of the Dauphiné.

The roads between Saint-Jean, Châtonnay, Artas and Villeneuve-de-Marc are made for unhurried riding. They twist across the hills with no particular logic, climbing over crests and dipping into small valleys, and they rarely carry more than the odd tractor or local car. Surfaces are mostly sound, though there is gravel at field entrances and the odd patch of broken tarmac in the shaded corners. The run west towards Vienne drops gradually towards the Rhône and makes a gentle way to wind the day down.

For a finish, the town has fuel, a supermarket and a couple of places to eat. Sit on the square for a while, watch the light turn gold over the rooftops, and let the engine tick as it cools.
t.near cilavegna@45.3,8.8:
Call Cilavegna a high point and anyone from the Lomellina will laugh: this corner of Lombardy, between the Ticino and the Sesia, is about as flat as land gets, a vast chequerboard of rice paddies, irrigation canals and poplar rows. But stand on the bank of a canal in spring, when the paddies are flooded and the whole plain becomes a mirror for the sky, with the snow-covered Alps floating above the horizon, and you will understand why people love it. Locals call it the mare a quadretti, the chequered sea.

Cilavegna itself is a farming town with a church, a square and a reputation for asparagus, celebrated each spring with a festival. The Lomellina is one of Italy's main rice-growing areas, and risotto is the local religion. The rice fields also support huge numbers of herons, egrets and other wading birds, which nest in colonies in the woods.

Just to the east lies Vigevano, home to one of the most beautiful squares in Italy, the Piazza Ducale, designed in the late fifteenth century for Ludovico Sforza, known as il Moro, with arcades on three sides and a castle behind. Leonardo da Vinci worked on irrigation projects in this area for the Sforza court.

The riding is flat and straight, with long views and very little traffic. Surfaces vary, and some farm roads are narrow and rough. Watch for tractors, mud and mosquitoes in summer. Fuel and food are available in Cilavegna, Mortara and Vigevano.
t.near linthal@46.9,8.9:
Linthal is the last real village at the head of the Linth valley in canton Glarus, a long way into the mountains and a place that the modern world mostly passes by. About a thousand people live here, among steep meadows, old wooden houses and the dark shapes of textile mills from the days when cotton printing ruled the valley. Above the village rises the Tödi, the highest peak of the Glarus Alps, at over 3,600 metres, with ice on its flanks and a long history of mountaineering. From the valley floor, in the right light, the glaciers look like they are poured down the rock.

For riders, Linthal is the start of the Klausen Pass, one of Switzerland's grand classic crossings, climbing to nearly 1,950 metres before dropping into Uri. The road was an official hill-climb race course in the 1920s and early 1930s, the Klausenrennen, when cars and motorcycles flew up the hairpins in front of crowds, and you can see why it was chosen. The surface is smooth, the bends are well engineered, and the views on the way up, with waterfalls pouring from the cliffs, are among the best in the central Alps. It is wide enough for confident riding, but traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, so aim for the morning.

Up the valley beyond Linthal, an aerial cable car and a funicular climb to Braunwald, a car-free village on a terrace, and a dam holds the Limmernsee in a high basin. The Pantenbrücke, a wooden bridge in the gorge, is a favourite with walkers.

Fuel is not available in the upper valley with any reliability, so top up in Glarus, about fourteen kilometres down the road, before setting off. The Klausen is closed in winter, normally from late October to early June, and in the shoulder seasons a sudden storm can bring snow and ice. Temperatures drop quickly, and the wind at the summit can be cutting. Cows grazing near the road are common, so be ready for a slow stretch. When you leave Linthal, the road begins to rise almost immediately, and you will feel the day tighten around you.
t.near valloire@45.1,6.4:
Valloire sits in a green bowl at about 1,430 metres, at the foot of the Galibier, and it feels like a proper mountain village rather than a purpose-built resort, which is rarer than it should be in the Alps. The old centre is a mix of stone chalets, small shops, and a church with an interior that is a riot of Baroque painting and gilding, a reminder that the Savoyard valleys were once rich in devotion and craft. In summer, cyclists and walkers fill the cafes, and in winter, the village becomes a ski resort.

The setting is lovely. The valley of the Valloirette runs toward the Galibier, with high meadows, scree slopes, and the glacier-tipped peaks of the Écrins beyond. Mountain flowers carpet the meadows in June and July, and marmots whistle from the rocks. The air smells of cut grass and pine, and the nights are cool even in summer. A short walk up a path from the village takes you into silence and big views.

For a rider, Valloire is the gateway to the Galibier, one of the great passes of the Alps. The road climbs from the village in a series of long bends, passing the last farms and then rising above the tree line into a barren landscape of rock and snow patches, and the summit stands at 2,642 metres. The ride is spectacular but demanding, with narrow sections, steep drops, and sudden weather changes, and the pass is usually open only from early summer to autumn. Before setting off, check the status, and keep a warm layer in the bag.

Valloire has fuel, though stations are small, so fill up when you can. Saint-Michel-de-Maurienne, about seven kilometres away down the valley, is the nearest bigger place, and Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne is larger still. The village has plenty of cafes, bakeries, and restaurants, and Savoyard dishes such as tartiflette, diots, and gratin dauphinois are on many menus. A pause here before or after the Galibier is a good idea. The best season is July to September, but late June brings the flowers, and autumn brings the clearest air.
t.near tiefencastel@46.6,9.7:
Tiefencastel sits at the bottom of a deep, narrow fold in the Graubünden mountains, at the point where the Albula river meets the Julia, and its name, the deep castle, is accurate in a geographical sense. The village is small, with a little baroque church on a rock above the river, and its importance is mostly as a junction: roads and railways from Chur, Davos, the Engadine and the Surselva meet here. For a motorcyclist, it is the start of the Julier Pass, one of the oldest crossings of the Alps, and the entry to a landscape that rises steadily from woodland to bare rock.

The Julier has been used since Roman times, and at the top, about 2,284 metres up, two stumps of Roman columns once marked the crossing. The modern road is wide and well surfaced, with long bends and gentle gradients, making it an easy pass to ride quickly or slowly. Beyond Savognin, the valley opens into pastureland and the forest thins, then the road climbs through bare terrain toward Bivio, a village where the Italian-speaking influence is visible in the architecture. From the top, the view descends to the Upper Engadine lakes, silver and blue under a wide sky.

At Tiefencastel itself, there are a few cafés and shops, but for fuel and bigger supplies, Lenzerheide is seven kilometres away and Chur, twenty-one kilometres, is the sensible choice. Riders sometimes miss that the pass is high and exposed, so it is wise to be full before you start. The region is Romansh-speaking in parts, and you will see signs in a language that most Swiss cannot read either. The local food leans on barley, cured meat and cheese, and a bowl of Bündner Gerstensuppe, the barley soup, is a comfort in cold weather.

The railway is part of the experience. The Albula line, with its viaducts and spiral tunnels, is a masterpiece of Alpine engineering, and the red trains of the Rhaetian Railway wind through the landscape like toys. If you hear a horn echoing through the valley, you can be fairly sure a train is coming. The pass is open in summer and closed or restricted in winter, so check conditions, and expect weather to change fast above the tree line.
t.near la punt chamues ch@46.6,9.9:
There are places in the Upper Engadine where the light behaves differently, and La Punt Chamues-ch is one of them. The valley here is high, around 1,700 metres, wide and flat-floored, with the young Inn river meandering through meadows and larch woods, and the air has a dry, thin brightness that makes distant peaks look sharp. The village is a cluster of traditional Engadine houses with thick walls, deep-set windows and sgraffito decoration scratched into pale plaster, and the language spoken here is Romansh, one of Switzerland's four national languages, in its local Puter form.

The road you came on, the Albula Pass, climbs to 2,315 metres from the Bergün side, and its character is quieter and calmer than many other Swiss passes. It is not as busy as the Flüela or the Julier, and its curves are rhythmic, with open views of rock and alpine pasture, and the surface is usually good. On the far side, you descend into the Engadine on a road that opens suddenly into this big, bright valley. Alongside, the Rhaetian Railway runs through the Albula tunnel under the pass, part of a line that is on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

La Punt is close to Zuoz, a more elegant village with a boarding school, and to Samedan, the larger town of the valley, six kilometres away, where you can find fuel, supermarkets and a hospital. The valley is also a place for Nusstorte, the walnut and caramel tart of Graubünden, which you should try with a strong coffee. The Engadine's reputation for sunshine is deserved, with more than three hundred days of it each year, though that does not mean warmth, and mornings can be cold even in summer.

The pass is closed in winter, normally from November until late spring, and snow can fall at any time of year at the top, so carry something warm. In autumn the larches turn gold, and the valley glows in a way that is hard to forget. Riders who have come over the Albula often stop here to rest, and an hour at a table outside a café, with the Inn rippling by and the peaks around, is a very good use of an afternoon.
