t.near silvaplana@46.5,9.7:
Silvaplana is where the Upper Engadine opens out into water and wind. The village sits on the edge of a lake of the same name, at around 1,800 metres, between the larger resort of St. Moritz and the little village of Sils, and above it the high peaks of the Bernina and Albula ranges hold glaciers in their cirques. The light here is famously clear, an effect of altitude and dry air that has drawn painters and thinkers for generations.

The lake is the thing. A steady wind blows up the valley most summer afternoons, known as the Maloja wind, and it has made Silvaplana one of the best places in Europe for windsurfing and kitesurfing. The water is cold and a deep blue, and the colourful sails on a clear day make a striking sight against the white of the mountains. Nietzsche spent summers in nearby Sils Maria and wrote some of his best-known work walking the lakeshore; a stone with a quotation still marks the place.

The road that ends the ride here is the Julier, one of the old Roman crossings, that climbs from the Surses valley to a pass of 2,284 metres and drops to the Engadine. The riding is wonderful: long, open bends, rocky slopes, and a wide view as you drop toward the lakes. The surface is generally good, and traffic is moderate, though summer weekends bring more. Wind and cold can make the top feel wintry even in July.

Silvaplana itself is small, with a handful of hotels, cafes and a few shops, and the nearby town of St. Moritz, with nearly five thousand people, is the place for fuel and larger services. Prices in the area are high, so it is worth knowing in advance. The Engadine is a place where Romansh is still spoken, and where houses have thick walls with small windows and the decorative sgraffito patterns typical of the valley. Evenings are cool even in summer, and a warm drink beside the lake is an ideal way to end the ride.
t.near brig@46.2,8.1:
Brig is a small town with a big palace, and its position at the foot of the Simplon Pass gives it a significance out of proportion to its size. It sits in the upper Rhône valley in the canton of Valais, where the river runs west to Lake Geneva, and a route over the mountains to Italy has existed here since Roman times. The Stockalperschloss, the biggest private residence in Switzerland when it was completed in the late seventeenth century, was built by Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper, a merchant who controlled the Simplon trade and became the richest man in the country. With its three onion-domed towers, named for the Three Kings, it dominates the old town and is open to visitors.

The Simplon Pass road is the reason riders come. Napoleon had a carriage road built over it between 1801 and 1805, so that his armies could cross to Italy, and it is still one of the great engineering works of the age. The road climbs in broad curves out of the Rhône valley, passes through galleries and over a famous bridge at the Ganter gorge, and crosses the top at about two thousand metres. The surface is good, the bends are open and consistent, and the views toward the Bernese and Valais Alps are huge. The pass is usually open from about May to October, and sections can be icy in the shoulder seasons, so check road conditions before you go.

South of the border lies the Italian valley of the Ossola, and Domodossola is a pleasant place for lunch. The Simplon Tunnel, a railway tunnel opened in 1906, runs far beneath the pass and was the longest tunnel in the world for much of the twentieth century. Naters, just across the river from Brig, is the starting point for the Aletsch Glacier region, the largest ice stream in the Alps.

Brig and Naters together have fuel, supermarkets and plenty of restaurants, and the town is a handy base. The Rhône valley can be hot in summer and windy in the afternoon, so start the pass early.

Raclette, melted local cheese scraped onto potatoes, is the Valais speciality, and a glass of Fendant, a crisp white wine, goes with it.
t.near lutry@46.5,6.7:
Lutry is where the Lavaux begins, if you come from Lausanne, and it announces the fact with vineyards that climb straight up behind the old town. The terraces, held by dry-stone walls that run for kilometres, rise from the shore of Lake Geneva to the ridge above, a staircase of green in summer and gold in autumn. They were first built by monks in the Middle Ages, and in 2007 UNESCO placed the whole landscape on its World Heritage list. Lutry itself is a lakeside town of nearly nine thousand people, with a medieval centre, a harbour and a promenade.

The old town has narrow, cobbled streets, stone houses with wooden shutters and a Romanesque church tower that rises above the roofs. Its priory dates from the Benedictines, who held the land and planted vines, and the traces of their work are everywhere, in the cellars, the walls and the layout of the terraces. Lutry's wine is mostly Chasselas, a white grape that produces a light, dry, mineral wine that tastes of the stone and the lake. It is the standard drink of western Switzerland, and pairs well with cheese fondue or a plate of fish from the lake.

For a rider, Lutry is the start of a gentle, rewarding ride along the Corniche de Lavaux, the narrow road that threads between the vines high above the lake. The bends are tight and the surface is smooth, with walls on both sides and sudden views across the water to the mountains of Savoy. Traffic can be an issue, because the road is narrow and popular with cyclists and walkers, and on weekends in the harvest season it can be very slow. The main road along the lake is faster but busier, with traffic lights and heavy lorries. For a quiet visit, aim for a weekday in spring or autumn, preferably in the morning, when the light is soft on the water.

Lutry is a town, not a village, so there are fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and restaurants, and Lausanne is only a few kilometres away if you need anything more. Parking can be tight in the old town, and motorcycle bays near the harbour are usually the easiest option. A coffee on the harbour front, with the sailing boats bobbing in the water, is a pleasant way to spend a short while.

In September and October, the grape harvest brings tractors and pickers to the terraces, and the air smells of crushed fruit and wine cellars. Walk up through the vines for a few hundred metres, and the view back across the lake is one of the best in the country.
t.near vevey@46.5,6.8:
Vevey is a lakeside town where the Alps seem to drop straight into Lake Geneva, and the light on the water can be so clear and bright that the mountains on the far side, in France, look close enough to touch. It is the capital of the Riviera vaudoise, about sixteen thousand people strong, with a long promenade, a market square lined with arcades and an air of calm prosperity. The town is the home of Nestlé, which started here in the nineteenth century, and the company's headquarters and food museum are a fixture on the waterfront.

Charlie Chaplin lived in the hills above Vevey for the last twenty-five years of his life, and a bronze statue of him stands on the lakeshore, with his cane and bowler hat. The great cultural event is the Fête des Vignerons, held roughly once a generation, with a huge pageant celebrating the winegrowers of the region, and the last edition took place in 2019. Look for the giant fork stuck in the lake, a sculpture placed there as a joke about the Alimentarium, and for the many cafés where you can have a coffee with a view.

The ride leading here follows the Lavaux, a steep terraced slope of vineyards that runs for about thirty kilometres along the lake and is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The terraces were built up by medieval monks, mostly Cistercians and Benedictines, over many centuries, and the vines, principally the white Chasselas, soak up three kinds of sun: direct, reflected from the lake and radiated from the stone walls. The roads are narrow, walled and twisting, with villages such as Cully, Lutry and Chexbres perched on the slope, and you need to ride at walking pace in some places.

Fuel, food and rest are no trouble in Vevey. The weather is mild by Swiss standards, though the wind called the bise can blow cold from the northeast in winter. Late September is the grape harvest, when the vineyard roads are busy with tractors and pickers, and a tasting in a winemaker's cellar is a fine way to end the day. Do not drink and ride, but do buy a bottle for later.
t.near altdorf@46.9,8.6:
Altdorf is the capital of the canton of Uri, a small town at the head of Lake Lucerne's southern arm where the Reuss river leaves the mountains and the Gotthard route begins. It is a practical, low-key place, flat and sheltered, with a pretty centre and a roar of traffic nearby from the motorway, and it is the sort of town where riders refill the tank, buy a coffee and look up at the wall of peaks above.

The centre of attention is Wilhelm Tell. The legend says that Tell, a crossbowman from Uri, was forced by the tyrannical Austrian bailiff Gessler to shoot an apple from his son's head, and that he later killed Gessler and helped spark the Swiss rebellion. In the main square stands a statue of Tell and his son, put up in the 1890s, and the story is told with pride. Historians doubt that Tell ever existed, but locals tend to treat that as irrelevant.

The roads from here are some of the best in Switzerland. South, the Gotthard route climbs through the Reuss valley, with its old stone bridges and the Devil's Bridge legend. East, the Klausen pass links to Glarus, and the Susten pass heads west toward Meiringen, with its sweeping bends and glacier views, closed in winter. Altdorf is also the gateway to the Axenstrasse, a lake-side road cut through rock, with tunnels, balconies and glimpses of the water far below. These are famous riding routes, and they get busy on sunny weekends.

Fuel is straightforward here, with several stations, and the town has plenty of cafes and bakeries. Altdorf lies at only 458 metres, so it warms up early, though the mountain passes above are still snowed up in spring. Give yourself time for breakfast before the big climbs. Note that the Gotthard road tunnel can have long queues, so plan around the holiday traffic.
t.near wildhaus@47.3,9.3:
Wildhaus is the village where Huldrych Zwingli was born, and that makes it, quietly, one of the cradles of the Swiss Reformation. Zwingli, who became the leader of the Protestant movement in Zürich and died in battle in 1531, was born in 1484 in a farmhouse here, and the small timber building still stands, now a museum. It is a modest place, a wooden house with low ceilings and small windows, and it gives a feel for the mountain farming community from which the reformer came.

The village sits at about 1,090 metres on a broad saddle, the Wildhaus Pass, between the Rhine valley and the Toggenburg, in a landscape of green meadows and wooded slopes. Above it rise the Churfirsten, a line of seven limestone peaks that stand like a wall along the north side of the Walensee, and which are among the most recognisable mountains in eastern Switzerland. From the village, the north face is a tall, sheer escarpment. Further north, the Säntis, the highest peak of the Alpstein, can be seen in the distance.

For a rider, Wildhaus is a lovely stop on the road between Buchs in the Rhine valley and the Toggenburg, with gentle bends, smooth tarmac and moderate gradients. The road is a pleasure at an easy pace, and the scenery is varied, with views of both the Churfirsten and the Alpstein. Traffic is light except in the ski season and on summer weekends. Weather can change quickly, and the pass is occasionally icy in winter, so keep an eye on the forecast.

The village has fuel nearby, small shops and cafes, and a handful of restaurants serving traditional dishes. The Toggenburg region is known for its cheese, its dairy products and a distinctive folk music tradition, the Naturjodel, which uses wordless harmonies, and which you may hear at a festival or in a restaurant on a Sunday. In winter the village is a ski resort, and in summer it is a hiking centre, with lifts that take walkers to the high pastures.

Grabs, about seven kilometres down toward the Rhine, is the nearest sizeable town and has more services. A coffee in the village, with a view of the Churfirsten, is a pleasant way to spend a short stop. Try a slice of Toggenburger Biber, the local gingerbread with almond filling, which is a good snack for the road.
t.near schwyz@47.0,8.7:
Schwyz is the village that gave Switzerland its name. The country's flag grew from the banner of this canton, and the oldest surviving federal charter, dated to 1291, is kept in a museum in town, written on parchment with seals that have survived seven centuries. If history is the thing for you, this is as close to the source as you can get, and a short walk in the old centre shows how modest the beginnings were.

The town itself is lively without being busy: a broad square with a baroque church, a town hall with painted facades showing a battle scene, and stately patrician houses built by men who had made fortunes as mercenary officers in foreign armies. Behind it all rise the Mythen, two sharp limestone peaks that look from the village like a pair of horns and dominate every photograph. The cloud sits on them often, and on a clear morning they are a fine sight with coffee in hand.

With fourteen thousand people, Schwyz has fuel, bakeries and sit-down restaurants, so as a start or a food stop it is easy. The start of the loop is the main reason to be here: from Schwyz the road climbs south and east into the hills, toward the Ibergeregg and the Pragel, a pair of passes that make a rewarding day. The first miles run through meadows dotted with fruit trees and farmhouses with deep-eaved wooden roofs, and the gradient builds gradually, so there is time to warm up the tyres and your rhythm.

Weather can be unpredictable here, because the Alps' northern edge catches the moist air coming from the lowlands, and a bright start can become grey by lunchtime. Plan accordingly, with a waterproof near the top of the luggage. The Föhn wind also blows through this region, warm and dry from the south, and on those days the air is incredibly clear but the gusts can be strong on the open stretches. In winter, the high passes close, but the town stays lively, and a bowl of something hot in a Gasthaus makes a fair reward for the effort.
t.near sarnen@46.9,8.1:
Sarnen is the capital of Obwalden, and it wears the title lightly. The town sits at the northern end of Lake Sarnen, a long blue lake in the middle of Switzerland, with the Pilatus above and a line of wooded hills on the other side. About nine thousand people live here, and the main street has the usual arrangement of bakeries, banks and cafes, with a large parish church that stands on a rise above the old centre.

What gives the town its identity is the Landsgemeinde, the open-air assembly where citizens once voted by raised hand. Obwalden held its last in 1998, and the stone ring on the Landenberg hill, where the assembly met, is still a place that people visit. The hill is named after a legendary bailiff in the William Tell story, and a path leads to the top, with views over the lake and the old town. Nearby, the village of Flüeli-Ranft is the home of Nicholas of Flüe, known as Brother Klaus, the fifteenth-century hermit who is revered as Switzerland's patron saint and credited with helping to hold the Confederation together.

As a food stop it is easy and pleasant. There are cafes on the lakeside, where you can sit with a view of the water, and restaurants serving local specialities such as cheese, sausages and dishes with potatoes and cream. Fuel is available, and the town is large enough to have everything a rider needs, from a tyre shop to a supermarket. Parking is straightforward near the lake.

The roads that leave Sarnen head in several directions: north toward Lucerne, east over the Glaubenberg, south along the lake to Giswil and the Brünig, or up toward Melchtal and the old pilgrimage valley. It is a hub, and in summer it is busy with traffic. Early mornings are calm, and in the late afternoon the light comes across the lake and turns the water gold, which is a good moment for a last coffee.
t.near giswil@46.8,8.1:
Giswil sits at the bottom of the Brünig road, and so it is a place where riders gather. The village, with about three and a half thousand people, lies in the valley of the Sarner Aa, at 485 metres, south of Lake Sarnen, between wooded hills and steep slopes. It is a quiet farming community in the canton of Obwalden, the heart of central Switzerland, and the main road runs through it on the way up to Lungern and the Brünig pass.

For the practical rider, Giswil is a gift. There are fuel stations, a bakery, small shops and a couple of inns, and it is the last easy place to fill up before the road climbs. Sarnen, the cantonal capital, is the nearest larger town, about eight kilometres north, with about nine thousand people and more choice. The lake at Sarnen is a good place to rest, with a lakeside walk and a shady park.

The riding begins at once. The road to Lungern climbs in a series of smooth bends beside the Lungerersee, a long, narrow lake with water of a deep green, then crosses the Brünig pass at around a thousand metres and drops into the Haslital near Meiringen. It is a gentle pass, wide and easy, but its corners are lovely, and in the early morning, with mist on the lake, it is one of the most pleasant rides in the Alps. The railway, a narrow-gauge line that climbs the pass with a cog section, runs alongside, and sometimes the trains and bikes share the same ridge.

Further afield, the Glaubenbielen road, the other half of the route, climbs west from Giswil through steep forest to a high pass, with narrow lanes, tight bends and a strong sense of being alone in the mountains. It closes in winter and can be icy until late spring. Giswil itself is a good base, and the evening light on the surrounding peaks is excellent.
t.near silvaplana@46.4,9.7:
Silvaplana is where the Upper Engadine opens out into water and wind. The village sits on the edge of a lake of the same name, at around 1,800 metres, between the larger resort of St. Moritz and the little village of Sils, and above it the high peaks of the Bernina and Albula ranges hold glaciers in their cirques. The light here is famously clear, an effect of altitude and dry air that has drawn painters and thinkers for generations.

The lake is the thing. A steady wind blows up the valley most summer afternoons, known as the Maloja wind, and it has made Silvaplana one of the best places in Europe for windsurfing and kitesurfing. The water is cold and a deep blue, and the colourful sails on a clear day make a striking sight against the white of the mountains. Nietzsche spent summers in nearby Sils Maria and wrote some of his best-known work walking the lakeshore; a stone with a quotation still marks the place.

The road that ends the ride here is the Julier, one of the old Roman crossings, that climbs from the Surses valley to a pass of 2,284 metres and drops to the Engadine. The riding is wonderful: long, open bends, rocky slopes, and a wide view as you drop toward the lakes. The surface is generally good, and traffic is moderate, though summer weekends bring more. Wind and cold can make the top feel wintry even in July.

Silvaplana itself is small, with a handful of hotels, cafes and a few shops, and the nearby town of St. Moritz, with nearly five thousand people, is the place for fuel and larger services. Prices in the area are high, so it is worth knowing in advance. The Engadine is a place where Romansh is still spoken, and where houses have thick walls with small windows and the decorative sgraffito patterns typical of the valley. Evenings are cool even in summer, and a warm drink beside the lake is an ideal way to end the ride.

t.near titisee neustadt@47.9,8.2:
Neustadt in the Black Forest has none of the lakeside bustle of its neighbour Titisee, and it is better for it. This is a working mountain town of about twelve thousand people on the Gutach river, with a solid church, a market square and a railway station where the Höllentalbahn from Freiburg arrives after its long climb. The line was an engineering feat when it was built in the nineteenth century, winding up the Höllental gorge with a steep rack section in its early decades, and the station is a handsome reminder of the days when the railway was the great modern invention.

The town has a long tradition of watchmaking, and the neighbouring village of Lenzkirch was home to one of the largest clock factories in the Black Forest in the nineteenth century. The local museum shows the craft, along with the wider history of the region. Above the town, the Hochfirst ski jump is one of the biggest in Germany, with a hill size that attracts competitors every winter, and a summer tour lets you stand at the top of the in-run and look down, which is dizzying.

For riders, Neustadt is a handy base for exploring the southern Black Forest. The roads leaving the town run in all directions over wooded ridges and past high farms, with a good mix of fast sweeps and tighter sections. Heading west, the B31 drops through the Höllental, a deep, narrow gorge with steep walls and a river far below, with tunnels and bends that need care in the wet. To the south, quieter roads climb toward Lenzkirch, Bonndorf and the Wutach gorge, where the landscape opens into fields and woods. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, particularly on the main roads, so side roads are better if you have time.

Neustadt has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. A bakery counter with a slice of Black Forest cherry cake and a coffee is a good start, and a traditional inn will offer smoked ham, a hunk of dark bread and a glass of local beer. If you want the lake, Titisee is only a couple of kilometres away.

Snow can arrive early here, so check the weather in autumn and spring. In summer, the cool air and shade of the forest are a relief from the heat of the Rhine valley.
t.near villingen schwenningen@48.1,8.5:
Villingen-Schwenningen is two towns that were made to share a name in 1972, and they still do not quite agree. Villingen, to the west, is a medieval walled town in the Black Forest, with gates, towers and a minster, once part of Austria and proud of its carnival, the Fasnet, in which masked figures in elaborate wooden masks and painted costumes parade through the streets in a thunder of whips and bells. Schwenningen, to the east, is younger and more industrial, a clockmaking town that grew in the nineteenth century, and it has the source of the Neckar river in a small park, marked with a stone.

That clockmaking is the reason for the ride. The Black Forest developed clocks in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, when farmers in long winters carved wooden wheels and built clocks to sell, and the craft grew into a major industry. Schwenningen became a centre for factory-made clocks and watches, with firms such as Kienzle and Mauthe, and the Black Forest cuckoo clock is a more rural cousin. The German Clock Route links museums, workshops and villages in the region, and you can follow the story across the hills.

The town has about eighty thousand people, so everything is available, including large fuel stations and supermarkets, and it is an easy place to begin. The Baar plateau around it is high, open and gentle, with farmland, wind and big skies, and the climate is cold by German standards, so mornings can be frosty even in spring. Riding west toward Furtwangen, the road climbs into the forest, with spruce on the hills and wooden farmhouses with huge roofs coming down almost to the ground, a style that has been used for centuries to shed snow.

The bends in the Black Forest are among the best in Germany, smooth, rhythmic and well surfaced, and weekend traffic of other motorcycles can be heavy. Speed limits are enforced in places, and some roads have noise restrictions for bikes on certain days, so check signs before you go. Autumn is clear and crisp, winter can be snowy, and the pace of life in the villages is slow. Try a slice of Black Forest cake in a village café, and you will understand why the region is famous for more than clocks.
t.near triberg@48.1,8.2:
Triberg is built in a steep, narrow fold of the Black Forest, a town that seems to have been poured down a gorge and set hard. Houses climb both sides of the Gutach valley, rooftops overlap, and the main street runs steeply uphill past shops full of cuckoo clocks, carved wooden bears and cherry schnapps. It is touristy, no question, but the tourists come because the place is the real thing, the heartland of the Black Forest clock trade, where families have been making timepieces in workshops since the eighteenth century.

The town's other big draw is the waterfall. The Gutach drops through a series of cascades in a wooded ravine just above the centre, a total fall of well over a hundred metres in seven stages, and it counts among the highest in Germany. A path with steps and bridges climbs beside it, and squirrels, who have learned that visitors carry nuts, will race along the rails to meet you. The spray, the smell of wet rock and spruce, and the roar of water make it a satisfying walk of an hour or so, best in spring, when snowmelt swells the flow, or after heavy rain.

Nearby Schonach claims one of the largest cuckoo clocks in the world, and rival towns argue with some energy about which one is biggest. The claim that the Black Forest cake was invented here is made by several places, and the argument has never been settled, but the cake itself, made with cherries, cream and kirsch, is easy to find in any café and generally excellent.

For riders, the approach is the reason to come. The B33 and the side roads that climb out of the Kinzig and Elz valleys wind through spruce forest in a long series of bends and hairpins, with the road gaining height steadily to over seven hundred metres around Triberg. Surfaces are good, the corners are smooth and well banked, and it is one of the classic bike roads of southwest Germany. That also means it is busy on fine weekends, with riders, cars and the occasional coach, and the police do monitor speed.

Triberg has about five thousand people and enough services for a stop: fuel, a supermarket, many cafés and restaurants. Parking is tight in high season, so arrive early or park low and walk up. Dress for cool weather, as it can be damp and cold even in summer.
